Alemanha planeja dobrar sua capacidade de data centers
11 de outubro de 2026
O futuro digital na Alemanhaestá tomando forma na cidade de Dietzenbach. Google, EdgeConnex e Maincubes – duas empresas de tecnologia americanas e uma alemã – reservaram terrenos para a construção de centros de dados (data centers) nessa pequena cidade próxima a Frankfurt.
Dietzenbach é um polo logístico nas proximidades do aeroporto da metrópole financeira e tem cerca de 35 mil habitantes. A região de Frankfurt é um dos locais mais atraentes do mundo para operadores de computação em nuvem.
À medida que a demanda por capacidade computacional continua crescendo, mais centros de dados estão sendo planejados no local.
Consumo de eletricidade e água
No entanto, a notícia sobre os planos para um quarto megacentro de dados encontrou resistência entre os moradores.
As dezenas de milhares de computadores instalados num data center precisam de um enorme fornecimento de energia para funcionar ininterruptamente.
Esses equipamentos geram grandes quantidades de calor e necessitam de sistemas de refrigeração, que, por sua vez, consomem enormes volumes de água.
As pessoas entrevistadas pela DW em Dietzenbach demonstraram preocupação com o aumento das contas de água e energia, além de possíveis elevações da temperatura local.
"Queremos saber duas coisas: quais são os benefícios para a comunidade local aqui em Dietzenbach? E quais são os impactos ambientais?", afirmou o morador Wilhelm Sauer, apontando para as quatro imponentes chaminés que se erguem do centro de dados da EdgeConnex.
Ele e outros ativistas locais acreditam que o impacto dos centros de dados sobre os recursos da região talvez não seja compensado pelo número relativamente baixo de novos empregos anunciados.
Já o prefeito de Dietzenbach, Dieter Lang, do Partido Social-Democrata (SPD), de centro-esquerda, mostra-se otimista. Segundo ele, cerca de cem empregos de alta qualificação deverão chegar à cidade por meio do centro de dados da Google. Ele também disse esperar benefícios para as finanças municipais por meio de impostos.
Mas a pesquisadora Tara Merk, do projeto Community Data Centers no Instituto Weizenbaum, é cética. Ela acredita que a Alemanha provavelmente arrecadará pouco com centros de dados operados por empresas americanas "porque os lucros podem ser tributados em outros lugares".
Em especial as grandes empresas de tecnologia, diz ela, não vão pagar seus impostos em Dietzenbach.
Falta de informação sobre data centers
Em agosto de 2026, o governo alemão lançou um cadastro nacional de centros de dados que lista consumo de energia e de água e medidas de eficiência energética dos centros já em operação.
No entanto, a lista inclui apenas cerca de 300 instalações, muito menos que os aproximadamente 2 mil centros de dados que, segundo o próprio governo, operam no país.
"Algumas empresas informam seus projetos menores, mas não os grandes", disse Werner Neumann, membro da diretoria da organização ambientalista Bund.

artigo.texto: Gil Torquato, Abranet: É difícil pensar na regulamentação do Redata ainda este ano Para o presidente da Abranet, a renovação do Congresso Nacional e a própria eleição presidencial deve provocar um delay. "É ruim, mas é o momento que estamos vivendo". Ele também defendeu o adiamento da Reforma Tributária. O presidente da Associação Brasileira de Internet (Abranet), Gil Torquato, defendeu ao participar de um painel na Futurecom 2026 que a regulação da Inteligência Artificial tem de ser “o mais cirúrgica possível e cobrir setores específicos para não inibir a inovação”. Segundo ele, quanto menos regulação será melhor para a IA, uma vez que é necessário estimular e não inibir o mercado. Em entrevista, Gil Torquato disse que as regulamentações têm de dar respaldo e segurança jurídica para assegurar os investimentos. Sinalizou ainda que uma agência para IA tem de ajudar nas diretrizes, mas não teria de ter uma visão punitiva. Gil Torquato é descrente da possibilidade de o Marco Legal de IA ser aprovado ainda este ano. “Houve uma renovação do Congresso e o tema tem de ser mais discutido”, pontuou. O presidente da Abranet falou também sobre o Redata. Ele também acha difícil ter a regulamentação ainda este ano – ela está com o poder executivo – diante das eleições presidenciais. “O Redata é muito importante, gostaria que saísse, mas acho que teremos um delay”, admite. E ao ser questionado sobre a Reforma Tributária, Gil Torquato lembrou que as empresas não estão preparadas e o próprio governo está atrasado. Ele defendeu o adiamento da vigência do novo regime. “É um tema sensível. Afeta todas as empresas e é preciso rediscutir as alíquotas”. Assista a íntegra da entrevista com o presidente da Abranet, Gil Torquato.

artigo.texto: How Chiplets Could Transform Server Design – And Data Centers Chiplets are reshaping CPU design, enabling data centers to do more without increasing space or power consumption. Since the advent of microprocessors more than 50 years ago, CPUs have typically been built as single pieces of silicon. As a result, servers and the data centers that house them have largely been designed around that model. However, that is beginning to change. The growing adoption of chiplets – small modular dies that can be combined in a single processor package – is giving chipmakers a new way to build CPUs. By improving manufacturing flexibility and enabling more specialized processor designs, chiplets could reshape not just server architecture but also how data centers approach compute density, power efficiency, and infrastructure planning. What Are Chiplets? A chiplet is a small integrated circuit designed to perform a specific function within a larger processing package. Depending on the design, chiplets may handle compute, input/output (I/O), cache, memory connectivity, or workload-specific acceleration, such as AI acceleration. When combined, chiplets can provide the same overall capabilities as a traditional CPU. The key difference is that, instead of manufacturing a processor as one large monolithic die, chipmakers can build it from multiple smaller dies assembled in a single package. The chiplet concept has existed for decades, and related multi-die approaches are not entirely new. But adoption accelerated in the late 2010s as chipmakers sought more efficient ways to improve processor performance, manage manufacturing complexity, and scale designs across different workloads. The Benefits of Chiplets A chiplet-based approach to CPU design offers several potential advantages. Reduced manufacturing costs. Smaller dies are often easier to manufacture with higher yields than a single large, complex die. If a single die has a defect, the loss is usually less significant than losing an entire monolithic processor. It can also be easier to engineer and optimize a smaller die for a specific function than to design one large chip that must handle multiple functions at once. Design freedom. By separating functions such as compute and I/O into different dies, chipmakers can tailor processor designs more efficiently for different types of workloads and product segments. Potentially higher compute density. In some cases, chiplets allow chipmakers to pack more processing capability into a single processor package, helping to enable more powerful servers without necessarily increasing physical server size. Supply chain flexibility. Because smaller dies are often easier and faster to manufacture than very large monolithic chips, chiplet-based designs may reduce some production constraints. That said, they do not eliminate supply chain risk altogether, because advanced packaging and integration can create bottlenecks on their own. In short, chiplets can make it easier for chipmakers to scale processor designs, improve yields, and optimize hardware for growing demand. What Do Chiplets Mean for Data Centers? Although chiplets directly affect processor design, their impact could extend well beyond the chip itself. One important implication is the potential for increased compute density inside data centers. If chiplets allow server vendors to deliver more processing power within a single server platform, operators may be able to support heavier workloads without expanding physical footprints at the same pace. Historically, higher compute density has often meant higher power draw and greater cooling requirements. Chiplets do not automatically solve that problem. However, if they enable more efficient processor designs or better performance per watt, they could help offset some of the infrastructure strain that typically comes with denser compute environments. A key result of greater chiplet adoption, then, could be data centers that support higher IT loads without requiring proportionally more space or power. In that scenario, existing facilities could become more valuable because operators would be able to do more with the infrastructure they already have. Chiplets may also help reduce the risk of server procurement delays by giving manufacturers more flexibility in how processors are designed and produced. This does not remove supply chain challenges altogether, but it could make sourcing CPUs and servers somewhat easier over time. In the longer term, chiplets could also encourage more specialized server designs. As chipmakers gain flexibility to mix and match dies optimized for different functions, server platforms may become increasingly tailored for workloads such as AI, analytics, storage, or high-performance computing. That would give data center operators more options, but it could also make infrastructure planning more workload-specific than it is today. A Shift Worth Watching Chiplets are no longer a futuristic concept. They are already becoming an important part of modern processor design, especially as chipmakers look for new ways to improve performance and efficiency. For data centers, the biggest impact may not come from chiplets themselves, but from the servers they enable. If chiplet-based designs continue to improve compute density, efficiency, and workload specialization, they could play a major role in shaping the next generation of data center infrastructure.

By improving manufacturing flexibility and enabling more specialized processor designs, chiplets could reshape not just server architecture but also how data centers approach compute density, power efficiency, and infrastructure planning. What Are Chiplets? A chiplet is a small integrated circuit designed to perform a specific function within a larger processing package. Depending on the design, chiplets may handle compute, input/output (I/O), cache, memory connectivity, or workload-specific acceleration, such as AI acceleration. When combined, chiplets can provide the same overall capabilities as a traditional CPU. The key difference is that, instead of manufacturing a processor as one large monolithic die, chipmakers can build it from multiple smaller dies assembled in a single package. The chiplet concept has existed for decades, and related multi-die approaches are not entirely new. But adoption accelerated in the late 2010s as chipmakers sought more efficient ways to improve processor performance, manage manufacturing complexity, and scale designs across different workloads. The Benefits of Chiplets A chiplet-based approach to CPU design offers several potential advantages. Reduced manufacturing costs. Smaller dies are often easier to manufacture with higher yields than a single large, complex die. If a single die has a defect, the loss is usually less significant than losing an entire monolithic processor. It can also be easier to engineer and optimize a smaller die for a specific function than to design one large chip that must handle multiple functions at once. Design freedom. By separating functions such as compute and I/O into different dies, chipmakers can tailor processor designs more efficiently for different types of workloads and product segments. Potentially higher compute density. In some cases, chiplets allow chipmakers to pack more processing capability into a single processor package, helping to enable more powerful servers without necessarily increasing physical server size. Supply chain flexibility. Because smaller dies are often easier and faster to manufacture than very large monolithic chips, chiplet-based designs may reduce some production constraints. That said, they do not eliminate supply chain risk altogether, because advanced packaging and integration can create bottlenecks on their own. In short, chiplets can make it easier for chipmakers to scale processor designs, improve yields, and optimize hardware for growing demand. What Do Chiplets Mean for Data Centers? Although chiplets directly affect processor design, their impact could extend well beyond the chip itself. One important implication is the potential for increased compute density inside data centers. If chiplets allow server vendors to deliver more processing power within a single server platform, operators may be able to support heavier workloads without expanding physical footprints at the same pace. Historically, higher compute density has often meant higher power draw and greater cooling requirements. Chiplets do not automatically solve that problem. However, if they enable more efficient processor designs or better performance per watt, they could help offset some of the infrastructure strain that typically comes with denser compute environments. A key result of greater chiplet adoption, then, could be data centers that support higher IT loads without requiring proportionally more space or power. In that scenario, existing facilities could become more valuable because operators would be able to do more with the infrastructure they already have. Chiplets may also help reduce the risk of server procurement delays by giving manufacturers more flexibility in how processors are designed and produced. This does not remove supply chain challenges altogether, but it could make sourcing CPUs and servers somewhat easier over time. In the longer term, chiplets could also encourage more specialized server designs. As chipmakers gain flexibility to mix and match dies optimized for different functions, server platforms may become increasingly tailored for workloads such as AI, analytics, storage, or high-performance computing. That would give data center operators more options, but it could also make infrastructure planning more workload-specific than it is today. A Shift Worth Watching Chiplets are no longer a futuristic concept. They are already becoming an important part of modern processor design, especially as chipmakers look for new ways to improve performance and efficiency. For data centers, the biggest impact may not come from chiplets themselves, but from the servers they enable. If chiplet-based designs continue to improve compute density, efficiency, and workload specialization, they could play a major role in shaping the next generation of data center infrastructure.

artigo.texto: Virginia Tops AI Data Center Readiness Ranking as Smaller Markets Advance TRG DataCenters’ August 2026 ranking places Virginia in the lead, while states with abundant power, low-carbon electricity, and favorable water conditions gain ground. Power supply and water availability could help states outside established data center hubs compete for AI infrastructure investment, according to a new survey of US states from TRG DataCenters. The report, published in August 2026, compares 24 states using measures of infrastructure scale and environmental exposure and points to a more geographically diverse market as AI demand expands. Virginia topped the August ranking of states positioned for AI data center growth, but the findings also suggest smaller markets can compete by offering a favorable combination of electricity supply, lower-carbon generation, and water availability. “When planning infrastructure for the long term, that balance between scale and resource efficiency matters as much as raw megawatts,” Chris Hinkle, CEO of TRG DataCenters, told Data Center Knowledge. TRG’s analysis considered mapped large-scale AI data center sites, power capacity, electricity use, estimated annual carbon emissions, and the proportion of mapped facilities in areas of high water stress. Capacity figures reflect the AI infrastructure included in TRG’s dataset and do not represent each state’s total data center market. Virginia’s Lead Comes with Water Constraints Virginia received a readiness score of 100, followed by Ohio at 88.2, Tennessee at 83.7, Georgia at 81.8, and Texas at 80.8. TRG’s dataset mapped seven large AI sites in Virginia totaling 1,085 MW of capacity, while Ohio and Tennessee showed higher mapped capacities – 1,410 MW in Ohio and 1,373 MW in Tennessee. Virginia’s advantage reflects performance across several measures, including lower estimated grid carbon intensity serving the mapped facilities. Hinkle said Ohio’s mapped AI capacity was around 30% greater, but the grid serving Virginia’s facilities had roughly one-third lower carbon intensity than Ohio’s. “As a result, the AI facilities in our dataset are associated with around 2.3 million tons of CO2 emissions annually, compared with roughly 4.5 million tons in Ohio and 4.3 million in Tennessee,” he said. Water – or lack thereof – is a complicating factor. About one-third of Virginia’s mapped data centers are located in areas of high water stress, compared with none in Ohio and just 7% in Tennessee. “One factor Virginia will need to continue managing as the market expands is site selection around water availability,” Hinkle said. Those differences make the ranking a starting point for evaluating markets rather than evidence that development conditions are uniform within a state. Smaller Markets Offer Competing Advantages South Carolina placed sixth with a score of 80.5, just behind Texas, despite having only one large AI site and 142 MW of capacity in the study. “What surprised us most was South Carolina,” Hinkle said. “It has just one large AI data center site and around 142 MW of capacity, yet it finished almost level with Texas in our overall readiness ranking, despite Texas having 13 large sites.” He attributed that performance partly to the state’s nuclear-heavy electricity supply and the absence of mapped facilities in areas of high water stress. Hinkle also pointed to New York, Iowa, and Mississippi. New York combined relatively limited large-scale AI capacity with one of the lowest-carbon grids in the dataset, while Mississippi already supported more than 500 MW of AI capacity. “States that can combine reliable power with a relatively low-carbon electricity mix and favorable water conditions could become increasingly attractive as demand expands,” he said. Texas Faces a Siting Challenge Texas had the largest number of AI sites in the study – 13, with a combined capacity of 1,301 MW. However, 58.8% of those facilities were located in areas of high water stress. Hinkle said he expects those conditions to influence cooling choices and project locations. “That is likely to encourage more sophisticated siting and infrastructure strategies rather than simply slowing development,” he said. “We could see greater use of approaches such as closed-loop or air-based cooling, recycled water, and locations where local water conditions are more favorable.” TRG notes that the water-stress measure describes facility locations and does not establish actual water consumption or the impact of individual cooling systems. Developers still need to assess those conditions at the project level. From Readiness to Deliverable Infrastructure Statewide advantages must also translate into infrastructure that developers can use. A relatively small share of statewide electricity use does not, by itself, establish that a particular site has power available for expansion. “Grid connections, transmission capacity, fiber connectivity, build-ready sites, and long-term power availability can all influence where major projects ultimately land,” Hinkle said. For emerging markets, those requirements determine whether attractive resource conditions can support projects at scale. For established hubs, the requirements shape where additional development can proceed. “The result could be a more geographically diverse AI infrastructure market as developers match projects with the locations best equipped to support them.”

artigo.texto: How to Secure Data Centers During the Construction Phase Before operations begin, layered defenses at the site and in the supply chain help prevent theft, vandalism, counterfeit gear, and covert endpoints. As data center build-outs accelerate, most conversations about physical security focus on operational facilities, with threats ranging from mundane events, such as break-ins, to novel threats like drone attacks. Yet the period of greatest exposure is often earlier: during construction. Sites are porous, contractor populations are large and fluid, and high-value materials and preinstalled equipment can be targeted or tampered with. Protecting the build phase should be a core pillar of any data center’s broader physical security strategy. Construction-Phase Risks to Data Centers Physical intrusions during construction come in many forms: Material theft. Theft of construction materials is common on open or lightly controlled construction sites. Copper, cabling, generators, and networking gear are all attractive targets, leading to financial losses and construction delays. Vandalism and sabotage. In some markets, community opposition to data center expansion can increase the likelihood of on-site disruption or damage. Deployment of spy devices. More covertly, malicious actors may attempt to plant devices – such as rogue wireless access points, small network switches, or hidden sensors – during construction to enable remote backdoor access once the facility is operational. Supply chain tampering. Risks also extend into supply chains: tampering with shipments, swapping components, or introducing counterfeit or compromised gear can create backdoors or degrade reliability before the facility ever goes live. Aerial reconnaissance or nuisance activity. Hobbyist drones can expose site layouts and procedures or create safety hazards. Practical Strategies to Secure Data Center Construction Sites While the overarching goal is simple – prevent unauthorized access to construction sites and their supply chains – executing this amid complex projects and large contractor populations is challenging. The following layered controls help reduce risk while maintaining construction speed. Establish a strong perimeter and active monitoring. Build robust physical barriers, ensure all ingress/egress routes are controlled, and funnel all foot and vehicle traffic through staffed gates. Pair this with temporary but professional-grade surveillance cameras covering the perimeter, material laydown yards, and sensitive areas; lighting designed with Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design principles; and motion or thermal sensors where feasible. Verify and control who enters the construction site. Vet contractors and delivery personnel before granting access, consistent with local laws and company policy. Require visible badges and use zoned access so workers can enter only the areas relevant to their tasks. This is no guarantee that bad actors won’t find their way in, but it’s one way to reduce risk. Grant access in phases. Bringing contractors on-site in smaller groups (e.g., having electricians complete their work before allowing HVAC workers to begin) reduces crowding and makes anomalous activity more visible. The trade-off is that this may slow construction by reducing the amount of work contractors can perform in parallel. Rope off construction areas. In addition to establishing a strong perimeter around the data center site, roping off or caging high-value storage (e.g., copper, cabling, generators, and networking equipment) provides another layer of defense against theft and sabotage. Harden the supply chain and track custody. Vet vendors for chain-of-custody controls, tamper-evident packaging, and secure transit practices. Upon receipt, record serial numbers and MAC addresses of networked devices, use barcodes or RFID to track movement, and keep sensitive equipment in controlled cages until deployment. Prepare for drone threats. Use drone detection where appropriate for visibility into potential aerial activity. Many forms of active drone interdiction are illegal, so coordinate with local authorities and legal teams, emphasizing deterrence, detection, and evidence capture rather than unlawful countermeasures. Validate what’s installed before commissioning. Another way to detect supply chain abuse is to compare installed assets against purchase orders and approved bills of materials. Conduct technical sweeps for unauthorized wireless signals or unexpected network endpoints to identify situations where someone installed a device that isn’t supposed to be included. Balancing Speed and Security Complete eradication of construction-phase physical security risks isn’t realistic, just as fully preventing cyberattacks isn’t. However, a multilayered defense strategy based on practices like those described above goes a long way toward reducing the likelihood and impact of intrusions, while improving your chances of detecting and remediating those that do occur.

artigo.texto: The hidden environmental cost of AI data centers September 4, 2026 Every question sent to AI models provides an instant reply that seems to appear out of nowhere, but answering queries requires physical infrastructure that consumes real energy, water and land. Somewhere around the world — maybe in Virginia, Sao Paulo or Hong Kong — a massive warehouse filled with fiber-optic cables and seemingly endless rows of humming servers is working to provide the processing power for the more than 2.5 billion questions ChatGPT alone fields daily. AI models, along with cloud storage, streaming, web hosting and social media, all have a very real physical footprint. If data centers were a country, their level of electricity use would make them the 11th largest electricity consumer in the world, according to researchers from the United Nations University. From energy to water to land, here's the real toll data centers take on the environment. An insatiable appetite for power Data centers are becoming some of the world's fastest-growing consumers of electricity. These warehouses of servers, routers and internet-connected devices run 24/7, while cooling systems operate continuously to keep the tech from overheating. In Frankfurt, Germany, the grid is currently so saturated that no new connections will be available until at least the 2030s. There, data centers consume about 41% of the city's electricity. In Dublin, it's double that. And data center electricity consumption is growing rapidly — it's expected to double by 2030 to about 945 terawatt-hours, around what Japan consumes annually, according to the International Energy Agency. How the AI boom could slow climate progress All that energy has to come from somewhere, increasing reliance on fossil fuels. One 2024 study found that more than half of the United States' data centers are powered by fossil fuels, emitting in excess of 105 million tons of CO2. Offsetting that would take more than 31,000 wind turbines running continuously for a year. The build-out is also keeping old coal plants alive. Utilities in the US have delayed the retirement of 15 coal-fired plants nationwide to meet surging demand, plants that together emitted nearly 65 million tons of greenhouse gases in 2023 alone. And utilities are also constructing new gas-fired power plants, with more than 100 GW of additional facilities across the country already announced. That would lead to more carbon emissions than burning 111 million pounds (50.4 million kilograms) of coal. Of course, data centers can also be powered by renewable energy. Pairing a facility with on-site renewables can ease pressure on the local power supply, and any surplus energy can even be sold back to the grid, making it more stable. However, using green electricity for data centers means there is less available for electrifying transport or decarbonizing other emissions-heavy industries. Hidden water demand Many data centers consume millions of gallons of water to stay cool. Servers generate constant heat, and water is one of the most effective ways to absorb and carry that heat away through evaporation. A single large facility can use up to 5 million gallons a day, roughly the same as a town of 10,000 to 50,000 people. About 80% of the water withdrawn for cooling simply evaporates; the rest becomes wastewater that can overwhelm local treatment systems never designed to handle that volume. In northern Virginia, the almost 300 data centers clustered in one region of the US state supply about a third of the world's online traffic. There, in what is known as the world's data center capital, facilities collectively used nearly 2 billion gallons of water in 2023. There are several more efficient ways to cool data centers. These include immersion cooling, where devices are bathed in a coolant, and closed-loop cooling systems which recycle water and can reduce freshwater use by up to 70%. Data centers are making cities hotter Cooling a data center doesn't get rid of the heat, it just moves it outside. That can exacerbate the urban heat island effect, which is when cities experience higher temperatures than rural areas. Researchers in Phoenix, Arizona, found a single large data center can emit as much waste heat as tens or even hundreds of thousands of households, raising nearby land surface temperatures by up to 9 degrees Celsius (16 Fahrenheit) and air temperatures by up to 2 degrees Celsius. Those effects can be felt as far as half a kilometer away. Since cities are already 0.5–4 degrees Celsius warmer than their surroundings, these higher temperatures can increase heat stress risks for nearby residents and push up air conditioning demand, requiring still yet more energy. Not all of that heat goes to waste: a growing number of data centers are capturing and piping it into nearby homes and businesses. This process, called thermal energy networks, can reduce data center power demand by up to 30%. Coal, gas and diesel all contribute to dirty air Powering and running data centers pollutes the air on two fronts. First, coal and gas plants release toxic particulate matter, which can lead to respiratory disease, heart disease, asthma and more health conditions for nearby communities. On-site diesel generators, used as backup power when the grid fails, also release harmful air pollutants. These generators pump out 200 to 600 times more nitrogen oxides than natural gas plants. One estimate found that when backup generators for all of Virginia's data centers were emitting at just 10% of their permitted level, they could contribute to 14,000 cases of asthma symptoms, more than a dozen deaths and up to $300 million in public health costs a year. Data centers take over large swaths of land Data center construction requires large plots of land to build on. artigo.texto: A Câmara dos Deputados aprovou nesta terça-feira, 13 de outubro, o requerimento de urgência do Projeto de Lei (PL) 3.716/2026, que propõe retirar dos geradores a obrigação exclusiva de custear a contratação de sistemas de armazenamento de energia por baterias como reserva de capacidade. Com a decisão, a proposta poderá ser votada diretamente pelo plenário, sem precisar passar pelas comissões. O requerimento de urgência foi apresentado pelo deputado Danilo Forte (PP-CE). Já o projeto é de autoria do deputado Arnaldo Jardim (Cidadania-SP). O PL revoga o parágrafo 6º do artigo 3º-A da Lei 10.848/2004, incluído pela Lei 15.269/2025, que determina que os custos das contratações de reserva de capacidade com baterias sejam rateados exclusivamente entre os agentes de geração, conforme regulamentação da Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel). Com a revogação, passaria a valer para as baterias a regra geral da lei, que prevê o rateio dos custos da reserva de capacidade entre os consumidores, assim como acontece copm as demais tecnologias contratadas nessa modalidade. Apoio das associações A aprovação da urgência ocorre após seis associações do setor elétrico divulgarem, em 7 de outubro, uma nota conjunta em defesa do projeto. As entidades argumentam que a regra atual estabelece tratamento diferente para as baterias em relação às demais tecnologias contratadas nos leilões de reserva de capacidade. O posicionamento foi assinado pela Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica e Novas Tecnologias (Abeeólica), Associação Brasileira dos Investidores em Autoprodução de Energia (Abiape), Associação Brasileira da Indústria do Hidrogênio Verde (Abihv), Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia (Absae), Associação Brasileira de Energia Solar Fotovoltaica (Absolar) e Associação Brasileira dos Produtores Independentes de Energia Elétrica (Apine). Segundo as entidades, a cobrança exclusiva dos geradores pode elevar os custos da energia elétrica para os consumidores, uma vez que os valores podem ser repassados às tarifas no mercado regulado e aos preços dos contratos no mercado livre. As associações também argumentam que os sistemas de armazenamento podem reduzir outros custos do setor elétrico. A nota cita estudo da Volt Robotics que estima economia superior a R$ 1,6 bilhão por ano para os consumidores, por meio da redução da volatilidade do Preço de Liquidação das Diferenças (PLD) e do acionamento de usinas termelétricas. As entidades defendem que os custos da reserva de capacidade sejam distribuídos conforme os benefícios proporcionados ao sistema e que baterias recebam tratamento equivalente ao das demais tecnologias que oferecem potência e flexibilidade.

artigo.texto:
A partir de 2027, os leilões de energia realizados pelo governo federal poderão contratar termelétricas movidas a biometano, biogás, biocombustíveis, além de hidrelétricas com a capacidade instalada de até 50 megawhats (MW) e soluções de armazenamento de energia, incluindo as baterias. As hidrelétricas de até 50 MW serão contratadas por meio de Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade no primeiro semestre de 2027. Neste tipo de leilão, o empreendimento fica disponível, mas só produz energia, quando é necessário ao Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN). A expectativa é de aumentar o mercado dos biocombustíveis com a realização destas novas concorrências.
Os novos leilões também devem aumentar a flexibilidade do sistema elétrico brasileiro. Serão contratadas térmicas flexíveis, que podem começar a gerar energia de uma forma mais rápida, quando for necessário. Atualmente, no Brasil, há térmicas que começam a produzir pela manhã, embora a sua energia seja necessária no final da tarde, quando as renováveis diminuem a sua produção.
>> Siga o canal da Movimento Econômico no WhatsApp
No primeiro semestre de 2027, devem ocorrer os seguintes certames: leilão para Contratação de Reserva de Capacidade para atendimento incluindo a contratação de centrais hidrelétricas com capacidade instalada de até 50 megawhats (MW) e Leilão para Suprimento aos Sistemas Isolados.
Já o leilão de potência, vai incluir as termelétricas e sistemas de armazenamento – em baterias químicas e no sistema hidráulico – e deve ocorrer no segundo semestre de 2027.
Portaria estabelece cronograma de leilões até 2029
O cronograma foi estabelecido para os leilões que serão promovidos entre 2027 e 2029 e estão na Portaria Normativa do MME nº 143, de 28 de setembro deste ano, publicada no Diário Oficial do dia 29. A portaria foi elogiada por agentes do setor por trazer previsibilidade na compra de energia e da potência instalada. A contratação desta última é importante para ter capacidade disponível para atender, rapidamente, aos horários de maior consumo, quando, por exemplo, a geração solar diminui.

artigo.texto: Você sabe carregar seu celular corretamente? Confira dicas para preservar a vida útil da bateria Conectar primeiro o carregador ou o celular? Onde deixar o aparelho? Usar o celular durante a carga tem problema? Veja alguns cuidados básicos Por O Globo Atualizado Há hábitos diários que repetimos sem nem nos dar conta. E, com certeza, carregar o celular é um deles. Tem quem demore até a bateria ficar no vermelho, outros preferem se precaver e, na primeiro oportunidade, dar aquela carga a mais por garantia. Apesar da duração das baterias poder variar entre as marcas e modelos, há alguns protocolos que merecem ser respeitados para prolongar na vida útil do aparelho, segundo especialistas. - Você é um dos 83 milhões de brasileiros endividados? Ferramenta do GLOBO ajuda a organizar suas contas; confira - Fim da escala 6x1: você trabalha mais ou menos do que a média no Brasil? E no mundo? Confira Pequenos cuidados podem ajudar a evitar, por exemplo, microdescargas causadas por flutuações de tensão. Aquela "escorregada" vez ou outra não compromete o aparelho, o problema está na recorrência de maus hábitos, em que, sucessivamente, vai mitigando o funcionamento. Mesmo nessa tarefa simples de carregar o celular, a ordem impacta no aparelho. Idealmente, você deve primeiro conectar o carregador à tomada, e só então conectar o cabo ao celular, dando início à recarga. Isso acontece porque o circuito interno precisa de alguns instantes para estabilizar o fluxo de energia. Na hora de desconectá-lo deve ser feito o caminho inverso, à fim de proteger os componentes, primeiro desconectando o celular do cabo do carregador, e só depois retirá-lo da tomada. Às vezes pode ser difícil ficar longe do celular, deixando-o recarregar sem uso. Responder uma notificação rápida, até vai, mas ações como jogar videogames ou assistir a vídeos em alta resolução geram um aumento de temperatura que afeta sua vida útil. Outro risco é tensionar ou dobrar o cabo durante esse manuseio, o que pode causar fissuras e rupturas comprometendo o carregamento e até estragando-o. Também está diretamente relacionado à temperatura do aparelho a superfície em que ele é mantido apoiado durante o carregamento. Materiais que ajudem a dissipar o calor, pois facilita o resfriamento durante o processo, dispondo o celular sobre móveis, como mesa ou escrivaninha, ou pedra, como mármore ou granito. Isto deve ser combinado a uma área bem ventilada e uma superfície seca. Deixar o aparelho sobre cobertores, travesseiros ou plástico deve ser evitado. O recomendado é escolher ambientes com pouca umidade, por isso, é importante evitar cômodos como banheiros e cozinhas, ainda para evitar risco de choque elétrico. Deixar o celular no chão também não é uma boa opção devido às chances de entrada de sujeira na porta de carregamento. Outros fatores que merecem atenção é o uso de carregadores de baixa qualidade, que causa tensões instáveis que danificam tanto a bateria quanto seus circuitos internos. O uso do acessório original ou de um certificado pelo fabricante garante a transferência segura de energia para o equipamento. E deixar o dispositivo conectado à tomada durante a noite é desnecessário para baterias modernas.

artigo.texto: Environment ministers, meeting in Luxembourg on Monday 12 October, held their first formal debate on the revision of the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS, or ‘ETS’) presented by the European Commission on 17 July (see EUROPE 13912/1). On the first question raised by the Irish Presidency of the Council of the European Union – the climate ambition of the proposed revision – little new emerged. Both camps are growing. The most ambitious countries – Denmark, Sweden, Finland, Spain, Portugal, the Netherlands and Luxembourg – want to change the current system as little as possible or propose a more demanding linear reduction factor, which determines how many allowances are removed from the European carbon market each year. Some of these countries, including the Nordic countries, opposed including international credits in the ETS, advocating domestic CO2 emissions reductions instead. Nevertheless, some of these same Member States favour the inclusion of carbon capture and storage (CCS) technologies, not least because they benefit from them (see EUROPE 13941/4). The countries calling for a further easing of the linear reduction factor are Poland, Austria, Slovakia, Slovenia, Estonia, Romania, Cyprus, Malta, Italy, Hungary, the Czech Republic and Belgium. Many of these countries also want to postpone or make optional ETS2, the system covering emissions from buildings and road transport, which is not due to enter into force until 2028. France and Germany clarify their positions. Germany and France clarified their positions on the various elements of the revision and they are both concerned about carbon leakage if the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) is not operational before the next phase of the ETS begins. Nine other Member States share that concern. “Work on the CBAM is not finished ”, French Minister for Ecological Transition Monique Barbut summed up. German Federal Minister for Climate Action Carsten Schneider told the press that “the free allocation of allowances must be conditional on investment commitments to ensure that companies and their expertise remain in Europe”. He also reiterated that any weakening of the ETS’s ambition would have to be offset by greater climate ambition in other sectors, echoing an argument put forward by Denmark. France, for its part, opposed the European Commission’s proposal to make free allowances conditional on investment in Europe. According to Monique Barbut, this would create an additional administrative burden for businesses. Use of European funds for modernisation and decarbonisation. Several Member States expressed alarm at the planned reduction in the Modernisation Fund’s allocation from 4.5% to 2%. These include Poland, Hungary, Romania, Slovenia, Croatia and Lithuania. In the forthcoming negotiations, the fact that several countries complaining about the reduction in this allocation also favour easing the ETS and reopening ETS2 could work against them. On the use of ETS revenues as an EU own resource – an issue being discussed in negotiations on the EU’s next Multiannual Financial Framework (see EUROPE 13957/1) – many Member States, including Belgium, Estonia, Hungary, Romania and Latvia, clearly opposed the proposal. As for extending the scope of the ETS to maritime transport, aviation and waste incinerators, Agence Europe will come back on this subject. (Original version in French by Nadège Delépine)

artigo.texto: JANESVILLE – This week, The Gazette is taking a closer look at three questions we originally wrote for a public forum we hosted Sept. 30 on the GM/JATCO ballot referendum that's set for the Nov. 3 election ballot. The referendum asks Janesville residents to respond “Yes” or “No” to a question that asks if they'd want voters to have the authority to decide whether to approve any development project worth more than $450 million at the GM/JATCO site. The Gazette didn’t get to all the questions we’d hoped to ask at our forum, so we posed three unasked questions to the public — and to panelists who attended the forum. We received several responses, and we plan to examine them this week in a three-part series, with each story focusing on one question and the range of views it drew from some of those who responded. The first question: Q: The Janesville City Council has approved a 12-month, citywide moratorium on all data center developments, which it says would allow the city more time to research and craft policy and guardrails tied to data centers. Should voters take that moratorium into consideration when deciding on the GM/JATCO site referendum in the Nov. 3 election? Why or Why not? Mandy Witt is a local commercial property realtor and one of the six panelists at our forum. She opposes the referendum because she says if it passes, it could bring unpredictability to decisions usually made based on local planning and economic development policies — structures developers are accustomed to working with. In her response to this question, Witt said she thinks a residents’ vote on projects bigger than $450 million at the GM site could deter developers. She thinks voters should pay attention to the moratorium’s intent, which she believes is to give the City of Janesville extra time to research data centers and develop standards and local protections for the projects. Witt points out a contrast between the two measures: The referendum would apply to a variety of large-scale projects at the GM/JATCO site, not just data centers, while the city moratorium only applies to data centers only. “I am voting “No” (on the referendum) because I want clear requirements, early communication, and a predictable approval process,” Witt said. “The moratorium provides an opportunity to develop data center rules. The referendum adds a separate voter approval requirement without establishing those rules or a timetable for that vote.” Cathy Erdman fronts SNOW Janesville, a grassroots group that advocates for south-side Janesville residents and businesses, and one of the six panelists at our forum. She was another forum panelist. Erdman supports a “Yes” vote on the referendum, which would give voters authority over whether to approve large-scale projects at the GM/JATCO site. She says she’s more interested in what a citywide data center moratorium eventually accomplishes than the city's stated intentions going into the moratorium. In her response, Erdman said she believes it’s impossible to separate data centers from the conversation on the GM/JATCO referendum – despite the city’s recent passage of a data center moratorium. Erdman points out the city’s nearly more than year-long rewrite of the city’s zoning code has rolled out during the period in which the city was considering a proposal by Viridian Partners. During that time, Erdman notes, planners have not written standards for data centers that would require impact studies, setback requirements or neighbor notification rules. She points out a zoning reboot with fewer data center rules than she thinks is appropriate could get approved before the city drafts and OKs companion ordinances tied to the moratorium. Meanwhile, Erdman said, a new data center proposal should come after the moratorium ends. Now, there’s no clarity on what new rules the moratorium will produce. She thinks that’s why voters should weigh both the moratorium and the possibility of data centers when they vote on the referendum. “Despite the presence of a moratorium, future data center projects at GM/Jatco remain a possibility, and that should be a part of a voter’s decision-making process,” Erdman said. “Voters should be asking 'What happens when the moratorium expires, and who should have the final say on any exceptionally large development project at the publicly-owned GM/Jatco site, including data centers?'" Elaine Strassburg is a Janesville resident who responded to The Gazette’s request for local reader feedback on our questions on the referendum. Strassburg opposes the referendum. In her response, she says she thinks residents should separate the city’s data center moratorium from their consideration of the GM/JATCO site referendum, in part because Strassburg takes a more measured stance on data centers. “I’m hopeful the strong feelings against data centers will motivate the industry to innovate because unless we put a lid on AI, and I doubt that will happen, we will need data centers,” Strassburg said. The city of Janesville cut short a due-dillegence process at the GM/JATCO site with data center developer Viridian Partners earlier this year after the company failed in six months to show any concerted plans on how it might pursue a data center project. Strassburg believes public pressure against against Viridian Partners’ proposal is what led the city to in turn enact a data center moratorium. She believes public pressure against data centers provides reason enough for the city to use the moratorium period to craft data center protections that respond to residents’ concerns. “Interested citizens had sufficient influence on city government to ensure there will be no data center anywhere in Janesville until environmental issues such as water and electrical usage, and noise levels of current data centers, are cared for to the satisfaction of Janesville citizens,” she said. Alyssa Capozziello fronts grassroots group No Janesville Data Center. She petitioned to get the referendum on the Nov. 3 ba

artigo.texto: The Nozu Project adds to Trina Storage's growing track record in Japan's utility-scale energy storage market. As deployment of grid-scale battery storage expands in the country, Trina Storage has established local capabilities to support projects from system configuration and technical consultation through delivery coordination and after-sales service. Through its team in Japan, Trina Storage works closely with customers and project partners to address local technical and project requirements, providing support throughout the project lifecycle. This local capability is complemented by Trina Storage's global experience in battery cell technology, system integration and utility-scale energy storage deployment. Dr. Leo Zhao, Head of Energy Storage (APAC), Trina Storage, said, "We are pleased to support Japan's growing renewable energy portfolio through the AEJ Nozu Battery Energy Storage System project. With Trinasolar's longstanding experience in solar and Trina Storage's growing presence in utility-scale energy storage, we see significant opportunities to support Japan's evolving energy needs. For Nozu and other projects in Japan, our focus is on combining advanced technology with strong local capabilities." Trina Storage is also supplying a 160MWh utility-scale BESS project in the Kyushu region, adding to its growing project track record in Japan. In September, it also signed an MoU with AMP-lify for approximately 1GWh of grid-connected BESS projects in Japan, featuring the latest Elementa 3 series. The MoU agreement, together with projects like Nozu, reflects Trina Storage's continued expansion in Japan as demand for utility-scale energy storage grows.

artigo.texto: - United States - / - Construction - / - NasdaqGS:MTRX 3 U.S. Infrastructure Stocks Tied To SPR Refill And Energy Storage Demand The U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve, sitting near multi decade lows, has turned what used to feel like a sleepy government stockpile into a live market risk. Supply shocks now carry more bite, and pricing power can shift quickly when barrels are scarce and storage is constrained. This piece walks through how that backdrop hits the SPR value chain and profiles 3 U.S. stocks whose businesses are directly exposed to those pressures. artigo.texto: Highlights - Repeat orders from a Hungarian partner. - Flow batteries support solar projects. - Long-duration storage demand rises. Invinity Energy Systems, a maker of vanadium flow batteries, secured new sales to a Hungarian partner for solar-plus-storage projects. The repeat order shows growing demand for long-duration energy storage as renewable energy expands. This update falls within our Energy Stocks coverage. Energy Storage for a Renewable Future Energy stocks include companies producing oil and gas, generating electricity and developing technologies for the energy transition. Invinity Energy Systems falls into the last category, manufacturing vanadium flow batteries that store energy for long periods. The company secured repeat sales to a Hungarian partner, adding to its growing presence in the Hungarian market. The systems will support solar-plus-storage projects, helping store solar power for use when the sun is not shining. What Invinity Does Vanadium Flow Batteries Invinity's batteries store energy in liquid electrolytes containing vanadium. Unlike lithium-ion batteries, flow batteries can discharge for many hours and degrade very little over time. Long-Duration Storage Flow batteries are suited to long-duration storage, providing power for several hours. This complements shorter-duration lithium-ion systems. Applications Invinity's systems support solar farms, wind projects, industrial sites and grid services. Why the Hungary Orders Matter Repeat Customer Repeat orders show that the customer is satisfied with performance, which builds credibility. Market Expansion Hungary is becoming an important market for Invinity, with multiple sales to the same partner. Solar Integration Pairing batteries with solar allows energy to be used in the evening, improving project economics. The Long-Duration Storage Opportunity Renewable Growth As wind and solar grow, storage is needed to balance supply and demand. Grid Stability Long-duration storage helps maintain grid stability during periods of low renewable output. Policy Support Governments are introducing support mechanisms for long-duration storage, including in the UK. Advantages of Flow Batteries Durability Flow batteries can operate for many years with minimal degradation. Safety They use non-flammable electrolytes, reducing fire risk. Recyclability Vanadium electrolyte can be reused, supporting circular economy goals. Risks to Consider Cost Competitiveness Flow batteries must compete with falling lithium-ion costs. Scaling Production Manufacturing at scale requires investment. Funding Growth companies may need additional capital. Order Timing Revenue depends on project timelines. How Investors Can Follow Invinity Readers will watch new orders, deliveries, manufacturing capacity, cost reductions and policy developments in key markets. The Role of Vanadium Vanadium is a metal that can exist in multiple charge states, making it ideal for flow batteries. Supply comes mainly from China, Russia and South Africa. Securing reliable vanadium supply is important for flow battery manufacturers. Why Europe Needs Storage European countries have ambitious renewable energy targets. Storage helps integrate renewables by smoothing output and reducing curtailment. Markets such as Hungary, with growing solar capacity, need storage to make the most of renewable generation. Hungary's Solar Growth Hungary has seen rapid growth in solar power capacity in recent years. As solar output rises, the grid faces challenges during peak production, when supply can exceed demand. Storage helps absorb excess solar power and release it later, improving grid balance and project returns. Repeat orders from a Hungarian partner suggest that solar developers in the country see value in long-duration storage. Building a track record in one market can help Invinity win business in neighbouring countries with similar needs. The UK Long-Duration Storage Scheme The UK government has developed a support mechanism for long-duration electricity storage, designed to encourage investment in technologies that can store energy for many hours. This scheme could create opportunities for flow battery manufacturers, including Invinity, by providing revenue certainty for projects. Competition in Energy Storage Lithium-ion batteries dominate the energy storage market because of falling costs and widespread manufacturing. Flow batteries compete by offering longer duration, greater cycle life and enhanced safety. The right choice depends on the application, with flow batteries suited to projects needing daily cycling over many hours. Manufacturing and Partnerships Invinity has worked with manufacturing partners to scale production. Expanding capacity while reducing costs is central to competing with alternative technologies. Partnerships can help share investment and accelerate deployment. Financial Considerations As a growth company, Invinity has invested heavily in product development and manufacturing. Revenue growth from orders like those in Hungary is important for reaching profitability. Investors watch cash balances, order backlogs and delivery schedules closely. The Energy Transition Context Global investment in renewable energy continues to grow, and storage is an essential part of integrating renewables into power systems. Long-duration storage is expected to become increasingly important as renewable penetration rises. Companies with proven technologies and growing order books may benefit from this trend. Why Durability Matters Energy storage assets are expected to operate for many years. Flow batteries can cycle many times with minimal degradation, which can lower lifetime costs. For project developers, durability and predictable performance improve the economics of storage investments. Final Thoughts Invinity Energy Systems' repeat Hungarian orders highlight demand for long-duration energy storage as renewable energy expands. Its vanadium flow batteries offer durability, safety

artigo.texto: The Andhra Pradesh Power Coordination Committee (APPCC), acting on behalf of Andhra Pradesh’s distribution companies (APDISCOMs), has invited proposals for developing 1,250 MW / 5,000 MWh of standalone Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) across three locations in the state. The projects will be developed under the Build-Own-Operate (BOO) model through tariff-based competitive bidding, allowing selected developers to build, own and operate the storage facilities. The initiative aims to strengthen energy storage infrastructure in Andhra Pradesh and support the integration and management of renewable energy. The proposed projects will be located at the Rayalaseema Thermal Power Plant (RTPP), Talaricheruvu Renewable Energy (RE) Project and NP Kunta RE Project. The tender provides an opportunity for battery energy storage developers to participate in large-scale standalone storage projects under a competitive procurement framework. The total planned capacity comprises three separate projects. The first project involves the development of a 500 MW / 2,000 MWh Battery Energy Storage System at the Rayalaseema Thermal Power Plant. The second project covers 250 MW / 1,000 MWh of storage capacity at the Talaricheruvu RE Project. The third project involves another 500 MW / 2,000 MWh installation at the NP Kunta RE Project. Together, these installations will provide 1,250 MW of power capacity and 5,000 MWh of energy storage capacity. The projects are structured to provide standalone battery storage facilities at designated locations, with developers responsible for implementing and operating the systems under the BOO arrangement. To facilitate project development, land will be provided to selected developers on a Right-of-Use (RoU) basis. The annual land lease charge has been set at a nominal rate of INR 1 per acre. This arrangement is intended to provide developers with access to the required land for establishing the battery storage installations at the identified project sites. APPCC issued the request for selection (RfS) document on October 7, 2026. The pre-bid meeting is scheduled for October 22, 2026, at 11:00 hours. Interested bidders must submit their pre-bid queries by 17:00 hours on the same day. The last date and time for submitting bids is November 23, 2026, at 17:00 hours. The technical bids will be opened on November 24, 2026, at 15:00 hours. Prospective bidders will need to follow the tender schedule and submit the required documentation within the specified deadlines. The cost of the RfS document is INR 3 lakh, plus 18% Goods and Services Tax (GST). The tender fee is non-refundable. Bidders must also submit an Earnest Money Deposit (EMD) of INR 5 lakh per MW of their quoted capacity. Permitted EMD instruments include a Demand Draft, Bank Guarantee, Payment on Order Instrument (POI) or Insurance Surety Bond. Additionally, selected developers will be required to provide a Performance Bank Guarantee (PBG) of INR 10 lakh per MW of contracted capacity before signing the Battery Energy Storage Purchase Agreement (BESPA). Through this procurement, APPCC is seeking developers to establish large-scale battery storage infrastructure across three strategic locations in Andhra Pradesh. The tender outlines the project capacities, land-use arrangements, financial requirements and bidding timeline for interested participants. artigo.texto: SINEXCEL Completes PCS Shipment for 100MW/400MWh Energy Storage Project in Chile VALLENAR, Chile, Oct. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- SINEXCEL (300693.SZ) has shipped all StellaON 1250K power conversion systems for RelyEZ Energy Storage Technology Co., Ltd.'s 100 MW/400 MWh battery energy storage project in Chile. The four-hour system in Atacama will charge during lower-demand periods and discharge at peak times, supporting grid flexibility and project returns. On-Schedule Delivery Supports Project Execution Large-scale overseas projects require production, inspection, and shipment schedules to remain closely aligned with on-site construction. SINEXCEL completed the full PCS order on schedule, helping RelyEZ Energy protect the timetable for transport, installation, commissioning, and grid connection. For a project of this scale, delays in a single batch can narrow the construction window. Coordinated delivery reduces uncertainty and helps local teams plan the next stages. StellaON 1250K PCS Built for Atacama's Demanding Conditions Energy equipment in Atacama must operate in an environment that can include high temperatures, dust, and sand. The StellaON 1250K PCS has a maximum efficiency of 99% and a rated-power efficiency of 98.5%. It supports operation from -40°C to 60°C, maintains full power output at 55°C, and has an IP65 protection rating. Maintaining rated output in high temperatures can reduce power derating and the need for additional capacity. Higher conversion efficiency also limits energy losses across repeated charge-discharge cycles, supporting stable operation and long-term returns. Strengthening Local Service Capabilities Across the Americas Following shipment, the project will move into on-site installation and commissioning. SINEXCEL has a dedicated after-sales team in Latin America and seven service centres across the Americas. Technical requests can receive a response within 30 minutes, backed by round-the-clock support and a seven-day spare-parts guarantee. SINEXCEL has deployed more than 17GW of energy storage capacity across over 5,000 projects and works with more than 600 partners in 60+ countries and regions. Following shipment, the Chilean project moves into its on-site delivery phase. SINEXCEL will continue to expand its local operations across Latin America, providing customers with support throughout the project lifecycle. About SINEXCEL Founded in 2007, SINEXCEL is a pioneer in energy storage, EV charging, and power quality solutions. With 17 GW of installed storage, 200,000 EV DC chargers, and nearly 20 million amperes of Active Harmonic Filters deployed, SINEXCEL partners with industry leaders to empower energy freedom. artigo.texto: O Brasil está vivenciando uma expansão acelerada de data centers, centros de dados digitais que movem a economia. A busca por energia estável e segurança levou esses empreendimentos para cidades do interior, como Varginha, em Minas Gerais. A previsão é de que o setor atraia até R$ 100 bilhões em aportes até 2030, redesenhando o mapa tecnológico do país. O Brasil está vivendo um grande crescimento na construção de data centers, que são estruturas essenciais para guardar e processar os dados da internet. Essa expansão, que pode atrair até R$ 100 bilhões de investimentos até 2030, está levando esses empreendimentos para fora das grandes capitais e para o interior do país. Muitas pessoas não percebem, mas toda a nossa vida digital depende de uma infraestrutura física enorme. A busca por energia elétrica estável e segurança está fazendo com que empresas de tecnologia instalem seus servidores em cidades menores, mudando a cara da infraestrutura digital do Brasil. - O setor de data centers no Brasil deve receber entre R$ 60 bilhões e R$ 100 bilhões em investimentos até 2030. - Varginha, em Minas Gerais, recebeu em setembro de 2025 o primeiro data center do Sul de Minas, com previsão de R$ 23 milhões em aportes. - O Brasil conta com cerca de 200 data centers, ocupando a 12ª posição no mundo e liderando a América Latina. - A energia é o fator mais importante: a demanda por conexão de grandes cargas deve somar 54,2 GW até 2038. - Construir um data center exige planejamento rigoroso de energia, refrigeração e conectividade antes mesmo de comprar os servidores. Como funciona a estrutura por trás da internet Segundo Henrique Reis, especialista em infraestrutura digital e fundador da Sourei, construir um data center não começa com a compra de computadores ou servidores. O primeiro passo é entender se a região tem energia elétrica estável e suficiente. É necessário verificar se há rotas diferentes de fibra óptica para conexão, se o sistema de refrigeração é adequado e se existe segurança para manter a estrutura funcionando 24 horas por dia, sem pausas. Uma decisão errada nessa fase inicial de planejamento pode atrapalhar toda a operação no futuro. A redundância, ou seja, a existência de fontes alternativas de energia e internet, é o ponto central. Se a eletricidade ou a internet falharem em uma única fonte, serviços de bancos, comércio online e empresas podem parar de funcionar. Henrique explica: Quando o usuário acessa um sistema, ele não vê o que existe por trás daquela aplicação. Há servidores, energia, refrigeração, fibra óptica e equipamentos trabalhando continuamente. O data center é justamente a estrutura que mantém essa operação disponível mesmo quando ocorre uma falha em algum componente. Energia define onde a tecnologia vai crescer A disponibilidade de energia elétrica é o principal fator que decide onde novos data centers podem ser construídos. Em São Paulo, por exemplo, estudos indicam que serão necessários cerca de R$ 1,6 bilhão em investimentos na rede de transmissão de energia para liberar espaço para novas conexões. Outras obras planejadas para 2026 devem aumentar ainda mais essa capacidade. Para o especialista, não basta apenas olhar a quantidade de energia disponível. É preciso garantir que ela seja estável e que haja espaço para expandir a capacidade futura. Como os servidores geram muito calor constantemente, a quantidade de energia e de sistemas de ar condicionado (refrigeração) precisa ser calculada com precisão. Um servidor trabalhando gera calor continuamente. Quanto maior a capacidade computacional instalada, maior também a necessidade de energia e refrigeração. Por isso, essas decisões precisam ser feitas em conjunto. Não adianta ter espaço físico se a região não consegue sustentar tecnicamente a operação, aponta Henrique. O interior entra no mapa tecnológico Com as grandes cidades ficando mais caras e complexas, a busca por novas áreas abriu espaço para cidades médias. Varginha, por exemplo, está localizada estrategicamente entre São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro e Belo Horizonte. A cidade possui acesso a redes de comunicação, aeroporto e uma atividade empresarial que exige serviços digitais. No entanto, trazer um data center para o interior não é apenas uma questão de encontrar terreno mais barato. É preciso analisar as rotas das fibras ópticas, a segurança do local, a distância dos principais pontos de conexão da internet no país e se há profissionais técnicos qualificados na região. O interior pode ter vantagens importantes, mas não basta disponibilizar uma área. É preciso saber por onde chegam as fibras, quais são as alternativas em caso de falha, como está a oferta de energia e se existe capacidade de expansão. Data center é uma decisão técnica antes de ser geográfica, afirma Henrique. O data center instalado em Varginha foi projetado para oferecer serviços como armazenamento de dados, cópias de segurança (backup) e processamento, conectando-se diretamente ao grande eixo econômico do Sudeste. artigo.texto: Recently, the strategic cooperation signing ceremony between Rockcheck New Energy Group and Suzhou Qingde Hydrogen Energy Technology Co., Ltd. was held in Tianjin. Relying on the Sunan Institute of Molecular Engineering at Peking University, the two parties will focus on the field of hydrogen agriculture to jointly develop and promote hydrogen molecular fertilizers, while deepening cooperation in hydrogen beauty and health and hydrogen industry sectors, working together to open up new tracks for diversified hydrogen energy applications. Peking University professor and doctoral supervisor Li Xingguo, Qingde Hydrogen Energy General Manager Xie Lei, and Rockcheck Group Director, Vice President, and Rockcheck New Energy Group Chairman Zhang Lihua attended the ceremony. Hydrogen energy industry enters a new era of multi-scenario large-scale application Currently, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT), the Ministry of Finance, and the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC) have approved five major urban clusters including Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei to carry out comprehensive hydrogen energy application pilot projects. China's hydrogen energy industry has officially moved from single-point breakthroughs in fuel cell vehicles into a period of multi-scenario large-scale application. The strategic cooperation between Rockcheck New Energy and Qingde Hydrogen Energy is an important initiative by the two enterprises to actively implement the national hydrogen energy pilot deployment, which will continue to broaden the boundaries of hydrogen energy applications and build a diversified hydrogen energy industry ecosystem. Strong alliance between technology R&D and scenario operations This cooperation achieves a strong alliance and complementary advantages between technology R&D and scenario operations. Rockcheck New Energy is a benchmark enterprise in the commercial and large-scale implementation of hydrogen energy, positioned as an integrated solution provider for the hydrogen energy industry. It has built an entire industry chain layout covering "production, storage, transportation, refueling, application, research, and equipment manufacturing," and created a "one core, two poles" development model centered on a digital and intelligent big data platform, with the "hydrogen +" economy and "vehicle +" economy as the two poles. To date, it hascumulatively put into operation 1,255 hydrogen fuel cell heavy trucks and 17 hydrogen refueling stations, with mature project implementation capabilities, rich multi-scenario operation experience, and a complete industrial supporting system. Qingde Hydrogen Energy is a hydrogen energy technology innovation enterprise relying on the Sunan Institute of Molecular Engineering at Peking University. The company has developed efficient and safe nano-hydrolysis hydrogen production materials, which are widely used in hydrogen molecular biomedicine and hydrogen agriculture. It holds multiple independent intellectual property rights and has carried out project cooperation with multiple industry leaders, demonstrating outstanding strength in technological innovation and commercialization of research outcomes. Industrial layout implemented across three major tracks According to the agreement, the two parties will implement industrial layout across three major tracks: first, jointly promote the civilian application, productization, and scenario-based implementation of hydrogen health technologies, creating a new sector in the hydrogen beauty and health industry; second, use hydrogen-enriched technology to empower the transformation of modern agriculture,jointly develop and promote hydrogen molecular fertilizers, and explore a new model of green, efficient, and low-carbon smart hydrogen agriculture; third, tap into the value of hydrogen energy storage, promote the large-scale application of hydrogen energy in scenarios such as renewable energy consumption and power grid peak shaving, and cultivate new growth poles for the hydrogen energy industry. The two parties will establish a special working group, build an industry-academia-research collaboration mechanism, and jointly carry out technical research, demonstration project construction, and market expansion, promoting the extension of hydrogen energy applications from transportation and logistics to diversified scenarios such as public health, modern agriculture, and new-type industry.

artigo.texto: SWI arrecada US$ 894 milhões para reestruturar a antiga mineradora de bitcoin da FTX, Genesis Digital, para IA O Grupo SWI afirmou que utilizará os recursos provenientes de uma captação de fundos de 800 milhões de euros (894 milhões de dólares) para transformar a Genesis Digital Assets, adquirida da falência da FTX, de um minerador de bitcoin para um data center focado em IA. - O Grupo SWI levantou 800 milhões de euros (894 milhões de dólares) de investidores institucionais, avaliando a empresa em 6,1 bilhões de euros, para expandir projetos de inteligência artificial e data centers na Europa e nos Estados Unidos. - A empresa planeja reutilizar as instalações nos EUA e na Suécia da Genesis Digital Assets, a mineradora de bitcoin anteriormente apoiada pela FTX que agora controla como SWI Digital, para cargas de trabalho de IA, enquanto vende os locais da unidade no Cazaquistão. - A estratégia da SWI reflete uma mudança mais ampla na indústria, à medida que os mineradores de bitcoin transformam conexões de energia e capacidade de data center em receita de IA e computação de alto desempenho. SWI Group (SWICH), que controla a mineradora de bitcoin Genesis Digital Assets, anteriormente pertencente à FTX, afirmou ter levantado 800 milhões de euros (894 milhões de dólares) junto a investidores institucionais para expandir seus projetos de data center e de computação em inteligência artificial (IA) na Europa e nos Estados Unidos. A empresa listada na Euronext Amsterdã, uma firma de investimentos focada em infraestrutura digital, anunciou o aumento de capital avalia-o em 6,1 bilhões de euros. Anunciou a aquisição de cerca de 40% da Genesis Digital em junho por 500 milhões de dólares, concluindo o aquisição em agosto com 70% dos direitos de voto e renomeando a unidade para SWI Digital. A estratégia da empresa ilustra o que se tornou uma operação conhecida para as empresas de mineração de bitcoin. Seu ativo mais valioso não são mais suas máquinas de mineração, mas as conexões de energia e os locais dos data centers que podem ser reaproveitados para clientes de IA. Mineradores de bitcoin assinaram mais de US$ 70 bilhões em contratos de IA e computação de alto desempenho, à medida que buscam uma receita mais estável do que a mineração de bitcoin atualmente oferece. A mudança do foco da mineração de criptomoedas para o processamento de computações de IA coloca a empresa na mesma corrida que os mineradores listados como a TeraWulf e Core Scientific , que estão convertendo o acesso à energia e a capacidade de data centers em negócios de hospedagem de IA. O CEO da SWI, Max-Hervé George, disse ao Wall Street Journal que ele “"juros zero” na mineração de bitcoin. A empresa está vendendo os sites da Genesis Digital Assets no Cazaquistão e pretende utilizar suas instalações nos EUA e na Suécia para cargas de trabalho de IA em vez disso. Alameda Research, a empresa de negociação de criptomoedas pertencente ao ex-CEO da FTX, Sam Bankman-Fried, investiu mais de US$ 1 bilhão na Genesis Digital Assets desde 2021 e detinha cerca de 20% da mineradora, informou o WSJ. FTX declarou falência em novembro de 2022, deixando esse investimento entre os muitos ativos analisados pelo espólio.
