GP Energy Tech Limited (âGP Energy Techâ or theâCompanyâ), a subsidiary of Gold Peak Technology Group Limited (âGold Peakâ) (SEHK: 40), is showcasing its Nickel-Zinc (NiZn) battery system at the Hong Kong Electronics Fair (Autumn Edition), held at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Center from October 13 to 16. With Manufacturing Twins and Speed to Scale at the core of its approach, the Company is advancing the development and scalable supply of backup power solutions for AI and cloud data centers, as well as other critical infrastructure. Speed to Scale: accelerating commercialization through smart manufacturing Drawing on Gold Peak's more than 60 years of experience in battery design, manufacturing and sales, GP Energy Tech is leveraging the Group's expertise in electro-chemistry and high-volume Nickel-based battery manufacturing to advance its NiZn battery systems. Through smart automation and replicable production processes, the Company is accelerating the transition from technology development to commercial application. While maintaining consistent quality and reliable delivery, it flexibly expands manufacturing capacity in line with customer demand, supporting the delivery of NiZn battery solutions at scale to meet growing demand for next-generation backup power. Alan Lo, Executive Vice Chairman of GP Energy Tech said:âThe value of NiZn technology lies in its ability to meet the industry's requirements for safety, power and sustainability simultaneously. By combining this technology with Gold Peak's more than 60 years of manufacturing experience, smart automation and Manufacturing Twins strategy, we are building scalable supply capacity. This is what sets GP Energy Tech apart. The rapid growth of AI and cloud services is creating new requirements for backup power in data centers and other critical infrastructure. Sophia Chong (left), Executive Director of the Hong Kong Trade Development Council (HKTDC), joins GP Energy Tech's management team for discussion on the development of the innovation and technology industry. It offers operators a backup power option for use with UPS systems. Its water-based, non-flammable electrolyte avoids thermal runaway risk in high-density computing environments, while its high-power density supports more efficient use of space, requiring 74% less floor space per MW than lead-acid systems. Its recyclability also supports resource circularity, enabling operators to balance performance and sustainability when deploying backup power. From cell to cabinet: supporting flexible deployment GP Energy Tech's NiZn battery solution features a modular design built around cells in cylindrical Sub-C format. Each pack contains 128 cells, with nine packs forming a module and ten modules integrated into a cabinet containing 11,520 cells. This architecture allows customers to deploy the solution flexibly according to their UPS system configurations, meeting the backup power requirements of different applications. The Company is also actively exploring battery backup opportunities in emerging 800 VDC power architectures as the power infrastructure needs of AI and cloud data centers evolve. Suitability will be further assessed through system-level testing and validation. Advancing commercialization through Manufacturing Twins strategy and industry collaboration GP Energy Tech's Manufacturing Twins strategy brings together manufacturing facilities in China and Malaysia to enhance flexibility in capacity allocation and strengthen supply resilience, providing reliable supply support for customers in different markets. The Company's first NiZn manufacturing facility in Dongguan, China, commenced operations in January 2026 and entered full mass production in mid-June. The first commercial order was delivered in August 2026. The Malaysian facility, part of the Manufacturing Twins strategy, is targeted to open in the third quarter of 2027. artigo.texto: The Lino Lakes City Council continues to have discussions around data centers. At the council’s most recent work session, Community Development Director Michael Grochala reviewed the city’s current land use regulations and provided an overview of data centers. “We’re hearing a lot more about them now,” Grochala said. “They’ve been around for years … but we’re seeing a lot more locally within the Twin Cities Metro Area and as a whole nationally.” What data centers do A data center is a facility that houses computer servers and related equipment used to process, store and distribute digital information. Grochala said data centers support cloud computing, artificial intelligence, data storage, online applications and other digital services. Unlike a typical office or commercial building, a data center is designed primarily to operate computer equipment. These facilities generally run continuously and require reliable electrical power, cooling systems, network connectivity and backup power, Grochala said. “The city’s zoning ordinance defines a data center as an establishment primarily involved in compiling, storing and maintaining information in digital form using a mainframe computer,” Grochala said. “The definition specifically excludes general business offices, computer-related sales establishments and business or personal service establishments.” Types and sizing considerations Data centers vary in size, ownership and function. Common types include enterprise, colocation and hyperscale facilities (see sidebar for more information). Grochala said the hyperscale data centers are driving concerns and interest. “These are much bigger facilities. These are over 200,000 square feet, some of them getting into the million-square-foot size,” he explained. “… These places are really pushing a lot of data, storing a lot of data and now computing, as AI is expanding.” Because these facilities differ in size, design and operating requirements, the appropriate location depends on the data center’s type and scale, available site infrastructure, surrounding land uses and local regulations. Potential sites may include industrial districts, technology or business parks, areas with existing or planned electrical and high-capacity fiber infrastructure, and locations with adequate water and wastewater infrastructure when water-based cooling is proposed. Under the city’s current zoning code, a data center is a permitted use in the Light Industrial (LI), General Industrial (GI) and Business Campus (BC) zoning districts. The LI district includes high-tech businesses and professional services. The GI district allows general industrial uses and services, including more intensive activities. The BC district supports employment-oriented development, including offices, services, research and development, data centers and light industrial uses. A data center proposed in one of these districts would not require rezoning, Grochala explained. However, the development would still need to comply with all applicable city building and development requirements. The city’s 2040 Comprehensive Plan provides the broader land-use framework for determining whether a proposed data center aligns with the city’s planned development pattern. Each proposal would be evaluated according to its location, design and development characteristics. Data centers may also be subject to state and regional regulations and approvals. Minnesota’s Business First Stop offers a coordinated resource for businesses and project proposers navigating state requirements. Depending on the project, those requirements may address environmental review, water appropriation and use, stormwater and wastewater, air emissions, electric generation or storage, utility interconnection, and building and plumbing standards. The city’s land use review and any applicable state or regional reviews are separate processes. A project must satisfy the requirements of each reviewing authority before the corresponding approvals or permits can be issued. Grochala said Lino Lakes’ location within the metropolitan area, access to major transportation corridors and established business campus and industrial areas may create opportunities for technology-oriented development. The city also participates in the Minnesota Technology Corridor, a regional economic development collaboration among six cities. The corridor encompasses development areas along I-35E and I-35W and identifies more than 1,500 acres of future development potential. According to the city staff report, supporting infrastructure includes proximity to I-35E, a fiber-optic backbone and two electric transmission lines. Council members share feedback, thoughts Council Member Julia Nelson clarified that no company has approached the city about building a data center. “I would be for anything that gives us the most power and control over this,” she added. Council Member Randy Rennaker, who brought this forward for discussion to the council in July, said he wants to make certain the city is protected and has the control of what type of facilities are built in the city. “I have friends and family who live in the city that can’t water their yard on a Monday or a Wednesday,” he added. “Some of these data centers are using exorbitant amounts of water. That’s just not right.” Council Member Chris Lyden asked Grochala if it would be possible to ban data centers in the specific zoning districts. Grochala said staff have not gone down the path of exploring prohibition, but the city could establish standards. There was no formal action taken by the council. It was discussion only.

artigo.texto: BYD is studying whether to manufacture lithium batteries in Argentina, Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno said on Thursday after meeting Stella Li, the Chinese electric vehicle maker’s executive vice-president. According to Quirno, the company was looking at “investment opportunities in Argentina linked to the lithium value chain, particularly in the production of batteries and energy storage systems”. He did not say how much BYD might spend or where the factory could go. The minister tied the talks to Argentinian President Javier Milei’s economic agenda, saying Argentina was positioning itself “as a platform for projects aimed at both the domestic market and exports”. Quirno credited the government’s policies with promoting investment and mining in the country. BYD has sold only imported cars in Argentina since it opened for business in October last year, and it has not announced production plans in the country. It sold 10,000 vehicles in August, including a Dolphin Mini in Rosario, and now has 21 dealerships, most of them in Buenos Aires. The company’s local subsidiary, BYD Auto Argentina SAU, registered with the Justice Ministry in August last year with a corporate purpose that already included making vehicles, batteries and auto parts, the South China Morning Post reported at the time. Christian Kimelman, who runs the Argentine operation, said a car factory was not on the table for now. “It is not in the plans, but anyone who knows the Argentine industry knows that, to lead the sector in the current context, you need to have some kind of vision in that direction,” he told Bloomberg Linea earlier this year. Kimelman said most of BYD’s supply for Argentina and Mexico would come from its factory in Camacari, in the Brazilian state of Bahia. The plant opened in October last year with capacity for 150,000 vehicles a year, and in March Li said it had orders for 50,000 cars from each country. Cars made in Brazil can enter Argentina largely duty-free under the automotive agreement between the two Mercosur members. Vehicles from outside the bloc pay a 35 per cent tariff, except for a quota of 50,000 units that Chinese brands have dominated. BYD has also kept shipping cars from China on its own vessels, and in January the BYD Changzhou unloaded more than 5,000 vehicles at the port of Zarate. The company registered 9,266 cars in Argentina in the first half of the year, according to the importers’ chamber. A lithium venture in Argentina would follow BYD’s failed attempt in Chile, where it had planned a US$290 million cathode plant in Antofagasta. The factory was meant to make 50,000 tonnes a year of lithium iron phosphate cathode material, using lithium from SQM at a preferential price. But BYD and Tsingshan, the other Chinese company Chile’s development agency, Corfo, picked for the scheme, both pulled out in May last year. At that time, Corfo blamed the collapse in lithium prices. -- SOUTH CHINA MORNING POST

artigo.texto: A joint South Korean research team has announced a finding that could accelerate the commercialization of next-generation lithium-metal batteries: a high-performance electrolyte formulation made entirely from two inexpensive, off-the-shelf solvents that battery researchers had long considered individually unsuitable — and had never thought to combine — tripling cycle life under demanding conditions compared with conventional electrolytes tested in identical circumstances. The result challenges a design principle that has dominated the field for decades. The Battery Chemistry That Could Double EV Range — and Its Long-Standing Problem Lithium-metal batteries have sat just beyond the commercial horizon for the better part of five decades. The appeal is straightforward: swap the graphite anode in today's electric vehicle batteries for lithium metal, and you can theoretically double — and in some research estimates multiply by up to ten times — the energy stored per kilogram. That translates directly into longer driving range without a heavier or larger battery pack, and into cheaper, more compact grid-scale energy storage systems. The obstacle is equally straightforward: lithium metal is exceptionally reactive. Every time a lithium-metal battery charges, the anode reacts with the surrounding liquid electrolyte. Those reactions build up a protective layer called the solid electrolyte interphase, or SEI, on the anode surface. On graphite, this layer forms once and stabilizes. On lithium metal, it cracks, regrows, and thickens with every cycle — consuming lithium and electrolyte irreversibly, promoting the growth of needle-like lithium dendrites that can short-circuit the cell, and triggering destructive side reactions at the cathode. The result is rapid capacity fade. Under the high-voltage conditions required to push maximum energy from a cell, the problem intensifies. The prevailing engineering response has been to use electrolytes that minimize the strength of the solvent's grip on lithium ions. Strongly solvating solvents — those that cluster tightly around a lithium ion in solution — raise the energy barrier for the ion to shed those solvent molecules and deposit as metal on the anode, a step called desolvation. Poor desolvation means uneven plating, which means a bad SEI, which means short cycle life. The conventional fix has been to use either expensive fluorinated solvents that bind lithium more weakly, or to dissolve lithium salts at very high concentrations to push the chemistry in a more favorable direction. Both approaches add manufacturing cost and complexity. An Unexpected Combination The team, led by Professor Song Hyun-kon of the Department of Energy and Chemical Engineering at the Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology (UNIST) and Professor Seo Dong-hwa of the Department of Materials Science and Engineering at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST), focused instead on two commodity chemicals that the battery field had previously ruled out: ethylene carbonate (EC) and sulfolane (SL). Both researchers are confirmed specialists in battery electrolyte design with a track record of publication in high-impact materials science journals. Both solvents are produced industrially at large scale and are inexpensive. Both had been excluded from lithium-metal battery electrolyte design for the same fundamental reason: they bind to lithium ions too strongly. EC in particular is a workhorse of the conventional lithium-ion battery industry — it is the primary solvent in most EV battery electrolytes today — but it is well-documented as incompatible with lithium metal anodes, where its tight grip on lithium ions and its tendency to decompose continuously at the reactive lithium surface rapidly degrade the cell. Sulfolane, a polar industrial solvent with similarly high binding affinity for lithium, had been studied as a battery solvent on its own and rejected for analogous reasons. What the UNIST–KAIST team found and reported in ACS Nano on August 11, 2026, is that mixing EC and SL at a 3-to-7 weight ratio — together with a lithium salt and a small quantity of an SEI-stabilizing additive — produces an electrolyte that behaves in a way neither solvent predicts individually. What Does 'Cooperative Solvation' Actually Mean? When EC and SL molecules are present together at that ratio, strong intermolecular forces arise between them — specifically, hydrogen bonds between EC's hydrogen atoms and SL's oxygen atoms. These inter-solvent bonds pull the two molecules toward each other rather than toward the lithium ion. The result is counterintuitive: each solvent's individual binding affinity for lithium ions is weakened by the presence of the other. The team called this mechanism cooperative solvation. The mechanism works through the structure of the lithium ion's immediate environment in solution. Normally, a lithium ion in an EC-based electrolyte is surrounded by EC molecules in what is called the first solvation sheath — typically four to six molecules arranged around the ion. When EC and SL are mixed in the cooperative ratio, both solvents appear simultaneously in that first solvation sheath in a new configuration that the team verified through computational modeling. The co-localized solvents effectively share the coordination of the lithium ion, and because they are also coordinating with each other through hydrogen bonding, the total binding energy available for each solvent to hold onto the lithium is reduced. Desolvation — the step where lithium ions must shed their solvent shell before depositing on the anode — becomes easier. "Mixing two strongly binding solvents to actually weaken their interaction with lithium ions represents a new design principle that overturns conventional electrolyte design wisdom," first author Jinki Hong stated in the research announcement. artigo.texto: More than 50 people marched to Ameren Missouri’s St. Louis headquarters Saturday to speak out against the company’s newly published plans to build more fossil fuel resources in the coming 20 years. The group wore nature-inspired costumes while holding signs calling for clean energy. The People’s Joy Parade and the Sierra Club organized the demonstration with speakers from Tenants Transforming St. Louis, the Missouri Coalition for the Environment and Labadie Environmental Organization. “We can create the clean energy future that we need. We can create it through people power, through love of our communities, and through good organizing,” said Jenn DeRose, the Sierra Club’s campaign organizing strategist for Beyond Coal in Missouri. She stressed the need to develop energy sources like solar and wind power with battery storage to make it available around the clock. Ameren Missouri recently released a new long-range plan that would significantly increase the amount of power plants in its portfolio to meet growing demand for electricity. The company said that growth is primarily driven by new large data centers moving to Missouri. The new resource plan increases the number of new natural gas power plants to nine while also extending the lives of two existing coal plants. Both resources emit planet-warming gases that contribute to climate change. Patricia Schuba lives near the Labadie Coal Plant, which will now operate all four of its units until 2042, rather than shuttering two units in 2036. The plant is about 35 miles west of St. Louis on the Missouri River. Schuba and other demonstrators hit a Labadie power plant piñata that was filled with candy made to look like coal. She said she is not normally that kind of person but feels “righteous rage” about the plans to keep the plant that she said has made her and her neighbors sick open longer. “We approached the solution in a peaceful way, but we need to express that we are very angry with these decisions,” Schuba said. “The people sitting in the building behind me make those decisions every day for all of us, for our children, for future generations, and we need to hold them accountable.” Ameren Missouri executive Ajay Arora told St. Louis Public Radio in September that keeping Labadie operating longer would save customers money. “Labadie remains one of the most affordable plants in the country and recognizing the economic conditions for all our customers and how important reliability and affordability is, that's really factored into delaying the retirement of a few of the Labadie units by a few years,” Arora said. On Saturday, the protesters said electricity is not affordable in the St. Louis region and condemned Ameren’s practice of disconnecting customers who are behind on their bills. “They say they care about affordability and that they're here to serve us. Is that true?” Sarah Watkins, an organizer with Tenants Transforming St. Louis, asked the crowd. “If Ameren cares so much about us, then why are tens of thousands of families losing their electricity every year?” Bills could rise again soon as Ameren is asking Missouri regulators to approve a rate increase for customers. Both the proposed rate increase and the new integrated resource plan are subject to approval by Missouri’s Public Service Commission.

artigo.texto: As the global transition toward renewable energy accelerates, the race to capture market share in storage and delivery is intensifying. Deciding between Eos Energy Enterprises (EOSE -5.16%) and Plug Power (PLUG -3.57%) is a choice between two distinct technologies. EOSE & PLUG: Performance Comparison Key Financial Metrics Eos Energy Enterprises specializes in zinc-based long-duration battery systems designed for utility and industrial applications. Plug Power focuses on building an end-to-end green hydrogen ecosystem, from fuel production to powering heavy machinery. Both companies are scaling rapidly but face different financial hurdles as they attempt to reach long-term profitability in the clean energy market. The case for Eos Energy Enterprises Eos Energy Enterprises designs zinc-based battery systems and is carving out a niche within industrial stocks. In its latest annual report, the company noted that two customers accounted for nearly 52% and 19% of revenue. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business, though it highlights the scale of its current utility-level partnerships. In FY 2025, revenue reached about $114.2 million, representing a roughly 632% increase over the previous year. The company reported a net loss of approximately $970 million for the period. This performance follows a net loss of nearly $686 million in fiscal 2024 as the company continues to invest heavily in its manufacturing capabilities. As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately negative 1.0x, indicating total liabilities exceed shareholder equity. The current ratio, which measures the ability to pay short-term obligations with short-term assets, is nearly 4.9x. Free cash flow, which is cash from operations minus capital expenditures, was roughly negative $265.0 million in FY 2025. The case for Plug Power Plug Power builds an integrated green hydrogen ecosystem, deploying over 74,000 fuel cell systems globally. In its latest annual report, the company disclosed that Walmart Inc. (WMT +1.55%) was its largest customer, representing approximately a quarter of revenue. Such high customer concentration adds a layer of risk to the enterprise as it navigates the high costs of hydrogen infrastructure. In FY 2025, revenue reached about $709.9 million, which is a roughly 13% increase from the prior year. The company recorded a net loss of approximately $1.6 billion for the same period. This trend follows a net loss of roughly $2.1 billion in fiscal 2024, showing a slight narrowing of losses even as the top line remains volatile. As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 1.0x, meaning total debt is roughly equal to shareholder equity. The current ratio is close to 2.3x. Free cash flow was approximately negative $662 million during FY 2025, reflecting the massive capital intensity required to build and operate hydrogen production facilities. Risk profile comparison Eos Energy Enterprises faces significant legal challenges from securities fraud class action lawsuits filed in 2026. These suits allege the company made misleading disclosures about its production ramp-up and quality issues at its Turtle Creek facility. The business also contends with competition from larger energy storage providers like Fluence Energy (FLNC -4.84%) and remains sensitive to changes in government subsidies. Plug Power is currently defending against multiple federal securities fraud lawsuits regarding its financial performance and Department of Energy loan status. The company suspended activities related to that loan program in November 2025, creating uncertainty about its path to low-cost capital. It also faces intense competition from established giants like GE Vernova (GEV -0.79%) while managing a complex supply chain for materials like iridium. Valuation comparison Eos Energy Enterprises is cheaper based on Forward P/E and earnings estimates, whereas Plug Power has a lower P/S ratio using sales over the past twelve months. Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers. Which stock would I buy in 2026? The current fiscal year, 2026, looks to be a major step forward for Eos Energy Enterprises. The business has already sold more products through the first half of the year than it did in all of 2025, shipping $126 million of gear to clients. The longer term should be much greater, too. Management says it has nearly $25 billion of business pipeline, meaning proposed energy storage developments Eos could bid on, and an $807 million backlog, which are firm orders for the company's products. 2026 revenue is expected to more than double. Recently, Eos scored a high-profile deal to support the PJM grid after joining with Alphabet Inc (GOOG +0.32%) and MN8 Energy on a solar energy storage project in West Virginia. Similarly, Plug Power's fuel cells run on clean-burning hydrogen, though creating hydrogen is often done in a process fueled by natural gas. Still, Plug Power sits firmly in the renewable energy niche, benefiting from many countries' moves toward green (non-fossil-fuel-derived) hydrogen. It is also benefiting from the datacenter boom and from restored tax credits that make its systems more affordable to deploy. For fiscal 2026, revenue growth is pretty good, with Wall Street analyst consensus predicting a nearly 15% increase to $812 million. The net loss is seen narrowing to about $580 million. Both businesses offer investors a way to play the rise in demand for power storage brought about by AI data center demand and the need for storage for renewable energy production. Eos, with its lower forward P/E and similar P/S ratio, seems to be the better bet for long-term investors.

artigo.texto: Why Choose TOPCon 3.0 Solar Modules? Vertex N G3 is built on Trinasolar's TOPCon 3.0 cell technology and incorporates four core technological upgrades. Ultra cell platform technology increases power output and bifacial performance. Multi-cut technology and edge passivation technology reduce current losses and improve shading and hot-spot performance. Ultra-high density packaging technology improves module efficiency and energy yield. A bifaciality of 85% ± 5% supports additional rear-side generation where site conditions allow, while the −0.26%/°C power temperature coefficient helps limit power losses in Vietnam's hot climate. A maximum annual degradation of 0.35% from the second year onward, backed by a 30-year power warranty, provides developers with a defined basis for modelling long-term output and project revenue. Solar and Battery Storage Applications in Vietnam Trina Storage also presented Elementa 3, its 6.25MWh utility-scale BESS built on in-house 587Ah cells. Elementa 3 supports renewable energy integration and flexible power supply, including in grid-connected projects, as Vietnam expands solar generation to meet growing demand from industry and AIDCs. Trinasolar's solar-plus-storage project at Corona Resort in Phú Quốc provides a local proof point of its PV and BESS delivery capabilities. The project combines a 3MWp solar installation with a 10MWh AC-coupled BESS retrofit, demonstrating how battery storage can be added to an existing commercial solar system. Vertex N G3 and Elementa 3 extend Trina's portfolio with higher module output and greater storage capacity per container, giving developers and EPC contractors greater flexibility in meeting project capacity and site requirements.

artigo.texto: O Nordeste estará no centro do debate energético nacional pelos próximos 10 anos e pode atrair quase 30% dos novos investimentos em data centers de grande porte, além de ampliar a produção eólica, fotovoltaica e de gás natural. As perspectivas constam no Plano Decenal de Expansão de Energia (PDE 2036), elaborado pela Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE), sob diretrizes do Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME). Divulgado no último dia 8 para consulta pública, o PDE atribui a atratividade do Nordeste aos data centers à presença de pontos de chegada de cabos internacionais de fibra óptica, à elevada disponibilidade de geração renovável e ao potencial de desenvolvimento econômico regional. Apesar dessas vantagens, o subsistema Sudeste/Centro-Oeste deverá receber a maior parcela dos novos investimentos em grandes data centers, estimada em mais de 65%, enquanto o Sul ficará com os 5% restantes. >> Faça parte do canal do Movimento Econômico no WhatsApp No cenário nacional, os centros de dados ganham importância com a digitalização da economia, a expansão dos serviços de armazenamento e processamento de informações e a disseminação da inteligência artificial. O PDE projeta que o consumo de eletricidade dos data centers no Brasil alcance aproximadamente 30 terawatts-hora (TWh) em 2036. Pelo porte dos novos empreendimentos, a tendência apontada é de busca por conexão direta à rede básica de transmissão. Demanda elétrica do Nordeste cresce acima da média nacional A expansão das atividades de comércio e serviços deverá impulsionar o crescimento da carga elétrica no subsistema Nordeste. O PDE estima avanço médio de 3,7% ao ano entre 2026 e 2036, a maior taxa entre os subsistemas e superior aos 3,3% previstos para o Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN). Segundo o relatório, a carga global nordestina deverá passar de 14.209 megawatts médios (MW médios) em 2026 para 20.462 MW médios em 2036. Esse indicador reúne o consumo final de eletricidade e as perdas verificadas entre a geração e o atendimento aos consumidores. Com isso, segundo o PDE, os data centers passam a exercer influência crescente sobre o perfil de demanda da classe comercial. Nacionalmente, a participação dessa classe no consumo de eletricidade deverá aumentar de 19% para 24% no período, enquanto a residencial recuará de 32% para 28%. Além dos centros de dados, o planejamento considera novas demandas associadas à produção de hidrogênio por eletrólise, que tendem a ocorrer apenas no segundo quinquênio, devido ao prazo mais longo de maturação dos investimentos, ainda em escala reduzida no horizonte analisado. Transmissão precisa atender novos consumidores e escoar renováveis A instalação de grandes consumidores, como data centers e plantas de hidrogênio, exigirá reforços na transmissão, segundo avaliação da Empresa de Pesquisa Energética. O PDE destaca um estudo para inserção dessas cargas no Nordeste e recomenda o Bipolo Nordeste II, que ampliará a capacidade de exportação de eletricidade da região para Sudeste e Sul. O empreendimento e as obras associadas deverão permitir a conexão de novos projetos de geração, consumo e armazenamento, além de fortalecer a estabilidade da rede e reduzir cortes de geração por restrições de confiabilidade. A redução mais ampla desses cortes, conhecidos como curtailment, também dependerá de armazenamento, resposta da demanda e maior flexibilidade das usinas. Nas simulações do plano, os cortes permanecem em patamar absoluto semelhante ao de 2026 ao longo do horizonte analisado. Trata-se de uma projeção sistêmica, sem previsão específica para regiões ou empreendimentos. Já sobre novos parques eólicos, solares e linhas de transmissão no Nordeste, o estudo indica que será necessário maior atenção aos impactos cumulativos sobre vegetação, fauna, paisagem e acesso das comunidades aos recursos naturais. O relatório também aponta riscos de conflitos pelo uso da água nas termelétricas e de pressão sobre comunidades, infraestrutura e ambientes marinhos nas atividades de petróleo e gás. Projetos de gás somam R$ 7,5 bilhões em infraestrutura As bacias de Sergipe-Alagoas, Parnaíba e Potiguar estão entre as principais contribuições à expansão da produção bruta nacional de gás natural, com uma projeção de atingir 308 milhões de metros cúbicos por dia em 2036. A produção líquida, descontados reinjeção, perdas, queimas e consumo próprio, deverá chegar a 135 milhões de metros cúbicos por dia, com destaque para o Sergipe Águas Profundas (SEAP) e os campos da Bacia do Parnaíba, no Maranhão. No Nordeste, três projetos de infraestrutura reúnem estimativas de aproximadamente R$ 7,5 bilhões. A maior parcela corresponde ao escoamento do SEAP, com R$ 6,8 bilhões, capacidade de 18 milhões de metros cúbicos por dia e operação prevista a partir de 2030. O projeto prevê processamento no ambiente marítimo e injeção direta na malha de transporte, por um gasoduto de 134 quilômetros. Na Bahia, a UPGN Miranga, da PetroReconcavo, tem investimento estimado em R$ 360 milhões e entrada prevista para 2028. A capacidade de processamento será de 950 mil metros cúbicos por dia, expansível a 1,5 milhão. Em Pernambuco, o terminal de regaseificação de GNL de Suape aparece com R$ 350 milhões, capacidade de 14 milhões de metros cúbicos por dia e operação considerada para 2027. Segundo o PDE, a ampliação da oferta de gás pode fortalecer o abastecimento industrial e a flexibilidade do sistema elétrico. Esses benefícios dependem da competitividade do combustível, da execução dos investimentos e das condições regulatórias. artigo.texto: Amwins Global Risks (AGR) is expanding its specialist commercial and industrial (C&I) insurance facility to cover battery energy storage systems (BESS) and electric vehicle charging infrastructure. The facility groups distributed assets under a single program, with deductibles scaled to individual site characteristics rather than to utility-scale norms. The structure is designed for portfolios that sit between the two ends of the existing insurance market: too small for utility-scale terms, too numerous to place site by site. Amwins has offered BESS cover through NARDAC, its specialist energy MGA, since March 2024, with capacity of up to $50 million per location backed by eight Lloyd’s syndicates. The C&I facility does not introduce new BESS cover so much as a new structure for it: a portfolio approach that groups multiple distributed sites under a single programme, with deductibles calibrated to individual asset scale rather than applied uniformly across the portfolio. The BESS insurance market has been expanding, but unevenly. A number of insurers have restricted or withdrawn capacity following battery fires in the UK and overseas, a trend documented by market participants including Allianz UK, which expanded its own BESS underwriting capability in July 2026 partly in response to gaps left by capacity withdrawals. That means brokers face a market where appetite and expertise are not evenly distributed. Allianz UK expanded its own BESS underwriting capability in July 2026, with its head of construction, engineering and energy insurance noting that early engagement with experienced underwriters is increasingly valuable given how quickly the risk landscape is developing. For C&I assets specifically, the challenge is structural as much as technical. Individual sites can be relatively small in value, but developers are assembling portfolios of dozens of them across multiple locations. Applying terms designed for a large utility-scale installation to a single C&I site can produce deductibles that are disproportionate to the asset’s value, making the insurance economically unworkable. The Amwins facility is designed to resolve that by underwriting at portfolio level while still assessing accumulated natural catastrophe exposure across individual locations. “Individual sites can be relatively small, but developers are increasingly building portfolios comprising numerous assets across multiple locations," said Tom Harries, director at Amwins Global Risks and partner at NARDAC. "Bringing those assets together allows us to underwrite them efficiently at portfolio scale, while still recognising the individual risk characteristics of each site.” The facility covers both construction and operational phases, including delay in start-up and business interruption cover. The EV charging component is primarily directed at the US market, where commercial charging infrastructure is being deployed at scale. Amwins Global Risks operates from London and places through the London market, giving US-based developers and their brokers access to London capacity for risks that the domestic US market has been slower to accommodate in structured form. Harries said the addition of BESS and EV charging reflects the increasing convergence of distributed energy technologies, and that the facility is designed to adapt as portfolios grow. “It allows us to focus on monitoring how the portfolio’s natural catastrophe exposure changes as new projects are added and gives developers the freedom to concentrate on building out their portfolios, knowing their insurance program can adapt and grow alongside them.” The C&I expansion follows AGR’s renewal and enlargement of a separate natural catastrophe facility for renewable energy projects in July 2026, which increased available capacity to $50 million per placement from $20 million and broadened cover to all major natural catastrophe perils globally. The two moves extend AGR’s distributed and renewable energy proposition across construction, operation and catastrophe layers within a matter of months.

artigo.texto: Ohio candidates for U.S. Senate As the country prepares to vote in this year's pivotal midterm election, the balance of power in Washington, D.C. is at stake, and once again Ohio finds itself in a decisive position. The results of our U.S. Senate race could tip the scales resulting in continuing Republican control, Democrats taking back power in Congress, or split control in the two chambers. On the table in Ohio is the remaining two years left on Vice President JD Vance's Senate term, left vacant when he became second in command following President Donald Trump winning the presidency in 2024. Governor Mike DeWine appointed then-Lieutenant Governor Jon Husted to temporarily take over that spot, and this year, Husted is running on the Republican ticket, hoping to retain the seat. On the Democratic side, Sherrod Brown is hoping to rejoin his former colleagues in the Senate, after losing his re-election bid to current Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno in 2024. Libertarian candidate Bill Redpath and Independent candidate Gregory Levy have also joined the contest. On Tuesday's edition of the "Sound of Ideas" hosted by Stephanie Haney, we'll share one-on-one pre-recorded conversations with Redpath and Levy. We previously shared Stephanie's one-on-one conversation with Brown in an episode of the "Sound of Ideas" that aired on Sept. 28. While we had an interview scheduled with Husted, his spokesperson told us he needed to reschedule due to Senate business, and never responded to our repeated requests to reschedule. The questions we've asked these candidates came from our own independent research, as well as conversations we had this summer with voters at libraries across Northeast Ohio as part of our Listen, Engage, Vote initiative. We also asked for input from our audience members on social media. Researchers are looking for ways to get people the help they need more quickly by using technology as an intervention tool, which can also be tailored to the individual. artigo.texto: Sungrow, a global supplier of photovoltaic (PV) inverters and energy storage systems, has announced the successful commissioning and commencement of commercial operations of a 10 MW/40 MWh Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) developed by WKV Hydro Technics (Pvt) Ltd in Galle, Sri Lanka. The project began commercial operations on September 10, 2026, and uses Sungrow’s PowerTitan 2.0 energy storage solution to improve grid stability, support peak demand management, and facilitate renewable energy integration. The project was developed by WKV Group, a subsidiary of Khen Energy Limited, and represents a significant addition to Sri Lanka’s growing energy storage infrastructure. The facility is designed to provide fast-response energy storage capacity, enabling the electricity grid to manage fluctuations in renewable energy generation and electricity demand more effectively. Sri Lanka is working toward achieving 70% of its electricity generation from renewable energy sources by 2030, with solar and wind power expected to play major roles in the country’s energy transition. As renewable energy capacity expands, the need for flexible grid-support technologies has become increasingly important. The country’s electricity demand typically peaks around 7 p.m., creating additional requirements for energy storage systems capable of supplying electricity during high-demand periods. The newly commissioned BESS is expected to strengthen grid flexibility by providing peak-shaving and frequency-regulation capabilities. The system can store electricity during periods of available supply and discharge it when required, helping improve electricity supply reliability and support the integration of variable renewable energy sources. The facility incorporates Sungrow’s PowerTitan 2.0 technology, which combines battery storage and power conversion systems (PCS) within an integrated AC-DC block. The solution features intelligent battery management and station-level control systems that continuously monitor battery performance and optimize operations to support long-term reliability. According to Sungrow, the system’s pre-assembled design simplifies installation and commissioning processes, contributing to a 50% reduction in grid-connection time. The technology is also designed to operate in challenging environmental conditions, an important consideration for the Galle project, which is located approximately 500 meters from the coastline. The coastal location exposes the facility to high temperatures, humidity, and corrosive conditions. Sungrow stated that PowerTitan 2.0 is engineered to withstand such environments and is designed for an operational lifespan of at least 15 years. The project also demonstrated an accelerated commissioning schedule through coordination between Sungrow and WKV Group. Thermal commissioning and pre-Site Acceptance Testing (pre-SAT) activities were completed within one week, followed by formal Site Acceptance Testing (SAT) and the commencement of commercial operations within five days. The accelerated delivery was supported by advance technical preparations, including system parameter configuration, auxiliary power arrangements, liquid-cooling inspections, and grid-connection planning. Sungrow’s technical and project delivery teams also provided on-site assistance throughout testing and commissioning. Commenting on the development, Sudath Pathmal, Chief Operating Officer of WKV Group, described the project as a technological milestone and a national achievement. He highlighted the importance of collaboration and innovation in strengthening Sri Lanka’s energy infrastructure and advancing its sustainability objectives. The commissioning of the 10 MW/40 MWh BESS highlights the growing role of utility-scale battery storage in supporting Sri Lanka’s renewable energy transition. With four hours of storage capacity at its rated output, the project is positioned to contribute to improved grid reliability, enhanced operational flexibility, and more effective utilization of renewable electricity. The development also strengthens Sungrow’s presence in the energy storage sector, demonstrating the application of its integrated battery technology in coastal environments and emerging renewable energy markets. artigo.texto: Michael Burry adds BYD shares after calling automaker a potential low-cost leader Michael Burry, the investor known for predicting the 2008 housing-market crash, added shares of Chinese electric-vehicle maker BYD Company BYDDY BYDDF in a portfolio reshuffle disclosed in early October. The purchase was reported in an October 6 portfolio update on Burry’s Substack. The update also included changes to his positions in JD.com JD and several other stocks. The number of BYD BYDDF shares purchased and the size of the position were not disclosed. Burry’s earlier analysis outlined the investment case for BYD BYDDF, highlighting its valuation, manufacturing scale and technology. He wrote, “I would be an aggressive buyer at HK$75 or better, if the thesis still holds at that time.” He also highlighted BYD’s BYDDF cost advantages from controlling more of its supply chain. “BYD is potentially the lowest-cost producer of vehicles in the world thanks to its vertically integrated model at scale,” he wrote. Battery technology is another part of the investment thesis. BYD’s in-house Blade battery uses lithium iron phosphate chemistry. Burry’s analysis highlighted the chemistry’s cost and safety advantages over nickel-manganese-cobalt batteries, while acknowledging its lower energy density. He also pointed to international expansion as a potential source of operating leverage. “I believe BYD is an exceptionally well-run and technologically advanced company today, and I believe long-term ROIC will settle above 10%,” Burry wrote. In his March analysis, Burry also compared BYD BYDDF with Tesla TSLA, noting that BYD generated more revenue despite having a much smaller market capitalization. The comparison underscored his view that investors valued the two businesses differently. Burry had indicated in September that he was monitoring BYD BYDDF. Asked about the stock, he said, “Yes, I am watching it,” after previously disclosing that he did not own shares. artigo.texto: The Custer County Board of Supervisors met for less than an hour on Tuesday morning inside the Custer County Courthouse. Following a public hearing late last month which saw no members of the public coming forward, the Board of Supervisors voted unanimously today to adopt the data center regulations recommended to them by the planning commission. Ahead of last week’s public hearing, Zoning Administrator Darci Tibbs explained the process that led to the regulations being drafted. “The purpose of these regulations is to not encourage or attract data centers, but to make sure that if one is proposed in Custer County, we have appropriate standards and safeguards in place to protect the health, safety, and welfare of our citizens, and to protect the ag and rural character of the county,” said Tibbs.” View the full data center regulation document here: Custer County Data Center Regulations The board also voted unanimously to put a 12 month moratorium in place regarding battery energy storage systems. This time period was stated to be so that more time could be given to researching them and to work toward regulations, much like the months long process ahead of the adoption of data center regulations. In board of equalization matters, tax corrections for the years 2023 through 2025 were made to change a stick built home to a mobile home resulting in over $2,000 back to the property owner. A motor vehicle exemption for Custer Care was also approved, at a loss to the county of $16 and change. Levy allocation requests for the upcoming fiscal year were approved unanimously for all subdivisions. View the levy allocations here: 2026-2027 Levies Custer County Sub-divisions County Assessor Elise Taylor came before the board regarding her department’s copier machine, stating that it is starting to show signs of failing. The current copier has been in use since around 2017 or 2018 and is owned, however repairs had become more frequent with parts being harder to find. Taylor said options of a $143 per month lease or purchase over $7,000 were available. Following a discussion about what budget the copier would have to come from and the fact that budgets were just passed and the copiers health was not a concern presented, discussions about its replacement fizzled out. A contract between Central Plains Valuations and the county’s assessor’s office was approved, capped at $8,000. The contract was stated to be the same as it had been since 2021. Supervisor Anne Gibbons was the lone vote of no. With no applications to cross right-of-way received, the meeting was adjourned at 9:52 AM.

artigo.texto: GLENDALE, AZ — The Phoenix area is experiencing a data center construction boom, transforming vacant lots and former farmland to meet digital demand in Arizona and beyond. Data centers keep the digital world running around the clock — streaming TV, cloud storage, banking, and artificial intelligence - but these facilities also require substantial power and water, which impact surrounding communities. DataCenterMap.com tracks locations worldwide and ranks Arizona eighth in the U.S. with 160 existing and proposed facilities statewide. Why is Arizona such a draw? "Land is inexpensive in Arizona; they require a lot of land to build," said Vijay Vittal, a professor at ASU's School of Electrical, Computer and Energy Engineering. Vittal said Arizona has also offered tax incentives and a geographic advantage "very close to the western tech markets" like California's Silicon Valley. Matt Bullock, Peoria's Mayor Pro Tem and owner of a data protection and cybersecurity company that works with data centers, echoed that assessment. "Arizona has one of the lowest seismic activity areas, unlike California or other parts of the country," Bullock said. "And because we have such wide open areas, it's very easy to get power and water infrastructure to data center locations." Data centers' demand for power and water — and the impact on nearby communities — is drawing pushback from some Arizona residents. April Butler lives near a proposed data center in Glendale called Project Eagle, also known as Project Baccara, located on Olive Avenue just east of the Loop 303. She says the project is massive. "The biggest part will be three data centers, and they're just back to back to back," Butler said. Butler and her neighbors spoke out at a Glendale City meeting in September. "I don't think we have a lot of laws in place to protect us," Butler said. "There are other states that were quicker enacting moratoriums and putting rules and guidelines in place to where it's a little bit more difficult to get those projects in." ABC15 is committed to finding the answers you need and holding those accountable. Submit your news tip to Investigators@abc15.com Peoria is also facing pushback over a large data center preparing to build there. Bullock said councilmembers are considering changes to zoning rules that would require special use permits for future data center projects or greater oversight. "To ensure they're using the reclaimed water, closed-loop [cooling systems], bring their own power, building parks and roads and things, and helping local schools," Bullock said. "That's how it should have been done all along, and now we're just catching up." As for Butler, she is standing her ground against Project Eagle. "Do you have any hope you can stop this from coming?" I asked her. "Absolutely," Butler said. A final vote on the formal land annexation and rezoning applications is expected at the Glendale City Council Meeting scheduled for October 27.

artigo.texto: Sodium-Ion Batteries and Storage Flexibility: Why Batteries are not a Bottleneck for a Fully Renewable Energy System Battery technology is frequently framed around a material bottleneck, but a recent study from LUT University researchers suggests that concern may be overstated. According to pv magazine, the analysis examines sodium-ion batteries as a promising alternative to lithium-ion batteries and finds that raw material availability need not constrain the scale of storage required for a fully renewable energy system. The study notes that sodium-ion batteries rely on abundant raw materials beyond the cathode, with hard carbon replacing natural graphite in anodes and aluminum substituting for copper as the anode current collector. Previous energy system simulations pointed to stationary battery demand approaching 75 TWh of capacity by 2050, while mobile batteries were estimated to dominate at up to almost 275 TWh of capacity by mid-century. A ratio of roughly 0.8 kWh of capacity per kW of installed solar PV capacity was identified for a cost-optimized, flexible global energy system run entirely on renewable energy. Including electronics and other applications, total battery demand could exceed 350 TWh of capacity by 2050. A bottom-up assessment spanning cell-level to system-level costs found sodium-ion batteries already close to cost parity with lithium counterparts. System-level costs were estimated at about EUR120 per kWh of capacity in 2025, and applying different learning rates could bring costs down to a range of EUR28.5 to EUR51.9 per kWh of capacity by 2050. The authors conclude that batteries are ruled out as a bottleneck on both raw material and cost grounds. They also note that sodium-ion batteries can serve as a drop-in technology produced on existing lithium-ion production lines. For solar PV prosumers who both produce and consume electricity, batteries are not strictly necessary for a secure supply. A grid connection allows surplus rooftop generation to be fed into the grid and reimbursed, with electricity drawn back during periods of low or no solar yield. Rising grid electricity prices and falling battery costs may nonetheless make adding a battery economically beneficial for optimizing overall energy supply costs. An initial cost-optimization study found that PV-battery systems are widely beneficial for prosumers in terms of total energy supply cost, with electrification of heat via heating rods or heat pumps identified as key. Residential rooftop PV yields about 18% less electricity than ground-mounted systems, yet very low-cost solar PV is not a limitation. Combining with stationary battery storage enables high demand and heat cover ratios globally, and battery capacity optimization depends on whether electric vehicles are included. High benefits were found for cars capable of supplying electricity to the system through vehicle-to-home arrangements. A follow-up study examined whether seasonal hydrogen storage benefits residential PV prosumer systems. Long-term storage was found to play only a niche role for Nordic countries in an off-grid scenario, even with significant cost reduction potential. The updated optimization model showed most regions reaching grid parity by 2035, with more than half having already reached parity in 2020. Batteries were confirmed to play an important role. For on-grid cases, a maximum battery-to-PV ratio of 1.6 to 1.8 kWh of capacity per kW was found, rising to 3 to 4 kWh of capacity per kW in off-grid cases. The electric vehicle fleet is growing quickly worldwide, already accumulating battery capacity on the terawatt-hour scale and driving solar PV capacity demand. Using this capacity for power system balancing is seen as a promising solution for systems with a growing share of variable renewable generation. Smart charging alone provides flexibility by raising electricity consumption during renewable generation peaks and reducing it during deficits. Vehicle-to-grid goes further, turning electric vehicles into distributed battery storage on wheels that can supply electricity to the grid during deficit periods. A study analyzing smart charging and vehicle-to-grid confirmed substantial system benefits. These technologies allow installed utility-scale battery storage capacity to be reduced by about 50%, indirectly lowering critical material use in batteries and reducing the need for other energy storage technologies. Enabling them alone may cut total annual system costs by about 4%. Vehicle-to-grid cannot be free for the system, however. Electric vehicle owners must be incentivized to participate and compensated for battery wear. The role and impact of vehicle-to-grid will depend strongly on the cost of this service, but even at EUR50 to EUR100 per MWh it still provides system benefits. The main challenge is the public infrastructure needed for electric vehicles to charge or feed high-quality AC power into the grid whenever parked, especially during the midday PV generation peak when additional storage capacity is most valuable. Flexibility is needed to mitigate the variability of renewable energy sources arising from their weather-dependent nature. Battery energy storage systems have gained widespread attention as a potential leading technology for this role, with advantages including high energy density, rapid response, reliable power delivery, sustained discharge capability, and geographical independence. Continued reductions in battery manufacturing costs have strengthened the role of battery storage in facilitating renewable energy integration, particularly for solar PV. artigo.texto: INDEPENDENCE, Mo. — KSHB 41 reporter Tod Palmer covers sports business and eastern Jackson County, including Independence. Share your story idea with Tod. — Independence approved new zoning requirements for data centers and battery energy storage systems within city limits. After several months of conversation and public hearings, the Independence City Council unanimously approved the changes Oct. 5 to its Unified Development Ordinance, or UDO, related to such projects. Independence initiated a moratorium on new data center projects, which passed in July, over the summer after Nebius broke ground in May 2026 on a hyperscale AI data factory in the Little Blue Valley and Patmos moved to build a data center farther south along Little Blue Parkway. The council approved the Nebius project in March despite strong organized opposition, which ultimately led to residents voting out several council members who supported the project. Council member Brice Stewart and Mayor Kevin King introduced a series of amendments, all of which were also adopted unanimously. One requires any new data center or BESS developments to be at least 1,000 feet from residences or other public spaces — schools, parks, recreation and playground facilities, daycares, nursing homes, hospitals or places of worship. It would allow for variances, if recommended by the city planning commission and approved by the city council. Other amendments were related to noise-impact assessments and mitigation plans, decommissioning data centers that cease operations for 12 months, and requiring generator compliance reports every six months rather than annually. The new regulations require any data center larger than 2.5 megawatts to seek a special use permit from the city. Independence, like many city and county governments, didn’t have specific zoning requirements in place for data centers and BESS projects, which “present unique land use considerations not commonly associated with traditional industrial development,” according to the Agenda Item Cover Letter. Those complicated issues include massive electrical demand, high water consumption, on-site backup power generation, consistent mechanical noise and other issues. “The City's current UDO does not contain use-specific regulations for data processing and hosting facilities,” according to the cover letter. “As interest in this development type continues to increase, staff believes additional standards are appropriate to provide clear expectations for future development while protecting surrounding properties and community resources.” —

artigo.texto: BYD Chases Global Crown Without America as Battery and Storage Bets Deepen Published on 10/12/2026 at 13:40 | Editorial boerse-global.de BYD has set its sights on becoming the world's largest automaker within five years, and it intends to get there without selling a single passenger car in the United States. The Chinese group is betting on purely organic growth, steering clear of the American market for now because regulatory hurdles facing connected vehicle software of Chinese origin make entry difficult. That global ambition is only partly reflected in the share price. The stock slipped 1.9% in the latest session to EUR 8.48, extending its year-to-date decline to 21%. A day earlier, the picture had looked brighter: BYD shares closed at EUR 8.65 on Friday, up 4.2%, lifted not only by company-specific news but by a broad recovery across Chinese automakers. According to media reports, the sector's rebound was a technical countermovement after several sessions of declines, with concerns about demand in the seasonal peak quarter and trade tensions between China and the European Union already partly priced in. Closing the Gap on Toyota and Volkswagen To narrow the distance to the industry leaders, BYD is pressing ahead with production capacity outside China. Toyota sold roughly 11.32 million vehicles worldwide in full-year 2025, Volkswagen around 8.98 million, while BYD delivered about 4.60 million. In the first half of 2026, Toyota notched 5.39 million sales, against 1.81 million for BYD in the same period. Management sees local supply chains as the key to closing that gap. Beyond plants already producing in Thailand and Uzbekistan, factories in Brazil and Indonesia are under construction. In Europe, the ramp-up at the Hungarian site is imminent, with series production slated to begin in the fourth quarter of 2026 once testing is complete. At the Paris Motor Show, Stella Li also held out the prospect of examining further European production locations in the medium term, with France among the candidates on the shortlist. Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying BYD? Public Fleets, Trucks and a Masdar Storage Deal Alongside its consumer passenger car business, BYD is broadening its international footprint in the public sector and adjacent technology fields. Overseas sales of passenger cars and pickups climbed 67.9% to almost 790,000 units in the first half of 2026. The company now supplies police forces and government fleets in several countries, including Mexico, Pakistan, the Philippines, Austria and Hungary. The commercial vehicle segment is expanding too. At its Huai'an plant, the 150,000th commercial vehicle in company history rolled off the line on October 9 — an all-electric Q3 tractor unit, underscoring the push into heavy long-haul transport. Outside vehicle manufacturing, BYD secured a battery storage agreement for 11.275 gigawatt-hours with energy company Masdar in the United Arab Emirates during the third quarter of 2026. Blade Battery Capacity Takes Precedence Operationally, BYD reports sustained strong demand for its models equipped with fast-charging capability. To safeguard delivery capacity over the long term, the company is giving top priority to expanding production capacity for the second generation of its in-house Blade battery. At the same time, the manufacturer is widening its model range at home. Pre-orders for the second generation of the Seagull have reportedly opened, with the official market launch planned for the fourth quarter. No official pricing has been disclosed so far. Geopolitics Keep Washington Off the Map On the international stage, management is pursuing a selective expansion strategy. Executive Vice President Stella Li, cited by Reuters, described geopolitical tensions as the single biggest challenge for the company's overseas business. For that reason, BYD will not bring passenger cars to the United States for the time being. Exports to other regions remain unaffected. In September 2026, the group sold 463,561 vehicles in total, a gain of 17.0% versus the same month a year earlier. Passenger car and pickup exports accounted for 180,700 units, up 153.9% from the prior-year figure. Ad BYD Stock: New Analysis - 12 October Fresh BYD information released. artigo.texto: UND in the Conversation: Data centers make heat all year long – here’s how the ground can hold onto it until winter Moones Alamooti, Assistant Professor of Energy and Petroleum Engineering at the University of North Dakota, explains in The Conversation how data centers generate waste heat year-round, and by storing that heat underground during warmer months, communities could reuse it in winter for heating buildings, reducing energy waste and reliance on fossil fuels. Editor’s note: The following article is written by Moones Alamooti and is an excerpt of the original article published by The Conversation. You can read the full article in its original format on their website. You have probably noticed it on a hot summer day: A basement feels cool even when the air outside is baking. The ground does not heat up and cool down as fast as the air does. A few hundred feet down, it stays close to the local yearly average all year, which can be around 50 degrees Fahrenheit (10 Celsius). In Verona, Wisconsin, the health software company Epic Systems has spent two decades turning that fact into infrastructure. It has drilled roughly 6,100 wells, 300 to 800 feet (90 to 240 meters) deep, that now heat and cool about 40 buildings on its own campus by using the waste heat from a 3.5-megawatt data center. What makes this setup unusual is not that Epic pulls heat out of the ground in winter – ordinary ground-source heat pumps do that in homes across the country. What’s uncommon is that Epic puts heat into the ground in summer and takes it back out months later. That matters more than it sounds because timing is what usually kills the idea of reusing a data center’s heat. Servers make heat every hour of the year. In most of the U.S., buildings need to be heated for only about four months. Piping it straight to nearby buildings works beautifully in February, but solves nothing in July. Storage is the missing piece.

artigo.texto: Mercado global de concentrados de eletrólito de ácido fosfórico: Tamanho, Tendências e Previsão até 2035 - Relatório completo em PDF · pacote de dados Excel · documento Word · apresentação executiva - Entrega por e-mail 24/7, inclusive fins de semana e feriados - Copiar e colar habilitado · formato pronto para impressão - Rodadas ilimitadas de esclarecimentos após a entrega Previsão do Mercado de Concentrados de Eletrólito de Ácido Fosfórico até 2035: Demanda por Energia de Backup em Data Centers Impulsiona o Crescimento Resumo De acordo com o mais recente relatório da IndexBox sobre o mercado global de concentrados de eletrólito de ácido fosfórico, o mercado entra em 2026 com fundamentos de demanda mais amplos, comportamento de compra mais disciplinado e uma arquitetura de oferta mais diversificada regionalmente. O mercado global de concentrados de eletrólito de ácido fosfórico entra em uma fase de expansão sustentada, com a demanda projetada para crescer a uma taxa anual composta de 6% a 9% entre 2026 e 2035. Essas formulações especializadas atuam como meio condutor em células a combustível de ácido fosfórico (PAFC), eletrolisadores e outros sistemas eletroquímicos, e seu desempenho é decisivo para a eficiência e a longevidade das unidades instaladas. O vetor de demanda mais poderoso é a implantação acelerada de sistemas PAFC para energia estacionária e backup em data centers e infraestrutura de telecomunicações, onde as exigências de confiabilidade são rigorosas e os ciclos de reposição geram demanda recorrente por concentrados. Os concentrados de alta pureza, que respondem por cerca de 70% a 80% do valor de mercado, alcançam um prêmio de preço de 25% a 40% sobre os graus industriais padrão, graças a limites de impurezas iônicas inferiores a 10 ppm. A oferta permanece concentrada em menos de uma dúzia de fabricantes especializados, com mais de 55% a 65% da capacidade produtiva localizada na América do Norte e na Europa Ocidental. A Ásia-Pacífico, excluindo Japão e Coreia do Sul, continua dependente de importações, embora a capacidade local de mistura e purificação esteja crescendo rapidamente. Ciclos de qualificação de 12 a 18 meses e padrões regulatórios divergentes aumentam a complexidade, mas o panorama geral aponta para um crescimento robusto até 2035. O cenário-base para o mercado de concentrados de eletrólito de ácido fosfórico prevê expansão constante entre 2026 e 2035, sustentada pelo uso consolidado e crescente de sistemas PAFC em aplicações de energia estacionária. Data centers, torres de telecomunicações, hospitais e edifícios comerciais adotam cada vez mais soluções de cogeração (CHP) e energia de backup baseadas em células a combustível para cumprir metas de descarbonização e garantir operações ininterruptas. Isso cria um duplo fluxo de demanda: os volumes de carga inicial para novas instalações e um mercado recorrente de reposição que já representa 30% a 40% das vendas de concentrados em volume. O segmento de reposição é particularmente resiliente, pois a degradação do eletrólito segue ciclos previsíveis, o que dá visibilidade aos fornecedores. Do lado da oferta, a capacidade está concentrada na América do Norte e na Europa Ocidental, mas novas unidades de mistura e purificação na China e na Coreia do Sul vêm reduzindo gradualmente a dependência de importações da Ásia-Pacífico. Espera-se que os preços se mantenham firmes para os graus de alta pureza, com as especificações premium sustentando uma vantagem de preço de 25% a 40% sobre os concentrados industriais padrão. A volatilidade das matérias-primas, ligada aos custos de rocha fosfática e energia, representa riscos de margem, mas contratos de longo prazo e barreiras de qualificação protegem os fornecedores já estabelecidos. A divergência regulatória, especialmente entre o REACH da União Europeia e as normas GB chinesas, pode retardar novos entrantes, mas não ameaça o crescimento geral do mercado. Até 2035, o índice de mercado deve alcançar 185 (2025=100), refletindo uma taxa anual composta de 6,8%. Vetores e Restrições da Demanda Principais Vetores de Demanda - Aumento da implantação de sistemas PAFC para energia de backup em data centers e telecomunicações, impulsionado pela necessidade de eletricidade confiável e de baixa emissão. - Adoção crescente da cogeração (CHP) em edifícios comerciais e hospitais, apoiada por incentivos governamentais e mandatos de descarbonização. - Demanda recorrente de reposição de concentrados de eletrólito, já que as pilhas PAFC instaladas exigem reabastecimento periódico, criando uma receita estável de pós-venda. - Expansão da infraestrutura de hidrogênio e das instalações de eletrolisadores, nas quais eletrólitos de ácido fosfórico são usados em certos processos eletroquímicos de alta temperatura. - Aumento do rigor das especificações de impurezas iônicas em membranas de células a combustível, favorecendo fornecedores de concentrados de alta pureza e elevando as barreiras de entrada. - Regionalização da fabricação de células a combustível na Ásia-Pacífico, sobretudo na China e na Coreia do Sul, impulsionando a capacidade local de mistura e purificação e reduzindo prazos de entrega. Possíveis Restrições ao Crescimento - Volatilidade dos preços do ácido fosfórico como matéria-prima, ligada aos custos globais de rocha fosfática e energia, gerando incerteza de margem e forçando renegociações de contratos. - Ciclos longos de qualificação de fornecedores, de 12 a 18 meses, que limitam o número de fontes viáveis e retardam a entrada de novos graus de concentrado no mercado. - Divergência regulatória entre os principais mercados, especialmente entre o REACH da União Europeia e as normas GB chinesas em evolução, elevando custos de conformidade e atrasando lançamentos de produtos. - Concorrência de químicas alternativas de baterias, como as de íons de lítio e as de fluxo, em algumas aplicações de energia de backup e armazenamento estacionário. - Altos requisitos de capital para manuseio em sala l

artigo.texto: Mercado global de cabos sensores de vazamento de água: Tamanho, Tendências e Previsão até 2035 - Relatório completo em PDF · pacote de dados Excel · documento Word · apresentação executiva - Entrega por e-mail 24/7, inclusive fins de semana e feriados - Copiar e colar habilitado · formato pronto para impressão - Rodadas ilimitadas de esclarecimentos após a entrega Mercado global de cabos sensores de vazamento de água: projeções até 2035 apontam expansão de data centers e automação industrial como motores do crescimento Resumo De acordo com o mais recente relatório da IndexBox sobre o mercado global de cabos sensores de vazamento de água, o mercado entra em 2026 com fundamentos de demanda mais amplos, comportamento de compra mais disciplinado e uma arquitetura de suprimento mais diversificada regionalmente. O mercado global de cabos sensores de vazamento de água está preparado para uma expansão significativa no período de previsão de 2026 a 2035, impulsionado pela demanda crescente por mitigação de riscos em ativos de alto valor e pela proliferação da infraestrutura digital. Esses cabos especializados, que detectam e localizam a entrada de água ou de líquidos condutivos, tornam-se indispensáveis em data centers, instalações industriais, edifícios comerciais e plantas de energia. O crescimento do mercado se sustenta na economia da prevenção de danos: o custo de uma paralisação ou de uma falha de equipamento provocada por vazamento supera em muito o custo dos cabos sensores, o que cria um ambiente orientado por especificação, no qual confiabilidade e integração de sistemas são fundamentais. À medida que as indústrias adotam cada vez mais tecnologias de IoT e de edificações inteligentes, os cabos sensores evoluem de alarmes autônomos para nós inteligentes dentro de sistemas de gestão mais amplos, exigindo APIs abertas e protocolos padronizados. A cadeia de suprimentos se divide entre a fabricação de controladores e circuitos integrados, de margem elevada, e a extrusão de cabos, de margem menor, o que molda a dinâmica competitiva. Regionalmente, a Ásia-Pacífico lidera a demanda devido à rápida construção de data centers, enquanto América do Norte e Europa seguem como polos de inovação. Espera-se que o mercado cresça a uma taxa composta de crescimento anual (CAGR) de 6,2% entre 2025 e 2035, alcançando um índice de mercado de 182 em 2035 (2025=100). Este relatório oferece uma análise abrangente da estrutura do mercado, de seus vetores e restrições, dos setores de uso final e das perspectivas regionais, com insights estratégicos para fabricantes, fornecedores e investidores. O cenário-base para o mercado de cabos sensores de vazamento de água prevê crescimento constante até 2035, com taxa composta de crescimento anual (CAGR) de 6,2% entre 2025 e 2035. Essa perspectiva é sustentada pela aceleração da construção de data centers e pela automação contínua dos processos industriais, que são os principais vetores de demanda. Nos data centers, a necessidade de proteger servidores e infraestrutura crítica contra danos causados por água é inegociável, e os cabos sensores são cada vez mais integrados a sistemas DCIM para monitoramento em tempo real. Em ambientes industriais, a detecção de vazamentos é vital para evitar paralisações, danos ambientais e riscos à segurança, sobretudo em plantas químicas, farmacêuticas e de processamento de alimentos. O setor de edifícios comerciais também vem adotando esses cabos para atender a códigos de obras e exigências de seguradoras. Avanços tecnológicos, como a integração de conectividade IoT e protocolos sem fio, ampliam o mercado endereçável para aplicações de retrofit e locais distribuídos. No entanto, o mercado enfrenta restrições, entre elas o custo inicial elevado, a complexidade de integração e a falta de conhecimento em algumas regiões. O cenário competitivo combina fabricantes especializados de cabos e empresas diversificadas de eletrônica, tendo a certificação e o suporte ao design-in como principais diferenciais. Até 2035, o índice de mercado deve alcançar 182 (2025=100), refletindo demanda robusta em todas as principais regiões, com a Ásia-Pacífico liderando em volume e América do Norte e Europa em valor. Vetores e restrições da demanda Principais vetores de demanda - Expansão acelerada de data centers e de infraestrutura de nuvem, que exige detecção confiável de vazamentos para proteger equipamentos de TI de alto valor. - Aumento da automação industrial e do controle de processos, contextos em que vazamentos podem causar paralisações dispendiosas e incidentes de segurança. - Códigos de obras rigorosos e exigências de seguradoras que obrigam a detecção de vazamentos em edifícios comerciais e residenciais. - Adoção crescente de IoT e de tecnologias de edificações inteligentes, que permite integrar cabos sensores a sistemas centralizados de gestão. - Maior conscientização sobre os custos dos danos causados por água e sobre os benefícios econômicos da detecção precoce em instalações de alto valor patrimonial. - Avanços tecnológicos no projeto de cabos sensores, como maior sensibilidade, durabilidade e conectividade sem fio. Possíveis restrições ao crescimento - Custos iniciais elevados de instalação e necessidade de integração especializada, o que pode desestimular a adoção em mercados sensíveis a preço. - Complexidade de adaptar cabos sensores à infraestrutura existente, especialmente em edifícios antigos e plantas industriais. - Falta de protocolos padronizados e problemas de interoperabilidade entre sistemas de diferentes fabricantes, o que dificulta a integração perfeita. - Conhecimento e compreensão limitados sobre os benefícios da detecção de vazamentos em economias emergentes, o que retarda a penetração de mercado. - Possíveis interrupções na cadeia de suprimentos e volatilidade dos preços de matérias-primas, que afetam a produção e a precificação dos cabos.
