artigo.texto: A White House executive order covering several categories of Chinese-made grid equipment could have a greater impact on battery storage supply chains than on transformers, circuit breakers or inverters, according to a new analysis by Rystad Energy. Executive Order 14421, signed by President Donald Trump on 26 August 2026, covers substation transformers, grid-connected inverters, battery energy storage systems (BESS), high-voltage circuit breakers and generation turbines. However, Rystad Energy notes that US dependence on China in several of these categories has already fallen significantly. The greatest exposure is now in batteries: China supplied 50% of the value of US lithium-ion battery imports in the 12 months to June 2026. “The supply chain problem created by the order falls most squarely on battery storage,” said Geoffrey Hebertson, Senior Analyst, Renewables and Power at Rystad Energy. According to the analyst, transformer and breaker markets had already largely shifted away from Chinese supply before the order was issued, while the battery market has yet to undergo a comparable transition. Source: Rystad Energy Grid Equipment Analysis; Rystad Energy Solar Solution; Rystad Energy Energy Storage Solution China accounts for half of US battery imports Rystad Energy’s analysis shows a significant difference across technologies. China accounted for only around 3% of US transformer imports and less than 1% of high-voltage circuit breaker imports by value in the 12 months to June 2026. In these categories, South Korea, Mexico and Canada together account for 74% of breaker imports and 48% of transformer imports. US reliance on China has also declined in the inverter market. The reported value of Chinese inverter exports to the United States fell by 34% between 2022 and 2025, as the 45X advanced manufacturing production credit supported the relocation of inverter assembly to the US. Rystad Energy expects US inverter manufacturing capacity to reach 126 GW by 2028. The picture is different for battery storage. After China, the next-largest suppliers of lithium-ion batteries are South Korea, with 15% of US imports, and Japan, with 13%, with no single alternative market currently able to match China’s scale. Data centers and AI increase exposure The executive order explicitly links the new security measures to the rapid growth of data centers and artificial intelligence, which are increasing electricity demand and the need for critical power infrastructure. The measure also covers uninterruptible power supply systems (UPS) used to support critical infrastructure, potentially extending its reach to behind-the-meter battery systems deployed at data centers to ensure power resilience. For Rystad Energy, this makes battery storage particularly important under the new policy, as large technology companies require growing volumes of storage to support the expansion of their facilities. December rulemaking will be decisive The final impact of the order will depend on rulemaking due by 24 December 2026. One of the main open questions is how the US Department of Energy will define a Covered Foreign Entity. Rystad Energy warns that a broad interpretation could also affect suppliers assembling equipment in countries such as South Korea or Mexico if they rely on Chinese-controlled components, capital or ownership structures. In that scenario, some of the supply sources currently viewed as alternatives to China could themselves fall under the restrictions. “If ownership is drawn broadly enough to follow Chinese capital into South Korean or Mexican assembly plants, the supply chain the tech industry is currently relying on to keep AI infrastructure buildout on schedule becomes part of the problem,” Hebertson said. Rystad Energy therefore considers the December rulemaking the most consequential stage in determining the true scope of the order, particularly for energy storage and the power infrastructure needed to support the expansion of data centers and artificial intelligence.

artigo.texto: Project doubles capacity of Bocanova site in one of the country's fastest-growing electricity load centers HOUSTON and OAKLAND, Calif., Oct. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Nightpeak Energy announced today the successful financial close and commercial operation of its 150 MW, two-hour duration Bocanova 2 battery storage project in Southeast Texas. The project reached commercial operation on September 17, doubling the Bocanova site's capacity to 300 MW and adding significant flexibility to the ERCOT grid as data centers and other large loads drive rapid growth in electricity demand. Bocanova 2 is the second phase of Nightpeak's battery storage development in Brazoria County, near the Houston metropolitan area. The first 150 MW phase, Bocanova 1, began commercial operation in August 2025. Bocanova 2 uses Tesla's Megapack 2 XL battery storage systems. Operating under a long-term offtake agreement with an investment-grade counterparty, the project was financed through a tax equity bridge loan and construction-to-term loan with MUFG Bank. U.S. Bank provided traditional tax equity. Paris Hays, Co-founder and CEO/CDO, Nightpeak Energy, said, "We're seeing large loads come to the grid at a pace and scale that is fundamentally changing how the power sector plans for new demand. Texas is at the forefront of that growth, and meeting it will require significant new infrastructure as well as resources that can respond quickly as conditions change. With 300 MW now operating at Bocanova, we're putting that kind of flexibility to work in one of the most dynamic power markets in the country. We're grateful to the City of Alvin, Brazoria County, and the local community for their support in bringing Bocanova to life." Since its founding in 2022, Nightpeak has developed and acquired a portfolio of over 1 GW of operating and de-risked capacity spanning gas-fired generation, battery storage and powered land development, and continues to advance an additional pipeline of flexible generation and large-load projects to meet growing demand in the U.S. About Nightpeak Energy Nightpeak Energy develops, owns and operates flexible power generation and large-load enablement assets that help meet growing electricity and AI demand while supporting a reliable, lower-carbon electric grid. Applying a technology-agnostic approach across gas-fired generation, energy storage, renewables, and large-load project types, the company combines generation and load into integrated solutions for its customers. Nightpeak is a portfolio investment of Energy Spectrum Partners VIII, LP, which is an infrastructure-focused private equity fund based in Dallas, Texas. Media Contact Ellie Malone [email protected] SOURCE Nightpeak Energy

artigo.texto: Battery Energy Storage System Plugs into the Smart Grid Enphase Energy introduced its first first commercial battery storage system. The all-in-one, grid-connected IQ Battery C80 will deliver 80 kWh of usable energy capacity and up to 40 kVA of continuous power in a single, compact enclosure, with battery packs and microinverters fully integrated. Available in capacities between 80 kWh to 2 MWh, the system is engineered for commercial, industrial, and multifamily applications where it can support demand charge management, time-of-use shifting, solar self-consumption, and other smart grid services and even participate in virtual power plants (VPPs). All models use active air cooling without the need for liquid cooling or external HVAC, helping simplify installation and improve reliability. Its modular architecture will allow customers to right-size projects and expand storage capacity over time, helping customers manage energy costs and maximize the value of onsite solar generation. The IQ Battery C80 will be available in two three-phase configurations: a 120Y/208 V model delivering 33 kVA for multifamily properties and smaller commercial buildings, and a 277Y/480 V model delivering 40 kVA for larger commercial and industrial applications. Both are based on the lithium iron phosphate (LFP) chemistry, deliver greater than 90% AC round-trip efficiency, and operate across an ambient temperature range of -22°F to 131°F. Shipments of the IQ Battery C80 are expected to begin in the first half of 2027. About the Author Lee Goldberg Contributing Editor Lee is the author of the popular PowerBites series. Lee Goldberg is a self-identified “Recovering Engineer,” Maker/Hacker, Green-Tech Maven, Aviator, Gadfly, and Geek Dad. He spent the first 18 years of his career helping design microprocessors, embedded systems, renewable energy applications, and the occasional interplanetary spacecraft. After trading his ‘scope and soldering iron for a keyboard and a second career as a tech journalist, he’s spent the next two decades at several print and online engineering publications. Lee’s current focus is power electronics, especially the technologies involved with energy efficiency, energy management, and renewable energy. This dovetails with his coverage of sustainable technologies and various environmental and social issues within the engineering community that he began in 1996. Lee also covers 3D printers, open-source hardware, and other Maker/Hacker technologies. Lee holds a BSEE in Electrical Engineering from Thomas Edison College, and participated in a colloquium on technology, society, and the environment at Goddard College’s Institute for Social Ecology. His book, “Green Electronics/Green Bottom Line - A Commonsense Guide To Environmentally Responsible Engineering and Management,” was published by Newnes Press. Lee, his wife Catherine, and his daughter Anwyn currently reside in the outskirts of Princeton N.J., where they masquerade as a typical suburban family. artigo.texto: DE SOTO, Kan. — KSHB 41 reporter Isabella Ledonne reports on stories in Overland Park, Johnson County and topics about government accountability. Share your story idea with Isabella. — The company behind one of the hyperscale data center proposal projects in De Soto, Kansas, announced it is preparing to provide direct credits of up to $1,000 for every household in the city. Digital Realty is preparing its 300-acre site for a data center at Astra Enterprise Park near the Panasonic Plant. Construction is expected to start in 2027. Beale Infrastructure has started construction on its data center campus down the road from Panasonic and Digital Realty's site. But even with the promise of Digital Realty's money, neighbors are still skeptical of what the project could mean for their everyday life. "Is that enough?" neighbor Sara VanDeCreek said. "How much is the value of our community?" Digital Realty reached out to me on Friday to announce the company is planning to give every household a yearly credit up to $1,000 for the next 10 years to be used for property tax and/or utility relief. —Watch: De Soto data center plans to offer $1,000 to households; neighbors skeptical— It's among the first in the Kansas City metro to offer an incentive directly to residents. "De Soto has a lot of people that could use $1,000 a year," VanDeCreek said. But to some neighbors, that check could mean something else. "It's a bribe, is what it looks like," neighbor Toni Caldwell said. "If you can't give us the true answers, then don't come to me with money and expect me to believe what's going on or accept that money." Both Caldwell and VanDeCreek have been outspoken against De Soto's two data center developments, even helping launch a petition earlier this month to block the development. They explained that petition has gained more than 400 signatures. Digital Realty's announcement to invest $20 million in a community fund in the form of direct relief for residents has been met with some skepticism. "They're not really answering the questions that we have," VanDeCreek said. "I don't think it sweetens the deal and I think it's purposeful that it's coming out right now before they ask for tax incentives to help with bonds." I asked Digital Realty why the company is offering this and if it's meant to offset any anticipated rise in residential electric and water bills with the operation of the data center. "This commitment is designed to deliver tangible benefits for De Soto residents while we invest for the long term," a spokesperson said over email. "It accelerates benefits the community will receive and is a reflection of our broader approach to responsible development, collaboration and being a good neighbor in our project communities." "A community partner first of all is transparent," VanDeCreek said. Neighbors are still wanting answers to their biggest concern: the long-term impacts of having data centers in the community. It's a question residents say they haven't gotten the answer to with either data center proposal. "A good community partner is one you can trust," Caldwell said. "I don't trust either one of them right now." Digital Realty did not make anyone available for an on-camera interview. "This community investment accompanies Digital Realty's entire development in De Soto and reflects our long-term commitment to local partnerships," a spokesperson wrote in a statement. "We look forward to continuing this investment in the community as the project moves forward." The company is expected to have a TIF district public hearing at the city council meeting on Nov. 19. The City of De Soto is helping Digital Realty with the distribution and plans for the direct relief payments, though no funds are expected to come out of the city's general revenue fund. “De Soto and the developers of Astra Enterprise Park have spent decades planning for the future of this historic site, with the City focused on ensuring its redevelopment creates tangible benefits and improves quality of life for our residents,” De Soto mayor Rick Walker said. “Digital Realty’s commitment builds on that vision in a meaningful way by investing directly in the people who call De Soto home.” —

artigo.texto: Chinese electric vehicles are often cheaper because manufacturers combine affordable batteries, integrated production, large supplier networks and intense domestic competition. These advantages reinforce one another, helping automakers reduce costs across the vehicle rather than relying on a single saving. The International Energy Agency’s manufacturing comparison found that battery-electric vehicle production costs were more than 30 percent lower in China than in advanced economies. Batteries accounted for around one-third of the difference, while a similar manufacturing gap existed for conventional cars. The comparison used standardized small SUVs and 2024 cost data; it is not a universal discount across all Chinese models. The IEA’s 2026 research shows how this industrial advantage translates into affordable vehicles, while examples from BYD and overseas markets demonstrate why prices vary by location. Battery Prices Give Chinese EV Manufacturers a Head Start BloombergNEF’s 2025 battery price survey recorded a global average lithium-ion battery pack price of $108 per kilowatt-hour, down 8 percent from 2024. China’s regional average was $84/kWh. North American and European pack prices were respectively 44 percent and 56 percent higher. These regional averages cover multiple applications and battery chemistries, rather than identical automotive packs. An illustrative 60-kWh pack shows the financial effect: This calculation demonstrates the sensitivity of vehicle costs to battery prices. It is not a quotation for a particular EV battery. Manufacturers can use lower battery expenditure to reduce selling prices, improve margins or add features without increasing the final price. LFP Batteries Lower Material Costs Lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, batteries avoid nickel and cobalt in their cathode chemistry, reducing exposure to these expensive materials. The IEA’s Global EV Outlook 2026 battery analysis says LFP accounted for more than 55 percent of EV battery deployment in 2025, up from nearly 50 percent in 2024. China also produced more than 80 percent of global battery output. LFP is particularly useful for affordable vehicles where manufacturers balance purchase price, range and battery size. Higher-energy-density chemistries remain relevant for other applications, so the cheapest chemistry is not automatically the best choice for every model. Battery sizing creates another saving. At an illustrative $100/kWh, reducing capacity from 60 kWh to 45 kWh lowers pack expenditure by $1,500. The trade-off is less stored energy, making vehicle efficiency and intended use important. BYD Combines Battery Expertise With Integrated Vehicle Technology BYD provides a practical example of integrating battery and vehicle development. The company highlights its Blade Battery, Cell-to-Body integration and 8-in-1 electric powertrain as important technologies across its electric lineup. BYD reported selling more than 4.6 million new-energy vehicles in 2025, including battery-electric vehicles and plug-in hybrids. Integrated development can help engineers coordinate battery packaging, electronics and drivetrain design. Producing key technologies internally can also reduce some purchasing layers and simplify component coordination. However, vertical integration requires capital and manufacturing expertise. It supports lower costs when internal production is efficient and volumes justify the investment. BYD’s example therefore combines two advantages: control over important technologies and a large vehicle business over which to spread development expenditure. Factory Scale Reduces Costs When Capacity Is Used China produced approximately 16 million electric cars in 2025, exceeding domestic demand by around 20 percent, according to the IEA. Electric-car exports doubled to more than 2.5 million. These figures include battery-electric cars and plug-in hybrids. Large production volumes can spread tooling, engineering and factory overhead across more vehicles. For example, assume a plant has $200 million in annual fixed costs. Producing 500,000 vehicles allocates $400 per vehicle; producing 250,000 allocates $800. This simplified illustration excludes variable costs but shows why utilisation matters. High capacity alone does not guarantee low costs. Underused factories can increase unit costs, while manufacturers may cut prices to maintain output and clear inventory. Supplier Concentration and Automation Improve Efficiency China’s advantage extends upstream into battery materials. In 2025, it accounted for approximately 85 percent of cathode active-material production and more than 90 percent of anode active-material production used in electric-car batteries. Concentrated supplier networks can shorten delivery routes, support engineering collaboration and enable larger component orders. The IEA’s EV manufacturing cost analysis also identifies manufacturing efficiency and automation as major contributors to battery cost competitiveness. Shared vehicle platforms provide another opportunity. Using common motors, electronics and battery systems across several models can reduce duplicated development and tooling. As an illustration, $600 million in platform development expenditure spread across one million vehicles equals $600 per vehicle, compared with $1,200 across 500,000. Price Competition Makes Chinese EVs More Affordable The IEA’s 2026 electric-car market analysis found that average battery-electric car prices in China fell more than 10 percent in 2025. Around 30 percent of BEV models had entry prices below $20,000. Nearly 70 percent of BEVs sold in China were cheaper than their conventional equivalents before government incentives, indicating that affordability extends beyond consumer subsidies. Competition encourages manufacturers to pass savings to buyers. artigo.texto: Câmara aprova urgência de projeto que muda rateio de custos para contratação de baterias elétricas A regra é um dos pontos mais controversos no setor elétrico para a realização do primeiro leilão para contratação de sistemas de armazenamento, previsto para dezembro A Câmara dos Deputados aprovou nesta terça-feira (13) um requerimento de urgência para a análise de projeto de lei que propõe alteração no rateio dos custos para contratação de baterias para armazenar energia elétrica. A regra é um dos pontos mais controversos no setor elétrico para a realização do primeiro leilão para contratação de sistemas de armazenamento, previsto para dezembro deste ano. Na prática, a medida possibilita que a proposta seja votada diretamente pelo plenário da Casa, sem ser analisada por comissões temáticas antes. A votação do mérito, contudo, deverá ficar para depois das eleições. De autoria do deputado Arnaldo Jardim (Cidadania-SP), o projeto revoga alteração legislativa feita no ano passado, que determina que os custos das contratações com baterias seja dividido exclusivamente entre os geradores de energia, conforme regulamentação da Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel). Com a revogação, a avaliação de alguns agentes do setor é de que os custos passariam a ser rateados entre os consumidores. Segundo o autor da proposta, o texto ainda deverá ser negociado com o governo. “Nós iremos aproveitar esse período dessa semana e a outra para arredondar o projeto, avançar no diálogo com o governo para votar após a eleição”, disse o deputado. Na justificativa da proposta, Jardim critica o dispositivo que determina que os custos da contratação de baterias para armazenamento de energia sejam divididos exclusivamente entre as empresas geradoras de eletricidade. Ele afirma que, como consequência, há “distorções relevantes na alocação de custos do setor elétrico” e que isso “compromete a segurança jurídica dos investimentos em geração de energia renovável no Brasil”. Segundo o parlamentar, o enfrentamento dos desafios operativos do Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN) passa pelo incentivo ao aumento da flexibilidade operativa do sistema. Em nota, a Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia (ABSAE), avaliou que o avanço da proposta é importante para ampliar a segurança jurídica e criar condições mais previsíveis para a realização dos primeiros leilões de baterias em larga escala no Brasil. "A entidade alerta que o cumprimento do cronograma dos leilões é fundamental para que os sistemas de armazenamento estejam disponíveis em 2028. O adiamento dos certames pode comprometer a entrada das baterias em operação no prazo previsto e aumentar o risco de déficit de potência e de apagão em períodos críticos de atendimento."

artigo.texto: Concept mockup to be showcased at the 2026 Paris Motor Show, with functional battery segment development planned as the next phase of cell and system integration work PARIS, Oct. 12, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- ProLogium today announced progress in its collaboration with Rimac Technology on next-generation electric vehicle battery pack development. The companies signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) in September 2025 to develop a next-generation battery platform and have completed a battery pack concept mockup, which will be displayed at the 2026 Paris Motor Show. The next phase will focus on developing a functional battery segment to establish a basis for testing the thermal management and cell-integration concepts and support battery pack applications in the battery electric vehicle (BEV) market. The collaboration combines ProLogium's next-generation cell technology with Rimac Technology's battery system development expertise, focusing on a pouch cell-to-pack architecture. Through a staged development path from concept mockup to functional battery segment, full-scale functional battery pack and in-vehicle testing, the companies will progressively evaluate cell and system integration approaches, connecting next-generation cell technology with automotive product development. From Concept Mockup to Functional Hardware Bringing cell technology into automotive applications requires more than cell-level performance. It also involves addressing thermal management, cell integration and battery pack architecture at the system level. With battery pack integration at its core, the collaboration brings together cell technology and systems engineering to examine the design requirements for next-generation batteries in automotive applications. The completed concept mockup is an initial milestone in this development process. The ongoing development will move the project from a conceptual representation toward functional hardware, using a battery segment as the platform for subsequent testing. This work will assess the feasibility of thermal management and cell-integration concepts and inform full-scale battery pack development. By developing a battery segment before expanding to a full-scale system, the companies will gather test results and design feedback at each stage to assess whether the integration approach can meet automotive battery-systems requirements. Vincent Yang, Founder and CEO of ProLogium, said: "Since jointly announcing our collaboration with Rimac Technology at IAA in 2025, both teams have continued to advance the project, translating our shared technical vision into concrete engineering development work. What we are presenting at the Paris Motor Show is the baseline of that collaboration. Building on the completed concept mockup and the functional segments currently in development, we are preparing to move into the development and production of a functional battery progressing toward a full-scale battery pack and subsequent vehicle integration validation. Bringing next-generation batteries to the automotive market requires more than cell technology. It also takes the engineering expertise to integrate those cells into a battery pack with optimized architecture and thermal management. We look forward to combining our technical strengths through hardware development and testing to address the engineering challenges of automotive integration and translate the value of next-generation cell technology into solutions that can be adopted in vehicles.” Daniel Kišić, Principal Product Architect of Rimac Technology said: "Rimac Technology is developing a scalable cell-to-pack integration technology for solid-state pouch cells, designed to meet and exceed the requirements the automotive industry is expected to set over the coming decade. A wide range of integration solutions is currently being evaluated and tested in parallel on functional battery segments, covering thermal management, swelling management, cell integration and system-level design. Some of these solutions are oriented towards maximum energy density and reduced space and weight, while others are oriented towards delivering performance. The work starts from vehicle-level requirements and aims to improve every aspect of the battery design by reducing complexity, combining functions and reducing weight. It does so with cost in mind, while still delivering state-of-the-art charging times and power output. Once validated at vehicle level, the solution is expected to deliver significant weight savings, improving driving efficiency and extending range. OEMs could then choose between more energy on board at the same weight, a smaller and lighter battery for the same range, or any combination in between.” A Clear Pathway to Full-Scale Battery Packs and In-Vehicle Testing According to Rimac Technology's current development roadmap, the functional battery segment currently in development is planned for display at CES 2027, with the full-scale functional battery pack identified as a development milestone for the second half of 2027. Subsequent targets include in-vehicle and public-road testing in the second half of 2028.These stages will progressively expand the scope of validation, from assessing integration concepts in a functional battery segment to a full-scale battery pack, followed by vehicle installation and road testing to evaluate system performance in an automotive environment. At the Paris Motor Show, the companies will present the concept mockup stage of the collaboration and outline the next steps in functional hardware development and integration validation. By combining cell technology with battery systems engineering, ProLogium and Rimac Technology will continue to advance next-generation battery integration technology development from concept design toward automotive applications. artigo.texto: ABB Broad industrial charger portfolio According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Industrial Battery Charger market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The global industrial battery charger market is a critical enabler of the energy transition, providing the power conversion backbone for grid-scale battery energy storage systems (BESS) and heavy-duty industrial electrification. Unlike consumer chargers, industrial battery chargers must manage high-power AC/DC conversion, grid-code compliance, and safety certification, making them high-value components embedded in bankable energy projects. Demand is bifurcating: standardized, cost-optimized chargers for containerized BESS versus customized, feature-rich systems for grid-support and harsh industrial environments. The competitive landscape pits diversified power-electronics giants against specialized OEMs with deep application engineering. Procurement is dominated by sophisticated buyers—BESS integrators, EPC firms, and utilities—who prioritize total cost of ownership and long-term service over upfront price. Supply chain resilience, particularly for SiC/GaN semiconductors and magnetics, remains a key concern. Regulatory frameworks and grid codes are primary product drivers, mandating advanced functionalities like fault ride-through and frequency regulation. As the market evolves through 2035, chargers will become intelligent grid-edge assets, with software-defined controls enabling active grid management. This report provides a structured analysis of market size, segmentation, demand drivers, competitive dynamics, and regional outlook, offering actionable insights for manufacturers, integrators, investors, and policymakers navigating this rapidly evolving landscape. The baseline scenario for the industrial battery charger market through 2035 anticipates robust expansion, underpinned by the accelerating deployment of grid-scale battery energy storage systems (BESS) and the electrification of heavy-duty transport and industrial processes. As renewable energy penetration rises, the need for flexible, grid-compliant charging infrastructure becomes paramount, driving demand for advanced chargers capable of bidirectional power flow, grid-forming capabilities, and seamless integration with energy management systems. The market is expected to grow at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 8.2% from 2026 to 2035, reaching a market index of 220 (2025=100). This growth is not merely volumetric; it reflects a shift toward higher-value, software-defined chargers that serve as intelligent grid-edge assets. Regionally, Asia-Pacific will remain the largest market, driven by China's dominance in BESS manufacturing and deployment, while North America and Europe will see strong growth supported by policy incentives and grid modernization initiatives. Latin America and the Middle East & Africa will emerge as opportunistic markets, albeit from a smaller base. Key risks include supply chain bottlenecks for specialized semiconductors, regulatory delays, and the potential for technology shifts that could disrupt incumbent product architectures. However, the long-term trajectory remains positive, with chargers increasingly viewed as strategic components in the energy transition. Grid-scale BESS represents the largest and fastest-growing end-use sector for industrial battery chargers. As utilities and independent power producers deploy massive battery arrays to store excess renewable energy and provide grid services, the demand for high-power, grid-compliant chargers surges. These chargers must manage bidirectional power flow, support grid-forming capabilities, and comply with stringent interconnection standards. The shift toward longer-duration storage and hybrid projects further amplifies charger requirements, as does the need for seamless integration with energy management systems. Demand-side indicators include renewable capacity additions, battery storage procurement targets, and grid stability mandates. Through 2035, this segment will remain the primary growth engine, with chargers evolving into intelligent grid-edge assets that enable ancillary services and enhance project bankability. Current trend: Rapid growth driven by renewable integration and grid modernization.. Major trends: Increasing adoption of grid-forming inverters for enhanced grid support, Standardization of containerized BESS solutions driving cost reduction, Integration of AI and predictive analytics for optimal charging and grid interaction, Growth in hybrid renewable-plus-storage projects requiring advanced charger controls, and Rising focus on cybersecurity and grid resilience. Representative participants: ABB Ltd, Siemens AG, Sungrow Power Supply Co., Ltd, Tesla, Inc, and LG Energy Solution, Ltd. The electrification of heavy-duty vehicles is a major demand driver for industrial battery chargers, particularly high-power DC fast chargers. Fleet operators are transitioning to electric buses, trucks, and port equipment to comply with emissions regulations and reduce operating costs. These applications require robust, high-power chargers capable of delivering rapid charging cycles and managing large battery capacities. The demand story is characterized by depot-based charging infrastructure, opportunity charging, and the need for smart charging to manage grid loads. Key demand-side indicators include fleet electrification targets, government subsidies for zero-emission vehicles, and the expansion of charging networks. By 2035, this segment will see significant growth, with chargers becoming more integrated with fleet management systems and renewable energy sources. artigo.texto: Microsoft Weighs 20% Cost Cuts In Azure Vertical Amid Soaring AI Data Center Spending: Report - Girish Bablani, president of Azure's software development group, instructed team leaders to identify ways to lower expenses by at least 20%, The Information reported. - The potential savings aim to help offset heavy capital expenditures for AI data centers and finance higher salaries to retain talent against competitors like Meta and Anthropic. - Scott Guthrie announced an internal restructuring elevating senior executive Arun Ulag to oversee key cloud units. Microsoft Corp.’s (MSFT) cloud business top executives have discussed strategies to cut expenses by at least 20%, reflecting growing pressure on major technology firms to fund artificial intelligence infrastructure. Girish Bablani, president of the Azure group that develops software for cloud servers, recently directed leaders in his roughly 11,500-person division to outline cost-saving proposals, The Information reported, citing people familiar with the matter. While the exact measures remain under consideration and could include parting ways with external contractors, the report did not state categorically whether internal discussions could lead to staff layoffs. However, a Microsoft spokesperson disputed the characterization of planned cuts, saying, "Azure leadership has not directed teams to develop cost-cutting plans. Every responsible company prepares for a range of scenarios and market dynamics, both positive and negative,” according to The Information. Balancing Infrastructure Costs And Talent Retention The potential cost-cutting comes despite strong financial performance for Azure. Microsoft recently disclosed that the cloud unit generated $101.9 billion in revenue for the 12 months ending in June—a 40% year-over-year increase—accounting for approximately 31% of the company's total annual revenue. In the June quarter alone, Azure’s revenue rose 43%. However, the rapid acceleration of AI deployment has driven massive capital expenditure on data center infrastructure, pressuring cash reserves. Similar financial pressures have affected competitors such as Amazon Web Services (AMZN) and Oracle (ORCL), both of which have implemented workforce reductions to protect cash flows amid rising AI expenses. Moreover, competitors like Meta (META) and Anthropic have aggressively targeted Microsoft personnel, forcing executives to offer counteroffers with higher compensation packages. Leadership Restructuring Alongside the cost discussions, Microsoft is reorganizing leadership within its cloud organization. In an internal announcement on Monday, Guthrie revealed that senior executive Arun Ulag will assume broader oversight across key divisions, The Information reported. Ulag, who previously managed Azure's database product line, will now oversee executives responsible for Azure Core—the business providing raw computing capacity to key clients, including OpenAI. His expanded purview includes senior leaders such as Bablani, Billy Anders, Douglas Phillips, Mark Russinovich, and former security chief Charlie Bell. The management shakeup reflects a broader push by Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella to elevate a new generation of leadership as several veteran executives step back or retire. artigo.texto: Estudo com o CPQD vai identificar áreas com potencial para expansão do setor até 2035 13/10/2026 Fonte: Magnific A Agência Brasileira de Desenvolvimento Industrial (ABDI) e o CPQD estão desenvolvendo um diagnóstico para identificar quais regiões brasileiras apresentam condições para receber novos data centers e quais dependem de investimentos em energia, conectividade e outros serviços essenciais. O levantamento produzirá uma Matriz de Atratividade Territorial e cenários para o setor até 2035. O estudo integra o Projeto ECOS – Data Centers Sustentáveis, iniciativa com duração de 24 meses que também prevê testes de tecnologias para melhorar a eficiência energética e operacional dessas instalações. A proposta é fornecer informações para decisões de investimento, planejamento territorial e formulação de políticas públicas. Além da infraestrutura disponível, serão examinados fatores como recursos hídricos, licenciamento, tributação, disponibilidade de profissionais qualificados e capacidade da indústria nacional de atender à demanda do setor. Matriz apontará potencial e gargalos regionais A Matriz de Atratividade Territorial será uma das principais entregas do diagnóstico. O instrumento deverá identificar localidades com condições para receber empreendimentos e aquelas que precisam de investimentos estruturantes, especialmente em transmissão de energia, telecomunicações e abastecimento de água. O trabalho abrangerá oito dimensões: panorama nacional e internacional; diagnóstico territorial; cadeia produtiva e desenvolvimento industrial; energia, sustentabilidade e infraestrutura; regulação e tributação; capital humano e inovação; soberania digital; e impactos, cenários e recomendações estratégicas. A metodologia combina levantamento de dados, entrevistas com representantes do mercado, consultas ao ecossistema, workshops e análises técnicas. Em setembro, durante a Campinas Innovation Week, em Campinas (SP), o projeto realizou um encontro para colher contribuições de participantes ligados à infraestrutura digital e à inovação. As informações serão incorporadas às demais etapas do levantamento. Além da matriz, estão previstas avaliações de impactos econômicos, sociais, ambientais e tecnológicos, projeções para o período de 2026 a 2035 e um roteiro estratégico para o desenvolvimento do setor. Quer receber notícias da ACAERT? Assine a newsletter - Assine aqui e receba por e-mail Indústria nacional entra no diagnóstico Outra frente do estudo será a identificação de oportunidades para fornecedores brasileiros de equipamentos, tecnologias e serviços associados à implantação e operação de data centers. A análise também considerará formação de profissionais, capacidades tecnológicas nacionais e os efeitos da expansão dessa infraestrutura sobre o desenvolvimento regional. Para o presidente da ABDI, Olavo Noleto, o objetivo é relacionar o crescimento da capacidade de processamento de dados à política industrial. “Com o Projeto ECOS, buscamos gerar inteligência, fortalecer a cadeia produtiva nacional e criar condições para que o crescimento desse setor se converta em desenvolvimento industrial, inovação e soberania para o Brasil”, afirma. Projeto prevê testes de eficiência energética Além do diagnóstico, a parceria entre ABDI e CPQD contempla uma jornada de inovação aberta, na qual empresas de data centers, startups e ambientes de validação poderão desenvolver e testar soluções para problemas operacionais do setor. Entre as tecnologias consideradas estão sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS), inteligência artificial, automação e ferramentas de monitoramento. As aplicações poderão envolver gestão térmica, redução do consumo de água, integração de fontes renováveis e confiabilidade operacional. Os projetos-piloto deverão gerar dados técnicos sobre desempenho e sustentabilidade das soluções avaliadas. “Com essa jornada, o projeto busca desenvolver modelos e soluções nacionais para o setor, alinhando o avanço tecnológico às metas ESG e posicionando o Brasil como referência na próxima geração de data centers sustentáveis e inteligentes”, afirma Sebastião Sahão Junior, presidente do CPQD. artigo.texto: Modelos de IA poderão em breve se ‘autorreplicar’ sem acesso a centros de dados, alerta Anthropic Em seus experimentos, empresa investigou se modelos de IA seriam capazes de encontrar dispositivos vulneráveis, copiar a si mesmos para esses aparelhos e continuar se espalhando sem ajuda humana A Anthropic afirmou, na segunda-feira (12), que seus experimentos sugerem que pequenos modelos de inteligência artificial podem estar a poucos meses de alcançar capacidade suficiente para se “autorreplicar” em dispositivos comerciais, como fornos “inteligentes” e televisões integradas ao sistema Android de marcas pouco conhecidas. Em seus experimentos, a Anthropic investigou se modelos de IA seriam capazes de encontrar dispositivos vulneráveis, copiar a si mesmos para esses aparelhos e continuar se espalhando sem ajuda humana. A empresa constatou que modelos pequenos, com menos de 30 bilhões de parâmetros, conseguiam executar as diversas etapas necessárias para a replicação. No entanto, a companhia também verificou que esses modelos de IA tinham dificuldades para concluir toda a sequência de etapas, do início ao fim. Em testes simplificados, nos quais algumas etapas de segurança foram removidas, a Anthropic constatou que o GLM-5.2 e modelos mais avançados eram capazes de realizar todo o processo de replicação de ponta a ponta. Modelos capazes de se replicar seriam difíceis de desativar, já que não existe um ponto central de desligamento. Além disso, diferentemente de softwares maliciosos convencionais, eles poderiam identificar e compreender dispositivos desconhecidos por conta própria, tendo como alvo processadores de centros de dados, alertou a Anthropic. A empresa concentrou sua pesquisa em dispositivos da chamada “internet das coisas”, tecnologia que conecta objetos físicos à rede de internet, como TVs com Android, eletrodomésticos e outros aparelhos conectados à internet, porque esses equipamentos geralmente apresentam sistemas de segurança frágeis. A gigante de IA também alertou que, se os modelos pequenos continuarem evoluindo no ritmo histórico, poderão se replicar de forma autônoma até o fim deste ano. Modelos pequenos capazes de se replicar por meio da transferência de seus próprios pesos deverão alcançar essa capacidade pouco depois. A Anthropic afirmou ainda que esses sistemas autônomos de IA provavelmente se replicariam lentamente e dependeriam de recursos computacionais amplamente disponíveis e relativamente pouco seguros. A companhia acrescentou que os sistemas devem ter sua segurança reforçada para dificultar a disseminação desses agentes de IA.

artigo.texto: Gentherm Major in CCS & seat climate According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Battery Thermal Management Components market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The global Battery Thermal Management Components (BTMC) market is a critical enabler of the electrification megatrend, providing the essential hardware that maintains optimal battery operating temperatures to ensure safety, performance, and longevity. This report delivers a comprehensive analysis of the market from 2026 to 2035, covering cooling plates, heat exchangers, thermal interface materials, coolant pumps, chillers, heating elements, temperature sensors, and insulation materials. The market is poised for robust expansion, primarily driven by the accelerating adoption of electric vehicles (EVs) and the rapid build-out of stationary energy storage systems (ESS) for renewable integration and grid stability. As battery technologies evolve toward higher energy densities and faster charging capabilities, the demand for more efficient and sophisticated thermal management solutions intensifies. The competitive landscape features established thermal management specialists, innovative pure-play component manufacturers, and vertically integrated battery and automotive OEMs. Key trends include the shift toward direct liquid cooling, the integration of smart thermal controls, and the development of sustainable, high-performance materials. This analysis provides stakeholders with a granular view of demand patterns across regions and applications, supply chain dynamics, and the strategic imperatives for success in a market fundamental to the global energy transition. The baseline scenario for the Battery Thermal Management Components market projects sustained growth from 2026 to 2035, with a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 14.2%, culminating in a market index of 380 (2025=100). This outlook is underpinned by the inexorable rise in global EV sales, which are expected to constitute a majority of new car sales in key markets by the mid-2030s, and the parallel expansion of grid-scale battery storage. The market will be characterized by a shift from air-cooled to more efficient liquid-cooled architectures, increasing the content and value of thermal management components per battery pack. Technological advancements will focus on improving thermal efficiency, reducing weight and cost, and enabling ultra-fast charging without compromising battery health. Supply chains will localize to mitigate geopolitical and logistical risks, with regional manufacturing hubs emerging to serve proximate automotive and ESS assembly plants. Pricing will trend downward for mature components due to scale economies, while advanced solutions like immersion cooling and phase-change materials will command premium pricing. The aftermarket for replacement components, particularly in industrial and telecom backup applications, will provide a stable secondary demand stream. Regulatory pressures, such as the EU's battery passport and carbon footprint rules, will increasingly influence material sourcing and component design, favoring suppliers with transparent and sustainable value chains. The EV sector is the dominant demand driver for battery thermal management components, accounting for the majority of market value. As EV adoption accelerates globally, the need for efficient thermal management becomes paramount to ensure battery safety, extend driving range, and enable fast charging. Currently, most EVs utilize liquid-cooled systems, which offer superior heat dissipation compared to air cooling. Through 2035, the demand will be fueled by the proliferation of EVs across all vehicle classes, from passenger cars to buses and trucks. The trend toward higher energy density batteries and ultra-fast charging (e.g., 800V architectures) will necessitate more sophisticated cooling solutions, such as direct cooling with refrigerants or immersion cooling. Demand-side indicators include EV production volumes, average battery pack size, and the penetration of fast-charging infrastructure. The aftermarket for thermal components in EVs will also grow as the fleet ages, though it remains a small share compared to original equipment. Current trend: Rapid growth, shifting toward liquid cooling and integrated thermal systems. Major trends: Shift from air-cooled to liquid-cooled systems for higher efficiency, Integration of thermal management with vehicle HVAC systems, Adoption of heat pumps for improved cold-weather performance, Development of immersion cooling for high-performance EVs, and Use of phase-change materials for passive thermal management. Representative participants: Valeo, Dana Incorporated, Mahle GmbH, Hanon Systems, Modine Manufacturing Company, and Gentherm. The ESS sector is a rapidly growing end-use market for battery thermal management components, propelled by the global transition to renewable energy and the need for grid stabilization. Large-scale battery storage systems, often housed in containers, require robust thermal management to maintain optimal temperatures and prevent thermal runaway. Currently, many ESS installations use air cooling for cost reasons, but as system sizes increase and energy densities rise, liquid cooling is becoming more prevalent. Through 2035, the demand will be driven by utility-scale projects, commercial and industrial installations, and residential storage. Demand-side indicators include renewable energy capacity additions, grid modernization investments, and government incentives for energy storage. The trend toward longer-duration storage will also influence thermal management requirements, as systems must operate reliably over many cycles. The ESS sector is expected to gain share as costs decline and deployments accelerate. Current trend: Strong growth, driven by renewable integration and grid stability.

artigo.texto: NTPC Arm to Start Commercial Operations of 500 MWh BESS Capacity 13 Oct 2026 2 Min Read CW Team Share NTPC Vidyut Vyapar Nigam (NVVN), a wholly-owned subsidiary of NTPC, plans to begin commercial operations of 500 MWh of battery energy storage capacity soon, its chief executive officer Somes Bandyopadhyay said on Thursday. Bandyopadhyay said NVVN also intends to commission an additional 500 MWh of capacity during the current financial year. The plans are part of the government’s scheme to support the development of 3,000 MWh of battery energy storage capacity through different modes. The comments were made on the sidelines of the 18th India Coal Summit, organised by the Indian Chamber of Commerce in New Delhi. NVVN is involved in developing large-scale Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) across the country as India expands its electricity storage infrastructure. A BESS uses batteries, either individually or more commonly in groups, to store electricity generated by power plants. The stored electricity can subsequently be supplied to the grid when demand rises or when renewable generation is unavailable. Battery storage systems are increasingly being used to help utilities manage peak electricity demand and improve grid reliability. They can store power during periods of lower demand or high renewable energy generation and release it during peak-demand periods, supporting the integration of intermittent sources such as solar and wind power. India is scaling up its BESS ecosystem through policy support and capacity additions as it seeks to strengthen the power grid and accommodate a growing share of renewable energy. NVVN’s planned projects are expected to contribute to the government’s broader effort to establish utility-scale storage facilities and improve flexibility in electricity supply. artigo.texto: VSL PowerHive, a wholly owned subsidiary of Vikram Solar Limited, has announced plans to establish a 7.5 GWh per annum Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) assembly facility at Oragadam, near Chennai, Tamil Nadu. The proposed plant is designed to expand to 15 GWh in subsequent phases and forms part of the company’s broader strategy to develop 30 GWh of total battery manufacturing capacity by 2030. The upcoming facility will be spread across approximately 1.65 lakh square feet and is scheduled for inauguration in January 2027, with commercial operations expected to commence in April 2027. The investment marks a significant expansion of Vikram Solar’s presence in the energy storage segment, complementing its existing solar manufacturing operations and supporting India’s growing demand for domestically manufactured battery storage solutions. The development comes amid increasing demand for energy storage infrastructure as India continues to expand its solar and wind power capacity. Battery energy storage systems are becoming essential for managing renewable energy variability, supporting grid stability, shifting surplus electricity to peak-demand periods and enabling round-the-clock renewable power supply. According to projections from the Central Electricity Authority (CEA), India will require approximately 47 GW of energy storage power capacity and 236 GWh of storage capacity by 2031–32. The anticipated growth in storage requirements is expected to create significant opportunities for domestic battery manufacturing and reduce dependence on imported energy storage technologies. As part of its long-term expansion strategy, VSL PowerHive also plans to enter battery cell manufacturing through a 7.5 GWh programme beginning in 2028. This initiative is intended to establish an integrated domestic battery manufacturing ecosystem, covering both battery cells and complete energy storage systems. The company is also developing indigenous battery technologies and has initiated multiple patent filings to strengthen its intellectual property portfolio and reduce reliance on imported technical expertise. Once operational, the Oragadam facility will manufacture lithium iron phosphate (LFP)-based battery energy storage systems for utility-scale and commercial and industrial (C&I) applications. Its product portfolio will include 5.016 MWh and 6.25 MWh liquid-cooled BESS containers, PowerHive P261 battery cabinets, utility-scale storage systems and renewable energy-integrated battery storage solutions. The proposed manufacturing operations will be developed under the Make in India initiative, with a focus on strengthening domestic energy storage production capabilities and supporting the country’s expanding renewable energy infrastructure. Commenting on the announcement, Gyanesh Chaudhary, Chairman and Managing Director of Vikram Solar, highlighted the importance of energy storage in supporting India’s transition towards reliable, round-the-clock clean electricity. He stated that the ability to store renewable energy efficiently would play a critical role in the next phase of India’s energy transition and emphasised the need to develop these capabilities domestically. Chaudhary further noted that the proposed facility would extend Vikram Solar’s participation in the clean energy value chain beyond solar power generation technologies into energy storage solutions. Arun Mittal, Chief Executive Officer of VSL PowerHive, highlighted the increasing demand for battery energy storage systems across India’s electricity sector. He stated that the company aims to establish advanced domestic battery manufacturing capabilities, beginning with 7.5 GWh of assembly capacity and subsequently expanding into cell manufacturing and an integrated battery production ecosystem. The planned facility is also expected to create skilled employment opportunities, support local talent development in advanced battery technologies and strengthen Tamil Nadu’s emerging clean technology manufacturing ecosystem. Through its phased manufacturing expansion and focus on indigenous technology development, VSL PowerHive aims to position itself as a domestic supplier of battery energy storage solutions for utilities, renewable energy developers and industrial consumers. The proposed 7.5 GWh facility, together with the company’s planned expansion to 15 GWh and its broader 30 GWh manufacturing target by 2030, represents a step towards strengthening India’s battery energy storage manufacturing capabilities and supporting the country’s transition to a more flexible, reliable and renewable energy-based electricity system. artigo.texto: - Energy - 2 min read India's battery energy storage sector set for 91% growth to 302GWh by FY32E: Nuvama Cumulative BESS capacity could rise to 302 GWh from 6.3 GWh, driven by renewable integration and falling costs, creating growth opportunities for domestic manufacturers. India's Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) sector is projected to register a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 91 per cent between FY26 and FY32E, according to a recent report by Nuvama. The expansion reflects a critical infrastructure cycle designed to support renewable integration, grid balancing, and round-the-clock power requirements across the country. The report noted that cumulative capacity will surge from 6.3 GWh to 302GWh over the same period, with annual additions climbing from 5.7GWh in FY26 to 56 GWh by FY32E. The report noted that the Central Electricity Authority (CEA) estimates national BESS demand at 236 GWh by FY32 and 1,840 GWh by 2047. "We estimate annual BESS additions to rise from 5.7 GWh in FY26 to 56 GWh by FY32E, taking cumulative capacity from 6.3GWh to 302GWh (91 per cent CAGR) over FY2632E," the report said. "With 89 per cent of current requirements met through imports, falling battery costs, alongside a likely ALMM-like framework, could accelerate adoption, localisation and domestic capacity growth. Although Li-ion occupies 98 per cent of the BESS market, sodium-ion technology and China+1 themes are an opportunity for India," the report added. Manufacturing economics reveal distinct margins across end-markets, with commercial, industrial, and retail segments yielding spreads of $18 to 23 per kilowatt-hour, corresponding to EBITDA margins of 17 to 20 per cent. By contrast, the utility segment records spreads of $8 per kilowatt-hour and an EBITDA margin of 9 per cent. "Our analysis shows attractive cell-to-pack manufacturing economics with materially differentiated spreads across end-markets," the report noted. "Even with low spreads of USD8/kWh (EBITDA margin 9 per cent) for the Utility segment, our calculation and channel checks indicate a one-to-two-year payback." The report also highlighted that while returns for an integrated BESS facility yield a modest internal rate of return of 12 per cent, domestic production maintains a distinct cost advantage through capital expenditure of $80 million per gigawatt-hour, coupled with production-linked incentive support of ₹181 billion for 50 GWh and competitive labour expenses. Cell-to-pack configurations demonstrate an internal rate of return of 31 per cent. "We believe with policy support, localisation and scale, integrated BESS could open up export-led growth," the report noted. Financially, BESS integration is estimated to contribute 17 to 60 per cent to company revenues by FY28. Premier presents an opportunity of ₹103 billion, representing 60 per cent of its projected FY28 revenue, while Vikram is positioned for a 54 per cent revenue uplift. "Despite early battery ambitions and potential BESS addition of 17-60 per cent to FY28E revenue, most listed solar/BESS players' earnings are yet to capture meaningful BESS contribution," the report stated. "At 17x FY27E EPS, solar/BESS trades at a 77 per cent discount to battery chemicals and a 64 per cent discount to battery IPP peers. As capacity ramps up, we believe BESS could emerge as a strong driver of earnings upgrade and valuation re-rating," the report said.

artigo.texto: Harrisburg, Pa. — The president of Concerned Citizens of Montour County was among the speakers at a state Capitol rally on Oct. 6, where organizers say more than 250 people from across Pa. called on Gov. Josh Shapiro and legislators to impose a moratorium on data center development. “All they have to fight with is money,” said Sam Burleigh, president and co-founder of the Montour County group. “We have collective voices, elective powers, constitutional laws, and home field advantage. Together we can beat them! Unite and fight!” Burleigh has also previously spoken at meetings focused on Muncy and Gregg townships' proposed data centers. The rally in the Capitol Rotunda was organized by the Better Path Coalition, No False Climate Solutions PA, and 30 partner organizations. Speakers addressed concerns including surveillance, affordability, impacts on health, the environment, and agriculture, threats from artificial intelligence to intellectual property, and the future being left to children. Speakers during the event criticized legislators for what participants described as “putting polluters before people via data center deals that were brokered outside of the public’s view.” The rally closed with speeches on what organizers called the state government’s failure to enforce Pa.’s Green Amendment, Article 1, Section 27 of the state constitution. “Once again, our elected officials are leaping before they look to do the bidding of an industry,” said Karen Feridun, co-founder of the Better Path Coalition and No False Climate Solutions PA and the rally’s emcee. “Governor Shapiro claims to have changed his position on data centers, but his recent Executive Order implementing his GRID initiative is all about making sure data centers are built, not taking the break the public is demanding to decide what role, if any, hyperscale data centers and generative AI should play in Pennsylvania.” Stuart Day of Ohio Valley Allies, who described himself as a Pa. farmer and investigative journalist, compared the expansion of hyperscale data centers to the shale-gas boom. “I believe AI and the infrastructure supporting it represent a transformative moment in human history — and decisions of that magnitude demand deliberation, transparency, and meaningful public participation. This development should not be foisted upon communities and landowners without independent economic and environmental analysis, strong oversight, enforceable protections, and an honest accounting of who receives the benefits and who carries the costs. Rural Pennsylvania has heard promises of salvation from outside industries before; we should have learned by now that something this consequential demands caution, wisdom, and a process with real teeth,” Day said. Hilary Flint, program director at Center for Organizing, said more than 40,000 people have joined the Pennsylvania Data Center Resistance Facebook group. “People understand that projects of this scale will shape their communities for decades, and they are saying no. This movement is growing, it is organized, and we will keep showing up because communities deserve more than a seat at the table. They deserve the power to say no to what gets built in their own backyards,” Flint said. The rally also launched a fall campaign of letters from specific groups of residents explaining why signers oppose data center development. The letters will be delivered to Gov. Shapiro, state legislators, and the winners of the upcoming election. Josephine Gingerich, health advocacy outreach coordinator at Physicians for Social Responsibility PA, led a delegation to Gov. Shapiro’s office to deliver a letter from 80 health professionals. Letters from faith leaders, artists and other creatives, and parents and guardians are open for signatures at bit.ly/NoDataCentersPA, with letters from other groups being planned. Maya van Rossum, founder of Green Amendments For The Generations and the Delaware Riverkeeper, said residents “have a true and enforceable right to pure water, clean air, and healthy environments” under the state constitution. “We are offended when our governor, legislators, or local officials throw out our environmental rights — the rights specifically respected in our state constitution’s declaration of rights — as a throwaway talking point. Our environmental rights are clear and enforceable here in Pennsylvania. When our governor, legislators, or local officials try to ignore or evade them, we will stand up and defend them.” Other speakers listed by organizers included representatives of the Phoenixville Liberation Center, March on Harrisburg, the Delaware Riverkeeper Network, Make the Road PA, Chester Residents Concerned for Quality Living, and the Intertwined faith community.

artigo.texto: Nippon Yusen Kabushiki Kaisha (NYK), NTT FACILITIES, INC., Eurus Energy Holdings Corporation e MUFG Bank, Ltd. (coletivamente, o "Consórcio") desenvolveram um novo conceito de centro de dados flutuante offshore baseado em porto como parte de seus esforços para realizar centros de dados flutuantes offshore. O conceito recém-desenvolvido deverá expandir as opções de implantação para centros de dados flutuantes offshore e acelerar sua aplicação prática. O rápido crescimento da demanda por centros de dados em todo o mundo intensificou desafios como a escassez de locais de desenvolvimento adequados e fornecimento de energia, bem como prazos de construção estendidos. Os centros de dados flutuantes offshore são considerados uma solução promissora para essas questões, tornando importante explorar múltiplos modelos de implantação para melhorar sua viabilidade e apoiar a implementação futura. Entre os conceitos em consideração, os centros de dados flutuantes offshore localizados mais longe da costa são considerados um modelo de implantação ideal porque podem utilizar mais facilmente fontes de energia renovável em larga escala, como a energia eólica offshore, ao mesmo tempo em que fornecem escalabilidade e independência operacional. Ao mesmo tempo, várias questões ainda precisam ser abordadas antes que a implantação offshore em larga escala possa ser realizada, incluindo acessibilidade, conectividade de telecomunicações de alta capacidade e configurações de fornecimento de energia independentes das redes de transmissão e distribuição convencionais. À medida que o Consórcio continuou a avaliar modelos de implantação adicionais adequados a diferentes casos de uso e condições de local, ele desenvolveu o novo conceito de centro de dados flutuante offshore baseado em porto. O conceito de centro de dados flutuante offshore baseado em porto prevê um centro de dados flutuante ancorado ao lado de um cais dentro de uma área portuária. Em comparação com os centros de dados flutuantes offshore projetados para operação em ambientes de mar aberto, o conceito baseado em porto pode ser implantado em uma ampla gama de locais, desde áreas metropolitanas até comunidades regionais. Além disso, pode utilizar a infraestrutura existente, aproveitando os recursos costeiros, incluindo instalações locais de geração de energia. Ambos os modelos de implantação, baseados em porto e offshore, compartilham vantagens exclusivas dos centros de dados flutuantes offshore. Ao combinar os benefícios da infraestrutura marítima com a flexibilidade de implantação, o Consórcio acredita que os centros de dados flutuantes offshore podem ajudar a resolver as crescentes restrições de disponibilidade de terra e fornecimento de energia, bem como a futura expansão da infraestrutura digital. Ao realizar o conceito de centro de dados flutuante offshore baseado em porto, o Consórcio visa acelerar a aplicação prática de centros de dados flutuantes offshore e abrir caminho para sua futura implantação mais longe da costa. Nippon Yusen Kabushiki Kaisha (NYK) Fundada em 1885, a NYK Line é uma empresa de logística global que se concentra em várias formas de transporte marítimo, como logística global e transporte de energia a granel, entre muitos outros negócios relacionados. Operando uma das maiores redes de transporte do mundo, a empresa possui e opera uma frota diversificada de transportadores de automóveis, transportadores de contêineres e transportadores de energia. Nos últimos anos, entramos ativamente em novas áreas de negócios, incluindo o negócio de descarbonização, alavancando o conhecimento e a tecnologia que cultivamos ao longo de muitas décadas no transporte marítimo. Através do desenvolvimento de tecnologia inovadora e criação de negócios, forneceremos novo valor que transcende os limites do negócio de transporte marítimo e contribui para a realização de uma sociedade sustentável. Neste projeto, a NYK Line supervisionará toda a iniciativa e promoverá o desenvolvimento do negócio de centros de dados offshore. NTT FACILITIES, INC. A NTT FACILITIES, INC. tem mais de 100 anos de experiência no projeto, construção e manutenção de edifícios de telecomunicações. A empresa é especializada na construção de centros de dados em larga escala, principalmente no Japão, América do Norte e região da Ásia-Pacífico, contribuindo para aproximadamente 70%* dos centros de dados construídos e operados no Japão. Neste projeto, a NTT FACILITIES realizará a verificação técnica para o projeto, construção e operação estável de centros de dados flutuantes offshore. Através deste processo de verificação, a empresa acumulará know-how de engenharia aplicável não apenas a ambientes offshore, mas também a futuros desenvolvimentos de centros de dados em uma ampla gama de configurações. Eurus Energy Holdings Corporation A Eurus Energy Holdings Corporation atua no negócio de geração de energia eólica e solar globalmente há mais de 30 anos e é a empresa líder do Japão em termos de capacidade de geração de energia eólica conectada à rede. Ao utilizar efetivamente a eletricidade gerada pela energia eólica offshore, que deve se tornar uma importante fonte de energia no Japão, a Eurus Energy visa promover a neutralidade de carbono dos centros de dados e contribuir para a realização de uma infraestrutura digital sustentável. MUFG Bank, Ltd. O MUFG Bank, Ltd. é uma subsidiária do Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group (MUFG), que define seu propósito como "Comprometido em capacitar um futuro mais brilhante" sob os princípios orientadores do MUFG Way. O MUFG está comprometido em enfrentar os desafios enfrentados por todas as partes interessadas, incluindo clientes, para realizar um ambiente e uma sociedade sustentáveis. Neste projeto, o MUFG Bank alavancará sua experiência financeira e ampla rede para explorar oportunidades de cocriação para negócios de centros de dados de próxima geração e considerar o fornecimento de suporte financeiro para empreendimentos relacionados.

artigo.texto: For many Indian businesses, the climate journey begins with a simple exercise: measuring their carbon footprint. But as India’s carbon market takes shape, knowing your emissions is only the starting point. A more important question then emerges: What do these numbers mean for business and what should we do next? India’s Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS) is moving from framework development towards implementation. Greenhouse Gas Emission Intensity (GEI) targets have been notified for energy-intensive sectors, and the compliance mechanism now covers 490 obligated entities across sectors1. For businesses, this means carbon is no longer just a number to measure and report at the end of the reporting cycle. It needs to be understood in the context of how the business operates and where there is scope to improve. Figure 1: Sector Covered Under CCTS CCTS: From Emissions to Performance Under the CCTS compliance mechanism, obligated entities are required to meet GEI targets. This means a company’s emissions are considered in relation to its output or production, rather than simply looking at how much it emits in total. Take a simple example. A company increases production, so its total emissions also go up. But if production grows faster than emissions, it is emitting less for every unit it produces. The opposite can happen too, emissions may come down, but if production falls even more, emissions per unit can increase. That is why total emissions alone do not tell the whole story. How Should Businesses prepare for CCTS? - Know Where You Stand The first step is to determine whether the company or its relevant facilities fall within the notified CCTS compliance mechanism. For covered entities, the management should know: - Notified target for its sector - The relevant baseline period - The applicable unit of production - Current emission intensity This should become a regular management metric rather than something reviewed only during reporting. - Build a Reliable Emissions Baseline A company cannot manage what it cannot reliably measure. Businesses should establish an emissions baseline covering relevant Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions, while assessing material Scope 3 categories where relevant. For CCTS-covered entities, particular attention should be given to the data required for calculating and monitoring GEI performance. The data should be accurate, consistent, traceable and supported by appropriate records. - Identify What Drives Emission Intensity Once the baseline is established, the next question is: what is driving our emissions? Figure 2: Factors Influencing Emission Intensity Identifying these drivers helps companies move from simply reporting an emissions number to identifying where intervention is possible. - Identify Reduction Opportunities The objective should not be to reduce emissions simply because a target exists. Companies should understand which interventions can improve both carbon performance and business efficiency. Potential areas may include: Figure 3: Potential Areas for Emission Reduction The right combination will depend on the company's sector, technology, production process and economics. - Understand the CCTS Gap Companies should establish a clear view of their position: Figure 4: Understanding the CCTS GAP This can help management assess whether existing measures are sufficient or whether additional interventions may be required. For an obligated entity, the assessment also provides an indication of whether the company is likely to outperform its notified GEI target or face a shortfall. Entities that perform better than their notified GEI targets may be eligible to earn Carbon Credit Certificates (CCCs). On the other hand, an entity that falls short of its target may need to purchase CCCs from the market and surrender them against its compliance obligation, in accordance with the applicable provisions of the scheme. - Strengthen MRV and Verification Readiness The CCTS framework includes a Measurement, Reporting and Verification (MRV) system, with annual verification of GHG emissions data and an ecosystem of Accredited Carbon Verification agencies. Companies should therefore ensure that: - Emission calculations are documented - Data sources are clearly identified - Methodologies and emission factors are consistently applied - Supporting records are maintained - Responsibilities for data are clearly assigned - Internal review and controls are established - Data can be traced back to source records The CCTS Readiness Checklist Before the compliance cycle becomes deadline-driven, management should be able to answer: Figure 5: CCTS Readiness Checklist From CCTS Compliance to Carbon Strategy This is where CCTS preparation needs to move beyond compliance and become part of the company’s broader carbon strategy. The biggest risk for businesses is to treat CCTS as a box-ticking exercise, limited to determining applicability, submitting data and meeting a notified target. Such an approach may address the immediate compliance requirement, but it does not help the business understand what is driving its emission intensity or how its performance can be improved. The real value of CCTS lies in using emission-intensity data to identify practical opportunities across operations, technology and investment planning. It can help companies assess energy efficiency, process performance, technology choices, capacity utilization and decarbonisation options in a more structured manner. Figure 6: CCTS Preparation Journey Starting early gives companies the time to understand the factors influencing their emission intensity, assess technically and economically viable reduction measures, and establish reliable data, monitoring and verification systems.
