artigo.texto: In between jeers and boos from an audience of Elizabeth Township residents, a Bucks County-based developer laid out an initial concept for a sprawling data center campus on a 549-acre former landfill bordering the Youghigheny River on Tuesday night. Tim Hendricks, a New Hope resident, told attendees that he hopes to develop a 20-building data center campus and associated natural gas power plant at a township-organized town hall meeting. Communications between Hendricks and local officials obtained by Pittsburgh’s Public Source last week revealed several project plans presented to the township over the summer. Those plans for a 549-acre parcel on Henderson Road near the Youghiogheny River included anywhere from 11 to 28 two-story data center buildings. They were met with opposition from some residents and advocates last week, and hesitancy from the local state representative. Hendricks provided few specific details regarding the final size, scope and environmental impact of the project at the town hall, stressing that the project was still in its development phase. “A project like this obviously has an impact on the community, everybody knows that,” Hendricks said. “We don’t know anything about what’s going to get approved.” Hendricks has not formally submitted any plans to the township or applied for any permits. “Frankly, Elizabeth Township deserves better than another sales pitch about how an industrial project is going to save this community,” said Joelle Whiteman, a township resident and local organizer for the D.C.-based advocacy organization Food & Water Watch, in an interview prior to the meeting. Whiteman is also a member of Protect Elizabeth Township, an environmental advocacy organization that was originally formed to oppose a power plant previously intended for the site. Whiteman, who has been collecting signatures for a petition to stop the development, said she has signed up 350 residents. Attendees, who nearly filled most of the Elizabeth Forward Middle School auditorium, raised questions regarding the water and energy demands of the site, its proximity to houses in the area, the planned natural gas plant and noise concerns. Many in the crowd held signs and wore pins opposing the project. The crowd applauded after one resident shouted, “We don’t want this.” Hendricks said he couldn’t provide specific numbers regarding the site’s water and electricity usage, but said that there was “no way” the site would have an impact on residents’ electricity bills. He also said it would use less water than “typical factories.” The data center buildings would be 2,000 feet away from the nearest homes in the township, a community of manufactured homes called Rolling Hills Village. Noise “will not exceed anything that exists today,” Hendricks said. “Everything is designed so far back from the homes that we don’t have [noise] as an issue.” Hendricks said the data center buildings would be around 150,000 square feet each, which would total 3 million square feet, dwarfing a planned site in Springdale Borough opposed by some local residents. “We’re at step one, maybe step two. There’s probably 100 steps,” Hendricks said, adding that he hadn’t previously attended a meeting this early on in a data center process. He said he’d have to obtain permits from the township, state and potentially the Federal government. State official not convinced State Rep. Andrew Kuzma, R-Elizabeth Township, previously expressed hesitation about some aspects of the project. In an interview after the meeting, he said he is opposed to the project in its entirety. “There is no end user, there are no facts that are in writing and it’s apparent a majority of the residents are against it,” said Kuzma. At the meeting, Hendricks said he was in discussion with end users but did not identify them. Hendricks said his role in the development is to identify the property and obtain all the required permits and approvals. Another person or company would build and operate the property, he said. The proposal became public on Sept. 15, when township commission President Josh Walls announced at a commission meeting that Elizabeth had been approached about a data center project. Tuesday’s town hall was moderated by Eric Piper, a township redevelopment authority member, who asked selected questions submitted by residents. Piper said he received 330 questions from residents that he condensed into 45. Elizabeth Township by the numbers - 22.8 square miles - 12,690 population - 92% white (vs. 76% countywide) - 5.7% in poverty (vs. 11.5%) - $80,589 median household income (vs. $78,548) - $167,000 median value of owner-occupied homes (vs. $227,600) Source: U.S. Census American Community Survey data compiled by Census Reporter The site could generate $125 million in annual tax revenue for the municipality and Elizabeth Forward School District, according to Hendricks’ emails to commissioners. Hendricks reiterated the $125 million number at the town hall. The township expects to bring in around $10.6 million in revenue in 2026, according to its budget. The district brought in $52 million in revenue during the 2024-2025 school year. “Everybody wants this township to be bailed out,” Whiteman said. “Seeing a number that high, I understand why some of the elected officials are like, ‘Oh, this could really save us.’” Walls said that he could not comment on the revenue figures because they were not prepared by the township or local taxing bodies. Walls also stressed that the development is still in the discussion phase. “There’s a lot of residents with very, very serious concerns. Without adequate answers to those, I could not personally support this project moving forward,” he said. artigo.texto: Nearly 4 million abandoned US oil wells could become underground batteries, with geothermal heat boosting storage output by 9.5% Abandoned oil wells may hold a second life as underground energy storage — and a Penn State study suggests trapped geothermal heat could make the whole system 9.5% more efficient. Renewable energy is growing fast — but the grid still goes dark when the wind dies and the sun sets. Solving that problem has sent engineers searching for new ways to store power at scale, from massive battery farms to pumped-water reservoirs. The answer, according to a new Penn State study, may already be in the ground. Across the United States, nearly 4 million depleted oil and gas wells sit largely forgotten — rusting relics of the fossil fuel era. Researchers now believe that infrastructure could be repurposed into something the clean energy transition urgently needs. Regions built around oil and gas extraction — western Pennsylvania, parts of Texas, Appalachia — face real economic disruption as fossil fuel production declines. A grid problem hiding in plain sight Renewable energy’s central weakness isn’t generation — it’s timing. Solar panels produce power at noon; demand peaks at dinner. Wind turbines spin through the night when most of the grid is asleep. That mismatch between supply and demand is one of the biggest structural challenges of the clean energy transition. Energy storage is the obvious fix, but storing electricity at grid scale is harder than it sounds. Battery farms help — they’re just expensive and limited in capacity. Pumped-water reservoirs work well where geography cooperates, which isn’t everywhere. Compressed-air energy storage, or CAES, offers another path. During periods of low demand, excess electricity compresses air and pushes it underground. When demand rises, that pressurized air drives turbines to generate power. It’s a proven approach in principle, but building the infrastructure needed to make CAES commercially viable has kept most projects on the drawing board rather than in the ground. What Penn State researchers discovered The Penn State team, led by Arash Dahi Taleghani — a professor of petroleum and natural gas engineering — proposed a way to change that equation. Their study, published in the Journal of Energy Storage, describes a geothermal-assisted CAES system built around depleted oil and gas wells. The key insight is thermodynamic. Deep underground, rock formations retain significant natural heat, and when compressed air is stored in those hot environments, its temperature rises. Higher temperature means higher pressure, and higher pressure means more energy stored in the same space. Using numerical modeling and simulation, the researchers quantified the effect: placing CAES systems in abandoned wells significantly increased air temperature, boosting efficiency by 9.5% over conventional CAES. “Without taking advantage of the geothermal setup, you could not get enough encouraging numbers,” Taleghani said. That efficiency gain, combined with cost savings from reusing existing wells, is what makes the economics potentially viable. Nearly 4 million wells — already in the ground The scale of America’s abandoned well problem becomes, in this context, an unexpected asset. The Environmental Protection Agency estimates approximately 3.9 million depleted oil and gas wells across the United States. Most sit idle — already drilled, already cased, already connected to the surface. Reusing those wells eliminates one of CAES’s biggest cost barriers. For an industry weighing whether a project pencils out, that upfront savings could tip the calculation. Pennsylvania illustrates both the opportunity and the urgency. State regulators estimate hundreds of thousands of orphaned and abandoned wells within its borders alone. Many are improperly plugged or structurally compromised, and when that happens, they can leak methane — a potent greenhouse gas — into the atmosphere and groundwater alike. Two problems, one solution Sealing a leaking well and converting it into an energy storage asset aren’t competing goals. They’re the same action. “If we use existing wells, we are basically hitting two birds with one stone,” Taleghani said. “First, we are sealing these wells. That stops any potential leaks. And then if we are repurposing these wells for energy storage, we are still using the infrastructure that is in place in these communities.” The social dimension matters too. Regions built around oil and gas extraction — western Pennsylvania, parts of Texas, Appalachia — face real economic disruption as fossil fuel production declines. Repurposing existing infrastructure could preserve technical jobs and keep communities tied to the energy sector rather than left behind by it. This research is part of Penn State’s Repurposing Center for Energy Transition, known as ReCET, and was funded by the U.S. Department of Energy. What comes next The 9.5% efficiency figure comes from modeling and simulation — no real-world pilot has been built and tested yet. The gap between a promising simulation and a functioning commercial system is significant, and worth being clear-eyed about. Challenges remain across several dimensions. Regulatory frameworks for underground energy storage in repurposed wells don’t fully exist. Each candidate well would need structural integrity assessments before it could be safely pressurized, and scaling the concept to a network capable of meaningfully supporting the grid is a separate engineering problem entirely. But if those hurdles can be cleared, the potential payoff is substantial. A validated system could simultaneously accelerate clean energy storage deployment and begin cleaning up nearly four million sources of legacy pollution — the kind of practical convergence that tends to attract serious investment. You can learn more about this discovery here: Penn State. “Reusing old oil and gas wells may offer green energy storage solution.” ScienceDaily

artigo.texto: With participation confirmed from 24 African countries and 45 countries globally, CMAS 2026 will bring together more than 100 speakers, over 50 investors, buyers and financiers, 20 African governments and more than 40 project developers in Kigali from 13 to 15 October. The diversity of participation reflects growing engagement with African carbon markets from governments, project developers, financiers and credit buyers. The international presence will bring African policymakers and projects into direct contact with organisations active across carbon markets globally. For Ibrahim Shelleng, Senior Special Assistant to the President on Climate Finance & Stakeholder Engagement for the Government of Nigeria, the Carbon Markets Africa Summit 2026 represents an opportunity for continental participants to play a central role in determining how the market develops. “This gathering of the leading players in African carbon markets represents a continental ownership in driving the future of carbon markets shaped by Africans, for the benefit of Africa.” Investor and buyer participation will add an important commercial dimension to the gathering. Dedicated Investor Roundtables will provide focused opportunities for capital providers, buyers and project developers to engage directly, while meetings across the summit will allow participants to identify potential partnerships and areas for further engagement. More than 40 project developers and project representatives working across sectors including nature-based solutions, agriculture, waste, clean cooking and carbon removals will also participate, providing investors and buyers with direct exposure to projects from across the continent. For Maggie Kinyanjui, Sourcing Manager, Africa, Climate Impact Partners, greater engagement between project developers, buyers and investors is essential to building a stronger African carbon market. “Africa should not just participate in carbon markets. We should help shape them. The opportunity is to build a market that attracts capital, rewards integrity and ensures that value reaches the countries and communities delivering climate impact.” The timing also coincides with an active period for international carbon markets. These discussions will take place at a time when key international carbon market rules and mechanisms continue to evolve. The Article 6.4 Supervisory Body, which oversees the Paris Agreement Crediting Mechanism, is holding its 23rd meeting this week in Bonn, immediately ahead of CMAS 2026. Amy Rhoades, Chief Communications & Engagement Officer, Carbon Standards, says meaningful engagement across the carbon value chain is critical to the growth of credible carbon removal solutions on the continent. “Africa isn’t waiting for global carbon markets to mature; it’s actively building them. At Carbon Markets Africa Summit, we’re not just sponsoring a conference, we’re engaging the policymakers, entrepreneurs, and buyers who are building the carbon removal ecosystem in Africa. That engagement is the future of credible CDR and that’s why Carbon Standards is in Kigali.” Against that international backdrop, discussions in Kigali will provide an opportunity for African governments and market participants to consider what developments in the global market mean in practice for the continent, while investors, buyers and project developers explore opportunities for greater cooperation. CMAS 2026 is hosted by the Ministry of Environment of Rwanda, with the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and African Development Bank (AfDB) as host organisations, the Development Bank of Southern Africa (DBSA) as host partner and AUDA-NEPAD as strategic institutional partner. With the summit now days away, Emmanuelle Nicholls, Portfolio Director, says the breadth of participation has been particularly encouraging. “The real opportunity lies in bringing decision-makers, financiers, buyers and project developers into the same room. Those conversations can help unlock investment, strengthen project pipelines and accelerate the partnerships needed to scale African carbon markets.” The scale and diversity of participation heading to Kigali reflect a market increasingly attracting attention from governments, investors, buyers and project developers alike. As these groups come together over three days, the focus will shift from market ambition to the partnerships and transactions needed to move implementation forward. CMAS 2026 takes place from 13 to 15 October 2026 at the Kigali Convention Centre in Rwanda.

artigo.texto: The handwritten warning was left at an Amazon data center construction site in suburban Virginia: A dozen pipe bombs scattered throughout the building would explode in the next half hour. Officers rushed to the scene as workers dropped their tools and fled. Bomb-sniffing dogs prowled every corner of the site. That April 22 message in the city of Manassas, authorities soon confirmed, was an empty threat – the latest in a string this year that has rattled the state and communities across the nation. As thousands of new data centers have been built to fuel the booming artificial intelligence industry, escalating public resentment against both the energy-sucking infrastructure and AI itself is roiling small towns and suburban communities from coast to coast, a CNN investigation has found. Police have been called into action to investigate dozens of threats to data centers, from bomb claims etched on bathroom walls to online incitements to “use bullets on city council members” to suggestions that protesters should “unalive” pro-development officials, according to a CNN review of more than 100 police reports filed since last year. Aside from rare cases like an Indianapolis council member whose home was sprayed with gunfire, those threats have rarely led to actual violence – but they’ve eaten up hundreds of hours of police time, alarmed workers and inflamed communities already on edge over the projects. That rising outrage has also inspired a growing police crackdown, including federal agencies tracking data center protests and local cops questioning vocal activists, and even filing criminal charges against critics that have later fallen apart in court. The police records as a whole paint a vivid picture of a national backlash against the rise of data centers and AI reaching a boiling point at a moment when the debate has become a key issue threading party lines ahead of the midterm elections. They also show growing concern among law enforcement agencies about extremist groups at opposite ends of the political spectrum hopping on the anti-data-center bandwagon. “Anti-technology extremist narratives appeal to a broad array of ideological movements – including anarchists, environmental extremists, and white supremacists – creating a common target between otherwise opposing movements,” Colorado state officials warned in an April bulletin for police agencies. A similar California memo warned in June of “a broad range of threat actors… mobilized by AI-related grievances.” Still, some people who have been charged with making threatening comments insist they’re not extremists and do not actually wish violence upon anyone. Rather, they say they were driven to take dramatic action by rising electricity bills, environmental worries or fears of AI. “I’m not really political,” Anthony Hinojosa, an Illinois man arrested in February over an alleged data center threat, told an investigator who interrogated him, according to police recordings. “I feel like we don’t have a vote.” But elected officials say the reports show how the battle over data centers and AI is entering dangerous territory, where they’re fearing for their lives just for doing their jobs. Minneapolis council member Michael Rainville was left pleading in an August letter to his constituents for a more peaceful dialogue over the issue. “Please stop the threats against me and my family,” he wrote. ‘Terroristic threats’ In early February, police in Troy, Illinois fielded multiple calls about ominous statements on a community Facebook page. At the time, the city had been debating whether to clear the way for a roughly 200-acre data center that backers said could create hundreds of jobs. Like similar proposals around America, the once-anodyne pitch had become hugely contentious. Views of data centers have soured significantly this year. Nearly nine in 10 Americans say they’re more concerned than excited about the rise of these facilities, a CNN poll conducted by SSRS found in September. Amid that debate, Troy officials confronted a tirade on Facebook: “My hypothesis is no one would want to be shot at so just start shooting the people involved and it’ll never be built,” Hinojosa, a 33-year-old lawn-care businessman, commented beneath a post about the proposed data center. When a user asked if he was really suggesting violence, Hinojosa responded, “for sure,” screenshots of his posts show. Later that day, officers knocked on his door. “You’re being placed under arrest for making terroristic threats,” an officer said. “I think people are taking things out of context,” Hinojosa told the authorities. He said he had been upset about the proposed data center’s potential strain on electricity and water supply, but he insisted he would not hurt anyone and his words had been misconstrued. “Over a misunderstanding you are literally going to ruin my life,” he said. “It just feels like the mayor of Troy and the city council, they’re just not really listening to the public.” Hinojosa, who described himself in police recordings as a moderate Republican, now faces felony charges for intimidation and harassment through electronic communication. He has pleaded not guilty. His lawyer declined comment, citing an upcoming trial. Hinojosa’s case is one of about 70 among the police reports CNN reviewed that include allegations of threats, intimidation or planned attacks – a collection showing a striking range of anger at AI infrastructure that at times has spilled into serious claims of potential violence. Dozens of additional police reports detail other security concerns, including scuffles at county meetings, calls for police patrols at local officials’ homes and confrontations with data center staff. Some even describe explicit calls for assassinations. “Time to use bullets on city council members. artigo.texto: BYD has unveiled its new Atto 8 at the Paris Motor Show, a large seven-seat electric SUV capable of charging its battery from 10% to 97% in just nine minutes using the manufacturer’s latest charging technology. The Atto 8 will sit at the top of BYD’s European SUV range, above models such as the Atto 3 and Sealion 7. Measuring just over five metres long, it will compete with large electric family SUVs such as the Kia EV9, Hyundai Ioniq 9 and Volvo EX90. Two versions have been announced, both featuring a large 115kWh battery. The rear-wheel-drive ‘Design’ model produces 456hp and offers a claimed driving range of up to 405 miles on a single charge, while the more powerful ‘Excellence AWD’ produces 764hp and has a range of up to 374 miles. The all-wheel-drive model can accelerate from 0-62mph in 4.6 seconds, compared with eight seconds for the rear-wheel-drive version. Rapid charging The Atto 8 will be the first BYD model in Europe to use the manufacturer’s second-generation Blade Battery, introducing its new Flash Charging technology. BYD claims the battery can be charged from 10% to 70% in five minutes, or from 10% to 97% in nine minutes, when connected to a compatible charger. Even in temperatures as low as -30°C, the manufacturer says a 20% to 97% charge can be completed in 12 minutes. These figures are considerably faster than the charging times currently offered by most electric SUVs, although achieving them will require access to BYD’s dedicated Flash Charging network. BYD plans to install 3,000 Flash Charging stations across Europe by the end of 2027. It has not yet confirmed how many will be located in the UK. Seven seats and plenty of equipment The Atto 8 has three rows of seats, with a 270-litre boot when all seven seats are in use. Folding the second and third rows increases luggage space to 1,960 litres, while an additional 136-litre storage compartment sits beneath the bonnet. Inside, both versions feature a 16-inch infotainment touchscreen with Google built-in, a ten-inch digital instrument display and a head-up display. Standard equipment includes leather upholstery, a panoramic glass roof and heated, ventilated and massaging seats in both the front and middle rows. Other features include three-zone climate control, wireless smartphone charging and a small refrigerated compartment that can also be used to keep food and drinks warm. The rear-wheel-drive model comes with a ten-speaker sound system, while the all-wheel-drive version gets a 21-speaker setup. When is it arriving? The BYD Atto 8 is expected to go on sale in European markets during the first three months of 2027. UK pricing, specifications and a customer delivery date have yet to be confirmed.

artigo.texto: Company Establishes Pilot Line in South Korea, Preparing 30MWh Sample Tests for North American Customers LG Energy Solution is accelerating the development of sodium-ion batteries as a potential next-generation growth driver, expanding its battery portfolio beyond conventional lithium-ion technology. The company has established a pilot production line in South Korea and is preparing to validate its technology with North American customers, positioning itself for an early entry into the emerging sodium-ion energy storage system (ESS) market. According to battery industry sources on Oct. 13, LG Energy Solution has established a sodium-ion battery pilot line at its Ochang Energy Plant in North Chungcheong Province. The company is currently conducting vehicle tests involving 12-volt and 24-volt batteries and plans to carry out sample testing for approximately 30 megawatt-hours (MWh) of sodium-ion ESS batteries with North American customers by the first half of 2027. Sodium-ion batteries use sodium instead of lithium as a key raw material, offering the potential for lower production costs and improved thermal safety. One of the technology's main advantages is the abundance and accessibility of its raw materials. Sodium is estimated to be approximately 1,200 times more abundant than lithium in the Earth's crust and can also be extracted from seawater, potentially reducing dependence on geographically concentrated supply chains. Sodium-ion technology also offers promising low-temperature performance. According to the performance figures cited in the industry, certain sodium-ion batteries can retain more than 90% of their charge capacity at temperatures as low as minus 40 degrees Celsius, although actual performance varies by cell chemistry and design. LG Energy Solution is pursuing a commercialization roadmap targeting 2027, initially focusing on automotive auxiliary batteries, uninterruptible power supplies (UPS) and stationary energy storage systems. The company eventually aims to expand into affordable electric vehicles as improvements in energy density make the technology suitable for a broader range of applications. It also plans to work with South Korean materials suppliers to establish a domestic sourcing network and strengthen its supply chain competitiveness. Competition is intensifying as other South Korean battery manufacturers advance their own sodium-ion development programs. Samsung SDI is developing UPS solutions for AI data centers and stationary ESS products using its proprietary technologies, with more detailed mass-production plans expected in 2027. SK On is also expanding its ESS development efforts, targeting completion of sodium-ion battery prototypes in 2027 and commercialization in 2028. Stationary energy storage is emerging as a promising initial market for sodium-ion technology because space and weight constraints are generally less demanding than those for electric vehicles. Although sodium-ion batteries typically have lower energy density than lithium-ion alternatives, their potential cost advantages and low-temperature performance could make them attractive for fixed-site applications. The South Korean government is also seeking to accelerate the commercialization of next-generation battery technologies. At a recent event, the deputy prime minister for economic affairs and the minister of climate, energy and environment pledged support for emerging technologies, including sodium-ion batteries, as part of the government's ambition to lead the next-generation battery market by 2035. Competition from Chinese manufacturers remains a major challenge. CATL, the world's leading battery manufacturer, unveiled a sodium-ion ESS product in June and announced plans for cumulative shipments of 1 gigawatt-hour (GWh) by the end of 2026. An LG Energy Solution representative said the company aims to establish a leading position in the emerging market by securing key technologies and supply chain capabilities at an early stage. The company's progress in customer validation, production readiness and cost competitiveness will be critical to determining how quickly sodium-ion batteries can become a commercially viable addition to its existing portfolio.

artigo.texto: Lithium Metal Battery Lifespan Extended Threefold — South Korean Researchers Overturn Electrolyte Design Convention South Korean researchers have developed an electrolyte technology that extends battery lifespan by nearly threefold by blending two commercial solvents previously deemed unsuitable for lithium metal batteries due to their strong lithium-ion binding properties. The approach resolves the rapid capacity degradation that occurs during high-voltage charging without relying on expensive specialty solvents or high-concentration salts. Professor Song Hyun-kon of the Department of Energy and Chemical Engineering at the Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology (UNIST) and Professor Seo Dong-hwa of the Department of Materials Science and Engineering at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) announced the findings on the 12th. The research was published in the August 11 issue of ACS Nano, an international journal in the nanoscience field. Unlike commercial lithium-ion batteries that use graphite anodes, lithium metal batteries employ lithium metal as the anode, theoretically enabling nearly double the capacity. They have been regarded as a key technology for extending electric vehicle driving range and increasing the capacity of energy storage systems (ESS). However, lithium metal undergoes unwanted side reactions with the electrolyte during charge-discharge cycles, sharply reducing lifespan — a problem that worsens under high-voltage charging conditions. 'Cooperative Solvation' Overturns Conventional Design Principles The research team focused on ethylene carbonate (EC) and sulfolane (SL). Both solvents had been excluded from lithium metal battery design because of their strong binding affinity for lithium ions. During charging, lithium ions must shed surrounding solvent molecules and deposit as metal on the anode surface. When solvents bind lithium ions too tightly, this process is impeded, causing uneven lithium deposition and capacity loss through side reactions with the electrolyte. The team inverted the conventional approach by mixing the two solvents at a 3:7 weight ratio and adding a lithium salt along with a small amount of electrode protective film stabilizing additive. The result defied expectations. Strong intermolecular forces — including hydrogen bonding between EC's hydrogen atoms and SL's oxygen atoms — emerged between the solvents, paradoxically weakening each solvent's individual binding affinity for lithium ions. The team characterized this phenomenon, in which the two solvents mutually influence each other to modulate lithium-ion binding and anion interfacial accessibility, as "cooperative solvation." Hong Jin-ki, the first author of the study, explained: "Mixing two strongly binding solvents to actually weaken their interaction with lithium ions represents a new design principle that overturns conventional electrolyte design wisdom. Beyond lithium metal batteries, this approach could be applied to enhance electrolyte performance in commercial lithium-ion batteries as well." Performance Validated Under High-Voltage Conditions Performance verification results were confirmed quantitatively. The new electrolyte achieved an initial Coulombic efficiency of 98.24% and an average Coulombic efficiency of 99.35%. Coulombic efficiency measures how much of the lithium deposited during charging can be recovered during discharge — higher values indicate less lithium is consumed during charge-discharge cycles. When applied to a high-nickel (NCM811) cathode battery and tested at 25°C with charging up to 4.5V, the battery retained approximately 80% of its initial capacity after 150 charge-discharge cycles. Compared with the conventional carbonate-based electrolyte, which fell below 80% capacity after roughly 50 cycles, the new electrolyte extended cycle life by approximately threefold under the same capacity retention standard. Note: Coulombic efficiency figures for the conventional electrolyte were not disclosed by the research team. Gas generation from electrolyte decomposition and nickel dissolution from the cathode material were also suppressed. This indicates that the major factors accelerating battery degradation under high-voltage charging conditions were simultaneously controlled. Professor Song Hyun-kon stated: "We improved electrolyte performance using commercial solvents without relying on expensive fluorinated solvents or high-concentration salts. We expect this will help extend the operational life of high-capacity lithium metal batteries for ESS and electric vehicle applications." Additional Validation Needed for Commercialization The study is significant in that it improved battery performance using only combinations of low-cost, commercially available solvents. However, 150 charge-discharge cycles remains a limited benchmark for real-world EV or ESS applications, as EV batteries typically require cycle lives in the thousands. Further validation is needed to confirm performance retention under long-term use, diverse temperature conditions, and fast-charging environments. The research team expects the technology can be extended beyond lithium metal batteries to high-voltage lithium-ion batteries and various next-generation battery systems, including sodium-ion and potassium-ion batteries. The research was supported by the Korea Evaluation Institute of Industrial Technology (KEIT) under South Korea's Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy, and the National Research Council of Science & Technology (NST).

artigo.texto: South Korea to Launch International Carbon Market Next Year with Blockchain-Based Credit Issuance South Korea will fully launch an international carbon market next year for trading overseas greenhouse gas reduction credits. The plan involves issuing reduction credits as carbon credits, trading them on the Korea Exchange, and enabling their use for corporate environmental, social, and governance (ESG) activities as well as national emissions reduction target compliance. Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Economy and Finance Lee Hyung-il presided over a meeting of economy-related ministers at the Government Complex Seoul on the 12th, where the government finalized the "Detailed Implementation Plan for the Global Verified Carbon Market (GVCM)." The GVCM is a market for issuing and trading carbon credits generated from overseas greenhouse gas reduction projects. The government has now specified the operational framework based on the roadmap announced in December last year. The core of this plan lies in ensuring credit credibility and activating trading. The government has decided to apply blockchain technology to data management. A dual-track approach will be adopted: core information such as project operators, reduction volumes, unique identification numbers, and reduction methodologies will be recorded on the blockchain, while remaining data will be stored in conventional databases. The intent is to apply the technology selectively to core information rather than uploading all data to the blockchain, thereby securing both management efficiency and stability. Credits will initially be issued in standard electronic form and traded on South Korea's voluntary carbon market exchange. Going forward, the government plans to consider parallel issuance in digital asset form, taking into account issuance and trading volumes, the status of digital asset legislation, and market confidence. The market's name has also been changed from "Global Voluntary Carbon Market" to "Global Verified Carbon Market." The change reflects the intent to encompass regulatory markets as well, based on the judgment that the previous name could give the impression that credits were only usable in voluntary markets. Credits are divided into two categories depending on whether the host country grants transfer authorization. "GVCM A" credits, which have received authorization, can be used for both regulatory compliance—such as fulfilling investor countries' Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) or the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA)—and ESG activities. "GVCM NA" credits, which have not received authorization, are limited to corporate voluntary environmental activities. However, GVCM NA credits can be converted to GVCM A status if the host country subsequently grants corresponding adjustment approval. The government is also reviewing options to link the GVCM with South Korea's domestic emissions trading scheme or greenhouse gas target management system, provided that credibility requirements, corresponding adjustments under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, and domestic legal participation conditions are met. The issuing body will consist of a board of directors, a technical oversight committee, and a secretariat. The board, composed of member countries, will determine policy direction and oversee the technical oversight committee. The technical oversight committee will decide on technical matters such as credit issuance, with expert members recommended by developing countries able to participate in issuance decisions. The secretariat will handle issuance, management, and registry operations. The Global Green Growth Institute (GGGI) is currently serving as interim secretariat, with a separate secretariat to be established upon official launch. The government is also prioritizing participation from developing countries. Governance has been designed so that developing countries can reflect their needs in operational processes and gain experience in carbon market operations. The approach respects participating countries' sovereignty when establishing operational regulations, emissions baseline setting, and sustainable development guidelines. Project sectors will be identified based on participating countries' development needs and South Korea's technological competitiveness. Examples include nature-based solutions such as mangrove forest restoration, agricultural waste treatment, methane capture, and energy efficiency improvements. The government is also in discussions with international organizations including the World Bank (WB) and the Green Climate Fund (GCF) to convert reduction volumes generated from existing reduction projects into GVCM credits. International carbon markets are gaining attention as a means to achieve national greenhouse gas reduction targets. This comes as major Paris Agreement parties anticipate difficulty in meeting their 2030 NDCs through domestic reduction efforts alone. However, the lack of standardized international market criteria has led to ongoing controversy over credit credibility and actual reduction effectiveness. The government has taken note of the international carbon market's growth potential. According to MSCI projections, the carbon credit market is expected to grow to $7 billion–$35 billion by 2030 and $45 billion–$250 billion by 2050. The government's assessment is that, as the boundary between voluntary and regulatory carbon markets weakens internationally, credits usable in both markets must be developed. The government plans to collaborate with GGGI to leverage networks such as the Indo-Pacific Economic Framework (IPEF) and the Asia-Pacific Carbon Market Roundtable (APCMR) to secure participating countries. artigo.texto: Seres Deepens Partnership with CATL as AITO Cumulative Deliveries Surpass 1.2 Million Units Chinese new energy vehicle manufacturer Seres (09927.HK) announced the signing of a long-term strategic cooperation deepening agreement with battery giant CATL (03750.HK), with both parties further consolidating their strategic partnership in areas including battery safety, supply chain coordination, and global ecosystem cooperation. Following the announcement, Seres' share price rose more than 4% in early trading on the Hong Kong stock exchange. Under the agreement, Seres' AITO brand has been equipped exclusively with CATL batteries across its entire lineup since the brand's inception, with cumulative deliveries surpassing 1.2 million units to date. Building on this milestone, AITO will continue to use CATL batteries across all models on a long-term basis, with cooperation spanning core areas including the expansion of "plant-within-a-plant" production capacity, the construction of a supercharging energy replenishment ecosystem, and the acceleration of global expansion. The signing ceremony was held in Chongqing on October 10, attended by Seres Group Chairman Zhang Xinghai and CATL Chairman Robin Zeng. Cooperation Focuses on Three Key Areas The deepening agreement clarifies both parties' continued commitment to the Chongqing production base. The Phase II "plant-within-a-plant" project for premium battery packs at Seres' super factory will be accelerated, while both parties will also deepen cooperation in supercharging, battery swapping, and battery services, jointly exploring innovative pathways for new energy vehicle energy replenishment ecosystems. On the global expansion front, both parties will work together to expand into overseas markets. The agreement also specifies that CATL will continue to increase investment in Chongqing, supporting the city's efforts to build a trillion-yuan premium intelligent connected new energy vehicle industrial cluster. Capital Market Reaction Seres' share price rose more than 4% in early trading on the first trading day following the announcement, with gains narrowing to 2.84% at HK$34.74 (approximately $4.4) as of press time, with trading volume of HK$13.6042 million (approximately $1.7 million). Market observers noted that the deepening cooperation between Seres and CATL helps stabilize the AITO brand's battery supply chain, particularly in premium battery pack capacity expansion. The "plant-within-a-plant" model effectively shortens supply chain distances and reduces logistics costs, which carries positive implications for Seres' gross margin improvement. Industry Background Seres and CATL have a long-standing cooperative relationship. The AITO brand, jointly developed by Seres and Huawei as a premium intelligent electric vehicle brand, has used CATL batteries across its entire lineup since launch, with both parties establishing deep ties at the battery technology and supply chain levels. The timing of this agreement coincides with intensifying competition in China's new energy vehicle market. As competitors such as BYD and Xiaomi continue to expand market share, battery supply stability and cost control have become critical competitive factors for automakers. Seres' decision to deepen its strategic cooperation with CATL at this juncture is being interpreted by the market as an important move to secure supply chain safety and enhance long-term competitiveness. Chongqing, as Seres' key production hub, has been actively promoting the development of the intelligent connected new energy vehicle industry in recent years. CATL's continued investment in Chongqing also aligns with the local government's policy objective of building a trillion-yuan industrial cluster.

Under the terms of the deal, Vattenfall will secure 100MW/400MW-hours (MWh) from a planned BESS near Meeden in Groningen province. The total project, developed and managed by Vopak, will have a capacity of 150MW and is expected to begin commercial operations in the second quarter of 2028. The agreement aims to support the balancing of fluctuations between electricity supply and demand as the Dutch power system incorporates increasing amounts of renewable energy. Battery storage enables the absorption of surplus electricity from renewable sources during periods of high production and can return power to the grid when demand rises or renewable output drops. According to Vattenfall, the secured BESS capacity will contribute to greater flexibility in its operations and aligns with the company’s objective to contract at least 1.5GW of BESS capacity across its core markets. Vattenfall wholesale energy head Erik Suichies said: “As the energy system becomes increasingly renewable, flexibility plays a crucial role in maintaining balance between supply and demand. Battery storage helps make better use of renewable electricity and contributes to a more reliable and efficient energy system. “We are pleased to partner with Vopak and support the development of large-scale energy storage in the Netherlands.” For Vopak, the deal represents a further step in its business expansion into electrical energy storage. Vopak battery energy storage solutions business development vice-president Jarno Veldhoven said: “With our aim to provide reliable and affordable battery systems to our customers we are excited to have Vattenfall as a long-term partner.” The partnership brings together Vattenfall and Vopak, both established players in the Dutch energy sector, and combines large-scale storage infrastructure with market expertise in flexibility optimisation. The companies aim to enhance the resilience of the Dutch electricity grid and support the integration of renewable energy sources. In July 2026, Vopak completed the acquisition of a 79% controlling interest in Green Energy Storage, a Netherlands-based developer specialising in BESS.

artigo.texto: Policy Update Anushree Khare BACKGROUND The Transformation of Industrial Carbon Pricing In the words of William D. Nordhaus: “Those who emit emissions do not have to pay to do so. Those who are affected by those emissions do not receive compensation. In short, carbon emissions represent a market failure which will require a price to be explicitly set.” During the formative years of industrial development, all forms of industry were able to treat the natural environment as their “free disposal” site for the effluents resulting from the combustion of fossil fuels. Economists recognized the discrepancy between the social cost of pollution and the private cost of pollution. They proposed remedies via tax (Pigou) or market based systems using well-defined property rights (Coase). These models provide the basis for modern-day international environmental policy. Although CO2 was historically viewed as a necessary by-product of large scale heavy industry, it is today becoming formally quantifiable and tradable on corporate balance sheets. Developing countries face two competing demands during this transition: - Expanding their primary sector to create jobs and build physical infrastructure and - Limiting emissions within an increasingly constrained global carbon budget. Market-based instruments in India initially focused on conserving energy before attempting to limit emissions directly. The Energy Conservation Act, 2001 empowered the Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE) to implement the Perform, Achieve and Trade (PAT) Scheme in 2012. Under PAT, each facility would receive plant-specific energy reduction targets. Facilities achieving better than specified standards were rewarded. Energy-Saving Certificates (ESCerts) could also be traded among facilities across different industrial sectors. Although significant cumulative energy savings were realized by PAT’s application, its reliance on Specific Energy Consumption (SEC) had a fundamental flaw. It failed to ensure emissions reductions when a facility optimizes its SEC but increases its total carbon emissions due to fuel choice or expanded production such as switching to carbon-intensive captive coal or scaling clinker output. India sought to address this divergence and bring its domestic policy into alignment with its revised Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC), specifically reducing the emissions intensity of GDP by 45% by 2030 compared to 2005 levels. To achieve this goal, India passed the Energy Conservation Amendment Act in 2022. Subsequent to the Ministry of Power issuing notification no. F.No. 12/14/2019-EMD dated June 28, 2023, titled “Carbon Credit Trading Scheme”, India transitioned from regulating input energy efficiency denominated in Mtoe… to regulating greenhouse gas emissions intensity measured in (tCO2e) the form of Carbon Credit Certificates (CCCs).With CCCs, India created a formal compliance mechanism where industrial emissions can be priced directly at the plant level. FUNCTIONING Market Design and Compliance Architecture The CCTS architecture distinguishes between two discrete but complementary markets: - a mandatory compliance market for energy-intensive sectors - a voluntary offset mechanism for non-obligated project developers Governance Nodes National Steering Committee for Indian Carbon Market (NSC-ICM): The NSC-ICM is co-chaired by the Secretary of the Ministry of Power and the Secretary of the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MOEFCC). It is responsible for governing the market design as well as establishing the trajectory for the market and providing guidance with respect to the Indian Carbon Market (ICM) registry. Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE): The BEE acts as the Administrator of the market. It shall recommend sectoral trajectories; define the methodology for Monitoring, Reporting and Verification (MRV) under the Indian Carbon Market and manage the ICM registry. Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC): The CERC regulates the trading of Carbon Credit Certificates (CCCs) in secondary markets through the approved domestic power exchanges such as India Energy Exchange (IEX) and Power Exchange India Limited (PXIL). Accredited Carbon Verification Agencies (ACVAs): Independent third-party auditors accredited by the BEE to audit annually the amount of greenhouse gases claimed by each production unit according to ISO 14064/14065 standards. The Rate-Based Intensity Metric The CCTS is different from the EU ETS because, instead of imposing an absolute emissions limit (i.e., limiting total gross tonnage of CO₂ emitted), the CCTS applies a rate-based emissions intensity cap-and-trade system. That design represents the economic realities of emerging economies such as India: industrial capacity must expand to meet infrastructure and urbanization demands, but it must do so cleanly. The compliance metric is the Greenhouse Gas Emission Intensity (GEI), defined as follows: GEI = (Direct Scope 1 Emissions + Indirect emissions Scope 2) Gross Equivalent Production Unit - Direct emissions (Scope 1) include emissions resulting from fossil fuel combustion, calcination, catalytic reactions, and on-site chemical reductions. - Indirect emissions (Scope 2) represent electricity consumed by a facility using state- and year-specific grid emission factors provided by the Central Electricity Authority (CEA). - Production units are measured per standard industry segment (for example, crude steel in metric tonnes,cement in clinker-adjusted metric tonnes; primary aluminium). PERFORMANCE The transition into CCTS is structured in multi-year compliance cycles, with the inaugural cycle covering FY 2025–26 and FY 2026–27. The scheme initially subsumes the heavy industrial sectors formerly regulated under PAT. Compliance targets are reset in triennial trajectories, requiring facilities to outpace business-as-usual technological advancements to generate surplus credits. artigo.texto: Planning commission weighs future of data centers in New Orleans The City Planning Commission has been tasked with recommending guidelines for data center creation in the city. Planning commission weighs future of data centers in New Orleans The City Planning Commission has been tasked with recommending guidelines for data center creation in the city. The New Orleans Planning Commission failed to approve a recommendation for data center creation guidelines Tuesday. Planning staff were tasked with creating definitions for data centers and making a recommendation for which, if any, should be allowed in New Orleans. The planning staff's recommendation was to prohibit large and hyperscale data centers, and allow small and medium data centers in certain parts of the city, with certain restrictions. According to their definitions, small data centers must be no greater than 20,000 sq. ft. and consume no more than 5 megawatts of power. Medium data centers must be no greater than 100,000 sq. ft. and consume no more than 20 megawatts of power. Large and hyperscale data centers are greater than 100,000 sq. ft. and consume greater than 20 megawatts of power. Planning commissioners decided the recommendation was not ready to go to City Council. They voted against approving the recommendation, and are now asking City Council to extend the moratorium on new data center creation. City Council approved a one-year moratorium back in January, in order to give the planning staff time to make a recommendation and come up with definitions. In the meantime, the commission is asking the planning staff to make amendments to the recommendation. They want to change the definitions for small and medium data centers. They are suggesting a small data center be reduced from 20,000 sq. ft. to 10,000 sq. ft. and the maximum usage be reduced from 5 megawatts to 3 megawatts. They also want the maximum size for a medium data center to be reduced from 100,000 sq. ft. to 50,000 sq. ft. and the maximum energy usage to be reduced from 20 megawatts to 15 megawatts. Their other suggestion is to increase the buffer between homes and data centers from 500 ft. to 1000 ft. The decision came after several people spoke against the recommendation during public comment, and a small group gathered outside City Hall ahead of the vote. The demonstration was led by members of the Party for Socialism and Liberation. They believe no type of data center should be allowed in New Orleans. They cited quality of life and environmental concerns, and said any new data center would put a strain on utilities. According to the planning staff report, it was found that many small data centers already exist in New Orleans. There are at least four operating in the downtown area. The report also says the biggest concern with new data centers is their impact on water and power usage. The item to approve a recommendation was originally on the agenda for the commission's August 25 meeting, and was deferred multiple times.

artigo.texto: This transition process creates a huge demand for resources to invest in technological innovation, transform production methods, use energy efficiently, and reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Expanding resources for green transformation At the seminar "Credit Policy and Carbon Market: Unlocking Green Capital Flows" organized by the Finance-Investment Newspaper on October 14th, Deputy Governor of the State Bank of Vietnam Nguyen Ngoc Canh emphasized that, in addition to resources from the State budget, capital markets, and money markets, developing new market mechanisms is crucial in mobilizing resources for green transformation. According to the Deputy Governor, by establishing quotas, measuring emission reduction results, and forming transaction prices for quotas and carbon credits, the carbon market creates a mechanism to convert emission reduction results into economic value. This provides businesses with additional motivation and resources to continue investing in the transition process, instead of relying primarily on bank credit. In recent years, the banking sector has gradually improved its policy framework, promoting green credit and managing environmental and social risks in lending activities. Capital flows are directed towards areas that bring environmental benefits, especially sustainable agriculture , green energy, and projects that reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Data from the State Bank of Vietnam shows that by the end of June 2026, outstanding green credit reached over VND 856 trillion, an increase of 9.87% compared to the end of 2025. During the period 2017-2025, green credit maintained an average growth rate of over 20% per year. Outstanding loans are mainly concentrated in agriculture, forestry, fisheries, and biodiversity conservation, accounting for over 31%; green energy accounts for nearly 28%. Notably, outstanding loans that have undergone environmental and social risk assessment reached over VND 6.2 million trillion, equivalent to more than 31.33% of the total outstanding loans in the entire economy. However, according to Deputy Governor Nguyen Ngoc Canh, the important thing for green credit is not only that the capital is disbursed to projects identified as green, but also that the results of energy saving, emission reduction, and environmental protection achieved by borrowers can be verified. From this perspective, green credit and carbon markets have a mutually supportive relationship. Credit provides resources for businesses to innovate technologically, improve energy efficiency, and thus generate emission reductions. Conversely, when carbon markets operate effectively, the recorded and commercialized emission reductions can generate additional revenue, improve cash flow, support debt repayment capacity, and enhance credit quality. Speaking at the conference, Pham Van Hoanh, Editor-in-Chief of the Finance-Investment Newspaper, argued that if the carbon exchange is the infrastructure of the market, then credit policy, the banking system, and the capital market are the driving forces for the green transition process. According to Mr. Pham Van Hoanh, a market that wants to develop sustainably needs not only an exchange, commodities, and trading regulations, but also liquidity, data, verification mechanisms, trust between buyers and sellers, and a sufficiently strong financial ecosystem. The crucial issue is how to gradually make carbon value a reliable factor in financial decisions, helping capital flow to the right, effective projects. Unblocking bottlenecks Despite the significant potential of the carbon market, translating emission reduction results into actual cash flow still faces considerable challenges. A project's ability to reduce emissions does not automatically guarantee carbon credits, buyers, or a sufficiently stable revenue stream for banks to consider granting credit. Dr. Nguyen Thi Thu Ha, Director of the Training School for Cadres and Deputy Head of the ESG Steering Committee of Agribank, analyzed that the capital needs for emission reduction projects often arise right from the preparation and implementation phases. Meanwhile, carbon credits can only be generated after emission reduction results are measured, reported, verified, and all related procedures are completed. The time gap between investment needs and the time when carbon revenue is generated is a challenge for both businesses and credit institutions. For agriculture and forestry, the dispersed nature of production makes the cost of measuring and verifying emission reduction results relatively high. If each producer has to carry out the entire process themselves, economic efficiency is difficult to guarantee. Meanwhile, linkages through cooperatives, raw material areas, or production chains require clear data governance mechanisms and benefit sharing. Based on this practice, Agribank proposes a "two-tiered cash flow" assessment principle. In this principle, cash flow from core production and business activities remains the foundation for debt repayment; carbon revenue is only considered as a supplementary source, depending on the level of legal, technical, and commercial certainty. From an international perspective, Mr. Bui Minh Giap, Chief Economist of the Asian Development Bank (ADB) in Vietnam, noted that the carbon market provides economic incentives for emission reduction, while credit provides the capital for investments. Of this, the capital needed for adaptation and resilience enhancement is approximately US$254 billion, and for emission reduction is approximately US$114 billion. artigo.texto: South Korea is set to launch the Global Verified Carbon Market (GVCM) next year, a platform for trading overseas greenhouse gas reduction credits. The initiative will utilize blockchain technology to record core data, aiming to enhance the credibility of carbon credits. Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Economy and Finance Lee Hyung-il announced the finalized “Detailed Implementation Plan for the Global Verified Carbon Market (GVCM)” after a meeting of economy-related ministers. The GVCM will facilitate the issuance and trading of carbon credits derived from international greenhouse gas reduction projects. Credits will be categorized into two types: GVCM A, usable for both regulatory compliance and voluntary environmental, social, and governance (ESG) activities when host countries authorize transfers, and GVCM NA, restricted to voluntary ESG purposes. The government plans to sign letters of intent with potential participating countries at COP31 next month and is in discussions with the World Bank and Green Climate Fund to convert existing project credits. Blockchain Integration for Enhanced Credibility A key feature of the GVCM is the integration of blockchain technology for data management. Core information, including project operators, reduction volumes, unique identification numbers, and methodologies, will be recorded on the blockchain. Other data will be stored in traditional databases. This selective application of blockchain aims to balance management efficiency with data integrity and stability. Initially, credits will be issued in electronic form and traded on South Korea’s voluntary carbon market exchange. The government is considering parallel issuance in digital asset form in the future, contingent on trading volumes, the evolving digital asset legislation, and market confidence. The market’s name change from “Global Voluntary Carbon Market” to “Global Verified Carbon Market” reflects its expanded scope to include regulatory markets. Dual-Track Credit System and Governance The GVCM’s dual-track credit system differentiates based on host country authorization. GVCM A credits, with host country approval, can satisfy regulatory requirements such as Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) under the Paris Agreement or the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA), as well as voluntary ESG activities. GVCM NA credits, lacking such authorization, are limited to voluntary corporate environmental initiatives but can be upgraded to GVCM A if corresponding adjustment approval is later granted. The government is also exploring links between the GVCM and South Korea’s domestic emissions trading scheme, provided that credibility standards, Paris Agreement Article 6 requirements, and domestic legal conditions are met. The issuing body will comprise a board of directors, a technical oversight committee, and a secretariat. The Global Green Growth Institute (GGGI) is currently serving as the interim secretariat. Governance structures are designed to ensure direct participation from developing countries, allowing them to influence operational processes and gain experience in carbon market management. The project sectors will align with participating countries’ development needs and South Korea’s technological strengths, encompassing areas like mangrove restoration, agricultural waste treatment, methane capture, and energy efficiency improvements. The anticipated growth of the international carbon credit market, projected by MSCI to reach $45 billion, $250 billion by 2050, underscores the significance of standardized and credible market criteria. The GVCM aims to address current controversies surrounding credit credibility and actual reduction effectiveness by establishing clear international market criteria. The government plans to leverage networks such as the Indo-Pacific Economic Framework (IPEF) and the Asia-Pacific Carbon Market Roundtable (APCMR) to secure participating countries. Full-scale operations are expected to commence after the establishment of the issuing body next year and the specification of project structures. The GVCM initiative aligns with the broader trend of major financial institutions exploring blockchain for core operations, as detailed in reports on how major financial institutions move core operations onto blockchain networks. This move also echoes the strategic planning seen in projects like the CENTEL Blockchain Roadmap, which pairs CNT participation with network plans, as highlighted in CENTEL Blockchain Roadmap Pairs CNT Participation With Network Plans. The involvement of entities like the World Bank and Green Climate Fund in such initiatives reflects a growing institutional interest in blockchain-based solutions for global challenges, similar to how Chainlink Co-Founder presented blockchain finance at a major banking conference. Frequently asked questions - What is the Global Verified Carbon Market (GVCM)? The GVCM is a platform South Korea will launch next year for trading overseas greenhouse gas reduction credits, utilizing blockchain for enhanced credibility. - How will blockchain be used in the GVCM? Blockchain technology will be applied to record core data, such as project operators and reduction methodologies, to ensure the credibility and stability of carbon credits. - What are the two categories of GVCM credits? Credits are divided into GVCM A, usable for regulatory compliance and ESG activities, and GVCM NA, limited to voluntary ESG purposes, based on host country transfer authorization. - Who will be involved in the GVCM's issuing body? The issuing body will consist of a board of directors, a technical oversight committee, and a secretariat, with plans for developing countries to participate directly. - When will the GVCM fully launch? The GVCM will fully launch starting next year, with plans to sign letters of intent at COP31 next month and establish the issuing body in the coming year.

artigo.texto: Regarding “Data centers are hot. We should use Lake Michigan to cool them” (Oct. 6): I think the idea of cooling coils under Lake Michigan for data centers has merit. Of course, a thorough environmental assessment would need to be done prior to moving forward. And with one reservation, the idea of data centers occupying former industrial sites in Chicago is also attractive. But what about the impact regarding electrical usage? Does Chicago have the capacity to support possibly multiple data centers? What impact would there be on residents’ electric bills if this were to go forward? While this is good news, there are still a few hurdles to get over before the city leaps forward. — Tom Canning, Homer Glen Cooling proposal’s flaws Regarding Joe Holberg’s op-ed, his mayoral candidacy, math knowledge and business ownership are impressive. But should he be promoting vast, expensive projects such as coolant loops “miles, perhaps tens or hundreds of miles, long and coiled far offshore at or near the bottom” of Lake Michigan to cool data centers? Holberg addresses the concern that this cooling loop plan for data centers might “cook the lake.” He writes that “setting a sealed coffee thermos in a swimming pool” wouldn’t change the pool’s temperature. He misunderstands heat exchange parameters with that inelegant comparison — a sealed, insulated thermos is not comparable to a metallic coil. He states without evidence that “we likely could not even marginally increase the temperature or create an environmentally noticeable impact.” Tell that to the fish. Taking his inexact idea of heat exchange even further, hot data centers “should have windows.” As every Chicago resident without air conditioning knows, opening windows does not satisfy the need to cool, and it would only add to atmospheric heat. He must know the heat has to go somewhere, as he quixotically writes “climate change increases the overall temperature throughout the year.” While seeming to minimize or disregard the impact of data centers on humans and the environment, Holberg spends several paragraphs addressing the saving of money. Normally, when I read commentary supporting the building of these projects, there seems to be an unbalanced emphasis on money, including arguments for creating jobs and adding to local tax bases. Does money have an overriding importance? What is the effect to our neighborhoods and communities, to our noise and pollution levels, to our air and water quality? Midway, Holberg proposes “a water and environmental study before a single pipe goes in, with the results and data published where anyone can read it.” Perhaps he should have opened with that. — Patrick Comer, Clarendon Hills More study is needed Joe Holberg’s op-ed contains sufficient information to earn further review and consideration. I was initially concerned about a few of the points, including that miles of coil in Lake Michigan would “not even marginally increase the temperature” of the lake. He saves himself by suggesting a study. Opening and closing windows to take advantage of Chicago weather vicissitudes seems simplistic, so it, too, needs deep study. More information about Toronto and Cornell University is intriguing and ought to provide a few clues. Although touting Cornell University’s prowess is gutsy, if not a welcome “first step”-like program. — Terrance W. Gainer, Wheaton Who committed these crimes? Regarding the story “Aldermen advance $261M police misconduct settlement” (Oct. 6): There is a proposed settlement to resolve 16 lawsuits filed against the city of Chicago by people who claim that they were victims of police misconduct by a former Chicago detective and that they were convicted of crimes they did not commit. Dozens of men have been issued certificates of innocence. Important questions come to mind: If the plaintiffs did not commit these crimes, who did commit the crimes? Have these investigations been reopened? Has anyone new been charged with or convicted of the crimes in question? Don’t the victims and their families deserve fresh investigations to identify the real perpetrators? — John Mulvey, Chicago Helping Chicago’s seniors Why do millions of budgeted 2026 funds go unspent while low-income seniors continue to struggle to access help for critical home repairs and modifications? We are still waiting. Approximately $6.3 million in unspent 2025 funds associated with the city’s Home Repair Program is being carried over into the next budget. At the same time, approximately $28 million in federal Community Development Block Grant funding is identified for administrative costs, including about $20.8 million carried over from 2025 and a new allocation of $7.3 million. artigo.texto: Nas colinas de Águas de Santa Bárbara, um município de cerca de 7 mil habitantes no interior de São Paulo, o Patria Investimentos está testando uma nova tese climática para o seu Reforest Fund. O Patria entrou no mercado de capital natural olhando para uma das apostas mais recorrentes da transição climática: o carbono. Acabou encontrando uma oportunidade menos óbvia – e bem mais saborosa: o avocado. É na região centro-oeste do estado de São Paulo que a gestora está investindo cerca de R$ 100 milhões para produzir a fruta, ainda pouco conhecida dos brasileiros. O projeto combina produção agrícola, restauração ambiental e geração de créditos de carbono. O Patria comprou duas fazendas que juntas somam mil hectares, e fechou uma parceria com a Jaguacy, que é um dos maiores produtores e exportadores brasileiros da fruta e vai tocar a operação. Hoje o Brasil produz pouco mais de 60 mil toneladas do abacate Hass, uma variedade criada na Califórnia há um século e que reina no avocado toast e nas saladas dos americanos. Boa parte da produção nacional é voltada para a exportação. O Reforest Fund foi desenhado para combinar diferentes fontes de capital – e diferentes interesses. De um lado estão investidores que olham para a agenda de restauração, biodiversidade e descarbonização. De outro, o capital mais tradicional, que precisa enxergar retorno, risco e previsibilidade de receita. “Ao longo do desenho do fundo, a pergunta era quanto da exposição ao mercado de carbono queríamos ter. É uma solução relevante, porque muitos dos esforços de descarbonização passam pelo mecanismo de offset. Mas o mercado tem se desenvolvido de uma forma que exige soluções mais customizadas. A gente sabia que o avocado preenchia essa lacuna,” disse Pedro Faria, sócio do Pátria e co-CEO da vertical de high growth. O fundo nasceu com a meta de mobilizar R$ 2 bilhões — e já chegou perto disso. Na primeira rodada, anunciada pelo Patria em 2025, foram captados R$ 100 milhões com a Desenvolve SP, a agência de fomento do Governo de São Paulo; David Vélez, o fundador do Nubank; Teresa e Candido Bracher, reconhecidos ambientalistas; e o Enseada, o family office dos Larragoiti. Mais recentemente, o fundo atraiu novos investidores – entre eles a Vale – e chegou a R$ 160 milhões. No momento, o Patria está em negociações com investidores institucionais internacionais. Outra frente de captação vem de instrumentos de capital catalítico – que aceitam maior risco, menor retorno ou prazos mais longos . No início do ano, o fundo foi um dos sete selecionados na chamada pública de mitigação climática que vai destinar R$ 4,3 bilhões em aportes do BNDESPar. Nessa frente, o veículo pode receber até R$ 500 milhões. Além disso, o Patria também vai acessar recursos do Fundo Clima e do terceiro leilão do Eco Invest. Os recursos do capital catalítico funcionam como uma espécie de colchão para atrair investidores. “O capital catalítico passa a ser uma camada de proteção. Nesse modelo, o dinheiro que pode ser ‘perdido’ é utilizado antes dos recursos do investidor tradicional,” disse Faria. A lógica adotada é que cada investidor também possa enxergar uma porta de entrada diferente para o mesmo ativo. Para uma empresa com metas de descarbonização e restauração, o projeto entrega atributos ambientais. É o caso da Vale, que entrou no fundo para acessar os créditos gerados pelo sequestro de carbono. Já para um investidor financeiro, a produção agrícola e a receita associada aos créditos ajudam a compor a equação de risco e retorno. “No nível da operação é um arranjo agroflorestal, no nível do fundo é um arranjo multifacetado de investidores entrando em cotas,” disse o executivo. Foi nesse desenho que o avocado ganhou espaço. Estima-se que o mercado global da fruta movimente cerca de US$ 20 bilhões por ano. O Brasil ocupa hoje a sétima posição entre os produtores, mas, na visão de Faria, tem condições para avançar bastante. “Quando você olha a questão de custo, competitividade e acesso a dinheiro, não há nenhuma razão para que o Brasil não esteja entre os três maiores produtores mundiais de avocado.” Para o Patria, os mercados europeu e asiático são o foco para a exportação. Em 2025, Japão e Chile passaram a importar a fruta do Brasil. A parceria com a Jaguacy, que cultiva 1200 hectares de avocado e atende clientes como Carrefour e Pão de Açúcar, garante não só a operação das fazendas como também o acesso à infraestrutura de processamento e aos canais de distribuição. A região de Águas de Santa Bárbara escolhida não foi por acaso. As propriedades estão em uma área de solo fértil, altitude adequada e disponibilidade de água, mas que também passou por ciclos de agricultura, pecuária e monoculturas que degradaram parte do território. O cultivo será feito em sistema agroflorestal, combinando as fileiras de avocado com espécies nativas, que protegem as árvores frutíferas contra potenciais danos causados pelo vento. Dos quase 1 mil hectares, a previsão é plantar cerca de 100 hectares neste semestre. A primeira colheita virá em quatro anos. O projeto também servirá como laboratório para o que pode vir depois. O Patria já identificou café e cacau como próximas culturas a serem desenvolvidas e vê espaço para levar o modelo a outros biomas. Para Faria, as mudanças climáticas estão tornando a produção de alimentos uma questão cada vez mais estratégica para o capital. A demanda global cresce, enquanto eventos climáticos mais frequentes aumentam o risco de choques de oferta. É essa combinação que transforma a agricultura resiliente em uma tese de investimento: produzir mais, restaurar áreas degradadas e, ao mesmo tempo, construir cadeias de alimentos menos vulneráveis às mudanças do clima. O avocado do Patria deverá ganhar mesas mundo afora. O carbono, por sua vez, fica como crédito para o planeta.
