artigo.texto: With participation confirmed from 24 African countries and 45 countries globally, CMAS 2026 will bring together more than 100 speakers, over 50 investors, buyers and financiers, 20 African governments and more than 40 project developers in Kigali from 13 to 15 October. The diversity of participation reflects growing engagement with African carbon markets from governments, project developers, financiers and credit buyers. The international presence will bring African policymakers and projects into direct contact with organisations active across carbon markets globally. For Ibrahim Shelleng, Senior Special Assistant to the President on Climate Finance & Stakeholder Engagement for the Government of Nigeria, the Carbon Markets Africa Summit 2026 represents an opportunity for continental participants to play a central role in determining how the market develops. “This gathering of the leading players in African carbon markets represents a continental ownership in driving the future of carbon markets shaped by Africans, for the benefit of Africa.” Investor and buyer participation will add an important commercial dimension to the gathering. Dedicated Investor Roundtables will provide focused opportunities for capital providers, buyers and project developers to engage directly, while meetings across the summit will allow participants to identify potential partnerships and areas for further engagement. More than 40 project developers and project representatives working across sectors including nature-based solutions, agriculture, waste, clean cooking and carbon removals will also participate, providing investors and buyers with direct exposure to projects from across the continent. For Maggie Kinyanjui, Sourcing Manager, Africa, Climate Impact Partners, greater engagement between project developers, buyers and investors is essential to building a stronger African carbon market. “Africa should not just participate in carbon markets. We should help shape them. The opportunity is to build a market that attracts capital, rewards integrity and ensures that value reaches the countries and communities delivering climate impact.” The timing also coincides with an active period for international carbon markets. These discussions will take place at a time when key international carbon market rules and mechanisms continue to evolve. The Article 6.4 Supervisory Body, which oversees the Paris Agreement Crediting Mechanism, is holding its 23rd meeting this week in Bonn, immediately ahead of CMAS 2026. Amy Rhoades, Chief Communications & Engagement Officer, Carbon Standards, says meaningful engagement across the carbon value chain is critical to the growth of credible carbon removal solutions on the continent. “Africa isn’t waiting for global carbon markets to mature; it’s actively building them. At Carbon Markets Africa Summit, we’re not just sponsoring a conference, we’re engaging the policymakers, entrepreneurs, and buyers who are building the carbon removal ecosystem in Africa. That engagement is the future of credible CDR and that’s why Carbon Standards is in Kigali.” Against that international backdrop, discussions in Kigali will provide an opportunity for African governments and market participants to consider what developments in the global market mean in practice for the continent, while investors, buyers and project developers explore opportunities for greater cooperation. CMAS 2026 is hosted by the Ministry of Environment of Rwanda, with the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and African Development Bank (AfDB) as host organisations, the Development Bank of Southern Africa (DBSA) as host partner and AUDA-NEPAD as strategic institutional partner. With the summit now days away, Emmanuelle Nicholls, Portfolio Director, says the breadth of participation has been particularly encouraging. “The real opportunity lies in bringing decision-makers, financiers, buyers and project developers into the same room. Those conversations can help unlock investment, strengthen project pipelines and accelerate the partnerships needed to scale African carbon markets.” The scale and diversity of participation heading to Kigali reflect a market increasingly attracting attention from governments, investors, buyers and project developers alike. As these groups come together over three days, the focus will shift from market ambition to the partnerships and transactions needed to move implementation forward. CMAS 2026 takes place from 13 to 15 October 2026 at the Kigali Convention Centre in Rwanda.

artigo.texto: NBC’s comedy show “Saturday Night Live” mocked “Shark Tank” investor Kevin O’Leary and his plans to build the massive Stratos data center in Utah — with a fake O’Leary calling it “the most evil name of all time.” “All I want is to buy up 40,000 acres of God’s untouched splendor and replace it with a very loud computer that steals your job,” actor James Austin Johnson said Saturday night from the show’s “Weekend Update” desk, wearing a bald cap to impersonate O’Leary, aka “Mr. Wonderful.” “Is it going to take up precious water? Absolutely. Is it going to provide a necessary service? Who’s to say?” Johnson’s O’Leary continued in a calm voice echoing the real O’Leary’s cadence. “But on the flip side, it’s going to make me a tremendous amount of money, and I think that’s great.” Anchor Colin Jost then noted that most Americans don’t want data centers near them, and Johnson’s O’Leary agreed, saying, “that’s why I’m building one in Utah.” He held up a map of Utah, with the Stratos site in Box Elder County ringed with a red target zone, which he said would be the area affected by noise and water pollution. “You have to understand — I don’t live there,” he said. Jost countered that other people do live there. “You’re missing the point,” the fake O’Leary replied. “That’s not real to me. … Those are Sims.” Johnson’s O’Leary then referenced one of the real O’Leary’s “Shark Tank” failures: “When I missed out on Scrub Daddy, I learned a very valuable lesson, which is I’m going to destroy the world.” Jost asked about the defamation lawsuit O’Leary is facing from activists protesting the Stratos project. The fake O’Leary noted that “yes, I made the mildly inflammatory claim that every single person in Utah who opposes me is a paid Communist super-agent from China. Was I wrong? Perhaps. But just because they’re not doesn’t mean they aren’t.” Last month, the real O’Leary’s lawyers filed a motion to dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that no “reasonable viewer” would have taken his claims that China funded his opposition as fact. Johnson’s O’Leary concluded the three-minute skit with another observation based on the real O’Leary’s “Shark Tank” experience: “When I missed out on Bombas socks, I could have gotten mad. But instead I made a decision: I’m going to make the future go away. And we’re doing just that in Utah.” Utahns by an overwhelming margin, 76%, don’t want more data centers built in the state, according to a survey released this month by Utah State University’s Community and Natural Resources Institute.

artigo.texto: Johannes Linder, Director, System Design & Innovation at BELECTRIC, a member of the Elevion Group, shared ideas on optimizing system designs for PV-plus-storage hybrid power plants, particularly in Germany, at the TaiyangNews Solar Power Plants & Storage Conference 2026. His presentation focused on hybrid system design optimization for engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) firms and investors. Linder shared a German co-located PV + battery energy storage system (BESS) system design case study with a 1:1 PV + BESS AC-coupled configuration as a reference project. In 2024, BELECTRIC simulated the project and found that a 58 MW BESS size corresponds to the project's highest Net Present Value (NPV). NPV, which indicates how much value a project is expected to add to a business in current monetary terms, is considered a key performance indicator (KPI) for optimization. Back then, the company could adjust BESS and PV size by optimizing the ratio of fixed-tilt and tracker-based systems within a given land area to get maximum BESS revenues. Linder argued that although these optimization types still apply to grey BESS, which charges itself from either PV or the grid, Germany has changed a few frameworks. These include regulations backed by grid oversizing, such as flexible grid connection agreements (FCAs), grid connection restrictions for grey BESSs, right balancing between the grid operator's acceptance and project profitability, and a focus on green BESS. Green BESS allows only renewable energy to charge it. From an investor's perspective, the company follows optimized system design in three stages: 1) Set the project frameworks; 2) Define technology and design parameters; and 3) Check sensitivities/critical assumptions. However, Linder noted that these procedures make hourly battery simulation challenging, with many possibilities and scenarios. The company has adopted a ‘practical’ four-step approach to address challenges. They are: pre-selection of PV system designs, BESS optimization for pre-selected designs, PV + BESS market value analysis and clustering, and simulation of all relevant scenarios. In a nutshell, this clustering of market value analysis reduces the need to handle too many simulations. Linder shared a case study for a PV + green BESS hybrid plant system design with an AC-coupled system architecture, no grid restrictions, and within 33 ha of land in Central Germany, following these steps. The simulation results showed that the optimized BESS size is 40% of PV MWp with a corresponding backup duration of 4 hours. For PV + BESS optimization, a 45 MWp PV array mounted on a fixed mounting structure with a 3P module mounting architecture at a 10° inclination angle showed the highest NPV and ranked first. In comparison, modules mounted on trackers, those installed along the east-west (E-W) direction, and those mounted vertically relative to flat land ranked at 178, 782, and 3,005, respectively.

artigo.texto: Planning for development is notoriously local in Pennsylvania, but one of the largest and most contentious building proposals in the region is now heading into a county-run public input process. Springdale Borough is one of around two dozen municipalities in Allegheny County that do not have ordinances establishing their jurisdiction over subdivision and land use decisions. Instead, the county carries out the process. Over the next two weeks, Allegheny County Economic Development’s (ACED) Planning Division will hold public meetings as part of this process for the proposed development of a data center campus, which has drawn opposition from residents of the borough and the surrounding community due to concerns over noise, air pollution and transparency from the developer Allegheny DC Propco LLC. The first meeting, which will be held virtually tonight, has even drawn a watch party organized by Save Allegheny Valley Environment (SAVE). SAVE Treasurer Marty Garrigan said that group has been educating residents on the process dictated by the county’s SALDO, or Subdivision and Land Development Ordinance. For Garrigan, the preferred outcome would be a denial. “We’re hopeful. In the worst case scenario, they would approve this with conditions. But that’s a scary thought, too,” he said. Anna Jewart, who serves as land use counsel for Allegheny DC Propco LLC, which recently rebranded as Dynamo DC, said that the SALDO process for major developments can be broken down into three steps: zoning approval at the local level, approval of the preliminary land development plan and final approval of the plan. The developer is on the second step. The ACED Planning Division has 90 days from its Oct. 28 meeting at Springdale Borough Municipal Building to issue its decision, she said. The county will accept written comments through Nov. 30. A preliminary approval would not allow Allegheny DC Propco to start building any structures or complete any grading work, she said. But because the Governor’s Responsible Infrastructure Development Standards now require local approvals to be complete before data center developers apply for Department of Environmental Protection permits, Jewart said an approved preliminary plan would allow Allegheny DC Propco to apply for those. “This is a big hurdle. And it takes a lot of work, a lot of engineering. But there is much more that has to be done still,” she said. One application, dozens of issues Last December, Allegheny DC Propco received approval from Springdale Borough Council to build the data center complex as a conditional use. The borough also granted the developer six variances. Lessons of Springdale: Towns must prepare if they want any say over data centers At the municipal level, the preliminary plan submitted as part of the SALDO process typically provides a broad overview of what’s being proposed, said Brigitte Meyer, a staff attorney for the environmental advocacy organization PennFuture. But that also depends on the town’s zoning ordinance and the level of detail it requires. The county’s SALDO requires preliminary applications to include a range of documents, including a description of the project and its purpose and maps of the development’s proposed location and surrounding developments. Depending on a site’s conditions, a developer might also have to submit reports that assess soil contamination, landslide proneness and subsidence risk. Allegheny DC Propco’s preliminary plan proposes transforming 47 acres of the former Cheswick Generating Station site into a data center campus that would include power generators, utility yards and stormwater facilities to support its operations. In response to the 182-page application, ACED’s Planning Division asked for correction of several inconsistencies. Some of those issues include: - Certification from the Allegheny County Health Department that it was notified about the proposal, as required, wasn’t included in the application. Notification to the Health Department would also trigger air pollution requirements for the facility, according to the county’s review. - Several concerns surrounding the application’s treatment of the St. Mark’s Lutheran Church cemetery, which sits to the west of the proposed data center campus. The review notes that there’s a call to move earth in proximity to existing headstones there, and a proposal to relocate access to the cemetery would require building a bridge. - Despite the plan showing that parts of the site are contaminated with methylnaphthalene and arsenic, the application did not signal that any remediation had been done. Two consultants — Mackin Engineers and Consultants and GFT Infrastructure, Inc. — also conducted reviews of the plan on behalf of the county and borough. Similar to the county’s internal review, the third parties took issue with missing or incomplete information throughout the plan. Jewart, counsel for the developer, said that the length of the county’s review was not surprising for a plan of this size. She also said that it’s standard for these reviews to include several reminders to obtain certain permits, some of which she said the developer cannot apply for at this time due to the state’s GRID Standards. Allegheny DC Propco has submitted a letter in response to the county’s review, she said, and plans to submit an updated plan ahead of the Oct. 28 meeting. In June, county Sustainability Director Brittany Prischak said the county is working on a model data center development ordinance that municipalities can adopt, but that the county was still figuring out its role in the evolving space. Harrisburg also has a role. According to the state’s data center permit tracker, the developer already has state water obstruction and encroachment permits, but still has to submit permit applications related to erosion control and brownfield cleanups. Mia Hollie is the economic development and housing reporter for Pittsburgh’s Public Source. She can be reached at mia@publicsou

artigo.texto: Words by Oliver Milman photographs by michael hauptman Our world is already beset by a climate crisis, galloping biodiversity loss, and a plague of plastic that has reached nearly every waterway and mountaintop. It may be unfortunate timing, then, that another—and perhaps final—environmental frontier is now rapidly coming into view: space. A slew of industrial projects designed for Earth’s orbit or other celestial bodies are currently underway. Some, like mining the moon for helium or reflecting sunlight back to Earth after dark with giant mirrors, remain out-there aspirations that may never materialize. Others are moving more quickly. Some of the world’s wealthiest people are determined that even if they cannot yet colonize other planets, they will soon be able to encircle our own with fleets of space-based data centers. Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin has applied to the Federal Communications Commission to launch 51,600 data centers, while Elon Musk’s SpaceX has even grander ambitions—a constellation of 1 million facilities, with testing set to begin next year. Google on October 1 launched Project Suncatcher, its orbital data center initiative exploring how to power AI in space, into low Earth orbit. The prospect of banishing data centers to space may appeal to people on Earth who abhor their explosive growth and decry their ravenous use of energy and water. In the United States, the issue has become so politically toxic that living next to a data center polls even worse than residing beside a nuclear plant. Musk has said space-based data centers will prove “ridiculously better” than their terrestrial counterparts. “Elon (Musk) and others in the industry are like, ‘Let’s take the data centers that no one likes in your backyard—it seems like there’s a lot of consensus on that—and put them into space where they won’t bother anyone,’” Jared Isaacman, administrator of NASA, said in August on the Pod Force One podcast. Isaacman has said separately that while countries like China escalate their space ambitions, the U.S. can win the “space race for sure, but the AI race, too.” The potential environmental payoff is substantial. The Department of Energy projects that data centers could account for as much as 12% of U.S. electricity demand by 2028, driven largely by the growth of AI. A large terrestrial data center can require around 100 megawatts of power and around 200,000 gallons of water a day for cooling, according to the Government Accountability Office. Moving some of that computing into orbit could, in theory, reduce the need for new power infrastructure, freshwater, and land on Earth. In sun-synchronous orbit, satellites could also receive near-continuous sunlight, allowing them to generate solar power without the nighttime interruptions affecting solar farms on the ground. Space could also shift one of the most resource-intensive parts of computing: cooling. Rather than consuming freshwater to carry away heat, an orbital data center would use large radiators to release that heat into space, though cooling in a vacuum remains technically difficult. For proponents, the appeal is that networks of solar-powered satellites could eventually take on some of the computing now driving the construction of energy- and water-intensive facilities on Earth. Whether that produces a net environmental benefit depends on what it takes to manufacture, launch, maintain, and ultimately dispose of them. But some experts are more wary. “Many issues occur with data centers in space that wouldn’t happen on Earth,” said Daniel Capper, a professor of philosophy at the Metropolitan State University of Denver and a proponent of space environmentalism. Even if the daunting cost and logistics of launching data centers into orbit can be overcome, adding 1 million large structures to low Earth orbit raises uncomfortable questions about energy, debris, and what happens when those structures eventually fall back to Earth. “A land-based data center can’t fall on your head. If one falls in this way, upon a city or in the ocean causing a tsunami, we are in big trouble.” Space-based data centers would be roughly the size of a tennis court, with only a fraction of the area housing computing equipment. The rest would be devoted to shielding the hardware from radiation, dispersing heat, and generating power. Should large, 5-gigawatt data centers make it into orbit, the solar arrays required to power them would also be sprawling—measuring more than six square miles, according to Starcloud, a company developing space-based data centers. All of that would require hundreds of rocket launches, generating additional emissions while adding large satellites to a band of space already cluttered with human-made debris. Around 30,000 pieces of tracked debris currently hurtle through orbit at roughly 10 times the speed of a bullet, posing a threat to satellites and other infrastructure we depend on for everyday functions such as GPS. “We have already entered a period of unstable debris growth in low Earth orbit; the amount of stuff in orbit will continue to grow even without human intervention,” said Cole Donovan, an advocate for the Stand Up for Science group who previously worked for the U.S. government on a new “air traffic control” system for various space actors. Satellites are equipped with automated collision-avoidance systems, but adding another million large objects could increase the risk of Kessler syndrome, a theoretical chain reaction in which collisions create more debris, which in turn triggers further collisions until parts of orbit become impossible for new missions. “We are already at the beginning of Kessler syndrome; if it gets extreme we will have to remain grounded,” said Capper. artigo.texto: New BYD Act 8: everything we know The new 7-seater electric SUV, which made its debut at the Paris Motor Show, sits at the top of the brand’s European range. It is set to arrive on European markets in 2027 Key points BYD unveiled the new Atto 8 – a seven-seater electric SUV that will sit at the top of the Chinese brand’s range – in a world premiere at the Paris Motor Show. Measuring 5.04 metres in length, 1.99 metres in width and 1.76 metres in height, the new Atto 8 features a three-row seating layout, complemented by a 270-litre boot capacity that expands to 1,960 litres when the second and third rows are folded down. The exterior design stands out for its Matrix LED headlights, slim daytime running lights and all-new light clusters, whilst the spoiler and aerodynamic features improve the car’s aerodynamic efficiency. There are two versions of the new SUV, both powered by the same second-generation 115 kWh Blade Battery. BYD Act 8: high-tech interiors Inside, the 2.39 m² panoramic roof, the 10.25-inch digital instrument cluster, the 26-inch head-up display and the 15.6-inch central touchscreen with Google Built-in immediately catch the eye. The seats in the first two rows are heated, ventilated and feature a massage function, whilst those in the third row have adjustable headrests. Three-zone climate control and leather upholstery come as standard. The standard equipment is rounded off by a 50 W on-board wireless charging pad and several USB Type-C ports. BYD Act 8: available engines The entry-level version of the BYD Atto 8 is the rear-wheel-drive Design model, which features a single 340 kW electric motor – equivalent to 462 cv – with a maximum torque of 365 Nm. It accelerates from 0 to 100 km/h in 8 seconds. The 115 kWh battery delivers a range of 653 km, the highest in the range. At the top of the range is the Excellence AWD. A second motor on the front axle is added to the rear motor to provide all-wheel drive. Power rises to 570 kW, equivalent to 775 cv, whilst torque reaches 775 Nm and acceleration from 0 to 100 km/h takes 4.6 seconds. The battery capacity remains unchanged at 115 kWh, but the combined range stands at 602 km – a result attributable to the presence of the second motor and the all-wheel drive system. BYD Atto 8: battery and charging Both versions feature the second-generation 115 kWh Blade Battery. This is the same technology that the Chinese brand uses in its flagship models, characterised by a high level of safety and remarkable energy density. New to the European market is the introduction of Flash Charging technology: for the first time on a BYD car sold in Europe, the battery can go from 10 per cent to 97 per cent in just 9 minutes. This places the new Atto 8 amongst the models with the fastest charging times in its segment. The combination of such a generous battery, two clearly differentiated power levels and ultra-fast charging makes the Atto 8 one of the most technically innovative new models amongst the seven-seater electric SUVs currently on the market.

artigo.texto: Professor da Universidade Estadual da Califórnia em Fullerton compara a expansão digital à infraestrutura de óleo e gás. Quando um data center chega a uma cidade, a promessa costuma aparecer na forma de arrecadação, aluguel de terrenos e obras de infraestrutura. O impacto mais persistente, porém, pode ficar longe dos usuários que utilizam serviços de nuvem, videoconferências e plataformas digitais. Uma pesquisa conduzida por David Adams, professor associado de Administração Pública da California State University, Fullerton, nos Estados Unidos, aponta que a expansão desses complexos segue uma lógica semelhante à do setor de petróleo e gás: o benefício se espalha, enquanto parte importante do custo permanece no território onde a instalação funciona. A análise foi apresentada em entrevista publicada em 12 de outubro de 2026 e reúne estudos do professor sobre energia, água, infraestrutura e atuação do poder público. Segundo a California State University, Fullerton, havia cerca de 7.000 edifícios de data centers em operação, propostos ou em construção nos Estados Unidos em 1º de setembro de 2026, com aproximadamente 2.100 unidades operando em cerca de 1.400 locais. O lugar escolhido depende de cabos e eletricidade Os data centers são estruturas que concentram servidores responsáveis por armazenar, processar e distribuir dados. Para funcionar, precisam de conexão rápida com redes de fibra óptica e fornecimento contínuo de energia. Por isso, o levantamento de Adams identificou uma tendência de localização próxima às rotas de cabos já existentes e às áreas com oferta energética considerada mais conveniente. Essa escolha produz efeitos diferentes dos gerados por uma fábrica tradicional. O empreendimento pode recolher impostos sem necessariamente criar uma grande demanda por moradias, escolas, transporte coletivo ou contratação permanente de trabalhadores. Para municípios e condados, a combinação parece vantajosa: entra uma nova fonte de receita, mas a população não cresce na mesma proporção. O problema aparece quando a análise considera o ciclo completo da instalação. Um campus de grande porte pode consumir eletricidade equivalente à de uma cidade pequena. Além disso, muitos equipamentos precisam ser resfriados continuamente, o que pode ampliar a pressão sobre os recursos hídricos, especialmente em regiões sujeitas a secas. A água economizada pode reaparecer na usina O sistema de resfriamento cria uma escolha difícil. Quando o operador utiliza ar para reduzir o consumo direto de água, a instalação tende a demandar mais eletricidade. Se essa energia for produzida em uma usina que também utiliza água, parte do consumo apenas muda de lugar dentro da cadeia de fornecimento. Esse deslocamento torna o impacto menos visível para a comunidade. A água pode não ser retirada diretamente pelo data center, mas ainda ser necessária na produção da energia que mantém os servidores ligados. A consequência é uma disputa por recursos que envolve empresas, concessionárias, governos locais, órgãos reguladores e moradores. A comparação com o petróleo e gás se estende ao risco de abandono. Adams avalia que a evolução tecnológica pode tornar determinados complexos pouco úteis ou economicamente inviáveis, deixando uma infraestrutura de grande porte sem função. O paralelo é feito com poços abandonados e órfãos, cuja manutenção e recuperação podem acabar recaindo sobre o poder público. O caso do Arizona expõe a divisão de responsabilidades Um episódio em Tucson, no Arizona, mostra como a aprovação pode atravessar várias instituições. Um empreendimento associado à Amazon Web Services adquiriu terras no condado, mas encontrou resistência da cidade para obter acesso à água. O projeto foi redesenhado para utilizar resfriamento a ar e, depois, buscou autorização para a conexão elétrica junto à Arizona Corporation Commission, reguladora estadual do setor de energia. Enquanto moradores participaram de manifestações e o conselho municipal rejeitou o projeto, a comissão estadual aprovou o acordo de fornecimento de energia. Como o condado já havia negociado o terreno, as decisões tomadas por diferentes órgãos produziram um resultado que contrariava a posição expressa no município. A situação, segundo Adams, deixa o público diante de uma dúvida prática: qual governo tem, de fato, poder para interromper ou alterar a instalação? O pesquisador afirma que um único empreendimento pode envolver até 15 governos, com participação de estados, municípios, condados, distritos especiais e comissões reguladoras. A fragmentação dificulta a fiscalização e pode fazer com que moradores procurem a instituição errada para apresentar reclamações sobre água, energia, zoneamento ou impactos ambientais. O que a experiência pode ensinar à Amazônia O debate também interessa aos estados amazônicos, onde a expansão da infraestrutura digital convive com rios estratégicos, sistemas elétricos ainda desiguais e municípios com capacidade administrativa variada. Acre, Amapá, Amazonas, Maranhão, Mato Grosso, Pará, Rondônia, Roraima e Tocantins podem enfrentar discussões semelhantes caso novos complexos de processamento de dados sejam planejados na região. A principal lição é que a autorização não deveria considerar apenas a área ocupada ou a arrecadação esperada. É necessário avaliar a origem da energia, a disponibilidade hídrica durante períodos de estiagem, a capacidade das redes de transmissão, o destino dos equipamentos ao fim da vida útil e quem pagará por eventuais reforços na infraestrutura. Na Amazônia, essa análise ganha peso porque o custo ambiental pode atingir comunidades que não são as principais beneficiárias dos serviços digitais. Uma instalação pode atender usuários de várias partes do país e do mundo, enquanto a demanda por água, eletricidade, estradas e terrenos se concentra em um município específico. artigo.texto: Peugeot is looking to bring back the spirit of its iconic RCZ coupe with the Peugeot RCZ Vision, a futuristic electric sports car concept that combines French design, advanced battery technology and a renewed focus on driving pleasure. Positioned as a successor to the original Peugeot RCZ, produced between 2009 and 2015, the RCZ Vision previews the brand’s vision for high-performance electric mobility. It introduces Peugeot’s new “Feline Future” design language while showcasing technologies intended to shape the company’s next generation of vehicles. The concept’s headline specifications include 500 horsepower, up to 600 km (373 miles) of range and a targeted energy consumption of 11.5 kWh/100 km. It also features a solid-state battery developed with Factorial Energy and a 1,000-volt electrical architecture designed to deliver exceptionally fast charging. Peugeot has not presented the RCZ Vision as a conventional production-car launch. Instead, it serves as a design and technology manifesto, offering a glimpse of what future Peugeot models could look like. Peugeot RCZ Vision Revives an Iconic Coupe The original Peugeot RCZ became one of the French automaker’s most distinctive modern models thanks to its sculpted bodywork, low roofline and characteristic double-bubble roof design. Although production ended in 2015, the coupe has since developed a following among enthusiasts and collectors. The RCZ Vision revisits that heritage with a more futuristic interpretation. Its proportions combine a low, wide stance with muscular bodywork, a compact-looking glass cabin and flowing surfaces intended to improve aerodynamic efficiency. The concept also introduces Peugeot’s “Feline Future” design philosophy, built around five principles: freedom, courage, elegance, inner force and instinct. Together, these ideas aim to create a car that looks powerful without appearing unnecessarily aggressive. At the front, ultra-slim lighting elements reinterpret Peugeot’s signature three-claw light design. An illuminated emblem, a distinctive RCZ graphic and intricately detailed air intakes give the concept a dramatic appearance. The rear continues the same minimalist approach, with integrated three-claw lighting and an active spoiler that remains hidden when the car is stationary and deploys while driving to improve aerodynamic performance. Peugeot has also retained the original RCZ’s distinctive double-bubble styling, reinterpreting it with slimmer, seemingly floating roof arches. The glass-bubble concept extends across much of the vehicle, creating a light and futuristic silhouette. 500 HP and Up to 373 Miles of Electric Range Beyond its styling, the Peugeot RCZ Vision showcases an ambitious electric powertrain concept. Peugeot targets 500 horsepower and a driving range of up to 600 km, equivalent to approximately 373 miles. The company also cites energy consumption of 11.5 kWh/100 km on the WLTP combined cycle, although the figure is marked as subject to confirmation. If achieved in practice, that combination would make the RCZ Vision an especially efficient proposition for a high-performance electric sports coupe. Its final range and consumption would, however, depend on the production specification, driving conditions and other factors. The concept is based on an architecture derived from Stellantis’ STLA One platform concept, designed to accommodate next-generation technologies and different battery solutions. A key highlight is the solid-state battery developed in collaboration with Factorial Energy. Solid-state batteries are attracting interest across the automotive industry because their potential advantages include higher energy density, reduced packaging requirements and improved charging performance. In the RCZ Vision, the battery is paired with a 1,000-volt electrical architecture. Peugeot targets a charging time of just 10 minutes to increase the battery’s state of charge from 10% to 80%. These figures describe the concept’s intended capabilities rather than verified performance from a production vehicle. Nevertheless, they illustrate Peugeot’s ambition to combine sports-car performance with more efficient energy use and shorter charging stops. Hypersquare Steering and Brake-by-Wire Technology The RCZ Vision is also a showcase for Peugeot’s next-generation driving technology, particularly its Hypersquare steering control and electronic vehicle-control systems. Hypersquare replaces the conventional round steering wheel with a distinctive rectangular control featuring four circular openings. The layout places key functions within easy reach, allowing the driver to keep their hands on the steering control. Combined with steer-by-wire technology, Hypersquare eliminates the traditional mechanical connection between the steering control and the front wheels. Instead, electronic systems manage steering inputs and adjust the steering ratio according to vehicle speed. At low speeds, the system is designed to make parking and tight manoeuvres easier by reducing the amount of steering input required. At higher speeds, the steering response is adjusted to provide greater stability and smoother control. The concept also introduces brake-by-wire technology, replacing the conventional hydraulic connection between the brake pedal and braking system with electronic control. Peugeot says this approach can improve braking precision and integrate regenerative braking more effectively, helping recover energy during deceleration. The RCZ Vision additionally previews Level 2++ automated-driving capabilities, including a hands-free function available on demand in city and highway environments. The precise operating conditions and availability of these features have not been detailed for a production vehicle. Importantly, Peugeot says the production version of Hypersquare will also feature in the next-generation Peugeot E-208, indicating that at least part of the technology is intended to extend beyond the concept itself. artigo.texto: UK bespoke raw materials company Avocet Materials Group is developing specialist lithium-ion battery components in Cheshire for high-performance applications including Formula One (F1), aerospace, defence, electric vehicles and energy storage, as it expands its advanced manufacturing and research capabilities. The family-owned business has established a 29-strong manufacturing and R&D operation in Holmes Chapel, producing components it says were previously manufactured only in Asia. It exports 99% of its battery products to international markets including China, Japan and the US. At the heart of its technology portfolio are lead tabs, small but critical metal components that connect a lithium-ion battery cell to an external circuit. Their properties can affect battery weight, conductivity and reliability, making precision manufacturing essential for demanding applications. One of Avocet’s innovations is Flyweight, a bimetallic lead tab designed for pouch cells and used in F1 battery applications to reduce battery system weight. The company is also developing DryTab, a next-generation surface technology that has secured government backing through the DRIVE35 programme. Avocet moved from specialist metals distribution into manufacturing during the Covid-19 pandemic. Supported by a £1.4m Innovate UK grant through the Advanced Propulsion Centre and further investment, it now operates through three businesses: Avocet Precision Metals, Avocet Battery Materials and Avocet Research Centre. Kieren Hall, CEO, said: “When you think that five years ago we didn’t manufacture anything, what we’ve achieved is pretty remarkable. We’ve built a manufacturing operation from scratch, developed our own technology and we’re now making specialist components for lithium-ion batteries in Cheshire for some of the most demanding applications in the world. “We’re exporting 99% of our battery products and selling into countries with some of the biggest battery industries in the world, including China and Japan. For a business of our size to be competing internationally at that level is something we’re incredibly proud of.” Turnover has grown from £1.5m to £3.5m, with sales increasing by around 25% this year. To support further expansion, Avocet is working with Made Smarter North West on manufacturing systems and digital infrastructure. The company has secured a £13,000 grant towards a £75,000 enterprise resource planning system, scheduled to go live in January 2027. The system will integrate operations across the business and support productivity and capacity growth. Avocet is also exploring automated inspection technology and artificial intelligence to improve manufacturing efficiency and decision-making as it develops its battery technology portfolio. artigo.texto: Los Angeles plans floating solar and iron-flow battery system on Encino Reservoir to generate and store electricity Los Angeles is pushing its green shift forward by deploying floating solar on a reservoir. The United States is actively pursuing its national climate goals to meet rising energy demands more sustainably. However, urban regions with the highest consumption and emissions struggle to raise renewable capacity. Ultimately, unused municipal reservoirs and floating photovoltaics can unlock local energy resilience, meeting rising demands more sustainably. Spatial limitations are a major bottleneck, which is why developers are turning to floatovoltaics. Will Los Angeles’ latest approved project serve as a vital blueprint for other cities? How U.S. cities struggle to progress in the clean transition The United States currently ranks 19th in the global renewable energy transition. Domestically, clean power generation accounts for 30% of total electricity supply. Despite this, the nation is still far from reaching its national climate mandates. This is because urban centers have concentrated, dense populations, industrial hubs, commercial infrastructure, and heavy transit networks. Cities’ extreme density accounts for more than 70 percent of global energy-related carbon emissions. In the U.S., electricity consumption and building operations drive roughly 40 percent of national greenhouse gas output. As industrial and transport electrification and AI data center infrastructure expand, power consumption will continue to surge. Consequently, energy demand is rising much faster than new power generation capacity can be added. This leads to a growing supply gap, threatening the stability of regional grids. To bridge this gap, rapid deployment of utility-scale renewable energy sources is key. Unfortunately, urban planners face significant spatial and economic hurdles. Structural obstacles faced in cities trying to go green Solar power has become a core pillar in America’s renewable energy shift, with capacity reaching major milestones in recent years. Currently, the nation’s total operational solar capacity is 299.4 gigawatts. However, this generation is highly concentrated in specific regions, and cities still face challenges raising solar production. Traditional utility-scale photovoltaic facilities require vast open land, roughly 5 to 10 acres per megawatt. Densely built urban regions cannot provide this footprint. Furthermore, U.S. permitting bottlenecks slow solar growth. This is because developments must navigate overcrowded grid distribution, complex zoning laws, and historic preservation rules. Additionally, limited undeveloped real estate in cities commands a premium market price. These high land acquisition costs make urban ground-mounted photovoltaic projects uneconomical. As a result, urban planners are forced to turn to dual-use infrastructure like floatovoltaics to generate localized clean power. In Los Angeles, a floating solar pilot project has been approved after the LADWP filed a formal Notice of Determination. The floatovoltaics project on the Encino Reservoir California’s solar-and-storage portfolio is set to increase, with the San Fernando Valley region of Los Angeles leading in innovation. A new floating solar project will be constructed directly on the Encino Reservoir. LADWP owns and manages the 960-acre site, which means private land acquisition was completely bypassed. The project will comprise a 5-megawatt floatovoltaic array covering 10 acres of the reservoir surface. There will also be a 30-kilowatt mounted solar system spanning 4,000 square feet on adjacent land. A 5-megawatt iron-flow battery system will ensure long-duration energy storage. Meanwhile, on-site transformers, inverters, and switchgear will be connected directly to an existing distribution line. The project achieved fast-tracked approval Regulatory review was quickly completed by filing a Mitigated Negative Declaration under CEQA. This bypassed a lengthy Environmental Impact Report. Environmental evaluations confirmed no significant ecological impact. By bypassing standard zoning delays, construction can proceed rapidly. With the environmental clearance completed, LADWP can proceed to procurement and development. The goal is to operationalize this project as a core clean energy pilot. The combined deployment of floating solar and local battery storage creates a vital blueprint for other urban regions nationwide. Ultimately, unused municipal reservoirs and floating photovoltaics can unlock local energy resilience, meeting rising demands more sustainably. Anke Maree is a writer with a clear and engaging editorial style. Her work focuses on making complex topics accessible, informative, and relevant for readers across different areas of interest.

artigo.texto: Gasgoo Daily presents a selection of the latest developments from China's automotive industry. Here are the key stories in this edition. CATL, SERES Deepen Strategic Partnership On October 10, 2026, CATL and SERES Group signed a long-term strategic cooperation agreement in Chongqing. All AITO-branded vehicles have been equipped with CATL batteries since the brand's launch, with cumulative deliveries exceeding 1.2 million vehicles. The two companies will continue their full-range battery partnership and deepen cooperation in three areas: Production capacity: Accelerate Phase II construction of the battery plant within SERES' super factory, with planned annual capacity of 10–12 GWh. Combined annual capacity for Phases I and II will exceed 20 GWh once completed. Charging services: Cooperate on fast-charging networks and battery services to build a full-lifecycle service system. Global expansion: Jointly explore overseas markets in Europe, the Middle East and Central Asia. Geely Galaxy ZJ700 Hits Market On October 10, 2026, Geely officially launched the Galaxy ZJ700, its first AI-powered all-terrain SUV, offering six variants. Built on Geely's GTA new-energy off-road architecture, the SUV combines advanced driver assistance, off-road capability and premium comfort. Its Qiankun H7 driver-assistance system uses a Thor-U chip delivering 700 TOPS of computing power. The sensor suite includes a 192-line LiDAR, three millimeter-wave radars, 11 high-definition cameras, 12 ultrasonic radars and two wading radars. The vehicle supports highway and urban Navigation on Autopilot (NOA), point-to-point parking navigation and multi-scenario automated parking assistance. Power comes from Geely's Leishen EM-T off-road hybrid system, combining a 2.0TD off-road hybrid engine with electric motors. Key performance figures include: Combined power: 830 kW Battery capacity: 47.14 kWh Pure electric range: 305 km Combined range: 1,770 km Fast charging: 10% to 80% in 10 minutes, with 6C charging support Wading depth: 800 mm Additional off-road features include mechanical differential locks and dual-chamber closed air suspension with CCD continuously variable damping. The SUV also supports a minimum turning radius of 3.36 meters and a "Waltz Turn" maneuver. GEENER, Wolfspeed Ink Deal Wolfspeed and GEENER recently signed a memorandum of understanding in Hangzhou to cooperate on silicon carbide (SiC) power modules. GEENER will prioritize Wolfspeed's SiC bare dies for integration into its next-generation power module platform, initially targeting applications such as main inverters for new-energy vehicles. Wolfspeed will leverage its established 200 mm SiC production lines to develop bare dies that meet or exceed GEENER's performance requirements, while providing stable supply and commercial support. The two companies will jointly engage with leading Chinese automakers on high-voltage electric vehicle platforms, aiming to secure vehicle design wins. The partnership combines Wolfspeed's SiC chip technology and manufacturing capacity with GEENER's expertise in module design, packaging and reliability validation. artigo.texto: A infraestrutura de nuvem da Yandex, uma das maiores empresas de tecnologia da Rússia, enfrenta uma grave crise após ataques com drones danificarem três de seus data centers. Os incidentes, registrados em outubro de 2026, provocaram interrupções operacionais e instabilidade em serviços de armazenamento, computação e inteligência artificial, levantando preocupações sobre a capacidade da empresa de manter suas operações durante emergências físicas. As instalações atingidas ficam em Sasovo, Kaluga e Vladimir. Entre os serviços afetados estão componentes do Yandex Cloud, o armazenamento compatível com S3, o Kubernetes e o Yandex Disk. Clientes também relataram falhas em requisições, dificuldades para baixar arquivos e respostas HTTP de erro. Diante do cenário, a empresa recomendou que os clientes recorressem a seus planos de recuperação de desastres enquanto a infraestrutura permanecesse instável. O episódio expõe uma fragilidade importante da computação em nuvem: embora os serviços pareçam funcionar de maneira virtual e distribuída, eles dependem de instalações físicas que podem ser danificadas. Para empresas que hospedam aplicações críticas, a crise reforça a necessidade de manter backups independentes, redundância geográfica e planos de continuidade operacional. Ataques com drones interrompem operações em três data centers da Yandex A sequência de ataques atingiu três instalações importantes da Yandex em poucos dias, reduzindo a capacidade disponível para executar aplicações e atender às solicitações dos clientes. A empresa, frequentemente comparada ao Google pelo conjunto de serviços digitais que oferece na Rússia, opera plataformas de busca, armazenamento, computação em nuvem e inteligência artificial. A interrupção simultânea de diferentes instalações representa um desafio maior do que a falha isolada de um servidor. Quando um data center inteiro deixa de operar, milhares de componentes podem ficar indisponíveis, incluindo servidores, sistemas de armazenamento e equipamentos de rede. A recuperação também depende das condições físicas do local e da possibilidade de transferir as cargas de trabalho para outras instalações. Sasovo, Kaluga e Vladimir foram atingidas em sequência Os incidentes foram registrados em três localidades russas durante outubro de 2026. Em Sasovo, na região de Riazan, um ataque ocorrido na noite de 7 para 8 de outubro provocou danos graves e levou ao desligamento da instalação. O local abriga parte da infraestrutura de computação utilizada pela Yandex, inclusive em atividades relacionadas à inteligência artificial. Em Kaluga, outro ataque, registrado em 9 de outubro, danificou módulos do data center e comprometeu parte de sua capacidade operacional. Embora a interrupção tenha sido parcial, a perda de recursos contribuiu para aumentar a pressão sobre a infraestrutura restante. Já em Vladimir, um ataque em 11 de outubro levou à suspensão das operações da instalação. A sequência dos incidentes reduziu a margem disponível para redistribuir serviços e manter a capacidade habitual da plataforma. Os episódios também levantaram preocupações sobre a concentração de recursos computacionais em instalações sujeitas a riscos físicos. Mesmo quando uma empresa mantém vários data centers, a redundância pode ser insuficiente se os locais compartilharem dependências ou se a capacidade remanescente não suportar a demanda. Yandex Cloud entra em modo de operação de emergência Durante a crise, a Yandex reconheceu dificuldades operacionais e orientou clientes a utilizar seus planos alternativos de recuperação de desastres, conhecidos pela sigla DR, de Disaster Recovery. Esse tipo de recomendação indica que a recuperação pode exigir mais do que uma manutenção convencional. A perda de instalações inteiras demanda avaliar equipamentos, reconstruir capacidade computacional, verificar a integridade dos dados e restabelecer as dependências necessárias para os serviços voltarem a funcionar. A ausência de uma previsão definitiva para a recuperação integral também dificulta o planejamento das empresas afetadas. Sem uma estimativa confiável, administradores precisam decidir se aguardam a normalização, transferem aplicações ou ativam ambientes alternativos. O cenário demonstra por que planos de contingência devem prever interrupções prolongadas, em vez de considerar apenas falhas temporárias de rede ou indisponibilidade de componentes individuais. Kubernetes, S3 e APIs enfrentam instabilidade A crise atingiu diferentes componentes do Yandex Cloud, plataforma utilizada para hospedar aplicações, armazenar dados e executar cargas de trabalho empresariais. Entre os serviços citados nos relatos sobre a interrupção estão Kubernetes, Object Storage compatível com S3, Container Registry, Console, APIs, IAM e serviços de bancos de dados. Também foram relatados problemas em componentes relacionados à inteligência artificial, incluindo o AI Studio. Os efeitos variam conforme o serviço e suas dependências. O Kubernetes, por exemplo, pode reiniciar contêineres e redistribuir aplicações entre nós disponíveis, mas não consegue compensar automaticamente a perda de toda uma instalação quando faltam capacidade computacional, armazenamento ou componentes essenciais do plano de controle. O armazenamento compatível com S3 também merece atenção. Muitas aplicações utilizam esse tipo de serviço para guardar documentos, arquivos de usuários, registros e cópias de segurança. Se as operações de leitura e gravação falham, o problema pode se propagar para sistemas que dependem desses dados. Da mesma forma, a instabilidade nas APIs e no IAM pode prejudicar a autenticação, o gerenciamento de recursos e a execução de operações automatizadas. Assim, uma interrupção física pode afetar tanto os usuários finais quanto as equipes responsáveis pela administração da infraestrutura. artigo.texto: I am writing today to address an integral piece of our local and national discourse: the debate over data centers. I am writing to challenge a recent letter I read in the local newspaper: “Nobody wants a data center in their backyard” (Sept. 8, Morgan Hill Times and Gilroy Dispatch). I respect the author’s perspective; many residents do not want data centers in their community, as there are negative externalities associated, such as water and power usage and the unsightliness of the power facilities associated with it. However, I believe that when it comes to such a contentious issue, we must tread carefully and treat the subject with the nuance it deserves. This article quickly served to attack the character of those in favor of data centers saying “the people who want the data centers are the same ones who never want them in their own neighborhood.” I, for one, can unequivocally refute this—I would love for more data centers to be built in San Martin, where I live, and Gilroy, where I was born and went to elementary school. Data centers are an opportunity to employ both blue collar and white collar workers—something that Gilroy would gladly take more of. Counties which host data centers experience a rise in local employment, total wages, median household income, business growth, construction revenue and tax revenue. I would love this for the South Valley, where I grew up, and in which not a single family member of mine worked, because of the lower wages compared to the rest of the Bay Area. The article continues to poke at Gilroy Mayor Greg Bozzo, and in reference to why he was allowing the data centers to be built, said he was “looking forward to an early and comfortable retirement.” The insinuation that Bozzo is looking out for his personal interest is a blatant attack on his character. As for how this got passed through without input from other stakeholders, the approved facility is more than a half mile away from the nearest residential area. The data center is being built in an area inhabited by the 145 Gilroy Outlets and other big box retailers and businesses. While I agree community input should be vital in a project like this, it is understandable that the Gilroy City Council would approve a project like this in an area which has hundreds of neighboring businesses, and no housing in close proximity. There are 107 data centers currently operating in Santa Clara County, and I contend this is a great thing. Data centers store data such as personal photos and database information for businesses. They stream media, like movies and TV shows into our homes. They help with cybersecurity, which protects local and corporate businesses from data breaches. They power online services, such as social media, online banking and the online print of the Morgan Hill Times, Gilroy Dispatch and Hollister Free Lance. They make our modern lives possible. When it comes to data centers, there are many issues that will arise. Seeing them in the community we live in and love can be difficult. It can seem that big tech companies and powers outside our control are dictating how our communities change. I am writing to say that these are entirely valid criticisms, but there are positive changes that come along with their construction, and they can serve to better our lives and the generations in the South Valley after us. Ellis Richardson San Martin

artigo.texto: Know Data centers prohibited under St. Pete’s city code According to Planning Director Derek Kilborn, data centers are neither permitted uses nor eligible for special exceptions. Standalone data centers, including large-scale facilities used to power artificial intelligence, are prohibited under St. Petersburg’s existing zoning regulations, according to a new memorandum from the city’s planning director. In an Oct. 9 memo to Mayor Ken Welch, Planning Director Derek Kilborn clarified how the facilities are classified under the city’s land development code. He concluded that data centers are neither permitted uses nor eligible for special exceptions. The determination comes as local governments across Pinellas County consider how to regulate the rapidly expanding industry amid concerns about electricity consumption, water resources and land availability. St. Petersburg’s zoning code contains a matrix identifying permitted land uses. Data centers are not included, and city regulations presume that uses not specifically listed are prohibited. Kilborn also examined whether data centers could qualify as similar to other permitted uses, including utility infrastructure, but found no sufficient justification. “For these reasons, Data Centers generally, and Large-Scale Data Centers explicitly, remain prohibited as a permitted, principal (P) or Special Exception (SE) use in the City of St. Petersburg,” Kilborn wrote. Gov. Ron DeSantis signed Senate Bill 484, which recognizes the infrastructure and environmental challenges of large utility users, like data centers, last May. However, DeSantis preserved local authority over land use regulation in the same bill, which took effect July 1. Under the new law, a large-scale data center is defined as a facility with an anticipated monthly peak electrical demand of at least 50 megawatts at a single location. St. Petersburg’s determination applies to standalone data centers regardless of whether they meet that threshold. The memo follows similar actions elsewhere in Pinellas County. Pinellas Park approved a one-year moratorium on data center development in August. Additionally, in September, county commissioners adopted a resolution restricting large standalone facilities in unincorporated areas. Unlike those actions, St. Petersburg’s memorandum simply clarifies that standalone data centers are already prohibited under existing regulations, and presumably no further action is needed to overhaul the law. It was not indicated whether the city has received any recent data center development proposals, or whether officials are considering changes to the zoning code.

artigo.texto: Pennsylvania launches interactive data center permit tracker amid environmental concerns PENNSYLVANIA (WHP) — Pennsylvania has launched a public map that will allow the public to track proposed data centers that are seeking environmental permits. The data center tracker is operated by the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection (DEP). The interactive map shows the locations of proposed data center projects in the Commonwealth and includes a list of environmental permits for each project and their status. Data centers have continued to be a point of contention in Pennsylvania, including as a talking point in the debate between Gov. Josh Shapiro and Treasurer Stacy Garrity. Shapiro started off the debate saying he's been listening to concerns of the people, and after doing so, drafted the "strictest guardrail in the nation" for data centers. He said it is important to protect air and water and that it must include local benefits. Meanwhile, Garrity discussed individual cases where people are fighting against data centers in their own backyard. Over the weekend, the Swatara Township Board of Commissioners approved community benefits agreements for a pair of proposed data centers. RELATED | Swatara Township approves community benefits plan for data center projects The types of permits and/or authorizations often associated with large-scale data centers include: - Earth disturbance and stormwater management - Wetland and waterway encroachment - Storage tanks - Air quality - Sewage facilities planning - Clean water To track the status of a permit authorization, use the DEP's permit tracker.

artigo.texto: Andhra Pradesh has issued a tender for 1,250 MW/5,000 MWh of standalone BESS with four-hour storage duration Winning bidders will sign 12-year BESPAs with state discoms Projects need to be set up across three locations under a build-own-operate model Andhra Pradesh has launched a call for the deployment of 1,250 MW/5,000 MWh of standalone battery energy storage system (BESS) capacity at selected project locations across the state. As the bid coordinator, the Andhra Pradesh Power Coordination Committee (APPCC) may procure up to 25% additional BESS capacity for each project under a green shoe option, amounting to 125 MW/500 MWh each for Projects 1 and 3, and 50 MW/200 MWh for Project 2. The tender documents state that the additional capacity will be included in the contracted capacity if allocated. To be set up under a build-own-operate (BOO) model, the capacity will be established at three locations. Of the total, 500 MW/2,000 MWh will be located at Dr. M.V. Ramana Reddy Rayalaseema Thermal Power Plant (RTPP). Another 250 MW/1,000 MWh will come up at the Talaricheruvu RE Project, and 500 MW/2,000 MWh at the NP Kunta RE Project. The entire 1,250 MW translates into 4-hour storage capacity. Bidders are required to design the BESS under Battery Energy Storage Purchase Agreements (BESPAs), ensuring the system can charge and discharge at a C-rate of 0.25. It must also be capable of being charged and discharged in blocks of either 50 MW/200 MWh or 100 MW/400 MWh, alone or in combination up to the total rate capacity specified for each location. Interested BESS developers are invited to submit bids for the grid-connected projects, each of which will be tendered, evaluated, and awarded separately, with tariffs determined independently. No viability gap funding (VGF) is available for these projects. APPCC has launched the call on behalf of AP discoms, namely Andhra Pradesh Central Power Distribution Corporation Limited (APCPDCL), Eastern Power Distribution Company of Andhra Pradesh Limited (APEPDCL), and Southern Power Distribution Company of Andhra Pradesh Limited (APSPDCL). State discoms will enter into a 12-year BESPA with the winning bidders to secure energy storage facilities on an on-demand basis. APPCC issued the tender on October 7, 2026. It will accept bids till November 23, 2026. Details of the tender are available on the APEPDCL website. Under its Integrated Clean Energy Policy 2024, Andhra Pradesh targets 25 GWh of BESS and 22 GW of pumped storage hydropower capacity by 2029 to accommodate growing renewable energy capacity. It also aims to add 78.5 GW of solar and 35 GW of wind capacity between 2024 and 2029.

artigo.texto: NYK-Led Consortium Develops Floating Data Center Concept for Ports A Japanese consortium led by shipping giant NYK Line has developed a new port-based floating data center concept designed to accelerate the commercialization of offshore data centers while addressing growing constraints on land availability, electrical power and construction timelines. The consortium, comprising Nippon Yusen Kabushiki Kaisha (NYK), NTT FACILITIES, Eurus Energy Holdings and MUFG Bank, envisions floating data centers moored alongside existing port quays, leveraging established shoreside infrastructure and local energy resources. Unlike floating data centers positioned farther offshore, which could directly utilize large-scale renewable energy sources such as offshore wind, the port-based model offers easier access, established telecommunications connectivity and more conventional power supply arrangements. The approach could enable deployment in locations ranging from major metropolitan ports to smaller regional harbors, potentially opening new opportunities for port authorities seeking to diversify waterfront infrastructure and services. The consortium sees the port-based concept as an intermediate step toward more ambitious offshore installations, where accessibility, telecommunications connectivity and independent power supply systems remain significant technical challenges. Under the initiative, NYK will oversee project development and business strategy. NTT FACILITIES will handle technical verification of data center design, construction and operations, while Eurus Energy will explore renewable power integration, particularly offshore wind. MUFG Bank will evaluate financing opportunities and potential business partnerships. The companies believe floating data centers could provide an alternative to conventional land-based facilities as global demand for digital infrastructure continues to expand. No construction timetable, project location, investment value or computing capacity was disclosed.

artigo.texto: DALLAS, Oct. 14, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Solidion Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ: STI) ("Solidion Technology" or "the Company"), an advanced battery technology solutions provider, today reaffirmed its commitment to address energy storage for artificial intelligence and data center infrastructure, centered on its PEAK Series uninterruptible power supply (UPS) system. As AI workloads increase the power density of data centers, operators face growing pressure on the systems that keep facilities running during grid disruptions. Uninterruptible power supply (UPS) batteries take up floor space that could otherwise hold AI servers and additional computing equipment, and they require periodic replacement. Solidion's approach is built around its PEAK Series, a UPS battery system built for AI data centers using its proprietary 5500 silicon-carbon anode cell, designed for AI data center environments and well positioned to address these evolving requirements. The Company's strategy focuses on three priorities: - Energy density and space efficiency: Based on Company testing, PEAK is designed to reduce UPS footprint by up to 30%, freeing floor space for servers. - Reliability and longevity: The 5500 cell is designed to last up to three times longer than conventional backup systems, reducing replacement cycles and maintenance. Solidion is focused on advancing technologies intended to support demanding data center operating environments. - Materials-level innovation: Solidion's portfolio of +385 patents covering silicon anodes, graphene and next generation battery chemistries, together with its pilot production facility in Dayton, Ohio, gives the Company a U.S. based foundation for developing data center energy storage. "AI infrastructure represents a compelling market for advanced energy storage," said Jaymes Winters, Chairman and CEO of Solidion. "Our focus is on translating our technology into practical commercial solutions that address real customer demand. We are not betting on which chips win; we are focused on supplying something every data center needs." Solidion intends to continue pursuing opportunities to apply its battery technologies directly to end users. About Solidion Technology, Inc. artigo.texto: In Bessemer, Alabama, a secrecy pact with the developer of a proposed $14.5 billion data center didn’t just keep city officials quiet. It required them to destroy records. In Salem, Oregon, a city council member learned of her city’s nondisclosure agreement only when the public did. In Pine Island, Minnesota, officials knew about a project for two years before residents heard a word. One resident told lawmakers the democratic process there had been “hijacked by big tech.” These aren’t isolated lapses. That’s how the artificial intelligence boom is being built: deals negotiated behind closed doors, with elected officials contractually barred from telling constituents what enterprise is coming, how much electricity and water the facility will consume, and what tax breaks it will get. The AI train has left the station. Secrecy is a choice, and it’s the wrong one. When University of Mary Washington sociologist Eric Bonds filed public records requests across Virginia, the nation’s data center capital, he found nondisclosure agreements in 25 of 31 localities. Why would any official sign away the public’s right to know? Towns and states are competing for these investments, and a developer that doesn’t get its secrecy can take its billions elsewhere. Red and blue states alike have signed. And the pushback is just as bipartisan: Republicans and Democrats in Congress have joined forces on a bill to ban the agreements. What do these contracts hide? Sometimes just the business’s name. In Spotsylvania County, Virginia, an agreement with Amazon kept the company’s water use confidential. Residents drink from that same public system, yet they couldn’t find out how much Amazon would draw from it. The industry’s argument isn’t frivolous. Once landowners learn a data center is the buyer, prices soar, Dan Diorio of the Data Center Coalition told Spotlight PA. Fair enough, for a land deal. That doesn’t require hiding a facility’s water and power use from the people who will live beside it. Microsoft said in March that it would end its nondisclosure agreements with local governments. Amazon Web Services CEO Matt Garman has since written that the company “ no longer use(s) nondisclosure agreements with the government agencies” it works with. Distrust breeds backlash: Garman counts more than 100 data center moratoriums under consideration nationwide. In Monterey Park, outside Los Angeles, 88% of voters banned data centers outright. Ending nondisclosure agreements only lets us see the bill. It doesn’t decide who pays it. That’s settled piecemeal, by utility commissions, county boards and water agencies, each with its own rules. Government often approves a data center with the same scrutiny as a shopping mall, by zoning boards never designed to handle infrastructure of national consequence. We’ve done this before. America didn’t build the interstate highway system by letting every county haggle over asphalt. It set national standards and built one network. The AI build-out deserves the same. Ohio offers a start. When data center demand outran central Ohio’s grid, regulators required large new facilities to pay for at least 85% of their expected power, for up to 12 years, whether they use it or not. The rules weeded out speculative projects, let new hookups resume, and aim to keep households from paying for power some server farm has reserved. Manufacturers have challenged it in court. However, it answers the question nondisclosure agreements never do: Who pays? California has gone further. Laws by San Diego state Sen. Steve Padilla and others order regulators to set separate electricity rates so data centers, not households, cover their grid upgrades, and require developers to report projected power demand when seeking local permits. Pima County, Arizona, went after the secrecy itself, capping nondisclosure agreements at two years and requiring disclosure at least 90 days before any county vote. Now, take these models national. Permit server farms like power plants. Before any council or county board approves a land sale, rezoning or tax break, require developers to disclose power, water and incentives. And make data centers pay. The servers are coming either way. What’s still up for a vote is whether Americans get to see the deal, and whether they’re the ones stuck paying for it.

artigo.texto: Ucranianos usaram drones para atingir três dos maiores data centers da Yandex, provocando quedas de serviço que revelam fragilidades na estratégia digital russa. Como começou a campanha de drones russos contra a Ucrânia? Em setembro passado, a Rússia iniciou uma série de ataques aéreos contra infraestruturas críticas ucranianas, incluindo centros de dados e redes de telefonia móvel. O objetivo declarado era interromper comunicações e limitar o acesso à internet em Kiev, afetando cerca de cem mil residências. Esses ataques faziam parte de um plano maior que também visava a rede elétrica, ferrovias e até blocos residenciais. Qual foi a reação da Ucrânia aos ataques russos? Como resposta direta, a Ucrânia passou a mirar instalações russas que sustentam serviços digitais essenciais. Em outubro, drones ucranianos atingiram um data center da Yandex na região de Sasovo, ao sudeste de Moscou, danificando equipamentos que hospedam dois dos três supercomputadores usados para treinar o modelo de IA YandexGPT. Que importância têm os supercomputadores da Yandex? Os dois sistemas afetados – batizados de Chervonenkis e Lyapunov – são baseados em gpus nvidia a100, reconhecidas pela alta performance em tarefas de aprendizado de máquina. O Chervonenkis registra cerca de 29,4 petaflops, ocupando a posição 101 no ranking Top500 de supercomputadores, enquanto o Lyapunov oferece 20,0 petaflops, posicionando‑se em 161. Essa capacidade permite à Yandex desenvolver modelos de linguagem avançados, aproximando‑se do que empresas como Google e Microsoft oferecem. Por que a infraestrutura russa parece vulnerável? Especialistas ligados ao círculo pró‑Kremlin, citados por pesquisadores independentes como ChrisO_wiki, alertam que a economia digital da Rússia está excessivamente centralizada. A maioria dos serviços de nuvem, busca e IA está concentrada em poucos data centers controlados por gigantes como a Yandex. Quando esses pontos críticos são atingidos, o efeito dominó pode comprometer desde serviços de streaming até plataformas de pagamento. O que o modelo descentralizado da Ucrânia oferece? A Ucrânia tem investido em soluções distribuídas, com provedores menores e redes peer‑to‑peer que dificultam a interrupção total. Essa arquitetura resiliente pode se tornar um exemplo para outros países que buscam reduzir a dependência de grandes provedores e melhorar a segurança nacional. Quais são as possíveis consequências para os usuários russos? - Interrupções temporárias em serviços de busca, mapas e assistentes virtuais da Yandex. - Impacto nas plataformas de e‑commerce que dependem da infraestrutura de nuvem da empresa. - Risco de atrasos nas atualizações de modelos de IA, prejudicando a competitividade da Rússia no mercado global. - Pressão para que o governo russo invista em redundância e diversificação de provedores. Como a comunidade tech brasileira deve interpretar esse conflito? Para os profissionais e entusiastas de tecnologia no Brasil, o episódio serve como alerta sobre a importância da arquitetura distribuída. Empresas que ainda dependem de um único provedor de nuvem podem considerar estratégias de multi‑cloud ou edge computing para mitigar riscos semelhantes. Além disso, o caso evidencia que a guerra digital pode ser tão decisiva quanto os combates tradicionais, influenciando políticas de segurança cibernética em todo o mundo. O que ainda não está claro sobre os danos aos supercomputadores? Até o momento, não há informações oficiais sobre o grau de comprometimento dos chips Nvidia A100 dentro dos sistemas Chervonenkis e Lyapunov. A complexidade de reparar ou substituir esses componentes pode levar semanas, e a Yandex ainda não divulgou um plano de recuperação detalhado. Para ficar no radar Os próximos dias serão críticos para observar como a Rússia reagirá a esses ataques. Se a estratégia de retaliação incluir novas ofensivas cibernéticas ou reforço de defesas físicas, o cenário digital da região pode mudar rapidamente. Enquanto isso, profissionais de TI no Brasil podem usar o caso como estudo de caso para reforçar a importância de arquiteturas resilientes e de um planejamento de continuidade de negócios robusto.
