artigo.texto: LOWELL — The Lowell residents who attended the city’s second meeting on data centers were virtually unanimous in their feedback to restrict future growth of the facilities in every district in the city. “The only way to protect our community from the environmental impacts that we know are caused by these data centers, particularly when these data centers are put in environmental justice neighborhoods, is to prohibit them … ,” the participants at Table No. 4 said during their presentation. The community engagement event was hosted on Oct. 7, by the Department of Planning and Development at the Senior Center on Broadway Street in the Acre neighborhood. Residents give city planners feedback More than 50 participants broke into a dozen small groups to discuss DPD’s two zoning options for consideration by the City Council for regulating data centers in the city, part of an overhaul of Lowell’s outdated zoning code. Option 1 is restricting future data center growth to 15 megawatts with climate-friendly infrastructure. Option 2 is that data centers are prohibited in every district. Lowell is currently home to a 352,000-square-foot data center in the city’s Sacred Heart neighborhood. Markley Lowell LLC operates the state-of-the-art data-storage and cloud-computing colocation data center that rents secure space to more than 500 clients to run their own technology. Its systems power and provide routing to a wide variety of private companies, state and local governments, internet companies and universities, including UMass Lowell. The privately owned company has faced some local headwinds, driven in part by consistent neighborhood opposition, as well as a national angst over the unchecked growth of hyperscale projects that are the backbone of the artificial intelligence revolution. Residents in the economic justice neighborhood have consistently testified to noise and air quality concerns, ongoing and disruptive construction projects and violations of approved permitting. “We say these are the rules in place, you can build your data center,” the moderator for Table No. 1 said. “Who’s going to enforce those rules? What are we going to do to make sure that they’re following them? And if they’re not, what is going to happen? Because we’ve seen it in other places where they come in, they say, ‘This is what we’re going to do,’ and then they far exceed that and it harms the community and the damage has already been done.” Markley Lowell only data center operating in Lowell Markley Lowell was not on DPD’s data center zoning agenda, but its shadow loomed over the residents’ workshopped conversations. When the Markley Group purchased the derelict and long-vacant former Prince Pasta plant in Lowell for $4 million in 2015, Lowell welcomed the high-tech center with a $77 million tax break. Over the past 10 years, the company embarked on a dramatic renovation and expansion, with founder and CEO Jeff Markley claiming to have invested at least $650 million in the site and related developments to date. The company’s power profile has expanded from seven to 23 diesel-powered backup generators, 16 chillers and two water towers to secure its growing energy needs. And despite significant pushback from both residents and the City Council, the company has continued to expand its footprint in Lowell. Both Markley Lowell and Jeff Markley have purchased multiple properties in and around its existing facility at 1 Markley Way. City lacks zoning on data centers The City Council unanimously passed a 360-day moratorium March 10 to allow the city to develop zoning around data centers in Lowell. Under the city’s existing zoning, the data center company is not required to divulge its long-term development plans for any of its new sites. But the parcels either contain or are colocated to generators of the scale needed to power data centers, perhaps even artificial intelligence. The company’s website recently added “Now available for your generative AI workloads.” DPD Deputy Director Camilo Espitia reminded participants that Markley’s current projects are “locked in.” “Whichever option we go with today is irrelevant to where Markley stands today,” he said. “They are grandfathered in and that business will keep operating. This is intended for any other land that has not been touched by data centers or that hasn’t been subdivided in the future for any other type of developer including Markley themselves.” At the end of the almost two-hour session, Assistant City Manager and DPD Director Yovani Baez-Rose thanked the community for their feedback. “We appreciate the fact that you’re taking time out of your personal lives to sort of help us frame what our community is going to look like moving forward,” she said. In late October to early November, DPD will present the data center ordinance to the City Council Zoning Subcommittee, followed by a final draft of the zoning ordinance to the council in early to mid-December. A Planning Board public hearing will be held in January, and the council will hold a public hearing and hold a vote later that month.

artigo.texto: Did Ukraine’s strikes on data centers really silence Russian bots? Russia's army of bots is apparently offline. At least, that's according to chatter on social media and even Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Over the past week, Ukrainian drones struck three data centers belonging to Yandex, the tech giant often called "Russia’s Google." The first strike happened on Oct. 8, followed by a second attack on Oct. 9. On Sunday, Oct. 11, a third strike damaged a Yandex data center in the Vladimir region, east of Moscow. The company said operations at that facility were completely suspended and some of its services were unavailable, according to the BBC. The attacks disrupted Yandex services, from its AI chatbot to its smart home devices. Per the BBC, the military strikes were meant to target "places that provide revenue streams for Moscow's war machine." You May Also Like Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum on Monday, Zelenskyy said "everyone noticed" a drop in Russian bot activity on social media after the strikes. On X, Reddit, and elsewhere, users in several Western countries reported seeing less right-wing activity in their feeds, from pro-GOP accounts in the U.S. to supporters of Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party. Czech member of the European Parliament Tomáš Zdechovský also pointed to claims that online support for the AfD had dropped after the strikes. This Tweet is currently unavailable. It might be loading or has been removed. The prediction market Polymarket’s X account was among those amplifying the claim. Take that with a grain of salt, though, as the account has a tendency for posting breaking-news-style claims without sources or verification. This Tweet is currently unavailable. It might be loading or has been removed. Much of the buzz traces back to a report from U24 Media, the media arm of United24, a platform run by the Ukrainian government. To its credit, U24’s own report is careful about what the numbers can and can’t prove. It cites an Oct. 12 analysis by The Deep Dive of data from Cloudflare Radar, which monitors internet traffic. According to that analysis, automated web traffic from Yandex’s network fell sharply after Oct. 8 and nearly disappeared by Oct. 11. At one point, it measured just 0.3 percent of the chart’s peak, compared with 88.2 percent at the same hour a week earlier. U24 also cites German tech publication t3n's report of a similar plunge — with bot traffic dropping to about 0.4 percent of the previous week’s level before bouncing back to around 20 percent later in the day on Oct. 11. The catch is that "automated traffic" and "Russian propaganda bots" aren’t the same thing. Automated traffic is any request sent to a website by software rather than a person. Most of it is mundane, e.g., search engine crawlers indexing pages or monitoring tools checking whether sites are up. Because Yandex runs Russia’s biggest search engine, its network constantly sends out crawlers to index the web. Knocking its data centers offline would bring traffic to a halt regardless of whether a single troll account went quiet. As U24 itself notes, the measurements show a sharp drop in automated network activity, but they can’t tell us whether propaganda bots disappeared or whether damaged infrastructure simply stopped producing ordinary automated traffic. The numbers also track how much traffic Yandex’s network sent relative to its peak, not how many social media accounts were active. Mashable has yet to see published evidence tying Russian influence operations on X or Reddit to Yandex’s servers specifically. Many of the claims to that effect are sourced from the same Cloudflare Radar and Deep Dive data reports that we cited here. Influence campaigns can run on infrastructure anywhere, and the accounts posting the content don’t have to live on Yandex’s network at all. It's easy to see why the claim has caught on, as social media platforms are rife with hyper-polarization fueled by ragebait political engagement. However, not all political content online comes from Russian bots. As The Atlantic's Ali Breland writes, operatives based in Eastern European countries like Latvia are paying people to post pro-GOP talking points — $3 for every 1,000 views. That also doesn’t mean the strikes had no effect online. Per U24, the bombings have found a way to rattle Russia’s internet, including widespread outages. Whether it also silenced Russia’s online propaganda machine is a much bigger claim. artigo.texto: ND counties talk about how to handle data centers BISMARCK, N.D. (KFYR) - The North Dakota Association of Counties said that data center construction should be considered on a county-by-county basis. The Association held its annual meeting this week in Bismarck. The group said questions about the size of data centers, proximity to urban and rural areas and potential tax benefits differ between counties. These differences are why it’s necessary for counties to have individualized zoning and planning rules. “There’s obviously people that are highly opposed, but we’re still gathering facts, getting the right information out there,” said Association President Nick Moser. “That’s one great thing about this event, is getting that information and getting the proper information to people is huge.” In Moser’s own county, Cavalier, data centers are not allowed within one mile of town. The noise from data centers only reaches 50 decibels at this distance, according to research. Moser encourages public hearings to ensure the correct information is being given to people. artigo.texto: BYD has launched its brand-new Festive Edition Sealion 7 SUV in India, which is priced at Rs. 50.60 lakh ex-showroom. The new edition is based on the premium trim and is limited to 150 units. BYD Sealion 7 Festive Edition The ultra-limited Festive Edition (150 units) was specifically introduced to capitalise on the Indian festive shopping season. It offers high-end buyers exclusivity through a unique Tan and Black interior treatment, maintaining momentum for a model that has quickly become one of BYD India's top sellers. Interior and Exterior Features The Sealion 7 festive edition features an 82.56 kWh Blade Battery and a rear-mounted electric motor that delivers 230 kW (308 hp) and 380 Nm of torque. The electric SUV can accelerate from 0 to 100 kmph in 6.7 seconds and has a claimed driving range of 567 km under the NEDC testing cycle. The Electric SUV is equipped with BYD's Cell-to-Body (CTB) technology, which integrates the battery pack into the vehicle's structural architecture. The festive edition also features torque adaptation control, which manages torque delivery based on traction conditions. These features were already seen in the premium model. The car comes with a 15.6-inch rotating touchscreen infotainment system, quilted Nappa leather seats, and a panoramic glass roof with an electric sunshade. It also comes with a dual-tone cabin treatment. It has 11 airbags and a five-star Euro NCAP rating. Other attributes include a DYNAUDIO system, ventilated front seats, driver's memory seats, a 360 camera, an ADAS suite, a panoramic glass roof, a powered tailgate, double-glazed glass, and a 12-speaker system. The Sealion 7 measures 4,830 mm in length, 1,925 mm in width, and 1,620 mm in height, with a 2,930 mm wheelbase. The cargo capacity is 500 litres at the back, expandable to 1,789 litres, and the frunk holds 58 litres. The Sealion 7 Festive Edition extends that approach, bringing a distinctive Tan & Black interior to the premium variant in a limited run for the festive season. At its core, it retains the technology, safety and performance that define the Sealion 7, while offering customers a differentiated expression of the model. Its biggest strengths are the Blade Battery, premium interior, 308 bhp performance and extensive equipment. The main point to remember is that this special edition is essentially the existing Premium variant with a different cabin colour scheme.

artigo.texto: Data center boom puts Republicans in a bind before midterm elections A year ago, there weren't many voters talking about data centers. Now, the massive facilities being built to satisfy the enormous computing needs of the AI boom have become one of the most explosive issues of the 2026 midterms, and their construction is opening a divide between the Trump administration and Republicans running in state and federal races this fall. When ChatGPT launched in late 2022, most data centers were being built in blue states. But by 2025, 68% of data centers online were in red states. Now, 75% of data centers under construction and 80% of data centers in the planning stage are in predominantly Republican states, according to new data from Cleanview Research, an independent energy market intelligence company tracking data center development. "Red states have more of a history of accepting large, energy intensive, infrastructure projects — even those that might have detrimental effects on communities," said Chris Millay, a data center analyst at the macroeconomic consultancy Greenmantle. He also points to the relative lack of environmental regulation and the availability of open land as reasons rural states are receiving more investment. President Trump sees the AI race as critical to the economy and national security, and he's one of data centers' biggest boosters. At a recent Ohio rally, he said of data centers, "We want them … look, there's so much money to be made for Ohio — you can't just turn them off. They'll go to China." He has repeatedly dismissed public opposition to data centers, posting on Truth Social that "the only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor." Mr. Trump has also resisted regulation, though he has called on developers to give back to local communities through education, lower taxes, job creation and energy cost protections. Red states may be hosting most of the boom, and increasingly, communities living next to data centers are pushing back. People who live near data centers have reported concerns about their property values, noise, higher energy bills and resource depletion. Meanwhile, calls for moratoriums are spreading through communities across the country. Overall, opposition to data centers outweighs support by 30 points, with polls showing the majority of Republicans oppose the construction of data centers near them. "It's such a consensus issue it's really impossible to take the other side," said Millay. "When voters see a politician who supports data centers, they think, 'Well, how am I going to trust him with my job?'" Some of the president's closest allies have begun to break with him on the issue. In Texas, which has the most data centers under construction, GOP Gov. Greg Abbott has paused environmental permits and grid connections for new data centers. Abbott, who is seeking a fourth term, is in a surprisingly close race against Democrat Gina Hinojosa. In Texas' tight Senate race, the Republican nominee, state Attorney General Ken Paxton, wants to end Texas' sales tax break for data centers. He has also said they should be held criminally liable if they power AI chatbots that endanger children. Data centers seem to be the single issue where Democratic and Republican candidates sound nearly identical. In Ohio, Amy Acton, the Democratic nominee for governor, said in a press release, "I am calling on our Statehouse to pass a conditional moratorium on data centers." Her GOP opponent, Vivek Ramaswamy, has gone further. He vowed to "issue an executive order on my first day in office to immediately halt the approval of any new data center project announcements in Ohio," and to keep that pause in place until lawmakers pass his "Ohioans-First" law, which would require data centers to provide free electricity to surrounding residents. A recent New York Times/Siena poll found that data centers are a weak point for Ohio Republican Sen. Jon Husted, with voters favoring his opponent by an 11-point margin on the issue. Campaigns have spent $45 million this year on ads that mention data centers — most of them in opposition — according to AdImpact. In Georgia, where candidates have spent nearly $13 million on ads mentioning data centers — more than any other state — the Republican gubernatorial candidate, Rick Jackson, is sticking with Mr. Trump. While the Democratic candidate, Keisha Lance Bottoms, is calling for a temporary moratorium on construction, Jackson says the decision should be left up to local officials. Jackson made the case for data centers at a recent press conference, saying he wanted "to educate people on the benefit if they want [a data center]." Some counties, he said, expect they "will have zero property taxes after the data center goes in." Effingham County, where OpenAI plans a $20 billion data center, has pledged to use some of that revenue to cut homeowners' property taxes. Because most of the next wave of data centers is largely planned in states Mr. Trump won in 2024, the choices Republican candidates make, siding with voters or with the president, could decide whether those projects are paused, made more expensive or even canceled.

artigo.texto: Marblehead could move to ban data centers under a new zoning bylaw, following a discussion at the Planning Board’s Oct. 13 meeting. Planning Board Chair Marc Liebman raised the possibility of prohibiting data centers in town, citing concerns about their impact on communities and pointing to similar efforts underway in Salem. “There’s all kinds of reasons why data centers create a strain on the communities they’re in,” Liebman said. Data centers are facilities that house computer servers and other equipment used to store, process and distribute digital information. Large facilities, including those supporting artificial intelligence, can consume substantial amounts of electricity and water and require extensive infrastructure. Liebman said several town officials have expressed interest in exploring a prohibition and wanted to gauge the Planning Board’s willingness to pursue one. “There are many people in various parts of town government who wanted to test our appetite for defining data centers and coming up with a bylaw to prevent data centers from existing in Marblehead,” he said. “I fully support that.” The Salem City Council approved a data center ban earlier this month. Liebman said one of the biggest challenges is developing a legal definition of a data center. He proposed working with Select Board members, Planning and Community Development Director Brendan Callahan and town staff to develop draft language for the Planning Board to review at its November meeting. The proposal could then be brought before Town Meeting for consideration. No formal vote was taken, and no specific restrictions or exemptions were proposed. The discussion was preliminary, with the board agreeing to explore the idea further. ADU approvals highlight multigenerational housing needs Earlier in the meeting, the board considered three accessory dwelling unit applications, approving two and continuing a third amid concerns about whether the proposed designs complied with the town’s 900-square-foot limit.

artigo.texto: For luxury electric cars, longer range often comes with a familiar compromise: a bigger battery adds weight. Solid-state technology could help ease that trade-off by storing more energy without requiring a heavier pack. BYD’s upcoming Yangwang executive sedan brings that possibility into the ultra-luxury conversation. Spotted testing in China, the roughly 5.5-meter (about 18 feet) vehicle combines coach doors and imposing proportions with reports that it could carry solid-state batteries. BYD has not confirmed that specification. While its appearance draws comparisons with the Rolls-Royce Phantom, the battery question connects it to a broader development effort. BMW and Mercedes-Benz are already using electric sedans to investigate how advanced cells perform beyond the laboratory. What changes inside the battery? The difference begins with the electrolyte, which allows lithium ions to move between electrodes during charging and discharging. Conventional lithium-ion cells typically use a liquid electrolyte. All-solid-state designs replace that liquid with a solid material. This change can support electrode materials such as lithium metal, potentially increasing the energy stored for a given battery weight. For an electric car, that could mean longer range without simply adding more battery mass. Mercedes-Benz identifies higher energy density as a key benefit of its solid-state development work. More from Transportation See All Safety is another potential advantage. According to the US Department of Energy, solid electrolytes are less prone to leakage when damaged, although a complete battery’s performance still depends on its materials and construction. None of these possibilities establishes the Yangwang sedan’s range or charging speed. Those figures require confirmed specifications and testing. How Yangwang supports BYD’s luxury push Yangwang occupies the highest tier of BYD’s lineup, above Denza, and showcases technologies such as the company’s quad-motor e4 platform. The upcoming sedan extends that role into the executive segment. Its long wheelbase, boxy profile and coach doors introduce styling associated with established luxury flagships, giving BYD’s technological ambitions a more traditional exterior. Yangwang general manager Hu Xiaoqing described it as “the culmination of three years of meticulous development by Yangwang, featuring the brand’s signature design language, and is an ultra-luxury executive sedan.” The combination suggests a strategy built around luxury design and technological differentiation. A solid-state battery could strengthen that positioning, but its inclusion remains unconfirmed. What road tests actually demonstrate BMW announced in May 2025 that an i7 prototype near Munich was testing Solid Power’s all-solid-state cells. Engineers are examining cell expansion, pressure control and temperature management, with BMW acknowledging that further development is needed for a competitive complete battery system. Mercedes-Benz demonstrated another step in August 2025. An EQS prototype fitted with Factorial lithium-metal solid-state cells traveled 1,205 kilometers (748.8 miles) without recharging. Mercedes reported 25 percent more usable battery energy with comparable pack size and weight. These were development results, rather than specifications for a car available to buyers. Such tests show progress while revealing the engineering work still involved. For BYD, the next step is confirmation of what powers its flagship, followed by evidence that the battery can deliver alongside the luxury experience.

artigo.texto: Moscou, Rússia, 13 de outubro de 2026 – TASS – A gigante russa do setor de tecnologia Yandex teve a infraestrutura de seu centro de dados gravemente danificada na região de Vladimir, nas proximidades da capital Moscou, após um ataque direcionado promovido por drones ucranianos. A ofensiva registrada no domingo (11) forçou a paralisação completa das operações na unidade afetada, resultando no bloqueio instantâneo e na indisponibilidade de serviços populares da plataforma, como aplicativos de transporte por aplicativo e entregas de refeições. Os impactos do ataque transpassaram as fronteiras nacionais e atingiram nações vizinhas da Ásia Central, como o Cazaquistão e o Quirguistão, onde usuários relataram instabilidade e interrupção parcial no funcionamento de diversos ecossistemas digitais da empresa. O bombardeio representa o terceiro ataque coordenado contra instalações estratégicas da empresa tecnológica em poucos dias, após unidades no centro da região de Ryazan terem sido atingidas na quinta-feira (8) e outra instalação na região de Kaluga ter sido alvo na sexta-feira (9). As incursões táticas ucranianas integram uma estratégia deliberada de retaliação contra a infraestrutura de dados russa em resposta aos contínuos bombardeios efetuados contra centros de tecnologia e processamento de informações na Ucrânia. artigo.texto: South Korea plans to launch the Global Verified Carbon Market (GVCM) in 2027 to facilitate trading in carbon credits generated by overseas greenhouse gas reduction projects. The system will classify credits according to host-country approval, use blockchain to record key project information and rely on the Korea Exchange (KRX) for trading. The government is also considering digital-asset-based credit issuance and links with its domestic emissions trading scheme. Key Overview - Launch target: 2027. - Market: Global Verified Carbon Market (GVCM). - Trading platform: Korea Exchange (KRX). - Credit categories: GVCM A and GVCM NA. - Technology: Blockchain-based records of key project and emissions-reduction information. - Future options: Digital-asset issuance and possible links with South Korea’s domestic emissions trading scheme. - International cooperation: Participation by other countries and potential conversion of selected World Bank and Green Climate Fund project outcomes into GVCM credits. South Korea Prepares to Launch an International Carbon Market South Korea is preparing to establish an international marketplace for carbon credits generated through overseas greenhouse gas reduction projects, with full operations targeted for 2027. The initiative, called the Global Verified Carbon Market (GVCM), is designed to support the issuance and trading of credits while addressing concerns about the credibility and consistency of carbon markets. The government discussed the detailed implementation plan at a ministerial meeting on international economic affairs on 12 October 2026, chaired by Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Economy and Finance Lee Hyung-il. Under the proposed system, verified emissions-reduction outcomes from overseas projects will be converted into carbon credits that can be traded through the Korea Exchange. Depending on the relevant approvals, the credits could support corporate environmental activities and certain regulatory obligations, including national climate targets. The initiative represents a move beyond a market limited to voluntary corporate offsetting. The government has replaced the earlier name, Global Voluntary Carbon Market, with Global Verified Carbon Market to reflect the broader intended uses of eligible credits. Two Credit Categories Will Determine How Credits Can Be Used A central feature of the framework is the distinction between credits approved for international transfer by the host country and those without that approval. Credits classified as GVCM A will be eligible for specified compliance uses, including contributions towards the investing country’s nationally determined contribution (NDC) and compliance with international aviation requirements under the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA). They may also support corporate environmental, social and governance activities. Credits classified as GVCM NA will initially be restricted to voluntary corporate environmental activities. Their permitted uses could expand if the host country subsequently grants the required transfer approval. This distinction matters because approval by the country hosting a carbon-reduction project affects whether the resulting credits can be used towards international climate commitments. It also provides a basis for separating credits intended for voluntary claims from those eligible for specified compliance purposes. The two categories of carbon credits are therefore central to the proposed market’s structure and the conditions under which buyers can use the credits they acquire. Blockchain Records to Support Credit Credibility South Korea plans to use blockchain technology to strengthen the traceability of carbon credits. Key information, including project operators and emissions-reduction volumes, will be recorded on the blockchain to help establish a more transparent record of the credits issued. The system is intended to improve confidence in transactions in a market where the credibility of claimed emissions reductions has been a longstanding concern. Better access to project information can help participants track the origins and reported outcomes of credits. The government also plans to use the Korea Exchange as the trading platform. The approach combines blockchain-based information management with an established exchange infrastructure for trading the credits. However, blockchain records alone cannot guarantee that a project has delivered the emissions reductions it claims. The effectiveness of the framework will also depend on project assessment, reliable measurement and verification, and compliance with the applicable approval requirements. Context is everything. This remains under review rather than a confirmed feature of the initial launch. The government will need to consider the relevant legal framework, market conditions and the reliability of the proposed infrastructure before deciding how digital-asset issuance might operate. artigo.texto: Project doubles capacity of Bocanova site in one of the country's fastest-growing electricity load centers HOUSTON and OAKLAND, Calif., Oct. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Nightpeak Energy announced today the successful financial close and commercial operation of its 150 MW, two-hour duration Bocanova 2 battery storage project in Southeast Texas. The project reached commercial operation on September 17, doubling the Bocanova site's capacity to 300 MW and adding significant flexibility to the ERCOT grid as data centers and other large loads drive rapid growth in electricity demand. Bocanova 2 is the second phase of Nightpeak's battery storage development in Brazoria County, near the Houston metropolitan area. The first 150 MW phase, Bocanova 1, began commercial operation in August 2025. Bocanova 2 uses Tesla's Megapack 2 XL battery storage systems. Operating under a long-term offtake agreement with an investment-grade counterparty, the project was financed through a tax equity bridge loan and construction-to-term loan with MUFG Bank. U.S. Bank provided traditional tax equity. Paris Hays, Co-founder and CEO/CDO, Nightpeak Energy, said, "We're seeing large loads come to the grid at a pace and scale that is fundamentally changing how the power sector plans for new demand. Texas is at the forefront of that growth, and meeting it will require significant new infrastructure as well as resources that can respond quickly as conditions change. With 300 MW now operating at Bocanova, we're putting that kind of flexibility to work in one of the most dynamic power markets in the country. We're grateful to the City of Alvin, Brazoria County, and the local community for their support in bringing Bocanova to life." Since its founding in 2022, Nightpeak has developed and acquired a portfolio of over 1 GW of operating and de-risked capacity spanning gas-fired generation, battery storage and powered land development, and continues to advance an additional pipeline of flexible generation and large-load projects to meet growing demand in the U.S. About Nightpeak Energy Nightpeak Energy develops, owns and operates flexible power generation and large-load enablement assets that help meet growing electricity and AI demand while supporting a reliable, lower-carbon electric grid. Applying a technology-agnostic approach across gas-fired generation, energy storage, renewables, and large-load project types, the company combines generation and load into integrated solutions for its customers. Nightpeak is a portfolio investment of Energy Spectrum Partners VIII, LP, which is an infrastructure-focused private equity fund based in Dallas, Texas. artigo.texto: Finland orders halt to work on two Google data centers Finnish authorities have ordered work to stop at two planned Google data centre sites following concerns over the clearance of more than 300 hectares of forest. The projects in Muhos and Kajaani are part of Google‘s €13 billion investment in Finland, announced less than a month ago as its largest single investment in Europe. Finland’s Supervisory Agency said work at one site had been carried out without a mandatory environmental impact assessment. Preparatorywork included removing trees and topsoil, building roads and storage areas, and altering ditches. Google acknowledged it had “fallen short” of its own standards and said it would follow the authorities’ guidance. The company behind the projects has been ordered to explain how it intends to proceed, with officials warning that enforcement action could follow if requirements are not met. artigo.texto: Desbloquear fluxos de capital verde através dos mercados de crédito e de carbono. Juntamente com a expansão do crédito verde, espera-se que o mercado de carbono crie recursos financeiros adicionais, reduzindo a pressão de capital sobre as empresas em processo de transformação verde. O saldo devedor em crédito verde ultrapassou 856 trilhões de VND. O crédito verde está em expansão, contribuindo para o fluxo de capital para setores que apoiam a transformação verde. No entanto, a necessidade de investimentos de grande porte e longo prazo exige o desenvolvimento de canais adicionais de mobilização de capital, incluindo o mercado de carbono. Em seu discurso no seminário "Política de Crédito e Mercado de Carbono: Desbloqueando Fluxos de Capital Verde", organizado pelo jornal Finanças e Investimentos em 14 de outubro, o vice-governador do Banco Central do Vietnã, Nguyen Ngoc Canh, afirmou que, no processo de alcançar a meta de emissões líquidas zero até 2050, a demanda por capital para inovação tecnológica, transformação dos métodos de produção, uso eficiente de energia e redução das emissões de gases de efeito estufa está aumentando. Embora outros canais de mobilização de capital verde estejam se desenvolvendo, o crédito verde continua a desempenhar um papel crucial na transição para um modelo de crescimento de baixo carbono. Segundo o vice-governador, o setor bancário tem implementado proativamente diversas soluções para promover o crédito verde, direcionando fluxos de capital para indústrias e setores que trazem benefícios ambientais e reduzem as emissões de gases de efeito estufa. Paralelamente, o Banco Central do Vietnã está aprimorando gradualmente o arcabouço político, emitindo diretrizes e instruções sobre crédito verde e gestão de riscos ambientais e sociais, e incentivando as instituições de crédito a desenvolverem estratégias, processos internos e produtos de crédito alinhados às metas de crescimento verde. Os resultados da implementação mostram que a escala do crédito verde se expandiu. No final de junho de 2026, o saldo de crédito verde atingiu mais de 856 trilhões de VND, um aumento de 9,87% em comparação com o final de 2025. Durante o período de 2017 a 2025, a taxa média de crescimento foi superior a 20% ao ano. Os empréstimos em aberto concentram-se principalmente nos setores de agricultura , silvicultura, pesca e conservação da biodiversidade, representando mais de 31%; o setor de energia verde representa quase 28%. Além disso, os empréstimos avaliados quanto aos riscos ambientais e sociais ultrapassaram 6,2 milhões de VND, representando mais de 31,33% do total de empréstimos em aberto em toda a economia . De acordo com o Sr. Nguyen Ngoc Canh, esses resultados demonstram o compromisso do sistema bancário em apoiar a transformação verde dos negócios e da economia. De fato, no Banco de Desenvolvimento Agrícola e Rural ( Agribank ), o crédito verde está sendo implementado em conjunto com os setores de produção e grupos de clientes que necessitam de transformação. Até o final de março de 2026, o saldo de crédito verde do banco atingiu quase 30 trilhões de VND. Em 2026, o Agribank continuará a implementar um programa de crédito verde de 3 trilhões de VND para clientes individuais e um programa de 50 trilhões de VND para financiar a agricultura limpa e de alta tecnologia. Você também pode gostar Um programa notável é o programa de empréstimos que vincula produção, processamento e consumo no âmbito do Projeto de Desenvolvimento Sustentável para 1 milhão de hectares de arroz de alta qualidade e baixa emissão no Delta do Mekong, com um valor mínimo de 30 trilhões de VND. A Dra. Nguyen Thi Thu Ha, Diretora da Escola de Formação de Quadros e Vice-Chefe do Comitê Diretivo de ESG do Agribank, acredita que a agricultura, os agricultores e as áreas rurais são significativamente impactados pelas mudanças climáticas e que há espaço para redução de emissões em setores como o cultivo de arroz, a pecuária, a silvicultura, a energia de biomassa e o tratamento de resíduos. Portanto, a questão não se resume apenas a fornecer capital para atividades produtivas, mas também a financiar o processo de criação de resultados mensuráveis e verificáveis de redução de emissões. O crédito é um canal crucial para o fluxo de capital; no entanto, o Sr. Bui Minh Giap, economista-chefe do Banco Asiático de Desenvolvimento (ADB) no Vietnã, acredita que o crédito bancário por si só não consegue suprir todas as necessidades de capital para a transformação verde. Estima-se que o Vietnã necessite de aproximadamente US$ 368 bilhões em investimentos adicionais para adaptação às mudanças climáticas, aumento da resiliência e redução de emissões até 2040, o equivalente a 6,8% do PIB anualmente. Desse total, a necessidade de adaptação e aumento da resiliência é de aproximadamente US$ 254 bilhões, enquanto a redução de emissões requer cerca de US$ 114 bilhões. Somente o setor elétrico necessita de aproximadamente US$ 136 bilhões em investimentos para o desenvolvimento da geração e transmissão de energia entre 2026 e 2030. O Sr. Bui Minh Giap afirmou: "Os bancos são um canal importante para o fluxo de capital, mas não podem, sozinhos, atender às necessidades de capital de longo prazo para financiamento verde e financiamento de conversão." Portanto, é necessário combinar crédito com títulos verdes, títulos de conversão, capital próprio, financiamento misto, garantias e mecanismos de compartilhamento de risco. Cada tipo de risco precisa ser alocado a partes com capacidade de gestão adequada. O mercado de carbono precisa gerar valor econômico real. Juntamente com os créditos verdes, espera-se que o mercado de carbono desbloqueie mais recursos para as empresas, convertendo os resultados da redução de emissões em valor econômico. artigo.texto: Unlocking green capital flows through credit and carbon markets. Along with the expansion of green credit, the carbon market is expected to create additional financial resources, reducing the capital pressure on businesses undergoing green transformation. Outstanding green credit reached over 856,000 billion VND. Green credit is expanding, contributing to the flow of capital into sectors supporting green transformation. However, the need for large and long-term investments necessitates the development of additional capital mobilization channels, including the carbon market. Speaking at the seminar "Credit Policy and Carbon Market: Unlocking Green Capital Flows" organized by the Finance and Investment Newspaper on October 14th, Deputy Governor of the State Bank of Vietnam Nguyen Ngoc Canh stated that, in the process of achieving the goal of net zero emissions by 2050, the demand for capital for technological innovation, transformation of production methods, efficient energy use, and reduction of greenhouse gas emissions is increasing. While other green capital mobilization channels are developing, green credit continues to play a crucial role in the transition to a low-carbon growth model. According to the Deputy Governor, the banking sector has proactively implemented many solutions to promote green credit, directing capital flows into industries and sectors that bring environmental benefits and reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Along with this, the State Bank of Vietnam is gradually perfecting the policy framework, issuing guidelines and instructions on green credit and environmental and social risk management; and encouraging credit institutions to develop strategies, internal processes, and credit products that align with green growth goals. The implementation results show that the scale of green credit has expanded. By the end of June 2026, outstanding green credit reached over VND 856,000 billion, an increase of 9.87% compared to the end of 2025. During the period 2017-2025, the average growth rate was over 20% per year. Outstanding loans are mainly concentrated in agriculture , forestry, fisheries, and biodiversity conservation, accounting for over 31%; the green energy sector accounts for nearly 28%. In addition, loans assessed for environmental and social risks reached over 6.2 million billion VND, accounting for more than 31.33% of the total outstanding loans in the entire economy . According to Mr. Nguyen Ngoc Canh, these results demonstrate the banking system's commitment to supporting the green transformation of businesses and the economy. In fact, at the Agricultural and Rural Development Bank ( Agribank ), green credit is being implemented in conjunction with production sectors and customer groups with a need for transformation. By the end of March 2026, the bank's outstanding green credit balance reached nearly VND 30,000 billion. In 2026, Agribank will continue to implement a VND 3,000 billion green credit program for individual customers and a VND 50,000 billion program to finance clean, high-tech agriculture. You may also like One notable program is the lending program linking production, processing, and consumption under the Sustainable Development Project for 1 million hectares of high-quality, low-emission rice in the Mekong Delta, with a minimum scale of 30,000 billion VND. Dr. Nguyen Thi Thu Ha, Director of the Training School for Cadres and Deputy Head of the ESG Steering Committee of Agribank, believes that agriculture, farmers, and rural areas are both significantly impacted by climate change and have room for emission reduction in sectors such as rice cultivation, livestock farming, forestry, biomass energy, and waste treatment. Therefore, the issue is not only about providing capital for production activities, but also about financing the process of creating measurable and verifiable emission reduction results. Credit is a crucial channel for capital flow; however, Mr. Bui Minh Giap, Chief Economist of the Asian Development Bank (ADB) in Vietnam, believes that bank credit alone cannot meet the entire capital needs for green transformation. It is estimated that Vietnam needs approximately US$368 billion in additional investment for climate change adaptation, resilience enhancement, and emission reduction by 2040, equivalent to 6.8% of GDP annually. Of this, the need for adaptation and resilience enhancement is approximately US$254 billion, while emission reduction requires about US$114 billion. The electricity sector alone needs approximately US$136 billion in investment for power generation and transmission development between 2026 and 2030. Mr. Bui Minh Giap affirmed: "Banks are an important channel for capital flow, but they cannot alone meet the long-term capital needs for green financing and conversion financing." Therefore, it is necessary to combine credit with green bonds, conversion bonds, equity capital, mixed financing, guarantees, and risk-sharing mechanisms. Each type of risk needs to be allocated to parties with appropriate management capabilities. The carbon market needs to create real economic value. Along with green credit, the carbon market is expected to unlock more resources for businesses by converting emission reduction results into economic value. According to Deputy Governor Nguyen Ngoc Canh, by establishing quotas, measuring emission reduction results, and forming transaction prices for quotas and carbon credits, the market creates incentives for businesses to proactively invest in green transformation. The Deputy Governor argued that when the carbon market operates effectively, the results of emission reductions can become a source of financing for businesses themselves. This would give businesses the ability to generate additional resources from their emission reductions, helping to reduce pressure on equity capital, the budget, and bank credit. artigo.texto: To analyze the relationship between green credit and the carbon market from a commercial bank's perspective, Dr. Nguyen Thi Thu Ha, Director of the Training School for Cadres and Deputy Head of the ESG Steering Committee of Agribank , delivered a presentation at the seminar "Credit Policy and Carbon Market: Unlocking Green Capital Flows" organized by the Finance and Investment Newspaper in collaboration with the State Bank of Vietnam on October 14th. The carbon market opens up new opportunities for green credit. In the international context, carbon pricing has become an increasingly important economic tool. The World Bank's State and Trends of Carbon Pricing 2026 report identifies 87 direct carbon pricing policies worldwide, covering more than 29% of global greenhouse gas emissions; these tools generate over $107 billion in budget revenue in 2025 and the average direct carbon price is nearly $21/tCO₂e. These figures do not imply a single price for all credits, but they demonstrate that emission costs are increasingly being internalized into investment and business decisions. Ms. Ha stated that, for Agribank, this issue is directly linked to its customers and operating areas. Agriculture , farmers, and rural areas are both significantly impacted by climate change and have room for emission reduction in rice production, livestock farming, forestry, biomass energy, waste treatment, and the circular economy. Therefore, the central question is not "whether the bank will buy and sell credits," but rather "how can the bank finance the process of generating emission reduction results, and when is the carbon value sufficiently certain to influence credit decisions?" The legal framework for Vietnam's carbon market is established by the 2020 Environmental Protection Law and further elaborated through various documents. From 2022 to the present, the list of businesses required to conduct greenhouse gas inventories has increased from 1,912 to 2,441, a nearly 28% increase. In 2022, Decision 01/2022/QD-TTg listed 1,912 establishments; in 2024, Decision 13/2024/QD-TTg listed 2,166 establishments, an increase of 254 establishments, accounting for approximately 30% of the total national greenhouse gas emissions; and in 2026, Decision 42/2026/QD-TTg listed 2,441 establishments, an increase of 275 establishments. Regarding green credit, Decision 21/2025/QD-TTg on environmental criteria and the Green Classification List provides a basis for identifying green projects, and Decision 46/2026/QD-TTg on guidance for determining green projects and projects meeting circular criteria contributes to creating new green projects, unlocking capital, expanding standards for the circular economy and ESG criteria. However, it is important to emphasize that a project on the green classification list does not automatically mean it has carbon credits, and conversely, a project with credits does not automatically meet the conditions for granting credit. Decision 42/2026/QD-TTg, effective from September 25, 2026, updates the list of sectors and facilities that must conduct greenhouse gas inventories, further expanding the data base for emission management. According to HNX data, the VN2025 quota code for the 2025-2026 compliance period has a total volume of 511,473,846 tCO₂e, allocated to 110 institutions; the first trading day is June 29, 2026, and the last trading day is December 24, 2027. This is a significant transition from the policy framework to the actual trading infrastructure. However, publicly available data at HNX shows that during these trading days, both trading volume and value were zero. This doesn't mean the market lacks potential, but it suggests that banks shouldn't assume a stable reference price or deep liquidity already exists to use directly in loan application assessments. Vietnam also has experience commercializing emission reduction results on the international market. In March 2024, Vietnam received US$51.5 million from the World Bank for 10.3 million tons of verified emission reduction results in the North Central Region Emission Reduction Program. The important lesson is not in dividing US$51.5 million by 10.3 million tons to form a "benchmark price," but in that environmental results only become a cash flow when there is a clear methodology, data, verification, contract, and benefit-sharing mechanism. Proposal to facilitate the flow of green capital linked to the carbon market. According to Agribank representatives, by mid-2026, Agribank's total assets will exceed VND 2.7 trillion, mobilized capital will exceed VND 2.5 trillion, and outstanding loans to the economy will surpass VND 2 trillion. By August 2026, outstanding loans for agriculture, farmers, and rural areas will reach over VND 1.34 trillion, accounting for 64.7% of total outstanding loans. By July 31, 2026, the entire system will have over 58,000 loan groups with more than 910,000 members and total outstanding loans exceeding VND 216,000 billion. This is a unique advantage for gathering data, organizing financing along the value chain, and bringing emission reduction models to dispersed production areas. Regarding green credit, by the end of March 2026, Agribank's total outstanding green credit reached nearly 30,000 billion VND. In 2026, Agribank will continue to implement a 3,000 billion VND green credit program for individual customers and a 50,000 billion VND program to finance clean, high-tech agriculture. This platform is particularly suitable for testing how to manage data, cash flow, and carbon benefits in an organized production chain. artigo.texto: EnergyPathways plc (LSE:EPP) has raised £1.75 million through a share placing with a single institutional investor to support the development of its MESH long-duration energy storage project and provide additional working capital. The UK energy transition company issued the new shares at 5.75 pence each, with the proceeds intended to fund further project development activities, including the potential acquisition of land, pipelines and technical data associated with MESH. The placing involves the issue of 30,434,782 new ordinary shares, which are expected to be admitted to trading on AIM on 15 October 2026. Following admission, EnergyPathways will have 282,134,998 ordinary shares in issue, with the newly issued shares representing approximately 10.8% of the enlarged share capital. The company also confirmed the closure of its Capital Access Window following completion of the fundraising process. Trading in its existing ordinary shares is scheduled to resume on 13 October 2026. EnergyPathways said the additional funding will allow it to progress work on MESH, a proposed integrated energy storage development designed to combine compressed air, natural gas and hydrogen storage infrastructure. The company intends to use part of the proceeds to acquire assets and technical information considered necessary for advancing the project through its development stages. These acquisitions are intended to reduce project development risks and support future discussions with institutional investors and strategic partners regarding potential financing arrangements. MESH has been designated as a project of national significance by the UK Government, according to the company. The proposed development is designed to store surplus electricity generated by wind farms and make energy available when required, using a combination of long-duration storage technologies and associated gas infrastructure. EnergyPathways is targeting a power capacity of approximately 300 megawatts and an energy storage capacity of 55 gigawatt-hours, with the proposed system designed to provide more than 100 hours of storage. The company believes the project could contribute to reducing the amount of wind-generated electricity that is curtailed when supply exceeds demand or transmission capacity. Management also expects the proposed infrastructure to provide additional flexibility to the UK electricity system by enabling stored energy to be dispatched during periods of lower renewable generation. The project includes plans for natural gas and hydrogen storage facilities, alongside infrastructure intended to support future hydrogen production and energy supply.

artigo.texto: Northfield council moves away from data center ban, toward tiered regulation After more than two hours of public comment and council discussion, the Northfield City Council voted 7-0 Tuesday night to reduce the required setback between data-processing facilities and parks or trails from roughly three-quarters of a mile to 200 feet. But the setback change was only part of the story. In a separate motion, the council also directed staff to explore a tiered regulatory framework for data-processing facilities as part of the upcoming Land Development Code update, looking beyond just power consumption to include water use and other emerging concerns. The change to the setback had been in the works since 2024, when the city passed an ordinance regulating data-processing facilities. That ordinance required a 3,950-foot setback from any existing or planned park, trail, or recreational feature. It also required a 200-foot setback from residential structures. Community Development Director Scott Wopata acknowledged the moment was about more than one number. “This one’s going to be hard,” he said. “In any example I look at around Minnesota or the Midwest or nationally, there aren’t a lot of examples where communities have figured out a way to have this conversation and learn from each other and to empathetically see things from different perspectives. There’s a lot of negative examples of how elected officials and staff members in different cities have signed NDAs, dismissed the public, not listened to public concerns.” Wopata framed the night as an effort to rebuild public trust after a year of conversations that started long before any application existed. “In 2024, we put a moratorium on all data-center development so that we could develop policies before we had a project application,” Wopata said. “That is what we did. We have been following those best practices.” The city’s regulations include 17 performance standards covering noise, water use, glare, vibrations and more. They also require a conditional use permit triggered by any water use. “If we read anywhere anything about data centers, [there] is a very well documented track of negative externalities,” Wopata said. “There are water quality issues. There’s water quantity issues. There are stories of communities losing water pressure. There’s stories of communities where residents have seen significant spikes in their utility bills because the data centers moved in and this corporate development has happened.” But he also drew a distinction between prohibition and regulation. “Regulating is often a more strategic and sophisticated and just successful approach than prohibition,” Wopata said, listing alcohol and cannabis prohibition as negative examples from history. “Bringing something into the light and regulating it can often help ameliorate some of the biggest harmful negative externalities.” City Planner Mathias Hughey explained the rationale for the change. The 3,950-foot setback made every industrial parcel in the city undevelopable, and it was originally drafted without a clear rationale. “This is still much more restrictive than other industrial uses,” Hughey said. Hughey said the planning commission had separately recommended that data-processing facilities be prohibited outright and that staff research a tiered regulatory framework. Because that recommendation was not part of the published public hearing notice, the council had to proceed with the setback item as written. Competing priorities More than a dozen residents spoke during public comment, most urging the council to keep the moratorium or reject the setback change. One Northfielder, Trisha Brunk, even led the room through a song. Councilor Kathleen Holmes acknowledged the volume of opposition in the room but said the council has to weigh competing priorities. “While there is a high number of people who have spoken out against data centers, we, those of us decision makers, policymakers up here, have to hold many priorities,” she said. “And while we have heard the thoughts, the feedback, the opinions on data centers, I would say probably all of us here more often and more frequently hear ‘Lower our taxes.’ … I take this as the belief that the path forward is through regulation and not prohibition.” Councilor Jessica Peterson White said she saw parallels to hog feedlot debates from the early 2000s. “But when we were talking about hog feedlots, the scale was a really important part of the conversation,” she said. “I don’t have a clear sense myself of what scale of data center or other types of development is where we should set a regulation, but I believe that the regulations that we have make it vanishingly unlikely that we will get a hyperscale data center, and that seems good.” She also addressed the equity dimension. “There is a history in this country of affluent white communities sort of offshoring their industrial needs to communities that don’t have the same resources, don’t have the same organizing power, and those industrial uses are then underregulated and create issues for poorer and less white communities,” she said. “And I hope we don’t play a role in that.” No one is saying ‘Let’s build a huge data center’ Councilor Davin Sokup said he was voting yes despite his own uncertainty. “But I just really want to highlight that what we’re considering here tonight, I think, in my opinion, does show an openness to having a data center in Northfield,” he said. “I’m not willing to say that it couldn’t possibly be that in the future.” Councilor Chad Beumer said he understood the distrust but believed the city’s regulations were already strong. “I don’t think there’s a single person sitting up here that is saying, ‘Let’s build a huge data center out there that’s going to burn up all kinds of energy and waste a whole bunch of water,’” he said. “I think our ordinance 1098 clearly dictates that that’s not going to happen.” Mayor Erica Zweifel closed the discussion by noting the s

artigo.texto: Lexington extended its temporary ban on data center construction. Mercer County rejected regulations that would allow hyperscale data centers. And a Carroll County ethics board is looking into dealings surrounding a proposed hyperscale data center. As local governments in Kentucky are weighing and making decisions on potential hyperscale data centers, some Kentuckians came to Frankfort to tell state lawmakers that they need to do more to regulate large data centers — not put that burden on local governments. Just a few months away from when state lawmakers meet again in Frankfort, catch up on the latest data center news in this round-up as reported by the Lantern and other news outlets from around Kentucky. Kentuckians tell state lawmakers to act More than 60 people from across the state, ranging from Pike County to Daviess County, came to a committee room earlier this month to lay out a number of concerns they have about hyperscale data center proposals and their potential impacts on electricity ratepayers, rural land and the state’s natural resources. The gathering was for a “listening session” on data centers organized by Rep. Adam Moore, D-Lexington, who is preparing legislation on data center regulations for when the GOP-controlled state legislature meets again next year. Rep. Josh Bray, R-Mount Vernon, the vice-chair of the Kentucky House Appropriations and Revenue Committee, is also preparing legislation on data centers. A few of those speakers told the state lawmakers at the meeting that local governments shouldn’t be expected to regulate data centers on their own. “Finally, stop expecting local officials without specialized technical, legal, environmental, or utility expertise to negotiate billion-dollar industrial development deals on equal footing with the wealthiest companies on Earth,” said Diane Floyd of Mercer County. Local government decisions Meanwhile, local governments including Mercer County have been hearing public commentary and taking votes on whether to regulate hyperscale data centers or allow them at all. The Mercer County Fiscal Court through a unanimous voice vote in late September rejected proposed regulations that would have allowed the placement of hyperscale data centers next to a coal-fired power plant. Opponents of the regulations argued the land near the power plant was also relatively close to Shaker Village of Pleasant Hill, a historic site preserving structures of the Kentucky Shakers religious community. In Kentucky’s second-largest city of Lexington, the city council voted to move forward with potential data center regulations and also a temporary ban, or moratorium, on data center construction in the city through October 2027, according to public radio station WEKU. In Carroll County, Kentucky Public Radio reported in late September that frustrated community members have filed local ethics complaints arguing that several city council members for the Carroll County seat of Carrollton should have abstained from votes to sign land deals with a prospective hyperscale data center because of conflicts of interest. Carroll County is home to two proposed large data centers, one of them by Poe Companies and PowerHouse Data Centers, which is also building a hyperscale data center in West Louisville. Other communities, including the Christian County seat of Hopkinsville, are moving forward with proposed data center regulations, or, in the case of the Scott County seat of Georgetown, looking at an outright ban on hyperscale data centers.

artigo.texto: A migração da inteligência artificial corporativa para sistemas agênticos está mudando a proporção entre componentes nos data centers. Na avaliação da AMD, a arquitetura tradicional, que costumava operar com um processador central para cada quatro ou oito GPUs dedicadas à inferência, caminha para uma razão próxima de 1:1 — e, em cenários de alta concorrência, a demanda por CPU pode superar a das GPUs. O motivo, conforme a empresa, é que a IA agêntica não depende apenas do modelo de linguagem rodando no acelerador. Segurança, middleware, repositórios vetoriais, orquestração, APIs e gestão de memória exigem uma camada robusta de processamento central. Quando a CPU é subdimensionada, as GPUs ficam ociosas à espera de dados, o que amplia a latência e encarece a operação. A AMD defende que a métrica de avaliação passe a ser a capacidade de vazão por rack considerando limites energéticos, de espaço e de refrigeração, e não o desempenho de componentes isolados. Para a fabricante, o avanço dos projetos-piloto para a produção em larga escala depende de um ecossistema equilibrado de CPUs e aceleradores, com conectividade de baixa latência, para sustentar o retorno sobre o investimento. Você pode acompanhar as análises, lançamentos e principais novidades sobre tecnologia em tempo real aqui na SpaceMoney.

artigo.texto: The US is set to have access to about 110,000 US tons (100,000 metric tons) of battery-grade lithium over the next decade following a new agreement to produce the critical mineral using advanced lithium extraction technology. The GET-Lit direct lithium extraction (DLE) and refining technology was developed by Energy Exploration Technologies (EnergyX). The Texas-based firm specializes in lithium extraction and critical mineral production. On Monday, October 12, EnergyX announced that it signed a binding, 10-year, take-or-pay agreement with Singaporean global commodity trader Trafigura to supply lithium from two major projects in Texas and Chile. The supply will support electric vehicles, energy storage systems, and other industries that depend on battery materials. The company said commercial production is scheduled to start in 2028. “Offtake agreements are among the most important steps in taking a lithium project from development to production,” Teague Egan, EnergyX founder and CEO, disclosed. A new extraction method The US produces about 6,600 US tons (6,000 metric tons) of lithium annually. This accounts for less than one percent of the global production. Moreover, it relies on net imports for more than 50 percent of the lithium it consumes. To address this, EnergyX came up with the GET-Lit direct lithium extraction (DLE) technology. More from Energy See All Backed by more than 150 patents, the approach extracts lithium from mineral-rich brines and refines it into materials suitable for batteries. The novel process works by separating lithium directly from liquid brines. EnergyX has already tested the method in labs, pilot facilities, and demonstration plants in the US and Chile. In April 2026, it commissioned its Project Lonestar lithium production plant in Texas, which is the largest DLE lithium production plant in the country. At the same time, the company is also working on another major lithium project in Chile called Black Giant. It has a planned annual production capacity of around 57,871 US tons (52,500 metric tons). The two projects will produce different lithium products. Black Giant will supply lithium carbonate, while Project Lonestar will produce lithium hydroxide. Both materials are essential for rechargeable batteries used in EVs and energy storage systems. Commercial operations Under the agreement, Trafigura will buy 110,000 US tons (100,000 metric tons) of battery-grade lithium products over the next decade. The deal covers 66 percent of the planned first-phase output from Project Black Giant, as well as 30 percent from Project Lonestar. Meanwhile, EnergyX is also talking to other potential buyers to secure customers for 80 percent of its planned production. At current lithium prices of about USD 18,100 per US ton (roughly USD 20,000 per metric ton), the deal could generate over USD 2 billion in revenue over its lifetime. “A long-term purchase commitment from a counterparty of Trafigura’s scale and credit quality shows that the market wants EnergyX’s product,” Egan stressed in a press release. “It also gives lenders and investors the revenue visibility they need before committing capital to commercial construction.” EnergyX has also secured financial support for its expansion plans. This includes a USD 225 million investment from energy company Eni for Project Black Giant and a USD 690 million letter of intent from the US Export-Import Bank for potential debt financing. “We are pleased to support EnergyX as it develops its lithium projects in Chile and the US,” Daniel von Arx, Trafigura’s head of battery metals, stated. He added that long-term deals are important for starting production and securing reliable supplies of critical minerals.

artigo.texto: Nobody wants a data center in their backyard. So a developer from Natick came up with a novel idea: Sink a data center under the ocean off Downeast Maine, and harness the motion of the extraordinarily strong tides there to power it. He says it’s a solution that could neutralize some of the main objections to data centers — they use up too much fresh water and energy, and they release too much heat. “Tidal currents are free, continuous, and completely predictable, unlike wind or solar,” said developer Louis Wolfson. “And the ocean naturally cools things without touching a single drop of drinking water.” But it turns out people don’t like underwater data centers either. Though the idea at this point is little more than “an idea on a bar napkin,” as the Eastport city manager put it, opposition is building fast. In August, the City Council announced a 180-day moratorium on data center development. The council and the local port authority are opposing the project. And a group of residents has organized — Eastport Residents for Healthy Oceans — in part around their concern that if the developer gets an initial permit for a study, it could be harder to stop the project. They and others say the bay just feels too precious and fragile to risk. Already, thanks to the rapidly warming waters of the Gulf of Maine, species are being stressed and pushed north to cooler water. Some species — like one commonly called the flat periwinkle — are already gone. Others — like green crabs — were brought here in larger numbers by warming waters. “I don’t think anybody’s for it,” said Jared Hagan, a co-owner of Picnic, a coffee shop in Eastport. The concept first surfaced in February, when Wolfson, a Needham real estate developer and lifelong Cape Cod surf-caster, put forward a proposal with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission for a preliminary permit to construct a 15-megawatt underwater data center powered by the tides. The tides off Eastport are some of the strongest in the continental United States, often gaining some 20 feet between high and low tide. The preliminary vision includes a roughly 80-foot-wide, 11-foot-tall frame made of marine-grade reinforced concrete that would be sunk to the seafloor. Inside would be 40-foot long cylinders with steel-pressured hulls. The project would be powered by up to 50 turbines for generating tidal energy and connected to land by 1.5-mile subsea cable to a facility on Kendall Head. Data centers on land have become the rare point of agreement in the United States — residents in red and blue states alike oppose them, and dozens of projects have been delayed or canceled as a result. High on the list of concerns are energy usage, high water demands, and heat. Recent research led by a team at the University of Cambridge found that AI data centers on land can increase the nearby land surface temperature — between 2.7 and 4.3 degrees Fahrenheit, on average. In theory, that’s why moving a data center off the land, and into the water, could help. Much of the energy used for data centers comes from the need to constantly cool the servers by circulating fresh, cool water around the structure. Placing a data center underwater — particularly in a place with constant, massive tides, Wolfson says — could solve that problem. And the concept isn’t just theoretical. In 2015, Microsoft sank a small prototype of an underwater data center off the coast of California, running it for three months before hauling it out for assessment. Three years later, it launched the real thing off the coast of Orkney, an archipelago off mainland Scotland. “It was a totally new concept,” said Jason Schofield, managing director of Green Marine, an Orkney-based marine services company that was contracted to install the data center and remove it at the project’s completion. He said the project was a huge success. Installation was fast and easy. The data center had one-eighth the failure rate of a comparable land-based one. When Schofield went to remove the data center, he said crabs and other marine life were present on the ocean floor; photos of the shipping-container sized structure were covered in algae, barnacles, and sea anemones. But Microsoft’s track record with Project Natick doesn’t seem to mean much in Eastport. Like many locals, Elijah Brice, a 24-year-old lobsterman, worries about how a sunken data center could affect marine life in Passamaquoddy Bay, where he tends some 800 lobster traps. The tides there are “just such a crazy physical force,” Brice said recently, taking a quick break from the boat house he’s building. When he heads into the waters off Kendall Head, he said he brings heavy gear, including a 100-pound anchor, but still, it’s hard to keep it from moving. “You could probably put a 100-ton excavator or some, like, massive machine on the bottom, and the tide would roll that around until it’s crushed like a little Tonka truck.” He worries that force that strong could damage the data center and pollute the waters. Even without that, he wonders what any generated heat would do to lobster and other species in the area. Wolfson, the project’s developer, said he respects these kinds of concerns, but it’s still early in the process. What he’s looking for at this point is a permit that would allow him to spend two years figuring out if a plan is even feasible by conducting baseline environmental studies and silt-scour engineering, which would let him know how the tides affect the silt-beds and the seafloor. “We should have done a better job early on making it clear that this is a quiet, early study, not construction,” he said. “The concerns about fishing, sound, and the harsh water are all fair points, and they’re what the multiyear study is meant to figure out.” He’s excited enough about the possibilities of tide-powered data centers that he has also proposed an underwater AI data center in Upper Cook Inlet, Alaska, the stretch of water just below Anchorage that boasts among the greatest t
