artigo.texto: Na manhã de 14 de outubro, o jornal Finanças e Investimentos organizou um seminário intitulado "Política de Crédito e Mercado de Carbono: Desbloqueando Fluxos de Capital Verde". Em sua apresentação, o vice-governador do Banco Central do Vietnã (SBV), Nguyen Ngoc Canh, enfatizou a relação complementar entre o crédito verde e o mercado de carbono na mobilização de recursos para o processo de transformação dos negócios e da economia . Converter os resultados da redução de emissões em recursos financeiros. Segundo o vice-governador Nguyen Ngoc Canh, para cumprir o compromisso assumido pelo Vietnã na COP26 de alcançar emissões líquidas zero até 2050, o Partido, o Estado e o Governo emitiram diversas diretrizes e políticas para promover o crescimento verde, a transição energética e o desenvolvimento de uma economia de baixo carbono. Esse processo exige recursos significativos para inovação tecnológica, transformação dos métodos de produção, uso eficiente de energia e redução das emissões de gases de efeito estufa. Portanto, além do orçamento estatal e do capital mobilizado nos mercados de capitais e monetário, outros mecanismos de mercado precisam ser desenvolvidos para complementar os recursos e criar incentivos econômicos para que as empresas reduzam proativamente as emissões. Ao estabelecer cotas, mensurar os resultados da redução de emissões e definir preços de transação para cotas e créditos de carbono, o mercado de carbono cria um mecanismo para converter os resultados da redução de emissões em valor econômico. Isso proporciona às empresas mais incentivos e recursos para continuarem investindo na transformação verde. Em 29 de janeiro de 2026, o Governo emitiu o Decreto nº 29/2026/ND-CP, que regulamenta o mercado interno de carbono, criando um arcabouço legal para a organização e operação do mercado e negociação de cotas de emissão de gases de efeito estufa e créditos de carbono. O mercado interno de carbono iniciou suas operações em 29 de junho de 2026. O mercado piloto foi inicialmente estabelecido com mais de 511 milhões de toneladas de CO₂ equivalente em quotas de emissão alocadas a instalações nos três setores de energia térmica, ferro e aço e cimento durante o período de 2025–2026. A fase piloto durará até o final de 2028, antes da transição para a operação totalmente obrigatória a partir de 2029. Bancos comerciais participam como bancos liquidadores; durante a fase piloto, o BIDV é o único banco liquidador no mercado. Do ponto de vista do setor bancário, o vice-governador Nguyen Ngoc Canh acredita que o papel de cada instrumento no processo de transição verde precisa ser claramente compreendido. O crédito verde fornece capital para investimentos, inovação tecnológica e desenvolvimento de indústrias e setores verdes, gerando, assim, resultados de redução de emissões. Esses resultados formam a base para a criação de bens no mercado de carbono. Por outro lado, um mercado de carbono que funcione de forma eficiente pode complementar as receitas das empresas através da redução das emissões, apoiar a produção e as operações comerciais e contribuir para a melhoria da qualidade do crédito bancário. “Quando o mercado de carbono funciona de forma eficaz, as reduções de emissões resultantes podem ser convertidas em recursos financeiros para as próprias empresas. Consequentemente, o desenvolvimento do mercado de carbono pode contribuir para reduzir a pressão sobre o financiamento de crédito verde”, afirmou o vice-governador. Em vez de dependerem principalmente de capital próprio, orçamentos ou crédito bancário, as empresas têm a capacidade adicional de mobilizar recursos a partir dos resultados de sua própria transformação. A longo prazo, esse mecanismo contribui para a diversificação das fontes de financiamento e facilita uma alocação mais eficiente do capital de crédito. No entanto, para o crédito verde, o requisito vai além do simples desembolso de fundos para um projeto identificado como verde; inclui também a verificação da economia de energia, da redução de emissões e dos resultados de proteção ambiental. A mensuração, o relato e a avaliação dos resultados da redução de emissões, juntamente com a negociação no mercado de carbono, podem fornecer informações adicionais para que as instituições de crédito monitorem a eficácia ambiental dos projetos, avaliem a eficiência do capital e aprimorem a supervisão dos fluxos de capital verde. Segundo Bui Minh Giap, economista-chefe do Banco Asiático de Desenvolvimento (ADB) no Vietnã, estima-se que o país necessite de aproximadamente US$ 368 bilhões em investimentos adicionais para adaptação às mudanças climáticas, aumento da resiliência e redução de emissões até 2040, o equivalente a 6,8% do PIB anualmente. Desse total, o capital necessário para adaptação e aumento da resiliência é de aproximadamente US$ 254 bilhões, e para redução de emissões, de aproximadamente US$ 114 bilhões. Especificamente para o setor elétrico, o Plano de Desenvolvimento Energético VIII revisado estima um investimento de US$ 136 bilhões para o desenvolvimento da infraestrutura de geração e transmissão de energia durante o período de 2026 a 2030. Segundo o Sr. Giap, as necessidades imediatas de capital concentrar-se-ão em energia limpa, na rede elétrica e na poupança de energia; seguidas pela produção industrial, transportes, agricultura e tratamento de resíduos. A procura é enorme, mas o capital só será desembolsado quando os projetos forem considerados eficazes, capazes de amortizar a dívida e quando os resultados da redução das emissões forem verificáveis. O mercado de carbono oferece incentivos econômicos para a redução de emissões, enquanto o crédito fornece capital para que as empresas façam os investimentos necessários. Essas duas ferramentas só são eficazes quando as instituições de crédito têm capacidade para avaliar o desempenho ambiental, as atividades de transição, o fluxo de caixa dos créditos de carbono e a capacidade de pagamento de cada projeto. artigo.texto: On the morning of October 14th, the Finance and Investment Newspaper organized a seminar titled "Credit Policy and Carbon Market: Unlocking Green Capital Flows." Speaking at the seminar, Deputy Governor of the State Bank of Vietnam (SBV) Nguyen Ngoc Canh emphasized the complementary relationship between green credit and the carbon market in mobilizing resources for the transformation process of businesses and the economy . Converting emission reduction results into financial resources. According to Deputy Governor Nguyen Ngoc Canh, in fulfilling Vietnam's commitment at COP26 to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050, the Party, State, and Government have issued numerous guidelines and policies to promote green growth, energy transition, and the development of a low-carbon economy. This process requires significant resources for technological innovation, transformation of production methods, efficient energy use, and reduction of greenhouse gas emissions. Therefore, in addition to the state budget and capital mobilized from the capital and money markets, other market mechanisms need to be developed to supplement resources and create economic incentives for businesses to proactively reduce emissions. By establishing quotas, measuring emission reduction results, and forming transaction prices for quotas and carbon credits, the carbon market creates a mechanism to convert emission reduction results into economic value. This gives businesses more incentive and resources to continue investing in green transformation. On January 29, 2026, the Government issued Decree No. 29/2026/ND-CP regulating the domestic carbon exchange, creating a legal framework for organizing and operating the market and trading greenhouse gas emission quotas and carbon credits. The domestic carbon market commenced operation on June 29, 2026. The pilot market was initially established with over 511 million tons of CO₂ equivalent to emission quotas allocated to facilities in the three sectors of thermal power, iron and steel, and cement during the 2025–2026 period. The pilot phase will last until the end of 2028, before transitioning to full mandatory operation from 2029. Commercial banks participate as settlement banks; during the pilot phase, BIDV is the sole settlement bank in the market. From the perspective of the banking sector, Deputy Governor Nguyen Ngoc Canh believes that the role of each tool in the green transition process needs to be clearly understood. Green credit provides capital for investment, technological innovation, and the development of green industries and sectors, thereby creating emission reduction results. These results form the basis for the creation of carbon market goods. Conversely, an efficiently functioning carbon market can supplement businesses' revenue through emission reductions, support production and business operations, and contribute to improving the quality of bank credit. “When the carbon market operates effectively, the resulting emissions reductions can be converted into financial resources for businesses themselves. Accordingly, the development of the carbon market can contribute to reducing pressure on green credit financing,” the Deputy Governor said. Instead of relying primarily on equity, budgets, or bank credit, businesses have the added ability to mobilize resources from the results of their own transformation. In the long term, this mechanism contributes to diversifying financing sources and facilitates more efficient allocation of credit capital. However, for green credit, the requirement goes beyond simply disbursing funds for a project identified as green; it also includes verifying energy savings, emission reductions, and environmental protection results. Measurement, reporting, and assessment of emission reduction results, along with trading on the carbon market, can provide additional information for credit institutions to monitor the environmental effectiveness of projects, evaluate capital efficiency, and enhance oversight of green capital flows. According to Mr. Bui Minh Giap, Chief Economist of the Asian Development Bank (ADB) in Vietnam, Vietnam is estimated to need approximately US$368 billion in additional investment for climate change adaptation, resilience enhancement, and emission reduction by 2040, equivalent to 6.8% of GDP annually. Of this, the capital needed for adaptation and resilience enhancement is approximately US$254 billion, and for emission reduction is approximately US$114 billion. Specifically for the electricity sector, the revised Power Development Plan VIII estimates a US$136 billion investment needed for power generation and transmission infrastructure development during the 2026-2030 period. According to Mr. Giap, the immediate capital needs will focus on clean energy, the power grid, and energy saving; followed by industrial production, transportation, agriculture , and waste treatment. The demand is huge, but capital will only be disbursed when projects are assessed as effective, capable of repaying the debt, and when the emission reduction results are verifiable. The carbon market provides economic incentives for emission reduction, while credit provides capital for businesses to make necessary investments. These two tools are only effective when credit institutions have the capacity to assess the green performance, transition activities, cash flow from carbon credits, and repayment capacity of each project. Facilitating capital flow while controlling risks. Over the years, the banking sector has implemented numerous solutions to promote green credit, directing capital towards industries and sectors that bring environmental benefits. The State Bank of Vietnam has gradually perfected the policy framework, issued guidelines and instructions on green credit, environmental and social risk management; and encouraged credit institutions to develop strategies, internal processes, and products consistent with green growth goals. artigo.texto: FISHKILL – Governor Kathy Hochul and U.S. Representatives Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Pat Ryan last Tuesday toured Fishkill Farms, a family-owned, multigenerational farm in East Fishkill, Dutchess County and held a roundtable discussion with several local farmers, advocates and businesses to discuss the impacts of hyperscale data centers. Today’s discussion highlighted New York’s nation-leading moratorium on hyperscale data center construction, which is helping to protect local communities amid concerns over water and land use, energy costs, and proposed data center development, including in East Fishkill. New York State is experiencing an unprecedented surge in proposals for data center development driven by artificial intelligence and other computing operations that could require massive amounts of energy and water to run and cool thousands of computer servers. This summer, Governor Hochul signed an Executive Order hitting pause on new hyperscale data center development. This action has temporarily paused discretionary State environmental permits for up to one year in order to build a regulatory framework that will protect ratepayers, the environment, the energy grid and communities across the state. By pausing discretionary state environmental permits for new hyperscale data center construction for up to one year and imposing strict new rules that hold data center developers accountable and ensure benefits for local residents, Governor Hochul’s moratorium is addressing the ongoing concerns being raised by communities statewide. “As artificial intelligence grows more powerful and transforms our world as we know it, I’m standing up for New York’s farmers, small businesses and families — ensuring they aren’t left behind,” Governor Hochul said. “I enacted a nation-leading data center moratorium to protect our communities and hold developers accountable because I believe New Yorkers deserve a say in the decisions that affect their future. I’m proud to stand with Representatives Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Pat Ryan as we deliver a government that’s committed to fighting for working families across New York.” Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said, “Across the country, Silicon Valley billionaires are trying to impose data centers on communities that don’t want them. Today, Governor Hochul, Representative Ryan, and I heard directly from Hudson Valley farmers on the impacts these data centers have on the farming communities in New York State. In July, Governor Hochul took action to protect farmers and working New Yorkers by instituting a one-year moratorium on data center construction. New York is once again showing Americans what is possible when we put working people at the center of our agenda.” Representative Pat Ryan said, “I’m so proud that here in the Hudson Valley we’re standing together and fighting back against these data center projects. We’re not going to let anyone — especially not a bunch of billionaire tech oligarchs — come in here and poison our water, drive up our utility bills, and build this powerful technology that even they acknowledge could have devastating impacts for humankind. This is a fight that transcends so many of the divides in our country right now because we’re all united in putting our community ahead of corporate profits. From our town boards, to the Governor’s nation-leading moratorium, to urgently needed action at the federal level, we’re going to continue our fight to ensure that we the people are the ones to decide what happens in our lives and in our communities.” State Senator Michelle Hinchey said, “Tech companies are racing to profit off the AI boom, building data centers wherever they can and leaving communities to bear the costs through increased pressure on water supplies, energy infrastructure, and utility bills. New York is responding the right way — with Governor Hochul’s nation-leading moratorium, which is critical to giving the state time to understand the risks involved and, above all, protect ratepayers from higher bills and our natural resources from depletion. New York has an opportunity to lead in responsible innovation, and I thank Governor Hochul for her leadership and Congresswoman Ocasio-Cortez for bringing this fight to the federal level.” State Senator Kristen Gonzalez said, “Across New York State, communities are struggling with the impacts of unchecked data center development from demands on our natural resources to strains on our energy grid. On my New York Fights AI Data Centers Statewide Tour, I visited 13 proposed or existing data centers and met with communities, just like East Fishkill, fighting to protect their air, water, and land. I want to thank the Governor for her first-in-the-nation moratorium on the largest data centers and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez for her work introducing federal data center legislation.” In the absence of guidance from the federal government, Governor Hochul has taken action to regulate AI by signing and championing the Responsible AI Safety and Education (RAISE) Act. Starting in November, New York will direct large frontier AI developers to register with the State and prepare for compliance with strict requirements on transparency, safety, and incident reporting as prescribed by the RAISE Act. Those strict standards require large frontier AI developers to report critical safety incidents within 72 hours. Beginning in January 2027, AI companies will be required to comply with those strict standards and provide regular reporting to the state’s new Office of Digital Innovation, Governance, Integrity and Trust (DIGIT) established within the New York State Department of Financial Services (DFS).

artigo.texto: Utex to Build 20 GWh Battery Storage Facility in Maharashtra ⚡ Quick Read - What happened: Utex New Energy, a Pagariya Group company, has announced a 20 GWh battery energy storage system assembly plant in Nagpur, Maharashtra, in partnership with ENcore Systems. - Why it matters: The facility will provide a significant domestic supply chain boost for BESS developers, featuring automated production lines capable of handling 628 Ah cells. - Watch: The phased rollout, starting with an initial 5.5 GWh capacity, as the company scales toward its 20 GWh target over the next two years. Background and Context The push for grid-scale energy storage in India has reached a critical inflection point, with the nation’s energy storage pipeline now exceeding 110 GWh. As renewable energy penetration increases, the demand for battery energy storage system (BESS) solutions for grid balancing and peak demand management has surged. Addressing this manufacturing gap, Utex New Energy, a Pagariya Group company, has signed a strategic agreement to establish a large-scale battery energy storage system assembly plant in Nagpur, Maharashtra. Key Details The project is structured in two distinct phases to ensure operational efficiency and technical precision. The initial phase will launch with an annual assembly capacity of 5.5 GWh. Utex New Energy plans to scale this footprint to a total of 20 GWh within the next one to two years. The facility will leverage advanced technology through a partnership with ENcore Systems, focusing on fully automated production lines. These lines will be equipped with high-precision robots supplied by Germany-based KUKA, capable of handling battery cells with capacities of up to 628 Ah. To maintain rigorous quality standards, the plant will utilize a Manufacturing Execution System (MES) integrated with SAP systems. This digital infrastructure will provide real-time oversight of production output, quality control, and operational performance, ensuring full traceability throughout the manufacturing cycle. What This Means for EPCs and Developers For EPC contractors and renewable energy developers, the localization of high-capacity battery assembly is a significant development. With India adding 8.2 GWh of battery energy storage in the first half of 2026 alone—a massive increase compared to previous years—the availability of domestically assembled, high-capacity cells will likely reduce lead times and logistics costs for large-scale storage projects. The ability to handle 628 Ah cells positions this facility to support the next generation of high-density storage requirements. What Happens Next As India continues to integrate variable renewable energy, the role of storage becomes paramount. With Rajasthan, Gujarat, and Maharashtra currently leading the storage landscape, the addition of a major assembly hub in Nagpur strengthens the regional supply chain. Stakeholders should monitor the commissioning of the first 5.5 GWh phase, as it will serve as a bellwether for the scalability of large-scale BESS manufacturing in India. This investment reflects the broader trend of the India renewable energy sector shifting from project deployment toward vertical integration and domestic manufacturing self-sufficiency.

artigo.texto: Cleveland City Council is preparing to extend the city’s moratorium on data centers for another three months. Council Member Brian Kazy said he plans to introduce legislation on Monday to continue the pause. Passed this summer, the moratorium was meant to give City Hall time to draw up regulations for the centers, which have become central to the artificial intelligence boom. Kazy, the chair of council’s Utilities Committee, convened a trio of public meetings on the topic. Council members also toured two local data centers, he said. He took away from the hearings that most people oppose the “hyperscale” centers that require large amounts of energy to power AI. He drew a distinction between those centers and small and medium-sized facilities that form part of the infrastructure of the internet. Now the city needs 90 more days “to assure that we get this thing right,” Kazy told Weekly Chatter. Democrats try to rock the southwest suburbs Strongsville is a Republican stalwart in strongly Democratic Cuyahoga County. But Democrats hope to unseat the suburb’s longtime County Council representative this fall. Council Member Mike Gallagher faces a Democratic opponent for the first time since 2010, when he originally won his seat with 59% of the vote. Democrats have already flipped the other two GOP seats on the 11-member council. Democratic challenger Courtney Scheff, an attorney and former prosecutor, has the support of County Executive Chris Ronayne, who has accused Gallagher of trying to “thwart progress.” A critic of the administration, Gallagher has embraced Ronayne’s opposition. Despite Ronayne’s support, Scheff told Weekly Chatter that she “absolutely” could serve as a check on the Democratic executive. Asked about the county’s budget troubles, she suggested consolidating programs and holding down department spending. Scheff said she wouldn’t have voted for a new building department the county created last year, for instance. Both candidates emphasized their ability to reach across the aisle. The Republican-leaning district reaches beyond Strongsville to include North Royalton, Berea, Olmsted Falls and Olmsted Township. President Donald Trump won the district by about 5 percentage points in 2024. Can a down-ballot Democrat win there? Scheff argued that, nationwide, voters are tiring of Trump and the GOP-controlled Congress. “Whether that translates into the district, I don’t know,” she said. “But I believe it will. I think that people are kind of fed up with the same old thing over and over again.” Rainbow Terrace family goes to court The estate of Cordale Sheffield, the man who died from burns he received in last year’s explosion and fire at Rainbow Terrace, has brought a wrongful death lawsuit over the blast. Sheffield’s estate is suing Enbridge Gas, the owner of the apartment building and others. Attorneys for the estate focused on a gas line at the site, writing that it was decades old. The suit also cites a finding by the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio that, after the blast, Enbridge removed pipes in such a way that they “could not be leak tested.” An investigation by the City of Cleveland pointed to a gas leak as the likely fuel for the explosion but said the ultimate cause was “undetermined.” A spokesperson for Enbridge declined to comment on the suit but wrote in an email, “Our thoughts are with everyone affected by this tragic event, particularly the Sheffield family.”

artigo.texto: Car changing is a big deal The new BYD Atto 8 is a large electric SUV which features the brand’s Flash Charging technology, and it also has up to 775hp. News editor Jamie Edkins is here to tell you all about it. Charging times are one of the main sticking points for long-distance electric car drivers. As someone with no way of charging at home, I find sitting in a car park for half an hour at a time to top up gets tiresome after a while, but BYD may have the answer to all of our prayers. It’s called Flash charging, and it’ll feature on the newly-revealed BYD Atto 8 as well as cars from its Denza luxury spin-off brand. It’s essentially a super high-powered charger which can get you back up on the road in as little as five minutes. Remember, you can buy a brand new or used car right here on Carwow. And you can sell your car, too. We’re here to help you through every step of your car-changing journey. New BYD Atto 8: batteries, range and Flash Charging The fastest chargers on offer in the UK right now top out at 480kW, but BYD has developed its new Flash Charging technology which can deliver up to 1,500kW from a single connector. In the BYD Atto 8, this means you can charge its 115kWh battery from 10-70% in just five minutes. 10-97% can also be achieved in nine minutes. Consumer writer Siobhan Doyle has tested BYD’s Flash Charging on the Denza Z9 GT, and she managed to get that car from 10-80% in six minutes and 28 seconds, while a full charge took eight minutes and 57 seconds. That car has a larger 122kWh battery compared to the BYD Atto 8 as well, so it’s certainly impressive. The fastest-charging electric car on sale right now is the Xpeng G6, and that car takes 12 minutes to go from 10-80%. BYD’s new tech cuts this time in half. There will be two versions of the BYD Atto 8 on offer. Both use a 115kWh battery, but the basic rear-wheel drive car gets 462hp and 405 miles of range. You can also get an all-wheel drive model with a whopping 775hp, but the added performance cuts your range down to 374 miles. New BYD Atto 8: interior and technology The Atto 8 will be BYD’s largest electric car, going up against other seven-seaters such as the Kia EV9 and Skoda Peaq. The interior is pretty standard fare for a Chinese EV. You get a large 15.6-inch screen in the middle, very few physical buttons and a tall centre console with a couple of wireless charging pads near the front. That screen features Google-based software, so you can have Google Maps and Google’s voice assistant without having to pair your phone to it. You can also get a temperature-controlled centre console which cools to minus six degrees, or warms up to 50 degrees. The front and outer middle row seats get heating, ventilation and massage functions as well. With all seven seats in place, you get 270 litres of boot space. This is almost 30 litres down on the Skoda Peaq, and it’s over 60 litres less than you get in a Kia EV9. You do get a 136-litre front boot though, beating the Peaq by almost 100 litres and the EV9 by 46 litres. When can I buy the new BYD Atto 8? The BYD Atto 8 will arrive in showrooms in early 2027, but BYD hasn’t said how much it’ll cost yet. Looking at its main alternatives and the performance on offer, you can expect a starting price of around £70,000. Car change? Carwow! Looking for a new set of wheels? artigo.texto: A senior Iranian official says Tehran finds the latest U.S. response to a proposal to end the war “insufficient” and warns of attacks on regional data centers and cables if fighting intensifies again. Meanwhile, Israel’s former attorney general took the witness stand in corruption cases against Benjamin Netanyahu, as the political future of the country’s longest-serving prime minister hangs in the balance with elections weeks away. Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Saturday. Read our full coverage here. Iran says latest US response is ‘insufficient’ The head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council says Tehran finds the latest response from the United States “insufficient” as efforts at negotiations to end the war and fully open the Strait of Hormuz limp along. The comments by Mohsen Rezaei, a former Revolutionary Guard commander, were carried by Iran’s state-run IRNA news agency. Rezaei added that Iran is no longer responding to the U.S. and said Washington must clarify certain issues, without giving details. He said the U.S. has accepted some of the seven conditions but others remain unclear. Iran’s delegation to the annual U.N. gathering of world leaders last month proposed a sped-up agreement that echoed the memorandum of understanding that collapsed days after the U.S. and Iran signed it in June. The new proposal was rejected, but the two sides have remained in contact via mediation. Rezaei also threatened “cables, data centers, AI facilities and other sites in the region” if intense fighting breaks out again. Meanwhile, the Guard’s navy warned that any ship on the strait that turns off navigation and identification systems would be “identified as hostile,” according to an IRNA report. Attacks on ships transiting the strait have increased since Iran’s proposal was rejected. One attack was reported Sunday. Former legal adviser testifies in Netanyahu corruption case Israel’s former attorney general took the witness stand in Netanyahu’s long-running corruption trial. Avichai Mandelblit indicted the prime minister seven years ago for fraud, breach of trust and accepting bribes. The charges were the first-ever against a sitting Israeli prime minister. Netanyahu was in the courtroom to hear Mandelblit testify. The prime minister handpicked Mandelblit, his former Cabinet secretary, for the attorney general job. His tenure ended in 2022. Netanyahu has been accused of offering or exchanging favors with wealthy associates and media moguls for political gain. He denies any wrongdoing. Saudi Arabia on alert as Houthis warn of new strikes A projectile struck the same passenger terminal at the Riyadh international airport that was hit on Saturday. The airport had been closed after Saturday’s attack, which killed 12 people, but Saudi authorities reported injuries in the latest attack. Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen claimed responsibility for both attacks on King Khalid International Airport, which has been targeted every day since Wednesday. Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, the Houthis’ military spokesperson, urged “everyone to take our warnings seriously” about the risks of flying in Saudi airspace. The attacks have marked a major escalation in the war between the Houthis and the kingdom, and complicated efforts to halt the U.S.-Iran war. Gaza residents return to rubble as strikes continue Residents in central Gaza returned home to assess the damage caused by Israeli strikes after they had been warned to evacuate the day before. Bassam Abed said at least 10 residences housing some 300 families were reduced to rubble, and families were not given enough time to flee. “Women slept outdoors. We did not take clothes,” Abed said. Israel’s military said it had targeted militant infrastructure, including a rocket launch site and a command center used by Hamas militants to attack soldiers. One year after Israel and Hamas reached a ceasefire deal, Israel continues to launch near-daily strikes. Netanyahu wants probe into ‘NAZA’ documentary Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has asked the attorney general and head of the Shin Bet security service to investigate people who participated in the new documentary “NAZA,” in which Israeli military insiders describe what they say was the reckless killing of civilians in Gaza. Netanyahu said the film, which debuted at the Venice Film Festival to a record 25-minute standing ovation, tells “a false, misleading and biased story that slanders the State of Israel” and its military. The documentary has angered and unsettled Israelis, whose view of the war in Gaza differs sharply from that of much of the world, where criticism of Israel’s actions in the Palestinian territory has grown. Netanyahu is fighting to stay in power in the Oct. 27 election, in which security is a major issue. Lebanese army says retired officer killed by Israeli shelling Lebanon’s army said it had recovered the body of a retired army officer who was killed by Israeli artillery fire while checking on his property in the southern town of Yater. It said Ali Abdul Hassan Sweidan was “directly targeted by a hostile Israeli tank” and called it “a flagrant violation of existing understandings.” An Israeli military spokesperson said they were not aware of the incident. Israel has occupied a large swath of southern Lebanon since the outbreak of its latest war with the Iran-backed Lebanese militant group Hezbollah in March.

artigo.texto: Data center ordinance dominates Harmony mayoral forum HARMONY, Minn. (KTTC) — Voters in Harmony packed the community center Tuesday evening to question their mayoral candidates and hear how each one plans to tackle local issues. The forum hosted by the Filmore County League of Women Voters featured candidates current Mayor Steve Donney, Kerry Kingsley, owner of Kingsley Mercantile, and Harmony Public Library assistant Sue Olinger. During the hour-long forum, the candidates covered a wide range of topics, answering questions on everything from election security in Fillmore County to how to maintain strong emergency services in small towns. The issue that drew the most attention was the city’s current data center ordinance. Candidates were pressed on where they stand, where they’re getting their information, potential incentives from developers, and what, if anything, might make them change their position. One candidate said she hopes to bring the town back together. “And with my volunteer service, I am working all the time on bringing more and more to the seniors of the community. I’m hoping that I can bring positive change and eliminate some of the current division,” Olinger said. KTTC offered each candidate a chance to interview. Mayor Steve Donney had to attend a city council meeting, and Kerry Kingsley declined. Harmony’s current data center ordinance is set to go in front of the planning and zoning committee at a special meeting on October 28 with a public hearing. artigo.texto: Drones ucranianos derrubam centro de dados do "Google da Rússia". Um ataque com drones desativou o grande centro de dados da Yandex em Vladimir, na Rússia, na manhã de 11 de outubro (horário local), interrompendo mais de 80 serviços. Segundo a mídia russa, o centro de dados da Yandex em Vladimir teve que interromper temporariamente suas operações, causando ampla interrupção em mais de 80 serviços, incluindo plataformas digitais e ferramentas de IA. Este é o terceiro ataque à infraestrutura de servidores da Yandex em quatro dias. Anteriormente, os alvos estavam localizados nas regiões de Ryazan e Kaluga. Especificamente, em 8 de outubro, drones ucranianos atacaram um centro de dados da Yandex em Sasovo (Ryazan), causando um incêndio e forçando seu desligamento completo, desativando a infraestrutura de servidores usada pela Russian Railways (RZhD), pela rede MegaFon e por diversas agências de notícias. No dia seguinte, 9 de outubro, drones atacaram outro centro da Yandex em Kaluga, a sudoeste de Moscou. A Yandex confirmou que vários módulos de hardware foram desativados. Você também pode gostar O Centro de Vladimir foi projetado para acomodar até 2.880 racks de servidores, representando um dos principais centros de processamento da Yandex. Após as explosões, a Yandex confirmou que as operações em seu centro de dados em Vladimir foram temporariamente suspensas. O incidente afetou diversos aplicativos para o consumidor, incluindo a assistente de voz Alice, o Yandex Music, a ferramenta de videoconferência Telemost e o Yandex Smart Home. Os sistemas empresariais hospedados na Yandex Cloud também sofreram interrupções nos serviços de computação, armazenamento e gerenciamento de banco de dados, incluindo Compute Cloud, Object Storage, Managed Kubernetes, PostgreSQL e ClickHouse. Além disso, ferramentas e interfaces de programação de IA, como a API YandexGPT, SpeechKit e Vision OCR, também foram afetadas. A interrupção se estendeu além dos aplicativos principais da Yandex e afetou plataformas de comércio de terceiros na Rússia e em países vizinhos. Usuários relataram falhas de conexão ao acessar aplicativos de bancos, transporte por aplicativo e varejo. Segundo o prefeito Vladimir, ataques com drones danificaram subestações locais, derrubando a rede elétrica da cidade. Na manhã do mesmo dia, aproximadamente 80% do fornecimento de energia elétrica nas áreas afetadas já havia sido restabelecido. Você também pode gostar O Ministério da Defesa russo anunciou que seus sistemas de defesa aérea interceptaram 479 drones ucranianos em 16 regiões, incluindo Vladimir, Belgorod, Bryansk, Kursk e Rostov. Especialistas militares ucranianos observam que o bloqueio sistemático de centros de dados e redes de comunicação corporativas interromperia a logística, a governança corporativa e prejudicaria as capacidades de comando digital da Rússia.

artigo.texto: Newswise — David Adams is an Associate Professor of Public Administration in the College of Humanities and Social Sciences who is an expert on data centers. CSUF News recently caught up with him to discuss water, energy, data centers, the government’s role in greenlighting data centers, and long-term impacts. CSUF News: What’s your research about? Adams: A lot of my research has been in oil and gas and energy infrastructure. I’ve been focused on that for a while, as well as water. My initial dissertation research focused on institutional collaboration in watersheds across the country and how people come together to improve water quality. I just published a book on that in May 2026 with Jonathan Fisk and John Morris, Navigating Water Quality Outcomes in American Watersheds (Cambridge University Press). I also have studied energy—oil and gas infrastructure. You are in the public administration division. How does this relate to oil and gas? Adams: I’m wondering how government agencies maintain legitimacy, achieve their goals, and serve every community fairly. Legitimacy means the public seeks their work as not just legal, but also important and valid. What’s the topic of your latest research? Adams: Data centers. A few of us working together on this research have come to realize that data centers are really similar to oil and gas infrastructure. The public initially sees a benefit in the build-out of a data center. If a new oil field is taken over by a gas company that comes in there, it builds out all the infrastructure, and there are a lot of jobs right away. Then, once it’s built or once the oil companies move on, the jobs go away. So [for energy companies], what’s still there is just the producing ground where the benefit is not local but spread out everywhere, while the cost is really local. Data centers are similar; they’re put in one spot by a multinational corporation whose dollars are everywhere. The people living in that area are getting some benefit from the build-out, but the costs are borne locally, and those benefits are spread across all of us. We’re all benefiting when there is a new data center put in the middle of the Sonoran Desert, right? Our phones work faster; we’re able to do cool, flashy things [on our computers]; we’re able to talk on Zoom. But the costs are really on the environment right there locally in Arizona, where the data centers operate. Quantify the data center story for us. What’s the scale of data center construction in the US? Adams: There are 7,000 data center buildings operating, proposed, or under construction across the country, and about 2,100 operating right now, on roughly 1,400 sites, as of September 1. Some of these are single buildings. Some of them are 30 buildings across 190 acres of land. What are the initial perceived benefits of data centers for cities? Adams: Cities and counties like the fact that the data center is a new source of tax revenue is coming in, but it’s not like it’s a factory that is going to require workers, apartment buildings, neighborhoods, new street maintenance and new school capacity. It’s just a new building that’s producing tax dollars and paying land rent. It’s great revenue. You don’t have to fund increased road pressure, but you don’t have to absorb new capacity of the schools to handle the students. [The city] is just getting more money. And the downside of data centers? Adams: The “down the road” risk for data centers for these communities is the same one we see with the abandoned and orphaned oil wells. The infrastructure is going to be stranded eventually, because the technology is going to move on. In the meantime, the environmental costs are local. A big campus can use as much electricity as a small city, and many data centers cool their servers with water, often in places like Arizona that are already short on it. When a data center switches to air cooling to save water, it uses more electricity, so some of that water use just moves to the power plant. Who makes the decision to approve a data center? Which governing body/bodies? Adams: The governance is so fragmented. There are so many different governments that are involved: state, local, special district, commissions. Tucson is a really interesting case. A developer with Amazon Web Services as its customer wanted to build a data center there. They went into the county and got a bunch of land. But the city said they couldn’t have access to water. Then they redesigned it to cool with air, so they didn’t need the city’s water. They then went to the Arizona Corporation Commission, the state utility regulator, and just asked for access to electricity. So the Commission approved the power deal. This was in contrast to the city, where the public showed up with signs and picketing and the council voted no. But the Commission said yes, and the county had already sold them the land. So what happened? The fences go up, the bulldozers come in, and all the public is standing there at the fence saying, “Look, we said no, why are you building these things?” And the whole thing was a mismatch of institutions. This is just one case in Arizona. There could be 15 different governments involved, and the public could be arguing with the wrong government. You have your own database on data center growth. What sort of information are you tracking? Any interesting trends? Adams: I really do have a huge database that I’ve gathered. I have gone out and searched maps to find where data centers are located. What I found so far is that the data centers are following the fiber. Where the internet cables already are, which is typically in more affluent areas, better educated, more money, that’s where these things are being located. They’re following that because that’s the best location for it because it’s the easiest access to connect to the infrastructure . What else? Adams: They’re also following the energy. artigo.texto: BYD has unveiled the all-electric Atto 8 at the 2026 Paris Motor Show, expanding the flagship SUV’s international line-up alongside the existing plug-in hybrid (PHEV) version. The EV variant also marks BYD’s debut of ultra-fast ‘Flash Charging’ technology, which can charge its 115kWh battery from 10 to 97 percent in just nine minutes. Meanwhile, the PHEV version continues with a 1.5-litre turbocharged four-cylinder petrol engine paired with either a 19kWh or a 35.6kWh battery. - Gets a 115kWh battery pack with a claimed WLTP range of up to 653km - ‘Flash Charging’ tops up the battery from 10-70 percent in 5 minutes - Exterior and interior design is similar to those of the PHEV version BYD Atto 8 EV powertrain details EV version is available in both RWD, AWD guises and supports ‘Flash Charging’ The BYD Atto 8 EV is offered with a 115kWh battery pack powering either a rear axle-mounted electric motor (RWD) or a dual-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) setup. The RWD version puts out 462hp and 365Nm, and does a 0-100kph run in a claimed 8 seconds. It has a claimed WLTP range of 653km. The AWD version has a combined output of 775hp and 775Nm, and does a 0-00kph run in just 4.6 seconds (claimed). It has a claimed WLTP range of 602km. The headline, however, is ‘Flash Charging’ support, a first for any BYD, which can recharge the battery pack from 10 to 97 percent in just nine minutes. This charging technology can top up the battery from 0 to 70 percent in just five minutes. In extremely cold temperatures as low as -30deg C, when charging power is drastically reduced, it takes only 12 minutes to charge from 20 to 97 percent. The BYD Atto 8 PHEV, meanwhile, continues with a 148hp 1.5-litre turbocharged 4-cylinder petrol engine paired with either a 19kWh or a 35.6kWh battery. The smaller battery has a FWD setup with 275hp output, while the larger battery has an AWD setup with a combined output of 481hp. BYD Atto 8 EV exterior design Save for new alloys and missing tailpipe, the EV’s exterior design mimics the PHEV’s Save for more aerodynamic alloy wheels and a missing tailpipe, the Atto 8 EV looks identical to the PHEV version. Up front, it gets a blanked-off grille with matrix LED headlights and a curved LED DRL bar, and a black section on the lower portion of the bumper with functional air inlets to cool the internals. A LiDAR sensor can also be seen on the roof. In profile, it sports black alloy wheels with aerodynamic inserts, flared wheel arches and slim roof rails. There’s a chrome strip on the front fender extending to the front doors and a black portion on the lower section of the doors. At the rear, it gets 'infinity knot' LED taillights with an illuminated BYD logo in the centre, and a roof-mounted spoiler. BYD Atto 8 EV interior and features 7-seater SUV gets dual digital screens, panoramic glass roof and 3-zone AC The interior design of the Atto 8 EV is identical to the PHEV. The dashboard continues with a 10.25-inch digital driver’s display, a 15.6-inch infotainment touchscreen and a 3-spoke steering wheel, thankfully with physical buttons and scrollers. The dashboard features slim air vents and a lot of soft-touch leather elements. It gets 7 seats in a 2+2+3 configuration, with a 270-litre boot space like the PHEV. However, it has a 136-litre frunk (boot space under the hood), which is unique to the EV version. The first and second rows feature heated, ventilated, and massaging seats. Other features include a panoramic glass roof, 3-zone climate control, a 21-speaker DiSound audio system, dual 50-watt wireless phone chargers and a front refrigerator that can cool to -6deg C and warm to 50deg C. Internationally, the BYD Atto 8 EV locks horns with the Kia EV9, Skoda Peaq and Hyundai Ioniq 9.

artigo.texto: Projects related to energy transition, green infrastructure development, green transportation, waste treatment, circular economy , and emission reduction activities often require large capital investments and long payback periods, while potentially involving technological and policy risks. Therefore, the challenge is not just how much capital is needed, but also where that capital comes from, with what terms and costs, and how the risks are distributed. Bank credit remains crucial, but it cannot alone meet the long-term capital needs. Along with credit, it is necessary to expand capital markets, green finance, climate finance, private capital, and risk-sharing mechanisms. But opening new channels of capital only solves half the problem. The harder part is determining what value a green project creates, where the risks lie, and to what extent that value can be converted into cash flow. This is where the carbon market becomes crucial. Carbon pricing creates an economic signal: emissions have a cost, while emission reductions can create value. For businesses, this signal can shift the balance between continuing to use high-emission technologies and investing in energy, fuel, or raw material-saving technologies. For projects that meet the credit mechanism, the resulting emission reductions can even become a source of revenue. However, carbon value only truly matters to investment decisions when businesses and investors have reason to believe that this value is clear, stable, and can be converted into monetary value. The gap between “potential emission reduction” and a tradable asset is therefore vast. Potential does not equate to tangible value. The creation of carbon value requires methodology, baseline data, and a measurement-reporting-verification (MRV) system, along with mechanisms for issuance, trading, and payment. Without one link, environmental value is not sufficiently solid to become a financial asset. Singapore's experience shows that a carbon market cannot be created solely through an exchange. The country combines price signals via carbon taxes with credit quality standards, international cooperation, and a financial services ecosystem. Policies create demand, standards build trust, and the financial system connects carbon value with capital flows. The lesson for Vietnam, therefore, is not just about building a place to buy and sell carbon credits, but about creating the necessary infrastructure for a market to form a reliable value. In Vietnam, this gap is evident in data and valuation, as emissions data remains fragmented, lacking sufficiently long data series and reliable benchmarks. Banks and investors struggle to reach a consensus on forecasting cash flows and pricing risks. Furthermore, the costs of due diligence, verification, and disclosure can also become a barrier for businesses. And especially, when information is not standardized, the "green label" alone is insufficient to build financial confidence. This also explains why green credit and carbon markets must be viewed within the same value chain. Capital needs arise very early, right from the project preparation stage, equipment procurement, technology investment, and production organization. Meanwhile, carbon revenue typically only emerges after emission reduction results are measured, verified, credits are issued, or sales contracts are formed. This gap creates a financial void that credit, bridge financing, guarantees, cash flow management, and combined financial mechanisms can fill. From a banking perspective, the appropriate approach is not to treat carbon credits as a guaranteed source of repayment from the outset. It's necessary to distinguish between cash flow from core business operations and carbon revenue. Core cash flow forms the foundation for repayment; carbon revenue is an additional layer and should only be recognized to the extent of certainty. Carbon value can impact the financial plan through three channels: reducing production costs through low-emission investments; reducing the need to purchase additional quotas for compliant businesses; or generating revenue from transferring emission reduction results or carbon credits. These three channels need to be quantified separately to avoid double counting or overestimating the potential for generating cash. On the capital market side, the requirements are similar. Carbon prices can only be passed on to the cost of capital when investors have sufficient information to assess risk. This requires verifiable data, consistent verification standards, clear disclosure, and post-audit mechanisms. When a project's emissions, emission reduction results, rights to carbon value, and projected cash flows are clearly defined, banks can better assess creditworthiness, and investors have a basis for valuing the asset. Therefore, unlocking green capital is not just about "getting more capital," but about creating a chain of links from emission reduction to data, from data to carbon value, and then to credit and capital markets. When this chain is transparent and reliable, the carbon market truly becomes a financial tool for green transition, instead of just a place to buy and sell credits. The ultimate measure lies not in the number of green labels or the scale of transactions, but in the actual emissions reduced, the number of projects funded, and the ability for the cost of capital to accurately reflect the quality, risk, and value of each project. The workshop focused on discussing the linkages between credit policy, carbon markets, and capital markets, thereby seeking solutions to unlock financial resources for the green transition process. artigo.texto: Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek has directed environmental regulators to temporarily stop issuing pollution permits to data centers, which would effectively pause most data center development in Oregon until next summer. Amazon — which has more than a dozen hyperscale data centers in Morrow and Umatilla Counties — said it was disappointed by the directive, with an executive at the company saying Kotek’s move could cost Oregon thousands of jobs and billions of dollars in planned investment. Data centers have played a growing role in the race for governor, with both Kotek, a Democrat, and her opponent Republican state Sen. Christine Drazan, saying they favor a moratorium on the high-tech developments. Both candidates have attacked one another for not doing more to crack down. Related: Amazon, data centers and the race for Oregon governor Kotek directed Oregon Department of Environmental Quality Director Leah Feldon to pause all air and water pollution permits for new or expanding data centers until July. The governor sent the directive in a letter to Feldon Friday, in response to an update on the agency’s air pollution permitting process. Kotek also told the agency to stop processing applications from cities and counties seeking to renew or modify wastewater permits to accommodate data centers. “This time limited pause will provide an opportunity for me to evaluate and digest recommendations forthcoming from the Advisory Committee, and to provide space for policy and/or regulatory reforms that may be considered in the upcoming 2027 session of the Legislature with my support,” Kotek wrote. The letter was obtained and shared widely by Oregon Rural Action, a grassroots nonprofit that advocates for social justice and environmental sustainability in Eastern Oregon. OPB obtained Kotek and Feldon’s interchange from Kotek’s office. “What this pause means is that everything — assuming it is implemented the way we think it will be — data center development will pause until the legislature has a chance to act over the course of the first half of next year,” said Kaleb Lay, Rural Action’s director of policy and research. The environmental permitting freeze would expand a previous moratorium that paused data center development on state-owned land. Without air or water pollution permits, most large data centers known as “hyperscalers” wouldn’t be able to build in Oregon, whether on public or private land. “This directive was issued abruptly, without meaningful stakeholder engagement of the workers, businesses, and municipalities it will affect,” said Shannon Kellogg, vice president of Amazon Web Services Public Policy for the Americas, in a statement. “Amazon has been a committed partner in Oregon for over 15 years, and we will continue to advocate for policies that protect communities and support responsible growth. Lay, with Oregon Rural Action, hopes the pause gives Oregon policymakers time to implement new laws regulating data centers, from the immense amount of water and electricity they consume to issues involving transparency and nondisclosure agreements. Pausing permits is not enough, Lay said. “What needs to happen at the Legislature, we need new laws to protect all of Oregon from these massive corporations.” Oregon’s next legislative session convenes in January. Lawmakers are expecting a wide range of bill proposals, particularly in response to policy directives from Kotek’s Data Center Advisory Committee.

artigo.texto: Americans are increasingly concerned about AI and data centers, and the impact of computing on climate change. A September poll by the Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research and the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago found that 53% are extremely or very concerned about the environmental impacts of AI—and that the majority of both Democrats and Republicans support policies including requiring data centers to use clean energy and pay for grid upgrades. We asked leading expert Andrew Chien to answer commonly asked questions about data centers. Chien is the William Eckhardt Distinguished Service Professor of Computer Science at UChicago. Before joining the University in 2011, he served for five years as the vice president of research at Intel Corporation. Since 2015, he and his research team have studied how to make computing more sustainable and grid-friendly. What is a data center? In the simplest terms, a data center is a room or building that’s full of computers. This can be a single room, a little building on the corner, or a few floors of a skyscraper, all the way up to huge, multi-acre complexes. What do data centers do? When people ask this, I explain by saying, “Data centers are where the Internet lives.” All the cloud computing and the data we use—your pictures, your social media and now AI chatbots—those are all supported by data centers. How has AI changed the need for data centers? The difference now is that AI-based services require massive amounts of power. When you used to type something into Google, it would search a copy of the internet. Now, when you ask a chatbot or an AI agent something, it literally performs a supercomputer-class numerical computation in order to figure out how to tell you that stuff. (It’s approximately a teraflop. That’s not quite the supercomputer of today—it’s a supercomputer of a few years ago—but it’s a gigantic amount of computation.) We also pioneered an approach we call “Middlebox.” The idea is to build a little energy station next to the data center. This means the data center itself gets highly reliable power (and doesn’t have to be flexible about when it runs computations). The combined data center + power station can also now actually reduce peak loads overall on the grid, in addition to supporting renewable energy by increasing consumption when there is excess energy from wind or solar. Remarkably, we did a study on this and showed that in the majority of cases, the data center companies would actually make money from doing this, because they can get better prices for energy and they don’t get charged extra for drawing power during peak usage times. So technically and economically, it’s absolutely clear that this is the right thing to do. All the technology is there. But the companies are not taking these steps. In fact, several of them are bringing lawsuits against attempts to regulate them. Are data centers good for a community? One thing to keep in mind is that data centers don’t employ a lot of people, relative to say, an automotive factory, or even a store of similar square footage. Once the initial construction is done, communities often see very little positive economic impact. One of the problems is that large data center companies have been pursuing aggressive business tactics. But they do so at the cost of alienating the local community and causing a backlash. For example, a common tactic is to come into a small town or county and tell the mayor, “We want to build a data center,” and the first thing they do is make the mayor sign a non-disclosure agreement about the discussions. When the deal is done, then the citizens hear about it—often with surprise and dismay. Worse, some of these deals carry NDAs into their operating stage—where the concessions or permits granted may not be known for many years—or ever. I think it’s a good idea to ban companies requesting or public officials signing such NDAs and require all such deals to be shared openly. This would decrease the information and power asymmetry, and force the data center companies to compete for community support! “If it’s really that important that data centers be built, let’s solve the problem in a way that works for everybody.” —Prof. Andrew A. Chien What do you think more people should know about data centers? Data centers don’t have to be built next door. With the modern fiber-optic internet, communication can travel across the country in less than 15 milliseconds. So, data centers don’t have to be anyplace that people don’t want them. They can be anywhere in the USA and serve AI to the entire population, businesses, etc. How do you recommend we solve the problem? National and state government needs to organize infrastructure for data centers. Coordinated regulation is needed because the companies are so powerful. It should be organized and planned to concentrate the data centers in “industrial” areas with power and networking infrastructure. If it’s zoned properly, it will reduce the impact on local community. Further, data center companies should REALLY cover the cost of new infrastructure—for its full lifetime of 15 to 30 years. They have plenty of profit. If it’s really that important that data centers be built, let’s solve the problem in a way that works for everybody. I think sometimes people feel that governments can’t force companies to change. But I don’t really believe that’s true. When I was at Intel, my experience was that if public policy changes, the companies change. The auto companies complied with the Inflation reduction act quickly. American tech companies comply with European policies in order to sell there. We should expect that companies will fight every step of the way to get more profit, but I still believe people can win that battle in the U.S. to reach a balanced solution where we can have the AI computing power we need, but the communities that host data centers get valuable training, community contribution,

artigo.texto: Rapid City to hold open house on proposed data center rules RAPID CITY, S.D. (KOTA) - Rapid City residents will have a chance to weigh in on proposed rules for data centers during a public open house on Oct. 14. The city’s Community Development Department will host the event Wednesday from 5 to 7:30 p.m. at City Hall in the Council Chambers and Circle of Friends Community Room. City staff will explain the proposed ordinance and collect public feedback. The proposal would expand rules adopted in December 2024, which defined data centers and allowed them in light and heavy industrial districts. New standards would address issues including setbacks from residential areas, power, water and sewer use, noise and vibration. The Planning Commission reviewed the proposal Sept. 10 but postponed further discussion until its Nov. 5 meeting to allow more time for revisions and public input. Residents are encouraged to attend the open house and share their thoughts before the proposal returns to the Planning Commission. See a spelling or grammatical error in our story? artigo.texto: Denver working group on data centers says they're off to promising start, "it exceeded my expectations" Denver's working group on data centers has officially begun meeting with the goal of creating policy recommendations for the city. The group, diversely composed of community members and experts in a multitude of industries, was created after the city council approved a moratorium to pause the construction of data centers in Denver. "This is an opportunity to be a part of democracy in action to help set the rules that we haven't had for these kinds of developments, and to make sure we're protecting Denver's resources and putting Denverites first," said Mark Orrs, who's on the working group. Orrs is an associate professor at Colorado School of Mines, and he's bringing his expertise to the table. "My training is in sustainable development, and I teach responsible engineering, specifically engineering for social and environmental responsibility," he explained. And one of the core questions at the center of the conversation is whether 'sustainable' and 'data centers' can exist in the same sentence. "There are new kinds of technologies coming out every day that might make them more sustainable," Orrs said. "But to date, what we've seen is a lot of unsustainable development in this area." Orrs is one of 26 individuals with diverse backgrounds chosen to participate from more than 250 applicants. But with honor comes enormous responsibility. "We know that others are looking to us, and to see how we decide to proceed, and that they will follow," said Orrs. "We are and have been the tip of the spear on this discussion," said Councilman Darrell Watson. "We are one of the first large municipalities to do a moratorium. We're one of maybe one that are building a working group with this very extensive application process." Watson represents District 9, where the controversial CoreSite facility in Globeville was recently built, which became the catalyst for the moratorium. "I think we have a unique process, and I do believe we're going to come up with a commonsense approach to regulating data centers," said Watson. For now, the working group is just getting started and met for the first time last week. "I thought it went about as well as I could have expected," said Orrs. "In fact, I said it exceeded my expectations." The next working group meeting will be on October 29, and although they are slated to meet through May, Watson says they'll continue to meet as long as necessary for the city council to create legislation.

artigo.texto: GIGante. A espanhola Aena assumiu a gestão do Galeão usando um trocadilho para mostrar o tamanho de suas ambições para o aeroporto do Rio de Janeiro. Os planos para o terminal passam por dezenas de novos voos em rotas internacionais e domésticas, além de projetos imobiliários incluindo um hotel, galpões, um hangar da Gol e até um centro de testes da BYD. Só essas iniciativas já totalizam R$ 1 bilhão em investimentos das empresas responsáveis nos próximos três anos, disse Santiago Yus, o CEO da Aena Brasil. Segundo ele, o aeroporto deve fechar este ano com 19,4 milhões de passageiros, comparado a 17,5 milhões em 2025, e ainda há muito espaço para crescimento diante de uma capacidade total estimada em até 37 milhões de passageiros/ano. “O Galeão é um aeroporto estratégico para o Rio de Janeiro e o Brasil,” Yus disse ao apresentar a estratégia para o terminal, que a Aena passou a administrar no último dia 6. Maior operador aeroportuário do mundo em número de passageiros, o grupo espanhol arrematou a concessão do Galeão num leilão realizado pelo Governo Federal em março, com uma proposta de outorga de R$ 2,9 bilhões. Após uma fase de transição junto aos antigos concessionários, a Vinci Compass e a Changi, a Aena chegou anunciando novas rotas e aumentos na frequência de voos para 30 destinos ao longo dos próximos meses. Ainda em outubro, a American Airlines começa a operar sete voos semanais para Nova York e amplia de sete para nove os embarques para Miami. A Air Canadá inicia três voos semanais para Toronto, e a Air France adiciona um voo para Paris aos dez já realizados. Em novembro, a JetSMART lançará três voos semanais para Assunção, e a Delta, três para Nova York; a Lufthansa passará a voar diariamente para Frankfurt, e a TAP vai adicionar um voo por semana para Lisboa e Porto. A partir de dezembro são previstas novas rotas para Toronto, Montreal, Dallas, Salta, Lima, Assunção e Mendoza, além de aumentos de frequência para Atlanta, Lisboa e Cidade do Panamá. Em janeiro, a Aerolíneas Argentinas começará a voar para Rosario, enquanto Latam, SKY e JetSMART vão quase dobrar a oferta de voos para Santiago, com esta última aumentando também os embarques para Córdoba. No plano doméstico, são previstos incrementos na frequência de voos da Latam, Azul e principalmente da Gol para diversas cidades nos próximos meses. No front dos projetos imobiliários, a Aena anunciou que a operadora bUP vai investir R$ 90 milhões em um novo hotel, com bandeira internacional ainda a ser definida. O empreendimento terá ao menos 232 quartos, podendo chegar a 426. O Galeão também receberá um centro de pesquisa e desenvolvimento e experimentação da BYD com capex de R$ 300 milhões, ocupando 184 mil m² e com previsão de criar 1,2 mil empregos. Estão previstos ainda um hangar de manutenção da Gol de mais de R$ 100 milhões; além de investimentos da Hire Capital em uma nova área de galpões industriais de R$ 430 milhões e uma expansão de galpão logístico de R$ 54 milhões. A Aena nomeou como novo diretor do Galeão seu executivo Felipe Cavalcanti, um ex-coordenador da Infraero que já foi responsável pela gestão do terminal entre 2018 e 2019, quando estava na RIOGaleão, a antiga concessionária. Com 46 aeroportos e 2 heliportos na Espanha, a Aena administra 35 terminais em outros países. No Brasil são 18, incluindo Congonhas. Os investimentos no País já somam R$ 15 bilhões quando incluída a outorga do Galeão.

artigo.texto: HELLENiQ ENERGY has commissioned a 100 MW/200 MWh BESS in Thessaloniki, Greece The facility uses LFP batteries and is designed to reduce renewable energy curtailment and improve grid flexibility The company is developing another 50 MW/200 MWh battery project in Florina HELLENiQ ENERGY has commissioned a 100 MW/200 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS), calling it one among the largest battery storage projects in Greece and Southeast Europe. Built at Thessaloniki, Greece, with an investment of approximately €50 million, it is developed by HELLENiQ Renewables, a subsidiary of HELLENiQ ENERGY as its maiden storage facility. The facility will store surplus renewable electricity and release it when demand increases. It will provide flexibility and balancing services to Greece’s national electricity transmission system, helping reduce renewable energy curtailment and improve grid reliability. The project is supported under Greece’s National Recovery and Resilience Plan, “Greece 2.0,” funded by the European Union’s NextGenerationEU program. The facility covers approximately 100,000 square meters and comprises three battery storage systems using lithium iron phosphate (LFP) technology with liquid cooling. HELLENiQ ENERGY said the battery system is expected to complete at least one full charge-discharge cycle daily, with its 200 MWh storage capacity. The 56 battery containers will provide enough energy to fully charge around 3,000 electric vehicles (EV). It includes a new 33/150 kV step-up substation and an underground high-voltage transmission line extending about 5 km to the Thessaloniki Extra-High Voltage Centre. The project was selected under the first competitive tender conducted by Greece’s Regulatory Authority for Waste, Energy and Water (RAAEY) for energy storage systems. The company is also developing a second battery storage project in Florina, Greece, with a planned capacity of 50 MW/200 MWh. Construction is expected to be completed in the near future. Its overall renewable energy and storage project portfolio under development exceeds 6 GW, including more than 1 GW of storage projects under development across Greece, Romania, Cyprus, and Bulgaria. Greece’s solar association HELAPCO calls energy storage the third pillar of Greek energy market going forward that will support the first two pillars of large commercial projects, and self-consumption. It estimates that more than 6 GW of battery storage capacity could be available by 2030, although around 8 GW may be needed to manage renewable energy curtailment in the country, exceeding the NECP target of 4.33 GW. HELAPCO also forecasts the country’s cumulative solar PV capacity to reach 20 GW by 2030 in its most likely scenario, with potential to rise to 27 GW, up from 13 GW interconnected as of May 2026.

artigo.texto: Power Secretary Pankaj Agarwal held a bilateral meeting with European Commission Director-General for Taxation and Customs Union Gerassimos Thomas in New Delhi to discuss India’s carbon market development, the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) and technical cooperation. Discussions covered carbon pricing, emissions monitoring, reporting and verification systems, and capacity building. Key Highlights - Power Secretary Pankaj Agarwal met EU Director-General Gerassimos Thomas in New Delhi to discuss carbon markets and CBAM. - India highlighted emission intensity reduction targets notified for 490 industrial units under the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme. - Non-fossil energy sources account for 308 GW of India’s total installed electricity generation capacity of 558 GW, according to the Ministry of Power. - India and the EU agreed to continue technical dialogue on carbon pricing, emissions monitoring and verification, and capacity building. New Delhi, Oct 14: Secretary, Ministry of Power, Pankaj Agarwal held a bilateral meeting with Gerassimos Thomas, Director-General for Taxation and Customs Union at the European Commission, in New Delhi to discuss India’s carbon market development, the European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) and opportunities for enhanced technical cooperation. The meeting focused on strengthening engagement between India and the EU on carbon pricing frameworks, emissions accounting and approaches to managing the climate-related aspects of international trade. During the meeting, Agarwal highlighted India’s progress under the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS), including the notification of emission intensity reduction targets for 490 industrial units and the development of a domestic carbon market. The scheme is part of India’s efforts to establish a framework for carbon credit trading and encourage industries to reduce the emissions intensity of their operations. The discussions also covered India’s progress in expanding non-fossil energy capacity as part of its broader energy transition. Agarwal noted that non-fossil sources accounted for 308 GW of India’s total installed electricity generation capacity of 558 GW. The expansion of non-fossil capacity is an important element of India’s strategy to diversify its energy mix and advance its climate and sustainability objectives. The meeting provided an opportunity to discuss the relationship between domestic carbon market mechanisms, industrial decarbonisation and international approaches to carbon-related trade measures. The European Commission delegation appreciated India’s progress in developing its carbon market and shared updates on the implementation of the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism. Both sides expressed willingness to continue technical engagement on the recognition of carbon pricing mechanisms, monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV) systems, and capacity building. They agreed to strengthen cooperation and maintain dialogue on carbon markets, CBAM-related methodologies and other areas of mutual interest. The India–EU meeting highlights the growing importance of technical cooperation on carbon pricing, industrial emissions and climate-related trade measures. Continued dialogue on the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme and CBAM methodologies could help both sides improve mutual understanding of their respective frameworks and identify areas for further cooperation.
