artigo.texto: (The Center Square) – The buildings that house thousands of computer servers powering cloud computing and artificial intelligence have increasingly caught heat over environmental and energy concerns. Another common criticism is that state and local governments offer data centers sweetheart deals to attract them, including tax breaks and other incentives, potentially leaving ordinary residents to shoulder some of the costs associated with their development. But the National Taxpayers Union has released a pair of studies in a series arguing that at least two common state tax policies treat data centers less favorably than other industries. Most states allow a tangible personal property tax on data centers, a tax the group contends is not only antiquated and generally harmful but disproportionately disadvantages data centers. The NTU also calls the tax an “international anomaly,” noting that “only seven of the 38 Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development countries tax tangible personal property at all, and among them, only Japan imposes them as broadly as the U.S.” A tangible personal property tax is a tax exacted on property “that can be moved or touched, such as business equipment, machinery, inventory and furniture,” as defined by the Tax Foundation. It’s paid annually and, like real estate property taxes, is calculated based on the assessed value of the property. For example, in some states, residents pay an annual property tax on their vehicles, often referred to as a car tax, based on the vehicle’s assessed value and the applicable tax rate. Data centers can pay tangible personal property taxes on their servers, networking equipment and other computer hardware, depending on state and local tax laws. Only, like with the car tax, the assessed value can be inaccurate. “Suppose the government thinks, ‘Well, your car is only two years old. It’s this make and model. You pay this much tax.’ But then you say, ‘Well, wait a minute! I drive this thing into the ground, and I’ve had to replace part of the suspension on it. It’s not in as good of shape as you think,’” NTU President Pete Sepp told The Center Square. Similarly, the assessed value of technology used in data centers can differ drastically from its market value — to the point that NTU argues state tangible personal property tax laws actually “discriminate against technology.” “The complex depreciation schedules required to value property are designed around manufacturing machinery that often performs at the same level after a decade or more of use,” NTU writes. “Applying the same standards to companies like data centers can significantly overvalue equipment like computer servers, which are often obsolete after three years.” And those depreciation schedules can also vary widely by state. In Florida, a three-year-old server is valued at 56% of its original cost according to its TPP tax law, while a handful of states would value that same server at 40% of its original cost. To avoid “discriminating” against technology-heavy industries like data centers, NTU recommends that states refrain from introducing new tangible personal property taxes but also avoid replacing existing ones with higher taxes elsewhere. And Sepp recommends going a step further. “State lawmakers should reform personal property laws so they’re uniform, neutral, simple and stable,” Sepp said in a statement. “Data centers are the manufacturing plants of the information age, and our laws should reflect that reality with equal treatment.” NTU also examined sales-and-use-tax exemptions in the first report of its series, addressing a more widely debated tax policy that has recently drawn criticism for its application to data centers. Thirty-three states offer a conditional form of the exemption to data centers (two offer it by right), but between May and August, eight states took steps to suspend or eliminate the exemptions “or benefit programs” for data centers, according to an analysis by S&P Global Market Intelligence. In the two states that offer sales-and-use-tax exemptions to data centers without having to meet special investment or employment requirements, the exemptions allow data centers to purchase computer servers, networking equipment and other hardware without paying applicable state and local sales taxes. Such exemptions are often perceived as unique to the industry, but that is a misconception, according to NTU Senior Fellow Jared Walczak, and “betrays a misunderstanding of how sales taxes are supposed to work.” There is a general consensus in tax policy that sales taxes should apply to final consumption rather than the inputs used to produce goods and services so as to avoid tax pyramiding, which occurs when a good or service is taxed multiple times at different stages of the production and supply chain, inflating the final consumer price. For example, if a data center pays sales tax on its computer servers, it may pass that expense along to businesses that use its computing services. Those businesses may then pass the added cost along to their customers through higher prices, which are taxed again when consumers make purchases. “No state’s perfect on exempting business inputs, but there are a few bright lines that basically all states adhere to,” Walczak told The Center Square. “They don't tax raw materials, and they almost always exempt machinery and equipment.” The vast majority of states offer sales tax exemptions for machinery and equipment used in manufacturing, while exemptions are also available for equipment used in industries such as agriculture, mining and energy production. “The problem is, where do data centers fit in that? Are they manufacturing? You know, what are they?” Walczak said. “A lot of states didn’t have a ready-made category for that.” Many states created similar exemptions years ago for data centers through incentive programs to help attract data centers, but unlike in manufacturing, in 33 states, data centers’ equipment

artigo.texto: BYD's Atto 8 Charges In Less Time Than You'll Spend Scrolling Netflix Tonight BYD’s Flash charging tech can charge from 10% to 70% in just five minutes. - BYD's electric Atto SUV charges faster than any rival – with the right charger. - The 115-kWh Blade battery can charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes. - Most potent version makes 764 hp and gives a 374-mile WLTP electric range. Fast electric SUVs are nothing new. But BYD's new Atto 8 is fast in a straight line and at the charging station. You might even spend less time topping up the battery than you would pumping gas into a combustion SUV and paying for it. The Atto 8 made its European debut at this week's Paris Motor Show, and on the stand, it doesn't look particularly groundbreaking. Sure, it's BYD's first three-row vehicle for Europe, where it will take on the new Skodq Peaq. But the design, a predictable mashup of existing BYD styling cues, is entirely forgettable. Review: The BYD Seal 6 Is A Perfectly Adequate EV Sedan, But That's About It It's a different story under the skin. The Atto 8 is powered by BYD's second generation Blade battery, and the generous 115 kWh capacity is actually the least interesting thing about it. Because the real story is the Atto 8's ability to charge that huge battery from 10-97 percent full in only nine minutes. And you can cut that almost in half by settling on a 10% to 70% fill, pulling the plug before the charge rate slows for the final push. Even in chilly (-30 C) weather, a 20-97 percent charge is done in 12 minutes. That compares with a 10% to 80% fill time of 28 minutes for the new Skoda Peaq. BYD's Flash Charging technology makes those feats possible, but only if you can find a Flash charger. The automaker is still building the infrastructure, so they're few and far between right now, although BYD says 3,000 Flash stations will be live across Europe by the end of 2027. Choose 456 HP Or 764 HP Both versions of the 198-inch (5 m) SUV get the same battery and charging capabilities, but not the same powertrain. The entry level Design comes with a 456 hp (462 PS / 340 kW) electric motor and rear-wheel drive. That might sound like a solid number of horses, but the weight of the huge battery means zero to 62 mph takes a leisurely 8 seconds. Atto 8 Excellence adds a second motor, boosting overall output to 764 hp (775 PS / 570 kW), and chopping the sprint time to 4.6 seconds. But it also chops the available range. The RWD 8 can over a respectable 405 miles (652 km) on a fill, and the dual-motor SUV, a less impressive 374 miles (602 km). 26-Inch Head-Up Display The Atto 8's flagship status in BYD's lineup means it comes loaded with standard equipment, including a panoramic glass roof, a 26-inch head-up display, and heating, ventilation and massage functions for both the front seats, and the outer pair in the middle row. Both models get dual 50W smartphone chargers, and Excellence models attempt to justify their name with a refrigerator. Will it also be excellent value? We'll find out later this year, closer to the spring 2027 on-sale date, by which time BYD might have plumbed in a few more Flash chargers.

artigo.texto: - Council seeks community input on data centers. Members of the Sioux Falls City Council's Regulatory Oversight Committee are meeting several times over the next couple months to put together regulations and ordinances related to data centers. And they want to hear from community members along the way. - Meetings will be held at 6 p.m. on Nov. 9, Nov. 30 and Jan. 4, with the goal to present final recommendations to the full council on Jan. 12. - "We’re trying to make sure that people can understand where we came from and what exactly the guardrails are that we’re putting in place," Councilor James Oppenheimer said. "So this is really an exercise in transparent governance." - There's also an opportunity to share feedback online on the city's website. - It's also unclear if any of these new ordinances or changes would impact the proposed Gemini data center in northeast Sioux Falls. Merkouris said the council has asked the city for a legal opinion on that. - Smithfield, take two. After having its initial conditional use permit overturned in court, Smithfield is going to re-apply, a Smithfield executive told The Dakota Scout this week. Find the full story here. - Erickson names next parks director. Mayor Christine Erickson on Tuesday announced the appointment of Brett Kollars as the city's next parks director. Kollars currently serves as the assistant director for the parks and recreation department, and has been interim director since Don Kearney retired this spring. His appointment now goes before the City Council for final approval. - Remembering Katherine Frank. Minnehaha County Sheriff's Deputy Katherine Frank, 26, died Monday after being shot in the line of duty on Friday night. The Sheriff's Office has established a memorial in her honor at the Law Enforcement Center on 4th and Minnesota, for those who wish to pay their respects. There's also a GoFundMe from the Minnehaha County Deputies Association that's raised more than $73,000 as of Tuesday night. - Frank's friends and colleagues shared memories of her life with Sioux Falls Live and Dakota News Now, and The Dakota Scout provided some important context on just how rare these types of incidences are in our community. artigo.texto: As ações da Enerflex Ltd. (NYSE:EFXT) sobem 5% nas negociações pré-mercado de terça-feira, após a empresa anunciar um contrato para fornecer mais de um gigawatt (GW) de equipamentos de geração de energia a gás natural com baixas emissões para um empreendimento de data center na América do Norte. O contrato amplia a presença da Enerflex no mercado de infraestrutura de energia dedicada para suporte a instalações de inteligência artificial e computação digital. Em conjunto com os projetos anunciados anteriormente, incluindo aproximadamente 450 megawatts (MW) divulgados em 1 de outubro de 2026, o novo acordo aumenta a carteira de projetos de geração de energia a gás natural da empresa para mais de 1,75 GW. As entregas referentes ao atraso estão programadas para se estender até 2028. Enerflex garante importante contrato de geração de energia para data centers O contrato recém-adjudicado está inserido na área de Sistemas de Engenharia da Enerflex e abrange o projeto, a engenharia, a fabricação e a montagem de unidades de geração de energia a gás natural. O equipamento será implantado em um centro de dados em desenvolvimento na América do Norte, fornecendo capacidade dedicada de geração de eletricidade. O projeto utilizará uma configuração “atrás do medidor”, permitindo que a energia seja fornecida diretamente à instalação sem a necessidade de conexão à rede elétrica convencional para o sistema de geração. Esses arranjos podem suportar grandes instalações industriais e de computação que exigem fontes de alimentação de energia substanciais e confiáveis. A Enerflex descreveu o equipamento como uma tecnologia de geração a gás natural com baixas emissões, embora o anúncio não tenha especificado dados de desempenho de emissões nem comparações com sistemas de geração alternativos. A empresa também não divulgou o valor financeiro do contrato, a identidade do cliente ou a localização exata do centro de dados. A carteira de pedidos de geração de energia ultrapassa 1,75 GW A Enerflex afirmou que sua carteira de projetos de geração de energia a gás natural para consumidores finais agora ultrapassa 1,75 GW. O total inclui o contrato mais recente para mais de 1 GW de capacidade e contratos previamente anunciados, incluindo aproximadamente 450 MW divulgados no início de outubro. A carteira de pedidos representa o trabalho contratado que a empresa espera executar nos próximos anos. A previsão é de que as entregas continuem até 2028, fornecendo um cronograma das atividades futuras de fabricação e execução de projetos. O aumento reflete a crescente demanda por infraestrutura dedicada à geração de eletricidade, à medida que os desenvolvedores expandem a capacidade dos data centers. No entanto, a empresa não forneceu uma discriminação detalhada do valor financeiro da carteira de pedidos nem do reconhecimento de receita esperado por ano. O cronograma e a rentabilidade de cada projeto dependerão dos prazos de fabricação, dos custos de execução e dos termos contratuais. A Enerflex planeja investir US$ 100 milhões em sua unidade fabril Para dar suporte à sua crescente carteira de projetos, a Enerflex autorizou um investimento de aproximadamente US$ 100 milhões em suas instalações e capacidades de Sistemas de Engenharia. Desse montante, US$ 15 milhões estão incluídos na previsão de despesas de capital da empresa para 2026. O programa de investimento tem como objetivo fortalecer os recursos de fabricação e operacionais necessários para executar contratos de geração de energia em larga escala. A Enerflex afirmou que os projetos serão entregues por meio de suas operações de fabricação na América do Norte. O investimento planejado surge em um momento em que a empresa expande seu papel no fornecimento de infraestrutura de energia modular para instalações com alto consumo energético. O anúncio não forneceu uma alocação detalhada do investimento restante nem especificou o cronograma para todas as despesas planejadas. A infraestrutura de IA impulsiona a demanda por energia dedicada A Enerflex atribuiu o crescimento de sua carteira de pedidos de geração de energia à demanda decorrente do desenvolvimento de inteligência artificial e infraestrutura digital. Os grandes centros de dados exigem um fornecimento substancial de eletricidade para operar equipamentos de computação, sistemas de rede e infraestrutura de refrigeração. A geração de energia instalada no próprio local de consumo pode fornecer uma fonte alternativa de energia para instalações que buscam capacidade dedicada sem depender de uma conexão convencional à rede elétrica para essa geração. Paul Mahoney, presidente e diretor executivo da Enerflex, destacou a demanda por esses sistemas. “A demanda por energia confiável e de primeira qualidade que não exija conexão à rede elétrica, e que dê suporte ao desenvolvimento de inteligência artificial e infraestrutura digital, continua a crescer”, disse Mahoney. “O nosso sucesso em garantir mais de 1,75 gigawatts em carteira de pedidos destaca as capacidades únicas da Enerflex em fornecer soluções integradas de design, engenharia, fabricação em grande escala e execução de projetos para geração de energia atrás do medidor.” Os comentários destacam o foco da administração no fornecimento de sistemas integrados de geração de energia para grandes projetos de infraestrutura. Os contratos podem gerar receita adicional com serviços A Enerflex afirmou que sua crescente carteira de pedidos de geração de energia pode criar oportunidades que vão além da entrega inicial dos equipamentos. Isso inclui o comissionamento, a instalação e os serviços pós-venda associados às unidades geradoras. A empresa também identificou uma demanda potencial por suporte digital por meio de seu ecossistema de Gestão de Desempenho de Ativos ReliaCore. Os sistemas de gestão de desempenho de ativos podem ajudar os operadores a monitorar equipamentos, avaliar as condições de operação e gerenciar as necessidades de manutenção. artigo.texto: The zoning amendment, filed by Mayor Dominick Pangallo in July, defines data centers within the city’s zoning ordinance, as a “facility, or portion thereof, primarily designed or used to house computer servers and related information technology infrastructure for the storage, processing, management, or transmission of electronic data.” City staff and legal counsel determined that data centers were already not an allowed use under the current zoning, but there was no language until now to explicitly define a data centers and prohibit its construction in the city. All councilors favored moving some version of the zoning amendment forward. Most of the discussion Thursday night centered around what version of the amendment would prevent potential loopholes for developers to exploit without inadvertently banning routine data processing uses for businesses such as hospitals and telecommunications. During a committee meeting Sept. 30, Councilor at-Large Ty Hapworth made a revision to specify that “a data center shall not include such computer servers and related information technology infrastructure that is accessory, incidental, and subordinate to a lawful principal use at the same facility or a portion thereof, however stored. This exception does not cover a separate business providing data storage, server hosting, distributing processing, or similar technology to third parties.” Several councilors agreed they need to revisit the new zoning change in the coming months, saying that what the mayor initially filed left them with little flexibility to more carefully define data centers without banning routine data processing. Legally, the council is unable to substantially change the language beyond the “four corners” of what was originally proposed in July. Since the council plans to revisit the matter soon, councilors Lydia King and Jason Sydoriak said it would be best to exclude Hapworth’s amendment in order to prevent potential loopholes. “We can all agree that nothing we can pass tonight is a comprehensive data center ordinance,” King said. “There is a lot of nuance that would go into (that), so anything we do tonight is effectively temporary... (But) by further clarifying accessory uses, we may have inadvertently introduced additional loopholes that would make this harder to hold up against in court if someone wanted to come and say they didn’t like a ruling they got from the city.” Other councilors disagreed. “I think this language is valuable to keep in here,” said Ward 6 Councilor Katelyn Holappa. “If this use is ‘accessory, incidental, and subordinate to a lawful principal use’ — all of those three things together, such as a hospital having a server room, we’re not making that impossible. That could cause problems for businesses that we’re not intending to put in here.” The vote to include Hapworth’s proposed language passed, with just King and Sydoriak in opposition. The committee had also approved a motion to strike language previously recommended by the Planning Board adding the language “and has an aggregate power demand of 2 Megawatts or higher” to the end of the definition of data centers. Councilors shared concerns that a use of up to 1.9 megawatts could still result in harmful impacts associated with data centers such as heat and noise. Ultimately, the council unanimously approved the zoning change to ban data centers, with plans to revisit the issue in the coming months to draft language that would give a more comprehensive definition of data centers. © 2026 The Salem News (Beverly, Mass.). artigo.texto: Energia DHL amplia rede global de logística especializada em baterias Companhia reúne mais de 20 instalações e prepara novos centros na Europa para atender aos setores automotivo, industrial e de armazenamento de energia A DHL está ampliando sua rede internacional de logística especializada em baterias, formada atualmente por mais de 20 instalações. A estrutura atende fabricantes de veículos elétricos, empresas industriais e projetos de energia, oferecendo serviços que vão do transporte de componentes e apoio à produção ao armazenamento, reparo e encaminhamento de baterias para reciclagem. A companhia prevê novas unidades na Europa até 2027. A rede reúne operações de três divisões do grupo — DHL Supply Chain, DHL Global Forwarding e DHL Express — para integrar transporte, armazenagem, procedimentos aduaneiros e serviços pós-venda. Segundo a empresa, os centros especializados também realizam diagnóstico, testes, carregamento, condicionamento e recebimento de equipamentos devolvidos pelos clientes. A expansão acompanha o aumento da utilização de baterias em diferentes atividades. Além dos automóveis elétricos, os equipamentos são empregados em máquinas industriais, operações de mineração e sistemas de armazenamento de energia. Alguns conjuntos pesam mais de 50 toneladas, o que exige veículos apropriados, equipamentos para movimentação de cargas pesadas e planejamento específico das entregas. O transporte desses produtos também está sujeito a requisitos de segurança. De acordo com a DHL, a classificação de baterias como mercadorias perigosas e as diferenças entre as regras aplicáveis ao transporte marítimo, aéreo e terrestre impõem cuidados com acondicionamento, documentação e fiscalização aduaneira. “A logística de baterias é fundamentalmente diferente das cadeias de abastecimento tradicionais”, afirmou Francisco Milián, responsável pela área de logística de entrada para a produção da DHL Supply Chain na Europa, Oriente Médio e África. Segundo ele, os clientes demandam serviços em todas as etapas, desde o fornecimento às fábricas até o recondicionamento, as devoluções e a reciclagem. Novas instalações Na Alemanha, a DHL disponibilizou recentemente 13 mil metros quadrados de armazenagem adaptada a baterias na cidade de Halle. Outra instalação está sendo preparada na Hungria, com início das atividades previsto para 2027. Nos Países Baixos, o grupo está construindo um centro em Holtum, com 17 mil metros quadrados para armazenagem e serviços especializados em baterias de alta tensão. A previsão é de que a operação comece no início de 2027. O empreendimento ficará próximo de instalações já utilizadas para atendimento à indústria automotiva, formando um complexo voltado também a sistemas de armazenamento de energia. Segundo a empresa, a concentração de atividades em centros especializados permitirá reunir operações de transporte internacional, liberação aduaneira, distribuição e atendimento após a venda. O serviço é destinado tanto à indústria automotiva quanto a fabricantes de equipamentos, empresas de energia e projetos relacionados a minerais críticos. Transporte de energia A DHL também atua na movimentação de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias, conhecidos pela sigla BESS, do inglês Battery Energy Storage Systems. Esses conjuntos armazenam eletricidade para utilização posterior e podem ser empregados em projetos de energia renovável e infraestrutura das redes elétricas. No primeiro semestre de 2026, a companhia transportou mais de 1.100 unidades BESS para diferentes mercados. Segundo o grupo, as entregas podem exigir transporte multimodal, içamento de cargas de grande porte e deslocamentos até áreas remotas, além do cumprimento das normas aplicáveis ao manuseio de mercadorias perigosas. O crescimento dessa atividade ocorre paralelamente à instalação de fábricas de baterias em diferentes regiões. A DHL aponta que a concentração de parte da produção na Ásia e a demanda em mercados como o europeu movimentam matérias-primas, produtos químicos, componentes, equipamentos industriais e baterias prontas entre continentes. “A transição energética está criando corredores comerciais e padrões de cadeias de abastecimento inteiramente novos”, afirmou Hendrik Venter, CEO global da DHL Supply Chain. De acordo com o executivo, fabricantes e operadores estão reorganizando suas redes para atender à produção de veículos elétricos, ao armazenamento de energia e aos empreendimentos de fontes renováveis. A logística para o setor de novas energias integra a Strategy 2030, plano de negócios do DHL Group. A área contempla oito segmentos: energia eólica, solar, veículos elétricos e baterias, armazenamento de energia em baterias, carregamento de veículos elétricos, infraestrutura de redes, hidrogênio e combustíveis alternativos.

artigo.texto: Alemanha planeja dobrar sua capacidade de data centers 11 de outubro de 2026 O futuro digital na Alemanhaestá tomando forma na cidade de Dietzenbach. Google, EdgeConnex e Maincubes – duas empresas de tecnologia americanas e uma alemã – reservaram terrenos para a construção de centros de dados (data centers) nessa pequena cidade próxima a Frankfurt. Dietzenbach é um polo logístico nas proximidades do aeroporto da metrópole financeira e tem cerca de 35 mil habitantes. A região de Frankfurt é um dos locais mais atraentes do mundo para operadores de computação em nuvem. À medida que a demanda por capacidade computacional continua crescendo, mais centros de dados estão sendo planejados no local. Consumo de eletricidade e água No entanto, a notícia sobre os planos para um quarto megacentro de dados encontrou resistência entre os moradores. As dezenas de milhares de computadores instalados num data center precisam de um enorme fornecimento de energia para funcionar ininterruptamente. Esses equipamentos geram grandes quantidades de calor e necessitam de sistemas de refrigeração, que, por sua vez, consomem enormes volumes de água. As pessoas entrevistadas pela DW em Dietzenbach demonstraram preocupação com o aumento das contas de água e energia, além de possíveis elevações da temperatura local. "Queremos saber duas coisas: quais são os benefícios para a comunidade local aqui em Dietzenbach? E quais são os impactos ambientais?", afirmou o morador Wilhelm Sauer, apontando para as quatro imponentes chaminés que se erguem do centro de dados da EdgeConnex. Ele e outros ativistas locais acreditam que o impacto dos centros de dados sobre os recursos da região talvez não seja compensado pelo número relativamente baixo de novos empregos anunciados. Já o prefeito de Dietzenbach, Dieter Lang, do Partido Social-Democrata (SPD), de centro-esquerda, mostra-se otimista. Segundo ele, cerca de cem empregos de alta qualificação deverão chegar à cidade por meio do centro de dados da Google. Ele também disse esperar benefícios para as finanças municipais por meio de impostos. Mas a pesquisadora Tara Merk, do projeto Community Data Centers no Instituto Weizenbaum, é cética. Ela acredita que a Alemanha provavelmente arrecadará pouco com centros de dados operados por empresas americanas "porque os lucros podem ser tributados em outros lugares". Em especial as grandes empresas de tecnologia, diz ela, não vão pagar seus impostos em Dietzenbach. Falta de informação sobre data centers Em agosto de 2026, o governo alemão lançou um cadastro nacional de centros de dados que lista consumo de energia e de água e medidas de eficiência energética dos centros já em operação. No entanto, a lista inclui apenas cerca de 300 instalações, muito menos que os aproximadamente 2 mil centros de dados que, segundo o próprio governo, operam no país. "Algumas empresas informam seus projetos menores, mas não os grandes", disse Werner Neumann, membro da diretoria da organização ambientalista Bund. Também não existe uma informação oficial sobre quantos centros de dados estão sendo construídos nem onde eles estão localizados. Para preencher essas lacunas, o projeto da sociedade civil Heisse Luft (Ar Quente) criou um mapa online dos centros de dados planejados em toda a Alemanha. O mapa é atualizado diariamente com informações obtidas por meio de contribuições das comunidades locais. "Em tese, essas informações já deveriam estar disponíveis", disse Tiziana von Witzleben, cofundadora da iniciativa Heisse Luft. Ela pondera que talvez o governo alemão não tenha capacidade para reunir e divulgar esses dados, mas acredita que parte da falta de transparência seja deliberada, especialmente por parte de gigantes como Google e Amazon. "Essas empresas são conhecidas por serem muito reservadas em relação ao que fazem. Porque sabem que, se contarem às pessoas, enfrentarão muitos protestos." Ao contrário dos Estados Unidos, onde surgiu um movimento nacional de protesto contra centros de dados, na Alemanha as manifestações continuam sendo um fenômeno predominantemente local. Em fevereiro, o conselho municipal de Gross-Gerau, na região de Frankfurt, votou contra um centro de dados de 2,5 bilhões de euros (R$ 14,7 bilhões) proposto por uma operadora americana. Segundo o jornal Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung, a decisão foi influenciada, ao menos em parte, pelos intensos protestos dos moradores preocupados com o calor residual gerado pela instalação. Em Maintal, outra cidade da região, um megacentro de dados da EdgeConnex enfrentou forte oposição devido ao plano de construir sua própria usina termelétrica a gás. O projeto de 1 bilhão de euros agora procura alternativas de energia numa região cuja rede elétrica já está próxima de seus limites. A corrida pelo poder computacional A Alemanha é o maior mercado de centros de dados da Europa, tanto em capacidade quanto em número de instalações. A região de Frankfurt/Reno-Meno, da qual Dietzenbach faz parte, concentra mais de um terço da capacidade total de centros de dados do país. A proximidade com o ponto de troca de tráfego de internet DE-CIX, em Frankfurt, torna a região especialmente atraente para operadores de computação em nuvem. Para atingir sua meta estratégica de dobrar a capacidade dos centros de dados até 2030, o governo alemão, formado por uma coalizão entre a União Democrata Cristã (CDU), de centro-direita, e o SPD, propôs alterar a legislação que regula o consumo de energia e a proteção climática. O Partido Verde questiona se essas metas realmente correspondem à demanda existente. Já o partido A Esquerda demonstra ceticismo em relação à expansão do setor como um todo. Ambos se opõem aos planos do governo de flexibilizar as regras para atrair mais centros de dados. No extremo oposto do espectro político, a Alternativa para a Alemanha (AfD), apoia a expansão dos centros de dados, mas critica a legislação que incentiva o uso de energias renováveis para alimentá-los. artigo.texto: The Chinese battery manufacturer leads with 26,574 patent families, supported by substantial research investment and rapid advances in power and solid-state battery technologies. China’s Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Limited (CATL) has surpassed South Korea’s LG Energy Solution to become the world’s leading company in battery patent holdings, highlighting China’s growing influence in the global battery technology sector. According to data released on October 6 by intellectual property consulting firm PatSnap, CATL recorded 26,574 simple patent families between October 2016 and September 2026. This places it ahead of LG Energy Solution, which holds 22,597 patent families, creating a gap of nearly 4,000. Simple patent families group patent applications covering the same core invention across different countries or regions. This method provides a clearer comparison of companies’ technological contributions while avoiding duplicate counting of identical inventions. CATL Strengthens Its Position in Battery Innovation The latest rankings reflect a significant shift in the battery industry, where Japanese and South Korean manufacturers historically held leading positions in research and development. LG Energy Solution now ranks second, while Panasonic has dropped out of the top ten with 4,994 patents. Toyota remains the only Japanese company among the leading ten. CATL’s growing patent portfolio is backed by substantial research spending. The company has invested more than 100 billion yuan, equivalent to approximately $14.9 billion, in cumulative research and development. PatSnap data further indicates that CATL holds 27,402 battery patents overall, including 16,722 filed during the past three years. These recent filings account for 61% of its total portfolio, demonstrating the pace of its technological expansion. Power Battery Patents Lead the Industry CATL has established a particularly strong position in power battery technology, holding 19,539 patents. Its portfolio is approximately 2.2 times larger than that of the second-ranked domestic competitor. During the past three years, CATL filed 12,084 power battery patents, significantly exceeding the 4,384 recorded by its closest domestic rival. Its recent filings also approach the combined 14,500 patents held by companies ranked second through fifth. Solid-State Battery Research Gains Momentum CATL is also expanding its presence in solid-state battery development, a technology widely viewed as important for the next generation of energy storage. The company holds 3,538 patents in this field, more than twice the total of its second-ranked domestic competitor. Of these, 2,763 were filed during the last three years, nearly matching the combined 2,891 patents recorded by domestic companies ranked second through tenth. The figures underline CATL’s growing technological lead and the increasingly prominent role of Chinese manufacturers in shaping the future of battery innovation.

artigo.texto: Data Centers and Public Health The rapid growth of AI and other digital services like search engines and cloud storage and computing is driving a major expansion of data center construction across the United States. As rapid expansion continues, it is necessary to account for related health impacts. Data centers can affect communities and their health in a variety of ways, including air pollution from the burning of fossil fuels, water use and pollution, excessive noise and light pollution, and land use and development. New facilities that are powered by fossil fuels can add to existing pollution and health burdens in communities already facing environmental injustices. Data centers are often placed and operated in the same communities already disproportionately impacted by environmental injustices: low-income, rural, immigrant/refugee, Indigenous communities and other communities of color, and other marginalized populations. It’s important to understand how data centers can affect health and the role public health professionals can play to advocate for transparent decisionmaking and protective policies. Latest Updates - Data Centers and Health: Understanding the Impacts and Taking Action AI data centers are expanding rapidly across the U.S., with growing implications for air and water quality, noise, energy costs and public health. This four-part webinar series equips health professionals and advocates with the evidence, messaging and actionable strategies needed to respond. Watch the recordings. - Q&A with NAACP: Addressing the growing environmental harms of AI data centers | Public Health Newswire From rising emissions to local air, water and noise pollution, AI data centers pose growing concerns about environmental justice and health equity. The NAACP has long been on the front lines of environmental justice and is addressing new threats as they arise. This March 2026 Q&A from Public Health Newswire talks with the NAACP to learn how communities and health professionals can respond. Read the article. How a Data Center Can Affect Health Energy, Air Pollution and Climate Health The energy demand created by data centers can drive grid expansion and fossil fuel energy generation, which can worsen air pollution, amplify the effects of climate change and create affordability concerns for households. Impact on Energy Grid In some areas, utility companies may need to expand or upgrade the power grid to meet data centers’ energy demand. Depending on how these upgrades are funded, this can increase energy costs for surrounding communities, contributing to financial stress and mental health impacts. Inadequate energy access can increase the risk of heat- and cold-related illnesses, such as heat stroke and inadequate blood circulation. Long-term socioeconomic implications of financial hardship can include food insecurity, increasing health disparities and chronic stress. Air Quality Data centers that rely on fossil fuels can increase air pollution, contributing to respiratory and cardiovascular disease, cancer, neurological disorders and reduced fertility. One high-growth model suggests that data centers may contribute to approximately 600,000 asthma cases in 2028, with an estimated public health cost over $20 billion. Climate Change Added CO₂ from data center operations accelerates climate change, contributing to more severe heat waves, storms and floods, which are all events that endanger both data centers and nearby communities and compound health risks ranging from heat stroke and respiratory illness to trauma and mental health impacts. The water consumption by data centers may exacerbate growing water scarcity caused by climate change and drought. Data centers can release excess heat that may raise temperatures in nearby neighborhoods. Some researchers have documented increased air temperatures up to 4°F, and this heat impact spanned approximately a third of a mile from the data center. Added heat may increase cooling needs and compound heat-health risks for people who are most vulnerable or unable to afford air conditioning. Water Use, Quality and Scarcity Cooling systems can strain local water supplies and raise concerns about water quality, drought and equitable access. The cooling systems used in data centers can strain local water resources and negatively impact water quality. There are also some concerns around incorporation of chemicals like PFAS in the cooling systems. These forever chemicals are long-lasting in the environment and high levels are linked with some cancers. The changes to water supply and quality may increase the risk of waterborne diseases, water scarcity, pollution ingestion and poor maternal outcomes. Noise, Light and Sleep Health Around-the-clock cooling equipment, fans, generators and construction can create disruptive noise, while nighttime lighting can interfere with sleep and daily rhythms. Noise Pollution Cooling systems, back-up diesel generators, fans and other machinery contribute to constant noise production, which can cause chronic sleep disturbance and stress, with the possibility of long-term conditions such as cardiovascular impacts. Noise pollution is of particular concern for children as it can impact cognition and may have lifelong health impacts. Light Pollution Data centers require lighting throughout the night which can disrupt the circadian rhythm of individuals exposed, impacting melatonin production, sleep cycles, mental health, cardiovascular health and overall quality of life. Beyond the Facility: Supply Chains and E-Waste Construction, mineral extraction and electronic waste create health and environmental impacts beyond the data center site. Beyond the direct health impacts of data centers, the processes required to build and maintain the facilities, such as mining rare-earth metals and concrete production, also impact health outcomes. artigo.texto: Morocco prepares to launch Africa’s first battery gigafactory Gotion Power Morocco plans to begin equipment commissioning in Kenitra, advancing major investment in battery manufacturing KENITRA, Morocco (MNTV) — Morocco is preparing to advance its electric vehicle battery manufacturing industry as Gotion Power Morocco plans to begin commissioning production equipment at its Kenitra gigafactory during the week of October 20. Moroccan subsidiary of China’s Gotion High-Tech announced the timetable for starting up equipment at the industrial facility, which is intended to produce lithium iron phosphate battery cells. The project’s first phase represents an investment of approximately 13 billion Moroccan dirhams, equivalent to about $1.3 billion, and targets an initial annual capacity of 20 gigawatt-hours. Located in Kenitra’s Atlantic Free Zone, the facility is designed to serve the automotive and energy storage industries. Its potential markets include Morocco, other African countries, Europe, the Middle East and the United States. Construction began in September 2025, with the company’s buildings and infrastructure completed over approximately 13 months. The project required large-scale shipments of production equipment from China, supported by Moroccan port and customs authorities. Gotion Power Morocco president Khalid Qalam described the equipment startup as an initial step toward developing a wider battery manufacturing ecosystem in the country. The company has recruited more than 400 Moroccan employees, including engineers, technicians and production workers. Many received training at Gotion facilities in China before joining the Kenitra project. The company expects the gigafactory to create more than 2,300 direct jobs when fully developed. Its longer-term plans include expanding production capacity and manufacturing battery materials for electric vehicles and energy storage systems. The project also forms part of a broader partnership involving Gotion and Volkswagen’s battery subsidiary, PowerCo. The companies announced a separate Moroccan joint venture in September to produce lithium iron phosphate cathode materials. That venture is expected to involve an investment of approximately €480 million, or about $547 million, with planned annual production capacity of 100,000 metric tons. The developments strengthen Morocco’s ambitions to attract advanced manufacturing investment and establish a larger role in international electric vehicle supply chains.

artigo.texto: Four-Hour Battery Storage Now Cheaper Than Gas Turbines: Report Lower battery costs, gas turbine shortages, and fuel volatility aid storage October 12, 2026 Follow Mercom India on WhatsApp for exclusive updates on clean energy news and insights Four-hour battery energy storage systems, utility-scale energy storage systems that are designed to discharge at their full rated capacity for approximately four hours, now cost less than open-cycle gas turbines across 43 markets, according to Wood Mackenzie’s latest global report on levelized cost of electricity (LCOE). This shift is driven by technological advancements and evolving market dynamics. Single-axis tracking solar is the lowest-cost new power generation option in 43 of the 48 markets analyzed. Wood Mackenzie attributed the shift to declining battery costs, gas turbine shortages, and volatile fuel prices. North America U.S. solar costs face pressure from tariffs, antidumping and countervailing duties, and Section 232 import restrictions. Utility-scale solar is partly insulated by 168 GW of safe-harbored capacity, although module prices are projected to rise 5% annually through 2030. Residential and commercial solar projects face greater cost pressures, with module prices expected to increase 6% in 2027 and 14% in 2028. Onshore wind’s LCOE is projected to decline 16% by 2060, driven by lower capital and operating costs, despite policy uncertainty and potential tariff impacts. Tax credits are expected to support battery storage economics despite foreign entity of concern restrictions and supply chain constraints. Storage costs could rise after investment tax credits phase out in 2038. Technological advances and domestic manufacturing expansion are projected to reduce storage LCOE by 10% by 2060. Growing data center demand is likely to constrain gas generation equipment supply through the late 2030s, keeping capital costs elevated. Latin America Single-axis tracking solar so far remains Latin America’s lowest-cost power generation technology in 2026. Its average costs are projected to decline 38% by 2060. Brazil, Chile, and Mexico benefit from strong solar resources and high capacity factors. Onshore wind’s average LCOE is projected to fall nearly 21%, from $73/MWh to $58/MWh by 2030, supported by the expansion of Chinese manufacturers and larger turbines. Grid-scale battery storage is expanding through renewable energy-linked mandates and standalone procurement. Its LCOE is projected to decline 42% by 2060. Offshore wind costs are expected to approach parity with combined-cycle gas turbines, before firming, in the early 2040s. Asia Pacific Utility-scale solar remains the most cost-competitive power source in Asia Pacific, although costs differ substantially across markets. In 2026, solar generation costs in the region’s most expensive market are over 200% higher than in the cheapest. The gap is expected to widen to 250% by 2030, despite declining costs across all markets. Onshore wind costs vary more than sixfold across the region. Greater penetration of Chinese turbine manufacturers and the adoption of higher-capacity turbines are expected to narrow the cost gap with coal in South and Southeast Asia. China has the world’s lowest grid-scale storage costs, more than 55% lower than the rest of Asia Pacific’s average of $134/MWh. Chinese equipment supply is expected to reduce the regional average to $92/MWh by 2036. Japan, Australia, and the Philippines face higher costs due to import duties, installation expenses, and domestic manufacturing policies. Offshore wind costs outside China are expected to decline significantly from the early 2030s. Europe Solar remains Europe’s cheapest power generation technology. The LCOE for fixed-tilt systems is projected to decline 22% by 2060, despite a 14% increase in capital expenditure (CAPEX) in 2026 due to higher module prices. Onshore wind CAPEX is expected to decline 2.5% annually through 2030 as manufacturers benefit from improved financial stability and growing demand. Higher capacity factors are expected to bring its LCOE to $60/MWh by 2060. Battery storage turnkey CAPEX rose 2%, the first increase in three years, as cell prices rebounded 10% from 2025 lows amid stronger demand and higher lithium prices. CAPEX is projected to decline 12% by 2031, although rising lithium prices could slow subsequent reductions. Europe has the highest fossil fuel generation costs among the regions analyzed, with carbon costs expected to exceed fuel costs by 2030. Offshore wind costs are projected to decline from the 2030s as supply chains stabilize and turbine prices fall. Middle East and Africa The Middle East and Africa have the lowest regional LCOE for single-axis tracking solar, at $37/MWh in 2026. Costs are projected to decline to $24/MWh by 2035, while solar LCOE in Saudi Arabia and the UAE could fall below $20/MWh by 2033. Onshore wind costs are declining as Chinese turbines become more competitive. Egypt and Morocco have low wind generation costs, supported by capacity factors of 40% to 45%. Four-hour battery storage costs in the region are estimated at $120/MWh in 2026 and are projected to decline 33% to $80/MWh by 2035. Battery storage is more cost-competitive than open-cycle gas turbines across the region’s gas markets, supporting the integration of solar and wind and reducing reliance on gas-fired peaking capacity. According to Wood Mackenzie, renewable energy LCOE across major markets, including single-axis tracking solar in the Middle East and Africa, recorded the lowest regional LCOE of $37/MWh as of November 2025, driven by technological advances, supply chain stabilization, and improved module efficiencies. Battery storage project costs hit an all-time low in 2025, even as other renewables rose, according to BloombergNEF’s LCOE 2026 report.

artigo.texto: AI introduces unprecedented challenges in data centers; not just in power, but in cooling, latency, deployment speed and geography. These challenges carry through all data center areas, or “subsystems,” to varying degrees. These different subsystems often require tailored solutions in an AI data center, removing them from any semblance of a typical “uniform” design. Setting a foundation for a successful AI implementation requires a cable infrastructure partner with the capacity, agility and resources to deliver high-performance cabling systems designed for real-world data center environments. It also requires an understanding of how AI implementation interacts with each subsystem in the data center, and what the people responsible for maintaining those subsystems can expect. There are four key subsystems: the Entry Point, Front End, DC Interconnect and Back End Subsystems. Entry point The Entry-Point subsystem is traditionally part of the data center gray space, supporting infrastructure by connecting the cable coming from outside the data hall to the cable within it. Moreover, the entry point is where those fibers are separated and directed to different areas of the facility. Increasing density demands from AI applications are driving increases of high fiber count cables coming into the Entry Point, and increasing power and cooling demands have further limited available gray space in the data center. This can cause complications for space utilization, cable management and labor, resulting in speed of deployment being the most critical issue related to the entry point. So how can data center operators mitigate this issue? Rapid and versatile installation is key; innovative splicing enclosures, splicing and interconnect trays and consideration of pre-terminated solutions can be vital. These solutions unlock a modular approach to infrastructure, allowing for rapid and easy upgrades as needs evolve and require much less time to install overall. Front end The Front-End subsystem is typically in the white space, where the computing occurs inside the data center, and is the layer that handles traffic between users, internal resources and external networks. Of the four subsystems, the Front End is least impacted by the addition of AI, buoyed above the waves that hit other subsystems by its established infrastructure. The Front-End Subsystem’s foundation has only received minor updates over the last five years. However, local code compliance is almost always a concern when expansions occur on the frontend, especially when those expansions are in other geographic locations. Global solutions can alleviate this concern, allowing you to utilize the same infrastructure across locations where local codes differ slightly. Data center interconnect The DC Interconnect subsystem is part of the data center’s gray space, or areas that provide critical support for computing, and often consists of multiple high strand count fiber cables running between facilities that connect pods across the network. Somewhat ironically, AI struggles with the capability that the DC Interconnect subsystem was designed to deliver: connection over distance. An AI cluster on the back end is treated as a single system, housed in one location that then must spread itself over the rest of the facility. As the size of AI clusters increases, expansion of the data center interconnect system also grows exponentially to ensure that communication between facilities at maximum throughput. However, the data center interconnect system is notoriously difficult to expand, demanding time and labor to add or replace cabling. Leaders can mitigate this issue by deploying infrastructure that can handle the higher densities AI requires, while also being built for rapid deployment. Leviton’s 1728-strand MMC trunks, which are part of the STRATA™ family of Hyperscale and AI data center solutions, allow for a much higher density footprint than traditional alternatives. Moreover, Leviton’s trunks are designed to be installed quickly and easily – a huge boon when recabling a traditionally labor-intensive subsystem. Back end Finally, there’s the Back End; the subsystem that houses the AI cluster, and where AI implementation really changes the subsystem’s status quo. As the density of the system increases to accommodate the AI cluster, cable management and power become critical. The substantial power demands of AI technologies require data center operators to find ways to do more with their established power infrastructure. The challenge of managing the increased density is one that data center operators are familiar with; doing more with less. This is where Very-Small-Form-Factor (VSFF) connectors, like MMC, come in. VSFF connectors meet the need for higher density at connect points, while taking up less space than their MPO alternatives. This enables operators to scale fiber capacity without proportionally increasing rack space, as demonstrated by solutions such as Leviton's STRATA™ family, which supports up to 3,456 fibers per rack unit using a 16-fiber MMC connector. As for maximizing the potential of established power infrastructure, utilizing power more efficiently in the data center often boils down to cooling. Immersion cooling is an emergent technology wherein servers are submersed in non-electrically conductive, thermally conductive fluids, offering almost-instantaneous heat dispersion for high-density networks. The success of immersion cooling depends not only on thermal performance but also on ensuring network infrastructure can operate reliably in submerged environments. Solutions such as Leviton TORRENT™ are designed to address this challenge by maintaining signal integrity and resisting degradation in dielectric cooling fluids. Greg Abbott and Attorney General Ken Paxton have adopted increasingly tough rhetoric against data centers, promising to crack down on hundreds of facilities that failed to disclose required information about their water use over the past five years. But the law that Texas political leaders are invoking carries a maximum fine of just $500 — a potentially negligible penalty that’s just a blip for large companies. Data centers use millions of gallons of water a year to run their facilities and cool their servers. Under state law, facilities that fail to complete required water-use surveys can be charged with a Class C misdemeanor, punishable by up to a $500 fine, and barred from certain state funding and environmental permits. But some experts say those consequences have significant limitations, raising questions about whether the state has the tools to force compliance from an industry expanding rapidly across Texas. State officials don’t know whether misdemeanor penalties have been issued against data centers, and the facilities aren’t eligible for state funding. Increasing fines for Class C misdemeanors in the Water Code would require state legislation. Lawmakers do not convene in Austin for the 2027 legislative session until January. “The governor is like, ‘Let’s enforce the laws on the books that weren’t being enforced.’ That’s not much in the way of incentive,” said Kathryn Guerra, who leads a watchdog campaign at the environmental nonprofit Public Citizen. “If those are the laws that we already have and nobody’s enforcing them, the data centers know.” Abbott’s office defended its enforcement crackdown by saying that the water board, along with other agencies including the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality, the Electric Reliability Council of Texas and the Public Utility Commission of Texas, will work together. “No other state agency will approve data centers until the Public Utility Commission, ERCOT, and the Water Development Board have the information they need to make informed decisions,” said Andrew Mahaleris, Abbott’s press secretary. Mahaleris added that the governor has recommended that data centers pay for their own electric infrastructure, use less water-intensive cooling technologies and add power generation to the state’s power grid. Cameron Poursoltan, the director of energy policy at Texas for the Data Center Coalition, said the organization, which represents many data center operators, supports annual water reporting because state and regional planners need accurate data to build a water plan that meets the needs of all Texans. The state already requires large water users, including data centers, to complete annual water use surveys. The Texas Water Development Board, the state agency tasked with overseeing the state’s water planning process and financing water projects, uses responses to assess the current demand and to plan for water needs 50 years into the future. But data centers have largely ignored the surveys. Or some argue they haven’t received them. Last year, 329 data centers were surveyed. Only about 30% responded. One lawmaker described the response rate as “pretty pathetic” at a legislative hearing this summer, despite the requirement being written into state law. Some data center operators have defended the low response rate, saying they have not received a survey. “Data centers take water stewardship extremely seriously,” Poursoltan said. He added that the organization has worked with TWDB to resolve “significant contact information and data discrepancies that contributed to the TWDB Water Use Survey’s initial lower response rate.” Tracking data centers in Texas The survey has long been the state’s only way to track how much water the rapidly expanding data center industry uses. Another effort to collect the information by the PUC this year has been voluntary and also had a low response rate. Now, amid growing scrutiny of data centers and their demands on Texas’ dwindling water supply, Abbott and Paxton are asking state agencies to enforce the existing law. The enforcement push comes as both Republicans face competitive elections and opposition to data center development grows. A University of Texas/Texas Politics Project poll released in August found that 57% of Texas voters opposed building a data center in their community. Republicans remained closely divided, with 45% supporting while 43% opposed local data center construction. Meanwhile, 75% of registered Texas Democrats oppose data centers. The water board, which collects the surveys to help plan the state’s water needs, has historically had little ability to enforce the requirement. Abbott has directed the agency to notify local prosecutors about noncompliant facilities, while Paxton has launched an investigation. But the board says it has no authority to prosecute violations itself, and state officials don’t know if fines have been issued against data centers. The state’s next steps could reveal how much leverage officials actually have. The water board is required to update Abbott’s office by Oct. 14 on the progress of its enforcement efforts. “We will continue working with state leaders to ensure our industry’s growth in Texas is responsible, transparent, and responsive to the communities where our members operate,” Poursoltan said in an email. Historically, the board relied on local law enforcement to ask for the list of noncompliant water users. artigo.texto: Fox stays positive on data centers even as public backlash grows The News Despite increasingly critical media coverage of AI and the spread of data centers across the US, one news network has been painting a more positive picture. More than half of the references to data centers on Fox News over the last two years would have left viewers with a favorable impression, compared to less than 10% on CNN and 5% on MS NOW, according to a new Semafor analysis of mentions of data centers on each network. The mentions were pulled from closed captions preserved by the Internet Archive, which keeps a digital, searchable library of recorded TV news. A pair of AI models from Anthropic and OpenAI scored each reference on its content, with the network's name removed. Mentions of data centers have, predictably, shot up across all three networks in recent months as political backlash against AI swells and the data centers themselves have become a salient issue ahead of the midterms. But Fox's opinion and morning shows, including, , and leaned on the promise of AI, economic investment and the race with China, skewing Fox's coverage more favorably, the analysis showed. The network's news shows were more measured. In an Aug. 23 monologue that at one point featured a chyron reading "The case for data centers," Fox host Brian Kilmeade acknowledged "real concerns," but argued that "saying no to data centers nationwide also means saying no to the tax dollars that can flow into a community. … If Americans don't build the infrastructure to meet the demand, somebody else will." On CNN and MS NOW, the criticism focused as much on the facilities' political toxicity as on harms like power bills or water use, casting them as unpopular with voters and a liability for politicians who back them heading into the midterms. Data centers "are driving up energy costs, sucking up water supplies, wiping out rather than creating jobs," MS NOW's Katy Tur said in May. "Politicians beware." Polling shows that across demographic groups, Americans hold increasingly negative views of data centers: More than half of Americans say data centers are mostly bad for the environment, Pew Research Center found last month, compared with 39% in January. Fox News did not comment for this story. Max's view The pro-data center programming on Fox News comes as the right tries to define its positions in an AI-fueled, post-Donald Trump future. Fox's favorable data center coverage mirrors Trump's position on their growth and the need for AI companies to help fuel the US economy. "The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor," Trump wrote on Truth Social in August. "If we kill the Golden Goose, you will only have yourselves to blame." But anger about data centers and the rapid advancement of AI represents a faultline within the MAGA coalition that swept Trump back into office. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., have questioned some data centers in their states, while Texas Gov. Greg Abbott seems to have flipped from supporting data centers to looking to slow their growth in his state amid a tougher-than-expected reelection campaign. Some on the right I have talked to in the last several months worry that Fox News, which Trump watches religiously, and other pro-data center voices are encouraging the president to take positions that are broadly unpopular with his rural and suburban base. "The Big Tech oligarchs, the guys driving AI, did a terrible job," Steve Bannon, a staunchly anti-AI Trump ally, told the Daily Signal in September. "They came in to try to muscle local communities, and particularly since President Trump's strongest base is in exurban and rural communities, that's where they were really the ugliest, and they haven't made their case, and they particularly haven't made their case at the local level about the economics of this, and the energy of this, and the water of this, and the manifestation of what these things are going to be used for." Room for Disagreement Not all of Fox's data center coverage has been rosy; its tenor grew slightly less favorable in 2026 compared to last year. artigo.texto: Bulgaria’s net electricity exports surged by 62% in annual terms from the beginning of the year to early October. They reached 3.5 TWh, compared to 2.16 TWh in the same period last year, driven primarily by increased generation from renewable energy sources, supported by energy storage systems. Data from Bulgaria’s transmission system operator (TSO) Electricity System Operator (ESO) show that the country produced 12.24% more electricity year-on-year, while domestic consumption grew by 8.45%, according to the Association for Production, Storage and Trading of Electricity (APSTE). Power generation from renewable energy sources reached 11.5 TWh, up by nearly 34% from the previous year. Renewables have accounted for nearly 80% of the country’s total power generation growth. The expansion of energy storage systems has been particularly remarkable The expansion of energy storage systems has been particularly remarkable. From the start of the year until October 4, grid-scale batteries delivered 1,720 GWh of electricity to the power system. It is a more than ninefold increase from just 190 GWh that was recorded a year earlier. This enabled cheap electricity generated during the day to be stored and used during hours of higher demand and higher prices, APSTE pointed out. Of note, Bulgaria’s BESS capacity is approaching 6 GW / 17 GWh. Eurelectric earlier said that 5.4 GW of BESS capacity accounts for 22.8% of total generation capacity in the country, making it one of the global leaders. Bulgaria remained a net exporter during the challenging summer in the region APSTE stressed that the benefits of the new energy mix became particularly clear during the summer. Despite prolonged heatwaves and low water levels on the Danube river that constrained nuclear and hydro power generation across the region, Bulgaria remained a net exporter and maintained prices lower than neighboring markets during key periods. This success was driven by a combination of solar power plants, battery storage, and the Kozloduy Nuclear Power Plant (NPP). Gazdov: While neighboring markets suffer from high prices and power shortages, Bulgaria generates and stores more and more of its own electricity “While neighboring markets suffer from high prices and power shortages, due to constraints on their nuclear plants and high natural gas prices, Bulgaria generates and stores more and more of its own electricity. This translates into more competitive prices for households and businesses, greater energy security, and a stronger position on the regional energy market,” APSTE chairman Nikola Gazdov explained. A striking example occurred on October 8, when Unit 6 of the Kozloduy NPP underwent planned maintenance and Unit 5 operated at reduced capacity due to low water levels on the Danube. Despite these constraints, in the early afternoon photovoltaic systems were producing nearly 4,300 MW, exceeding total national demand of 4,100 MW, while batteries were charging at over 4,000 MW, storing cheap electricity for peak evening demand, the update reads. Wind is the solution for cheaper electricity in the winter However, APSTE warned that the successful expansion of solar energy and batteries is not enough. In the winter, solar generation decreases while demand rises. To secure more of cheap domestic power during the colder months, Bulgaria must accelerate wind energy deployment. Since 2020, PV capacity in the country has grown by about 600% to nearly 7 GW, while BESS capacity is close to 6 GW / 17 GWh. APSTE estimates that total investments in photovoltaics, batteries, and related infrastructure since 2020 have reached approximately EUR 7 billion. However, Bulgaria has only 716 MW of installed wind capacity, with no major new wind farm built since 2013. Wind power complements solar with a different daily and seasonal generation profile, capable of providing substantial power output during winter, APSTE added. Gazdov: Sun and batteries have significantly enhanced Bulgaria’s energy security “Sun and batteries have significantly enhanced Bulgaria’s energy security amid one of the most severe energy crises. This is very important, but it is not enough. We must build on this success by attracting investment into wind power as well,” he said. This road will secure cheaper local electricity not only in the summer, but also in the winter, Gazdov added. Achieving this does not require new subsidies, but clear rules and a genuine easing of construction procedures for new capacity, in his view. According to APSTE, Bulgaria could attract over EUR 4 billion in additional private investment in wind farms and energy storage systems by 2030, provided institutions ensure predictable regulations and remove unnecessary administrative constraints, including for projects located outside renewable energy acceleration areas.

artigo.texto: Residents weigh in on year-long data center pause CHARLOTTE, N.C. – Dozens of people sounding off about whether Charlotte should move forward with data centers in the city. City council hosted a public hearing to extend the data center moratorium. Across the country, conversations about data centers have been getting heated but the discussion at the government center Monday night was subdued. More than 30 residents on both sides of the argument signed up to speak at the hearing. Back in June, the council voted in favor of a data center moratorium that runs out in November. The moratorium temporarily paused any new data center applications or development. This did not stop projects that are already under construction like the large scale data center under construction in University City. The moratorium was supposed to give staff time to research potential ways to regulate data centers and address environmental concerns. The city started a task force and hosted forums for residents to weigh in while working on regulations. More than 100 days later the work isn’t done. “Staff need additional expertise and capacity to develop the tools needed to ensure responsible data center development,” Heather Bolick, Chief Sustainability & Resiliency Officer for City of Charlotte said. “An extension of the moratorium would allow us to develop needed tools.” Some residents encouraged the city to speed up the process of writing regulations for data centers. “We believe that this moratorium is an impractical tool that risks sending the wrong signal about our region’s economic readiness,” Rob Nanfelt, Executive Director of Real Estate and Building Industry Coalition said. “However, since city staff and council require more time to study infrastructure impacts, we firmly believe the path forward lies in collaboration, not exclusion.” Other residents say the city cannot afford to rush the process to regulate data centers. “The purpose of a moratorium is not to stop progress; is to create the space for informed progress,” Rev Dr Janet Garner Mullins, Charlotte resident said. “Tonight is not about whether data centers belong in Charlotte. It’s about whether or not Charlotte has done enough homework before writing rules that would shape our future.” Some councilmembers suggested city staff research what other cities are doing to regulate data centers. Council will vote on whether to extend the moratorium at the October 22nd meeting. If passed the action would extend the moratorium until October of 2027.

artigo.texto: The flagship seven-seater is BYD’s first vehicle in Europe to feature its second-generation batteries and Flash Charging tech, delivering over 400 miles of range. BYD launches new flagship Atto 8 in Europe “BYD is all about turning intelligence into reality,” Stella Li, the company’s executive vice president, said on Monday. The Atto 8 is the “perfect example,” Li added, featuring its latest breakthrough tech, including its second-generation Blade Batteries and Flash Charging system. Introduced at the Paris Auto Show, the flagship SUV is the first BYD vehicle to feature its Flash Charging system, enabling it to recharge just as fast as filling up at the gas station. It takes just five minutes to charge from 10% to 80%. A full recharge, or going from 10% to 97%, takes just nine minutes. According to BYD, that’s about a third of the time rival SUVs take to go from 10% to 80%. Even in temperatures as low as -30°C, it requires only 12 minutes for the vehicle’s battery to recharge from 20% to 97%. Measuring 5,040 mm long, 1,996 mm wide, and 1,760 mm tall, the Atto 8 is about the size of other full-size electric SUVs, such as the Hyundai IONIQ 9 and Kia EV9. BYD’s flagship SUV comes in two all-electric variants with the choice of rear- and all-wheel-drive powertrains. The Design RWD model has a single rear motor producing 456 hp (340 kW) and 269 lb-ft (365 Nm) of torque, which BYD said delivers a 0 to 62 mph time of eight seconds. Powered by a 115 kWh BYD Blade 2.0 battery, the Atto 8 offers an impressive WLTP range of up to 405 miles (600+ km). For example, BYD said the flagship SUV offers enough electric range to drive from London to Edinburgh. The Atto 8 Excellence AWD, on the other hand, adds a front electric motor for a combined output of 764 hp (570 kW) and 572 lb-ft (775 Nm) of torque. The added power delivers a sports-car-rivaling 0- 62 mph acceleration time of 4.6 seconds and a WLTP range of 374 miles. Inside, natural light fills the spacious cabin thanks to a 2.39m2 panoramic glass roof. Both Atto 8 variants have a 10.25″ digital instrument cluster, a 26″ head-up display, and a 15.6″ central infotainment touchscreen with Google Built-in. BYD said the Atto 8 is specifically tailored for those looking for a “zero compromise” seven-seat SUV. The front seats and outer seats of the middle row feature heating, ventilation, and massage functions. Rear passengers get their own air-conditioning control panel. All seats are upholstered in genuine leather. The Design RWD model features a 10-speaker sound system, while the Excellence AWD gains a 21-speaker DiSound audio system, plus an added front refrigerator. With the second and third rows folded, the Atto 8 offers up to 1,960L capacity. Even with all three rows up, the full-size SUV offers 270L of luggage space. Plus, there’s a 136L frunk (front trunk). BYD said dealers in Europe will begin selling the Atto 8 in the first quarter of 2027. Prices have yet to be announced, but given it will be positioned above the Ti 7, a plug-in hybrid seven-seat SUV, it will likely start at slightly over £47,995 ($65,000) on the road in the UK. In Europe, BYD currently sells the Tang, an electric seven-seat SUV. In Germany, the BYD Tang typically starts at €75,000 ($84,000), but it’s currently on sale for €47,990 ($54,000).
