artigo.texto: Modelos e plataformas de IA Flex adiciona módulos de IA fabricados em fábrica ao portfólio de data centers modulares Adicione Unite.AI às suas fontes preferidas no Google Em 12 de outubro de 2026, a Flex anunciou um portfólio ampliado de soluções modulares pré-fabricadas para data centers, projetadas para acelerar a implantação de fábricas de IA de próxima geração. O portfólio inclui os novos Axiom AI Modules, que integram energia, computação de alta densidade e resfriamento líquido avançado em sistemas fabricados em fábrica, que, segundo a Flex, podem reduzir os prazos de implantação em até 50% em comparação com a construção tradicional. O portfólio ampliado faz parte do segmento de Infraestrutura de Nuvem e Energia da Flex, que a empresa planeja separar e transformar na Axiom Solutions International, Inc., uma empresa independente de capital aberto, no primeiro trimestre do ano-calendário de 2027. A Flex afirmou que, à medida que a infraestrutura de IA cresce em escala e densidade de potência, os operadores de data centers enfrentam complexidade cada vez maior na distribuição de energia, no resfriamento, na integração da computação e na implantação. Chris Butler, que deverá ocupar o cargo de diretor de tecnologia e estratégia da Axiom, afirmou que atender a essa demanda em escala exige mais do que melhorias incrementais. Em vez disso, descreveu uma abordagem em nível de sistema que combina tecnologias de energia, computação e resfriamento com manufatura avançada para simplificar a integração, acelerar a implantação e fornecer fábricas de IA em escala. Por dentro dos Axiom AI Modules Segundo o comunicado, os módulos integram componentes essenciais da infraestrutura de IA em três categorias. Um rack de energia de 800 VDC oferece conversão e distribuição de energia de alta eficiência para a infraestrutura de IA de 800 VDC de próxima geração e a computação de alta densidade. Unidades avançadas de distribuição de resfriamento fornecem resfriamento líquido para controlar o calor gerado por cargas de trabalho de IA que consomem muita energia, enquanto racks de TI de alta densidade integram servidores de IA, redes e interconexões de alta velocidade para dar suporte à computação de IA de próxima geração em escala. A Flex afirmou que transferir a integração de infraestruturas complexas do local do data center para um ambiente de fábrica controlado permite montar, integrar e testar os módulos em paralelo ao desenvolvimento do local, reduzindo a complexidade no local e ajudando os clientes a disponibilizar capacidade de IA mais rapidamente. Uma página de recursos da Flex publicada em 12 de outubro de 2026 informa que os módulos são pré-fabricados e comissionados em um ambiente de fábrica controlado, com racks de TI e a infraestrutura de suporte essencial integrados em um único sistema antes do envio. Os módulos incluem estruturas de corredores, unidades de distribuição de líquido refrigerante, redes secundárias de fluidos, painéis de energia remotos, controles, sistemas de distribuição elétrica, sistemas de gerenciamento da qualidade da água e componentes de segurança e detecção de vazamentos. Prazos de implantação estimados A página de recursos apresenta uma comparação estimada entre a implantação modular pré-fabricada e a construção tradicional com estrutura montada no local para um projeto de fábrica de IA, tomando como referência os 18 meses, ou 78 semanas, da construção tradicional. Nesse modelo, afirmou a Flex, os Axiom AI Modules podem reduzir os prazos de implantação em até 50%, de 78 semanas para apenas 39 semanas. A Flex atribuiu a aceleração a cinco fatores: padronização do projeto e integração em fábrica; fabricação em fábrica e construção no local em paralelo; redução da instalação, dos testes e do comissionamento no local; controles integrados e testes no nível dos racks; e menos alterações em etapas avançadas, retrabalho e falhas de instalação em campo. A empresa declarou que os prazos e as economias reais de implantação variam conforme o escopo do projeto, as condições do local, os requisitos de projeto e outros fatores. Presença industrial e separação da Axiom A Flex afirmou que está desenvolvendo ativamente soluções modulares pré-fabricadas para hiperescaladores em suas unidades em todo o mundo, com o apoio de mais de três milhões de pés quadrados de capacidade dedicada à fabricação de infraestrutura de data centers nos Estados Unidos. Em conexão com a separação proposta, Flex apresentou à Comissão de Valores Mobiliários dos Estados Unidos (SEC), em 5 de outubro de 2026, uma declaração de procuração no formulário Schedule 14A. A declaração de procuração foi enviada ou divulgada por outros meios aos acionistas para solicitar sua aprovação das propostas relacionadas à cisão. A declaração de registro da Axiom no formulário Form 10, referente às suas ações ordinárias, foi apresentada à SEC em 15 de setembro de 2026. Em um comunicado separado, de 5 de outubro de 2026, a Flex informou que havia firmado um acordo para vender US$ 2,0 bilhões em ações preferenciais conversíveis Série A da Axiom a fundos afiliados à General Catalyst e à Koch Equity Development, além de coinvestidores, com um valor empresarial inicial de US$ 37,5 bilhões para a Axiom. Revathi Advaithi, CEO da Flex e futura CEO da Axiom, afirmou que o investimento “fornece financiamento por meio de capital próprio para nossa aquisição da EPC Power, anunciada recentemente, e permitirá que a Axiom tenha um balanço sólido enquanto nos preparamos para nos estabelecer como uma empresa independente de capital aberto”. As ações preferenciais conversíveis pagam dividendos em dinheiro de 10,0% ao ano antes da separação. Depois dela, a taxa cai para 6,0% ao ano se pagos em dinheiro ou 7,0% ao ano se pagos na forma de dividendos não pecuniários, sujeita a aumentos após o quinto aniversário da separação e a certos outros ajustes. A General Catalyst terá o direito de indicar um diretor para o conselho da Axiom após a conclusão da separaç

artigo.texto: - The BRICS Business Council has proposed a voluntary carbon market framework for agriculture and nature-based solutions, with farmers positioned to receive most credit-sale proceeds. - The plan calls for shared carbon accounting standards, digital monitoring and links to existing international carbon registries. - Projects in India involving rice cultivation and soil carbon illustrate how carbon-credit revenue could support more sustainable farming practices. Intergovernmental organization BRICS, bringing together eleven major emerging markets and developing countries of the world, has proposed a framework for agricultural carbon credits intended to channel climate finance directly to farmers while expanding the supply of nature-based credits available to corporate buyers. The proposal was presented by the bloc’s Agribusiness Working Group at the BRICS Business Council’s annual meeting in New Delhi, as reported by India’s The Economic Times. The council included the recommendations in its annual report, which was submitted to BRICS leaders at the closing ceremony of the group’s 18th summit. In addition to the five original member states, namely Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa, six new members have joined in recent years: Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The proposed BRICS voluntary carbon market would cover agriculture and nature-based solutions. It would remain open to domestic and international buyers and connect with established voluntary carbon registries, rather than operate as a separate system. The framework also calls for a common carbon classification system across member countries, allowing carbon sequestered through farming practices to be measured and credited on comparable terms. A shared digital platform for monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV) would aim to reduce the costs that have made carbon markets difficult for smallholder farmers to access. Indian Projects Offer A Potential Model Under the proposal, farmers, farmer organizations and Indigenous communities would be the primary beneficiaries, receiving most proceeds from credit sales. Companies seeking to address emissions and financial institutions developing green portfolios would provide buyer demand, while governments could use the system to support national climate commitments and attract green finance. Existing projects in India offer examples of how the approach could work. Google has agreed to buy 1 million credits over four years from Bengaluru-based Mitti Labs, supporting changes in irrigation practices among more than 70,000 smallholder rice farmers across three states. The project aims to cut methane emissions by about half and water use by nearly 40%. Relevant: Google To Buy 1M Rice Methane Carbon Credits From India’s Mitti Labs The proposal’s wider ambitions face a practical challenge: making carbon measurement and verification affordable across fragmented agricultural landholdings. Pilot projects between BRICS members are intended to test compatibility between systems before broader implementation. The framework’s success will depend on whether credit revenue reaches farmers promptly while maintaining credible verification and affordable participation. artigo.texto: Chinese battery manufacturer Contemporary Amperex Technology Company Limited (CATL) announced that it has signed a new long-term strategic cooperation agreement with local automaker Seres Group, strengthening their existing long-term partnership. CATL confirmed that since Seres launched the Aito brand, all Aito models have been equipped with CATL batteries, with cumulative deliveries exceeding 1.2 million units to date. The two companies have now agreed to deepen strategic collaboration across three key areas: Production Capacity Expansion: the two companies plan to accelerate the implementation of Phase 2 of the 'Plant in Plant' project at Seres' manufacturing hub in Chongqing, which involves adding 10–12 GWh of annual battery production capacity, bringing total battery production capacity to over 20 GWh. Supercharging and Energy Replenishment Ecosystem: CATL and Seres will focus on expanding supercharging networks and battery services, creating a full-lifecycle service system to further enhance the user experience. Global Market Development: the two companies also plan to work together to explore overseas markets, including in Europe, the Middle East and Central Asia, bringing "high-quality products and services" to more global customers and supporting the transition to intelligent electric mobility in key markets. "CATL, Seres strengthen their long-term battery partnership" was originally created and published by Just Auto, a GlobalData owned brand.

artigo.texto: AI data centers got the "Weekend Update" treatment on "Saturday Night Live" this week. Comedian James Austin Johnson portrayed "Shark Tank" investor Kevin O'Leary on the sketch comedy show, during which he addressed the dispute over the real O'Leary's proposed data center in Utah, known as the Stratos Project. "It's very simple. All I want is to buy up 40,000 acres of God's untouched splendor and replace it with a very loud computer that steals your job," Johnson's O'Leary said. "Is it going to take up precious water? Absolutely. Is it going to provide a necessary service? Who's to say? But on the flip side, it's going to make me a tremendous amount of money, and I think that's great." The "SNL" version of O'Leary said he understood that some Americans were concerned about data centers near their homes. (An actual May Gallup poll found that over half of American surveyors opposed constructing AI data centers in their local area.) "These things are terrible and shouldn't be anywhere. That's why I'm building one in Utah," he said. Data centers are a contentious issue in the United States. Leading tech companies rely on AI data centers to power their systems and products. Supporters say they'll create new jobs, bolster the economy, and help the US defeat China in the race to control the global AI market. Residents in the places where they are being built, however, are often much less excited about them. The Utah project, backed by O'Leary Digital, has drawn criticism from many local residents over concerns that the data center could strain local resources and worsen the environment. Some residents are also upset over what they consider a lack of transparency from O'Leary and local leaders. Critics of the Stratos Project have staged protests, created petitions, and taken legal action to stop its construction. O'Leary scaled back the data center's size from about 40,000 to just over 20,000 acres after public pushback. He has said he remains undeterred, though. "There are bumps in the road. There's litigation. There's misinformation. There's propaganda. You name it. But if you know what you're doing is right, you make it, you get there," O'Leary told Business Insider in June. "Persevere." During a May interview on Fox News, O'Leary said said some critics of the project have ties to the Chinese Communist Party, a claim he later walked back. A Utah advocacy group that has publicly opposed the project filed a defamation lawsuit against Fox News and O'Leary in July. On "Saturday Night Live," Johnson's O'Leary acknowledged the incident. "I made the mildly inflammatory claim that every single person in Utah who opposes me is a paid communist super agent from China. Was I wrong? Perhaps. But just because they're not, doesn't mean they aren't," he said. He added, "I'm going to make the future go away. And we're doing just that in Utah."

artigo.texto: Seres Group has signed a long-term strategic agreement with Contemporary Amperex Technology (CATL) in Chongqing, securing CATL battery supply for every AITO model in its line-up. Concluded on 10 October 2026, the pact also enlarges their shared battery production and adds joint work on supercharging, battery services and overseas markets. AITO, the premium brand Seres develops with Huawei, has used CATL packs in every model since launch, with deliveries now past 1.2 million vehicles. Extending that arrangement across the full range gives Seres supply certainty and hands CATL a customer with proven volume. Production is the most concrete strand. The partners will fast-track phase two of their plant-in-plant facility inside the Seres Super Factory, adding 10 to 12 GW/h a year for a combined total above 20 GW/h. Building batteries inside the vehicle plant is meant to sharpen cost competitiveness, and the expansion also supports Chongqing’s drive to build a cluster of intelligent connected electric vehicle makers. Beyond the factory, the companies plan supercharging networks and battery services that follow a car through its whole life. They will also seek buyers together in the Middle East, Central Asia and Europe, a spread that gives AITO growth options outside the EU, where China-built electric cars face extra import duties. Source: CATL

artigo.texto: Priorizar a melhoria do quadro institucional e garantir o funcionamento eficaz da bolsa de carbono. Para garantir a implementação eficaz de tarefas essenciais relacionadas às mudanças climáticas, o Vice-Ministro da Agricultura e do Meio Ambiente, Le Trong Yen, solicitou ao Departamento de Mudanças Climáticas que priorize a conclusão do projeto de lei que altera e complementa diversos artigos da Lei de Proteção Ambiental, bem como os projetos de decretos e circulares que orientam sua implementação. Ao mesmo tempo, ele instou à aceleração da pesquisa e do desenvolvimento da Lei de Mudanças Climáticas. Com relação ao mercado de carbono, o Vice-Ministro orientou a implementação da Conclusão nº 71-KL/TW, de 17 de julho de 2026, do Comitê Central do Partido, sobre a gestão e o uso de créditos de carbono para servir ao desenvolvimento socioeconômico sustentável e garantir a segurança nacional, em um espírito de estreita ligação com a prática, criando uma fonte de bens e um mecanismo de negociação transparente para que a troca opere de forma eficaz, trazendo benefícios práticos para as pessoas e as empresas. Ele também orientou a aceleração da conclusão do banco de dados nacional sobre mudanças climáticas, conectando-o ao Centro Nacional de Dados do Ministério da Segurança Pública , para servir efetivamente à gestão, operação e exploração de recursos pela sociedade. Ao mesmo tempo, o Departamento está preparando meticulosamente cenários para a participação em negociações internacionais na próxima conferência COP 31, visando afirmar a posição do Vietnã e suas contribuições responsáveis no cenário internacional. Segundo o Diretor do Departamento de Mudanças Climáticas, Nguyen Tuan Quang, nos últimos três meses de 2026, o Departamento concentrará todos os recursos na conclusão do sistema de documentos legais imediatamente após a aprovação da proposta de emenda à Lei de Proteção Ambiental pela Assembleia Nacional; na implementação da Conclusão nº 71-KL/TW, de 17 de julho de 2026, sobre a gestão e o uso de créditos de carbono para servir ao desenvolvimento socioeconômico sustentável e garantir a segurança nacional, e da Conclusão nº 75-KL/TW, de 28 de julho de 2026, do 3º Plenário do 14º Comitê Central do Partido Comunista do Vietnã sobre proteção ambiental e resposta proativa às mudanças climáticas na nova era; na aceleração da reforma dos procedimentos administrativos e na continuidade da coordenação da operação da bolsa de carbono; na organização da reunião do Comitê Conjunto Vietnã-Japão em outubro; na preparação meticulosa da delegação internacional e na modernização da infraestrutura do Banco de Dados Nacional de Mudanças Climáticas. Você também pode gostar Olhando para o futuro, até 2030, a unidade definiu como foco continuar a aprimorar o quadro político, pesquisando proativamente e preparando uma proposta para a Lei de Mudanças Climáticas, com um plano para submetê-la à Assembleia Nacional em 2029. Nos primeiros nove meses de 2026, o Departamento prestou consultoria proativa e concluiu diversas tarefas essenciais, conforme diretrizes do Comitê Central, do Governo e da liderança do Ministério. Entre elas, o Departamento liderou o desenvolvimento do plano de gestão e utilização de créditos de carbono, que serviu de base para a publicação da Conclusão nº 71-KL/TW pela Secretaria. Simultaneamente, o Departamento colaborou com o Ministério do Meio Ambiente na elaboração da Conclusão nº 75-KL/TW, de 28 de julho de 2026, do Comitê Central do Partido Comunista do Vietnã, sobre proteção ambiental e adaptação proativa às mudanças climáticas na nova era; e concluiu e submeteu para publicação o Programa de Ação Governamental completo e o Programa de Ação do Ministério para a implementação dessa conclusão. O Departamento coordenou-se estreitamente com o Departamento do Meio Ambiente para finalizar o projeto de lei que altera e complementa diversos artigos da Lei de Proteção Ambiental, para que o Governo o apresente à Comissão Permanente da Assembleia Nacional. O projeto encontra-se atualmente em fase de revisão técnica para garantir sua apresentação em tempo hábil à Assembleia Nacional, para apreciação e aprovação na sessão de outubro. O progresso na elaboração de documentos políticos e legais, de acordo com o programa de trabalho de 2026, está dentro do cronograma, sem atrasos em nenhum documento. De agora até o final do ano, o Departamento continuará a desenvolver um Decreto e uma Circular em paralelo com o projeto de alteração e complementação de diversos artigos da Lei de Proteção Ambiental, visando garantir a coerência do sistema jurídico. O Departamento recomendou ao Ministério que submeta ao Governo uma Resolução aprovando o Acordo de Implementação do Artigo 6º do Acordo de Paris entre o Governo do Vietname e o Governo de Singapura. Atualmente, o Governo aprovou acordos bilaterais de troca de créditos de carbono com Singapura e o Japão; relativamente à Coreia do Sul e à Suíça , o Departamento está a promover negociações técnicas, prevendo-se a assinatura até ao final do ano. Você também pode gostar Em relação aos inventários de gases de efeito estufa, o Departamento mantém inventários em nível nacional, organiza sessões de treinamento para orientar empresas no cálculo e na redução de emissões e está estabelecendo um sistema online de relatórios de inventário para reduzir custos e melhorar a transparência dos dados. Além disso, o Departamento está finalizando um plano para preparar a participação da delegação vietnamita em importantes conferências internacionais sobre o clima ainda este ano.

artigo.texto: Wood Mackenzie: Four-Hour Battery Storage Beats Gas Peaking on Cost Across 43 modeled markets, four-hour battery storage costs less than open-cycle gas turbines. Wood Mackenzie details cost trajectories for solar, wind and storage by region. Wood Mackenzie says its latest global report on levelized cost of electricity (LCOE) shows four-hour battery storage is cheaper than open-cycle gas turbines in all 43 markets where both technologies were modeled. According to the firm, gas turbine shortages and fuel volatility are raising peaking costs, while expanding battery manufacturing is pushing storage costs down. On the financing side, Lydian Energy and Infranity closed a $300 million credit facility for energy storage. The report covers Europe, North America, Latin America, Asia Pacific, the Middle East and Africa. Middle East, Africa and China lead on costs In the Middle East and Africa, utility-scale solar already stands at an LCOE of $37/MWh. The cost of four-hour storage is forecast to fall a further 33% to $80/MWh by 2035, which would place it ahead of gas peaking in every gas market in the region. China remains the global benchmark, with storage costs more than 55% below the Asia Pacific average excluding China. "This economic shift is decisive and widening," said Ahmed Jameel Abdullah, principal analyst at Wood Mackenzie. He said gas turbine shortages and rising fuel volatility are driving up peaking costs, while expanding battery manufacturing continues to push storage costs down. He noted that a similar transformation has already reshaped baseload economics. Company Wood Mackenzie: company profile Solar dominates baseload generation According to the report, single-axis tracker solar is the lowest-cost new-build technology in 43 of the 48 modeled markets, with onshore wind leading in five. In Saudi Arabia and the UAE, the most competitive markets, solar LCOE is on track to fall below $20/MWh by 2033. In Latin America, solar PV with single-axis tracking remains the lowest-cost generation technology in 2026, with average costs expected to fall 38% by 2060. Brazil, Chile and Mexico hold a structural advantage tied to their solar resources and high capacity factors. The regional average onshore wind LCOE is expected to fall nearly 21% by 2030, from $73/MWh to $58/MWh, as Chinese manufacturers intensify price competition and larger turbines lift yields. Grid-scale storage LCOE is forecast to fall 42% by 2060, and offshore wind would approach combined-cycle gas turbine parity only in the early 2040s. Asia Pacific: sharp regional gaps In Asia Pacific, utility-scale solar remains the most cost-competitive source, but regional disparities are stark. In 2026, solar generation in the highest-cost market is more than 200% more expensive than in the lowest, a gap expected to widen to 250% by 2030. Onshore wind costs range more than six times between the cheapest and most costly markets in the region. China posts a benchmark grid-scale storage LCOE more than 55% below the rest of Asia Pacific average of $134/MWh. That average is expected to fall to $92/MWh by 2036, but Japan, Australia and the Philippines would remain at a premium because of import duties, elevated installation costs and domestic manufacturing policies. artigo.texto: To keep up with artificial intelligence, Illinois needs batteries big enough to keep its air conditioners running on hot summer nights and to replenish its electrical grid during winter storms lasting for days. The state took a step in this direction Monday when Richardson Electronics said it would expand production of commercial-scale storage batteries at its factory in La Fox, a suburb west of Chicago. Richardson, a diversified manufacturer of power products, expects to sell batteries worldwide. But company officials say they’ll deploy many of their batteries in Illinois because of the state’s hefty tax incentives for renewable power and for batteries that make solar and wind less intermittent. When layered on top of each other, Illinois and federal tax incentives add up to almost the entire cost of one of Richardson’s storage batteries, said Scott DuBois, director of the company’s storage operations. The battery, which the company plans to build at its La Fox site next summer, would be able to store 5 megawatts of power and will cost about $3 million. It will be the largest battery ever connected to the grid by an Illinois company, Richardson officials said. Without more batteries, Illinois will be even more reliant on dirty, expensive electricity imports from other states and more likely to delay the natural gas power plant closures it’s planned for years to clean the air. “We are depending on out-of-state resources to essentially keep the lights on,” said Matthew Tomc, vice president of regulatory policy and energy supply for Ameren, which serves customers in downstate Illinois. “There are many states building new generation, but it’s not built yet. So there are reliability issues first and foremost,” Tomc said. “And it raises the risk that you have price spikes seasonally, namely in the summer, right when you’re trying to meet those capacity requirements.” Tomc’s not alone in sounding the alarm. PJM Interconnection, the regional grid that includes northern Illinois, 12 other states and the District of Columbia, could face 13 days of service interruptions a year by 2030 in a worst-case scenario, Pennsylvania regulators said last month. PJM’s longstanding goal has been to have just one day of service interruptions every 10 years. Prices already are climbing. Commonwealth Edison customers in northern Illinois pay an average residential bill of $141 per month, according to Heatmap News and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. That’s up just 4% since 2021, partly because PJM imposed price caps last year. Ameren customers downstate pay an average of $224, up 51% in five years. The downstate area is part of the Midwest Independent System Operator grid or MISO, which also serves 14 other states from Mississippi to North Dakota as well as Manitoba. To blunt further increases, Richardson and its supplier Gotion, a Chinese-owned company with a $2 billion factory in Manteno, Illinois, start with 4,500 battery cells, each about the size of a college textbook. For their biggest batteries, they will then stack, weld and seal the battery cells, cooling equipment and electronic controls inside a metal box resembling a 20-foot shipping container. DuBois wouldn’t give a precise estimate for how big Richardson’s battery business will get. But he said he expects exponential growth. Gil Quinones, ComEd’s chief executive, is thinking big, too. “If the majority of our residential, commercial and industrial customers put in batteries, that’s going to be a big win for the state,” Quinones said. “It could increase the capacity utilization for the grid we’ve already paid for, and have a chance to really put downward pressure on prices for everybody,” Quinones said. Because Richardson sees itself as an engineering specialist rather than a high-volume manufacturer, it will focus on customized storage systems for so-called microgrids. These are clusters of solar and wind operators that can either supply electricity directly to nearby users or buy and sell power as a group into the regional grid. One of the company’s first orders, for example, came from a microgrid serving seven remote communities in Alaska. Illinois needs more batteries to unlock the full potential of its growing wind and solar capabilities, according to consultants to the Illinois Power Agency and other state regulators in a report last month. Illinois will need 50 gigawatts of installed solar and wind capacity by 2050 to get close to its goal of using only non-carbon sources to generate electricity by then, the agencies said. But regional grid operators still regard wind and solar as too intermittent. As a result, the state will be able to count only about 6 gigawatts of its renewable output as the baseload power electricity grids need to operate around the clock. With additional batteries, Illinois could make its solar panels more productive and reliable by, for example, storing the power they generate during the day and then pumping it into the grid or nearby homes and businesses after the sun goes down. In addition to more batteries, the Ameren service area downstate will need 9 gigawatts of out-of-state imports by 2045, according to the Sept. 24 consultant report to the IPA. That’s more than half the Ameren area’s total requirement of 16 gigawatts of round-the-clock power in 2045. The ComEd service area will need 4 gigawatts of out-of-state imports, or about 13% of its baseload requirement. The imports will include power produced by new natural gas plants that Illinois ratepayers will help build in other states. Illinois can’t build these plants because of the state’s clean air rules. (NYSE American: GPUS), an artificial intelligence ("AI") data center company ("Hyperscale Data" or the "Company"), today announced that it has amended the At-the-Market ("ATM") Issuance Sales Agreement (the "Agreement"), dated June 18, 2026, by and between the Company and Spartan Capital Securities, LLC, as sales agent (the "Agent"), reducing the aggregate amount that may be sold pursuant to the Agreement from Three Hundred Million Dollars ($300,000,000) in shares of the Company's Class A common stock, par value $0.001 per share (the "Common Stock") to One Hundred Million Dollars ($100,000,000), including the shares of Common Stock that have been sold pursuant to the Agreement through an amendment to the Agreement (the "Amendment"). The Company has sold 121,827,841 shares of Common Stock and raised approximately $49.8 million in gross proceeds, or approximately $0.41 per share, pursuant to the ATM. "Based on our current capital plans, we do not believe the additional $200 million of ATM capacity is currently necessary," said Will Horne, Chief Executive Officer of Hyperscale Data. "Reducing the size of the ATM reflects our commitment to disciplined capital management while preserving financial flexibility to support our AI data center strategy. We believe that our equity is significantly undervalued and this $200 million reduction will limit the dilution to our equity and is in the best interests of our stockholders. Our focus remains on deploying capital prudently and building long-term value through the buildout of our Michigan AI data center (the "Facility") to initially support the 20 megawatts of critical compute capacity of our neocloud customer. It is our intention to augment the Facility buildout costs with debt financing and preliminary estimates on the existing buildout indicate that the Facility will support project debt financing between $100 million to $150 million." The Company may evaluate capital markets options in the future as appropriate and in the best interests of the Company and its stockholders. This press release shall not constitute an offer to sell or the solicitation of an offer to buy, nor shall there be any sale of shares of the Common Stock in any state or other jurisdiction in which such offer, solicitation or sale would be unlawful prior to registration or qualification under the securities laws of any such state or other jurisdiction. For more information on Hyperscale Data and its subsidiaries, Hyperscale Data recommends that stockholders, investors and any other interested parties read Hyperscale Data's public filings and press releases available under the Investor Relations section at hyperscaledata.com or available at www.sec.gov. In addition, ACG is actively engaged in private credit and structured finance through Ault Lending, LLC, a licensed lending subsidiary. Hyperscale Data's headquarters are located at 11411 Southern Highlands Parkway, Suite 190, Las Vegas, NV 89141. artigo.texto: From pressures facing Iowa farmers to the costs of major industrial projects, Iowa’s U.S. Senate candidates outlined their priorities and challenged each other’s records in their second and last debate Tuesday night. Iowa Rep. Josh Turek, D-Council Bluffs, and U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson, R-Iowa, faced off in their second debate for U.S. Senate hosted by WHO-13 in Des Moines. The candidates continued to highlight hot button issues, discussing the importance of agriculture and economic developments throughout the state. The debate also covered immigration enforcement, rural healthcare, and Social Security with the candidates offering differing approaches to border security, access to care, and retirement benefits. Questions about transgender athletes in women’s sports and congressional stock ownership prompted further exchanges, alongside criticism of each other’s voting records and personal finances. On agriculture and economic development, the candidates debated how to expand markets for Iowa farmers and attract investment while protecting taxpayers from the costs and risks of major projects. Agriculture continues to be a top priority The candidates offered differing views on tariffs and farmland ownership, with both emphasizing the need to support Iowa farmers. Turek criticized the administration’s tariffs and said they have hurt farmers by limiting markets and increasing costs. He supports targeted tariffs to protect American manufacturing but opposed those he said burden agriculture and small businesses. “Our farmers rely on open markets and free trade more than any other group,” he said. He also called for year-round E-15 sales, mandatory out-of-origin labeling, and a federal right-to-repair law allowing farmers to repair their equipment. He urged Congress to pass a farm bill before adjourning. Hinson defended tariffs as a tool to counter unfair trade practices while acknowledging farmers’ uncertainty. She said she has raised their concerns directly with President Donald Trump and pointed to agricultural exports and trade negotiations as signs of progress. “Nobody loves tariffs, but what I like even less is an unlevel playing field for Americans and for our farmers,” she said. Hinson emphasized preventing foreign adversaries from purchasing agricultural land, particularly near sensitive military sites. Turek agreed restrictions on foreign ownership were important but said large corporations posed the greater concern, pointing to pressures facing small family farms. Data centers, industrial projects raise economic questions Both candidates opposed a federal moratorium on new data centers but differed on how to oversee the projects and who should pay for the infrastructure needed to support them. Turek demanded no further tax breaks for multinational tech firms and suggested requiring closed-loop water circuits that reuse water to reduce data centers’ consumption of local water supplies. “We should be doing what we can to protect Iowa and to protect the tax rates here,” he said. He opposed using taxpayer funds for the reopening of the Duane Arnold nuclear plant — a facility near Palo, northwest of Cedar Rapids, that shut down in 2020 — if most energy is diverted to Google. Hinson, on the other hand, maintained that data center regulation should occur at the local level rather than through a federal moratorium and supports reopening Duane Arnold to help meet rising electricity demand. “It is really critical that we have enough energy production in this country to handle the necessary needs of whether it’s a data center or another big energy consumer,” she said. “We want to reinvigorate American manufacturing in this country.” Questions about taxpayer protections extended to the proposed steel plant in southeast Iowa, with both candidates saying Iowans should not bear infrastructure costs if the project falls through. Turek said he supported the $15 billion Masabi Metallics steel plant’s job potential but questions the risks associated with a $770 million federal loan given the company’s history of bankruptcy. He argued companies should cover their own infrastructure. “There’s no upfront state money,” he said. “The incentives are only there if they provide the actual jobs and metrics achieved.” Hinson said she views the plant as critical for national security and the domestic steel supply chain, though she agrees taxpayers should not be held liable if the project fails or is scaled back. “We need definite accountability measures built in,” Hinson said. “And I think what’s important about the policies we’ve put into place is that they are going to supercharge potential future investments just like this one.”

artigo.texto: LOGAN, Utah — Before a crowd here at Utah State University on Tuesday night, Republican Congressman Blake Moore and Democratic challenger Peter Crosby debated a number of big issues facing the newly-formed Second Congressional District. It was a collegial, policy-focused debate where they presented their views for northern Utah. Both were quizzed on data centers, a particularly hot topic in the district, where celebrity investor Kevin O'Leary's plans for a massive data center have sparked significant public protest. Both candidates agreed local control is best. "Data centers are a part of our immediate future, right? There's no question. We're all using cellphones. We're all, you know, doing some type of AI utilization and whatnot, but the issue is, we cannot have this kind of situation take over the way that it did and that people have to be brought along," Moore said, pointing to what was being done on a congressional level. "There's good, strong legislation that should have passed in the Senate, but it didn't, to make sure electricity costs don't go up for residents and the Department of Defense is doing a unique thing where they're going to start to use more of their resources and their land in a more productive way, which is a good change that's happening." Crosby said he had been involved in some of the pushback on data centers. "I think as we talk about the future of data centers in Utah specifically, we have to acknowledge that local control is oftentimes being ignored because external pressure coming from the top down is forcing a decision against the will of local residents," he said. "That's inappropriate. I am all for a future where local communities decide whether or not that kind of infrastructure is appropriate for them, and what we have seen in Box Elder is a direct counter to that reality." The two expressed a desire to save the Great Salt Lake, but offered differing viewpoints on water policy. "I don't want the federal government making water policy for the state of Utah," declared Crosby. "I think that's a bad road to head down. The state of Utah has to decide: Are we a state that grows to 10 million people? Are we a state that decides to fully invest in Silicon Slopes? Are we a state that decides to maintain local resiliency in agriculture? We can't have all three." But Moore said he has already been passing legislation to help the lake, though he acknowledged President Trump's pledge of a billion dollars for the lake is unlikely to get through Congress. "We were able to do bite-size projects to help funding the support from different elements of the of the lake that the state is actually leading a lot of the effort and then of course you're seeing the White House now get involved, so it's nice to be able to see a throughput," he said. Crosby was critical of Moore's votes on President Trump's Big, Beautiful Bill. Moore defended his work to mitigate tariffs, even noting that he had removed some of the harsher impacts on a major northern Utah employer. "There is a lot of pain with this and every time that Procter and Gamble has reached out to our office, we've gone and actually successfully been able to mitigate their issues," Moore said. "If I may say, Procter and Gamble, that's great, but none of the small business owners seem to receive the same attention," Crosby countered in a rebuttal. But the candidates both pledged ongoing support for Hill Air Force Base and bolstering northern Utah's aerospace industry. They also supported agriculture, a major industry in the area. The poll commissioned by the Utah Debate Commission that put the two men on stage on Tuesday night shows a closer race than some might like. Voters surveyed had Moore in the lead at 39%, with Crosby close behind at 34%. Nearly 11% of voters remained undecided and third-party candidates took the rest. Speaking to FOX 13 News after the debate, Moore believed voters would stick with him. "We’re confident where we are, we’re going to continue to drive the message home and I look forward to the opportunity to continue on the things I've been working on," he said. Crosby told FOX 13 News after the debate he and volunteers for his campaign would be out engaging voters. artigo.texto: O Sindicato dos Trabalhadores da Construção Civil do Vietnã promove a transformação verde e a redução das emissões. Aumentar a conscientização sobre a redução de emissões, promover práticas ecológicas e o uso eficiente de recursos são tarefas essenciais realizadas pelo Sindicato dos Trabalhadores da Construção Civil do Vietnã para contribuir com o alcance dos objetivos de desenvolvimento sustentável. Integrar a transformação verde nas atividades sindicais. O Sindicato dos Trabalhadores da Construção Civil do Vietnã (VCPTU) desenvolveu recentemente um plano para organizar campanhas de conscientização, treinamentos e workshops com o objetivo de aprimorar o entendimento de dirigentes, membros e trabalhadores do sindicato em relação à redução de emissões, à transição verde e ao desenvolvimento econômico de baixo carbono. O plano visa fortalecer o papel dos sindicatos na promoção de práticas sustentáveis, utilização eficiente de recursos e proteção ambiental, garantindo, ao mesmo tempo, os direitos e interesses dos trabalhadores durante o período de transição. De acordo com as diretrizes do Sindicato dos Trabalhadores da Construção Civil do Vietnã, os sindicatos filiados integrarão a disseminação de informações sobre créditos de carbono, práticas de economia de energia, uso eficiente de recursos e redução de emissões em suas atividades sindicais, adequadas às suas condições específicas. Além disso, promoverão a reutilização, a reciclagem e a redução de resíduos, e incentivarão a aplicação de soluções sustentáveis e ecologicamente corretas para a produção, os negócios e o consumo. Por meio dessas atividades, o Sindicato contribui para a formação de um estilo de vida sustentável, promovendo a produção verde e o consumo de baixo carbono, protegendo o meio ambiente e adaptando-se às mudanças climáticas. A Confederação Vietnamita de Sindicatos (CĐXDVN) também orienta todos os níveis de sindicatos a participarem proativamente, contribuindo com ideias para a construção e o aprimoramento de mecanismos, políticas, leis , programas e projetos relacionados à redução das emissões de gases de efeito estufa, inventários de gases de efeito estufa, desenvolvimento de mercados de carbono, gestão de créditos de carbono, transição verde e proteção da camada de ozônio. Dá-se ênfase ao conteúdo diretamente relacionado aos trabalhadores, contribuindo assim para o aumento da competitividade nacional, a integração proativa na comunidade internacional e a conquista dos objetivos de desenvolvimento verde e sustentável. Você também pode gostar Além disso, o incentivo à participação de entidades econômicas, empresas e trabalhadores na criação, negociação e utilização de créditos de carbono baseia-se em princípios de mercado, transparência, concorrência leal e eficiência. Os créditos de carbono são reconhecidos como uma força motriz para a inovação tecnológica, a melhoria da eficiência energética e de recursos e a promoção do desenvolvimento sustentável. Na promoção da transição verde e da redução das emissões, o Sindicato dos Trabalhadores da Construção Civil do Vietnã enfatiza o papel do sindicato no monitoramento da implementação das diretrizes do Partido, das políticas e leis estatais nessas áreas, bem como no desenvolvimento do mercado de carbono e na garantia da transparência em sua implementação. O monitoramento também se concentra na implementação de políticas e programas que apoiam a transformação tecnológica, a economia de energia, a produção mais limpa e políticas relacionadas. Por meio disso, os sindicatos em todos os níveis compilam e relatam prontamente as questões emergentes, especialmente o impacto da transição verde e da redução de emissões no emprego, na renda, nas condições de trabalho, na segurança e saúde ocupacional e nos direitos e interesses dos trabalhadores. É dada especial atenção aos grupos de trabalhadores que correm o risco de serem afetados pela transição, a fim de abordar prontamente as questões relacionadas aos direitos dos trabalhadores e às condições de trabalho. Paralelamente às suas atividades de monitoramento, o Sindicato dos Trabalhadores da Construção Civil do Vietnã visa integrar a redução de emissões, a utilização eficiente de recursos, a conservação de energia, a economia circular e a adaptação às mudanças climáticas ao movimento "Verde - Limpo - Bonito, Garantindo a Segurança e Saúde Ocupacional" e a outros movimentos de emulação relevantes. Com base nas condições reais, os sindicatos em todos os níveis, unidades e empresas incentivam seus membros e trabalhadores a propor e implementar iniciativas e modelos para economia de energia, uso eficiente de recursos, redução de emissões e proteção ambiental. Essas iniciativas devem estar vinculadas ao objetivo de melhorar as condições de trabalho, prevenir acidentes e riscos e construir uma cultura de segurança no local de trabalho. Identificar, elogiar e replicar iniciativas e modelos práticos e eficazes que sejam adequados às condições de produção e negócios das empresas e às atividades sindicais também recebe atenção, a fim de incentivar soluções com aplicação prática. Além de promover e incentivar práticas sustentáveis, o Sindicato dos Trabalhadores da Construção Civil do Vietnã concentra-se em aprimorar as habilidades de seus dirigentes em diálogo e negociação coletiva. O sindicato também incentiva a inclusão de critérios para a construção de uma cultura de segurança no trabalho na avaliação da qualidade dos acordos coletivos de trabalho, utilizando-os como base para revisar e premiar órgãos, unidades e empresas com bom desempenho em segurança e higiene no trabalho. Outra tarefa é promover a aplicação da tecnologia da informação e da transformação digital na disseminação, gestão, monitoramento e avaliação da segurança e saúde ocupacional. artigo.texto: Flex Expands Prefabricated Modular Data Center Portfolio to Accelerate AI Factory Deployment Integrated solutions combine power, compute and cooling to speed deployment by up to 50% News summary - Introduces AI Modules that integrate power, compute and cooling in prefabricated modular solutions to accelerate AI factory deployment by up to 50% - Enables faster deployment of next-generation AI infrastructure through factory-built, integrated systems - Strengthens Flex's Cloud and Power Infrastructure portfolio, which Flex plans to separate into Axiom Solutions International, Inc. (Axiom), in the first quarter of calendar 2027 SAN JOSE, Calif. , Oct. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Flex (NASDAQ: FLEX) today announced an expanded portfolio of prefabricated modular data center solutions designed to accelerate deployment of next-generation AI factories. The portfolio includes new AI Modules that integrate power, high-density compute and advanced liquid cooling into pre-engineered, factory-built systems, enabling customers to reduce deployment timelines by up to 50% compared with traditional construction approaches. The expanded portfolio is part of Flex's Cloud and Power Infrastructure (CPI) segment, which Flex plans to separate into Axiom, an independent publicly traded company, in the first quarter of calendar 2027. "Meeting the demands of AI infrastructure at scale requires more than incremental improvements. It requires rethinking how power, compute and cooling work together as a system," said Chris Butler, expected Chief Technology and Strategy Officer at Axiom. "Our system-level approach brings these critical technologies together with advanced manufacturing to simplify integration, accelerate deployment and deliver AI factories at scale." As AI infrastructure grows in scale and power density, data center operators face increasing complexity across power delivery, cooling, compute integration and deployment. Addressing these challenges requires a more integrated approach to designing and deploying the critical infrastructure that supports next-generation AI factories. The Axiom AI Modules integrate critical AI infrastructure into pre-engineered, factory-built systems, including: - 800 VDC Power Rack: Delivers high-efficiency power conversion and distribution for next-generation 800 VDC AI infrastructure and high-density compute. - Advanced cooling distribution units (CDUs): Provide liquid cooling to efficiently manage the increasing heat generated by power-intensive AI workloads. - High-density IT racks: Integrate AI servers, networking and high-speed interconnects to support next-generation AI compute at scale. By shifting complex infrastructure integration from the data center site to a controlled factory environment, the Axiom AI Modules are assembled, integrated and tested in parallel with site development. This approach reduces on-site complexity and helps customers bring AI capacity online faster. Flex is actively building prefabricated modular solutions for hyperscalers across its global footprint, including more than three million square feet of dedicated data center infrastructure manufacturing capacity in the U.S. With deep expertise across power, compute, cooling and systems integration, Flex has the scale and capabilities to support rapid AI infrastructure deployment across regions. The four-hour system in Atacama will charge during lower-demand periods and discharge at peak times, supporting grid flexibility and project returns. On-Schedule Delivery Supports Project Execution Large-scale overseas projects require production, inspection, and shipment schedules to remain closely aligned with on-site construction. SINEXCEL completed the full PCS order on schedule, helping RelyEZ Energy protect the timetable for transport, installation, commissioning, and grid connection. For a project of this scale, delays in a single batch can narrow the construction window. Coordinated delivery reduces uncertainty and helps local teams plan the next stages. StellaON 1250K PCS Built for Atacama's Demanding Conditions Energy equipment in Atacama must operate in an environment that can include high temperatures, dust, and sand. The StellaON 1250K PCS has a maximum efficiency of 99% and a rated-power efficiency of 98.5%. It supports operation from -40°C to 60°C, maintains full power output at 55°C, and has an IP65 protection rating. Maintaining rated output in high temperatures can reduce power derating and the need for additional capacity. Higher conversion efficiency also limits energy losses across repeated charge-discharge cycles, supporting stable operation and long-term returns. Strengthening Local Service Capabilities Across the Americas Following shipment, the project will move into on-site installation and commissioning. SINEXCEL has a dedicated after-sales team in Latin America and seven service centres across the Americas. Technical requests can receive a response within 30 minutes, backed by round-the-clock support and a seven-day spare-parts guarantee. SINEXCEL has deployed more than 17GW of energy storage capacity across over 5,000 projects and works with more than 600 partners in 60+ countries and regions. Following shipment, the Chilean project moves into its on-site delivery phase. SINEXCEL will continue to expand its local operations across Latin America, providing customers with support throughout the project lifecycle. Our Data Center Info Hub features an interactive map, data center profiles, frequently asked questions, and a form to ask us your questions about data centers in your area. Data centers have become a central issue in Oklahoma’s midterm elections, with gubernatorial candidate Mike Mazzei (R) saying he supports them with guardrails, and Democratic nominee Cyndi Munson promising a day-one moratorium. Related Story: Mike Mazzei and Cyndi Munson share their stances on Oklahoma data center development Driven by affordable land, access to power, and growing demand for cloud and AI services, companies ranging from global tech giants to regional providers are expanding their presence in Oklahoma. According to the US Data Center Map, data as of Oct 2026. https://dcmap.us, Oklahoma has: - 64 data center projects overall - 34 operational data centers - 6 data centers under construction - 20 data centers planned - 2 paused data center projects - 2 inactive data centers Below is a running list of data center projects across the state. This article will be updated as new facilities are announced, approved, or completed. Claremore Project Mustang (Approved) Project Mustang is an approved data center development at the Claremore Industrial Park by Beale Infrastructure. Plans call for multiple data center buildings and office space, with power supplied by Grand River Dam Authority and water and wastewater services provided by the City of Claremore. City leaders say the property is already zoned for industrial use and that the developer would pay for required infrastructure upgrades. The Claremore City Council approved plans Monday, May 18, for “Project Mustang.” Claremore City Hall reached standing-room capacity during the meeting, with dozens of people waiting outside and rotating in to comply with fire code limits. Public comment lasted nearly two hours before the council voted on the proposal. Related Story: Claremore approves Project Mustang data center plan The agreement allows Beale Infrastructure to seek a 25-year ad valorem tax exemption for each phase of the project. Company representatives said the development would still contribute more than $250 million toward Rogers County schools, municipal services and community programs over time. Some residents have raised concerns about water usage, environmental impacts and transparency. City officials and the developer say the project would not raise taxes or utility rates and could bring long-term investment and jobs. Muskogee County Google Data Centers (Summit and Council Hill) (Early Development) Google plans to build two new data center campuses near Summit and Council Hill as part of a $9 billion investment in Oklahoma. The facilities are expected to support Google’s cloud and AI services, including Search, Maps and Google Cloud. Cerebras Systems operates a 10-megawatt data center in Oklahoma City in partnership with Scale Datacenters. The facility supports large-scale AI computing and uses a closed-loop, direct-to-chip liquid cooling system. artigo.texto: TI unveils new ADC to enable nanosecond-level telemetry and minimize downtime in AI data centers As AI workloads increase in volume and complexity, Texas Instruments is delivering the essential solutions needed to power, monitor and optimize AI data centers News highlights: - TI's ADC34DSO75 is the industry's highest performance 3 gigasamples per second ADC, enabling 24/7, low-power, event-based remote monitoring at nanosecond resolution – thousands of times faster than what current solutions offer. - The LMI800PS is the industry's first 800V isolated hot-swap controller, replacing a complex discrete solution requiring five integrated circuits with a single high-density package that delivers in-rush current and power path protection. - The LMK6B is a bulk acoustic wave-based oscillator that delivers best-in-class jitter performance and power-supply rejection ratio. SAN JOSE, Calif. , Oct. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- At the Open Compute Project (OCP) Global Summit, Texas Instruments (TI) (Nasdaq: TXN) debuted the first analog-to-digital converter (ADC) to enable 24/7, low-power, event-based remote monitoring at nanosecond resolution. As AI workloads rapidly increase, data center operators face significant challenges around power instability, inadequate real-time monitoring and signal degradation, all of which can lead to costly downtime. TI is addressing these challenges through its new ADC device and other analog solutions designed to tackle the challenges of scaling artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructures. Demonstrations on display in TI's booth, No. E45, at OCP include: - Real-time nanosecond-level telemetry: TI's ADC34DSO75 is the industry's highest performance 3 gigasamples per second (GSPS) ADC, enabling 24/7, low-power, event-based remote monitoring at nanosecond resolution – thousands of times faster than what current solutions offer. Existing monitoring solutions often fail to detect the nanosecond-level power-rail glitches that cause costly, unplanned downtime in data centers. By combining ultra-high-speed sampling with advanced on-chip digital signal processing in a small form factor, the ADC34DSO75 detects and captures transient fault events in real time. As the industry's first solution to offer fully remote, event-based telemetry, the device eliminates the need for on-site debugging and oscilloscopes. By providing continuous, high-resolution monitoring of low-voltage, high-current power rails, the ADC34DSO75 helps data centers minimize downtime – which can cost operators hundreds of thousands of dollars an hour – while optimizing grid power efficiency. This compact, efficient solution offers hyperscalers unmatched remote diagnostic capabilities at a fraction of the size and cost of conventional monitoring methods. - Reliable high-voltage power delivery: The LMI800PS is the industry's first 800V isolated hot-swap controller, replacing a complex discrete solution requiring five integrated circuits with a single high-density package that delivers in-rush current and power path protection. The integration of an isolated bias supply and PMBus telemetry reduces board area by more than 60% and simplifies high-voltage designs. The LMI800PS enables safe power insertion and fast fault isolation, meeting safety standards with 5kVrms reinforced isolation and more than 8mm creepage. This prevents a single load failure from disrupting the shared power bus and maximizes data center stability. Supporting both ±400V and 800V distributions, the device provides a scalable solution for diverse rack architectures, accelerating the deployment of high-efficiency power systems required for next-generation AI infrastructures. - Ultra-low jitter signal integrity: The LMK6B is a bulk acoustic wave (BAW)-based oscillator that delivers best-in-class jitter performance and power-supply rejection ratio (PSRR). As data center transmission rates approach 3.2Tbps, the margin for timing error shrinks significantly, and even minute jitter can increase bit error rates and cause system instability. The LMK6B provides industry-leading jitter performance of 9.6fs at 625MHz, ensuring reliable performance and preserving signal integrity for next-generation, AI-driven networking infrastructures. "As AI workloads drive massive scale, the need for real-time visibility and architectural stability has never been greater," said Karthik Vasanth, vice president and general manager for TI's Data, Converters and Clocks business unit. "By delivering industry-leading solutions for high-speed telemetry, advanced power protection and precision timing, TI is enabling hyperscalers and operators to design the next generation of AI data centers with optimized performance and minimal downtime." More details Also at OCP, TI Power Electronics Engineer David Reusch will present "800V Data Center DC/DC Design Considerations, Topology Comparisons and Trade-Offs," on Oct. 15 at 2:45 p.m. in room 230A. See ti.com/ocp for more information. For more information on the ADC34DSO75, read the technical article "The power glitches AI data centers can't see." About Texas Instruments Texas Instruments Incorporated (Nasdaq: TXN) is a global semiconductor company that designs, manufactures and sells analog and embedded processing chips for markets such as industrial, automotive, data center, personal electronics and communications equipment. At our core, we have a passion to create a better world by making electronics more affordable through semiconductors. This passion is alive today as each generation of innovation builds upon the last to make our technology more reliable, more affordable and lower power, making it possible for semiconductors to go into electronics everywhere. Learn more at TI.com. artigo.texto: Trending PANAMA -- Conversations surrounding Battery Energy Storage Systems have been held in the recent past in the village of Panama, and during their most recent meeting the village board dove more into the research behind the hazards associated with the systems. Originally, the village was meant to have someone who has done research on BESS as they appear around the county come to talk, but as that person could not make it, the village board looked at the research that was sent along to them at their October meeting. Mayor William Schneider said BESS are being seen more in the northern parts of the county, but it is anticipated that they will start to drift towards the areas around the village soon, so the village is looking to be prepared, especially with the increase in usage of solar farms. The man who sent the research to the village is a scientist and aerological engineer, who has worked with the town of Ripley on this subject as well, outlining some potential hazards with BESS. "One of the things that can create an issue is if they start a reaction and overload and start a fire," Schneider said. "These particular lithium ion thermal batteries, they call them runaway events, and what happens is they cannot be put out with water or foam and it basically has to burn until the modules in the container are consumed." The additional problem with that, Schneider said, is that there are several containers or modules that sit close by each other, so if one was to catch on fire the process could cause issues with the one sitting next to it and cause that one to catch on fire as well. Emergency responders then have to cool the existing ones that are not on fire until the first one burns out, and there is no time frame on how long that could take, needing to be done continuously and for many hours. "The problem is if the cooling issue were to stop somehow or be prolonged, the other units could start a chain reaction," Schneider said. Other potential issues about BESS that connect to the fire issue that were outlined for the village include the possibility of toxic runoff that could get into the groundwater and surrounding water ways, along with toxic gases that can come off as containers fail, meaning responders need full respiratory protection and that, Schneider said, would most likely mean the hazmat team would have to come in as well, and residents would likely have to be evacuated. Schneider also addressed liability concerns with the companies that come in and build the systems, with the liability then falling back on the municipalities and residents. "So this is something we're going to need to take a look at," Schneider said. "I've reached out to the town because I want to know what their language is on these systems, and then I'm also going to reach out to the lawyer to find out if the town has a particular law regarding these, do we have to reinvent it for the village or does that also cover us as we are inside the town itself. I know that can be a sticky point in certain circumstances, so I want to make sure we have all of our t's crossed and i's dotted." While nobody has asked about putting these systems in the village, Schneider said it is something the village needs to prepare for as they are not sure what will happen once nearby proposed solar farms are put in and functioning. It was noted that the village does not have to put in BESS, and the thought would be that the village would not due to the dangers. "Especially in a village that is one square mile and 450 residents and we have major waterways and most everybody's got groundwater, we don't have a public water system, these are all very high concerns," Schneider said. "I'm also very concerned as a retired emergency services and hazmat responder. It's dangerous for everybody all the way around." Schneider added that emergency services are not prepared for something like these systems either, citing similar potential dangers that come with fires in electric vehicles, though those are on a smaller scale. After talking with the town and lawyers, Schneider said the village could come back with a resolution against allowing BESS in the village, if that is the way everyone decides that they want to go. Conditional use permits or variances were also discussed, as technology has the ability to change years into the future. Having to deal with electric buses as the state continues to push for them was also brought up and noted that the village will have to deal with that at some point as well. "There's all of these little intricate things that we don't know enough about right now," Schneider said. "We need to see how some of this plays out. So, the safe thing would be to do this, cover the bases, and then as technology increases, gets better, safer, then the village can relook at the issue again." The village also briefly discussed upcoming fall related items, including Trick-or-Treat hours being from 5 p.m. to 7 p.m. on Halloween, and village leaf pickup being scheduled for November 4, with a rain date of November 5. Residents are also asked to bring their leaves out to the curbside for leaf pickup.

Set us as preferred California has always hidden the true price of progress somewhere beyond the horizon. The water arrives from a distant river. The electricity crosses a mountain range. By the time the benefits reach us, the damage has been assigned elsewhere. Now the future is arriving in windowless buildings. Data centers are rising from industrial corridors and farmland with the appetite of cities. They pull electricity by the hundreds of megawatts. Inside, servers build fortunes. Outside, residents open their utility bills and wonder what will remain. Before California approves another facility, every host community deserves an answer: What will this project make better here? Gov. Gavin Newsom recently signed seven laws that begin to make the hidden costs visible. Until those are in effect, a company could arrive with the appetite of a city and quietly leave its bill for wires and water with people who never asked for it. Now utility regulators must reckon with what it takes to serve that appetite. The rates and connection terms are meant to make new users shoulder their share of the grid and the electricity it must supply, instead of loading those costs onto a family studying its bill. Regulators must now make that promise real. The water, too, must come into the open. Data centers are water guzzlers, using huge volumes for cooling. Before construction, a developer must show where that water will come from, how the facility will fare in drought and who will pay for the new pipes. After the servers begin to hum, estimates must give way to actual water use. State planners will gain an account of energy consumption and efficiency. A town needs numbers it can see. And the project can no longer pass under a blanket environmental exemption. A quicker path through court is reserved for facilities that meet demanding conditions on clean power, water and protection of ratepayers. In California, speed must be earned. These laws draw a floor beneath the bargain. They do not guarantee that a neighborhood gains something lasting from the land, power and water it commits. California should establish a “community benefit standard” for every new data center and major expansion. Protect the resources of the place. Pay every cost the project creates. Then deliver a public benefit that residents can see, measure and enforce. The first requirements are obligations, not generosity. Developers must disclose projected electricity demand, water consumption, emissions, noise and infrastructure needs. That includes drought, extreme heat and nearby projects. Households cannot pay for capacity reserved by a corporation that may never use it. No company should receive applause for obeying environmental law. Efficient cooling is not a community gift when the machinery is necessary to run the servers. A research grant cannot excuse an unacceptable water plan. Public benefits cannot purchase permission to pollute a neighborhood or drain an aquifer. Only after those tests are met does the additional bargain begin. Each major project should fund at least one substantial technology program tied to an identified public need. Residents and public agencies would help choose the priority. California should measure what changes, not what gets announced. One developer might finance advanced water reuse with a local district beyond what is required to address its own demand. The compact would state how much freshwater demand must be eliminated, how savings will be verified and who will operate the system. Buying equipment would not count. Producing verified water savings would. Another facility might guarantee computing capacity to California hospitals and universities studying rare diseases, cancer or wildfire behavior. The agreement would specify secure access, support and computing hours, and bind the tenant. Researchers would receive usable capacity, not whatever remains after commercial customers finish. A third project could finance batteries and controls that keep a clinic, cooling center or water system operating during an outage. The equipment must serve the public in an emergency. Backup power reserved for company servers would not qualify. Every project must still provide a direct local benefit. A statewide research program may supplement that commitment, but it cannot replace it. The compact would name beneficiaries, funding, responsible parties, milestones and penalties for failure. Its duties would survive a sale or tenant change. Independent verification would report delivery, not spending. If one method underperforms, the agreements between data centers and communities should permit another. The obligation itself remains. Contribution levels should reflect project size. Small facilities could pool resources. Large campuses could not divide themselves into smaller applications to escape responsibility. Broader innovation contributions should be legally sound and separate from required mitigation. Projects with unacceptable impacts should be rejected or relocated. Those meeting environmental standards and securing credible, enforceable benefits deserve coordinated reviews and clear timelines. The Legislature has drawn the line against making families pay for the servers that power someone else’s fortune. The industry can meet that line by showing, in public and before construction, how it will protect the grid and water system. Then it can show what it will build for the people living outside its walls. For too long, California has sent the rewards of progress in one direction and the damage in another. If our communities are asked to power the future, that future must also power them. Dean Florez is a former California Senate majority leader, representing portions of the Central Valley. artigo.texto: Chuyển đổi số từ dữ liệu: [Bài 4] Xây nền tảng số cho thị trường carbon Dữ liệu hạn ngạch phát thải khí nhà kính, tín chỉ carbon, các tổ chức tham gia thị trường carbon tại Việt Nam được quản lý tập trung, thống nhất trên một nền tảng số. O setor de agricultura e meio ambiente está focado na padronização, interconexão e exploração de bancos de dados, na inovação de métodos de gestão e no atendimento às pessoas e empresas. Em resposta ao Dia Nacional da Transformação Digital, em 10 de outubro de 2026, com o tema "Da arquitetura, plataforma e dados a resultados tangíveis", o jornal Agricultura e Meio Ambiente publica uma reportagem especial intitulada "Transformação Digital a partir de Dados", esclarecendo o papel dos dados na inovação de métodos de gestão, na melhoria da eficiência operacional, na otimização do uso de recursos e no atendimento às pessoas e empresas. A transição para uma governança orientada por dados. O Departamento de Mudanças Climáticas (Ministério da Agricultura e Meio Ambiente) desenvolveu e implementou o Sistema Nacional de Registro de Cotas de Emissão de Gases de Efeito Estufa e Créditos de Carbono. Em junho de 2026, o sistema começará a operar em paralelo com a bolsa de carbono nacional. Isso pode ser considerado um passo significativo na transformação digital do setor agrícola e ambiental, contribuindo para a modernização da gestão estatal em resposta às mudanças climáticas e para o desenvolvimento de um mercado de carbono no Vietnã. Segundo o Sr. Nguyen Thanh Cong, Vice-Chefe do Departamento do Mercado de Carbono (Agência de Mudanças Climáticas), o sistema ajuda a transformar os métodos de gestão, passando de processos administrativos tradicionais para um ambiente digital. Através do sistema, os dados sobre quotas de emissão de gases de efeito estufa, créditos de carbono e participantes do mercado são gerenciados de forma centralizada e uniforme em uma plataforma digital. Os dados garantem precisão, transparência, rastreabilidade e controle sobre as flutuações históricas. Em particular, o Sistema Nacional de Registro é um componente crucial da infraestrutura digital que serve à operação do mercado de carbono do Vietnã, desempenhando um papel de ligação entre a gestão estatal e as atividades relacionadas à custódia, negociação e pagamento de cotas de emissão de gases de efeito estufa e créditos de carbono. “A construção deste sistema não só atende aos requisitos operacionais do mercado de carbono doméstico, como também cria uma base para a conexão e troca gradual de dados com os mecanismos de cooperação internacional sobre carbono, conforme o Artigo 6 do Acordo de Paris. Isso apoiará o alcance das metas de redução de emissões de gases de efeito estufa, a transição verde e o compromisso do Vietnã de atingir emissões líquidas zero até 2050”, afirmou o Sr. Nguyen Thanh Cong. As principais funções do sistema O sistema nacional de registro serve para gerenciar de forma centralizada e uniforme as operações relacionadas ao registro, emissão de códigos, rastreamento de propriedade, transferência e uso de cotas de emissão de gases de efeito estufa e créditos de carbono, em conformidade com a lei . Você também pode gostar O Departamento de Mudanças Climáticas está oferecendo treinamento para organizações e empresas sobre como participar do mercado de carbono. Foto: Trung Nguyen. Em primeiro lugar, o sistema facilita o cadastro, a configuração e a gestão de contas eletrônicas para agências e organizações participantes do mercado de carbono. Isso inclui o gerenciamento de informações dos titulares das contas, o controle de transações e o monitoramento do saldo de cotas de emissão de gases de efeito estufa e créditos de carbono para cada conta. Essas atividades são realizadas eletronicamente, simplificando o processo de cadastro, aprimorando as capacidades de controle e aumentando a eficiência do processamento de transações. Para quotas de emissão de gases de efeito estufa e créditos de carbono, o sistema registra e armazena informações sobre as quotas alocadas e os créditos de carbono elegíveis; atribui códigos, gerencia a quantidade, o status e o histórico de alterações de cada unidade de carbono. Por meio de uma gestão centralizada e unificada, o sistema permite o rastreamento das quotas de emissão de gases de efeito estufa e dos créditos de carbono ao longo de sua existência e utilização. Isso garante transparência, rastreabilidade e reduz o risco de dupla contabilização e reutilização de uma mesma unidade de carbono. A imagem ilustra o número de série da quota de emissão de uma organização/empresa. Foto: VNEEC . Além disso, o sistema suporta operações relacionadas a depósitos, saques, transferência de titularidade fora da bolsa, uso de créditos de carbono para compensar emissões, pagamento, transferência e empréstimo de cotas de emissão de gases de efeito estufa, conforme regulamentado. O sistema está conectado e troca dados com sistemas de custódia, negociação e pagamento para garantir a sincronização entre as informações de registro e as atividades de negociação no mercado nacional de carbono. Além das funções já mencionadas, o sistema também permite pesquisar, agregar, analisar estatisticamente e gerar relatórios com dados sobre o registro e o uso de cotas de emissão de gases de efeito estufa e créditos de carbono. Essas funções auxiliam os órgãos de gestão estatal no monitoramento das operações de mercado, na verificação e cruzamento de informações e na supervisão do cumprimento das normas pelas instalações emissoras. Os dados também contribuem para o planejamento e a implementação de políticas de redução de emissões de gases de efeito estufa e desenvolvimento do mercado de carbono no Vietnã. Preparativos passo a passo para o lançamento oficial do mercado de carbono. Segundo o Sr. Nguyen Thanh Cong, no próximo período, o Ministério da Agricultura e do Meio Ambiente continuará a concentrar-se no aperfeiçoamento, aprimoramento e expansão das funções do Sistema Nacional
