artigo.texto: A auxiliar de saúde Jessica Kivell, mãe e moradora de West Memphis, no Arkansas, pediu à Comissão de Serviço Público do Arkansas os registros públicos sobre quem pagaria por um data center do Google na região. Em vez de respostas, ela recebeu o título de ré numa ação judicial movida pela utilidade elétrica Entergy Arkansas, responsável por construir a usina solar que abasteceria o projeto, publicada pelo site The Intercept nesta terça-feira, 13 de outubro de 2026. Os documentos obtidos por Kivell indicavam que o Google cobriria apenas um terço do custo da nova usina solar, contrariando a promessa de que os consumidores de energia não arcariam com a conta. Ela compartilhou os registros com o jornal Arkansas Democrat-Gazette, que os publicou. A Entergy Arkansas então processou Kivell, o Democrat-Gazette, o repórter do jornal e o Arkansas Times, que afirmou nem ter tido acesso aos documentos. A empresa alegou que a comissão errou ao liberar os registros, que eles conteriam segredos comerciais e que os réus deveriam ser impedidos de discuti-los, com retirada do que já havia sido publicado. A utilidade também contestou os cálculos do jornal sobre a divisão de custos com o Google. A coluna é assinada por Seth Stern, diretor de defesa da Freedom of the Press Foundation, que classifica o caso como uma ação estratégica contra a participação pública, o chamado SLAPP, um processo cujo objetivo é silenciar críticos pelo custo da defesa. Pelo menos quatro decisões da Suprema Corte dos EUA rejeitam censura prévia que tente recolher registros liberados pelo governo, mesmo por engano. No caso Florida Star contra BJF, envolvendo a publicação do nome de uma vítima de estupro, o tribunal considerou inconstitucional punir veículos por divulgar informação que o próprio governo havia liberado. A corte já chamou a censura prévia à imprensa de a mais grave de todas as violações à Primeira Emenda. O juiz federal Lee Rudofsky negou o pedido de ordem de mordaça de emergência da Entergy, que em seguida desistiu da ação. O processo, porém, já havia custado dinheiro, tempo e sono aos réus. Kivell, que correu ao tribunal ainda com o uniforme de trabalho para a audiência, chegou a chorar no corredor do fórum. Como o caso tramitou na Justiça federal, os réus não puderam recuperar as despesas advocatícias. O Arkansas é um dos 40 estados americanos com lei antisslapp, mas a proteção não alcançou o caso, e a coluna defende uma lei federal contra processos destinados a calar a liberdade de expressão.

artigo.texto: A $410 million bet on Australia's biggest AI infrastructure IPO turned into a one-day stock rout for Maas Group, the industrial supplier caught holding Firmus equity nobody else wanted at the marketed price. Shares in Maas Group Holdings cracked as much as 30% in Sydney trading last Thursday. They closed down 22.4%, wiping out roughly A$517 million, or about US$340 million, in market value, then slid further on Friday and Monday. The trigger was the client it had quietly bet big on: Firmus, the Nvidia-backed AI data center operator, had just pulled its roughly A$7 billion ASX float. Investors refused to clear the offer even after the indicative price was cut from A$11 to A$8.25. StartupFortune covered the IPO withdrawal itself last week. What's new is who actually ate the loss, and it wasn't a hedge fund or a bank underwriter. It was a Dubbo-based construction and quarrying company that had piled A$410 million, including a A$300 million top-up in August, into a 3.2% stake in a business it also supplies through its JLE Group subsidiary. That's the uncomfortable mechanics of an AI infrastructure boom running years ahead of the capital markets built to fund it. Maas wasn't a passive financial investor chasing yield. It was a contractor who put real money into its own customer's growth story. Then it watched that customer's implied valuation collapse from almost A$44 billion to roughly A$33 billion in 48 hours of bookbuilding, before the whole deal got shelved entirely. The spark wasn't investor squeamishness about AI in the abstract. It was something far more specific: CDC Data Centres CEO Greg Boorer said on a podcast that CDC's partnership with Firmus on Project Southgate was no longer going ahead. The project had been announced just last October as a plan to build up to 1.6 gigawatts of AI factories across Australia, with a potential A$73.3 billion in investment behind it. Two people involved in the IPO transaction said institutional orders started pulling out the next day. Firmus co-CEOs Oliver Curtis and Tim Rosenfield pulled the $44 billion float on October 9 after bookbuilding stalled, with partner CDC Data Centres having already exited a $73 billion build-out only 2.5% complete. - nvidia backed AI data centre IPO withdrawn - Australian tech IPO cancelled after investor backlash The scale of the shortfall says everything. Project Southgate was supposed to scale toward 1.6 gigawatts by 2028. Firmus and CDC ended up deploying about 42 megawatts, about 2.6% of the original ambition, before calling it off. Boorer put it plainly: the two companies had made "other choices" about how to develop data centers that diverged from what CDC had envisaged. Layer that on top of Firmus's other problem and the IPO's failure looks less like bad timing and more like investors doing basic diligence. Only about 5% of the data center capacity Firmus has already sold to customers is actually built and running, well behind the roughly 25% completion rate at listed rival NextDC. Meanwhile Firmus is carrying close to $30 billion in debt against that unbuilt capacity. Two months before the float, a private funding round had priced the company at $10.5 billion. The IPO was asking the public market to pay more than three times that figure for a business that, by its own numbers, had delivered a fraction of what it had promised. Firmus says it will now chase private market capital instead, with a person involved in the process telling reporters a Nasdaq listing could follow down the line. The company declined to confirm that plan on record. Who's actually left holding the bag This is the part that should worry anyone watching the broader AI infrastructure trade, not just Firmus specifically. Banks and bond investors have spent recent months growing warier of data center debt generally, as the gap between promised AI compute capacity and physically delivered capacity widens across the sector. IREN is the AI data center firm serving a reported $9.7 billion Microsoft GPU cloud contract from its Childress, Texas campus. It raised $2.3 billion in convertible notes in December 2025 and arranged $3.6 billion of GPU financing in 2026 as it funded its buildout. Firmus's collapse is the clearest data point yet for what happens when that gap gets priced by a public market instead of a private one willing to take management's word for it. Maas Group's trading halt, imposed the morning after the IPO fell apart pending a "material announcement" about its contractual arrangements with Firmus, tells you how tangled supplier and investor relationships have become inside Australia's AI buildout. Maas isn't just exposed through its equity stake. JLE Group, its subsidiary, has construction and infrastructure contracts tied to the same Firmus campuses that are, by Firmus's own account, only 5% complete. A failed IPO doesn't just dent a balance sheet. It can slow or stall the actual construction pipeline that a supplier depends on for revenue. Frankly, the $340 million wiped off Maas in a single session is a cleaner measure of AI infrastructure risk than any valuation multiple Firmus or its bankers floated during the roadshow. Paper valuations can be marked up by a term sheet. A 22% single-day drop in a real, profitable industrial company's share price is money that doesn't come back just because the next funding round prices higher. artigo.texto: Meta has continued its PR blitz in support of its artificial intelligence push. On Oct. 8, the company published a new overview of data center myths as it works to counter negative sentiment around its massive infrastructure developments. In order to fuel its AI push, Meta needs to process increasing amounts of user data, which is why the company is spending hundreds of billions of dollars to build new data centers across the U.S. But the impacts on regions where these projects are being developed have been significant. Some regions have reported water contamination and impacted utilities, as well as damage to local infrastructure. Indeed, Time Magazine reported in July that only a third of Americans approve of the pace of data center development. Meanwhile, more than 300 cities, towns and counties have enacted bans or moratoriums on the construction of hyperscale data centers. Meta knows that this backlash could derail its AI push, which is why it’s been working to counter the negative reports about data center impacts with explainers from its own team about the main concerns with data center developments. In this latest iteration, creator Tom Shaw addressed three myths about data center development: - Regarding concerns about excess water usage and limiting water resources for local residents, Shaw said water usage for cooling Meta’s data centers is “permitted, metered, and counted in the local water plan, not carved out of it.” Shaw also said that many of Meta’s data center facilities use less water annually than an average U.S. golf course does in the same amount of time. - On power usage, Shaw said that Meta works with utility companies years before data center work begins in order to ensure that any new infrastructure is built and installed ahead of time with no impact to local supply. - Shaw also said that Meta’s data center developments create jobs in both the construction phase, and in the ongoing management phase. Shaw added that this often means Meta becomes the biggest employer in regions where data centers are installed. Meta is hoping that by addressing these concerns it can lessen community opposition and ensure that it can continue to build its massive data centers without facing negative public sentiment. Data center concerns have become a political issue, with some candidates using their support of, or opposition to, data centers in order to win support. U.S. President Donald Trump, however, has made his stance on data center development clear. As reported by ABC News, last month Trump said in a social media post: "The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor. If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign." Yet, even with the president’s backing, Meta knows the negative impacts of its developments could have longer-term impacts for its business, which is why the company is working hard to counter concerns.

artigo.texto: Dive Brief: - Electricity affordability, data center development and antitrust issues were top concerns voiced about the proposed NextEra Energy-Dominion Energy merger at a hearing held by the Virginia State Corporation Commission at the Fairfax County Government Center on Friday. - Most of the state and local officials who spoke at the hearing asked for the merger to be denied or allowed contingent on guarantees like Virginia Clean Economy Act compliance, data centers paying for infrastructure costs, and prohibitions on regulated utilities making campaign contributions. Local business and union leaders spoke in favor of the deal, citing job creation and the need to meet electricity demand. - Virginia Del. Irene Shin, D, who represents parts of Fairfax County, cited the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s Sept. 23 letter to Dominion and NextEra calling their merger application incomplete and requesting more information on issues like rate impacts. “I'm surprised that the SCC has moved forward without doing the same,” she said, urging the commission to reject the merger. Dive Insight: The meeting was the second of two local in-person hearings in Virginia, with the first held Oct. 7 in Newport News. The SCC will also hear public testimony through telephonic hearings on Nov. 5, 9 and 10; the evidentiary hearing in the case begins Nov. 17. Under the case’s current 180-day review clock, the SCC is set to make a decision in the case in January. Virginia’s lieutenant governor, Ghazala Hashmi, D, said in a Tuesday report that she has concluded the merger is “not in the best interest of Virginians” following a five-city listening tour across the state. Gov. Abigail Spanberger, D, has not taken a definitive position on the deal but has called herself “skeptical” about it. In August, Spanberger filed with the SCC to be a respondent in the case. At the Oct. 9 hearing, Alexandria City Councilman John Taylor Chapman said, “Ultimately, our concern is that the creation of the nation's largest electric utility will put Alexandrians at risk of runaway utility costs with limited recourse. Utility costs have risen dramatically over the last several years.” Virginia Sen. Jennifer Boysko, D, whose statement was read by her chief of staff, Karen Harrison, did not speak for or against the merger but said she was concerned about ratepayer burden and “the lack of clear language in the merger proposal for ratepayer protection.” Boysko’s statement asked for a “clear commitment” to the VCEA. U.S. Rep. Eugene Vindman, D, said in his comments that he believes the proposed merger is “a bad deal for Virginians,” citing rising energy bills along with Dominion’s existing status as a monopoly utility. “This commission has a responsibility to protect Virginia ratepayers,” he said. “NextEra sees enormous profits to be made in Virginia, particularly with the explosion of data centers,” Vindman said. “That is crystal clear. Data centers need to pay their fair share. Virginia families should not have to subsidize corporate expansion through higher utility bills.” Don Slaiman, the political coordinator for the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers Local 26, which represents electrical workers in the D.C., area, said he had not planned to speak “because our unions are still negotiating with NextEra and Dominion.” Slaiman didn’t give his opinion on the merger, but said he felt the need to respond to the negative comments previous speakers had made about data center development. “If we did not have data centers to store this data and we reserved it to private service, we'd be using almost half of our grid instead of the 6% or 7% we're using now,” Slaiman said. “So unless you're ready to curb your own digital footprint, I would not admonish this industry so much, which has provided fantastic jobs for my membership.” State Del. Kirk McPike, D, whose district covers part of the city of Alexandria, said he is opposed to the merger unless there are “ironclad guarantees that costs will not increase for Virginia taxpayers, that large energy users like data centers will pay for their own infrastructure and energy usage,” that VCEA commitments are met in a timely manner “and that you'll never see the sort of corruption scandal that occurred in Florida occur here in Virginia.” NextEra agreed in June to pay a $150 million settlement over allegations that it lied about its involvement in political interference schemes in Florida. Shin’s comments also cited concerns about Florida Power & Light’s “Robo memo” which is filed in the SCC’s case docket but which the public has yet to review. Clean Virginia noted in a Sept. 2 motion to compel that the memo is titled, “Florida Power & Light Officers’ Potentially Unlawful Conduct Through Third-Party Consultants and Vendors.” SCC Chief Hearing Examiner Mathias Roussy ruled Oct. 2 in favor of the release of the Robo memo. Shin also said she has concerns about whether NextEra will commit to meeting Virginia’s clean energy goals if it acquires Dominion, saying previous responses from company representatives on the topic “[sounded] like a company laying the groundwork to walk away from the VCEA.” “When Dominion was asked about the VCEA, its executive vice president told the commission, ‘I am still your throat to choke,’ and that was a shocking thing for me to hear as a legislator,” she said. State Del. John McAuliff, D, who represents the 30th District in western Loudoun County and campaigned against data center development in 2025, expressed concerns about NextEra and Dominion's history of political contributions. “If we move forward with anything like this, we have to prohibit regulated utilities from making campaign contributions to the elected officials who oversee them,” McAuliff said.

Sign up for Grist’s weekly newsletter. Cindy O’Neil understands the boom-and-bust cycles of industry. Her husband spent years working in Carbon County’s namesake coal mines. In this pocket of central Utah, energy and the economy have long been intrinsically linked, at great sacrifice to county residents. “We’ve had the coal. We’ve dealt, the whole community, with black lung,” O’Neil said. “The explosions, the fires, and all the things that came along with it.” But a new industry and type of energy production is about to move near her rural home. And she says it has her and her neighbors even more worried than they were about the dangers that came from their long history with coal. “It’s all descending, these data centers,” said O’Neil, who tracks mysterious new projects in the works and shares updates on Facebook community pages. “They’re setting these things within a couple of miles of homes.” Her latest updates involve a lot of chatter about Valar Atomics, a nuclear startup. The company plans to build a mega-complex of 456 small modular reactors — a still largely untested and unproven technology in the United States — on the vast tracts of Bureau of Land Management land in the county. The project will store radioactive waste, according to a report from National Public Radio, and power an array of industrial activities, including data centers. “Project Beehive” has support from the state of Utah, and will include a square mile of state-owned trust lands. Another data center complex planned for the county, Altigen Energy’s “Jurassic Spark,” will cover hundreds of acres and include a massive natural gas plant. It’s an abrupt shift. Carbon County’s coal mines produced nearly 10 million tons of coal in 2006. But a shift to cheaper energy sources, like renewables and natural gas, along with depleted supplies in the coal seams, sank the region’s main economic engine in just a few decades. Since 2023, not a single pound of coal has been mined in Carbon County. “They say everything’s left us, and if we don’t grab these table scraps we’re not going to get anything,” said O’Neil. “I don’t think our county has to take the table scraps.” None of Carbon County’s new data center plans call for coal. The Utah Trust Lands Administration recently agreed to lease a square mile of its state-owned land for up to 100 years to Valar Atomics. The nuclear startup intends to use that lease to run some of its small modular reactors, process its uranium TRISO-fuel to feed the reactors, build water desalination, manufacture steel, refine critical minerals — and support data centers. The Valar site is expected to generate $35 million in lease rents over 50 years, according to information the Trust Lands Administration staff presented to its board last month. Revenue collected from the project benefits Utah schools. (The state agency declined to comment on the Valar project.) During that September board meeting, three Carbon County residents who are employed or expected to be employed by Valar spoke in favor of the project. All three of the Carbon County commissioners also voiced their support. “[We] realize that this topic is a hot button now, along with data centers,” said Larry Jensen, one of the commissioners. “It’s important that you understand that the Carbon County commissioners are committed to allowing these things to move forward. Even with the pushback — we realize that there are a few in our community who will push back — but the silent majority are the ones that we really represent.” Cheryl Lupo, a longtime resident of the county, balked at that assertion. She is running for a seat on the county commission this year. As an unaffiliated candidate, she had to collect 300 signatures to land on the ballot. She said the opinions she heard during that process were overwhelmingly opposed to data centers and nuclear plants. “People are up in arms,” Lupo said. “Torches and pitchforks. Because they’re not being heard.” Gov. Spencer Cox (R), U.S. Sen. John Curtis (R), and other high-ranking Utah officials welcomed Valar to the state earlier this year, allowing it to test its “Ward250” microreactor at the San Rafael Energy Lab in neighboring Emery County. Valar announced it had achieved “self-sustaining criticality” in June — a process where atoms split and maintain a steady fission chain reaction without being fed more neutrons. The company has plans to power a 30-megawatt nuclear-powered AI data center in Emery County, too, in partnership with the computer-chip giant Nvidia. Small modular reactors have yet to be deployed for commercial use in the United States. During the recent Trust Lands Administration meeting, Mike Nelson, the board’s chair, seemed to acknowledge that the deal with Valar came with some unknowns. “We weren’t always sure what to ask about,” Nelson said, while offering praise for the nuclear startup, “and probably still aren’t sure of everything to ask about because this is a first, right?” Utah has a troubled history with nuclear testing. Lupo’s mother was 38 years old when she died, and Lupo believes the cause was downwind effects from radioactive weapons testing in nearby Nevada during the 1950s. Her mother lived in Carbon County at the time. She believes the fallout caused her grandfather’s death, too. “I will never, ever be a proponent of nuclear,” Lupo said. Even before the proposal to build Valar’s complex started causing a stir, rumors swirled about the possibility of another data center campus in Carbon County. Altigen, a company that builds natural gas power plants for data centers, has selected an area east of Wellington for its 1,200-acre “Jurassic Spark” project — nearly double the size of the Valar campus, according to meeting minutes from the local Community Economic Development Board. artigo.texto: Estudo identifica como reduzir falhas em baterias de sódio Simulações computacionais mostram como ajustar eletrólitos para proteger áreas sensíveis das baterias e prolongar sua vida útil Baterias de íons de sódio despontam como uma alternativa viável às populares baterias de lítio, graças à maior abundância e distribuição de sua matéria-prima. No entanto, para melhorar seu desempenho, é preciso resolver um gargalo técnico: a formação de dendritos, estruturas que reduzem a vida útil e causam falhas de segurança no componente. Um estudo computacional realizado pelo Centro de Inovação em Novas Energias (CINE) mapeou esse processo em escala atômica, oferecendo orientações concretas para controlar o fenômeno e, dessa forma, melhorar o desempenho das baterias. As baterias de íons de sódio destinam-se a diversas aplicações, com destaque para o armazenamento de energia em larga escala, a integração de fontes renováveis às redes elétricas e a eletrônica portátil. Apesar de seu potencial, possuem densidade de energia menor que as baterias de lítio. Na prática, isso significa que precisam de mais volume e peso para armazenar a mesma quantidade de energia. Para superar esse desafio tecnológico, é fundamental compreender, em escala atômica, os mecanismos que regem as interações entre o ânodo —eletrodo em que os íons de sódio ficam armazenados durante a descarga da bateria— e o eletrólito —substância que permite o transporte dos íons de sódio entre os eletrodos. Cientistas do programa de Design Computacional de Materiais do CINE estudam um aspecto crítico dessas interações: a formação de uma camada muito fina na superfície do ânodo. Chamada de interface de eletrólito sólido (SEI, na sigla em inglês), essa camada se forma a partir da decomposição de componentes do eletrólito. Quando a SEI é de boa qualidade, protege o ânodo de reagir continuamente com o eletrólito e permite, ao mesmo tempo, a passagem de íons de sódio durante os ciclos de carga e descarga da bateria. Por outro lado, quando a SEI tem baixa qualidade, ela racha e cresce de forma irregular, favorecendo a formação de estruturas de sódio em forma de agulha — os dendritos —, que constituem uma das principais causas de falhas e riscos à segurança das baterias. A equipe do CINE se propôs a compreender os processos de formação da SEI em escala atômica. Esse objetivo só poderia ser alcançado com o uso de ferramentas computacionais, já que um estudo experimental seria inviável por causa da natureza ultrafina, quimicamente heterogênea e dinâmica da SEI. “Em nosso projeto, selecionamos alguns eletrólitos e um tipo de ânodo —o de sódio metálico— e simulamos como moléculas individuais dos eletrólitos interagem com esse ânodo”, detalhou Juarez L. F. da Silva, professor do Instituto de Química de São Carlos da Universidade de São Paulo (IQSC-USP) e coordenador do programa de Design Computacional do CINE, liderou a pesquisa. Inicialmente, os autores utilizaram simulações computacionais baseadas na física quântica para construir um modelo de uma superfície de sódio metálico com defeitos. “As superfícies reais desses ânodos nunca são perfeitamente lisas. Elas apresentam pequenos aglomerados de átomos em relevo e minúsculas cavidades onde faltam átomos”, explicou Tapasendra Adhikary, primeiro autor do artigo e pesquisador de pós-doutorado no IQSC-USP. Com esse modelo, a equipe simulou interações com 22 espécies químicas encontradas em eletrólitos de baterias. De acordo com Tapasendra, o objetivo foi compreender quais moléculas do eletrólito se fixam em cada local do ânodo e por quê, para projetar eletrólitos capazes de controlar a formação da camada SEI. Receita de bons eletrólitos Dessa maneira, a equipe conseguiu investigar como os componentes do eletrólito interagem, em escala atômica, com um ânodo de sódio com defeitos e como essas interações moldam os estágios iniciais da formação da SEI. “A descoberta fundamental é que essas irregularidades na superfície do sódio funcionam como pontos críticos de atividade química”, disse Tapasendra. Em outras palavras, o local em que uma molécula se fixa depende fortemente da geometria da superfície. Com base nos resultados, os autores formularam orientações concretas para desenvolver eletrólitos que promovam a formação de camadas SEI de boa qualidade. “Primeiro, deve-se dar preferência a sais que liberam fluoreto, uma vez que o fluoreto se liga com especial força aos sítios de defeito reativos e forma fluoreto de sódio — uma camada inorgânica resistente e muito eficaz em vedar esses pontos vulneráveis e bloquear o crescimento de dendritos”, sugeriu Tapasendra. A 2ª orientação consiste em combinar esses sais liberadores de fluoreto com solventes de carbonato cíclico para criar condições favoráveis à formação de uma camada protetora rica em fluoreto e carbonato nos pontos mais vulneráveis do ânodo. Além disso, os autores destacam a importância de desenvolver e testar formulações de eletrólitos levando em conta superfícies de eletrodos reais e imperfeitas, em vez de superfícies planas idealizadas. Isso porque a rugosidade da superfície determina onde e como a camada protetora se forma. Este texto foi publicado originalmente pela Agência Fapesp, em 7 de setembro de 2026. artigo.texto: Consumer Liaison Group explores growing role of energy storage The third 2026 meeting of the Consumer Liaison Group (CLG) centered on batteries, energy storage, and the future of the electric grid, examining how storage technologies are evolving, the role they can play in supporting grid operations and reliability, and their potential to help meet New England’s changing energy needs. A video recording and summary of the Sept. 24 meeting in Portland, Maine, are available online. Drew Landry, CLG Coordinating Committee member and Maine’s deputy public advocate, began the meeting with opening remarks and provided an overview of the group as well as the critical roles of ISO New England. He introduced the topics of discussion and described innovations in battery technology. Heather Sanborn, Maine’s public advocate, discussed electrification during her keynote address, noting that demand growth from heat pumps and electric vehicles (EVs) has largely been offset by declining industrial consumption. She highlighted findings from the ISO’s 2050 Transmission Study, describing how it showed the potential cost savings of reducing peak demand. The audience followed up with questions on load growth trends, EV charging timing, stakeholder coordination, solar incentives, and utility data transparency. The first panel discussion was moderated by Cole Cochrane, policy affairs lead at Powertown and a Coordinating Committee member, and featured Greg Geller, Stack Energy Consulting; Kelly Kaufmann, ReVision Energy; Jessica Robertson, New Leaf Energy; and Elio Torres, Powertown. The panelists examined how market reforms, incentive programs, and interconnection processes affect energy storage development. They emphasized the need for better alignment between wholesale markets and retail programs, more predictable revenue streams, and reduced barriers to battery deployment. Audience questions focused on the impact of FERC Order No. 2222 and market complexity on storage participation. The ISO’s Eric Johnson, executive director of External Affairs, and Ruben Flores-Marzan, policy advisor for environmental and community affairs, provided a regional grid update covering market, planning, and policy developments. Highlights included consumer engagement opportunities and community outreach activities, growing battery participation on the system, market trends, transmission planning initiatives, and large load integration efforts. Audience questions focused on battery visibility in ISO-NE tools and maintaining a safe, affordable resource mix. The final panel discussion, moderated by Landry, featured George Baker, Gridworks Consulting; Ian Burnes, Efficiency Maine Trust; Al McBride, ISO New England; and Ethan Tremblay, Maine Department of Energy Resources. They discussed the growing role of energy storage in New England, highlighting state initiatives, battery participation in ISO-NE markets, and the reliability and operational benefits storage can provide. Audience questions focused on battery deployment, interconnection challenges, and opportunities for greater participation in wholesale markets. The next CLG meeting, scheduled for Dec. 2 in Boston, will include the biennial election of the Coordinating Committee. - Categories - Events - Tags - consumer liaison group

artigo.texto: 'People are big mad in Texas': Hinojosa challenges Abbott's data center policies DALLAS - Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic nominee for Texas governor, discussed her stance on data centers during a press conference in Dallas on Tuesday. What they're saying: Hinojosa said she believes Texans should "have a seat at the table" when it comes to deciding whether there are data centers in their communities, and called for lawmakers to pass legislation putting more protections in place. She also took aim at her opponent, Gov. Greg Abbott’s attitude toward AI data center development by criticizing the rapid expansion in the state and blaming it on tax breaks and other incentives. "There's no protections for people to have a seat at the table to decide if and how they come into their communities. There is no protection for water or electricity costs," Hinojosa said. "We are left to fend for ourselves under Greg Abbott, and people are big mad in Texas about the data centers." Abbott pauses data center permits, calls for more regulations The other side: Abbott, who previously welcomed the artificial intelligence industry, appears to have shifted his stance. The governor ordered a pause on some data center approvals in August, and a month earlier said he wants to ban data center development in rural Texas neighborhoods. "We must prohibit them from building AI data centers in rural Texas neighborhoods, and we must eliminate the tax break they are getting," Abbott said during a campaign stop in Bullard. "They must be responsible for funding their own projects here in Texas." Hinojosa echoed a need for a moratorium, but said she believes her opponent's pause on data center development is "in name only." "I could issue a moratorium, but it would be in place until laws are passed to accomplish those things," Hinojosa said, referring to her calls for more guardrails and stricter protections. Abbott's office has previously emphasized his willingness to work with lawmakers, pointing to a letter the governor sent to the Public Utilities Commission of Texas and the Electric Reliability Council of Texas in June. The letter laid out some of his ideas, which included having the legislature repeal sales tax exemptions. Data centers remain a major topic of debate in Texas Big picture view: Data centers have been a major topic of debate in the state, which has seen hundreds spring up in recent years. The concerns of local leaders and residents mainly center around noise, light and water pollution. A resident of the Joppa community who spoke Tuesday also shared concerns with locals being included in discussions, saying she did not know a data center was being built in her neighborhood until it was already there. "We do not want one," she said. "However, it is now up and running, and we are faced with the challenge of having the data center less than 0.3 miles, 1,500 feet -- not 15 miles, but 1,500 feet – from our community." The Source: The information in this article comes from a press conference held by Democratic gubernatorial nominee Gina Hinojosa in Dallas, as well as previous reporting on data centers.

artigo.texto: PowerCo × Gotion: Volkswagen’s LFP Battery Push Builds European Independence Three Joint Ventures Span Cells, Cathode Material and Cross-Regional Supply €1.6 Billion Investment Fills Critical Technology Gap Restructuring and Profit Targets Frame Broader Group Renewal Volkswagen Group and its battery subsidiary PowerCo have formed a landmark partnership with Gotion High-Tech to establish Europe’s first large-scale production of lithium‑iron‑phosphate (LFP) batteries, a chemistry poised to dominate affordable electric vehicles but currently manufactured almost entirely outside the continent. The agreement creates three joint ventures across Spain, Slovakia and Morocco, combining Volkswagen’s platform and vehicle scale with Gotion’s proven LFP manufacturing expertise. Announced against a backdrop of sweeping restructuring across the Group, the move underscores a dual imperative: to secure supply chains for the next generation of accessible EVs and to restore profitability amid intense global competition. The LFP Opportunity and the Gap LFP batteries are central to affordable electric mobility: they use no nickel or cobalt, offer exceptional longevity and safety, and deliver compelling cost advantages. Yet Europe has no meaningful domestic LFP production capacity, even as demand is projected to surge from roughly 10% of the market today to between 40% and 60% by 2030. Closing that gap is not merely about supply — it is about who controls the technology, the manufacturing infrastructure, and the value chain. Thomas Schmall, Volkswagen Group Board Member for Technology and PowerCo Supervisory Board Chairman, described the partnership as “a major breakthrough” that makes Volkswagen the first European automaker to cover the entire battery value chain from development and cathode processing through to cell production. Three Sites, Complementary Roles Each facility is designed with a distinct strategic purpose and ownership structure: - Valencia, Spain — The flagship hub. PowerCo holds a 51% majority stake in the gigafactory currently under construction, which will be reoriented to produce PowerCo’s Unified Cell in LFP format. Gotion invests approximately €1.1 billion for its 49% share, reflecting the site’s centrality to Volkswagen’s volume plans. Because the plant is still being built, it can be engineered for LFP from the ground up rather than retrofitted, a decisive advantage in speed and efficiency. - Šurany, Slovakia — Gotion holds a 51% majority here, converting an existing cell plant to supply LFP batteries for both electric vehicles and stationary energy storage systems (ESS). Serving two markets from one line provides operational flexibility as EV adoption rates evolve, giving the facility a second, more stable revenue stream. PowerCo contributes around €470 million across this and the Kenitra site combined for its 49% stakes. - Kenitra, Morocco — Upstream security. Gotion holds 51% in a new facility producing LFP cathode active material, diversifying supply sources and expanding the regional value chain beyond cell assembly alone. All three ventures will operate under joint management, combining PowerCo’s cell design and platform integration strengths with Gotion’s manufacturing process expertise. Frank Blome, CEO of PowerCo, emphasised the partnership’s resilience: “It strengthens the resilience of our value chain, accelerates industrialization and combines PowerCo’s capabilities with the strengths of a long-standing partner.” Broader Restructuring Frames the Push The battery initiative advances alongside a comprehensive Group-wide efficiency drive unveiled by CEO Oliver Blume at the June 2026 annual general meeting. Volkswagen targets annual net savings exceeding €6 billion by 2030, including roughly 50,000 job reductions across the Group, 35,000 at Volkswagen AG alone, with over 28,000 departures already agreed through collective bargaining. Factory costs in Germany fell by more than 20% in 2025, and the Group aims to lift operating return on sales from 3.3% in the first quarter of 2026 to between 8% and 10% by decade’s end. Pressures are intense: first-quarter profit dropped 28.4% to €1.56 billion, revenue fell 2.5%, and US tariffs alone cost an estimated $4 billion annually. In this context, LFP leadership is not just a technology play; it is a pathway to lower vehicle costs and restored margins. Strategic Alignment and Shared Evolution Concurrent with the joint ventures, Volkswagen is selling down a 5.3% equity stake in Gotion to optimise capital structure while retaining full board representation and voting rights, a financial recalibration that leaves the strategic partnership intact. Gotion Chairman Li Zhen characterised the relationship as transcending typical supplier-customer ties: “Six years of close collaboration have built deep mutual trust… together we are accelerating our global strategic cooperation.” Realising the ambition will depend on execution at scale. LFP manufacturing differs materially from nickel-rich chemistries, requiring new materials, electrode processing, and pack design. Running dual-product lines in Šurany adds further operational complexity. As the Group acknowledged, covering the value chain on paper is one thing; delivering consistent yield, ramp-up speed, and quality cell by cell is where the claim will be proven. The PowerCo–Gotion alliance answers a defining question for European automotive: who will build the batteries that power mass-market electrification? By combining European industrial ambition with proven LFP expertise, Volkswagen is positioning itself to lead the transition while strengthening supply chain independence. Success will not be measured in announcements, but in affordable vehicles rolling off production lines powered by cells made on the continent and in the resilience of a partnership built to last. artigo.texto: Aurora neighbors call for removal of police chief, end to data centers in city During Monday's Aurora City Council meeting, neighbors called for a data center moratorium and for Aurora's police chief to be removed. City council unanimously passed an ordinance that will keep data centers from being built in some areas. It's a step toward limiting where data centers can be, not banning them entirely. The city of Aurora has nine existing data centers, with five in various stages of the development process. Many public commenters Monday spoke out against data centers. "We need a moratorium on all data centers!" one Aurora neighbor said, and was met with loud cheers from the audience. "I do not want this data center to be built near my home building this data center will affect all the creatures. Please don't build this data center, thank you," a young boy said on the record. City council voted unanimously to approve the first reading of an ordinance that would prohibit new data centers from being built in areas zoned "mixed-use office/institutional," where they could be located near schools, homes and assisted living facilities. It would not ban data centers citywide. While several commenters spoke directly in support of the ordinance, many Green Valley Ranch neighbors shared concerns about the proposed Trident data center that could move in near their homes. That area falls under different zoning, and it would not be impacted by the ordinance. "Reverse the A-D zoning; stop the Trident's data center," one woman said. Many in the audience cheered. There are currently no submitted development applications for data centers in "mixed-use office/institutional" zoned areas. City council will have its final vote on the ordinance on Oct. 26. If passed, the ordinance would likely take effect 30 days later. Throughout the meeting, dozens of community members stood with signs depicting the faces of Black men killed by police, demanding the removal of Todd Chamberlain as Aurora's police chief. Activists and community members staged a sit-in at the meeting. They said they won't leave city hall until officials agree to meet with them directly about their demand for new leadership in Aurora's police department, and make a termination plan for the police chief. They say it comes after their concerns over deadly police shootings and transparency have gone ignored. "We are tired of people being murdered by the Aurora Police Department," one activist said. "We will not leave this building until we have a termination date and strategy for Chief Todd Chamberlain," said MiDian Shofner, CEO of Epitome of Black Excellence and Partnership. Shofner said some council members indicated a meeting could take place after Monday's council meeting, but the demonstrators say they won't leave the building until there is a termination plan for Chamberlain. As of 10 p.m. Monday, the activists were still in the building. Aurora's leaders shared the following comments on the sit-in: Statement from Mayor Pro Tem Alison Coombs and Public Safety Committee Chair Rob Andrews, "We have reached out to all concerned parties and are actively working to schedule a meeting at the earliest opportunity." "We recognize and respect the importance of ensuring that every voice is heard, and we welcome the opportunity for open, honest, and constructive dialogue." "We remain committed to transparency, meaningful community engagement, and fostering an environment where residents feel comfortable expressing their perspectives, feedback, and concerns. We believe that listening to one another is essential to building trust and finding solutions that move our community forward." Statement from City Manager Jason Batchelor, "I welcome discussions with all community members on city issues and look forward to having a meaningful dialogue." "Crime in Aurora is down across every major category – murder, sexual assault, aggravated assault, robbery, burglary, larceny and motor vehicle theft. Total crime in Aurora is down 10% from this time last year and 38% from September 2024, when Todd Chamberlain was sworn in as chief." "In a recent community survey, nearly 74% of Aurora residents rated the job that APD is doing as fair, good or excellent. A similar survey at the start of the consent decree in 2022 had 57% expressing the same opinion." "The city of Aurora continues to make significant progress and improvements, including being in "substantial compliance" or "right track, 75-99% complete" on all mandates outlined in the state-mandated consent decree." "The city also continues to move forward with the Office of Public Safety Accountability, a city function that the city began contemplating before the consent decree process began in 2021. Applications for the Public Safety Accountability Manager closed in September and candidate review is underway. Community engagement, including a meet-and-greet with candidates, is planned as the process continues." "I stand behind the ongoing work and continuous improvement at APD."

artigo.texto: The Greek Ministry of Environment and Energy presented a bill of law setting detailed rules for the development of projects for data centers in the country. Greek authorities have witnessed a steep rise in interest in data centers. Independent Power Transmission Operator (IPTO or ADMIE) saw applications rise from 5 GW to 9 GW in just two months in the summer. The proposal for the new law is attempting to clarify the regulatory framework concerning the connections to the power network, as well as establish specific requirements. IPTO to handle requests above 10 MW When it comes to oversight, IPTO will have to include data centers in its ten-year development plan, separately from other large consumers. The operator is called to categorize availability at extra-high-voltage substations. They can be free, partially congested or fully congested. These estimations will be updated every two months to provide timely information to the market. As for the licensing process, IPTO will be responsible for data centers above 10 MW, with Hellenic Electricity Distribution Network Operator (HEDNO or DEDDIE) handling requests below that capacity. Projects won’t be allowed to be segmented into smaller parts for benefiting simpler regulations. Power must be 60% renewable Investors would be required to submit letters of guarantee for EUR 200,000 per MW, with a three-year duration. When ready, the operator would provide them with a three-year connection offer, at which point developers need to submit a report with the project’s technical features and a power supply agreement. Consumed electricity must be at least 60% renewable in origin. Data centers can connect directly to neighboring renewable electricity and energy storage facilities, or sign power purchase agreements (PPAs). Data centers above 200 MW would benefit from priority in their connection, although with certain caveats. The owner must establish that 80% of the electricity will come either from a distributed power producer, or from energy storage with a six-hour injection duration.

artigo.texto: Leader Energy breaks ground on 100-MW battery project in Malaysia It is scheduled for commissioning in 2027 under Malaysia’s MyBeST programme. Malaysia-based Leader Energy Group Berhad has begun construction of a 100-megawatt (MW)/400-megawatt-hour (MWh) battery energy storage system (BESS) in Pajam, Negeri Sembilan. The facility is scheduled for commissioning in 2027 under Malaysia’s Battery Energy Storage System bidding programme (MyBeST). It is expected to improve flexibility in Peninsular Malaysia’s electricity grid, supporting renewable energy integration and helping manage changes in electricity supply and demand. Administered by Malaysia’s Energy Commission, MyBeST comprises four grid-connected BESS projects, each with a capacity of 100MW/400MWh. Together, the projects represent 400 MW of power capacity and 1,600 MWh of energy storage capacity. The programme supports Malaysia’s goals of reducing reliance on fossil-fuel peaking plants, lowering electricity system costs over time and achieving the National Energy Transition Roadmap’s target of 70% renewable energy capacity by 2050. Leader Energy’s project forms part of this national effort to develop energy storage infrastructure alongside renewable generation. “As Malaysia’s renewable energy capacity grows, the electricity system needs greater flexibility to manage when power is available and when it is needed,” said Dato’ Sean H’ng, Executive Deputy Chairman and Group CEO of Leader Energy. “Storage helps meet that need.”

artigo.texto: Mount Pleasant finalizes 2-year data center development pause MOUNT PLEASANT, S.C. (WCSC) — Mount Pleasant is officially pausing any possible data center development. Mount Pleasant town leaders finalized a moratorium, buying time to figure out where these facilities belong and where they don’t. The originally proposed moratorium was for 120 days, but the council extended that pause to two years, giving the town time to study where and how data centers could fit into the community. “We are starting to feel the pressure, predominantly upstate, but we’re certainly starting to feel it in the region,” Michelle Reed, the town of Mount Pleasant’s director of planning, land use and neighborhoods, said. Across the country, towns and cities are working on ways to manage data center development. Mount Pleasant’s code allows data centers in some commercial and industrial zones. “They were actually permitted in area-wide business two, light industrial and our economic development properties. We don’t have a lot of light industrial, but we have a lot of AB2 properties. Most of them are not vacant, but that doesn’t mean we wouldn’t lose a use and perhaps a data center could come in,” Reed said. “It gives us time to study the issue and to make sure that we’re protecting our residents and protecting our natural resources,” Daniel Brownstein, a member of Mount Pleasant Town Council, said. Power usage, water and noise are all major concerns that the town is looking to address. “There are environmental impacts that we want to look at as well, and make sure we have the proper locations for them, proper buffering, those sorts of things if we were to have one come to the town,” Reed said. Those are concerns that environmental groups also want at the forefront of the conversation. “Recent analysis from the Sierra Club is warning that the data centers under development right now could reverse 15 years of climate progress in just three years,” Taylor Allred, State Energy and Climate Program director at the Coastal Conservation League, said. “Pivoting away from evaporative cooling technology that uses a lot of water toward more closed-loop systems that use less water. And that’s generally a good thing, but there are some concerns that need to be addressed with those systems. For one thing, they tend to use more energy. And the power plants that produce that energy use water too. Not to mention air pollution and other issues. Potentially, some of the coolants used in some of these closed-loop systems could be hazardous. So, making sure that containment and spill avoidance is properly accounted for is really important too.” But not every data center looks like the massive campuses being built by big tech companies. This moratorium applies to facilities of at least one megawatt, and the town says it’s working to avoid unintended consequences for local businesses. “The video game developer that just needs some of their data, but they don’t need a huge system; they have to get it from somewhere. And so, that’s what we’ve been helping do. Smaller scale, up to 1 MW of compute can actually fit in a 20-ft by 8-ft container and take up less than half an acre of space. The sound is no more than a commercial air conditioning unit and it doesn’t use any more water than like a regular garden at your house,” Andrew Harris, a local business owner and resident in Mount Pleasant, said. “There are a lot of industries and businesses, commercial centers, strip malls, parking lots of a Target where those owners of those properties are interested in somehow figuring out a way to increase income. We install the canopy solar that feeds EV charging, but that canopy solar also can feed these data compute centers, which allows that landowner or business owners to actually get a little bit more income based on selling that kind of compute versus a corner of their parking lot that otherwise was sitting vacant.” The town will study suitable locations and development conditions, then recommend changes to its zoning code and comprehensive plan. If a data center development is proposed, the town says it should go through a public approval process. “The people of South Carolina deserve to have a seat at the table with respect to the future of data center development in our state,” Allred said. “The real work begins with making sure that we’re limiting it and making sure that if there were a data center to come to town, that there would be a public process for it to go through rather than our current zoning code which would just allow it by right without a public process,” Brownstein said. Rules around data center development are expected to be taken up in the State House. Environmentalists say that will be a key test: whether statewide standards could be enough for Mount Pleasant, or whether the town will need stronger protections of its own. For now, this creates a temporary pause on accepting, processing or approving applications, permits or other requests related to data centers in Mount Pleasant. Copyright 2026 WCSC. artigo.texto: CATL Largest global volume According to Wood Mackenzie's newest outlook, the worldwide energy storage sector is entering a period characterized by both scale and complexity. The firm projects that cumulative capacity will exceed 7 TWh by 2035, while demand growth during 2026 alone will be near 30 percent. What matters more than the speed of expansion, however, is how the market is composed. China and the United States continue to hold the top two positions among national energy storage markets, but in 2026 Europe's yearly installations surpassed annual US energy storage capacity for the first time, claiming second place behind China. Government-led tenders remain the principal force in the utility segment, having cleared more than 80 GW of de-rated capacity worldwide, with India contributing the largest single share. Poland has emerged as the top emerging market globally, buoyed by capacity-market auctions and a grid lacking flexibility. Demand signals in mature utility markets are equally solid. Contracted offtake for storage has exceeded 130 GW, with utility power purchase agreements and tolling deals combined representing over three-quarters of all contracts signed, based on the firm's global offtake tracker. Within the residential landscape, the centre of gravity has moved southward. Australia has displaced Germany as the world's foremost residential energy storage market, with over half a million installations supported by its Cheaper Home Batteries subsidy, while the US market shrinks this year as tax credits grow less accessible. Wood Mackenzie forecasts commercial and industrial storage capacity as a separate category, and the breakdown reveals that industrial demand is substantially larger in certain regions. In the most recent market outlook update, Wood Mackenzie alters the way the utility energy storage market is measured. The utility segment is now divided into three parts — standalone, solar-paired and wind-paired — rather than one, since each is expanding for distinct reasons, at varying speeds and in different locations. Standalone projects continue to lead and will do so through 2035. Yet paired capacity is no longer negligible: nearly one-third of the storage anticipated to come online by 2035 will be located alongside a wind or solar plant. The revised breakdown reveals how dissimilar the regions are, owing to their differing policy and economic parameters. Europe is the most standalone-dominated market globally, with the vast majority of its utility pipeline unpaired. Nevertheless, it is also set for the quickest expansion in paired capacity, as deteriorating economics for standalone solar drive developers toward co-location. This positions Europe as the market most likely to move rapidly toward co-location as an economic remedy for stranded solar projects in markets such as Spain or Germany. The Americas occupy the opposite position. In the US, nearly half of utility storage additions are solar-paired — a legacy of the ITC pairing requirement in the early days and now poor solar capture rates in key markets like CAISO. That proportion is anticipated to decline as storage extends into lower solar-penetration states, where standalone economics perform better. Data centre-linked battery projects are also emerging in the US, though not all are paired with wind or solar: gas-plus-storage pairings are the new co-location favourites for emerging data center projects. Asia Pacific falls in between, with solar pairing the fastest-growing utility category, driven mainly by India, which has surpassed Australia as the region's largest utility-scale market. Regulatory changes are pivotal here: India's new rules will mandate that solar and wind projects commissioned after July 2027 incorporate co-located storage equal to at least 10 percent of capacity, increasing to a four-hour minimum duration from 2029. Aging storage assets will only begin to come offline and be replaced at scale after 2030, contributing 40 GWh of repowered capacity by 2035, led by the US, Japan and Germany. This marks the first indication of a market mature enough to require replacement, which has earned a reporting line in the latest energy storage outlook. Wood Mackenzie is holding a global energy storage outlook webinar on 3 November to examine which markets and segments are shaping the future of global energy storage. Anna Darmani serves as a research director on the Wood Mackenzie Power & Renewables team, leading the EMEA energy storage team. She previously worked at EIT InnoEnergy, developing innovation and technology roadmaps and contributing to EU research and advisory projects. artigo.texto: It’s not just your electricity bill that could be going up — it sounds like the massive boom in AI data centers is making practically everything more expensive. As the Washington Post reports, officials at the Federal Reserve are starting to sing a different tune after blaming president Donald Trump’s tariff war on rising prices, admitting that the explosion in “AI-related investments” is contributing to inflationary pressures. That’s on top of Trump’s Iran war already sending the price of oil soaring. Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago president Austan Goolsbee told Semafor that AI-tied inflation is “jumping out of its lane.” “Prices are going up in spaces that are not just components in data centers and the directly adjacent industries,” he said. “I’m getting increasingly nervous that that’s just straight, old-fashioned overheating demand.” In economics, overheating occurs when aggregate demand outpaces productive capacity, leading to demand-side inflation, higher prices, and eventually reduced demand and consumption. In the worst case scenario, overheating can even trigger a recession. “It takes a long time for overheated demand to get going, and once it’s going, it’s hard to get rid of that,” Goolsbee added. While the prices for groceries have yet to be directly impacted, economists are wondering whether it’s only a matter of time. Worse yet, whether raising the interest rate, which makes borrowing more expensive and lowers consumer spending, will be able to meaningfully address rising inflation, is also starting to look less like a certain bet. The Fed raised interest rates in September, the first time in three years, as inflation proves tough to beat. Futures markets expect yet another increase later this month, according to Reuters. Meanwhile, the tens of billions of dollars being spent on AI data centers are starting to mask some fundamental problems plaguing the US economy, triggering fears over what it could look like if the AI bubble were to burst. Sectors that have already seen instant knock-on effects from the construction boom have been consumer electronics becoming practically unaffordable, as well as a major shortage in skilled labor available for housing projects. According to Goolsbee, “it’s clear what the Fed has to do” if inflation “remains persistent:” continue raising rates. But as tech companies show no signs of slowing down their extreme levels of spending, that lever may end up driving up the cost of investment — a reality that would make things tougher for AI companies as well. artigo.texto: Cabinet greenlights lithium mining to boost local battery manufacturing Cabinet has approved support for lithium mining and local battery production in a push to lower the cost of solar-powered irrigation for Ugandan farmers. The decision, taken on October 12, 2026, links investment in battery manufacturing to the government’s six-point irrigation strategy. Minister of ICT and National Guidance Justine Kasule Lumumba said locally produced batteries would help reduce the cost of solar-powered water pumping and piping on farms and in gardens. The government will support investors in lithium mining and battery production to speed up implementation of the strategy, she said. The move builds on earlier efforts to turn Uganda’s mineral resources into finished products. In December 2023, President Yoweri Museveni backed a proposal by investors from London-based Strand Hanson Limited to mine lithium in Ntungamo District and manufacture electric vehicle batteries locally. He urged them to link extraction with processing and identified Kiira Motors as a potential customer. Government-backed researchers have also investigated lithium resources elsewhere. A Ministry of Finance monitoring report for the 2023/24 financial year recorded preliminary sampling and analysis of lithium sites in Mayuge and Buhweju districts under a battery development project. Uganda already has businesses assembling lithium battery packs. Soleil Power began operations at its purpose-built factory in Kirolo, Wakiso District, in July 2025. The company assembles imported cells into batteries for homes, businesses and electric motorcycles, according to an account published on its website. That reliance on imported cells shows the gap between assembling batteries locally and producing their core components from Ugandan minerals. Busitema University has pursued a Shs1.75 billion research project aimed at developing batteries using locally available materials. The university says minerals must undergo purification to meet battery manufacturing standards. Under Cabinet’s irrigation plan, the Ministry of Agriculture will work with the Ministry of Water and Environment to extend water supplies to farms and gardens. In districts with reliable water sources, the government will invest in systems to transport water to agricultural land. Elsewhere, it plans to draw irrigation water from nearby seasonal streams and rivers. The ministries will also rehabilitate small and large irrigation schemes and dams to improve their operation and restore water delivery to the farms they serve. Cabinet further approved support for fish farming in Busoga, Bukedi, Greater Luwero, Lango, West Nile and the Kigezi lowlands. Regional mechanisation centres will receive additional machinery. Farmers will access the equipment at affordable rates to construct farm dams and fish ponds. Cabinet directed the Ministry of Finance to release funds for the strategy. Lumumba’s account did not specify the funding amount, the investors to receive support or when lithium extraction would begin.

artigo.texto: As Georgia becomes one of the fastest-growing markets for data centers, voters are approaching their ballots wondering where candidates stand on their development — especially southeast Georgians who soon will see a hyperscale OpenAI data center built in their "backyard." One of the most significant races for data center development is the state Public Service Commission, which has five seats, and is the regulatory body for Georgia Power and other state utilities. While the PSC doesn't decide where data centers are built, it does make decisions on how much energy power companies serve these facilities and for how much. In August, PSC members reviewed and approved the large load contract for Georgia Power to serve electricity to the future OpenAI data center in Effingham County. Two seats are up for election in November. Republican Joshua Tolbert and Democrat Shelia Edwards are competing for the District 5 seat, while Democratic incumbent Peter Hubbard and Republican former PSC member Fitz Johnson are facing off — again — for District 3. District 5: Tolbert vs. Edwards Tolbert, who has an engineering background in building power plants, said he believes Georgia should welcome businesses that want to invest in the state from factories to data centers. However, he said local communities should be able to decide whether they want data centers and where they should be located. He criticized the lack of transparency with Effingham County's OpenAI announcement. "Number two, if they do decide they want a data center, that should not come on the financial backs of the local members of the community," Tolbert said. "That is where the PSC comes in." The PSC should be ensuring that data center development does not shift costs onto residential customers or other communities, he said. Tolbert also said there is a difference between the direct cost of electricity and less obvious costs associated with serving massive new loads. "It's very easy to make sure the data centers pay for the electricity they use," he said. "The part that's more challenging is adding infrastructure, whether it's transmission lines or pipelines or purchasing fuel reservations. How are those costs being allocated? How are they being paid for?" Tolbert was also critical of the PSC's 2025 decision to approve roughly 10 gigawatts of new generation. He said he objected because much of the projected demand was speculative at the time. "If the forecast is wrong, who's paying for that," he said When approaching large load contracts as a PSC commissioner, Tolbert said he would scrutinize the contract's collateral, termination provisions and payments to determine whether the data center is paying more than the incremental cost of serving it. He also supports considering solar and other generation technologies as part of Georgia's energy mix, but said power companies must evaluate resources according to the particular needs of the grid rather than selecting technologies in advance. Edwards has a background in Cobb County politics and working in the Kennedy Space Center's Space Shuttle Program. She ran for the Georgia PSC in 2022, but her race was taken off the ballot because of a voting-rights lawsuit that was ongoing at the time. Edwards is back and when it comes to data centers, she said both the state and local governments have offered too many incentives to data center companies, causing development to move too quickly. "They should have to pay their own way," she said. "You kick women and children off of welfare, but you allow these companies to come into our state and get corporate welfare." Edwards also criticized the state for a lack of regulations for things such as data center's water usage, noise pollution and ensuring ratepayers are protected from paying for increased energy demand. She also called for greater transparency around large-load contracts. When it comes to approaching these contracts, Edwards said she would push for fewer redactions and an end to nondisclosure agreements. She said Georgia residents should be able to see what they are paying for and how major projects, like OpenAI's, affect utility costs. She said she also wants contracts to include clearer plans for water use and community benefits as well as protections for ratepayers, ensuring data center companies are paying for needed infrastructure and not receiving abatements or incentives. Edwards said she would like to push for utility companies powering data centers to look into more renewable energy resources, including solar. She said she also worries about strains on power grids, particularly in severe storm-prone south Georgia. Edwards said she also questions the long-term risk of building large amounts of infrastructure around an industry that is expanding rapidly but remains relatively new. "If that bubble bursts," she asked, "who's left holding the bill?" Hubbard said Georgia has provided substantial incentives to data centers while also allowing them to access electricity under favorable large-load arrangements, thus "rolling out the red carpet," for them. When approaching large load contracts, Hubbard said he would push for additional safeguards, including financial protections if projects terminate early. artigo.texto: Em outubro de 2026, drones ucranianos atingiram um centro de dados de inteligência artificial da Yandex, empresa russa frequentemente chamada de “o Google russo”, e tiraram a estrutura de operação, segundo a Ars Technica. A publicação Ars Technica não divulgou a data exata nem a localização da instalação atingida. Também não foram informados números sobre prejuízos financeiros ou quantidade de servidores danificados. A Yandex domina serviços de busca, mapas e plataformas digitais na Rússia, e expandiu sua infraestrutura para processamento de inteligência artificial. A empresa não se pronunciou publicamente sobre o incidente, segundo a Ars Technica. O ataque ao centro de dados de IA demonstra que a guerra entre Rússia e Ucrânia passou a mirar a infraestrutura computacional que sustenta tanto a economia de guerra quanto sistemas de vigilância. A computação de alto desempenho se tornou um ativo estratégico. Diferentemente de alvos tradicionais, a neutralização de um data center de IA compromete a capacidade de processamento massivo de dados, essencial para logística, inteligência e monitoramento em tempo real. A Ars Technica destacou que o ataque representa um precedente em conflitos armados, ampliando o escopo de alvos para infraestrutura digital crítica. Segundo a Ars Technica, a paralisação do centro de dados interrompeu serviços associados à Yandex, mas a extensão do impacto sobre usuários e clientes corporativos não foi detalhada. O episódio consolida a infraestrutura de inteligência artificial como frente de batalha na guerra entre Rússia e Ucrânia, de acordo com a Ars Technica.

artigo.texto: Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN) and Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG) (NASDAQ: GOOGL) are two of the biggest spenders in the artificial intelligence (AI) industry. Each has a sprawling cloud computing business with far more demand than capacity, so they're spending unprecedented amounts of money to expand their data center footprints. For 2026, Amazon plans to spend about $220 billion on capital expenditures, while Alphabet expects to lay out about $200 billion. Nearly all of that will go toward building out data centers. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » While I think both stocks are strong investments, I believe Amazon has far more to gain. But don't sleep on Alphabet, as it's growing at an incredibly fast rate. AWS is a major part of Amazon's overall picture The reason why I think Amazon has more to gain from its cloud computing investment is the position of Amazon Web Services (AWS) within Amazon as a whole. In Q2, AWS accounted for about 21% of Amazon's total revenue. However, AWS produced 60% of Amazon's operating profits. That's a natural result of the fact that e-commerce and retail generally are relatively low-margin businesses; AWS' operating margin is far higher. This magnifies the effect that revenue growth from AWS has on the overall company's profitability. So its net sales rose 20 year over year in Q2, but its operating income increased by 43%. As Amazon continues to invest big time in AWS, its added capacity will translate directly into impressive revenue growth and even larger profit growth. Likewise, Alphabet is benefiting from Google Cloud's growth, but not to the same degree. The company's core business is advertising from its Google family of products, and that already has a pretty strong operating margin. Companywide, Alphabet had an operating margin of 34% in Q2. Google Cloud did slightly better, with a 36% operating margin, but since it's already pretty close to the company's overall margin, it doesn't have the outsized effect on profits that AWS has on Amazon. But don't disregard Google Cloud, either. Google Cloud's revenue growth in Q2 was 82% year over year, while AWS's was 37%. That mismatch shows how Alphabet is rapidly expanding its cloud segment. However, it's doing so off a much smaller base. Amazon is the world's largest cloud infrastructure provider, with a 28% market share as of Q2. While No. 3 Alphabet is slowly cutting into that lead, it still accounts for just 15% of the market. Google Cloud booked $24.8 billion in revenue in Q2, while AWS booked $42.2 billion.

artigo.texto: On Maxxen Day 2026, Maxxen Energy opened its factory in Türkiye to the European energy storage industry and showed the most advanced BESS factory in Europe. Maxxen Day 2026 brought together more than 300 guests from 18 European countries and nearly 120 companies across the battery energy storage system (BESS) value chain. Discussions covered the technology landscape, market outlook and revenues, financing, risk management, as well as project development and scaling, according to Maxxen. Maxxen Day 2026 welcomed energy industry executives, investors, project developers, technology companies and business partners from all across the European continent, from the UK to Türkiye. In just nine months, the company has delivered more than 600 MWh across 20+ projects Maxxen Energy’s factory in Aydın, Türkiye, opened in December 2025. In just nine months, the company has delivered more than 600 MWh across 20+ projects, reaching nearly 5% of the European grid-scale BESS market. Maxxen believes this makes it the fastest-growing European BESS manufacturer ever. At the event, Maxxen also announced its membership in SolarPower Europe. Valiente: We are shaping the future of the industry, together Ruben Valiente, Managing Director of Maxxen Energy, said that on Maxxen Day it opened its factory in Türkiye to the European battery storage industry and showed what the company believes is one of the most advanced BESS factories in Europe. “We also believe Maxxen is the fastest-growing European BESS manufacturer ever, with more than 600 MWh delivered in just nine months. It was a privilege to host guests from all across the European continent, from the UK to Türkiye. Many told us it was one of the best industry events they had attended. None of this happens without people and culture,” he stressed. He thanked the Maxxen Energy team, and colleagues in Türkiye in particular, who work tirelessly and welcome everyone with great warmth. “As a European company, we are proud to contribute to Europe’s energy transition, and we look forward to doing so alongside our peers at SolarPower Europe,” Valiente added. The future of Europe’s energy storage market took centre stage Sessions explored the technology landscape, market dynamics and revenue outlook for Europe’s energy storage market. Panels looked at how to finance the investments needed to meet the growing demand for flexibility, and at the role of risk management and insurance in securing that financing, Maxxen said. Project developers shared what they learned moving from their first projects to large-scale portfolios, and the challenges of scaling. Sessions and panels featuring international companies including Benchmark Mineral Intelligence, Wood Mackenzie, Clean Horizon, Solas Capital, Volteo Capital, Gresham House, Munich Re, Zagope, Luxera and Crowmie brought perspectives from across the BESS value chain. Guests saw the factory in action After the sessions, the programme continued with factory tours and product presentations. Guests followed the production of battery systems step by step and spoke directly with Maxxen’s engineering and technical teams. A networking gathering gave participants time to continue the conversation and build new business connections. On the second day, guests took part in a cultural programme showcasing the heritage of the Aegean region, Maxxen pointed out.
