artigo.texto: A Tower Semiconductor (NASDAQ:TSEM) e a Semtech Corporation (NASDAQ:SMTC) expandiram sua parceria de fabricação de longo prazo por meio de um novo acordo plurianual, projetado para aumentar a capacidade de produção de silício-germânio (SiGe) para produtos avançados de conectividade de data centers. Anunciado em 13 de outubro de 2026, o acordo fornecerá à Semtech capacidade de produção dedicada nas instalações de fabricação da Tower Semiconductor nos Estados Unidos, Israel e Japão. O acordo visa atender à crescente demanda por tecnologias de interconexão óptica e de cobre de alta velocidade utilizadas em infraestrutura de inteligência artificial e centros de dados. O acordo ampliado dá continuidade a uma parceria que já dura aproximadamente 20 anos e inclui planos para desenvolver futuras gerações de tecnologia de conectividade. Os detalhes financeiros do acordo não foram divulgados. Capacidade dedicada de SiGe em três regiões de fabricação Nos termos do acordo ampliado, a Semtech garantirá capacidade de fabricação dedicada de SiGe nas instalações da Tower Semiconductor em três países. A distribuição geográfica tem como objetivo melhorar a resiliência do fornecimento e proporcionar maior flexibilidade de fabricação à medida que a demanda por componentes avançados para centros de dados aumenta. A tecnologia de semicondutores SiGe é utilizada em aplicações de alta frequência que exigem alto desempenho de sinal e transmissão de dados eficiente. A Semtech utiliza os processos de fabricação SiGe da Tower para diversos produtos de seu portfólio de integridade de sinal, incluindo amplificadores de transimpedância, drivers de modulador, drivers de laser e equalizadores lineares. Esses componentes suportam comunicações de alta velocidade, processando, amplificando e mantendo os sinais elétricos usados em sistemas de interconexão óptica e de cobre. As empresas esperam que a capacidade de produção adicional ajude a Semtech a atender às futuras necessidades dos clientes, ao mesmo tempo que apoia o desenvolvimento de redes de data centers cada vez mais avançadas. Ao garantir recursos de produção em várias regiões, a Semtech também visa reduzir sua dependência de locais de fabricação individuais. Acordo prevê suporte para conectividade de 800G, 1.6T e futura de 3.2T A expansão da produção abrange várias gerações de tecnologia de interconexão de alta velocidade. As empresas afirmaram que o acordo dará suporte aos produtos de conectividade atuais de 800G e 1,6T, bem como às futuras tecnologias que operam em velocidades de 3,2T e superiores. Esses avanços estão se tornando cada vez mais importantes à medida que as cargas de trabalho de inteligência artificial criam uma demanda maior por conexões de alta largura de banda entre sistemas de computação. Os modernos centros de dados de IA exigem que grandes volumes de informações se movam entre processadores, servidores e equipamentos de rede. À medida que a infraestrutura de computação se expande, o desempenho das interconexões pode influenciar a eficiência geral do sistema e a capacidade de suportar cargas de trabalho cada vez mais complexas. Os produtos de conectividade óptica e de cobre da Semtech são projetados para atender a esses requisitos por meio de processamento e transmissão de sinal de alta velocidade. O acordo de fabricação ampliado tem como objetivo fornecer a capacidade de produção necessária para dar suporte às gerações sucessivas dessas tecnologias. A Semtech destaca a importância da conectividade com IA O presidente e diretor executivo da Semtech, Hong Hou, enfatizou a crescente importância da infraestrutura de conectividade no suporte a sistemas de inteligência artificial. “A conectividade tornou-se um fator crucial para determinar o alcance da escalabilidade dos sistemas de IA”, disse Hou. “Atender a essa demanda exige planejamento de capacidade a longo prazo e compromissos firmes com nossos parceiros de fabricação.” Seus comentários refletiram a crescente importância dos componentes semicondutores que possibilitam a comunicação entre os sistemas de centros de dados. Com o crescimento da infraestrutura de IA, os fabricantes buscam garantir que a disponibilidade de componentes de rede acompanhe a demanda por equipamentos de computação. A ampliação da parceria com a Tower tem como objetivo proporcionar à Semtech maior visibilidade sobre sua futura capacidade de produção. A Semtech recebe o Prêmio de Inovação em Tecnologia Óptica O anúncio surge na sequência do recente reconhecimento do trabalho da Semtech em conectividade óptica de alta velocidade. Na Conferência Europeia de Comunicação Óptica (ECOC) 2026, a Semtech recebeu um prêmio de Inovação em Componentes Ópticos por sua família de amplificadores de transimpedância de 224 Gbps por canal. Os produtos são projetados para óptica linear plugável e são fabricados utilizando a tecnologia de processo SiGe da Tower Semiconductor. Os amplificadores de transimpedância são componentes importantes em receptores ópticos, convertendo sinais de corrente elétrica gerados por fotodetectores em sinais de tensão que podem ser processados por outros sistemas eletrônicos. O prêmio destacou uma família de produtos desenvolvida por meio da relação de fabricação já estabelecida entre as empresas. Também demonstrou a aplicação da tecnologia SiGe da Tower em equipamentos de comunicação óptica de alta velocidade. As empresas pretendem consolidar essa colaboração no desenvolvimento de futuros produtos de interconexão para aplicações em centros de dados. artigo.texto: Microsoft Pushes Custom AI Chips with Azure Maia 300 Microsoft unveiled Maia 300, its third-generation AI chip, as Maia 200 goes live, powering Copilot. Microsoft on Monday (Oct. 12) unveiled Maia 300, its third-generation in-house AI accelerator, and said that Maia 200 is now in production, powering Copilot and other Microsoft cloud services. The company said it plans to scale deployments of its Azure Maia processor family at multi-gigawatt scale in 2027, positioning Maia as a primary inference system for Microsoft products and services, according to a blog post by Scott Guthrie, Microsoft’s executive vice president, cloud + AI. Microsoft said Maia 200 is deployed across its data centers in the US, Europe, and Australia, delivers up to 1.7 times more tokens per watt than leading GPU infrastructure, and powers built-in AI capabilities in Microsoft Teams, Copilot, and Cowork. By the end of the year, the chip is also expected to power GitHub Copilot and Microsoft Foundry, a platform for developing, deploying, and managing AI applications and agents, according to Guthrie’s blog post. Maia 300, which Microsoft said will be deployed in production in 2027, is designed with an inference-first architecture optimized “for long-context, memory-intensive, and decode-heavy AI workloads,” according to the blog post. The company said the chip is expected to deliver 40% more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU-based systems and, in a full 96-accelerator rack, up to seven times the rack-scale token throughput of Maia 200. Like other hyperscalers, Microsoft continues to rely heavily on Nvidia and AMD GPUs for AI workloads. At the same time, it has spent the last few years building its own custom silicon to improve performance and efficiency across its infrastructure and cloud services. Unlike Amazon Web Services, which offers Trainium and Inferentia chips via public cloud instances, and Google Cloud, which provides access to its TPUs, Microsoft has not made Maia available to customer workloads via Azure instances. In Monday’s blog post, the company did not say whether that could change in the future. Because Microsoft is using Maia primarily for internal workloads, the competitive dynamic is different from a traditional chip war among hyperscalers, said Matt Kimball, vice president and principal analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy. This is about Microsoft and other cloud providers delivering services faster, more efficiently, and more reliably. “That’s good for the customer because they’re getting better quality of service, and it’s good for the cloud provider because they’re doing it at lower cost, which means they’re more profitable,” Kimball said. Kimball said that Maia 300 appears to represent a significant step forward in Microsoft’s custom silicon strategy. “Maia 100 was a proof of concept. Then 200 came out, and they solved the issues they had seen in the 100. They are powering GitHub and Copilot,” he said. “It validated the design choices they were making, and 300 was where they said, ‘Let’s go big,’ and that’s what you are seeing with the Maia 300.” Microsoft’s plan to deploy the Azure Maia family at multi-gigawatt scale suggests broad global adoption across its infrastructure, Kimball noted. “It’s going to be used very broadly to support their workloads across the globe,” he said.

artigo.texto: Damion Smy Toyota agrees to $750 million HiLux, Prado DPF class action settlement 9 Hours Ago Deputy News Editor The Peugeot RCZ Vision has been revealed at the 2026 Paris motor show, with the French brand saying the sleek electric coupe concept previews the look of its future models both inside and out, as well as groundbreaking technology including solid-state batteries. A follow-on from the original petrol-powered RCZ coupe, based on the Peugeot 308 hatch and sold in Australia between 2010 and 2015, the four-seat RCZ Vision concept wraps the brand's upcoming technologies in its 'Feline Future' design language. This includes advanced solid-state battery tech, which promises to be safer and cost less than conventional lithium-ion batteries, as well as being much faster to charge and offer between 20 and 50 per cent longer range per charge. While not confirmed as a production model, the RCZ Vision teams a 1000V electrical architecture with Peugeot's higher-density, space-saving solid-state battery tech. This enables a 500hp (373kW) power output, yet with low claimed energy consumption of just 11.5kWh/100km, with the automaker targeting a 600km WLTP range from a battery pack that's only 110mm thick. Developed with US battery firm Factorial Energy, with which Peugeot parent company Stellantis entered an agreement in 2021, the solid-state battery enables a claimed 10-80 per cent charge in as little as 10 minutes. Beyond its battery tech, the RCZ Vision shows off Peugeot's upcoming design principles, which include an aggressive, muscular stance and new three-claw headlights, also seen on the E-T16 concept revealed in Paris, as well as three-claw tail-lights and an active rear spoiler. Massive 21-inch front and 22-inch rear forged aluminium alloy wheels complement its aggressive haunches, including triangular details in a nod to the original RCZ, while another reference to the original is the double-bubble roof design, which sits above a transparent glass cockpit. The cabin includes the 'Hypersquare' steering wheel seen in the E-T16, along with the 2025 Polygon and the 2023 Inception concepts. The Hypersquare wheel has been confirmed as a feature on the production version of the next-generation 208 hatchback, which is expected to be revealed in 2027, with the 2008 small SUV expected to follow. The RCZ Vision features variable-ratio steer-by-wire steering, reducing driver hand movements at low speeds while adjusting for smoother steering at higher speeds. The RCZ Vision is also the first Peugeot to use brake-by-wire technology, which replaces the conventional hydraulic connection between the brake pedal and calipers with electronic controls. Peugeot says this brings more precise braking modulation and greater efficiency through improved integration of regenerative braking. The Hypersquare steering wheel is teamed with the latest version of Peugeot's i-Cockpit, featuring transparent micro-LED displays positioning configurable data directly in the driver's field of vision, as well as a floating central display angled towards the driver. The recycled-leather-trimmed seats are asymmetrical and offer additional support towards the centre of the vehicle, while the centre console features physical machined-aluminium controls arranged on a piece of frosted glass. Space efficiency measures include movable air vents, which can be stowed when not in use, while a Serica analogue clock forms part of the cabin design. Peugeot's multiple concepts at its home motor show come as the French brand receives greater attention from parent company Stellantis. Earlier this year, Peugeot was named as one of four priority brands by Stellantis, alongside Jeep, Ram and Fiat, ahead of other marques in its stable including Alfa Romeo, Chrysler and Citroën. This bodes well for its future in Australia, after local importer Inchcape, which also distributes brands including Subaru, Deepal and Foton here, announced it would hand back the local Peugeot distribution rights it has held since 2017. A new Australian importer is yet to be officially announced and nor has Stellantis resumed local Citroën distribution following Inchcape's decision to cease distributing the smaller French brand in 2024, ending 102 years of sales in Australia. artigo.texto: Renewable energy producer R.Power is nearing completion of its first utility-scale BESS project in Romania, the 127MW / 254 MWh Scornicesti BESS. EPC contractor Parapet, working with R.Power’s in-house EPC management team, commenced construction in spring 2026. It has, over the past three months, laid foundations and deployed all 46 battery units and 23 containerised medium-voltage transformer stations. Scornicesti BESS will be one of the first assets of its kind in Romania, and one of the largest BESS assets to enter operation in Central & Eastern Europe (CEE). Connecting Scornicesti directly to the high-voltage national transmission grid, operated by Transelectrica, is a major undertaking that goes well beyond a standard project and has required extensive design works. Once connected, expected in late 2026/early 2027, the project will become a strategic energy asset for Romania’s national energy system. R.Power secured a €46 million financing package for the project in June 2026. Under the terms of the deal, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) provided €44 million in investment and bridge financing, while Polish development bank Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego (BGK) issued a €2.3 million bank guarantee to secure the long-term optimisation contract in place with regional trading partner GEN-I. The project, located in Olt County, is co-owned through a JV with France’s Eiffel Investment Group. “As a utility-scale asset connected to the national transmission grid, Scornicesti BESS will actively support the stabilisation of Romania’s energy system.” said Florin Federenciuc, R.Power Country Head for Romania. “By integrating BESS at the heart of its energy transition, Romania is strengthening its grid resilience and supporting the roll-out of renewable energy generation. Having contracted our first Romanian PV assets just two years ago, we are proud to now be playing this vital role in one of Europe’s fastest growth energy transition markets. “Together with EBRD, BGK, Eiffel Investment Group and GEN-I, we look forward to completing the final phase of construction and commissioning and getting this strategic asset to work”. Scornicesti BESS forms part of one of Central and Eastern Europe’s largest utility-scale energy storage pipelines. R.Power’s BESS portfolio in operations and under construction in CEE currently stands at 0.9 GW / 3 GWh, with an additional 0.7 GW / 2.8 GWh of commercialised, ready-to-build projects.

artigo.texto: Peugeot RCZ Vision previews a solid-state battery and 1000V charging Peugeot RCZ Vision is a 500 hp concept with a 110 mm solid-state battery, up to 600 km of range and 10–80% charging in 10 minutes. A 110 mm-thick solid-state battery, 500 hp and a 10–80% charge in ten minutes: Peugeot has presented an unusual continuation of the RCZ story. The RCZ Vision remains a concept and brand manifesto, but it showcases design and technologies Peugeot links to its future models. The key feature is a 1000V electrical architecture and solid-state battery cells developed with Factorial Energy. The concept uses an architecture based on the STLA One platform. Peugeot quotes up to 600 km of range and a target combined WLTP energy consumption of 11.5 kWh/100 km. The company explicitly says that consumption figure still has to be confirmed. The original RCZ is referenced by the sports-coupe format and its distinctive double-bubble roof. The new car is far more futuristic, with a low silhouette, pronounced fenders, a transparent upper body section and an active rear spoiler that deploys while driving. Inside, there is a Hypersquare control and Steer-by-Wire with no mechanical steering connection to the wheels. RCZ Vision is also Peugeot’s first model to demonstrate Brake-by-Wire electronic brake control. The concept differs from the former coupe by much more than the absence of a petrol engine. Peugeot presents RCZ Vision as a showcase for solid-state batteries, a 1000V architecture, X-by-Wire technologies and a new generation of the i-Cockpit driver interface. Peugeot has not announced a production date, a final production specification or a price. It is therefore too early to call RCZ Vision a confirmed return of the RCZ to showrooms: for now, the company has revived the idea of the coupe as a concept and shown technologies that could reach future Peugeot models.

artigo.texto: PHOENIX — Gov. Katie Hobbs and her Republican opponent, U.S. Rep. Andy Biggs, have one thing they can agree on: data centers. Both reject calls for a moratorium on new data centers proposed by Attorney General Kris Mayes, with Hobbs saying it’s not the right approach. "I think there are places where data centers make sense, and they're an important part of the high-tech economy that we're growing here,” she told reporters last month. Biggs agrees. After last week’s gubernatorial debate, he said local communities should have the final say. “There are many who don't want them at all, and others that are willing to investigate and are thinking about getting them,” he said. Do you have a concern in your community or a news tip? We want to hear from you! Connect with us: share@abc15.com He pointed to Marana’s decision to approve a data center after Tucson’s city council rejected a proposal for a Project Blue facility, saying “the company’s moving to Marana.” However, the Marana facility is one of up to three sites Project Blue’s developer, Beale Infrastructure, is working on. The company moved the proposed Tucson facility to just outside the city, in an unincorporated part of Pima County, after the city rejected the project. Biggs and Hobbs both say Arizona needs state standards for water and power use at data centers. “That data centers pay for themselves,” Hobbs said. “That they're not raising utility costs on Arizonans. That they're using water sustainably, and that they're addressing real and valid community concerns about data centers in neighborhoods.” She pushed for the repeal of state tax incentives for data centers – a tax break she voted for when she was a lawmaker in the state Senate. Hobbs negotiated a three-year moratorium on the incentives in this year’s budget with legislative Republicans. “We landed in a good place, and we can still have conversations about the water use, the energy use,” Hobbs said in July. Biggs, who voted against the incentives when he was in the Senate, said he wants to get rid of them permanently if elected governor. “Well, the first thing we're going to do is, we're not going to provide taxpayer subsidies or incentives for data centers to come in here,” he said. Biggs said he’s met with industry leaders and told them they don’t need the incentives. “I haven't had anybody say that they would leave without those incentives or with the constraints that I've proposed,” he said. Biggs has proposed developers pay for all the needed infrastructure and that data centers not “encroach on current and future natural growth of water and energy policy.” Hobbs, who has said she still supports a repeal of the tax breaks, said the current three-year freeze on new applications is an opportunity to craft a data-center policy. "I understand that many Arizonans are worried about data centers, and we want to make sure we're addressing those concerns in the right way,” she said. Meanwhile, Mayes is holding a town hall in Mesa on Oct. 14 to discuss her proposed statewide moratorium on new data centers. “We need a temporary ban,” she told reporters after last month's attorney general debate. “We need a pause so that we can get our hands around this situation.” Mayes said she’s working on a plan for a new approval process that would allow communities to vote on data center projects and create a commission to review proposed data centers like the Arizona Power Plant and Transmission Line Siting Committee does for energy projects.

artigo.texto: GreenYellow and Tilt Energy Partner to Deploy Battery Storage at Industrial Sites GreenYellow finances and operates the batteries, while Tilt Energy handles their dispatch and market valorisation. The two companies launch a behind-the-meter storage offer with no upfront investment for industrial and commercial sites. GreenYellow and Tilt Energy announce a partnership aimed at accelerating the deployment of Behind-the-Meter (BTM) electricity storage systems in the industrial and commercial sectors. According to the two companies, the offer is built on an integrated, contractually backed Battery Energy Storage System (BESS). Energy storage is drawing in other players across different segments, such as Trinasolar, which is unveiling 760 W solar modules and battery storage in Vietnam, or, on the gas side, Naftogaz and Siemens Energy, which are considering five compressor units for Ukrainian gas storage. GreenYellow describes itself as an industrial orchestrator of flexible electrification since 2007, and Tilt Energy as a specialist in valorising electrical flexibility. A split of roles between financing and dispatch GreenYellow designs, finances, builds, operates and maintains the energy storage infrastructure. Tilt Energy handles its real-time dispatch and valorises the flexibility on electricity markets. The two companies say this complementarity gives customers access to a solution combining infrastructure, financing and energy management. They state that the offer allows customers to benefit from storage flexibility with no upfront investment, no exposure to electricity market risk and with contractually guaranteed performance. Company GreenYellow: company profile Three obstacles identified by the partners According to GreenYellow and Tilt Energy, many companies remain held back despite growing interest in batteries. The partners cite three obstacles: the level of initial investment, the technical and operational complexity of projects, and uncertainty around flexibility revenues. In the proposed model, GreenYellow bears the investment and performance commitments are contractualised. Operation of the asset and valorisation of its flexibility are entrusted to specialists, and the customer receives a turnkey solution. The two companies specify that the offer goes beyond a simple "Battery-as-a-Service" formula, without the customer having to handle the complexities of financing, operation and valorisation. Storage integrated into flexible electrification GreenYellow places this offer within a broader vision of flexible electrification. The company says the aim is not only to install a battery but to integrate it into a package combining energy efficiency, electrification of uses, local renewable power generation and smart management. "Electricity storage should no longer be considered as a mere energy technology, but as a full-fledged industrial infrastructure," says Mathieu Cambet, Strategy Director at GreenYellow. He adds that companies need solutions that improve their efficiency and resilience without tying up more capital. The context described by the partners combines volatile electricity prices, growing electrification of uses and the development of renewable energy. - Gas44.1 % - Nuclear16.1 % - Coal15.7 % - Solar10.6 % - Wind8.3 % - Hydro3.5 % - Bioenergy0.9 % - Other fossil0.5 % - Other renewables0.4 %

artigo.texto: Maxxen Day 2026 welcomed energy industry executives, investors, project developers, technology companies and business partners from all across the European continent, from the UK to Türkiye. Maxxen Energy’s factory in Ayd?n, Türkiye, opened in December 2025. In just nine months, the company has delivered more than 600 MWh across 20+ projects, reaching nearly 5% of the European grid-scale BESS market. Maxxen believes this makes it the fastest-growing European BESS manufacturer ever. At the event, Maxxen also announced its membership of SolarPower Europe. The future of Europe’s energy storage market took centre stage Sessions explored the technology landscape, market dynamics and revenue outlook for Europe’s energy storage market. Panels looked at how to finance the investments needed to meet the growing demand for flexibility, and at the role of risk management and insurance in securing that financing. Project developers shared what they learned moving from their first projects to large-scale portfolios, and the challenges of scaling. Sessions and panels featuring international companies including Benchmark Mineral Intelligence, Wood Mackenzie, Clean Horizon, Solas Capital, Volteo Capital, Gresham House, Munich Re, Zagope, Luxera and Crowmie brought perspectives from across the BESS value chain. “We are shaping the future of the industry, together” Ruben Valiente, Managing Director of Maxxen Energy, said: “At Maxxen Day we opened our factory in Türkiye to the European battery storage industry and showed what we believe is one of the most advanced BESS factories in Europe. We also believe Maxxen is the fastest-growing European BESS manufacturer ever, with more than 600 MWh delivered in just nine months. It was a privilege to host guests from all across the European continent, from the UK to Türkiye. Many told us it was one of the best industry events they had attended. None of this happens without people and culture. My thanks go to the Maxxen Energy team, and to our colleagues in Türkiye in particular, who work tirelessly and welcome everyone with great warmth. As a European company, we are proud to contribute to Europe’s energy transition, and we look forward to doing so alongside our peers at SolarPower Europe.” Guests saw the factory in action After the sessions, the programme continued with factory tours and product presentations. Guests followed the production of battery energy storage systems step by step and spoke directly with Maxxen’s engineering and technical teams. A networking gathering gave participants time to continue the conversation and build new business connections. On the second day, guests took part in a cultural programme showcasing the heritage of the Aegean region.

artigo.texto: The News Despite increasingly critical media coverage of AI and the spread of data centers across the US, one news network has been painting a more positive picture. More than half of the references to data centers on Fox News over the last two years would have left viewers with a favorable impression, compared to less than 10% on CNN and 5% on MS NOW, according to a new Semafor analysis of mentions of data centers on each network. The mentions were pulled from closed captions preserved by the Internet Archive, which keeps a digital, searchable library of recorded TV news. A pair of AI models from Anthropic and OpenAI scored each reference on its content, with the networkâs name removed. Mentions of data centers have, predictably, shot up across all three networks in recent months as political backlash against AI swells and the data centers themselves have become a salient issue ahead of the midterms. But Foxâs opinion and morning shows, including My View with Lara Trump, Fox & Friends, and Life, Liberty & Levin, leaned on the promise of AI, economic investment and the race with China, skewing Foxâs coverage more favorably, the analysis showed. The networkâs news shows were more measured. In an Aug. 23 monologue that at one point featured a chyron reading âThe case for data centers,â Fox host Brian Kilmeade acknowledged âreal concerns,â but argued that âsaying no to data centers nationwide also means saying no to the tax dollars that can flow into a community. â¦ If Americans donât build the infrastructure to meet the demand, somebody else will.â On CNN and MS NOW, the criticism focused as much on the facilitiesâ political toxicity as on harms like power bills or water use, casting them as unpopular with voters and a liability for politicians who back them heading into the midterms. Data centers âare driving up energy costs, sucking up water supplies, wiping out rather than creating jobs,â MS NOWâs Katy Tur said in May. âPoliticians beware.â Polling shows that across demographic groups, Americans hold increasingly negative views of data centers: More than half of Americans say data centers are mostly bad for the environment, Pew Research Center found last month, compared with 39% in January. Fox News did not comment for this story. In this article: Maxâs view The pro-data center programming on Fox News comes as the right tries to define its positions in an AI-fueled, post-Donald Trump future. Foxâs favorable data center coverage mirrors Trumpâs position on their growth and the need for AI companies to help fuel the US economy. âThe only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,â Trump wrote on Truth Social in August. âIf we kill the Golden Goose, you will only have yourselves to blame.â But anger about data centers and the rapid advancement of AI represents a faultline within the MAGA coalition that swept Trump back into office. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., have questioned some data centers in their states, while Texas Gov. Greg Abbott seems to have flipped from supporting data centers to looking to slow their growth in his state amid a tougher-than-expected reelection campaign. Some on the right I have talked to in the last several months worry that Fox News, which Trump watches religiously, and other pro-data center voices are encouraging the president to take positions that are broadly unpopular with his rural and suburban base. âThe Big Tech oligarchs, the guys driving AI, did a terrible job,â Steve Bannon, a staunchly anti-AI Trump ally, told the Daily Signal in September. âThey came in to try to muscle local communities, and particularly since President Trumpâs strongest base is in exurban and rural communities, thatâs where they were really the ugliest, and they havenât made their case, and they particularly havenât made their case at the local level about the economics of this, and the energy of this, and the water of this, and the manifestation of what these things are going to be used for.â Room for Disagreement Not all of Foxâs data center coverage has been rosy; its tenor grew slightly less favorable in 2026 compared to last year. âItâs taxing our system way too much on water, agriculture land, or electricity. Weâre gonna implode,â the Texas agriculture commissioner said in an interview on a weekend Fox show in August. âWe just canât do it. Thereâs not enough.

artigo.texto: Microsoft purchases over 600 acres in Woodward to build a data center In a residents-only community meeting Monday night, Woodward’s mayor and Microsoft representatives unveiled plans for the company to build a data center within city limits. More than 200 residents gathered in the auditorium of Woodward-Granger High School to hear details about the project and express their opinions. It comes as Microsoft purchased over 600 acres of land in Woodward late last week. The land was purchased from an independent seller, not from the city. It’s already zoned for industrial use, which includes data centers. Tempers flared within the meeting, with one person being escorted out by police as Microsoft officials and Mayor Todd Folkerts answered questions about the project. Many said they were frustrated at the lack of community involvement in the project. “Is this something that we get a vote on? I mean, something this big, the community should get to vote on instead of doing back-ended deals,” one resident said. Folkerts said residents would not get to vote on the matter, but city council would vote on negotiations between Microsoft and the city. Microsoft representatives said the project would bring dozens of jobs, increase the tax base, and would not impact utility costs for residents. Something Folkerts says is necessary. “I can safely say I have not seen a single one of you at a budget meeting when we try to balance a budget for this community,” he said to the crowd. “We have to find revenue sources for our community.” But frustrations extended beyond the data center. The meeting, which replaced the city’s regular city council meeting, was open to Woodward residents only. Attendees had to show proof of residency to get inside, and several people were turned away. Randy Evans, president of Iowa’s Freedom of Information Council, was one of the people turned away. He said requiring proof of residency goes against Iowa’s open meeting laws. “It runs counter to the openness that the public meetings all guarantee,” Evans told KCCI. “From my vantage point, it erodes the trust and confidence, and the respect for Woodward city government.” Microsoft said the building has not been designed, and doing so would take roughly two years before construction could even begin.

artigo.texto: Indiana utility regulators unanimously approved a plan for utility AES Indiana to build the solar, battery storage and electric line project needed to power a 390-megawatt Google data center project in Monrovia. At the Oct. 7 meeting, the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission said the proposed project meets a 2025 state law that requires data centers and other large electricity users to cover 80% of costs reasonably assigned to it. The law also requires the plan to protect existing and future customers. The Monrovia project is the first data center filed under the new law. AES estimates the infrastructure investment at $1.3 billion. AES Indiana says Google will pay all of the costs. But the order says it is reasonable for existing customers to be assigned a share of the cost upgrades. The Citizens Action Coalition objected to this. AES Indiana says Google’s payments to the utility system will make up for customers’ costs. The Monrovia project, southwest of Indianapolis in Morgan County, will include two battery energy storage systems and a solar facility. The total project cost is $737.3 million. Commissioner Joby Jerrells said AES Indiana had testified that Google would pay for at least 100% of the costs under the requirement. “Not only does this agreement satisfy the statutory requirement, it exceeds it substantially,” Jerrells said. Regulators put their approval in a written order. It explains the energy project is designed to mainly serve large electricity customers, like the Google data center, while protecting current AES customers. Several groups joined the case, including the Indiana Office of Utility Consumer Counselor, a consumer watchdog; Citizens Action Coalition, a nonprofit consumer advocate; the AES Indiana Industrial Group; and several residents of Morgan County. Brian A. Wright, an electric utility analyst with the consumer counselor’s office, testified that power line transmission upgrades wouldn’t be necessary without the data center’s energy needs. The office did not oppose the plan. “What we’re concerned about is a $74 million set of transmission upgrades that AES Indiana identified that it had to make specifically because this Google data center is being added to the grid,” Ben Inskeep, program director at Citizens Action Coalition, said. AES US Utilities CEO Gustavo Garaviglia said in testimony that Google will pay $32.3 million for direct connection facilities, while $73.8 million in network upgrades will be included in AES’s transmission rate base and recovered in future retail rates. Bickey Rimal, vice president of consulting firm Concentric Energy Advisors, testified for AES that it wouldn’t be reasonable to assign all transmission upgrades to Google because the utility hadn’t done that with a customer in the past, and the upgrades would benefit all customers. The commission agreed. Inskeep said the data center, not the customer, should foot the upgrade costs. “We already have high bills here in Indianapolis,” he said. “We don’t need more rate increases caused by data centers to be added on top.” In a statement, AES Indiana President Brandi Davis-Handy called the approval “an important milestone.” The company has said that the partnership with Google protects existing customers. “None of those costs are shifted to existing AES Indiana customers,” it said. Google’s head of data centers in the Americas, Will Conkling, said that the company is paying for 100% of its electricity and any new infrastructure required to serve them. AES said the agreement will benefit customers by spreading fixed costs to more users and bring the cost per customer down, and that its modeling estimated about $770 million in savings during the term of the project. The contract with Google lasts at least 15 years, according to AES, and includes assurances that customers won’t get stuck paying for upgrades if Google scales back or leaves the project. AES also requested to keep certain information confidential, including portions of temporary, electric and construction service agreements and testimony. The Citizens Action Coalition raised concerns about that. The commission approved the request for confidentiality because the information includes trade secrets exempt from public disclosure under state law. A spokesperson for AES Indiana, Claire Rice, said in response to emailed questions seeking details about the agreements and what customer protections exist, that the company’s filings could be found in the case. “I want to clarify that the agreements are filed publicly with only certain competitively sensitive and confidential information redacted. The terms and details of the customer protection provisions and customer benefits have not been redacted,” she said. The electric, construction and temporary service agreements are filed as exhibits, but they include many redactions, including dollar amounts, rate schedules and timelines. The utility commission recently agreed to reconsider its June approval of a rate increase for AES Indiana. It will consider evidence related to the Monrovia data center project and the announced acquisition of AES’s parent company by BlackRock and other investors. The review will continue into 2027. artigo.texto: Câmara aprova urgência para PL que muda divisão de custos de armazenamento de energia Em redação dada pela lei de 2025, foi fixado que os sistemas de armazenamento de energia, na forma de baterias, terão custos de contratação rateados apenas entre os geradores de energia A Câmara dos Deputados aprovou nesta terça-feira (13) o requerimento de urgência do projeto de lei que abre margem para o custo da contratação de baterias ser arcado pelos usuários finais de energia elétrica do Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN), incluídos os consumidores. Ainda não há data para a votação do mérito do texto (PL 3716/2026), que deve ficar para após o segundo turno. Em redação dada pela lei de 2025, foi fixado que os sistemas de armazenamento de energia, na forma de baterias, terão custos de contratação rateados apenas entre os geradores de energia. Isso gerou críticas do setor e um dos argumentos é a falta de um tratamento isonômico. As baterias serão contratadas na modalidade de "reserva de capacidade". Em geral, os custos administrativos e financeiros e os encargos tributários precisam ser rateados entre todos os usuários finais de energia elétrica do SIN, incluídos os consumidores. A exceção, contudo, foi dada aos sistemas de armazenamento de energia. A proposta de mudança é do deputado Arnaldo Jardim (Cidadania-SP). O tema é controverso porque a Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) já está trabalhando na regulamentação do tema com base na legislação em vigor. Os inéditos leilões para baterias estão previstos para dezembro. Em nota conjunta, um grupo de seis entidades apontou que o armazenamento de energia, inclusive em baterias, é capaz de reduzir outros encargos suportados pelo consumidor ao otimizar a operação do parque gerador em suas diversas fontes. Foi citado estudo da Volt Robotics, ao demonstrar que as baterias podem reduzir a variação do preço da energia (PLD) e o acionamento de termelétricas, gerando economia superior a R$ 1,6 bilhão ao ano para o consumidor. "Os custos da reserva de capacidade são distribuídos entre todos os usuários finais, conforme parâmetros definidos em lei. Porém, apenas os sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias são tratados de maneira diversa, sendo custeados exclusivamente pelos geradores e sem definição legal dos parâmetros de custeio", apontou o grupo de entidades. Assinaram a nota conjunta: a Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica e Novas Tecnologias (ABEEólica), a Associação Brasileira dos Investidores em Autoprodução de Energia (Abiape), a Associação Brasileira da Indústria do Hidrogênio Verde (ABIHV), a Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia (ABSAE), a Associação Brasileira de Energia Solar Fotovoltaica (Absolar) e a Associação Brasileira dos Produtores Independentes de Energia Elétrica (Apine). O que diz a ABSAE? A Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia (ABSAE) disse em nota que o avanço da proposta com urgência aprovada hoje "é importante para ampliar a segurança jurídica e criar condições mais previsíveis para a realização dos primeiros leilões de baterias em larga escala no Brasil". "A aprovação da urgência representa um avanço para que o Congresso discuta o tema com a celeridade necessária. Em paralelo precisamos olhar para o prazo dos leilões: o sistema elétrico necessita de potência adicional em 2028, e é plenamente possível corrigir a isonomia no rateio enquanto prossegue o cronograma. Assim vamos equilibrar segurança energética, redução de custos sistêmicos e segurança jurídica", afirma Fabio Lima, diretor-executivo da ABSAE.

artigo.texto: Contemporary Amperex Technology (CATL) has published results in all three waves of the Global Battery Alliance (GBA) battery passport pilot, a record the Chinese battery maker says no rival has matched. The latest round covered cell producers with nearly 80% of global capacity, ahead of a full certification scheme due in early 2027. The pilot is building a shared method to track, measure and verify the environmental, social and governance (ESG) record of a battery over its life. CATL’s entry this year reported ESG data for every stage of supply, from mining and refining through materials, cells and packs. That breadth matters as passports move from trial to obligation. EU rules will require digital passports for electric vehicle batteries from February 2027, giving suppliers with verified upstream data an edge with European automakers. CATL joined at the GBA’s first proof of concept in January 2023, and in the second wave sought separate passports for its Shenxing and cell-to-pack batteries, with results checked by an independent auditor. It also says its core operations are carbon neutral and targets a carbon-neutral value chain by 2035. In a statement, Dennis Pan, Head of Sustainable Development at CATL, said: “The GBA Battery Passport pilot program provides an effective methodology for the industry to monitor, quantify and demonstrate ESG performance across the battery value chain. It helps the industry better prepare for future sustainability risks and challenges.” Source: CATL

artigo.texto: ACC (Automotive Cells Company) JV Stellantis, Mercedes, Saft Exide Technologies, headquartered in France, has introduced Solition Powerflex, a modular battery energy storage system (BESS) intended for commercial and industrial use, renewable energy integration, e-mobility infrastructure and agricultural facilities, ESS News reported. The product combines a 261 kWh LFP battery with a 125 kW bidirectional power conversion system (PCS) housed in an outdoor cabinet. In grid-connected setups, as many as 15 cabinets may be paralleled, delivering a maximum combined capacity of 3.915 MWh and 1.875 MW of power output. Off-grid installations can accommodate up to five cabinets. Within each cabinet sit five battery packs, each rated at 52.25 kWh and based on 314 Ah LFP cells. Charge and discharge rates reach 0.5C, while the system runs at 400 V AC and either 50 Hz or 60 Hz. Per the manufacturer's technical datasheet, nominal round-trip efficiency stands at 86%, inclusive of auxiliary power consumption. The IP55-rated outdoor cabinet has dimensions of 1,000 mm x 1,420 mm x 2,250 mm and a weight of approximately 2,720 kg, taking up roughly 1.42 m2. It is built to run at ambient temperatures from -20 C to 50 C, with power derating kicking in above 45 C. A dual-loop liquid cooling and heating system handles thermal management, using separate circuits for the battery and the power conversion system, rated at 5 kW and 3 kW respectively. Built into the cabinet are a battery management system, energy management system, PCS, thermal management and fire protection equipment. Safety provisions encompass automatic aerosol fire suppression, emergency shutdown, audible and visual alarms, explosion relief devices and a dedicated external firefighting interface. Exide stated that the system features a European-developed Storage Control System (SCS) that permits integration with on-site generation assets, grid operators and energy markets. Applications supported include peak shaving, self-consumption optimization, spot-market trading and ancillary services. The control platform further delivers remote monitoring, over-the-air software updates and interfaces for third-party systems. Exide noted that its digital architecture encompasses encrypted remote connections, EU-based data hosting and multilayer access controls. Serge Arbes, senior business director global, energy solutions, at Exide Technologies, said organizations increasingly want to boost energy resilience, integrate renewable generation and optimize energy costs. He added that Solition Powerflex was created to meet these evolving requirements, pairing a scalable architecture with advanced control capabilities in a solution able to adapt to shifting business needs. Standard warranty terms were not disclosed by Exide. The technical datasheet notes that battery capacity and system warranty conditions can be obtained upon request. artigo.texto: O novo "reduto" da China em sua ambição de construir o maior centro de dados do mundo. A área parece uma miragem de alta tecnologia. Fileiras de enormes centros de dados, tanto recém-concluídos quanto em construção, erguem-se em meio a planícies onduladas e campos de girassóis e sorgo. Os edifícios ostentam os nomes de algumas das maiores empresas de tecnologia da China , desde a gigante de hardware Huawei e a plataforma de mídia social Kuaishou até a provedora de serviços VNET. Todas estão concentradas em uma área constantemente movimentada por atividades de construção e operação. Esta é Ulanqab, uma cidade na Região Autônoma da Mongólia Interior, na China, localizada na orla do Deserto de Gobi. Ela está se tornando rapidamente um dos polos de dados que impulsionam o poderoso boom da inteligência artificial (IA) na China, posicionando o país como o único rival verdadeiramente formidável dos EUA em sua ambição de domínio tecnológico. Quase 90 data centers estão planejados para serem construídos nesta cidade com menos de 2 milhões de habitantes. Ulanqab possui um número crescente de centros de dados de IA e big data, demonstrando as vantagens que a China está ganhando na corrida para desenvolver tecnologias que podem moldar o século XXI. As estruturas gigantescas aqui foram construídas em ritmo acelerado. Grande parte do Parque Industrial de Big Data de Bayin, densamente construído, foi formada em apenas dois anos. Isso demonstra a capacidade de construção rápida da China. Ventos fortes, sol intenso e vastos espaços abertos proporcionam à região acesso a energia verde barata e abundantes recursos de terra. Ulanqab faz parte da visão de Pequim de expandir rapidamente sua infraestrutura de dados. Essa é uma prioridade fundamental para o governo chinês, que vê a IA como um motor de crescimento crucial para sua economia em desaceleração, em meio a uma população em declínio. “A China abriu os braços para a IA”, disse o presidente chinês Xi Jinping em uma conferência global sobre inteligência artificial em Xangai, em julho passado. Ele mencionou iniciativas para integrar a IA em diversas áreas, da saúde aos eletrodomésticos, e elogiou os esforços para integrar a IA na indústria como um dos destaques da modernização da China. Segundo estatísticas oficiais, mais de 700 milhões de pessoas na China utilizam atualmente IA. O plano de integrar a IA na manufatura, na indústria e no cotidiano também exige enorme poder computacional. No mês passado, a China anunciou um plano de US$ 560 bilhões para expandir rapidamente sua infraestrutura de informação nos próximos cinco anos. Empresas privadas de tecnologia também estão aumentando seus investimentos em infraestrutura de IA, embora ainda estejam muito atrás de suas contrapartes do Vale do Silício, nos EUA. Segundo a empresa de pesquisa Rhodium Group, o investimento total de empresas chinesas listadas na bolsa nesse setor dobrará este ano, chegando a aproximadamente US$ 139 bilhões. No entanto, esse valor ainda representa menos de um quinto dos US$ 800 bilhões investidos em data centers de IA por empresas americanas. As empresas chinesas também enfrentam outro desafio sério: o fornecimento limitado de hardware de ponta para equipar data centers. As proibições de exportação dos EUA restringem o acesso aos melhores chips de IA, como alguns modelos da Nvidia e da AMD, enquanto a China também limita as importações de alguns chips de desempenho inferior. Os fabricantes nacionais de chips estão correndo para alcançar a concorrência, mas a tecnologia ainda está atrás da dos EUA, e o fornecimento dos modelos mais avançados continua escasso. "Considerando o custo total de construção de um centro de dados, os chips são o fator mais importante, e a China simplesmente não tem chips suficientes", disse Nick Corvino, pesquisador da Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. Você também pode gostar No entanto, o que a China não tem em termos de chips e capital de investimento pode ser compensado por outra vantagem: eletricidade abundante e acessível, grande parte da qual é energia verde. Fontes de energia em excesso Enquanto os centros de dados com alto consumo de energia pressionam a rede elétrica dos EUA, a China adicionou capacidade de geração de energia entre 2022 e 2025 equivalente à capacidade total de todas as fontes de energia industrial dos EUA até o final de 2025. artigo.texto: Amazon recently followed Microsoft’s lead and said it will no longer use nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) while negotiating with local governments over data centers. On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Sean O’Kane, Rebeccan Bellan and I discussed Amazon’s announcement, which came in the middle of a longer blog post making the case that data centers are actually good for communities. Rebecca was a bit skeptical that the recent spate of data center moratoriums will have a lasting effect, especially since the moratoriums only last for a year or two and “these data centers aren’t coming online for the next two, three, four, five years,” though I countered that data center backers definitely seem worried. Sean, meanwhile, suggested that a big reason for the backlash is the industry’s poor communication. “We’ve seen, through a lot of the controversy and backlash to AI and data centers, that the industry just does a really poor job explaining itself, and that they are obviously and constantly frustrated with the fact that most people can’t envision a world in which this stuff is useful for them,” he said. Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity. Sean O’Kane: It’s an interesting thing that it was sort of buried in the blog post and part of a larger story that Amazon’s clearly trying to tell. I guess I understand why they weren’t putting it in the foreground, but to me, this is at the root of so many of the problems that the tech industry currently faces when it comes to AI broadly, but data centers in particular. There are so many things that could be said about whether or not people should be worried about the effect that data centers have on their property values, on their electricity bills, on their water usage in the area, and whether or not those things are real problems, inflated problems, etc. etc. I think so much of that just really goes back to the fact that a lot of these projects are being negotiated essentially in secret. Sometimes they’re being negotiated [with the public knowing] that it’s a data center, but just not knowing who’s actually going to use it or occupy it at any point. This is a long-standing issue with the tech industry. I always go back to the mid-2010s when Uber was expanding really fast. Uber was one of the companies that really used this tactic a ton when it came to working with local governments. In particular, I remember I was working at The Verge at the time and we had a freelancer write a story about a city outside of Orlando where Uber was trying to negotiate tax subsidies to subsidize rides for people to use public transit after the Uber trip. The whole thing was negotiated in secret. And not only that, which was frustrating on its face, but also, because of the secrecy, you could just see Uber getting really comfortable with asking for a lot of other stuff, too. So there needs to be more of this. I’m glad Amazon’s doing this. We’ll see if it actually does have any positive effect, but people are pretty entrenched right now. Rebecca Bellan: Yeah, I’m curious about what effect this will have and whether it will lead to communities successfully delaying or or killing any infrastructure that the companies need to build. What I’ve heard from some people I’ve spoken to, who deal with data centers every day, a lot of these moratoriums that are getting passed — and there are a significant number of them, including one recently in San Francisco, which is pretty ironic — but they’re only for like a year or two years. But these data centers aren’t coming online for the next two, three, four, five years. All of the buildouts are going to be massively delayed for a number of reasons from zoning to funding. Of course, if the pushback keeps going, then it might have an effect, but I often wonder just how much of an effect this political pushback is having on this. Anthony Ha: The moratorium I’m most familiar with is the one in New York. I believe it’s a one year moratorium, and that’s on permits for large projects. [Technically, it’s until the state finalizes an environmental review process, which is expected to take a year.] So already, there’s some wiggle room within that. And often, they’re framed as: “It’s not like we think [data centers are] bad, let’s not do this. It’s [that] we need to take the time to study this.” Which gives them a lot of room to say later on, “Actually, we’ve decided this is great. We love it.” But you can tell that the people trying to build these data centers are worried, which is why you have these unhinged tweets from people like Trump or David Sacks. Only time will tell in terms how long and how deep that [community] resistance is, but I do think they are worried. It’s also noteworthy that Microsoft, earlier this year, made a similar announcement about not using NDAs. I don’t think that getting rid of the NDAs automatically is going to make the people who opposed these data centers be like, “Great, let’s let’s do it. I’m in.” But I think the beginning of that conversation is, “Well, we don’t even know what the heck you’re doing, because you’ve negotiated all this stuff in secret.” So it does seem like a good first step. Sean: The larger problem here is just a communication problem, right? This is a problem I think that goes across the entire tech industry, but it’s especially acute now, because we’re living in the era of “going direct” and “you don’t need to talk to the media, the media is dead,” etc. And I’m not trying to beat that horse, because we’re in the media and [we] think we’re still relevant. artigo.texto: - The companies are developing the new module because their customers are asking for it - Customers want to embrace more powerful technology for AI workloads with something they’re familiar with - The new modules will increase bandwidth density from 200 Gbps-per-lane to 400 Gbps-per-lane. OCP GLOBAL SUMMIT, SAN JOSE, CALIFORNIA — Cisco and Nvidia this week unveiled plans to develop an ultra-dense small form factor pluggable (USFP) optic module for AI data centers. The USFP is capable of 400 Gbps-per-lane and is expected to deliver 4x the bandwidth density and 1.3x the power efficiency of 200 Gbps-per-lane optics. The companies are developing the USFP because their hyperscaler and neocloud customers are asking for it. The customers want to extend their use of octal small form factor (OSFP) modules but scale from 200 Gbps-per-lane to 400 Gbps-per-lane. With USFP, they can embrace next-generation optical technology for AI workloads without overhauling their data center infrastructure. Fierce asked Will Eatherton, Cisco SVP of Engineering, to break down all this information for us. He said pluggable modules are used in AI data centers to connect servers — which house the GPUs — to the switches. The modules “have the fiber optic pigtail coming out of them, and these plug into both servers as well as into the switches, and then the optic runs between, and that's how you connect up your cluster of hundreds of thousands to millions of GPUs,” he said. The current OSFP technology is topping out, and data centers need an upgrade for the future. In terms of the increase in “lanes,” this refers to the tiny copper pathways that carry electrical signals between the chip and the optical module. Eatherton said others are working on different solutions to increase bandwidth for pluggable optic modules in data centers. For instance, Arista and Broadcom are working on a solution called XPO that involves liquid cooling going to the module. And co-packaged optics (CPO) is another alternative. But Eatherton said Cisco has gotten feedback from its customers that what they really want is something that's like the old thing, but in the next generation. For their USFP, Cisco and Nvidia will work with a variety of vendors. “These modules will have massive engineering,” said Eatherton. “You have an ecosystem. So, what we're announcing is we have simulated and tested and are ready for this module to move into the next stage. And Cisco and Nvidia will champion it.” They will work with connector vendors and then go through a process of forming an open standard. And that’s why they announced the new product at the Open Compute Project (OCP) event, because OCP is all about open technologies that aren't proprietary or locked in. Interestingly, even though Cisco and Nvidia are working together, and Arista and Broadcom are working on the competing standard XPO, Eatherton said that ultimately, everyone will probably support both standards just to cover their bases in terms of providing customers whichever product they want. Although Cisco and Nvidia are not giving specifics about roadmaps or timelines for their USFP, Eatherton said everything is moving so fast it will take a matter of months, not years. Its target market for OSFP are the AI hyperscalers, neoclouds, telcos around the world that are creating sovereign AI clouds, and even high end-enterprises. artigo.texto: SAN ANTONIO – Residents gathered at Northwest Vista College on Tuesday to voice concerns about data center development in San Antonio and discuss what regulations city leaders should consider as they prepare to update the city’s land development rules. The town hall, hosted by District 6 Councilman Ric Galvan, the Greater Edwards Aquifer Alliance and Public Citizen, focused on issues including water use, electricity demand, noise, zoning and the effects of data centers on nearby neighborhoods. The meeting also gave residents an opportunity to learn about the city’s process for updating its Unified Development Code and share feedback on proposed data center regulations. The city’s Development Services Department is drafting regulations for data centers, with City Council expected to vote on the rules in the near future. Randy Sipe said residents need more notice about proposed projects before permits are approved and construction begins. “When you first notice them, it’s too late to do anything because I’ve been to some meetings before and unfortunately the permits are done and over,” Sipe said. “So once they break ground, there is no stopping them.” Luis Leon said he is concerned about how data center development could affect future generations, particularly access to water and electricity costs. “I’m concerned about the future of my descendants,” Leon said. “I want to know that they’re going to be OK, that they’re going to have water and the cost of electricity.” Residents also discussed where data centers should be allowed, how noise should be controlled and what requirements developers should meet. Potential policy changes discussed at the meeting included establishing a clear, updated definition of a data center, revisiting zoning qualifications, strengthening site plan requirements and updating fire and building codes. Galvan said San Antonio has just under 30 data centers within city limits, with 18 or 19 located in District 6. “A little under 30 data centers here in San Antonio city limits, with 18-19 of them here in District 6,” Galvan said. “We’ve seen them grow over time with rapid development over the last 15 years.” Galvan said the city and its residents need to understand how local policies could affect future projects and the communities where they are built. “It’s incumbent on us to make sure we’re understanding what’s going on and how local policies can help impact some of the developments here so our communities aren’t left behind,” he said. Organizers said the town hall was intended to bring more residents, particularly those on the far West Side and in District 6, into discussions about data center development. Annalisa Peace, executive director of the Greater Edwards Aquifer Alliance, said she hopes the city’s development code will be updated to address the growth of large-scale data centers. “We hope that the City will be amending the UDC to accommodate new hyperscale data centers with regulations that best serve the citizens of San Antonio,” Peace said. No official decisions were made at Tuesday’s citizen town hall. The feedback comes as the city works to develop regulations for data centers and prepares for further City Council consideration of updates to the Unified Development Code. Read also:

artigo.texto: Colorado can help lead data center construction — in space | PODIUM Across Colorado, proposals for new data centers are running into fierce opposition. Residents are worried about noise, water use, health risks and high electricity costs. Six municipalities, including Denver, have imposed bans, caps or moratoriums while they figure out how these massive facilities could affect their communities. Local officials cannot ignore voters’ concerns. But the response to new data centers can’t simply be “no” because there’s too much at stake. Abundant computing power is critical to U.S. medical and scientific progress, military and intelligence capabilities and economic growth. Recommended Stories So it’s exciting Colorado may soon have an opportunity to play a key role in developing another option: moving some of that computing infrastructure off the ground and into space. In June, Colorado U.S. Sen. John Hickenlooper joined Texas U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz in introducing the NEW HORIZON Act, which would direct the Department of Defense to establish a pilot program to test orbital data centers and space-based cloud computing. Currently in early-stage development by well-known companies like Google, SpaceX and Amazon — as well as new entrants like Starcloud and Sophia Space — orbital data centers would put computing, storage and networking equipment aboard state-of-the-art platforms in low-Earth orbit. Then, instead of sending data collected by satellites back to Earth, the orbital facilities would process and store much of that data in space. Sen. Hickenlooper’s proposed program would start small, testing whether orbital computing can quickly, safely and reliably process satellite imagery, national-security information, weather observations and other data already being generated in space, while also assessing key cybersecurity and compatibility issues. But there’s much bigger potential here. If powerful computing systems work reliably in space, we may be able to move into orbit some of the intensive computing now performed in massive ground-based data centers. That would allow us to expand America’s computing capacity without putting so much pressure on local power grids, water supplies and communities. Colorado is an obvious place to start making this happen. Aerospace is one of our defining industries, and we’re also home to important military installations, research universities, federal laboratories and innovative startups. As Sen. Hickenlooper put it, “Space innovation and military preparedness are Colorado’s bread and butter.” It won’t be easy. Launching equipment into space is expensive — and incredibly complex. Computers in orbit have to withstand intense radiation, and keeping powerful processors cool is a serious engineering challenge. Space-based data facilities would also mean more orbital congestion, debris and collision risks. And when something breaks, sending someone up to fix it is a lot harder than calling a technician to a building in Denver or Colorado Springs. But those aren’t reasons to walk away. Rather, as many tech-industry leaders have argued, they’re reasons to start innovating and experimenting with new technologies, including the power systems, cybersecurity, heat management and radiation-resistant hardware that could make commercial orbital data centers possible. Colorado can demonstrate leadership quickly. State agencies, universities, aerospace employers, federal installations and startups can pursue research funding, host demonstrations, train workers and ensure Colorado companies are competing to participate in NEW HORIZON pilot programs. Orbital data certainly won’t arrive soon enough to resolve today’s thorny local disputes. But decisions we make today could determine where the new orbital computing industry takes root in the years to come. Colorado can get there early — creating jobs, developing new national security technology and giving future policymakers another way to meet America’s growing demand for computing power. The fights over data centers happening across Colorado highlight why this idea is worth pursuing. Communities shouldn’t have to choose between protecting their residents and resources and building the infrastructure America needs to power the next generation of innovation. Colorado has the scientific talent, national-security expertise and industrial capabilities to help find another way: up. Kyle Shannon of Denver is chief executive of Storyvine and founder of AI Salon. Dave Cavossa of Washington, DC., is president of the Commercial Space Federation.

artigo.texto: Vikram Solar Subsidiary Plans 7.5 GWh BESS Assembly Plant in Tamil Nadu VSL PowerHive plans to expand from battery storage system assembly into cell manufacturing, building towards an integrated domestic battery manufacturing ecosystem. October 13, 2026. By News Bureau VSL PowerHive, a wholly owned subsidiary of Vikram Solar, has announced plans to establish a 7.5 GWh per annum Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) assembly plant at Oragadam, near Chennai, Tamil Nadu. The facility is designed to scale up to 15 GWh in later phases and will anchor PowerHive's broader roadmap to build 30 GWh of total battery manufacturing capacity by 2030. Spread across approximately 1.65 lakh sq. ft., the facility is slated for inauguration in January 2027, with commercial operations expected to begin in April 2027. The development comes at a time when energy storage has moved to the centre of India's clean energy agenda. As solar and wind capacity grows, storage has become critical to keeping the grid stable, shifting renewable power to evening peaks and enabling round-the-clock clean energy. The Central Electricity Authority projects that India will need about 47 GW /236 GWh of energy storage by 2031-32. Meeting this need at scale will require a strong domestic manufacturing base and reduced reliance on imported systems. Complementing that, PowerHive's ambitions extend well beyond assembly. The company will move into cell manufacturing with a 7.5 GWh programme from 2028, a key step towards building a fully integrated battery manufacturing ecosystem in India, from cell to system. Backing this roadmap, PowerHive is developing indigenous battery technologies and has already initiated multiple patent filings to strengthen its technology ownership and reduce reliance on imported know-how. Once operational, the plant will assemble Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP)-based energy storage systems for utility-scale and Commercial and Industrial (C&I) applications. The portfolio will include 5.016 MWh and 6.25 MWh liquid-cooled BESS containers, PowerHive's P261 battery cabinets, utility-scale energy storage systems and renewable energy-integrated storage solutions, all to be manufactured in India under the Make in India initiative. Gyanesh Chaudhary, Chairman and Managing Director, Vikram Solar, said, "Storage is the bridge between India's renewable ambition and round-the-clock clean power. As the country scales up solar and wind, the ability to store that energy reliably will define the next phase of the transition and that capability must be built in India. The new plant is a decisive step in that direction and extends Vikram Solar's role in the clean energy value chain from generating power to storing it." Arun Mittal, CEO, VSL PowerHive, said, "Energy storage is what makes renewable power dependable, and demand for it in India is rising faster than ever. With this development, we are setting out to build world-class battery manufacturing capability in the country, starting with 7.5 GWh of assembly and progressing to cells and an integrated ecosystem. Our aim is to give utilities, developers and industries a future-ready, domestically built storage partner for the decades ahead." Through the upcoming facility, PowerHive plans to create skilled jobs, develop local talent in advanced storage solutions and strengthen the local industrial ecosystem, supporting Tamil Nadu in building a thriving clean-tech industry. please contact: contact@energetica-india.net.

artigo.texto: The ongoing festive season has brought a curated update to BYD’s electric SUV portfolio in India. The premium Sealion 7 is now available in an exclusive Festive Edition; however, this package does not introduce extra mechanical power or a new battery layout. Instead, BYD has focused its attention on elevating the cabin experience, offering this special edition in a strictly limited run of 150 units nationwide. The BYD Sealion 7 Festive Edition enters the market priced at Rs 50.60 lakh (ex-showroom). It is based directly on the high-spec Premium trim, which carries a sticker price of Rs 49.90 lakh, positioning this limited-run model at a premium of Rs 70,000 over the standard variant. What is new on the Sealion 7? The primary differentiator for the Festive Edition is found entirely within the interior. It introduces a sophisticated Tan and Black dual-tone theme that seamlessly accents the leather-appointed seats, layered dashboard, door cards, and the floating center console. The rest of the extensive equipment list is carried over directly from the high-end Premium trim. Core feature highlights include: - 15.6-inch rotating touchscreen - 10.25-inch driver display - Head-up display - Panoramic glass roof with electric sunshade - Ventilated front seats - Driver seat with memory function - Powered tailgate - 19-inch alloy wheels - 360-degree camera - 11 airbags - Level 2 ADAS - 12-speaker Dynaudio sound system - Dual-zone climate control - Double-glazed glass - All-LED lighting The SUV also gets leather upholstery, ambient lighting and auto-tilting ORVMs with memory function. On the exterior, the Festive Edition retains the identical styling cues, aerodynamic character lines, and 19-inch alloy wheels of the regular Premium variant, keeping changes strictly interior-focused. Battery and performance Under the skin, the Festive Edition uses the same 82.56kWh battery pack as the standard Premium model. This battery powers a rear-mounted permanent-magnet synchronous electric motor that puts out a healthy 308bhp and 380Nm of peak torque. BYD claims a 0-100km/h time of 6.7 seconds. The claimed range stands at 567km on the NEDC test cycle. The battery uses BYD’s Blade Battery technology and Cell-to-Body construction. The Sealion 7 also gets Intelligent Torque Adaptation Control, or iTAC, as part of its electric powertrain setup. The Festive Edition is offered only with the Premium specification. BYD has limited production to 150 units across India, making it a fairly small run. BYD Sealion 7 price in India What else from the brand? Beyond the core BYD lineup, the manufacturer is actively preparing to venture deeper into the ultra-luxury EV segment by introducing its premium sub-brand, Denza. Having officially teased its Indian entry, the luxury marque is widely expected to debut with two flagship models: the Z9 GT and the D9. The Denza Z9 GT is a high-performance electric shooting brake driven by a massive 122.5kWh battery pack and a triple-motor layout, generating a staggering 1,156hp and achieving a 0-100km/h sprint in just 2.7 seconds. Concurrently, the Denza D9 will cater to the executive segment as a large, ultra-luxurious electric MPV featuring a plush three-row, 2+2+3 seating configuration with individual rear captain’s chairs.
