artigo.texto: Back in my corporate days, I started every new project with one rule: you can't control what you don't measure. Twenty years in energy added a second half to it. You can't sell what you can't prove. In the power business, nobody ever asked me to take my own word for anything. The meter did the talking instead. It sat at a defined point, recorded continuously, and both sides of every contract trusted it. Today I develop AI data centers and keep running into the opposite problem. Operators measure everything, from GPU utilization and node uptime to power draw and temperature at the rack, yet almost none of it counts outside their own control room. It's their own data, collected their own way and shown when they choose to show it, so enterprise customers and capacity buyers end up taking the operator's word for what a facility actually delivered. Hyperscalers get past that on brand and scale. Mid-market operators cannot, and as I see it, that's one of the biggest commercial handicaps they carry. It has nothing to do with how well they run their sites. The market has noticed. Buyers now use independent assessments of AI cloud operators to decide where their workloads go. The money side has noticed too. CoreWeave's $8.5 billion facility, secured against its infrastructure and a contract with a strong customer, has a fixed-rate tranche priced at around 5.9%, while its own unsecured five-year bonds sit close to 10%. Part of that gap is the hardware pledged behind the deal, but the rest, as I read it, is a contract that gave lenders something to rely on beyond the company's own word. Lenders will finance what they can check. With no record of your own, you borrow against someone else's name or pay a few hundred basis points more, and deals take longer either way. The dashboard was never built to answer this Here's a distinction I keep coming back to. A dashboard answers the operator's question: "How is my facility performing?" The person across the table is asking something else: "Can I rely on this when I sign a contract?" Running the first instrument harder won't answer the second. In my experience, three things separate a record somebody else can rely on from good monitoring. The readings need to be collected in a way the other side recognizes, at a defined point and interval, just like the meter. The record needs to be continuous, bad quarters included, because a history with the worst months taken out isn't really a history. And it has to stay blind to what customers are actually computing, the way a meter sees kilowatt-hours but not what you use them for. What I'd start writing down today You don't need new instrumentation for any of this, just a decision about what to keep and the discipline to keep it. Building uptime isn't the best place to start, because a building can be up while half the chips inside it are failing. I'd track how many contracted GPU hours actually turned into usable work after failures, restarts, and degraded links. The industry calls this goodput, and it's what a customer is really paying for. I'd keep the incident history beside it: what failed, how often, and how fast it was replaced. How an incident was resolved is something an outsider can check. Then there's how a site behaves when power gets tight, and that's the one I'd pay most attention to, because the grid side has made up its mind. This May, after incidents in which a gigawatt or more of computing load dropped off the grid unexpectedly, NERC, North America's grid reliability body, issued a rare top-level alert. It told grid operators to tighten how large computing loads are studied, tested, and connected. Load behavior now has to be measured to a standard, rather than described by the operator. Finally, I'd write the methodology down: what's measured, where, how often, who may check it, how long it's kept. That costs almost nothing and gets skipped most. A two-year record can't be built backwards, which is why I'd start now. A power plant with a certified generation and dispatch history talks to the market very differently from one showing its own charts, because a stranger can act on it without knowing or liking the operator. The meter is coming Every mature infrastructure industry eventually got its meter. Electricity has certified metering, and telecom carriers that compete every day still settle with each other against a shared record. AI infrastructure is young and still runs mostly on trust and brand, and I don't think that phase lasts. When a neutral way to record what a facility delivered arrives, I expect it to favor the operators who kept honest, continuous records all along, and that's where a mid-market operator can actually win against a hyperscaler. You don't win in infrastructure by promising the most. The winner is the one who can prove what they've already delivered. artigo.texto: Câmara aprova urgência de PL sobre divisão de custos de baterias Votação do mérito deve ficar para depois das eleições; projeto impacta leilões de dezembro A Câmara dos Deputados aprovou o regime de urgência do projeto de lei 3.716 de 2026, que altera a divisão dos custos de contratação de baterias no setor elétrico. A proposta enfrenta divergências entre agentes do setor, e ainda não há prazo para a votação no Legislativo. A aprovação do texto pode afetar os primeiros leilões de armazenamento de energia em larga escala no Brasil, marcados para dezembro. Com a aprovação da urgência, o projeto passa a tramitar de forma acelerada e pode ser votado diretamente no plenário da Câmara, sem precisar passar pelas comissões temáticas. O texto ainda precisa ser analisado pelos deputados e, se aprovado, seguirá para o Senado. A expectativa do setor é que a votação do mérito do projeto só aconteça depois das eleições. Os leilões estão marcados para os dias 2 e 4 de dezembro, com contratos de 15 anos e início do fornecimento previsto para agosto de 2028. Em setembro, o diretor da Aneel (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica), Gentil Nogueira, afirmou que uma alteração na legislação às vésperas dos leilões poderia levar ao adiamento das disputas por até 30 dias, para permitir a adaptação das regras. De autoria do deputado Arnaldo Jardim (Cidadania-SP), o PL 3.716 de 2026 propõe revogar um dispositivo da lei 15.269 de 2025 que determina que os custos da contratação de reserva de capacidade por baterias sejam pagos exclusivamente pelas empresas geradoras de energia. Com a mudança, as despesas passariam a seguir a regra geral da reserva de capacidade e seriam divididas entre os usuários finais do SIN (Sistema Interligado Nacional), incluindo consumidores e autoprodutores. A proposta é apoiada por associações ligadas à geração de energia solar e eólica, além de produtores independentes e empresas de armazenamento. As entidades argumentam que as baterias beneficiam todo o sistema elétrico ao armazenar eletricidade para utilização nos horários de maior demanda. Por isso, defendem que o custo seja distribuído de maneira proporcional entre os beneficiários. Manutenção da regra atual Do outro lado, as distribuidoras defendem a manutenção da regra atual. A Abradee (Associação Brasileira de Distribuidores de Energia Elétrica) argumenta que a expansão das fontes renováveis, especialmente solar e eólica, contribuiu para a necessidade de contratar baterias. Na avaliação da entidade, os geradores devem arcar com os custos, uma vez que os consumidores já financiam a expansão dessas fontes por meio de subsídios incluídos nas tarifas de energia. Em nota, a Absae (Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia) classificou a aprovação da urgência como um “avanço” para ampliar a segurança jurídica dos leilões. A entidade defende a mudança na divisão dos custos, mas afirma que a discussão no Congresso não deve comprometer o calendário dos leilões. Eis a íntegra (PDF – 166 kB). A associação alerta que um eventual adiamento pode comprometer a entrada dos sistemas de armazenamento em operação em 2028 e aumentar o risco de deficit de potência e de apagões em períodos críticos de atendimento. Durante uma audiência pública que inaugurou as contribuições dos agentes do setor para o edital do leilão, o adiamento foi discutido. Beneficiados pelo PL em discussão no Congresso temem que o certame seja realizado antes da eventual aprovação da lei. A Aneel, até o momento, tem assegurado que manterá o cronograma, salvo se a lei for alterada durante os 30 dias que antecedem o leilão. Nesse caso, poderá adiar em até 30 dias a realização do certame para que empresas possam adaptar suas propostas.

artigo.texto: Eskom has launched a process to select a strategic partner to help deliver the 1.5GW Tubatse pumped-storage scheme, a landmark project in Limpopo set to become South Africa’s largest energy-storage programme. As a flagship development in Eskom Green, an unbundled renewable energy subsidiary of the state power utility, the project will provide the long-duration energy storage needed to integrate increasing volumes of renewable energy into the national grid, strengthen energy security and support South Africa’s transition to a more resilient, low-carbon electricity system. “As South Africa advances its energy transition, long-duration storage will be essential to maintaining a reliable and resilient power system. Tubatse will provide the flexibility needed to integrate increasing volumes of renewable energy while strengthening grid stability and security of supply,” Eskom group CEO Dan Marokane said in a statement on Tuesday. Last week, electricity & energy minister Kgosientsho Ramokgopa said the government would prioritise the procurement of 4,600MW of battery energy storage systems and 5,000MW of gas-to-power under its integrated resource plan unveiled last year. The combined allocation of 9,600MW responds to the electricity system’s immediate requirements for storage, flexibility and dispatchable supply amid increasing curtailment, which occurs when available generation cannot be accommodated due to network constraints or operating conditions, including periods when supply exceeds demand. South Africa plans to build 14,000km of new high-voltage transmission lines over the next decade, at an estimated cost of R440bn, to connect new wind, solar, battery storage and gas generation projects to the national grid while strengthening the network to support changing electricity flows. The just-launched request-for-qualification process for Tubatse is the first stage of a competitive exercise to identify a partner with the financial strength, technical expertise, development experience and long-term commitment required to advance the scheme, Eskom said on Tuesday. The proposed facility will provide about 21 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of energy storage through four reversible pump-turbine units. A gigawatt-hour is a unit of total energy equal to 1-billion watt-hours (Wh) delivered or consumed over an hour. Able to generate at full output for up to 14 hours, the scheme will help balance the power system, support greater renewable energy integration and enhance grid reliability. Eskom Green is targeting up to 6GW by 2030, with plans to expand its clean energy portfolio to 21GW by 2035 and up to 32GW by 2040, including 5GW of hydro and pumped storage. “Tubatse is … a cornerstone of Eskom Green’s ambition to develop the infrastructure required for a modern, low-carbon electricity system. By combining Eskom’s development experience with private-sector expertise and investment, we aim to unlock the full potential of this project while supporting economic growth, localisation and skills development,” Eskom group executive for renewables Rivoningo Mnisi said. Tubatse will store surplus electricity when demand is low and release it during peak demand, when wind and solar output drops, or when the grid is under strain. This will help reduce wasted renewable energy, make better use of existing generation and strengthen security of supply. The project has been classified as one of the top 12 national priority projects by Infrastructure South Africa and forms part of the country’s just transition programme towards cleaner renewable energies. Tubatse builds on more than two decades of Eskom’s experience in operating and maintaining pumped storage schemes and conventional hydropower plants, including the delivery of the 1,332MW Ingula pumped storage scheme commissioned in 2017. The power utility currently operates 2,732MW of pumped storage capacity across Drakensberg, Palmiet and Ingula, as well as 661MW of conventional hydroelectric capacity, primarily at Gariep and Vanderkloof. The required land has been secured, environmental authorisation has been granted for the scheme, and key technical studies and access-road designs have reached an advanced stage, Eskom said. Grid connection studies have also advanced, and the department of water & sanitation has confirmed water availability from De Hoop Dam. “Together, these milestones distinguish Tubatse from an early-stage concept and provide prospective partners with the opportunity to invest in an advanced development platform where critical enabling work is either complete or well progressed,” the utility said. artigo.texto: Madison County planning commission votes against battery energy storage facility Madison County’s Planning Commission has given a unanimous unfavorable recommendation for zoning changes to allow a proposed battery energy storage facility. IPR’s Thomas Ouellette reports. Audio Transcript Developers with Jupiter Power want to build two battery energy storage system facilities in the county. Battery storage facilities hold surplus energy from a local power grid in large lithium batteries until it’s needed in times of peak power use. These kinds of facilities do not generate any power on their own. As part of hours of deliberation, Nat Drucker with Jupiter Power addressed several concerns from residents – like capping the number of total batteries, draining water to an independent system, and taking precautions against fire. “We hope that all of this shows and demonstrates that we are absolutely willing to work with people.” Drucker said. “And we’re working to do this better, and to provide this very important piece of infrastructure that is going to help keep this county, and this part of Indiana, moving forward.” The rezoning was proposed last month with the planning commission, but Jupiter Power developers at that meeting requested a continuance to better respond to concerns and questions. Despite that new information, members of the public remained firmly against the battery storage facility. Former Madison County Council member Ben Gale was among them. “So the numbers we’re seeing up here, I don’t buy them,” he said. “I’ve been through the process before, I see how it works, and the promises made up front are never what ends up working.” Officials with Jupiter Power say neither project involves a large building. The sites instead feature “container-based” energy storage. After the unfavorable recommendation, the project will now move to the county commissioners to consider and vote on the rezoning request. If it were to be approved in Madison County, Jupiter Power says the first site, Liberty 1, would start construction in 2027 and be operational in 2028. Indiana Michigan Power has an agreement with Jupiter Power to purchase the battery storage facility upon its completion. The second site, Liberty 2, is significantly bigger, and has a longer development time. No long-term ownership of the site has been determined yet. Thomas Ouellette is our reporter and producer. Contact him at thomas.ouellette@bsu.edu.

artigo.texto: A data center moratorium could once again be moving forward in Michigan City, but who controls the language is a topic of debate. The city council introduced, then tabled, an ordinance last month, to give the city’s planning department a chance to weigh in. But this week, council members announced a new ordinance, similar to the last one. It would suspend the approval of new data center developments, until the city adds regulations to its zoning ordinance or until July 31, 2028. It explicitly excludes both phases of Google’s current development. Council member Bryant Dabney said the pause would let city officials evaluate the Google project, before allowing more. “Not something that we heard happened in Texas or in Tennessee or wherever it may be. We’ll be able to get real data regarding noise, water usage, energy and so forth, from a data center right here in Michigan City,” Dabney said. But the sponsors of the original ordinance complained that they weren’t consulted about the new one. Council member Joseph Nelson called it disingenuous. "I worked my butt off for this, me and Nancy [Moldenhauer] and a lot of good people," Nelson said. "So, for you to come in and swoop and do this and not speak to me or Nancy about this, I do not appreciate that." Reaction from residents was mixed. While they want a moratorium, they had concerns with the way the ordinance was written and presented. Just Transition Northwest Indiana Executive Director Ashley Williams opposed letting the moratorium end as soon as new regulations are adopted. “It pauses just long enough to create an illusion of action while the planning department skates in an M-3 Data Center zoning district that we know it’s been working on behind the scenes, without public knowledge or input up until this point,” Williams told council members. Residents also voiced concerns about Google’s data center, including potential emissions from diesel generators and the storage of diesel fuel. Since the ordinance wasn’t filed in time for the council to take official action Tuesday, a formal first reading is scheduled for the next meeting.

artigo.texto: On the morning of October 14, 2026, the Finance and Investment Newspaper, in collaboration with the State Bank of Vietnam, organized the seminar "Credit Policy and Carbon Market: Unlocking Green Capital Flows," focusing on discussing the linkages between credit policy, the carbon market, and the capital market, thereby seeking solutions to unlock financial resources for the green transition process. In his keynote address at the workshop, Deputy Governor of the State Bank of Vietnam Nguyen Ngoc Canh highly appreciated the initiative of the Finance and Investment Newspaper in organizing the workshop "Credit Policy and Carbon Market: Unlocking Green Capital Flows" today. This is a practical forum for management agencies, credit institutions, businesses, and experts to participate and exchange ideas on an issue that is becoming increasingly important for the green transformation of the economy : mobilizing and effectively utilizing capital for this process. In fulfillment of Vietnam's commitment at COP26 to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050, the Party, State, and Government have issued many important policies and guidelines to promote green growth, energy transition, and the development of a low -carbon economy. This transition requires significant resources for investment in technological innovation, transformation of production methods, efficient energy use, and reduction of greenhouse gas emissions. In this context, in addition to resources from the state budget and mobilization from the capital and money markets, it is necessary to simultaneously develop other market mechanisms to mobilize more resources and create economic incentives for businesses to proactively reduce emissions, including the carbon market. Through the establishment of quotas, measurement of emission reduction results, and the formation of transaction prices for quotas and carbon credits, the carbon market creates a mechanism to convert emission reduction results into economic value. This provides businesses with additional motivation and resources to continue investing in the green transition process, instead of relying primarily on bank credit. On January 29, 2026, the Government issued Decree No. 29/2026/ND-CP regulating the domestic carbon exchange, creating a legal framework for organizing and operating the market and trading of greenhouse gas emission quotas and carbon credits. The pilot market is initially being established with a scale of over 511 million tons of CO2, equivalent to the emission quotas allocated to facilities in the three major emitting sectors: thermal power, iron and steel, and cement, during the 2025-2026 period. The pilot phase will last until the end of 2028, before entering the full mandatory operation phase from 2029. In this market, commercial banks participate as settlement banks; during the pilot phase, BIDV is the sole settlement bank in the market. Deputy Governor Nguyen Ngoc Canh stated that, from the perspective of the banking sector, it is necessary to clearly recognize the role of green credit and the carbon market in the green transition process. First, green credit provides capital for investment and technological innovation, creating resources for the development of green industries/sectors, thereby resulting in reduced emissions. The emission reductions from projects funded by banks will create the basis and commodities for the development of the carbon market. Conversely, an efficiently functioning carbon market will support businesses by providing them with stable revenue and cash flow from emission reductions, which will support their production and business activities, improve their bank credit quality, and enable them to purchase carbon credits to meet the stringent standards of import and export activities. For green credit activities, it is important not only that the disbursed funds for a project are identified as green, but also that the results of energy savings, emission reduction, and environmental protection achieved by the borrower are verified. Measuring, reporting, and evaluating emission reduction results, as well as trading quotas and credits in the carbon market, can provide additional information to monitor the environmental outcomes of a project. This helps credit institutions assess the effectiveness of capital utilization and enhance the management and supervision of green capital flows. According to the Deputy Governor, in reality, over the past years, the banking sector has proactively implemented many solutions to promote green credit, directing capital flows into industries and sectors that bring environmental benefits and reduce greenhouse gas emissions. The State Bank of Vietnam has gradually perfected the policy framework, issued orientations and guidelines on green credit, environmental and social risk management; and encouraged credit institutions to build strategies, internal processes, and develop credit products suitable for green growth goals. While other green capital mobilization channels are developing, green credit continues to play a crucial role as an important resource for developing green industries/sectors and supporting the transition of the growth model to a low -carbon economy. From the early years of green credit implementation (2017) to the present, green credit activities have expanded both in terms of credit scale and the level of participation of credit institutions. By the end of June 2026, outstanding green credit reached over VND 856 trillion, an increase of 9.87% compared to the end of 2025, with an average growth rate of over 20% per year during the 2017-2025 period, mainly concentrated in agriculture , forestry, fisheries and biodiversity conservation (accounting for over 31%), and green energy (accounting for nearly 28%). artigo.texto: Jones holds Huntsville rally, calls for Medicaid expansion and data center regulation HUNTSVILLE, Ala. (WAFF) - Doug Jones held a rally in Huntsville Sunday as he seeks to become Alabama’s first Democratic governor since 2003, with 23 days remaining until the Nov. 3 midterm election. The former senator discussed issues he said are important to Alabama communities, including expanding Medicaid to help rural areas where hospitals have closed or are at risk of closing. Jones also called for stronger regulations on data centers, including limits on tax incentives and requirements to address their power and water use. Jones points to consistency Jones said his consistency in office should speak to voters. Voters in attendance said they are ready for the change Jones is talking about. Congressional candidate speaks at rally Andrew Sneed, the Democratic candidate for Alabama’s 5th Congressional District, also spoke at the rally. Sneed is facing incumbent Dale Strong in the Nov. 3 election. Sneed said people at the event were given the space to be heard. Jones and Sneed will both be on the Nov. 3 ballot. Tuberville rally set for Thursday Jones’ opponent in the governor’s race, Sen. Tommy Tuberville, will hold a rally Thursday. The Marshall County Republican Club is hosting the event, called “Liberty on the Lake.” Organizers say the event is free and open to anyone in the community who wants to hear from Tuberville. It will run from 4:30 to 6 p.m. Thursday at the Marshall County RSVP building on Highway 431. Strong has not advertised any upcoming campaign events on his social media pages or campaign website. artigo.texto: The Kremlin in Moscow is investigating how much financial loss Yandex -- which supports AI and search in Russia -- has incurred after last week's drone attack on three of its data centers. One of the data centers is used to train its AI models. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said it was too early to assess whether users had suffered financial losses from outages, Reuters reported. Asked by Reuters whether the government was considering a mechanism to compensate users, he said Yandex was "currently facing difficulties," adding that "the matter is being discussed by the government, but the company is taking urgent steps to address the consequences of the attack." Media reports in Russia are calling Yandex,Russia’s largest technology company." Last week it announced that two of its data centers were struck by drones. “Serious" damage was reported at all three locations. advertisement advertisement In a statement posted on Friday, Yandex said operations at its Sasovo facility were “completely halted,” while part of the infrastructure in Kaluga was “disabled.” The Vladimir facility was taken completely offline on Sunday, according to the company. "Data centers are the 'iron heart' of Yandex," according to a post on the company’s website translated into English from Russian. “Their operability is critical for services that have become part of people's everyday lives. Millions of users check traffic and build routes, listen to music, watch movies, order groceries, and get answers to questions. Our technologies help hundreds of thousands of companies run their businesses: taking orders, serving customers, and interacting with partners.” Following the attacks on the Sasovo and Kaluga facilities, a third Ukrainian drone strike hit Yandex's Vladimir data center on Sunday, Oct. 11, forcing a complete shutdown of operations at that site. The Sasovo data center is noted for housing two of Yandex's top supercomputers equipped with Nvidia A100 chips used to train its YandexGPT AI models. Chinese conglomerates represent one of the largest foreign ad segments on Yandex today that leverages search, video, and geotargeted navigation ads across Yandex Maps and Navigator, according to Google Gemini. These recent targeted drone strikes hit a company still trying to recover from a recent restructuring following a corporate split in 2024. Yandex is based in Russia. It has retained the brand’s name and continues to operate as Russia's leading search engine and AI lead. Its Dutch parent company rebranded as Nebius Group. Yandex still dominates domestic search with the most market share in the region, but it is currently battling infrastructure challenges after Ukrainian drone strikes targeted several of its data centers and supercomputers. In 2024, Yandex NV, the parent company of the Russian search engine at the time, agreed to sell its assets in Russia to a group of local investors for $5.2 billion in one of the largest corporate exits from Russia since Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine. Nebius Group, which now focuses on AI, found that its shares fell 2% on Tuesday -- opening at $200.50 versus a prior close of $210.06, while trading volume reached nearly 6.94 million shares, according to MarketBeat. The company does not sell advertising space or operate an advertising network. Unlike its predecessor Yandex, focused on digital advertising, Nebius has completely exited the consumer-facing ad-tech industry.

artigo.texto: Eskom lança rodada de qualificação para programa de 6 GW de renováveis e armazenamento A Eskom, estatal de energia elétrica da África do Sul, iniciou uma etapa de solicitação de qualificação (RFQ) para selecionar desenvolvedores de energia renovável para a fase inicial de uma iniciativa destinada a implantar até 6 GW de capacidade de geração renovável e armazenamento em escala de utilidade. Segundo comunicado da empresa, essa primeira fase representa um conjunto inicial de projetos que chega a até 6 GW, abrangendo energia solar fotovoltaica (PV), sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS), energia eólica e tecnologias renováveis adicionais.A própria Eskom fornecerá projetos que incluem não menos de 2 GW de solar fotovoltaica, além de 1 GW / 4 GWh de BESS, que os parceiros estratégicos selecionados poderão complementar com projetos próprios ou originados por eles. Esses parceiros formarão uma lista de colaboradores pré-qualificados para codesenvolvimento e coinvestimento, cuidando do desenvolvimento, do financiamento e da implementação ao longo de um prazo de cinco anos. Os desenvolvedores que se qualificarem serão convidados a participar de rodadas competitivas de contratação posteriores, por meio de uma ou mais solicitações de propostas (RFPs). O portfólio pretendido inclui projetos originados pela Eskom em terrenos de propriedade da estatal e em locais de geração atuais, além de projetos de propriedade de parceiros estratégicos ou originados por eles, que poderão ser desenvolvidos, adquiridos ou executados em conjunto com a Eskom ou sua divisão Eskom Green. Espera-se que cada projeto seja organizado por meio de uma sociedade de propósito específico (SPV) dedicada e com patrimônio segregado, com financiamento estruturado principalmente em uma estrutura de project finance com recurso limitado ou sem recurso. Em julho, a Eskom apresentou a Eskom Green como parte de uma abordagem de reestruturação mais ampla que abrange o esforço de desmembramento iniciado em 2023. Pressão financeira e reformulação do mercado Mesmo com esses passos, a Eskom continua a enfrentar pressão financeira. A estatal ainda depende de geração a carvão e de usinas de pico movidas a diesel. Os gastos com diesel permanecem na casa das centenas de milhões de randes sul-africanos, embora tenham caído consideravelmente em comparação com o ano anterior. Ao mesmo tempo, a África do Sul avança com reformas no mercado de eletricidade, entre elas propostas para criar um mercado atacadista de eletricidade que pode alterar a posição da Eskom no setor elétrico. Analistas alertaram que medidas regulatórias que favoreçam os ativos a carvão da Eskom poderiam desestimular o investimento privado e corroer ganhos de eficiência, possivelmente elevando os custos de eletricidade de longo prazo para os consumidores. A capacidade solar instalada total da África do Sul agora ultrapassou 10 GW, após 1,6 GW ter sido adicionado em 2025. Este relatório fornece uma análise aprofundada do mercado de células solares e diodos emissores de luz na África do Sul, cobrindo tamanho de mercado, crescimento, demanda, oferta, fluxos comerciais, preços, cenário competitivo e previsões até 2035. O estudo é projetado para fabricantes, distribuidores, importadores, exportadores, investidores, equipes de compras, consultores e equipes de estratégia que precisam de uma visão consistente e orientada por dados da dinâmica do mercado e de uma definição analítica transparente do escopo do produto. artigo.texto: Media gets first look at Project Jupiter AI data center in Santa Teresa Oracle and Stack Infrastructure offered a first glimpse of Project Jupiter, a $165 billion AI data center under construction in Santa Teresa, highlighting its progress, technology, and workforce impact. Media gets first look at Project Jupiter AI data center in Santa Teresa Oracle and Stack Infrastructure offered a first glimpse of Project Jupiter, a $165 billion AI data center under construction in Santa Teresa, highlighting its progress, technology, and workforce impact. Media crews were invited for the first time to tour Project Jupiter, a $165 billion AI data center under construction in Santa Teresa, which began building within the past year. The tour showcased several aspects of the roughly 1,400-acre campus, including energy solutions, construction progress, and workforce details. Oracle highlighted Bloom Energy's fuel cell technology, which uses natural gas to generate electricity without burning it. The company explained that this system will reduce air pollution and water usage. Visitors were also shown Building A, one of four planned data center buildings, and its cooling system. "It's a closed-loop cooling system, and so what that means is the project is not continuously consuming water for data center operations," Josh Timberlake, SVP of site strategy at Stack Infrastructure said. The equipment staging area was another stop on the tour, where materials and equipment are managed. Stack Infrastructure, the company developing and building the campus, shared workforce details, saying, "We have just about 4,400 construction workers working here full time. 1,200 of those are New Mexicans. Over 600 of those are from Doña Ana County." The tour concluded inside one of the data halls, where rows of server racks will eventually fill the space. Over the past year, Project Jupiter has faced community concerns regarding water use, air quality, and transparency. During a Q&A session, Oracle executives addressed these concerns, saying, "We're committed to New Mexico at this point. So we're making sure we do everything right. We're taking the feedback we need to adjust something. We keep adjusting till we get to making sure we come through on our New Mexico economic benefit." Oracle noted that this was the first time media had been allowed inside the construction site but assured it would not be the last. The company emphasized its commitment to keeping the community informed as construction progresses. Stack Infrastructure stated that the number of construction workers on-site is expected to grow to nearly 7,000, and hiring for permanent data center operations jobs has already begun.

artigo.texto: St. Joseph City Council postponed vote on data center study contracts ST. JOSEPH, Mo. (KQTV) -- The St. Joseph City Council postponed two ordinances related to zoning and development guidelines for potential data center projects on Monday evening. The council postponed the ordinance after questions arose about whether the proposed consultants do business with data centers. One company recommended for a contract denied having business ties to data center development. "Any affiliation with data centers or data center developments was asked. I want to drill down on that with one company in particular that was mentioned," City Manager, Mike Schumacher said. During the meeting, several residents urged council members to consider how data center development could affect the community, with some also raising concerns about the proposed contract with GBA Inc. GBA Inc. provides turnkey data center services for handling the entire planning, designing, construction and maintenance process. The council is considering a contract with GBA Inc. for up to $42,440 to study data center development and recommend zoning changes and development guidelines. The review would address electric and water infrastructure, land use, environmental impacts, public services, costs and community concerns. "You're not gonna get accurate, fair information from somebody that makes their living building data centers," St. Joseph resident, Debra Miller said. "I opposed spending over $42,000 for a company that you can't trust is going to give you the best results that take in the consideration of the residents of St. Joe." The council is also considering a contract with Renew Missouri Advocates for up to $10,750 for community outreach and legal services related to data center development. The firm would also recommend zoning updates and potential changes to the city’s code of ordinances. One resident also urged the city to revise the ordinance language. "Please amend these bills and work toward that goal, and then I will say thank you for pursuing zoning restrictions, and regulations that protects the health, and well being of the citizens of St. Joseph," St. Joseph resident, Deb Ballin said. The council plans to review the language of both proposed ordinances before bringing them back for a vote at its next meeting. The council voted on a development plan for Bryan St. Joseph Apartments. The complex would be at 5408 N. Pointe Drive, behind the YMCA. The ordinance will allow the city to issue up to $40 million in bonds to help Bryan St. Joseph Apartments LLC build a 180-unit market-rate apartment complex. The project will receive property tax abatements on the improvements and a sales tax exemption on construction materials. The council voted to withdraw the request to add 55 parking spaces along Southwest Parkway between Fleeman Street and Mason Road. The school district requested the ordinance be withdrawn because they want to continue to evaluate the parking needs at Benton High School. The next city council meeting will take place on Monday, Oct. 26th, in the Council Chambers at City Hall.

artigo.texto: BYD reveals Atto 8 in new fully-electric iteration; previously PHEV only BYD has revealed the all-electric Atto 8 at the 2026 Paris Motor Show. The flagship electric SUV has up to 653km of claimed range and a new Flash Charging technology that can charge the battery from 10 to 97 percent in just nine minutes. New Delhi: BYD has expanded its flagship Atto 8 SUV lineup by introducing a fully electric version at the 2026 Paris Motor Show. Joining the existing plug-in hybrid (PHEV) model, the new Atto 8 EV offers strong performance, a large battery pack, and the Chinese manufacturer’s latest charging technology. The biggest highlight is BYD’s new Flash Charging system, which makes its debut on the Atto 8 EV. The technology promises exceptionally short charging times, allowing the battery to gain a substantial amount of charge in just a few minutes. The electric SUV will be available in rear-wheel-drive (RWD) and all-wheel-drive (AWD) configurations, with the latter producing a combined 775hp. In terms of design, the electric version remains largely identical to its plug-in hybrid counterpart, apart from a few EV-specific changes. BYD Atto 8 EV: Battery, range and performance The BYD Atto 8 EV uses a 115kWh battery pack across both powertrain configurations. Buyers can choose between a single-motor rear-wheel-drive setup and a more powerful dual-motor all-wheel-drive version. The RWD variant produces 462hp and 365Nm of torque. BYD claims it can accelerate from 0 to 100 kph in eight seconds, while delivering a WLTP-certified driving range of up to 653km. The AWD model uses two electric motors to generate a combined output of 775hp and 775Nm. With the additional power and traction, the SUV can complete the 0-100 kph sprint in a claimed 4.6 seconds. However, its WLTP range is slightly lower at 602km. One of the most significant developments introduced with the Atto 8 EV is BYD’s Flash Charging technology. The system is designed to drastically reduce charging times, making longer journeys more convenient. As per BYD, the technology can replenish the battery from 10 to 97 per cent in just nine minutes. The manufacturer also claims that charging from 0 to 70 per cent takes only five minutes. BYD says the system can maintain impressive charging performance even in extremely cold conditions. At temperatures as low as -30 degrees Celsius, the battery can reportedly be charged from 20 to 97 per cent in approximately 12 minutes. These figures show the maker’s claimed charging capabilities. It is with actual charging times depend on factors such as charger compatibility, battery temperature and charging conditions. BYD Atto 8 EV: Exterior design The Atto 8 EV carries over most of its styling from the PHEV version. The most noticeable differences are the redesigned aerodynamic alloy wheels and the absence of an exhaust outlet. At the front, the electric SUV features a closed-off grille, matrix LED headlights and a curved LED daytime running light strip. The lower bumper incorporates black trim and functional air intakes intended to help cool the vehicle’s components. A LiDAR sensor is placed on the roof, indicating the presence of advanced driver-assistance hardware. The side profile of the Atto 8 EV features black alloy wheels with aerodynamic inserts, prominent wheel arches and slim roof rails. A chrome accent runs from the front fender towards the front doors, while black cladding covers the lower portion of the doors. At the back, the SUV gets distinctive infinity-knot-inspired LED tail lamps, connected by a design element incorporating an illuminated BYD badge. A roof-mounted spoiler completes the exterior styling. BYD Atto 8 EV: Interior and features On the inside, the Atto 8 EV shares its dashboard design and overall layout with the plug-in hybrid version. The cabin has a 10.25-inch digital instrument cluster and a large 15.6-inch touchscreen infotainment system. A three-spoke steering wheel houses physical buttons and scroll controls, while the dashboard incorporates slim air-conditioning vents and extensive soft-touch leather surfaces. The SUV offers a seven-seat configuration arranged in a 2+2+3 layout, with individual seats in the second row. Boot space sits at 270 litres, identical to the PHEV model. However, the fully electric Atto 8 benefits from an additional 136-litre front storage compartment, or frunk, made possible by the absence of a combustion engine. Comfort features include heating, ventilation and massage functions for both the first- and second-row seats. Other equipment highlights include a panoramic glass roof, three-zone automatic climate control and a 21-speaker DiSound audio system. The SUV also comes with two 50W wireless smartphone chargers and a front-mounted refrigerator capable of cooling its contents to -6 degrees Celsius or heating them to 50 degrees Celsius. In international markets, the BYD Atto 8 EV will compete with other large electric SUVs, including the Kia EV9, Hyundai Ioniq 9 and Skoda Peaq. Click for more latest Auto news. artigo.texto: SACRAMENTO, Calif. — There are many issues Sacramento retiree Laureen Anderson said she is driven to speak out on, like reminding people to get out and vote early. Another she said are data center’s impacts on communities and the environment. “I’m very passionate about; I do not want data centers in our area,” Anderson said. “We don’t have enough water. It takes gallons and gallons of water every day to maintain it [a data center].” Anderson isn’t alone in her opposition. Several California communities have moved to temporarily pause or restrict new data center development. And beyond water consumption, there’s another concern, said Anderson. “Also, the electricity, that’s an issue too,” she said. The potential impact on electricity rates and who should pay for major grid upgrades are at the center of a California Public Utilities Commission review of an agreement between utility company PG&E and Google to connect a massive 250-megawatt data center in San Jose. The power needed for the center, sizeable to say the least, said assistant attorney at The Utility Reform Network, a utility watchdog organization, Elise Torres. “At 250 megawatts, it’s approximately the entire load of Marin County,” Torres said. “So that gives you a sense of the scale of just this one facility.” The commission has repeatedly postponed a vote on the agreement. One possible sticking point is a proposed requirement for Google to pay an additional upfront advance toward infrastructure costs, a first for data centers, said Torres. “My speculation is that Google and PG&A are both unhappy about the current provision in the draft resolution that requires Google to pay $600,000 per megawatt,” Torres said. That would amount to as much as $150 million, intended to protect other electricity customers from potentially being left with the costs of major grid upgrades. PG&E argues the upgrades were already planned, would move forward without Google, and would benefit thousands of homes and businesses. Google said the site will feature research and development facilities as well, and reports have noted the company said it will mainly use recycled water. The commission’s eventual decision could have implications well beyond this project, said Torres. “I personally think whatever they decide here, you know, will give us a big indicator of what they’re going to do in Rule 30,” Torres said. “And, will probably be the same standard they apply to exceptional case filings going forward.” Rule 30 is a broader set of proposed standards that the commission is considering for connecting large electricity customers to the transmission grid. Other environmental impacts Torres said he worries about are their potential to produce a large amount of e-waste, and also because they need so much energy, it may make it harder for the state to move away sooner from fossil-fueled power plants. As for Anderson, she said she’s not entirely opposed to data centers, but wants stronger oversight. “It really does need to be regulated, totally, totally regulated by the feds, by the state, by local [governments],” Anderson said. “They need to get together and regulate.” So, as she said, they truly can benefit every community that encounters them.

artigo.texto: Containerized Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) Technology Innovation Key Trends, Growth Drivers and Opportunities Introduction to containerized BESS technology Containerized Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) technology is transforming the way utilities, independent power producers, and commercial enterprises store, manage, and dispatch electricity. Powered by lithium-ion and emerging sodium-ion chemistries, advanced battery management systems (BMS), power conversion systems (PCS), thermal management, and cloud-based energy management software, modern containerized BESS units deliver real-time control and grid-scale flexibility. From utility-scale renewable integration and peak shaving to commercial microgrids, EV charging hubs, and remote industrial sites, the technology is becoming an integral part of the global energy transition and the decarbonization of power networks. History of containerized BESS technology The containerized BESS industry has evolved from small stationary battery banks and UPS installations into modular, factory-assembled, plug-and-play energy storage ecosystems. Advances in lithium-ion cell density, power electronics, liquid cooling, fire suppression, and digital monitoring have enabled containerized systems to support renewable firming, frequency regulation, demand response, and resilience for critical infrastructure. Standardized 20-foot and 40-foot containers now allow rapid deployment, scalable capacity expansion, and lower installation costs compared with traditional brick-and-mortar storage plants. Benefits of containerized BESS technology Containerized BESS technology offers numerous advantages across utility, commercial, industrial, and residential environments: - Rapid deployment through factory-built, pre-tested modular containers. - Scalable capacity that can be expanded block by block as demand grows. - Enhanced grid stability, frequency regulation, and renewable energy firming. - Lower installation, civil work, and land acquisition costs. - Seamless integration with solar, wind, EV charging, and microgrid ecosystems. Current market size and growth trends of containerized BESS industry The containerized BESS market is experiencing robust growth as renewable penetration, grid modernization, and energy security become mainstream priorities. According to MarketsandMarkets, the global containerized BESS market size was valued at USD 13.87 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach USD 35.82 billion by 2030, growing at a CAGR of 20.9% from 2025 to 2030. Rising adoption of utility-scale storage, commercial microgrids, and AI-driven energy management continues to accelerate market expansion across North America, Europe, and Asia Pacific. Key drivers and factors influencing the future of containerized BESS technology AI, IoT, 5G, cloud analytics, and edge intelligence are enabling more capable containerized storage systems across industries. - artigo.texto: Demand for data center labor is up, but can Indiana’s workforce growth match the pace? (Inside INdiana Business) - With large technology companies offering hefty wages and enticing incentives as a wave of data center developments washes across the state, now seems a good time to be a skilled tradesman in Indiana. But it’s a different story for contractors focused on wrapping up other projects. For them, the unprecedented number of data center projects and the benefits that come with them are becoming a hard-to-beat competitor. READ ORIGINAL REPORT HERE: Demand for data center labor is up, but can Indiana’s workforce growth match the pace? Several area industry leaders IBJ spoke with said Indiana’s current workforce might not be able to keep up with the rapidly rising demand for skilled electricians, pipe fitters and builders — even though national statistics show that labor numbers are growing steadily. Over the past decade, the number of construction workers in Indiana has increased by 37%, from 132,300 in August 2016 to 181,300 in August 2026, according to the latest federal labor statistics. And across the state, data center projects already under construction are employing thousands, with Google alone expected to employ about 5,000 workers daily across three sites. And they’re paying well — at least one data center project is reported to be paying workers $5,000-$6,000 a week. Major opportunities With the increased media and public attention on data centers over the past year or so, some might think they are a fresh concept, but that’s not necessarily the case. Data centers have existed for years. They are typically large facilities that support cloud computing and infrastructure for everyday internet uses. Advocates compare them to power plants or water treatment facilities. But in recent years, they have become more prominent and more controversial, likely because of the artificial intelligence boom. While supporters say data centers mean more economic development for communities and workers, opponents say the facilities’ staggering energy and water usage will strain local resources. According to the International Energy Agency, a conventional data center might have the capacity for 10 to 25 megawatts of power — which is equivalent to the annual electricity consumption of 10,000 to 25,000 homes. But a hyperscale, AI-focused data center can have the capacity of 100 megawatts or more, equivalent to about 100,000 households. Several large data center projects are already under construction in Indiana. For example, Meta is building a massive $10 billion, 1,500-acre data center campus at the LEAP Research and Innovation District in Lebanon. And Google is working on three data centers in the state: one in Fort Wayne, one in Morgan County and another in Michigan City. And three other projects were approved in Indianapolis before the City-County Council put a moratorium in place through the end of next year. While some of these facilities might only establish several dozen permanent jobs once complete, the size of the projects means building them will take years — and require lots of workers. Google’s projects, for example, are expected to support thousands of trade jobs daily, according to a spokesperson. In Fort Wayne, where Google is investing $847 million to build a 900-acre campus, about 3,000 workers are on site every day. The Morgan County project, which recently saw the topping out of its first building, has over 750 daily workers — 80% of whom are local and regional hires — and the company’s Michigan City data center is projected to have about 1,500 workers daily during “major construction phases.” (For reference, about 1,500 are still working on Indiana University Health’s new downtown hospital, according to recent IBJ reports.) In Lebanon, Meta’s project is expected to employ 4,000 skilled workers on site during peak construction. Once complete, there will be about 300 operational jobs. In Decatur Township in Marion County, Sabey Corp. was able to get a $4.3 billion, 1-million-square-foot data center project approved before Indianapolis put a moratorium in place. Economic development officials have called the project the largest private capital investment in the city’s history. The Indianapolis project would be the company’s largest data center development. Sabey Corp. CEO John Sabey told IBJ he expects the project to break ground in spring 2027, but that depends on when the company can get through the permitting process and resolve an ongoing legal challenge from several Decatur Township residents. Sabey said the company does not have exact figures, but he estimated the number of workers on site could reach 500 to 1,000, if not more, depending on when the project gets underway. David Peterson, the CEO and president of Indianapolis-based electrical contractor ERMCO, said data center projects have created a “tremendous” opportunity for the trades. Peterson said ERMCO now has 1,200 electricians on site at a data center in Fort Wayne he would not name. He did not disclose specifics of the other projects the company is working on, other than saying that another two are in Indianapolis. Intense competition Data center development not only creates tons of jobs for skilled tradespeople. The pay and incentives are also significant. “We have electricians on some of our work sites, with the amount of time that they’re working in overtime, they’re making, you know, $250- to $300,000 a year in some cases,” Sabey, the data center developer, said. According to Jon Hooker, president and executive director of the Central Indiana Building Trades Council, Meta is paying electricians about $10 above the union pay scale to work on its Lebanon site — which is equivalent to about $5,000 to $6,000 a week. It is “just almost unheard of,” Hooker said. artigo.texto: Data Centers Voters in Six States Will Decide Future of Data Center Construction September 24, 2026 | Kim Miller October 13, 2026 | Billy Culleton Key Takeaways: The sheer power demand from data centers has recently pushed state lawmakers to consider new policies that allow large energy users to access dedicated power sources without everyday ratepayers shouldering the cost. These arrangements, called "behind-the-meter" or "bring-your-own-power," share the same goal: addressing public concern over rising electricity costs while giving data center developers alternatives to lengthy utility interconnection queues. While utilities and large-load users have long negotiated power purchase agreements for generation, state policymakers are seeking to make behind-the-meter arrangements more common and easier to establish. This type of legislation saw more activity in 2025 than in 2026 but is likely to remain of interest to state lawmakers as more data centers connect to the grid. Last year, seven states enacted legislation allowing data centers to source their own energy. In May 2025, Oklahoma Governor Kevin Stitt (R) signed SB 480, which exempts large users from being defined as public utilities if they provide their own electricity. The bill also allows data centers to contract with regulated and non-regulated utilities to house onsite generation. Ohio lawmakers followed suit by enacting a sweeping energy bill (HB 15) that removes barriers for large energy users to self-generate power, either directly or through a third party. In addition, the bill removed previous rules requiring self-generation sources to be located on a customer's premises. In Utah, lawmakers created a pathway for behind-the-meter generation by allowing large-load users to enter the competitive market if an agreement is not reached with the utility within 90 days. SB 132 allows data centers to source energy from the grid through a third-party supplier or from a source entirely separate from the grid. Texas, a state known for its energy production, also enacted a major bill in 2025 that addressed behind-the-meter options for data centers. SB 6, which broadly sets standards for how data centers can interconnect with the grid, allows large-load users to connect directly to an existing stand-alone generation source. The bill also requires utility regulators to direct data centers to source energy from backup generators during emergency power situations. Finally, New Hampshire lawmakers allowed off-grid power generation for large users, with the main caveat being that they have to be completely independent of the grid (HB 672). Bills that create this type of arrangement, called "consumer-regulated electricity" (or CRE) were also considered in Maryland (HB 1219 & SB 947), Illinois (HB 4163), New Jersey (A 5431), and New York (S 8037). However, none of these bills advanced out of their committee of origin. Behind-the-Meter Behind-the-meter refers to energy generation or storage systems that are located on the customer's side of the utility meter, allowing large users like data centers to generate or source their own electricity independently from the main utility grid. These arrangements can reduce reliance on the grid and help avoid passing costs onto other ratepayers. Consumer-Regulated Electricity (CRE) Consumer-regulated electricity (CRE) is a system where large energy users, such as data centers, operate their own private electricity networks or source power independently, rather than relying solely on traditional public utilities. This model allows for greater flexibility and can help large users avoid regulatory and cost structures imposed on standard utility customers. Some behind-the-meter bills explicitly make it possible for multiple large users to source off-grid power through microgrids. As part of their efforts to attract more data center development, West Virginia lawmakers created a microgrid program (HB 2014) that allows data centers to operate in certified microgrid districts. The law gives the state authority over local governments in regulating microgrids as part of its effort to attract data center users to West Virginia. In New Mexico, lawmakers enacted microgrid legislation that is more regulatory in nature. HB 93 allows customers to enter agreements with investor-owned utilities in the state for microgrid operation, including generation and distribution for onsite use. By the time legislative sessions kicked off in January 2026, data centers had become one of the most contentious issues facing lawmakers, especially at the local level, where moratoriums were being enacted. Because of this, the politics of enacting laws that speed up the process for data centers to connect to the grid became more challenging. New Jersey lawmakers enacted a pro-clean-energy measure (A 796) that directs the state's Board of Public Utilities to create energy rates that encourage large loads to bring their own generation and storage, as long as it comes from non-carbon-emitting sources. Additionally, lawmakers in Arizona (HB 4097) and Virginia (SB 751 & HB 1087) considered bills that provide pathways for large users to source behind-the-meter power. In Louisiana, a failed attempt (SB 490) to create a pathway for behind-the-meter power sourcing encouraged the Louisiana Public Service Commission (LPSC) to open its rulemaking docket on private-use electrical networks. Meanwhile, proposals in Connecticut and Maryland made behind-the-meter generation a requirement to enter the market rather than an option that data centers could exercise. Maryland's SB 596 and HB 940 banned large-load customers from connecting to the grid unless 25% of their capacity is met by either backup storage or a demand-response program. Connecticut's HB 5469 requires load customers of 50 MW and above to receive 100% of their electricity from a colocated source or off-grid supplier. artigo.texto: Last year, the Springdale Borough council gave the green light for a new massive data center to be built in the small town outside of Pittsburgh. But it's actually Allegheny County that will give the project final approval — and organizers say there's still an opportunity for the public to weigh in. The Springdale data center could draw as much power at one time as nearly 200,000 homes. It has gotten pushback from locals worried about noise, pollution, property values, and rising utility bills. Marty Garrigan has been organizing against the center with the group Save Allegheny Valley Environment (SAVE). He said it’s not too late to push back on the computing warehouse “Many people thought that this whole thing was a done deal when the borough voted in favor of it,” Garrigan said. “But the county has the final say here.” Springdale Borough Council voted to grant the project a conditional use permit in December. Several members of council said during the vote that they did not want the data center in the borough, but felt they had to approve the application to avoid a costly lawsuit. Allegheny County must approve the center’s land development plan before the project can move forward. The plan lays out the details of how the facility would be built, connected to utilities, and landscaped. County staff made 97 comments on the data center’s preliminary application, noting errors and unanswered questions. For example, the comments note that “no evidence has been provided” that conditions related to noise mitigation will be met. A virtual hearing is set for Wednesday, Oct. 14 at 6 p.m. An in-person hearing is scheduled for Oct. 28 at 6 p.m. at the Springdale borough building. Written comments will be accepted until Nov. 30. “This is an opportunity for us to increase public awareness and relay the dangers that this behemoth poses,” Garrigan said. Garrigan’s group plans to drive a billboard truck around the area for the next two weeks, to remind people that the center is “not a done deal.” SAVE is hosting an in-person gathering for the county’s virtual hearing at the Pittsburgh Shrine Center at 1877 Shriners Way in Harmar Township. Garrigan said volunteers can help people register to speak during the hearing. The group has also launched a fundraiser for possible legal and expert fees if the data center does get county approval and the fight moves to the courts. “We've had an estimate from an attorney who's fought these kinds of things before that would be $20,000 to continue on with the fight for an appeal to the county,” Garrigan said. “And that's just the first level of courts.” The data center, which has been dubbed “Springdale Dynamo” in a nod to the area’s industrial history, is financially backed by the New York-based hedge fund Davidson Kempner. A website for the project shows it could draw up to 240 megawatts of power, up from the company’s original proposal of 180 mw. Recent increases in electricity prices have been attributed to the projected growth of data centers and other heavy power users.

artigo.texto: NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WTVF) — Before Nashville's next large data center can power up, it will have to clear a new set of rules aimed at limiting the impact these facilities can have on surrounding communities. Metro Council approved new zoning regulations for data centers in July, creating five classifications based on factors including size and electrical load. The regulations prohibit the largest category, campus data centers, countywide. Councilmember Rollin Horton, a sponsor of the legislation, described Nashville's approach this way during an interview with NewsChannel 5: "Nashville has passed some of the strictest rules and regulations protecting all of Davidson County from the dangers of data centers." The regulations followed significant public debate over data center development in Nashville, particularly after plans emerged for a DC BLOX facility next to the Nashville Zoo. In July, more than 100 people spoke in opposition to data center development during Metro Council public hearings. Under Nashville's new framework, allowable data centers face different requirements depending on their size. Small data centers have a 100-foot separation requirement from specified sensitive uses, while medium facilities generally face a 500-foot requirement. Large facilities face a 2,640-foot, or half-mile, separation requirement. Sensitive uses identified by the framework include residences, schools, daycares, religious institutions, parks and zoos. A new Metro Data Center Impact Assessment & Policy Recommendations compared Nashville's regulations with policies being adopted or considered in other communities. It found Nashville's requirements for small and medium facilities generally align with other jurisdictions, but said the half-mile buffer for large facilities makes Nashville"somewhat of an outlier." "We set very strict distance requirements, especially compared to other cities," said Horton. "And so I think it's important not just that we look at how we can continue to improve our regulations, but make sure that there's no effort to water down or weaken them." The regulations include more than where facilities can be built. They require closed-loop cooling systems, establish daytime and nighttime noise limits, require 24-hour noise monitoring and require utilities to confirm they have capacity to serve a proposed project. New data centers must also provide renewable energy systems accounting for at least 15% of annual power use. Despite concluding that the city's framework provides a strong foundation for addressing many known risks, Metro's report identifies several issues officials say warrant further evaluation. Among them are vibration, increases in background noise and potential contaminants in wastewater discharged from cooling systems. Nashville currently limits data center noise at the property line to 65 decibels during the day and 55 decibels at night. But the report says the city could consider another safeguard limiting how much a facility can increase the existing background noise around it, even if it remains below those absolute limits. Vibration is another area Metro says needs further research. The new regulations do not establish a separate vibration limit or require a vibration impact assessment comparable to the required noise assessment. Metro also wants to further study wastewater from closed-loop cooling systems. The report says that discharge can potentially contain substances including heavy metals and PFAS and recommends determining whether existing contaminant standards adequately capture potential data center process-water impacts. The report does not say Nashville's water has been contaminated by data centers. "I think we have the strictest and most comprehensive rules in the entire country. That said, this is a very fast-evolving industry. So I think it's important that we continue to monitor how the industry develops and make sure that our rules and regulations stay one step ahead of the industry," said Horton. Perhaps one of the biggest questions is what happens when Nashville's framework encounters a new proposal. Metro's report says the city has yet to apply the new regulatory framework to a new data center proposal, meaning some challenges remain relatively unknown. The report recommends several changes to how Metro implements the rules, including required pre-application coordination, completeness reviews and phased approvals tied to utility milestones. It also recommends forming a working group involving Metro, Nashville Electric Service and the Tennessee Valley Authority to develop compliance procedures, coordinate enforcement and determine whether additional resources will be needed as applications, inspections and monitoring begin. The young patient was in Houston, and her life-saving liver here in Nashville. With the grounding of all civilian aircraft, how could it be done? “Nobody ever said this isn’t possible.” - Rhori Johnston

artigo.texto: The construction workers building Meta's largest-ever data center are arriving in a tiny Louisiana town with more than specialized skills and manpower. They've also got cash to spend. It's a fact that local entrepreneurs are leveraging to build new businesses. "It's been a good opportunity for everybody," David Rodgers, the cofounder of Ice Queen, a local business, told Business Insider. "I tell people, you can't stop it unless you have $50 billion. You might as well get on board and go with the flow." Meta said the data center, dubbed Hyperion, will span nearly 10 million square feet in rural Holly Ridge and will support more than 7,500 jobs at peak construction. That's a workforce larger than the population of Aspen, Colorado. While the influx of workers is straining the local housing market and disrupting aspects of daily life, their presence has also boosted the region's economy. Spinning straw into gold Holly Ridge is a very small sliver of the nearly 19,600 residents in Richland Parish, where agriculture has been the main industry for decades. Before Meta arrived, the smattering of towns, villages, and unincorporated areas that make up Richland Parish hadn't seen significant economic growth in years. Tim Allen, a Richland Parish restaurant owner, lived through that stagnation in the nearby town of Rayville. "Rayville has been a small community my whole life, and it's been in decline over the last several years. We have a lot of people whose children are moving out, and they usually don't come back," Allen said. "Growing up, downtown Rayville had multiple businesses, hardware stores, and clothing stores. One by one, they shut down until only a couple of stores were left." When Meta announced its project in 2024, Allen and his family were among those who saw an opportunity to turn things around. "Since Meta's announcement, we've seen old businesses revitalize and new ones open, including ours," Allen said. Holy Tacos opened in April 2025. TJ and Kaycie Weed, also based in Rayville, said the new demographic created by Meta's project has boosted their sales. They first opened their café, HeBrews Coffee & Eats, near the end of 2021. "When we first started, we thought 30 tickets was a good day," TJ said. "Now, we're hitting 30 tickets before the first hour and a half through the drive-thru alone. We're probably hitting 130 tickets now." The café in Rayville is a brick-and-mortar, but the couple has two franchise locations, including a food truck that opened in 2025 directly across the street from the construction site in Holly Ridge. They said the Holly Ridge location opened specifically because of Meta. "Holly Ridge does most of the catering. If it's any of the businesses under the umbrella of Meta, I send it to Holly Ridge," TJ said. The wave of construction workers inspired Rodgers and his former business partner, Linda Edwards, to cofound Ice Queen in 2025. The business sells $3 bags of ice to subcontractors and companies working on the Meta project. The parish has weathered several heat waves this summer, making ice a necessity for outdoor trade workers. Since July, residents have seen temperatures reach 100 degrees Fahrenheit more than two dozen times. The pair keeps the ice bags in a large tractor-trailer parked near the construction site and has a separate ice truck available to make deliveries. Ice was only the beginning, though, and soon Ice Queen transformed into a one-stop shop of sorts for the work crews. Coffee machines. Cups. Sugar packets. Fridges. Microwaves. Straws. You name it, Ice Queen tries to supply it. Robert Cleveland, president and CEO of the local economic development authority, Grow NELA, said the economic growth happening in Richland Parish is undeniable. Data collected by Grow NELA shows that Richland Parish's annual sales tax revenue jumped from $21 million in 2024 to $39 million in 2025. At the end of 2026, Grow NELA expects the parish will see $92 million in annual sales tax revenue. Richland Parish has gained more annual sales tax revenue in 2025 alone than in the last 20 years combined, Grow NELA says. "We have a number of small businesses that have propped up and have grown significantly because of the project," Cleveland said. Supply and demand Part of the business growth in Richland Parish is supplying construction workers with what they need while they are away from home: lodging, food, and basic necessities. Angel and Bryan Crawford, for example, chose to address the housing market gap with their rental company, Parish Line Properties. The couple owns a mobile home park called Antley Pines that opened in 2025. "We added two homes last December, four this May, and our last four in July. All the homes were secured by deposits from Meta workers before we even got them into the park," Angel said. A fully-furnished four-bedroom, two-bathroom mobile home that's eight miles from the construction site costs an average of $3,000. The couple previously worked in the nursing field, but decided to dive into real estate and property management after becoming empty nesters. "In 2024, we started buying older houses that had been on the market for a long time or needed a lot of work. We had a vision to create a mobile home park and already purchased some land when we heard about Meta's data center," Angel said. The company now owns 18 rental properties, 14 of which the owners have set aside as workforce housing. "Location is very important to Meta's workers because they work six to seven days a week and 12-plus hours a day. They leave around 4:30 in the morning, and they don't come home until 7 at night," she said. Those long days can be taxing, making places like HeBrews Coffee & Eats popular with workers. Shelbie Stephenson, owner of the Holly Ridge location, said they deliver 450 lunch plates to the Meta work site twice a month. Stephenson said they also do breakfast and coffee catering several times a month. "We have done 900 burritos and 2,500 cups of coffee

A Câmara dos Deputados aprovou, nesta terça-feira (13/10), o requerimento de urgência para o projeto de lei 3716/2026, que altera o rateio dos custos da contratação de sistemas de armazenamento (BESS). O PL, de autoria de Arnaldo Jardim (Cidadania/SP), altera a Lei nº 15.269/2025, que estabelece que o custo do armazenamento é arcado pelas geradoras de energia. A nova proposta estabelece a divisão dos valores com os consumidores. O pedido de urgência foi apresentado à Mesa, nesta terça, pelos deputados Danilo Forte (PP/CE), Evair Vieira de Melo (Republicanos/ES), Vitor Lippi (PSD/SP) e Isnaldo Bulhões Jr. (MDB/AL). Agora, o texto segue direto para plenário. O PL ainda não tinha sido distribuído para nenhuma comissão. A matéria é apoiada por diversas organizações do setor que esperam a mudança na divisão do rateio antes dos leilões de baterias, marcados para 2 e 4 de dezembro. A Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia (Absae) defende que o avanço da proposta é importante para ampliar a segurança jurídica para os certames e que a legislação estabelece um tratamento desigual para o armazenamento. “A aprovação da urgência representa um avanço para que o Congresso discuta o tema com a celeridade necessária. Em paralelo precisamos olhar para o prazo dos leilões: o sistema elétrico necessita de potência adicional em 2028, e é plenamente possível corrigir a isonomia no rateio enquanto prossegue o cronograma”, disse o diretor-executivo da Absae, Fabio Lima, em nota. Já a Associação Brasileira dos Produtores Independentes de Energia Elétrica (Apine) considera que a aprovação sinaliza uma sensibilidade do Congresso Nacional em relação à necessidade de debater o tema. “A tramitação célere é fundamental para o setor, tendo em vista que a matéria ainda será submetida à análise do Senado Federal”, afirmou a associação, em nota. O tema integra as prioridades da Agenda Legislativa de 2026 da Apine, que busca por soluções estruturais para os cortes de geração de energia (curtailment) .
