artigo.texto: New tool kit helps Minnesota cities prepare for when big tech's data centers come to town Go Deeper. Create an account or log in to save stories. Like this? Thanks for liking this story! We have added it to a list of your favorite stories. Quick Read Big tech’s giant data center proposals have touched raw nerves in several Minnesota towns, sparking firestorms of criticism aimed at local government leaders, some of whom signed non-disclosure agreements to keep project details secret until after elected officials approved the plans. Seeing how data centers have churned up local politics and spurred newcomers to run for office, some city administrators came together to seek help. The end result is a new toolkit developed by researchers at the University of Minnesota to help local government officials better understand and weigh the pros and cons of having Google, Meta or some other big tech company build a massive data center in their community. "The way we've been framing it is how do you proactively address a data center?” said Elise Harrington, a University of Minnesota public affairs professor who is the tool kit project lead. “How do you think about it before you have one?" It’s the culmination of a year of research by the University of Minnesota and the Freshwater Society, a water conservation nonprofit. It was developed to help city leaders separate facts from fiction and to guide what city codes they can enact to mitigate environmental impacts if big tech pitches in their city next. Turn Up Your Support MPR News helps you turn down the noise and build shared understanding. Turn up your support for this public resource and keep trusted journalism accessible to all. Arming local leaders with facts Harrington and her group of researchers released the tool kit last Friday afternoon in Rochester, where dozens of city planners, administrators and elected officials from cities and towns across southeast Minnesota gathered for a workshop to learn about the tool kit and try it out. Al Roder, city administrator for the nearby town of Byron, is part of the reason this tool kit exists in the first place. He and some of his peers in other southeast Minnesota cities had been talking a couple of years ago about how they could prepare for the seemingly inevitable arrival of data center proposals. “We just started having a conversation about data centers and how do we answer all these questions with facts instead of emotions?” Roder said. “Because so much of what I hear is emotional arguments for or against. Where are the facts?” He had observed how these emotions had created deep rifts in cities like Pine Island, about 20 minutes away, after Google proposed its Project Skyway data center there, dividing residents into heated factions of those who support the data center and those who vehemently oppose it. Roder and his counterparts in nearby Stewartville and Lewiston wanted to get ahead of such controversies. If Google or some other big tech company came to Byron, Roder wanted to be armed with facts and have city rules preemptively laid out for prospective data centers. “These are rules that we decided before we were in the heat of battle,” Roder told MPR News. “These are the conditions that we would find acceptable for our community. It's easier to do that before somebody's knocking on the door.” So they reached out to the community development folks at the University of Minnesota Extension for help gathering facts they could use to guide these discussions. What does the tool kit include? The guide, which will be made available to the public Wednesday, includes sections on how data centers can impact energy and water usage, and how these impacts can be regulated at the local level to manage environmental impacts. It also includes guiding questions for city leaders to ask if they get an inquiry from big tech about a data center proposal as well as examples of how to address data centers in local code. That’s why Greg Krushke attended the workshop. He's the community development manager for the city of Owatonna, and he’s in the midst of modernizing the city’s zoning and subdivision code that was developed back in the 1980s. He hopes the tool kit will help inform how they write the code and what is included in it. He said it’s especially helpful to come together with peers at a workshop like this one to talk with one another and share experiences. "What are they learning from others, and how can we be able to apply some of this and be able to use it to help ourselves and our neighbors?" Krushke said. A regional approach Andi Sutton, executive director of the Southeast Regional Sustainable Development Partnership with University of Minnesota Extension, said she was thrilled that so many local government decision makers showed up for Friday’s workshop in Rochester. Local data center decisions are not made in a vacuum, and she hopes the workshop, which has convened leaders from across the region, will spark these conversations early since the environmental impacts of data centers don’t stop at city borders. That’s especially true in southeast Minnesota, which has a unique geologic landscape. It’s made of karst, a type of rock that’s very porous. “It means that the way that water moves through our region is different from other parts of Minnesota,” Sutton explained. “We have sensitive aquifers. We have water that’s in use for agricultural purposes, for ecosystem purposes. So what one community does with the water that they have will very quickly and inevitably have an effect on another community.” Sutton hopes this workshop jump starts these conversations and leads local planners to ask their neighbors questions as they weigh the pros and cons of data center proposals; questions like, “Who is my neighbor in terms of energy, water, infrastructure or roads?” “All of these questions get pushed to their limits by data centers as a development opportunity,” Sutton said. “We're so grateful that we're able to h

artigo.texto: Abstract: Photovoltaic (PV) systems are renowned for low electricity generation costs, but their intermittent and non-dispatchable generation poses significant challenges to grid stability and curtailment. Concentrated solar power (CSP), equipped with thermal energy storage (TES), can provide firm, dispatchable power, but its wide deployment is constrained by high capital and operating costs. To address limitations of PV and CSP systems, this study proposes an operation strategy for hybrid PV-CSP plants to utilize the thermal storage capacity of CSP systems. The proposed strategy utilizes stable power supply and grid capacity constraints to guide TES systems operation, providing a methodology for determining supply target power, followed by system simulation, techno-economic evaluation and capacity parameter optimization. Over an annual simulation, the hybrid plant achieved an average monthly target-fulfillment rate of 93.5 %, indicating robust operational performance. The effects of various capacity parameters on system operation are evaluated, with capacity allocation optimized based on metrics of levelized cost of energy (LCOE) and channel utilization rate (CUR). Analysis of capacity parameters demonstrates that the rated output power of CSP systems exerts the most substantial impact on hybrid system operations. Optimization results demonstrate that configuration combining large-scale PV with thermal energy storage-dominated CSP systems (Mode I) could achieve 40–50 % CUR at 0.06–0.07 $/kWh LCOE, while the hybrid system pairing small-scale PV with large-capacity CSP plants (Mode II) attains 70–80 % CUR with 0.08–0.086 $/kWh LCOE. PV-CSP hybrid power systems effectively address operational challenges inherent in sole PV and CSP systems. Bo Wang, Tao Ma, Yanjun Dai, Wentao Xie, Peng Xue, Simulation and techno-economic optimization of a PV-CSP hybrid system with thermal energy storage under stability-oriented operation strategy, Journal of Energy Storage, Volume 150, 2026,120371, ISSN 2352-152X, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.est.2026.120371

artigo.texto: O Valor Econômico informa que a expansão dos investimentos em data centers no Brasil começa a provocar uma reação regulatória nos Estados, com propostas que vão da concessão de incentivos locais a novas exigências sobre uso de água, licenciamento ambiental e transparência. Dos 16 projetos apresentados nas assembleias estaduais em 2026, oito criam restrições ou ônus aos empreendimentos. As propostas favoráveis eram maioria no ano passado, segundo levantamento da Innova Assuntos Públicos obtido com exclusividade pelo Valor. O estudo mapeou 20 projetos de lei e de lei complementar sobre data centers em 11 assembleias legislativas entre 2025 e outubro de 2026. Em todo o ano de 2025 foram registradas quatro iniciativas, valor que saltou para 16 no acumulado deste ano até outubro. Dos 20 projetos, nove são restritivos, sete favoráveis, dois misturam incentivos e exigências e dois são considerados neutros. Itaipu emite alerta de cheia no rio Paraná A Comissão Especial de Cheias da Itaipu Binacional divulgou, no domingo (11), um boletim hidrológico indicando perspectiva de elevação rápida do nível do Rio Paraná nos próximos dias, com risco de impactos em estruturas e residências do lado brasileiro do rio. No domingo, por volta de 10h, a cota registrada do rio era de 110,4 metros na Ponte de Amizade, em Foz do Iguaçu (PR). A projeção é de que o nível poderá subir até 115,10 metros na segunda-feira (12) e até 115,14 metros na terça (13), segundo o boletim. Paulo. Crucial no desenvolvimento de São Paulo, o complexo foi fundado pela Light em 10 de outubro de 1926 e está hoje sob gestão da Emae (Empresa Metropolitana de Águas e Energia), cujo controle a Sabesp assumiu em fevereiro deste ano. A usina fica em Cubatão (SP) e continua em plena atividade. Ainda mantém parte de suas características originais, mas já não opera da mesma forma como fazia no passado. Desde 2012, afinal, a Henry Borden trabalha sob o regime de disponibilidade. Funciona assim: em vez de vender energia ao mercado, ela recebe para garantir que sua produção esteja sempre à disposição do ONS, o operador nacional do sistema elétrico, que pede eletricidade sob demanda — que costuma ser solicitada quase todos os dias. Australiana compra projeto de terras raras próximo de mina de Serra Verde A australiana Alvo Minerals anunciou a assinatura de um contrato definitivo para adquirir, em etapas, até 100% da brasileira Mata Azul S.A., responsável pelo projeto de terras raras Bluebush, em Goiás, localizado a cerca de 40 quilômetros da mina Serra Verde, recentemente adquirida pela americana USA Rare Earth por US$ 2,8 bilhões. O montante já supera em mais que o dobro o valor das negociações de todo o ano de 2025, que somaram US$ 2,3 bilhões. Os dados indicam que 42% dos US$ 8,2 bilhões negociados entre 2025 e 2026, até 2 de outubro, estavam relacionados a projetos de terras raras. Os dois principais anúncios envolveram as aquisições da mineradora Serra Verde, em Minaçu (GO), pela americana USA Rare Earth, no valor de US$ 2,8 bilhões, e o projeto Caldeira, em Caldas (MG), pela australiana Lynas, por US$ 672 mi. (Agência Infra) A corrida das indústrias do Rio para entrar no leilão de gás da União Reportagem da Agência Eixos indica que ao menos sete indústrias do Rio de Janeiro correm contra o relógio para avançar com as documentações com a CEG e a CEG Rio, nos próximos dias, para migração para o mercado livre de gás natural. As empresas miram o leilão de gás da União, marcado pela Pré-Sal Petróleo S.A. (PPSA) para 22 de outubro. O edital do certame, publicado na semana passada, admite a habilitação de indústrias que ainda estão no mercado cativo. Quem entra assim fica obrigado a comprar por meio de comercializadora. O prazo da primeira etapa de habilitação terminou ontem (12/10). Na habilitação, a empresa deve enviar o protocolo de pedido de migração e indicar o estado onde está localizada a unidade industrial que vai receber o gás. O estado pode ser trocado depois, mas só com o aval da PPSA. De acordo com a reportagem, a expectativa é que a fila de migrações no Rio enfim destrave, após o acordo assinado entre o governo do Rio, a Agenersa e a Naturgy, para encerrar a disputa judicial sobre a abertura do mercado no estado. África bate recorde de energia solar, mas dados oficiais não registram avanço, diz relatório A África registra recorde na instalação de painéis solares em 2026, com 17 GW (gigawatts) previstos até o final do ano, um aumento de 45% em relação a 2025 e o equivalente a 1,2 vez a capacidade da usina hidrelétrica de Itaipu. No entanto, o avanço não aparece nas estatísticas oficiais por conta de limitações nos dados nacionais, dizem as organizações Ember e African Tech Futures Lab. Para contornar informações desatualizadas, as entidades analisaram as importações de placas solares da China, de onde vêm 94% dos painéis instalados no continente. (Folha de S. artigo.texto: However, there may be at least one issue where the board's 21 members can find consensus. "The county board is pretty unified in all things related to data centers right now — very cautious, very much in favor of having strong regulations, very much in favor of transparency," Farney said. In that vein, two items related to this topic will be discussed at tonight's committee-of-the-whole meeting: an ordinance prohibiting nondisclosure agreements and a resolution against property-tax incentives for hyperscale data-center developments. No final action will be taken during the meeting. "These are all commitments that we have made," said board member Emily Rodriguez, who chairs the data-center activities task force. "We are not interested in anything that dodges taxes, for example. That's something we all agree on on the data-center task force. We also all agree that nondisclosure agreements are bad governance and that folks should be embarrassed to sign them, and data centers should not ask that of local governments." The proposed ordinance against NDAs states that such agreements have "become an issue with other units of government in local and national news." If approved, the ordinance would prohibit county board members and county employees from entering into NDAs regarding county business — in any situation, not just instances where data-center developers are involved. As for the other piece of legislation, the proposed resolution would prohibit "the negotiation of tax-abatement agreements, payment-in-lieu-of-taxes agreements and other concessions for the development and construction of hyperscale data centers within Champaign County." "No data-center applications have yet been submitted to the county for rural Champaign County, but rumors and public outcry have prompted the need for a formal position," the resolution states. The two proposals come after the village of Mahomet announced on Sept. 28 that it was in talks with Clean Cloud Energy about a potential data center project in "a rural area west of Champaign" that falls within Mahomet's extraterritorial jurisdiction. One week later, the village announced the end of those discussions amid public opposition, including concerns about transparency. Farney, who wrote the resolution against tax incentives for hyperscale data centers, sent a draft to the board's policy and finance committee chairs on Oct. 5. "And like a half-hour later, somebody texted me the article that says, 'Hey, Mahomet's saying they're backing off,'" he said. "But I wanted to get that out there right away for the county to actually be able to do something immediately. We don't have to go through the same processes that we do for the zoning ordinance change in order to put a policy in effect for tax breaks for developments. And so I wanted to have something on record." When asked how payment-in-lieu-of-taxes agreements work, Farney said it's his understanding that data-center developers sometimes offer to make payments to communities while also entering into agreements for long-term property-tax abatements or reductions. Farney said that such agreements end up "being a benefit to the developer and not to the taxing bodies within the area as far as collecting the full value of property taxes." "Basically, what I'm saying is, if you want to build a data center here, then you're going to have to do it by our ordinances, which are going to be very stringent when the data-center task force gets done with their work," he told The News-Gazette. "You're also going to have to play by the rules that are in place for every other taxpayer in the county, as far as the county's portion of the tax bill goes. And so we're not going to give any incentives for data centers. If they can make it, they're gonna make it on their own." It's his hope that other governments and taxing bodies will enact similar policies and form a united front. Champaign County currently has a moratorium on the development of data centers with "at least 10,000 square feet of processing area"; the ban is currently set to end in April. The county also created the data-center activities task force to draft planning and zoning regulations for such developments. A previous statement from Leslie Farmer, Clean Cloud Energy's director of environmental and permitting, indicated that the company may still be considering the project, just not in partnership with Mahomet. "Clean Cloud Energy has decided not to seek annexation into the village of Mahomet following discussions with village leadership," she said. "We respect Champaign County's ongoing review of data-center regulations and will evaluate our project's development in accordance with the framework established by the county." Documents released by the village on Sept. 28 following a Sept. 14 Freedom of Information Act request by Mahomet resident John Bambenek show that Clean Cloud Energy began talking with Mahomet officials about the project in December. The village entered into a nondisclosure agreement with the company in early 2026 but was released from the agreement on Sept. 16. Communications between the village and Clean Cloud Energy included multiple drafts of a proposed redevelopment and annexation agreement. Both Farney and Rodriguez said that if a municipality annexes an unincorporated area, that land would no longer be subject to the county's moratorium or zoning regulations on data centers. "I was very surprised to hear that Mahomet was in those discussions, knowing that the county was working on a data-center ordinance," Farney said. "... I knew immediately, 'OK, this is how the data-center developers are trying to do an end-around around the county and any other entities that are trying to regulate this.'" Rodriguez said that the situation in Mahomet resulted in "broken trust," making it important for the county to "codify" its position. artigo.texto: Studina BESS is a 100 MW/200 MWh project in Olt County. Like nearby project, Scorniçesti (127 MW/254 MWh) – which is now nearing completion – Studina is a standalone system that will add significant storage capacity to the Romanian network, supporting grid stability, and energy security. R.Power has appointed an experienced contractor to handle balance of plant and high-voltage grid connection works for the project, which will connect to the national distribution grid. Construction is now expected to begin in 4Q26 this year, ahead of an expected connection date in 3Q27. The project sits within a wider CEE pipeline that includes 0.9 GW/3 GWh of assets in operation and under construction, alongside 0.7 GW/2.8 GWh of commercialised, ready-to-build projects. “Having advanced our flagship Romanian BESS, Scorniçesti, through financing, commercialisation and construction, we are now pleased to set the wheels in motion for Studina, which will play an equally important role in supporting the regional energy transition,” said Florin Federenciuc, R.Power Country Head for Romania. “Romania is a pace setter for grid scale storage adoption, not just in CEE but across Europe as a whole, and we are proud to be contributing to that momentum.” For more news and technical articles from the global renewable industry, read the latest issue of Energy Global magazine. artigo.texto: A heated debate is ongoing within the European Union regarding the EU Emissions Trading Scheme (EU ETS). In July, the European Commission presented a proposal to revise the scheme, and on 12 October this became the subject of political debates held by the Council of the EU. The Council has stated its aim to combine stronger climate ambitions with support for industrial competitiveness. This was reported by the Council of the European Union. The EU ETS is the bloc’s key climate policy instrument, which helps to reduce emissions and is the world’s first and largest carbon market. It requires companies to pay for their CO₂ emissions. Supporters of the EU ETS believe it encourages businesses to invest in the ‘green’ transition, whilst opponents see it as placing excessive financial pressure on them. "We must ensure that the EU Emissions Trading System is fit for the next decade. Our aim is to align our carbon market with our climate ambitions in a way that also ensures the competitiveness of our industry,” emphasised Dara O’Brien, Ireland’s Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment, who currently holds the presidency of the Council of the EU. They added that the review of the EU ETS should align the carbon market with the EU’s climate target – to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 90 per cent by 2040. The ministerial discussions are focusing on the trajectory of the annual emissions cap after 2030, as well as the use of international carbon credits and carbon sequestration projects. The debate also assessed the proposed mechanisms for financing and allocating free allowances. Some politicians expressed the view that the EU ETS should be extended to cover aviation, shipping and the waste management sector. O’Brien noted that they would aim to reach agreements on the revision of the ETS by December 2026. At the same time, according to data from Politico, the three largest political groups in the European Parliament are set to oppose any watering down of the emissions trading scheme. It was previously reported that the European Parliament intends to make significant amendments to the European Commission’s proposal. In particular, the Member States wish to require 75 per cent of ETS revenues to be reinvested in the eco-modernisation of businesses A number of countries will call for the cancellation of the revocation of ‘excess’ quotas in the Market Stability Reserve. As a reminder, the European Commission presented its proposal to reform the EU carbon market on 17 July. It includes, in particular, an increase in funding for decarbonisation, an extension of the period for receiving free allowances, and a reduction in the level of allowances transferred to the market stability reserve. Work is continuing in Ukraine on the legislative framework for establishing a national emissions trading scheme. In addition to the draft bill from the Ministry of Economy – which was drawn up taking into account feedback from experts and stakeholders – there are three parliamentary proposals. A detailed comparison of these can be found in the article by EcoPolitika.

artigo.texto: EPC contractor, Parapet, working with R.Power’s in-house EPC management team, commenced construction in spring 2026. It has, over the past three months, laid foundations and deployed all 46 battery units and 23 containerised medium-voltage transformer stations. Scornicesti BESS will be one of the first assets of its kind in Romania, and one of the largest BESS assets to enter operation in Central & Eastern Europe (CEE). Connecting Scornicesti directly to the high-voltage national transmission grid, operated by Transelectrica, is a major undertaking that goes well beyond a standard project and has required extensive design works. Once connected, expected in late 2026/early 2027, the project will become a strategic energy asset for Romania’s national energy system. R.Power secured a €46 million financing package for the project in June 2026. Under the terms of the deal, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) provided €44 million in investment and bridge financing, while Polish development bank Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego (BGK) issued a €2.3 million bank guarantee to secure the long-term optimisation contract in place with regional trading partner, GEN-I. The project, located in Olt County, is co-owned through a JV with France’s Eiffel Investment Group. “As a utility scale asset connected to the national transmission grid, Scornicesti BESS will actively support the stabilisation of Romania’s energy system.” said Florin Federenciuc, R.Power Country Head for Romania. “By integrating BESS at the heart of its energy transition, Romania is strengthening its grid resilience and supporting the roll-out of renewable energy generation. Having contracted our first Romanian PV assets just two years ago, we are proud to now be playing this vital role in one of Europe’s fastest growth energy transition markets. “Together with EBRD, BGK, Eiffel Investment Group, and GEN-I, we look forward to completing the final phase of construction and commissioning and getting this strategic asset to work.” For more news and technical articles from the global renewable industry, read the latest issue of Energy Global magazine. With insights from experts such as Everllence, BW Ideol, EM&I, Watson Farley & Williams, and many more, make sure to check out this issue now.

artigo.texto: Principais Pontos - As ações da Enerflex subiram 13% hoje após a empresa vencer um contrato para construir mais de um gigawatt de unidades de energia a gás natural para um data center norte-americano. - O contrato eleva o backlog de energia behind-the-meter da Enerflex para mais de 1,75 gigawatts, com entregas até 2028, e as estimativas de receita dos analistas foram definidas antes deste anúncio. - A Enerflex não divulgou o valor em dólares do contrato e está investindo cerca de US$ 100 milhões para expandir as instalações de Sistemas de Engenharia que irão construí-lo. - O CIBC elevou a recomendação da ação para Outperformer com um preço-alvo de US$ 35, e o relatório do terceiro trimestre será a próxima oportunidade para ver quanto vale o backlog em dólares. Enerflex (EFXT) As ações subiram 13% hoje após a empresa fechar um pedido de mais de um gigawatt de energia a gás para um único data center. Antes da abertura, a Enerflex anunciou que construirá unidades de energia a gás behind-the-meter para "um grande desenvolvimento de data center na América do Norte". Este novo contrato sozinho é mais que o dobro dos aproximadamente 450 megawatts anunciados em 1º de outubro. Somando esses e outros contratos, seu backlog de energia behind-the-meter agora ultrapassa 1,75 gigawatts, com entregas até 2028. O CEO Paul Mahoney atribuiu a demanda à IA e destacou o "sucesso da empresa em garantir mais de 1,75 gigawatts de backlog" (comunicado à imprensa). Às 10h, o CIBC elevou a recomendação da ação para Outperformer, de Neutral, com um preço-alvo de US$ 35. Gigawatts em um negócio de US$ 3,5 bilhões O backlog de Sistemas de Engenharia da Enerflex estava em US$ 1,5 bilhão no final de junho, acima dos US$ 1,1 bilhão no final de 2025, e a maior parte dos 1,75 gigawatts anunciados hoje foi contratada após esse período. A empresa não divulgou um valor em dólares para o novo contrato nem nomeou o cliente. O contrato chega a um negócio cuja receita tem se mantido estável, em US$ 3,52 bilhões em 2025, embora os analistas projetem US$ 4,37 bilhões até 2028... Essas estimativas são de 9 de outubro, antes do contrato de hoje. Com entregas ocorrendo até 2028, eu esperaria que os números de 2027 e 2028 sejam revisados para cima. Agora a Enerflex precisa construí-lo Para construir tudo em suas plantas norte-americanas, a Enerflex autorizou cerca de US$ 100 milhões para expandir suas instalações de Sistemas de Engenharia, e apenas US$ 15 milhões disso estão no guia de gastos de capital deste ano. A administração espera que isso aumente significativamente a capacidade de receita do negócio. É muito trabalho novo dependendo de um cronograma que se estende até 2028, então um atraso ou um custo excedente em um pedido na escala de gigawatts teria um impacto forte. A ação ainda não está esticada A Enerflex já negociava a 14x o lucro futuro no último fechamento, bem acima de sua média de cinco anos de 9,7x... Ao preço desta manhã, está próximo de 16x, ainda bem abaixo de seu pico de 23,8x em janeiro de 2022. E o preço-alvo de US$ 35 do CIBC está confortavelmente acima mesmo do preço de hoje. Eu posso ver a visão do mercado sobre a Enerflex mudando ainda mais a partir daqui. Por anos, o mercado precificou a empresa como uma fabricante de equipamentos a gás, e um pedido na escala de gigawatts é um forte sinal de que o negócio é algo mais do que isso. Os analistas também ainda não incorporaram o contrato em suas estimativas, o que deixa espaço para os números se ajustarem. Claro, ainda não sabemos quanto tudo isso vale em dólares. O relatório do terceiro trimestre da Enerflex é a primeira chance de descobrir. Então, quanto vale realmente a ação da Enerflex? artigo.texto: Growth through decarbonisation: Why the EU must stand firm on emissions trading EU Climate Week began in Brussels on 12 October. The EU itself should remember that the economy can grow while emissions fall. Technology Industries of Finland does not support erratic climate policy. We support a predictable investment environment, a strong and long-term emissions trading system, electrification and clean domestic energy. Climate action is still sometimes approached with caution on the grounds that it is too expensive. Europe’s own figures tell a different story: between 1990 and 2024, the EU’s GDP grew by more than 70 percent, while net greenhouse gas emissions fell by 40 percent. Since the launch of emissions trading in 2005, emissions in the sectors covered by the system have halved. The Commission wants to support the continuation of climate policy because it links climate policy more closely to competitiveness, affordable energy and reducing strategic dependencies. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen outlined the bigger picture in her State of the Union address in September: “The transition is complex, and we have to adapt our approach and learn along the way. But Europe can, must and will stay the course on its climate goals.” The Commission has also consistently promoted the phase-out of Russian fossil energy imports, with transition periods. In Finland, security is understood broadly. Climate policy is also not seen as a separate cost item, but as part of building self-sufficiency and resilience. In Finland, the volatility of fossil fuel prices is visible in transport and logistics costs. In the marine industry and heavy transport, the transition to clean electricity and clean fuels is beginning. We need a major leap in electrification One of Finland’s strengths is that electricity is more than 95 percent emission-free and among the most competitive in Europe in terms of price. Growing electricity consumption creates demand, but networks are now starting to become a bottleneck. At the same time, the Confederation of Finnish Industries’ green investment data window, Fingrid’s assessments and the Finnish Wind Power Association’s own figures all point to strong readiness to unlock new production potential. In addition, Finland’s existing nuclear power capacity is being renewed, and readiness to produce electricity and heat with small modular reactors is being built in several locations. The Finnish economy needs a major leap in electrification, supported by hydrogen, clean fuels and other solutions. This electrification leap is the next growth step, and both society and companies must be brought on board. We cannot afford to stumble now. Emissions trading rewards the most efficient solutions Technology Industries of Finland has defended the EU Emissions Trading System as the cornerstone of climate policy because it is a market-based tool. In addition, it generates revenues that should be allocated to accelerating the transition in the sectors affected by emissions trading. It puts a price on emissions but leaves companies free to choose the means. Emissions are reduced where it makes the most sense and where it is most cost-effective. For the sake of the EU’s own competitiveness, this should not be distorted with state aid. Countries and companies that have invested early are now in a stronger position. Weakening emissions trading would punish frontrunners and would not eliminate regulation as it would simply be replaced by more detailed, less market-based and less efficient steering. Freedom from fossil fuels is also security policy Europe’s dependence on imported fossil fuels is both an economic and a security policy risk. Russia’s war of aggression has shown how energy can be used as an instrument of pressure and as a means to finance a war economy. Every unit of energy saved or produced cleanly in Europe reduces the need to transfer wealth outside the Union. According to Eurostat, the EU is moving in the right direction, but slowly. Energy import dependency has decreased: in 2022, net imports accounted for 63 percent of the EU’s energy, and in 2024 the figure was still 57 percent. Yet in 2025, oil, gas and solid fossil fuels worth EUR 337 billion were still imported into the EU. In other words, we remain heavily dependent on energy whose price is determined elsewhere. Fossil fuels are still needed in transport, heating and industry. But dependence — the obligation to buy — can be reduced especially through electrification, clean electricity production, a sufficient and smart grid, and energy efficiency. These are precisely the areas where Finland has solutions to offer. When carbon has a price, demand is created for clean technology. At the same time, the trade balance, security of supply and Europe’s own strategic autonomy are strengthened. Bringing the handprint into EU climate policy European solutions can also reduce emissions outside Europe. In Finland’s case, this export-driven carbon handprint is larger than the emissions of our emissions trading sector. There is therefore evidence of the positive impacts of technology exports. However, the EU has not yet strongly embraced the carbon handprint in its climate policy. Could the handprint be brought more firmly into the core of EU climate policy, alongside the carbon footprint? I am in Brussels for Climate Week — let’s discuss.

artigo.texto: Câmara aprova urgência do PL que faz rateio de custos de baterias elétricas Projeto ainda precisa passar pelo plenário, o que deve ficar para o período pós-eleitoral; setores argumentam que proposta traria maior segurança jurídica e previsibilidade para o setor elétrico A Câmara dos Deputados aprovou nesta terça-feira um requerimento de urgência para o projeto de lei que muda a proporção de rateio dos custos de baterias elétricas. O projeto em si, no entanto, deve ser votado no plenário da Câmara apenas após o segundo turno das eleições presidenciais, marcado para 25 de outubro. Com a urgência aprovada, o texto do deputado Arnaldo Jardim (Cidadania-SP) se torna uma "prioridade" dos trabalhos legislativos. Na prática, o projeto altera uma revogação de uma lei de 2004, determinando que os custos das contratações de baterias sejam divididos entre os geradores e os consumidores de energia elétrica. Atualmente, uma regulamentação da Aneel (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica) determina a exclusividade para agentes do setor, o que produz, segundo o autor do projeto, "distorções na alocação de recursos". Ainda há a necessidade de negociar a tramitação da proposta junto ao governo federal para que vá de fato a voto. A proposta também depende de aprovação do Senado Federal para se tornar lei. Setores argumentam que a legislação atual cria um cenário de insegurança jurídica aos leilões de bateria que estão previstos para dezembro deste ano, além de acentuar a imprevisibilidade das tratativas do setor de energia. A proposta corrigiria "assimetrias" do modelo atual. As entidades Absae (Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia), Absolar (Associação Brasileira de Energia Solar Fotovoltaica), Apine (Associação Brasileira dos Produtores Independentes de Energia Elétrica), Abeeólica (Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica e Novas Tecnologias) e Abiape (Associação Brasileira dos Investidores em Autoprodução de Energia) emitiram uma nota em apoio ao PL. “Todas as tecnologias e soluções que prestam serviços semelhantes aos usuários devem estar sujeitas ao mesmo regime jurídico, permitindo alocação e comparação justa dos custos. Por isso, as regras de custeio da reserva de capacidade devem ser as mesmas para todas as soluções eventualmente contratadas”, diz o comunicado. O principal ponto de convergência entre as entidades é de que a manutenção do modelo atual pode elevar o custo de energia para o consumidor, tendo em vista que os custos refletem diretamente no preço da energia que chega às casas brasileiras.

Battery Storage Four-hour battery storage now beats gas peaking in 43 markets Storage LCOE falls below open-cycle gas turbines Gas shortages and scale widen the cost gap Stock video by ROMAN ODINTSOV via Pexels Oct 12, 2026 Four-Hour Battery Storage Beats Gas Peaking on Cost in All 43 Wood Mackenzie Markets Four-hour battery storage has reached a cost milestone, with its levelized cost of electricity falling below that of open-cycle gas turbines in every one of the 43 global markets modeled by Wood Mackenzie, according to the firm's latest Levelized Cost of Electricity report. The analysis, reported by pv magazine, also finds that single-axis tracker solar is now the cheapest new-build power source in 43 of the 48 markets studied. Wood Mackenzie principal analyst Ahmed Jameel Abdullah described the economic shift as decisive and widening, noting that gas turbine shortages and rising fuel volatility are lifting peaking costs while expanding battery manufacturing keeps pushing storage costs lower. The report attributes the change to advancing technologies and manufacturing scale that are redrawing global power market dynamics. North America as an exception North America stands apart from the global trend in long-term cost trajectories, shaped by domestic trade policies, supply chain protections, and load pressures. Unlike international markets that benefit from low-cost Chinese equipment exports, developers in the United States and Canada face near-term cost headwinds, with solar costs remaining elevated under tariffs, anti-dumping and countervailing duty actions, and Section 232 import restrictions. Utility-scale solar developers retain a buffer from 168 GW of safe-harbored capacity, but module prices are projected to rise by roughly 5 percent annually through 2030. Distributed generation faces greater pressure, with residential and commercial solar module prices forecast to increase 6 percent in 2027 and a further 14 percent in 2028. Storage incentives and load growth For energy storage, federal tax credits under the Inflation Reduction Act continue to offer a competitive advantage, helping offset strict Foreign Entity of Concern sourcing restrictions and domestic supply bottlenecks. A temporary cost increase is anticipated when the Investment Tax Credit phases out in the late 2030s, but hardware commoditization, alternative cell chemistries, and localized manufacturing expansion are expected to bring long-term storage LCOE down 10 percent by 2060. At the same time, substantial load growth from data center development is prompting utilities to reassess capacity planning. Thermal capital costs remain elevated because of a supply deficit cycle in gas generation equipment through the late 2030s, which strengthens the long-term economic case for paired renewables and storage despite near-term headwinds. Faster declines abroad Outside North America, storage and solar costs are declining more quickly owing to unhindered supply chain integration. The convergence of falling storage costs and high gas turbine prices is changing how grid operators plan baseline and peaking capacity, and the underlying economics continue to favor renewable-plus-storage builds over new thermal peaking plants. Abdullah said the structural shift being tracked is no longer only about renewables becoming competitive, but about storage and solar together redefining the economics of a power system. He added that the combination of falling storage costs and strong renewable resources is closing off the economic case for new gas peaking capacity globally. artigo.texto: Dive Brief: - The global failure rate for lithium-ion battery energy storage systems, on a per-GWh basis, fell 98% from 2018 to 2025 and 50% from 2024 to 2025, the Electric Power Research Institute said in a new analysis of its BESS failure incident database. - Stationary energy storage systems’ annual failure rates range from 0.04% to 0.14%, according to the analysis. That is comparable to the 0.1% annual failure rate for oil-filled electrical transformers, EPRI said in the report, Risk Factors and Failure Statistics of Lithium-Ion BESS. - Safety reviews and, in some cases, retrofits can mitigate failure risk and improve reliability in older systems, which tend to fail at higher rates than newer systems built under stricter codes and design practices, EPRI said. Dive Insight: Ninety-three percent of the BESS safety incidents EPRI reviewed worldwide resulted in no injuries or fatalities, according to the report. In the United States, no reported injuries or fatalities have occurred as a result of BESS failures since April 2019, when an explosion at an Arizona Public Service facility seriously injured four firefighters. A post-incident report by Underwriters Laboratories, the global safety science organization known as UL, noted that the APS installation was commissioned before the initial release of NFPA 855, the safety standard that governs energy storage systems today. Lakshmi Srinivasan, a senior technical leader with EPRI’s energy storage program and a principal investigator on the report, told Utility Dive that battery systems deployed over the past five years appear significantly more reliable than earlier vintages. The trend continues today. “There are things we know in 2026 that were not necessarily understood in 2019 or 2020, when the older systems were being put in place,” Srinivasan said in an interview. The most dramatic BESS failure in the U.S. involved a utility-scale installation inside a 1950s-era turbine hall at a decommissioned thermal power plant near Santa Cruz, California, known as Moss Landing. In January 2025, thermal runaway in one of the units caused fire to spread throughout the indoor facility and ultimately destroyed most of the 300-MW battery array. Thick smoke emanated from the facility for days, but no injuries were reported and subsequent soil and water monitoring found no significant threats to human health or the environment. Experts later told Utility Dive the incident was a “learning opportunity” for the energy storage industry. Indoor BESS facilities fail at higher rates and sustain more damage on average than outdoor facilities, according to EPRI’s report. Propagation-prevention measures within battery units and fire walls or similar barriers between units can mitigate fire’s spread within indoor facilities, EPRI said. Vistra commissioned Moss Landing in 2020. BESS facilities commissioned before 2021 account for just 3% of global energy storage capacity, according to the report. It’s worthwhile for owners of those older facilities to run thorough risk assessments of them and take corrective action if warranted, Srinivasan said. For example, the 2019 incident in Arizona showed a need for older BESS facilities to address explosion risk, which represents “a different risk than fire and a bigger one from a personnel and equipment standpoint,” Srinavasan said. Explosion-mitigation retrofits range from what she called “a relatively low-difficulty change,” like installing flammable gas detectors inside battery enclosures, to more significant projects like installing new ventilation systems or making structural upgrades to direct pressure waves upward and away from first responders, Srinavasan said. Those last two types of projects generally require changes to battery unit envelopes, which could void the manufacturer’s warranty or interfere with other aspects of the system’s design, Srinavasan said. In some scenarios, it could make more sense to prematurely decommission an outdated, higher-risk system, she added. Although newer battery systems appear to be safer than early-vintage systems, local permitting remains challenging in some jurisdictions due to limitations in the NFPA 855 standard that lead most developers to apply for exemptions to allow for higher energy densities or other project modifications, Srinavasan said. To assist local authorities that may lack in-house expertise, New York added a requirement to its fire code — which took effect in January — that those authorities can make energy storage developers pay for independent technical reviews of exemption applications, she added. Correction: We have updated this story to remove a reference to a new NFPA standard expected this fall. NFPA 855 will remain the key standard for battery energy storage systems.

artigo.texto: A Youdera assinala 11 anos de atividade com mais de 2.500 projetos de energia solar realizados em Portugal, Espanha e Suíça e pretende reforçar a aposta em sistemas locais que combinam produção fotovoltaica, armazenamento em baterias e gestão de energia, foi divulgado em comunicado. Segundo a mesma fonte, cinco anos depois de iniciar operações em Portugal, a empresa está a direcionar a sua atividade para soluções de energia descentralizada instaladas nas próprias instalações dos clientes, do lado do consumo, o chamado modelo behind the meter. A estratégia passa por combinar a produção solar com baterias e ferramentas digitais de gestão de energia. Segundo a empresa, a plataforma tecnológica, que recorre a inteligência artificial, permite otimizar a utilização da energia produzida localmente e a eletricidade adquirida à rede. A evolução do modelo de negócio acompanha também um reforço da capacidade de investimento. No início de 2026, a Youdera fechou uma ronda estratégica com a Amundi Energy Transition, associada a um plano de implementação de 150 milhões de euros para infraestruturas de energia distribuída. O financiamento deverá ser aplicado na instalação de novos sistemas, na incorporação de armazenamento em ativos existentes e na aquisição de projetos e portefólios já em operação nos três mercados onde a empresa está presente. “O quinto aniversário de operação da Youdera em Portugal é uma ocasião especial. Temos muito orgulho no trabalho que temos feito no país até aqui”, afirma Pedro Miranda, cofundador e CEO da Youdera. A empresa, acrescenta, começou por financiar projetos solares e evoluiu para um modelo em que constrói e opera sistemas locais de energia nas instalações dos clientes, combinando produção, armazenamento e gestão. A Youdera estabeleceu como objetivo alcançar 500 megawatts (MW) de potência instalada em Portugal, Espanha e Suíça até 2030, através da construção de novos sistemas de geração e armazenamento e da aquisição de projetos e portefólios em funcionamento. Em Portugal, a empresa mantém o foco no desenvolvimento de sistemas locais de energia destinados sobretudo ao setor empresarial, num contexto de procura por soluções que permitam reduzir custos energéticos e aumentar a previsibilidade do consumo. O modelo Energy-as-a-Service adotado pela empresa prevê que os clientes não tenham de realizar o investimento inicial nos equipamentos, ficando a Youdera responsável pelo financiamento, instalação e operação dos sistemas.

artigo.texto: Topeka City Council hears presentation on proposed data center, discusses sales taxes TOPEKA, Kan. (WIBW) - Sales taxes and data centers were a few of the topics discussed at the Topeka City Council on Oct. 13. Council members heard a presentation from Metropolitan Topeka Airport Authority (MTAA) President Curtis Sneden on a proposed data center at Forbes Field. The proposed spot is by Southwest Topeka Boulevard and 77th Street. Many council members raised questions surrounding the transparency of the data center since MTAA has not disclosed who the developer is. “All developers have a different approach. They worry about their proprietary information, and that’s fair, but eventually, you can’t do it forever, you got to have an honest conversation with the community,” Spencer Duncan, Topeka Mayor, said. There is no contract with the county due to the moratorium in place. Council members also raised questions about how the data center might affect the airport and frequency and transmission waves, but MTAA said there shouldn’t be any interruption. Mayor Duncan emphasized the importance of not only meeting with council but talking with the community as well. “Starting with who you are is usually the best place,” Duncan said. “There’s a reason we walk up to people and introduce ourselves first, because that’s how you start to build trust. That, I think, was the biggest ask you heard tonight: it’s hard to have an honest conversation with people who we don’t know who you are.” The full presentation on the potential data center can be viewed here. Topeka City Council also continued discussions on potential sales taxes to fill projected budget gaps. Council is considering the following four tax question possibilities: - A half-cent sales tax that would raise about $20 million a year for city services like fire, police and public works - A one-tenth of a cent sales tax that would generate about $4 million a year for affordable housing and homeless services - Renew a current half-cent sales tax for infrastructure, which expires in 2029 - It would keep collecting with no tax increase - Create an independent City Auditor Office that reports directly to the City Council to review spending and performance. Council must make a decision by next week for any of these possible questions to appear on ballots in March 2027. “We will make some decision next week because we have pressing deadlines, election deadlines,” Duncan said. “What I think will happen is, personally, I don’t think we’re ready to send anything at this time to the public without some more public conversations. We might consider something as it relates to housing and homelessness issues.” More about the sales taxes the city is considering can be found here. The city also discussed Fiscal Year (FY) Goals in 2026 along with plans for 2027 through 2030. What’s been accomplished and what the city is still aiming to do can be found here. Copyright 2026 WIBW. artigo.texto: A Câmara dos Deputados pode votar na tarde desta terça-feira, 13 de outubro, o requerimento de urgência do Projeto de Lei (PL) 3.716/2026, que altera o rateio dos custos da contratação de sistemas de armazenamento de energia por baterias (BESS). A proposta busca transferir aos consumidores o custeio atualmente atribuído aos geradores e tem o apoio de seis associações do setor elétrico, que defendem a mudança para garantir isonomia entre as tecnologias contratadas nos leilões de reserva de capacidade. Caso a urgência seja aprovada, o projeto poderá ser analisado diretamente pelo plenário, sem precisar concluir a tramitação nas comissões. O PL 3.716/2026 revoga um dispositivo da Lei 10.848/2004, incluído pela Lei 15.269/2025, que determina que os custos das contratações de reserva de capacidade com baterias sejam rateados exclusivamente entre os agentes de geração, conforme regulamentação da Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel). Em nota conjunta divulgada em 7 de outubro, seis associações do setor elétrico defenderam a aprovação urgente do projeto. As entidades argumentam que o modelo atual cria uma diferença de tratamento entre as baterias e outras tecnologias que prestam serviços de reserva de capacidade, cujos custos são distribuídos entre os usuários finais de energia elétrica. O posicionamento é assinado pela Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica e Novas Tecnologias (Abeeólica), Associação Brasileira dos Investidores em Autoprodução de Energia (Abiape), Associação Brasileira da Indústria do Hidrogênio Verde (Abihv), Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia (Absae), Associação Brasileira de Energia Solar Fotovoltaica (Absolar) e Associação Brasileira dos Produtores Independentes de Energia Elétrica (Apine). As entidades alertam que a atribuição dos custos exclusivamente aos geradores pode encarecer a energia elétrica para os consumidores e reduzir a competitividade da indústria brasileira. Modelo de custeio das baterias Na avaliação das associações, a reserva de capacidade tem como objetivo garantir a segurança do suprimento de energia elétrica, assegurando potência e flexibilidade para a operação confiável do Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN). Esses atributos podem ser fornecidos por diferentes tecnologias, que, segundo as entidades, devem receber tratamento equivalente. Atualmente, os custos da reserva de capacidade são distribuídos entre os usuários finais, conforme os parâmetros legais previstos no artigo 3º-A da Lei nº 10.848/2004. No entanto, os sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias recebem tratamento diferente, com os custos atribuídos exclusivamente aos geradores, conforme determinou a Lei n° 15.269/2025. Para as entidades, essa regra cria um descompasso entre a natureza sistêmica do serviço prestado, a distribuição de seus benefícios e a responsabilidade pelo pagamento dos custos. Baterias podem gerar economia de R$ 1,6 bilhão por ano As associações argumentam que os sistemas de armazenamento de energia, inclusive os baseados em baterias, podem contribuir para reduzir outros encargos pagos pelos consumidores ao otimizar a operação do parque gerador. Como exemplo, a nota cita um estudo da Volt Robotics segundo o qual os sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias podem reduzir a variação do Preço de Liquidação das Diferenças (PLD) e o acionamento de usinas termelétricas, gerando uma economia superior a R$ 1,6 bilhão por ano para os consumidores. O documento também destaca que atribuir legalmente os custos aos geradores não impede que eles sejam repassados aos consumidores finais. No mercado regulado, as entidades mencionam o reconhecimento, pela Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel), da inclusão integral e automática desses custos nas tarifas de energia. No mercado livre, o impacto pode ocorrer por meio de renegociações ou reajustes de preços. Já na autoprodução de energia, os custos podem ser incorporados aos preços de bens e serviços, afetando a competitividade da indústria brasileira. As associações acrescentam que o pagamento do encargo pelo segmento de geração pode elevar os custos para os consumidores devido ao repasse dos valores, acrescidos de tributos e despesas administrativas. Data centers e hidrogênio verde entram no debate A nota também relaciona a expansão da eletrificação da economia à necessidade de discutir a responsabilidade pelo custeio da reserva de capacidade. Segundo as entidades, novas cargas, como veículos elétricos, data centers e projetos industriais eletrointensivos, incluindo parques produtores de hidrogênio verde, influenciam a demanda máxima de energia e o déficit de capacidade do sistema. Na avaliação das associações, esses consumidores também podem contribuir para reduzir o déficit de capacidade caso recebam sinais econômicos adequados para ajustar sua demanda. Por isso, as entidades defendem que as baterias sejam tratadas em igualdade com as demais soluções de capacidade, considerando os atributos de potência e flexibilidade. O objetivo, segundo a nota, é permitir a contratação da tecnologia mais eficiente para cada cenário e reduzir os custos finais com transparência.

artigo.texto: Some Nevada unions love data centers. Now they just have to convince everyone else. Data centers have fast become the political bogeyman of 2026, with nearly every candidate seeking to outfox their opponent in attacks on "Big Tech" and "dirty data centers." In a September poll, nearly 6 in 10 registered voters in Nevada said they oppose the construction of new data centers. Not everybody in the state hates them, though: Electrical and construction unions that benefit from data center projects say the facilities can be a force for good in Nevada — and they're figuring out how they can prove it to everybody else. "There is not a one-size-fits-all situation for how to move forward with this, but there are so many possibilities of how to do that and still check all the boxes of ensuring that ratepayers are protected, that we are good stewards of the earth," said Ronald Young, the political director for the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers (IBEW) Local 357 in Southern Nevada. Some unions see it differently. A few view data centers as threatening their members, doing more to fuel automation via artificial intelligence (AI) than to power Nevada's economy. Advocates for construction counter that while AI acceleration is scary, it's inevitable, making it pointless for Nevada to pass up on economic opportunities that would flow elsewhere. It's led to nuanced discussions as unions representing thousands of workers try to navigate the best approach on young, fast-moving technologies driving demand for new data centers. As 2027's legislative session approaches, unions that work on data center projects say guardrails on their use of water and energy are necessary but that an all-out moratorium could cost Nevada. "Everything's so expensive, and I think if we can turn this into something where locals are getting good-paying jobs, good-paying union jobs, that's a win on top of everything else, right?" Young said. "But it's got to be done smart." Todd Vachon, a professor at Rutgers University who studies labor movements, said he believes concerns about AI will cause a split among organized labor nationwide. "It creates this friction within labor itself," Vachon said, between the primarily blue-collar groups that construct the centers and the white-collar groups who feel threatened by them. "The data centers are actually going to undermine the livelihoods of the white-collar workers if AI advances rapidly and actually does start replacing professional jobs and administrative work, clerical work, writers, creative people, artists." Fears of automation are not theoretical in Nevada, where some service-based workers in casinos and hospitals view AI as an existential threat. In August, Rep. Ro Khanna (D-CA) came to Las Vegas for a roundtable titled Workers over Machines, where he, Rep. Steven Horsford (D-NV) and leaders from trucking, hospitality and other industries discussed how to protect workers without being enemies to growth. Leaders from a range of different unions emphasized in conversations with The Nevada Independent that questions over data centers aren't yet causing major fissures in Nevada's labor community, but there are some disagreements. Brian Lenihan, a steward with the Service Employees International Union (SEIU) Local 1107 and an engineer with Clark County, said he is pro-innovation but is skeptical of rampant data center construction, especially in Southern Nevada. He said he distinguishes between data centers that power the internet and "the superpower, water-intensive, noisy, horrific data centers that people don't like." Kenneth Gillingham, an energy professor at Yale, told The Indy there are differences between traditional data centers that have been around for decades and data centers that are now being built to power AI. The latter have greater computational demands, said Gillingham, and therefore require more floor space, more power and more water. Lenihan also said he doesn't find electrical unions' arguments about economic benefits very compelling, arguing those groups could get jobs elsewhere. "Instead of saying we want data centers, what if they said we are going to do a tax cut for everyone to get solar?" he asked. "How much more money do you think IBEW could get from having more electricians wiring up solar facilities?" The electrical unions' view Electrical unions know data centers will be one of the biggest ticket items in the 2027 Legislature, and they say they want more regulations, too. "I don't think the concern is misplaced entirely. … We are in a spot in time where we can either do great things or we could totally screw it up," said Young, adding he disagreed with both those calling for an all-out moratorium and those calling for no regulations. "You need to have some kind of guardrails, because it affects everybody." Jacob Haas, business manager at IBEW Local 401 in Northern Nevada, told The Indy he believes data centers should have regulations similar to those governing "any other building." That means ensuring data centers pay for their own power and don't pass energy price hikes onto consumers, he said. And it means ensuring all facilities use closed-loop cooling systems, a far less water-intensive approach that Southern Nevada has already required of new data centers since 2023. But Haas and Young also emphasized the benefits of data centers when built responsibly. "If data centers weren't here right now, I think Nevada would be in a huge recession," said Haas, adding that roughly 3,000 of his workers are currently staffed on data center projects. He also said the maintenance and upkeep of the centers is so labor-intensive that workers return to the facilities constantly, ensuring jobs aren't just temporary. According to the online tracker Data Center Map, there are 76 data centers built or planned in Nevada. artigo.texto: The Louisiana Tax Commissionâs approval of a motion establishing average economic lives for data center equipment and infrastructure marks a step toward statewide property tax valuation guidelines for this type of technology. The test of good policy is whether the guidelines reasonably reflect equipment value, giving taxpayers and local governments a predictable basis for assessments while accounting for advances in technology. The motion, approved at the LTCâs Sept. 23 tentative adoption proceeding, establishes three equipment categories with different average economic lives. Economic life refers to how long equipment is expected to remain economically useful, rather than simply how long it can operate. The motion would divide data center equipment into: - Computer, networking, and storage equipment and electronic controls, with a five-year average economic life - Power, cooling, and fixtures, with a 12-year life - Electrical infrastructure, with a 15-year life The LTC also approved a notation recognizing data centers as a new property category beginning in 2027 and stating that the provisions should apply until sufficient additional operational or market data becomes available to support revisions. Before the motion was approved, the Louisiana Association of Business and Industry and Advantous Consulting proposed three-year economic lives for servers, networking equipment, and storage systems, and eight-year lives for power and climate-control infrastructure. The proposal emphasized how advances in technology can reduce equipment value and how the economic life of supporting infrastructure may depend on the computer equipment it serves. They also proposed applying percent-good factors without cost indices. Percent-good factors estimate the percentage of equipmentâs value remaining as it ages. Cost indices adjust acquisition costs for changes in price levels. Separately, the West Feliciana Parish assessor requested that the LTC staff work with the Louisianaâs Assessorsâ Association to develop data center guidelines. The LTC subsequently asked industry representatives and assessors to form a working group to collaborate on a proposal for the Sept. 23 tentative adoption hearing. LAA filed a rebuttal to put its position in the record while the working group was being organized. It opposed LABIâs broad equipment categories and shorter economic lives, recommending more detailed classifications with lives ranging from five to 25 years. LAA also opposed eliminating cost indices and questioned reducing equipment value based on anticipated advances in technology. The approved motionâs five-year life for computer, networking, and storage equipment is consistent with LAAâs recommendation, but the motion uses different classifications and lives for supporting infrastructure. The proposal, rebuttal, and subsequent approval of the motion from the LTC illustrate the challenges of valuing data center equipment and infrastructure and, more broadly, property affected by rapidly evolving technology. The selected economic lives affect equipment valuations and property tax burdens. Longer lives generally result in higher valuations for equipment of the same age and cost and, all else equal, higher property tax burdens than shorter lives. These lives guide valuation rather than require equipment to be written down to zero. Existing LTC rules also allow a different economic life or other valuation adjustments when supported by evidence. Determining economic life can be challenging because itâs hard to discern how long property remains economically useful, rather than simply how long it can operate. For example, servers and artificial intelligence accelerators may remain operational, but newer technology may make them less competitive and reduce their market value. Supporting infrastructure presents additional challenges. Power and cooling systems may remain operational for many years, but their economic usefulness can depend on the technology they support. Changes in computing requirements or facility design may require substantial modifications or limit alternative uses. However, systems that can support newer computing equipment without substantial modifications may remain useful beyond the life of the original servers. Economic lives are also only one component of valuation. The disagreement over cost indices concerns whether adjusting acquisition costs for price changes accurately reflects equipment value when newer technology may reduce that value. Existing LTC rules generally apply both cost indices and percent-good factors: Acquisition costs are adjusted for price changes, then reduced to account for depreciation. The rules also allow separate adjustments for obsolescence, or losses in value caused by factors such as outdated technology or changes in economic conditions, when supported by evidence. The approved data center motion doesnât include the proposed exclusion of cost indices. The data center schedule would extend an existing valuation practice to a new equipment category. Louisiana already publishes economic lives and valuation factors for numerous categories of business personal property. Other states, such as Alabama, also use depreciation schedules for business equipment. A statewide schedule can be sound tax policy if its classifications and economic lives reasonably reflect market value. Consistent guidelines can improve predictability, help reduce valuation disputes, and account for losses in value as technology advances. But lives that are too long can overstate value and increase taxpayersâ burdens, while those that are too short can undervalue equipment and reduce the local tax base. Revisiting the guidelines as more data becomes available would help address both risks. artigo.texto: BYD leads Tesla in electric car sales through September 2026, while Geely and Volkswagen are strengthening their positions through expanding model ranges and regional growth. The race among the world’s largest electric vehicle manufacturers is becoming more competitive. Sales volumes matter, but battery costs, affordable models, overseas expansion and profitability determine which companies can sustain growth. Among BYD, Tesla, Geely Automobile and Volkswagen Group, BYD recorded the highest battery electric vehicle sales in 2025. Its lead continued during the first nine months of 2026, although the companies’ results reveal different strengths and challenges. EV Sales Comparison: Why Vehicle Categories Matter Electric vehicle comparisons require consistent definitions. Battery electric vehicles (BEVs) run entirely on electricity, while plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs) combine rechargeable batteries with combustion engines. BYD and Geely sell both categories. Tesla sells battery electric vehicles exclusively. Comparing BYD’s combined plug-in sales with Tesla’s deliveries would therefore overstate BYD’s advantage in the fully electric market. The following table compares reported BEV sales for four major manufacturers. It is a selected comparison rather than a complete global ranking. The figures show that Geely Automobile exceeded one million BEV sales and finished ahead of Volkswagen Group in this comparison. Differences in reporting scope still matter when assessing market position. BYD vs Tesla in 2026: Who Is Selling More Electric Cars? BYD sold 1,629,957 passenger BEVs between January and September 2026, according to its September 2026 sales disclosure. Tesla delivered 1,324,681 vehicles over the same period, based on its three quarterly announcements. That puts BYD ahead by approximately 305,000 vehicles, or 23 percent relative to Tesla’s deliveries. These are year-to-date results, so they do not establish the final 2026 outcome. www1.hkexnews.hk BYD’s results also demonstrate why the BEV–PHEV distinction matters. Its passenger BEV sales increased 1.5 percent year on year through September, while PHEV sales fell 10.2 percent. Total new energy vehicle sales, including commercial vehicles, declined approximately 3.9 percent. Growth in fully electric cars therefore coexisted with weaker overall plug-in sales. www1.hkexnews.hk For manufacturers, a broad product range provides access to different buyers. Compact electric cars target price-sensitive customers, while plug-in hybrids appeal to drivers seeking electric commuting with combustion-engine flexibility. Tesla: High Volumes From a Concentrated Product Range Tesla delivered 486,532 vehicles in the third quarter of 2026, according to its Q3 production and delivery report. Model 3 and Model Y accounted for 478,237 deliveries, approximately 98.3 percent of the quarterly total. Other models contributed 8,295 vehicles. This concentration supports large production runs, but it makes performance heavily dependent on two core models. Pricing, product updates and competition in the electric sedan and SUV segments consequently have a substantial influence on Tesla’s sales. Tesla retains a strong position at the individual-model level. The IEA estimates that Model Y represented nearly 8 percent of global BEV sales in 2025, while Model 3 accounted for approximately 3.6 percent. Geely: Rapid EV Growth Across Multiple Brands Geely Automobile’s BEV sales increased 86 percent to 1,073,805 vehicles in 2025. It also sold 613,962 plug-in hybrids, taking combined plug-in sales to approximately 1.69 million, according to Geely Automobile’s 2025 sales announcement. Its reported portfolio includes Geely, Zeekr and Lynk & Co. These figures should not be confused with the entire Zhejiang Geely Holding portfolio, which includes additional automotive businesses. The brand mix creates several routes to growth. Geely addresses mainstream demand, Zeekr competes in premium electric vehicles, and Lynk & Co expands the group’s electrified offering. Financial performance adds another perspective. Geely Automobile reported RMB173.6 billion in first-half 2026 revenue, up 15 percent, and a 17.9 percent gross margin. These are company-wide figures covering its business, rather than standalone EV profitability measures. Volkswagen: European Growth Offsets Weakness in China Volkswagen Group delivered 983,100 BEVs in 2025, an increase of approximately 32 percent. Fully electric vehicles represented 10.9 percent of its total deliveries, according to its Volkswagen Group’s 2025 global delivery results. Regional performance varied sharply: Europe: 742,800 BEVs, up 65.9 percent. China: 115,500 BEVs, down 44.3 percent. United States: 72,000 BEVs, up 45.7 percent. Within the group, Škoda delivered 174,900 BEVs, increasing 119.8 percent, while Audi delivered 223,000, up 35.6 percent. These examples show how growth across several brands can support group performance even when one major market weakens. Volkswagen’s challenge is to convert growing electric vehicle demand into consistent performance across regions, where prices, competitors and customer preferences differ. Affordable Models Are Reshaping EV Competition The market extends beyond these four manufacturers. Smaller, affordable vehicles are gaining significant volumes alongside premium SUVs. The IEA estimates that Geely’s Geome Xingyuan accounted for 3.5 percent of worldwide BEV sales in 2025, followed by the Wuling Hongguang Mini EV at 3.1 percent and BYD Seagull at 3 percent. These examples demonstrate that manufacturers can build scale by meeting everyday transport needs. Purchase price, practical range and access to charging can be more influential than maximum battery capacity. artigo.texto: Slovenia’s Velenje coal mine is one of the sites within international project GeoSolar for exploring the possibility of converting coal mines into underground thermal energy storage facilities. The idea is to store solar energy collected during the summer in mines and use it for district heating in winter. An increasing number of coal mines in Europe are reaching the end of their operational lives. In this context, the issues of just transition and sustainably reusing the mining infrastructure are becoming increasingly important. The Velenje coal mine, the last one in Slovenia, is also shutting down in the coming years. It is operated by state-owned firm Premogovnik Velenje. The mine supplies lignite to coal power plant Termoelektrarna Šoštanj (TEŠ), currently the main district heating source in the Šalek valley, where preparations are underway to switch to alternative energy sources. How coal mines could store thermal energy The GeoSolar project could offer a solution for giving coal mines a new lease of life. European coal mines contain millions of cubic meters of mine water, with temperatures ranging from 20 to 30 degrees Celsius. Such a level is insufficient for direct use in district heating, but coal mines are often located near cities and towns with high seasonal heat demand, making them suitable for repurposing. The project envisages installing solar thermal systems on rehabilitated mining land to heat mine water to temperatures of 70 to 90 degrees Celsius during the summer. In winter, the hot water would be pumped to the surface and used for district heating. The cooled water would then be returned to the underground system to continue the cycle. Feasibility of the solution is being assessed in Slovenia and Poland The feasibility of applying this solution is being assessed at coal mines Velenje in Slovenia and Bolesław Śmiały in Poland. The project is coordinated by the Utrecht University and involves other partners from the Netherlands, Slovenia and Poland. It began in 2025 and is scheduled to run for 42 months. It is co-funded by the European Union’s Research Fund for Coal and Steel (RFCS). Project partners met in Velenje on October 5 to present their findings so far on the feasibility of the proposed solutions and agree on criteria for further research. In the next phase, they will develop more detailed models and compare the solutions based on the characteristics of the two mines.
