artigo.texto: By — Jessica Hill, Associated Press Jessica Hill, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/ai-data-centers-are-coming-for-federal-land-and-roiling-nevada-governors-race Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter AI data centers are coming for federal land and roiling Nevada governor's race Politics Oct 13, 2026 2:20 PM EDT BOULDER CITY, Nev. (AP) — Janelle Sorenson loves the clear night skies in Boulder City, less than an hour's drive from the bright lights of the Las Vegas Strip. It's a small, quiet town, and she thinks an artificial intelligence data center would ruin the community and scar the desert landscape. So over the summer, she joined with other residents to successfully oppose plans for one of the giant computing warehouses that have popped up around the country. But their victory was short-lived. The developers withdrew their application and instead sought adjacent land owned by the federal government — and the U.S. Bureau of Land Management signed off. "Not only did we not get to decide anything or have a say," Sorenson said, "we were just really kept in the dark." The Townsite data center was the first in the country to be approved on federal public land, though construction is stalled after a judge ruled that the government couldn't use an old environmental review from when the project was intended to be a solar farm. Tech companies are eager for vast tracts to build data centers that can be as large as 70 football fields, and Townsite could set a precedent for similar projects on federal property with more than a dozen others in the planning stages. President Donald Trump has been a steadfast supporter of the artificial intelligence industry, which he views as a source of economic growth and part of a global competition with China. However, data centers have been unpopular in many communities as voters worry about higher electricity bills, declining water supplies and other impacts. In Nevada, where 80% of the land is owned by the federal government, Townsite and other projects have become a dominant issue in the battleground state's closely watched governor's race. Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo, one of his party's most vulnerable incumbents, doesn't outright oppose building data centers on public lands, as long as they have community support. He recently signed an agreement with Trump's Republican administration to streamline infrastructure projects, which could include data centers on federal lands. Democratic nominee Aaron Ford, the state attorney general, has pledged to oppose data centers on public lands, saying affordable housing should be the priority. Both say the projects, whether on public or private land, must follow state rules, such as requiring data centers to cover their own energy costs and protecting water supplies, or they would lose eligibility for state tax abatements. Voters across the political spectrum unite against data centers Sorenson, the Boulder City resident, considers herself to be liberal, but she said her conservative neighbors are on the same page as she is. "We're all aligned on this," she said. Autumn McGrath-Shook, who lives in the same town, said she recently left the Republican Party and registered with the Green Party over data centers, though she still identifies as conservative. Worried about the environmental impact on wildlife, she joined forces with "these crazy libs" to oppose the project. Data centers have quickly become a "catalyzing issue" in the midterms, catching many politicians flat-footed, said David Damore, a political science professor at the University of Nevada Las Vegas. Some state leaders who were previously supportive of data centers have rushed to respond. For example, Republican Texas Gov. Greg Abbott paused data center approvals until audits are completed, and Democratic Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro signed an executive order removing data center proposals from a fast-track permitting process and requiring them to receive local approval before seeking state approval. READ MORE: Data center controversies have transformed midterms. Here's where different groups stand In August, Ford announced his plan to pause new tax abatements for data centers while an audit is conducted to see if the projects have fulfilled promises about producing tax revenue and economic benefits. In September, Lombardo, who has said data centers provide enormous economic opportunity for Nevada, signed an executive order placing more guardrails on data centers and requiring them to pay more taxes to support schools. The two have successfully "muddied the waters" on their data center positions, Damore said. Lombardo criticized Ford for co-sponsoring 2015 legislation that created the state's tax abatement program for data centers, a measure that received bipartisan support. Ford criticized Lombardo for giving more than $200 million in tax breaks to data centers, which is connected to the legislation that Ford co-sponsored. Ford told The Associated Press that he would use "every tool" at his disposal to prevent data centers from skirting state guardrails, including withholding tax abatements and pursuing litigation. Lombardo, whose campaign declined to make him available for an interview, has a similar pitch. His office said he would not hesitate to confront the federal government to advocate for Nevadans. But that's not good enough for McGrath-Shook, who is on the fence in the governor's race. She thinks Ford is soft on crime, but she views Lombardo as more pro-data centers. "I would much rather vote for Lombardo than Aaron Ford in a normal world," she said. "But with the looming data centers, it really changes the landscape — and literally." artigo.texto: NIL elabora modelo de contrato de financiamento para apoiar projetos de redução de emissões Natural Investment Lab desenvolve modelo de contrato para facilitar financiamento de projetos de carbono no Brasil Apontada como um dos principais entraves para que projetos de reflorestamento e de Redução das Emissões por Desmatamento e Degradação Florestal (Redd+) consigam acessar linhas de financiamento, a modelagem dos contratos passará a ter um padrão, que está em desenvolvimento pelo Natural Investment Lab (NIL). A minuta desse contrato modelo foi apresentada publicamente durante a Semana do Clima que aconteceu recentemente em Nova York e, para elaborá-la, o NIL conversou com 25 importantes instituições. Entre elas, Itaú BBA, Regia Capital, Systemica, Petrobras e Regreen. No próximo passo, o rascunho do contrato modelo será colocado em audiência pública e deve ganhar destaque durante a COP31, que acontecerá entre os dias 9 e 20 de novembro na Turquia. A meta é concluir o trabalho até o final deste ano. O NIL aposta no processo de amadurecimento desse mercado, que já vem durando mais de 20 anos e que deverá elevar o carbono ao status de commodity, com possibilidade de ser negociado internacionalmente "A ideia é preparar os desenvolvedores dos projetos de produção de carbono para que consigam lidar com todas as exigências com as quais vão se deparar quando tentarem acessar recursos", explica Fabiana Philipi, gerente de projetos da Climate Venture, organização que lidera o NIL. Ela pondera, no entanto, que o documento de referência poderá ajudar os outros players desse mercado, como os compradores e financiadores do mercado de carbono. Segundo Philipi, as propostas de produção de carbono bem elaboradas têm forte demanda e o objetivo é ajudar desenvolvedores de todos os portes, desde empresas já consagradas como Re.Green e Mombak, até aquelas que estão dando os primeiros passos. As maiores compradoras dos créditos de carbono brasileiros, atualmente, são as big techs, principalmente a Microsoft. A minuta apresentada em Nova York refere-se a contratos offtake - compra mínima garantida - que são acordos jurídicos firmados entre comprador e vendedor de uma mercadoria, antes dela entrar em produção. O documento apresenta cláusulas referentes à estrutura comercial, como preço, pagamento e financiamento, garantias, recebíveis e financiadores, ciclo de vida dos créditos, entrega e titularidade, falha de entrega, entre outros O NIL é um laboratório de investimentos criado a partir de uma iniciativa que reúne o Banco do Brasil, o Instituto Itaúsa, o Instituto Clima e Sociedade (iCS) e a internacional Gfanz. O seu objetivo é atrair e estruturar financiamentos, além de promover inovação financeira, para ampliar a chamada economia de Soluções Baseadas na Natureza (SbN).

artigo.texto: Battery storage is scaling faster than almost any other grid resource in the U.S. As transmission and distribution networks accommodate increasing shares of solar and wind power, Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) are emerging as one of the most effective technologies to enhance grid flexibility, stability, and resilience. What was once considered a niche solution is now becoming strategic infrastructure. But deployment is outpacing the industry's confidence in how these systems will perform on the grid, under stress, and over decades of service. Closing that gap requires connecting independent testing, grid modeling, and owner oversight across the full project lifecycle. Today's BESS installations play a far broader role than simply storing surplus electricity. Modern battery systems support frequency regulation, voltage control, peak shaving, congestion management, renewable integration, and ancillary services. Their fast response times allow them to react within seconds to grid disturbances, making them valuable assets for balancing increasingly dynamic energy systems. At the distribution level, utilities are evaluating BESS solutions to postpone costly network reinforcements, increase renewable hosting capacity, and improve power quality. Energy storage can support local grids by reducing transformer overloads, mitigating voltage deviations, and managing demand peaks driven by electric vehicle charging and growing electrification. At KEMA Labs, battery research is complemented by the multidisciplinary expertise of the Digital Lab, which combines battery testing with Electromagnetic Compatibility (EMC) testing and Accelerated Life Testing (ALT). This integrated approach clarifies how batteries, power electronics, control systems, and communication devices interact within BESS architectures. Its expertise also extends to plant controllers and IEC 61850 testing, helping assess communication between grid-connected assets, including BESS, and network operators. Beyond operational benefits, the business case for energy storage is evolving rapidly. BESS operators can stack multiple revenue streams, combining ancillary services, energy arbitrage, capacity or resource adequacy contracts, and congestion management. This evolution is encouraging larger-scale deployment and attracting investment across global markets. However, growth also brings technical and operational challenges. A modern BESS comprises battery cells, racks, Battery Management Systems (BMS), energy management systems, power conversion systems, transformers, cooling systems, and fire protection solutions. Each component influences efficiency, safety, and lifetime. Owners also need confidence in grid interaction, as inverter-based resources respond to disturbances differently from conventional generators. That confidence starts before a project is energized. Grid integration studies, including system impact, harmonic and power quality, temporary overvoltage, insulation coordination, and ride-through assessments, determine whether a BESS will support the grid or introduce new risks. Detailed Electromagnetic Transient (EMT) models capture inverter and plant controller behavior, helping identify control interactions and compliance issues early. Models, however, are only as good as the data behind them. Independent testing laboratories such as KEMA Labs, the testing Division of CESI Group, evaluate batteries under realistic operating conditions. Dedicated facilities can reproduce environmental and electrical stress, including extreme temperatures, humidity, charging and discharging cycles, and accelerated aging scenarios. These tests provide insight into battery performance, reliability, degradation, and expected service life. Recent KEMA Labs’ research on Lithium Iron Phosphate (LPF) batteries demonstrates the value of testing and modeling. Laboratory aging campaigns supported semi-empirical and thermal models for predicting capacity fade, State of Health, and battery lifetime under real-world operating conditions. The study highlighted temperature and State of Charge as key factors affecting degradation, providing insights for battery operation and long-term asset management. The greatest value comes when these disciplines are connected. Laboratory results can validate simulation models so planning studies reflect equipment behavior rather than relying solely on vendor data. Owner's engineering carries that discipline through procurement, factory acceptance testing, commissioning, and performance verification. Within CESI Group, KEMA Labs and EnerNex, the Group’s U.S. grid innovation company, link what is proven in the laboratory with how a system performs on the grid. Once a system is in service, combining laboratory test data with BMS information enables aging models to predict capacity fade, State of Health, and Remaining Useful Life. These capabilities support optimized maintenance, improved operational efficiency, and better-informed investment decisions. As energy storage moves from pilot projects to mainstream infrastructure, utilities and developers should require validated models early, confirm them against test and commissioning data, treat testing and performance verification as core project requirements, and use owner's engineering services to ensure that installed systems match what was studied and contracted. The future power system will require unprecedented flexibility, and battery storage is uniquely positioned to provide it. Realizing that potential will depend on robust testing, accurate modeling, and technical oversight working together across the full lifecycle of every project.

artigo.texto: Lithium-ion batteries use a small amount of glue, called a binder, to hold their internal components together during many charging cycles. Most binders contain fluorine, which means toxic solvents are needed during manufacturing, and hazardous waste is produced when the batteries are recycled. Engineers from the University of California, San Diego, and the Toyota Research Institute of North America have developed a fluorine-free binder that dissolves in water. Their findings appear in Nature Communications. Their studies show that a simple mix of two affordable polymers, polyacrylic acid and carboxymethyl cellulose, can replace toxic ingredients without losing performance. To connect the polymers, the researchers used citric acid, which is also found in citrus fruits. The new binder lasted through thousands of charge cycles and worked with different battery types, including common graphite and silicon anodes. “But that same stability also makes batteries much harder to recycle,” said Zheng Chen, a professor at the UC San Diego Jacobs School of Engineering, referring to conventional fluorine binders. Making Battery Recycling Easier Advertisement Traditional battery production uses large drying ovens to remove toxic solvents, which adds extra cost and uses a lot of energy. “Those extra steps significantly increase the cost and energy use — as well as the environmental impact — of battery manufacturing,” said study first author Jiao Lin, a postdoctoral researcher in Chen’s lab. The new design removes those steps completely. To recycle a battery with the new binder, workers soak the parts in water. The binder dissolves, so the electrode material separates easily from the metal foil without leaving behind tough chemical residues. When the team used the recovered materials to make new batteries, they worked just as well as those made with traditional parts. Next, the researchers plan to increase production for commercial use and adjust the formula for different types of batteries in the industry.

artigo.texto: Rep. Jay Dean, Fantasha Allen share thoughts on data centers in Texas House District 7 race Hear where the candidates stand on data centers, school vouchers, and other topics. LONGVIEW, Texas (KLTV) - The contest for who will represent Texas House District 7 pits incumbent state Rep. Jay Dean (R-Longview) against Democratic nominee Fantasha Allen. Dean is running for a sixth term. “This train has sort of left the station,” Dean said, referring to data center construction. “Those companies did a terrible job of getting out front in their public relations to explain and make sure people understood exactly what they are and what they are not.” “I like the idea of the power that they need, that they build their own power plants,” Dean added. Allen said data center constructions should be up to local citizens. “If the people in that county do not want the data centers there, they shouldn’t be there,” Allen said. “I do see a lot of people say that when a data center is built by them, they’re losing water and their electricity bill is going up,” added Allen. “I won’t want that for East Texas because most of us here are already living paycheck-to-paycheck.” The district includes Gregg, Harrison, and Marion counties. artigo.texto: Ataques de drones desativam centros de dados de empresa russa de IA Empresa russa de tecnologia perdeu total ou parcialmente a operação de unidades em 3 regiões do país em 3 dias consecutivos A Yandex, empresa russa de tecnologia e IA (inteligência artificial), informou neste domingo (11.out.2026) que seu centro de dados na região de Vladimir foi totalmente desativado depois de um ataque de drones. Ninguém ficou ferido, mas alguns serviços da companhia estão indisponíveis para os usuários. A unidade de Vladimir é a 3ª instalação da empresa a perder total ou parcialmente a operação em 4 dias, segundo a Reuters. A sequência de ataques afeta a infraestrutura digital da companhia, que tem papel central no desenvolvimento de inteligência artificial na Rússia. Ataques em 4 dias Na 6ª feira (9.out.2026), drones ucranianos atingiram um centro de dados da Yandex na região de Kaluga, a sudoeste de Moscou. Segundo a empresa, a unidade ficou parcialmente fora de operação. Na 5ª feira (8.out.2026), um ataque ucraniano desativou o centro de dados da companhia em Sasovo, a sudeste de Moscou. A instalação abriga 2 dos 3 supercomputadores usados no desenvolvimento dos modelos de IA da Yandex. Conhecida informalmente como “o Google da Rússia”, a empresa oferece serviços digitais e desenvolve tecnologias de IA no país. A perda de capacidade em seus centros de dados pode afetar o funcionamento de seus serviços e o desenvolvimento desses sistemas.

The requirement is part of a new rulebook that the Paris Agreement carbon market regulator – the Article 6.4 Supervisory Body – approved last Friday for programmes that aim to cut emissions by distributing new and cleaner cookstoves in regions that still burn wood or charcoal for cooking. These are the UN mechanism's first rulebooks for cookstoves, one of the carbon market’s most popular credit types and also one of its most criticised for overstating climate benefits. Cleaner cooking projects in the UN carbon market will have to set aside a share of their credits to insure against the risk that the trees they save are lost to fire, drought or logging, after the market’s regulator rejected calls to exempt the sector. The requirement is part of a new rulebook that the Paris Agreement carbon market regulator – the Article 6.4 Supervisory Body – approved last Friday for programmes that aim to cut emissions by distributing new and cleaner cookstoves in regions that still burn wood or charcoal for cooking. These are the UN mechanism's first rulebooks for cookstoves, one of the carbon market’s most popular credit types and also one of its most criticised for overstating climate benefits. But if those trees later burn in a wildfire or are logged, the carbon stored would be released anyway, erasing the climate benefits of the credits. Several carbon credit developers, conservation NGOs and the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) disputed that cookstove projects face this risk, in what critics described as a “coordinated lobbying campaign”. They argued that, unlike forest protection schemes, this type of credit represents a "flow" of avoided emissions rather than a "stock" of stored carbon that can be released. They also warned that requiring a buffer would impose disproportionate costs and undermine the financial viability of these activities. But the UN carbon market regulator was not persuaded by the argument. It decided that projects would have to protect against this reversal risk by handing over a percentage of credits to a so-called “buffer pool” instead of selling them. 'New paradigm' The amount of credits to be given up is calculated by applying different methods for natural risks, like wildfires, droughts or hurricanes, and human-caused ones, such as logging or land clearing. For natural risks, project developers will need to apply local risk values derived from new modelling published by a group of independent scientists. Campaigners have broadly welcomed the decision. Federica Dossi, an expert at Brussels-based advocacy group Carbon Market Watch, said it sets a new paradigm for calculating reversal risk based on empirical data. “This approach is grounded in science and we hope to see this now being adopted by other carbon crediting mechanisms in the voluntary market,” she added. Backers claim this method is more rigorous than current practice in the voluntary carbon market, which largely relies on expert guesswork. artigo.texto: The two candidates running for Wisconsin's 7th Congressional District met Wednesday for what could be their only debate before the November election. Republican Michael Alfonso and Democrat Fred Clark met in Duluth, Minnesota, for the debate hosted by WDIO-TV. Among the issues discussed was Enbridge's Line 5 pipeline, which has faced renewed scrutiny following a major natural gas liquids spill in Iron County and environmental concerns surrounding construction of its reroute around the Bad River Reservation. When asked about Line 5, Alfonso expressed support for the pipeline. He also said protecting northern Wisconsin's lakes, forests and farmland doesn't have to come at the expense of building energy infrastructure. “Line 5 is one of these things that brings costs down for every single family in Northern Wisconsin. I really look at this issue and say, if you truly want prices to come down, how can you not support it.” Alfonso had earlier said Clark opposed Line 5. Clark disputed that claim and said his concerns were with Enbridge's environmental record. “I have put out a statement calling on the Wisconsin DNR to hold the Enbridge company accountable for the set of environmental problems they've had. This company has not operated in good faith and until they're willing to do that, we need the state to hold them accountable and stop work until there are reforms.” The candidates were also asked about data centers, which have become a growing concern in Wisconsin over their potential impact on water supplies and electricity costs. Clark called for state and federal regulations to protect communities from the environmental and financial risks of data center development. “We need that badly to protect our water resources, absolutely, to make sure that consumers of energy are held harmless by the huge power demand these things generate, absolutely,” Clark said. Alfonso agreed that water use and electricity costs need to be addressed, but said local communities should decide whether to allow data centers. “If you were to ask me, do I want a data center in Hayward, Wisconsin, where I live? Absolutely not,” Alfonso said. “But I'll tell you what, the federal government does not have a role in stepping in and telling local municipalities what they can and cannot do.” Clark then questioned Alfonso about President Donald Trump's efforts to limit state regulation of artificial intelligence. "So are you willing to tell the president that he's wrong to want to preempt states from having regulations around artificial intelligence and that he's wrong to let Mark Zuckerberg and Jeff Bezos basically run the table the way they want to with AI and data centers?” Clark asked. Alfonso responded that Trump supports local control. “President Trump was actually very clear with this. He said, if you're a local municipality and you don't want one, you don't need one. President Trump truly listens to the people,” Alfonso said. “I mean, when we look at issues like the data center issue, it's very clear. People in northern Wisconsin don't want it. But I can't say the same for Kansas. I've never been there. If they want one, it's not the federal government's job to step in and say, no, it's the state or local government.” The full debate is available to watch on WDIO-TV's website.

artigo.texto: Iniciativa prevê compensação de cerca de 10 mil toneladas de CO₂ equivalente por ano com créditos certificados de parques eólicos A Azul Conecta, responsável pela operação regional da Azul, firmou parceria com a Auren Energia para compensar as emissões de carbono associadas ao consumo de combustível de todos os voos realizados pela companhia ao longo de 2026. A iniciativa integra o programa voluntário Conecta NetZero e prevê o uso de créditos de carbono certificados, sem custo adicional para os passageiros. A compensação será feita com créditos gerados pelos complexos eólicos Ventos do Piauí I e Ventos do Araripe III, que integram o portfólio de geração de energia renovável da Auren. O volume estimado de emissões a ser compensado é de 10 mil toneladas de dióxido de carbono equivalente (tCO₂e) por ano. Os créditos possuem certificação do Verified Carbon Standard (VCS), administrado pela Verra, e passaram por processos independentes de validação e verificação. Também tiveram sua elegibilidade reconhecida para a fase piloto do CORSIA, mecanismo da Organização da Aviação Civil Internacional (ICAO) voltado à compensação de emissões da aviação internacional. Após a utilização, as unidades serão aposentadas no registro da Verra em nome da Azul Conecta, impedindo seu uso em novas compensações. A iniciativa integra a estratégia de descarbonização da Azul, que inclui renovação e modernização da frota e medidas de eficiência operacional. Entre 2019 e 2025, a companhia reduziu em cerca de 20% sua intensidade de carbono, indicador que relaciona as emissões de CO₂ ao volume transportado. A empresa também possui metas climáticas validadas pela Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi), alinhadas à trajetória de aquecimento global de 1,5°C. “A sustentabilidade é um dos pilares da estratégia da Azul e o Conecta NetZero representa mais um avanço concreto em nossa jornada de descarbonização. Ao compensar integralmente as emissões associadas ao consumo de combustível dos voos da Azul Conecta por meio de créditos certificados, reforçamos nosso compromisso de combinar eficiência operacional, inovação e responsabilidade ambiental”, afirma César Grandolfo, diretor de Relações Institucionais, Tributárias e de Sustentabilidade da Azul. Para a Auren, a parceria amplia as possibilidades de aplicação dos créditos gerados por seus ativos de energia renovável. “A parceria mostra como a geração de energia renovável pode contribuir também para a descarbonização de outros setores da economia. Ao levar créditos de carbono gerados a partir dos nossos ativos eólicos para uma iniciativa voltada ao setor aéreo, mostramos como nosso portfólio pode apoiar diferentes empresas em suas estratégias climáticas”, afirma João Guillaumon, vice-presidente de Clientes e Comercialização da Auren Energia. Mercado de créditos de carbono Cada crédito de carbono corresponde a uma tonelada de dióxido de carbono equivalente (tCO₂e) que deixou de ser emitida ou foi removida da atmosfera. Esses instrumentos podem ser utilizados por empresas para compensar emissões associadas às suas operações, desde que observados os critérios de certificação e integridade ambiental. A Auren já comercializou mais de 7 milhões de créditos de carbono para clientes em mais de 20 países. Segundo a empresa, seu portfólio registra mais de 1,2 milhão de toneladas de CO₂ evitadas e certificadas por ano, com créditos provenientes de projetos de geração de energia renovável e de preservação de florestas nativas. artigo.texto: Statesboro District 2 candidate Kathleen Keehner focuses on data centers, youth programs Kathleen Keehner is one of three candidates running for Statesboro City Council District 2 STATESBORO, Ga. (WTOC) - Statesboro residents will vote in just over three weeks to fill the city’s District 2 council seat, which has been vacant for nearly five months. The special election is a three-person race. Kathleen Keehner is one of the three candidates seeking the seat. Background Keehner became a homeowner in Statesboro last year when she bought a house to raise her newborn son. She said she is now looking to represent the city’s District 2. “I have a lot of ideas for the future because my son is going to be living here for the foreseeable future,” Keehner said. Data centers Keehner said her motivation for running centers on data centers. In August, Statesboro City Council approved a zoning map amendment that would allow a data center to be built within city limits. Because District 2 was unrepresented, Mayor Jonathan McCollar broke a tie to push the approval despite resident protests. Keehner said she began paying closer attention to local politics when talk of data centers began to increase in the state. She said if elected, she would vote against any data center application. “This race, it’s deeper than just surface level who’s going to win for city council, yeah the city council is made up of five people who vote on decisions, but those decisions can shape the future,” Keehner said. Budget priorities City council members are tasked with approving the city’s annual budget. Keehner said if elected, she plans to devote more taxpayer dollars to creating programs and safe spaces for the city’s youth. “Since we lost the boys and girls club in 2025, we haven’t had any major investments in young people’s programs. So, I would like to reallocate funds, I know that there was a brand new park that they spent over one million dollars on in Whitesville that is farther away from the west side,” Keehner said. Qualifications Keehner does not have experience serving as a public official. She said her qualifications come from being an active member of her community. “Because I do talk to my constituents, I am out here in the streets, I think that qualifies me more than a leader that doesn’t care about the next person, you know,” Keehner said. Keehner said voters should consider who has their best interest at heart. “It’s important to vote for somebody who you know has your best interest at heart, I think that it is important to vote for somebody who doesn’t have deep ties and deep relationships with people who are already proving not to care about you or what you’re concerned with,” Keehner said. artigo.texto: Power Grid Corporation of India Limited (POWERGRID) has invited online bids for the development of a 187.5 MW / 750 MWh Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) in Telangana. The project aims to strengthen electricity grid stability and support the integration of renewable energy into the power network. The tender has been published through the company’s PRANIT Portal, inviting eligible firms with the necessary technical and financial capabilities to participate in the bidding process. The project is designated as Package TS-BESS-01 and carries Tender Reference Number CC/T/W-BESS/DOM/A02/26/14098. The proposed battery storage system will have a power capacity of 187.5 MW and an energy storage capacity of 750 MWh, equivalent to four hours of storage at full output. The project is expected to contribute to the development of energy storage infrastructure required to support the increasing share of renewable energy in the electricity system. The tender falls under the Tariff Based Competitive Bidding (TBCB) route and is classified under works related to power and energy projects. Interested bidders can access the tender documents through POWERGRID’s official tendering platform using RFX Number 5002005732. Participants are required to examine the tender conditions and pre-qualification requirements before submitting their bids. According to the tender details, the participation fee has been fixed at Rs. 25,000. The tender value and earnest money deposit (EMD) are listed as zero on the portal. Prospective bidders should refer to the official tender documents for the applicable eligibility conditions, technical specifications, commercial requirements and other instructions governing participation. The tender schedule specifies October 12, 2026, at 7:50 PM as the commencement date and time for both document sales and soft copy bid submissions. The document sale period will remain open until October 17, 2026, at 11:55 PM. The deadline for submitting bids is October 19, 2026, at 11:00 AM. The bids are scheduled to be opened on October 19, 2026, at 11:30 AM, providing a short interval between the submission deadline and the opening process. Interested companies must complete the required procedures within the prescribed schedule to ensure their participation in the tender. The tender is being managed by Satyam Gupta, Engineer (CS), at POWERGRID’s corporate office. The office is located at Saudamini, 3rd Floor, Plot No. 2, Sector 29, Gurugram, Haryana. The proposed Telangana BESS project comes amid growing requirements for flexible electricity infrastructure to accommodate variable renewable generation. Battery storage systems can store electricity when supply is available and discharge it when demand rises or renewable generation declines. Such capabilities can help balance supply and demand, improve grid flexibility and support the reliable integration of solar and wind power. Through this tender, POWERGRID is advancing the development of large-scale battery storage infrastructure. The project represents another step towards strengthening India’s electricity network and meeting the operational requirements of a power system increasingly supported by renewable energy sources. artigo.texto: Richardson Electronics, ComEd, trumpet company’s battery storage system plans Richardson Electronics, state lawmakers and ComEd officials gathered Monday to celebrate the Kane County company’s plan to build the largest commercial battery energy storage facility on ComEd’s Illinois grid. “Take it from somebody in the energy industry. This is a very big deal,” said Gil Quinones, ComEd’s chief executive officer and president. The facility, which will have containers with battery energy storage systems, or BESSes, will be built at the rear of Richardson’s headquarters in La Fox. It is intended to serve as a model for potential customers. The facility would be capable of storing up to 5 megawatt-hours of power. “We have learned that standing still is not an option,” said Edward Richardson, chief executive officer and president of Richardson Electronics. His father founded the company in 1947, selling military-surplus electronic supplies such as walkie-talkie batteries. “We’re here because we believe battery energy storage will be claiming an increasingly important role in the future of energy infrastructure,” Richardson said. “The demand for power continues to grow. The ability to store energy, improve reliability and support a more resilient grid becomes increasingly important.” Richardson said the company’s manufacturing experience, engineering expertise and customer relationships help as it grows its global power-management program, which focuses on “green” energy applications. “We believe it has significant long-term potential,” he said. In August 2025, Illinois officials announced the company would receive tax credits for the project through the state’s Re-imagining Energy and Vehicles Program. According to the state, Richardson was investing $8.5 million in the project. The agreement with the state calls for Richardson to add 54 full-time employees at the La Fox site. “The fact is, our energy future depends on having enough power to support growing communities and local economies. Battery storage helps make power available when and where it’s needed most. This is critical for grid stability,” Quinones said. He said batteries will store energy when it is cheap and abundant, to be available when power is scarce and expensive. He said using batteries also “buys valuable time needed to make infrastructure investments needed to bring excess energy onto the grid.” The company is still designing the project. The building size will depend on how many 44-ton battery energy storage systems it will contain, said Scott DuBois, the company’s director of business development. Meanwhile, it is looking to lease space in which to build BESSes, he said. Richardson Electronics sells engineered solutions, green energy products, power grid and microwave tubes and related consumables, power conversion and radio-frequency and microwave components, CT X-ray tubes, and customized display solutions. ssarkauskas@dailyherald.com

artigo.texto: New Peugeot RCZ Vision: solid state battery, 493bhp, and a mad steering wheel A warm welcome back for Peugeot's stylish small coupe. But that wheel? Yeesh... Peugeot is feeling funky. In fact, its new design language is feeling feline, so much so that it’s actually called ‘feline future’. Peugeot wants to be the left-field, extrovert French brand, without being self-consciously wacky. The RCZ Vision showcases the direction of travel. A crisply resolved coupe with echoes of its forebear – which ran from 2009 until ’15 and shifted a healthy 68,000 units – there’s plenty to like on the surface. But actually the bigger stories here are within and beneath, because this car introduces us to two significant developments – both of which are actually coming down the pipe. Core to the RCZ is the STLA architecture, a modular mega-platform that will underpin in excess of 30 new cars across the Stellantis constellation, to the tune of two million vehicles per year by 2035. Coupled to it is a new software and control system called STLA Brain, fast-tracking the company’s ability to deliver autonomous driving capability and innovations such as steer-by-wire. That’s also key to the RCZ Vision. Peugeot was one of the first to genuinely reimagine the car interior, with its odd but also oddly effective i-Cockpit. This new concept car develops the theme in various ways: highlights include ‘mobile’ air vents that can disappear when not in use, an aluminium centre console topped with frosted glass, and a transparent micro LED display screen above the wheel, which can be configured to show as much or as little as the driver wants to see. You might like Well, we say wheel. The dominant innovation inside the RCZ is clearly the so-called Hypersquare, which groups switchgear into four rings. That’ll take some getting used to, but we suspect the ergonomics are sound. Another head-spinner is the arrival of steer-by-wire; yep, there’s no mechanical linkage here, everything is 100 per cent electronic. And fast: the maximum wheel rotation is a little less than one turn compared to the three turns lock-to-lock that we’re used to. A variable steering ratio means that you’re not all at sea at motorway speeds, and vibrations and torque steer are now relics of a different era. The RCZ – and indeed all future Peugeots – will brake-by-wire too. What of the propulsion? The STLA One platform can accommodate ICE, but not here. On the RCZ Vision, we’re talking about a solid-state battery built on a 1,000 volt architecture so that it can charge from 10 to 80 per cent in 10 minutes. Most of the big players are exploring solid state, whose primary benefit is a superior energy density in a more compact configuration. Peugeot is collaborating with a company called Factorial Energy in order to deliver this (Stellantis has a 9.5 per cent equity stake). The company says the RCZ has a power output of 491bhp, is targeting a range of 375 miles, and can deliver 5.4mpkWh overall. Back to the new design language. Peugeot’s design director Matthias Hossann says it’s predicated on five key principles: freedom, courage, elegance, instinct and inner force. Answers on a postcard – if anyone remembers those – as to the meaning of the last one. The RCZ is an undeniably pretty thing, if not as outré as some of its previous concepts (it’s worth looking those up – as far back as you care to go). The horizontal light ‘claws’ are present and correct at the front and rear, and there’s a micro-perforated RCZ graphic across the bumper. The original’s glass bubble roof treatment reappears, and the slinky silhouette is made possible thanks to a battery that’s just 110mm thick. Forged aluminium wheels help reduce weight; they’re 21in upfront, 22in at the rear. Top Gear Newsletter Get all the latest news, reviews and exclusives, direct to your inbox. Note the triangular motifs, another callback to the original. Inside, there’s a dashboard clock from French specialist Serica, enough physical switchgear to satisfy analogue ideologues, and Pelinova recycled leather that uses offcuts that would otherwise be heading to the bin. No word yet on whether the RCZ is destined for production. But a whole heap of the tech and thinking it contains is 100 per cent happening. Good news.

artigo.texto: More than 40 University of Michigan staff, students and Ypsilanti community members gathered in the Trotter Multicultural Center Monday evening for a data center teach-in by Stop the Data Center, an advocacy organization against the the University’s planned Ypsilanti Township data center in collaboration with Los Alamos National Laboratory. Ypsilanti Township residents organized a presentation arguing the data center is another expression of the military-industrial-academic complex, which they said only serves to advance the United States’ hegemony while ignoring local communities. The presentation then shifted to discussing new ideas to secure their collective goal: ending the development of the research computing center. At the event, assistant information professor Justine Zhang said residents opposing the center are worried about toxic chemicals and the other potential consequences of proximity to data centers. “(The project is) proceeding in spite of opposition from people in Ypsilanti and beyond, who do not want a project that will extract land, water and capacity from the community while extending the infrastructure of U.S. imperialism,” Zhang said. “Our task is to collectively analyze and strategize around these developments, so we act in solidarity with our friends, coworkers, neighbors and comrades to the data center.” Ypsilanti Township resident Robin Wylie, the School of Public Health Epidemiology staff member, said he was concerned about a recent letter from Los Alamos handed out to the community during a September town hall. The letter claimed the proposed site was only a research computing facility that would allow scientists from Los Alamos to work more closely with U-M faculty and students to explore fields like brain cancer surgery outcomes, extreme weather predicting and various other scientific and engineering challenges. “Even at the town hall meetings, we keep asking, ‘What are we going to get out of this?’” Wylie said. “They don’t have an answer for us. We’re not — Ypsilanti is not — benefiting at all from this.” Wylie also said the statement highlighted the benefits the project could provide to the University, but it did not explain how the center would affect local communities. In an interview with The Michigan Daily, Wylie expressed concerns about his community’s safety given the health complications the project may cause. “Toxic chemicals will probably be used in the cooling system, and they can leak in the data center,” Wylie said. “They’ve been known to cause serious health problems. I don’t know how they’re going to prevent that from happening. How are they going to? It’s right next to a river.” University librarian Craig Smith said he worries the project is fully in the power of the University’s Board of Regents, instead of the local community. Smith also questioned why the University is providing nearly $850 million in funds, despite Los Alamos having greater access to the facility. “In our group, we were reflecting on the fact that Los Alamos is going to have 90% access to this data center, and U-M is going to have 10%,” Smith said. “Why are we doing this? We’re paying $800 million for this thing, and we’re getting 10% out of it.” LSA freshman Katrina Hunter told the Daily she was concerned that the majority of the student population remains unaware of the University’s affiliation with Los Alamos for the data center project. She said she believes more students would get involved in anti-data center activism if they were made aware. “I think getting a collective body of students aware of it, and then we can maybe move on to protesting, handing out flyers, talking to students, getting people outside petitioning or talking to town offices, calling up and going to board meetings,” Hunter said. “We can get more involved. Once we go to board meetings we can talk to officials and try to push our way into getting the students and community of Ypsilanti involved.” Daily News Contributor Elise Maurer can be reached at elisemau@umich.edu.

artigo.texto: By Shereen Siewert | Wausau Pilot & Review A Town of Wausau ordinance sharply restricting where and how data centers can be built goes before Marathon County supervisors Thursday, as the county considers its own rules. The board meets at 6 p.m. Thursday, Oct. 15, in the Assembly Room of the Marathon County Courthouse, 500 Forest St. Thursday’s session is an educational meeting where supervisors review and discuss items; votes are scheduled for Tuesday, Oct. 20. Public comment is limited to items on the agenda. The Town of Wausau adopted the data center ordinance Aug. 3, following a public hearing that drew 14 residents. According to town minutes, Supervisor Steve Buntin told the audience the town attorney recommended an ordinance because the town had nothing on the books and the state exercises no control over data center siting. The ordinance is modeled on one adopted in the Town of Saratoga in Wood County and is, in Buntin’s words, “very restrictive.” Planning commission minutes note the audience “was not in favor of data centers being located in the township.” Under the ordinance, data centers could be built only in the town’s manufacturing district and only with a conditional use permit. Buildings would have to sit at least 200 feet from every property line, parking lots at least 100 feet, and no structure could exceed 35 feet in height. Noise at the property boundary could not exceed 60 decibels. The definition covers cryptocurrency mining, blockchain processing and server farms. Developers would have to submit an environmental and community impact analysis before any public hearing, including an evaluation of effects on emergency services, water supply, school district budgets and municipal revenue. Any facility relying on private wells would need a water feasibility study mapping every well within 1,000 feet and the geology within a mile. No certificate of occupancy could be issued until the utility verifies that supply lines and substations can carry the load without shortchanging other customers, and until the developer shows the cooling system “will not negatively impact the surrounding region.” Because the Town of Wausau operates under county zoning, state law requires county approval of town ordinance amendments. The county’s review is procedural; the application form signed by town officials states that the county does not assess the legality or enforceability of the language and that the town bears full legal responsibility for the ordinance. The county’s Environmental Resources Committee voted Sept. 29 to forward the ordinance to the full board. The voice vote was not unanimous. At the same meeting, the committee began laying groundwork for a countywide data center ordinance. Committee members directed staff to research state regulations, water usage, cooling systems, electricity demand, noise, lighting, traffic and utility infrastructure, and asked for an educational presentation before deciding which zoning districts might allow data centers. The ordinance itself notes that “the development of data centers is swiftly increasing across the State of Wisconsin.” Rietbrock wind and solar rules Supervisors will also review wind and solar siting ordinances from the Town of Rietbrock, in the Athens and Edgar area west of Wausau. Both cleared the Environmental Resources Committee on non-unanimous voice votes. The wind ordinance incorporates the state Public Service Commission’s wind siting rules, known as PSC 128, including noise limits of 50 decibels during the day and 45 at night and the state’s setback table. The ordinance’s findings run to 25 clauses and cite infrasound, wildlife deaths, property values, drainage, road damage and the town’s desire to “maintain the pastoral, rural nature of this region.” The solar ordinance is unchanged from a version the town board passed in 2025 but never submitted to the county. According to town minutes, the Environmental Resources Committee required a fresh public hearing, which the town held Aug. 25. The town board approved both ordinances that night. Cherokee Park expansion The board will consider buying up to 15 acres of wooded land adjoining Cherokee Park in the Town of Hull at $4,450 per acre, a cost not to exceed $66,750. The 65.5-acre park sits on the Big Eau Pleine River. According to a memo from Parks, Recreation and Forestry Director Jamie Polley, the adjacent landowner approached the county about selling the wooded portion of the property, which includes land along the river that the public cannot currently reach. Adding the acreage would open room for trails and river access, Polley wrote. The owner would be required to survey the land and split off the wooded acres as a separate parcel. Money would come from the county’s Parkland and Products account, which has a balance of about $344,400, or from state Knowles-Nelson Stewardship funds if available. Other business Supervisors will review a resolution authorizing staff to proceed with the fourth phase of construction on the county’s planned new highway facility. The resolution and supporting documents were not included in the agenda packet released Friday. As previously reported, the board will also vote on sweeping roughly $388,750 in unspent American Rescue Plan Act funds from 11 completed projects into the Regional Forensic Science Center. Federal rules require all ARPA money to be spent by Dec. 31. The largest unspent balance, $164,198, comes from medical examiner vehicle purchases. A new Solid Waste Department policy would cut landfill tipping fees for 60 days following any declared emergency. Residents, contractors, haulers and municipalities bringing certified disaster debris to the county landfill in Ringle would pay the contract hauler rate. The board directed staff to write the policy following severe weather events earlier this year. artigo.texto: Why Should Delaware Care? Local governments across Delaware have passed regulations on data centers, citing fears about their massive energy use and effects on the environment. But Dover’s data center moratorium is the first in the state, potentially marking a shift in how far municipalities will go to address these concerns. The Dover City Council on Monday unanimously approved a 18-month moratorium on the construction of data centers in Delaware’s capital city. The moratorium is the first of its kind in Delaware, and follows more than a year of discussions and debate across the state over how much the fast-growing industry could impact power bills and the local environment. Dover’s new ordinance now pauses the city’s official review of proposals for large energy-use facilities, including data centers that use more than 30 megawatts of electricity. That amount of electricity is roughly equivalent to the energy use of 24,000 homes. During the 18-month pause, city officials will research the effects data centers could have on the city; whether they should be allowed to be built; and how to regulate them if they are built. “This is not a ‘no’ to data centers. This is, we need to figure it out before we can say, ‘yes,’” Councilwoman Donyale Hall, who introduced the ordinance, said in an interview. Hall said the council will now decide the most cost-effective way to study the issue. The moratorium passed with little discussion on Monday evening, except from Councilman Brian Lewis, who said called for a ban on construction of the facilities in the city, despite potential economic benefits they could bring. “To me, the environment, people’s health and our infrastructure are more important than jobs in the city,” Lewis said. Dover officials have already been approached about potential plans for more than one data center project in the city, Hall said. She said she did not have information about the developers. And they have not yet submitted a formal application to the city, so the potential projects will not move forward at least until the moratorium is over. While Dover is the first city in Delaware to pass a data center moratorium, it is not alone. Almost every state in the country has at least one municipality that has either banned data centers or imposed a moratorium, according to the artificial intelligence research site, Programs. A boom in the construction of data centers to power the artificial intelligence industry has sparked a nationwide backlash to the facilities. Opponents say they are noisy, use too much water and cause power bills to surge. Proponents say they bring much-needed jobs and tax revenue. New Castle and Kent counties also recently approved rules limiting where a data center could be built in their unincorporated areas. Those regulations include buffer requirements, noise limits and bans on cooling systems that consume large amounts of water. When debating the regulations last summer, Kent County officials also expressed a willingness to consider an outright county-wide ban on the fast-growing industry. Adding to the county regulations are new rules state lawmakers passed in June through a slate of bills. Among those is one that would require developers to supply all of the power a data center facility would use for the first 10 years of its operations.

artigo.texto: GEORGE TOWN: A 31-year-old man was injured while trying to put out a fire at an electric vehicle (EV) battery storage room in Jalan Jelutong yesterday. The Penang Fire and Rescue Department received an emergency call at 3.42pm. Its assistant operations director, John Sagun Francis, said the fire involved a battery storage room measuring about 10sq ft. An estimated 85 per cent of the premises was damaged. "The victim was injured while attempting to put out the fire. "He received initial treatment from the Emergency Medical Rescue Services (EMRS) team before being taken to Penang Hospital for further treatment," he said in a statement. Firefighters from the Jalan Perak station, assisted by teams from the Lebuh Pantai and Paya Terubong stations, were deployed to the scene. John said the team used two water lines fitted with two 60-metre jets and a hose reel to extinguish the blaze. "The fire was brought under control at 4pm and fully extinguished at 4.10pm. "Firefighters then carried out overhaul operations to ensure there were no further hazards," he added. The operation ended at 5.57pm, after which the case was handed over to the Fire Investigation Unit for further action.

artigo.texto: Data centers were on tap for both the Pulaski County Quorum Court and the Little Rock Board of Directors on Tuesday night, with the city’s measure going forward for a vote next week and the county’s legislation pulled for further study. Little Rock City Director Kathy Webb tried and failed to get an 18-month moratorium passed in August – it tied on a 4-4 vote – and now has come back with a six-month pause, which was brought up at Tuesday night’s agenda meeting. There was little discussion and no vote taken. Webb said she had talked to her constituents, some of whom thought a year and a half was too long and others who thought six months wasn’t long enough. Her proposal allows for another six-month delay if more time is needed to study a data center proposal. Asked if she thinks she has the votes this time around, Webb said she hopes so. “If we were in the Legislature, lawmakers have those kinds of conversations every day,” she said. “But we can’t do that on the board so I depend on the people I’m working with to have those conversations with other board members. I can say this, there will be several co-sponsors this time.” Google has proposed a 100-megawatt, $1 billion data center that would be located on 380 acres in the Port of Little Rock area. The Board of Directors passed an ordinance in June outlining data center regulations, but it has been criticized for not going far enough. About a block and a half away from City Hall, at the county’s administration building, the Quorum Court’s own agenda was getting underway, but a proposed piece of legislation was pulled before it could be considered and placed on the full Quorum Court’s agenda. The proposed ordinance was written by Justice of the Peace Douglas House, who said he had taken his proposal off the agenda after talking with members of the county’s planning staff who had questions about some of the particulars. House, who was appointed by Gov. Sarah Sanders, is serving until the end of the year and took the place left vacated by Phil Stowers, who resigned in June. He said he has worked on the ordinance as an alternative to one proposed by Justice of the Peace Julie Blackwood. Blackwood’s ordinance was passed last month on an 11-4 vote and sets out detailed conditions under which large industrial projects, like data centers, can operate. After that vote, County Judge Barry Hyde vetoed the measure because, among other objections, he thinks the county will be sued if the ordinance passes. House’s ordinance includes some of the same topics as Blackwood’s measure, but makes an exception for a large data center project being pushed by AVAIO Digital. That project, located near Wrightsville, is estimated to be worth $21 billion and need 1 gigawatt of electricity to operate. House said he also thinks the county will be sued if the Avaio project is included in any legislation that slows the construction process that is now underway. “I am 99.9% sure that will happen,” House said after the meeting. House said if the Quorum Court overrides Hyde’s veto, thereby confirming the passage of Blackwood’s ordinance — nine votes are needed — he will toss his proposal in the trash, noting that his time on the Quorum Court will end soon after. If the justices of the peace fail to override the veto, he said he will continue pursuing his proposal.

artigo.texto: SMM, October 13: Entering September, the sodium-ion battery industry chain's "advancing amid divergence" operating pattern further evolved. The electrolyte segment continued its "capacity without volume release" logic, with top-tier players' shipments highly concentrated and growth mainly flowing to undisclosed major clients. The window for scaled-up breakthroughs is expected to materialize in Q4 with GWh-level order fulfillment. In the battery cell segment, order deliveries were released intensively amid the "September-October peak season" signals, but actual project implementation pace clearly lagged plans, with regional and application-based divergence intensifying. 1. Electrolyte: Ample Capacity in Wait for GWh-Level Batch Implementation According to an SMM survey, sodium-ion battery electrolyte production rose 24% MoM and surged 115% YoY in September, sustaining high growth momentum. Production was highly concentrated, with top-tier players' shipments showing a clear breakaway lead. This round of growth likely flowed to major clients not yet publicly disclosed, and scaled shipment growth is likely delayed to Q4. September data largely reflected early stockpiling and small-batch deliveries on top of existing capacity. From an operational perspective, the number of industry players remains limited. Traditional lithium battery electrolyte leaders still attach relatively low priority to sodium-ion battery business. Apart from a few major clients, they have yet to form bulk supply to publicly disclosed entities, with only sporadic deliveries mentioned in financial reports. Downstream demand exhibited "small-batch, project-based" characteristics—some battery cell manufacturers' sodium-ion battery shipment volumes were relatively small, with cylindrical products shipped only intermittently in small batches, mainly targeting start-stop and small power applications, and no scaled energy storage application has yet formed. On the capacity side, since lithium battery electrolyte capacity is highly interchangeable with sodium-ion battery electrolyte capacity, overall industry capacity is ample with no obvious supply gap. However, it is worth noting that the current high returns in the lithium battery industry may crowd out sodium-ion battery electrolyte capacity. Enterprises' production scheduling priorities will continue to revolve around lithium battery business, leaving uncertainty in the pace of sodium-ion battery capacity release. On prices and raw materials, finished electrolyte prices remained generally stable in September, while core raw materials fluctuated slightly. NaPF6 prices were relatively stable: September production pulled back from August's unusually high level but was clearly better than the same period in previous years' normal levels. The core driver of this round of rise came from marginal improvement on the demand side. Upstream and downstream players across the industry chain generally held no additional inventory, with production strictly following produce-based-on-sales. Downstream electrolyte plants made temporary purchases as needed without advance stockpiling. Despite NaPF6's favorable storage conditions and longer shelf life than similar lithium chemical products, enterprises still scheduled production based on fixed sales, reflecting the industry's prudent judgment on the pace of demand realization. Competitive landscape-wise, the entire industry is waiting for top-tier players to deliver GWh-scale volume signals. Notably, some battery cell manufacturers have adopted low-price selling strategies right after production line commissioning and at the initial mass production stage, a commercial logic that remains to be validated over time. Looking ahead, if demand from key clients ramps up as expected in October, electrolyte and upstream NaPF6 shipments are poised for a step-change increase. SMM expects sodium-ion battery electrolyte production to rise 2% MoM and surge 146% YoY in October. II. Battery cells: Clear peak season signals, but rollout pace falls short of expectations According to SMM survey, sodium-ion battery cell production rose 1% MoM and surged 120% YoY in September, with the sodium-ion battery market showing initial signs of the "September-October peak season." Constrained by the requirement that energy storage projects generally must be connected to the grid before year-end, order deliveries are being released in a concentrated manner; however, from the perspective of project implementation, actual progress is clearly lagging behind plans, with schedule pressure and execution gaps coexisting. Regionally, utility-scale energy storage in China is concentrated in northern regions such as Hebei and Inner Mongolia, while overseas commercial and industrial storage demand is concentrated in Europe and Australia. Domestic commercial and industrial storage has yet to gain traction, presenting a three-way divergence in the demand geography: "northern storage leading, European and Australian commercial and industrial following, and domestic commercial and industrial yet to start." From an operational perspective, mainstream producers' monthly battery cell output remains at the tens of megawatt hours level. On the capacity side, some battery cell manufacturers' new bases in Sichuan will begin production and ramp up in late October, while some existing bases face clear capacity gaps that need to be filled through toll processing. Toll processing business is mostly focused on energy storage projects, with order demand expected to last until year-end. On the technology roadmap, current capacity is concentrated in the polyanion route, demand for cylindrical start-stop battery cells is steadily rising as winter approaches, and orders for prismatic energy storage battery cells remain at high levels, with route and product differentiation trends continuing. artigo.texto: Supermicro expande seu portfólio de projetos de computação aberta integrada para acelerar as implantações de data centers de IA em escala de rack AGÊNCIA DE COMUNICAÇÃO Conteúdo de responsabilidade da empresa 14 de outubro de 2026 - O portfólio integrado baseado no Open Compute Project (OCP) abrange sistemas de IA/HPC em escala de rack, racks ORv3 e ORW, alimentação de 48V CC, redes e soluções de refrigeração líquida para viabilizar a computação de maior densidade em data centers existentes e novos - O portfólio abrange desde a infraestrutura até operações inteligentes, incluindo fluidos de resfriamento DCBBS, CDUs integradas ao rack (in-rack), switches e o pacote de software de gerenciamento de sistemas da Supermicro para a gestão da infraestrutura - O Supermicro DCBBS reúne essas tecnologias baseadas em OCP em soluções integradas em escala de rack, simplificando e acelerando a implementação de recursos de computação, energia, rede e refrigeração para reduzir o tempo de entrada em operação (TTO). SAN JOSE, Califórnia, 14 de outubro de 2026 /PRNewswire/ — A Super Micro Computer, Inc. (NASDAQ: SMCI), uma provedora de soluções completas de TI para IA, empresas, armazenamento e 5G/Edge, com destaque para as soluções Data Center Building Block Solutions® (DCBBS), anunciou hoje um portfólio expandido de sistemas, racks e trocadores de calor de porta traseira (RDHx) certificados como Open Compute Project Accepted(TM). Com o suporte do DCBBS, o portfólio de soluções pode ser incorporado em implantações completas de ponta a ponta, em escala de rack e cluster. “O boom da IA redefine a forma como os data centers são projetados, construídos e implementados, e a Supermicro lidera essa transformação com o DCBBS”, disse Charles Liang, presidente e CEO da Supermicro. “Ao integrar computação, redes, energia, refrigeração avançada, software e serviços em soluções validadas em escala de rack, ajudamos os clientes a simplificar a complexidade e acelerar o caminho da inovação até a produção. O DCBBS possibilita que os clientes reduzam o TTM e o TTO ao oferecer infraestrutura essencial de IA de forma mais rápida e eficiente.” As soluções OCP da Supermicro já estão disponíveis; clique aqui para saber mais. Ao aproveitar as melhores práticas da comunidade OCP e o design e serviços do DCBBS, os operadores de data centers podem aumentar a densidade de computação e a eficiência energética para cargas de trabalho de IA e HPC com base em uma infraestrutura aberta e validada em escala de rack — desde sistemas e barras de distribuição até o resfriamento em nível de rack e de data centers — para implementar soluções de alta densidade de forma mais eficiente e acelerar o tempo de lançamento no mercado (TTM) e o tempo de operação (TTO). “Os clientes precisam de uma infraestrutura aberta e flexível que possa ser dimensionada de acordo com as demandas em rápida evolução da IA, ao mesmo tempo que se adapte à realidade de seus data centers”, disse Dirk Van Slyke, vice-presidente de Marketing da OCP. “Ao reunir sistemas, racks, energia e refrigeração aceitos pelo OCP em soluções validadas em escala de rack, a Supermicro ajuda os clientes a simplificar a integração, maximizar a capacidade e a eficiência das instalações e acelerar a implantação da infraestrutura de IA de produção.” Os racks ORv3 e ORW substituem as fontes de alimentação e os cabos individuais por servidor por uma barra de distribuição CC centralizada de 48 V, permitindo que os clientes otimizem seus sistemas de CPU e GPU para racks de computação de maior densidade. Essa densidade é ainda mais reforçada pelo sistema de resfriamento líquido DLC-2 Direct-to-Chip da Supermicro, que remove o calor de forma mais eficiente de CPUs, GPUs e outros componentes críticos, enquanto o calor residual pode ser removido do rack por meio de unidades de resfriamento ORv3 RDHx especialmente desenvolvidas, sem a necessidade de adaptações adicionais nos sistemas de ar-condicionado do data center. As unidades RDHx da Supermicro podem ser montadas na parte traseira de racks ORv3 e ORW, removendo o calor residual do ar de exaustão dos servidores antes que ele entre na sala do data center. O portfólio abrange capacidades de refrigeração de 10 kW a 120 kW, oferecendo aos operadores uma maneira prática de aumentar a densidade de racks tanto em novas instalações de IA quanto em data centers existentes. Os modelos alimentados por corrente contínua conectam-se à barra de distribuição do rack para reduzir a quantidade de cabos, enquanto os designs incluem ventiladores redundantes N+1 para garantir o tempo de atividade e um sistema anticondensação inteligente para evitar danos causados pela umidade a outros componentes dentro do rack. Os operadores podem monitorar e gerenciar todo o portfólio de componentes DCBBS, por meio do SuperCloud Composer®, utilizando protocolos padrão do setor. Além disso, os softwares da Supermicro, como o SuperCloud Director, o SuperCloud Automation Assistant e o SuperCloud Developer Console, possibilitam que as empresas gerenciem e operacionalizem todos os aspectos das modernas fábricas de IA, centros de dados corporativos e infraestrutura NeoCloud, por meio de uma solução unificada de controle de software. Como parte do portfólio do DCBBS, a Supermicro também oferece um portfólio abrangente de soluções de rede para IA, que variam de switches Ethernet 800G e 1.6T com refrigeração a ar ou líquida, incluindo plataformas Co-Packaged Optics (CPO) de última geração baseadas no silício de comutação Broadcom Tomahawk 6, otimizadas para racks EIA ou ORv3. O sistema operacional de rede SONiC Advanced da Supermicro Enterprise oferece aos clientes a flexibilidade de selecionar a arquitetura de rede que melhor atenda às suas necessidades de desempenho, energia, escalabilidade e implantação, à medida que a IA e os ambientes de data center de grande escala continuam a evoluir. The event brings together industry professionals focused on advancements in battery technology, electric vehicles, and manufacturing innovation. As manufacturers continue to advance electric vehicle and battery production, maintaining product quality and identifying defects throughout the manufacturing process remain critical priorities. ViewTech Borescopes will showcase its remote visual inspection solutions, demonstrating how video borescopes can help quality control and maintenance teams inspect internal components, identify potential defects, and improve inspection efficiency. ViewTech’s screen replicator tablet delivers a larger, wireless viewing experience for the VJ-4 video borescope, allowing inspectors to mirror the borescope’s display and remotely control its functions. Featuring a rugged 11-inch screen, the tablet enables inspection teams to view live footage on a larger display while maintaining convenient control of the borescope, supporting greater visibility and flexibility during inspections. “Reliable inspection is essential for maintaining quality and production efficiency,” said Joel Greene, ViewTech Borescopes Sales Consultant. “Our video borescopes help technicians inspect hard-to-reach areas and identify potential issues, while ODIN Borescope Report Maker turns inspection findings into professional reports easily shared with technicians, engineers, decision-makers, and customers.” Attendees are invited to connect with the ViewTech Borescopes team at booth 825 during the show to learn how remote visual inspection technology can support manufacturing quality control, reduce the need for unnecessary teardown, and help identify potential problems before they progress further into production. For manufacturers unable to attend the event, ViewTech Borescopes offers a no-obligation demonstration program, allowing prospective customers to evaluate a video borescope in their own facility. About ViewTech Borescopes ViewTech Borescopes is a leading provider of remote visual inspection solutions, offering video borescopes and inspection technologies designed to help professionals efficiently examine difficult-to-access areas. artigo.texto: Badland Batteries has officially opened a new 80,000-square-foot lithium-ion battery cell manufacturing facility in Fargo, North Dakota, expanding domestic production capabilities for unmanned aircraft systems, defense platforms, robotics and other autonomous technologies. The Badland Batteries manufacturing facility, which celebrated its grand opening on October 8, 2026, represents an investment in rebuilding the U.S. battery supply chain and reducing dependence on overseas manufacturers for critical energy storage technologies. The facility combines automated and operator-controlled manufacturing equipment to produce lithium-ion pouch cells, with the capacity to manufacture more than 15,000 battery cells per day as production scales. Badland Batteries Manufacturing Facility Opens in North Dakota The new Fargo facility is designed to manufacture lithium-ion pouch battery cells for defense, aerospace and autonomous systems applications. The 80,000-square-foot plant incorporates a combination of automated manufacturing processes and equipment operated by personnel. According to Badland Batteries, the facility is intended to support domestic battery production while providing greater control over materials, manufacturing quality and supply chain traceability. “Opening this facility marks an important step forward in building a secure and resilient battery supply chain here in the United States,” said Terri Zimmerman, CEO of Badland Batteries and Packet Digital. “Simply put, we believe that America should build its own batteries, and this facility represents years of work towards that goal and demonstrates our unwavering commitment to supporting our nation’s defense.” New Facility Targets Drone and Autonomous Systems Batteries The manufacturing operation is focused on producing battery cells for technologies that require reliable and domestically sourced power systems. Target applications include: - Unmanned aircraft systems - Military and defense platforms - Autonomous vehicles - Robotics - Aerospace technologies - Commercial autonomous systems Battery technology is a critical component of electric unmanned aircraft, affecting flight endurance, payload capacity and operational reliability. Badland Batteries is positioning its domestic production capabilities to support growing demand from U.S. defense and commercial customers. “These battery cells will help power today’s and tomorrow’s cutting-edge autonomous and UAS systems, which are critical to our nation’s security,” Zimmerman said. Domestic Battery Supply Chain Reduces Foreign Dependence According to Badland Batteries, more than 80% of batteries and critical materials used in autonomous systems are manufactured overseas. The company identifies this dependence as a significant supply chain vulnerability for U.S. defense and advanced technology programs. Badland Batteries describes its Fargo operation as the first UAS-specific battery manufacturing facility designed to control the complete manufacturing process, beginning with raw material sourcing and qualification. The company plans to use domestic or allied-sourced raw materials with full traceability. This approach is intended to strengthen supply chain security while giving customers greater visibility into the origins and production of critical battery components. Integrated Battery Cell and Pack Manufacturing The new facility will handle lithium-ion pouch cell production, beginning with raw material sourcing and in-house material qualification. Once cells are manufactured, they can be transported to Badland Batteries’ existing manufacturing and assembly facility located approximately one mile away. That second facility provides the capability to assemble completed cells into customer-ready battery packs. The combined operations create a manufacturing workflow covering: - Raw material sourcing - Material qualification - Lithium-ion cell production - Battery cell manufacturing - Battery pack assembly - Customer-ready power systems The company said this integrated approach is intended to provide a reliable domestic source of batteries for UAS and other autonomous platforms. Production Capacity Exceeds 15,000 Battery Cells Per Day Badland Batteries said the new facility has the ability to produce more than 15,000 lithium-ion battery cells per day. The company also designed the manufacturing operation with the flexibility to increase production as demand grows. The announced figure represents the facility’s production capacity rather than a confirmed current daily output. Actual production volumes, battery cell specifications and customer delivery schedules were not disclosed in the announcement. The manufacturing capacity is intended to support growing demand for domestically produced energy storage technologies across defense, aerospace and autonomous systems markets. Federal Investment Supports North Dakota Battery Industry The facility opening brought together federal, state, local, industry and military representatives. U.S. Senator John Hoeven highlighted the importance of domestic battery manufacturing for national security and economic competitiveness. “Building a strong domestic battery ecosystem is critical to our nation’s economic competitiveness and national security,” Hoeven said. “That’s why we’ve worked over the last six years to secure more than $50 million in federal funding to advance these efforts in North Dakota.” Hoeven said the Badland Batteries investment supports efforts to expand American manufacturing, create skilled employment opportunities and reduce reliance on foreign suppliers. The announcement does not specify how much of the referenced federal funding was awarded directly to Badland Batteries.
