artigo.texto: At 5 a.m. in Northern Virginia, chefs are already preparing chicken and chile roja enchiladas, fried shrimp tacos, and big batches of rice and beans to feed thousands of data center construction workers. By late morning, a crew brings the food from the off-site kitchen to a break tent where workers can pick up lunch without leaving the worksite. They don't pay: The Big Tech companies spending billions on AI infrastructure foot the bill. On an average day, National Jobsite Catering serves about 1,500 meals at each of its dozen data center construction sites across Northern Virginia, Texas, Ohio, Louisiana, Nevada, and Georgia, founder Scott Kaplan tells me. The busiest sites serve twice as many. After one to three years, the crews wrap up and move on. Kaplan, whose business used to consist of a fleet of food trucks catering one-off events along the East Coast, designed a venture that can follow them. If you build it, they will cook. National Jobsite Catering is part of the economic ecosystem being generated by America's data center boom. The tech giants leading the AI buildout are expected to spend more than $5 trillion on technology and data centers through 2030, with more than 1,500 data centers already in the works in the US. The room where a worker sleeps, the gym he hits before his shift, his parking spot, his lunch — these are all provided by a growing network of businesses. Local firms in the suburban and rural areas where the bulk of data centers are being built can get a windfall from a single project, but a more lasting proposition is the opportunity to serve site-to-site as construction crews move around. Whether that translates into lasting benefits for host towns is at the heart of growing pushback against the wave of data centers popping up across the country. Kaplan recognized the new opportunity a few years ago when a hyperscaler hired him to bring trucks to a site outside Philadelphia to feed 2,500 workers. "Literally the town that it was in had one restaurant — and it was in a strip club," he says. To avoid a lunch-hour bottleneck, Kaplan proposed preparing meals in a temporary kitchen and bringing them to the site. After replicating this model for other projects, his company now has 20 full-time employees and partners with established local vendors, helping them add equipment and plan production. He estimates a project can employ about 15 local people in kitchen, delivery, and distribution roles. "They know what they're doing," Kaplan says of the local partners. "But they've never cooked for 1,000 to 3,000 people." Since pivoting to data centers exclusively four years ago, revenue has gone up 10X, Kaplan says. Before thousands of construction workers can arrive on-site, they need somewhere to leave their cars — a logistical challenge that's creating a new market. WhereiPark began as a marketplace for city parking spots, but its fastest-growing business now comes from leasing lots near data center construction sites. General contractors have asked WhereiPark to find as many as 2,000 spaces for a project. A church lot used mainly on Sundays might work, as might a struggling shopping center or a nearby fairground or casino. In more remote locations, a contractor may need to grade and stripe land. Local landowners, meanwhile, earn temporary income from unused space without selling the farm. "If there's nowhere for the construction workers to park, the thing doesn't get built," says Joshua Eisen, WhereiPark's chief revenue officer. A team in Toronto does much of the search via property data, calls, and emails; a partner or the general contractor then inspects a prospective lot locally. The company also partners with shuttle operators to ferry workers between the lots and construction sites. For a builder juggling several projects, that means one contact and billing relationship instead of a new search and lease negotiation in every town. A completed facility the size of a Walmart might have just 50 spaces, so most lots return to their previous use. WhereiPark can repeat the search around another project without owning land. With global AI investment expected to exceed a trillion dollars in 2026 alone, companies of all sizes are getting in on the gold rush. Food services and facilities management giant Aramark launched a new division called Nexus earlier this year, which offers hotel-like amenities, fitness centers, and recreation to help attract skilled workers. The company noted that Nexus contracts carry higher-than-average profit margins. Executives projected that three initial data center sites could each generate Aramark about $150 million in annualized revenue once fully running. The data center housing business has a precedent in the oil patch, where companies have long followed temporary crews from project to project. Target Hospitality, a $1.8 billion company that has housed oilfield workers and operated two Texas detention centers for ICE, is building and operating accommodations for data center construction crews, including a $550 million deal for a 4,000-bed facility in North Texas. The company advertises furnished bedrooms equipped with small fridges and microwaves, as well as communal dining, gyms, and WiFi. Its modular assets can be redeployed elsewhere. In August, the company said it has secured contracts representing more than 9,000 beds and $1.4 billion since January. Facing growing opposition, hyperscalers have pitched the AI buildout as an engine of economic development, promising spillover benefits for local areas. Microsoft's "community-first" promise cited its experience in Washington state to estimate that for every direct construction job created, another is generated in sectors including security, maintenance, retail, and food service. While spillovers certainly occur, the exact level varies project to project. artigo.texto: Hoymiles HiOne All-in-One BESS Powers Thai Homes with More Resilient, Flexible Energy Systems By PR Newswire BANGKOK, Oct. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Thailand’s hot and humid climate, growing household electricity demand and the need for greater power reliability are driving more homeowners to look beyond solar generation alone. Hoymiles’ HiOne all-in-one BESS system, paired with HiBox gateway, is helping households in Bangkok make better use of solar power, manage electricity consumption and maintain power availability during grid interruptions. Meeting Thailand’s Growing Residential Energy Needs For Thai households, hot climate drives heavy air-conditioning use, while high electricity costs and power interruptions create demand for systems that offer more than daytime solar generation. The market is also moving toward wider residential solar adoption. According to the Department of Alternative Energy Development and Efficiency (DEDE), Thailand had 3,310 MWp of cumulative rooftop solar capacity by the end of 2024. In 2026, the government also introduced a residential solar feed-in program targeting up to 500 MW of capacity nationwide, allowing eligible households to sell surplus solar electricity to utilities at THB 2.20/kWh under 10-year power purchase agreements. In this context, local installer COMSYS SOLAR has deployed Hoymiles HiOne systems with HiBox gateway across multiple residential properties in Bangkok. Configurations include 10kW or 12kW of solar capacity with 8kWh or 16kWh of storage, allowing each system to be matched to the household’s energy needs. Flexible Solar-plus-Storage for Greater Energy Resilience Hoymiles’ HiOne BESS integrates the inverter, battery and energy management system (EMS) into a minimalist, space-saving design. With maximum efficiency of 98.5% and more than 8,000 battery life cycles, HiOne combines efficient energy conversion with long-term performance. New and existing batteries can be mixed through built-in DC-DC technology, with storage capacity expandable from 8 to 64kWh. Its AI-powered time-of-use (TOU) optimization adjusts charging strategies based on electricity prices and household consumption patterns to maximize self-consumption and reduce electricity costs. The HiBox gateway serves as a central hub for whole-home backup, providing seamless off-grid switching to help keep household appliances running during grid outages. It also supports system expansion through an additional inverter, compatible third-party generators and PV inverters, as well as smart load management through its Smart Port. Hoymiles’ HiOne helps Thai households make better use of locally generated solar power while adapting to changing electricity demand. The multiple installations by COMSYS SOLAR in Bangkok demonstrate how flexible system configurations can meet diverse household energy needs and support more resilient residential energy use. artigo.texto: Developer Returns With A Second Proposal For A Zoning Overlay To Facilitate Apartments In Proximity To Pearl River Transit Station The developer of Jefferson Arms, a proposed 88-unit residential project in Pearl River’s CO (Commercial) zone, returned to the Orangetown Town Board last week asking the town board to advance a proposal that would create a Development Enhancement (DE) Overlay Zone in Pearl River’s downtown. The DE Overlay would allow rental apartments on parcels of land of at least one acre in size and within 1,000 feet of the Pearl River commuter train station. The developer first appeared in May, with a proposal that would allow a 4-story building with 109 apartment units and 132 parking spaces at 10 Jefferson Avenue. In a new iteration, the developer scaled back its project to 88 units (65 units per acre) in a three-story building with below ground parking. Jefferson Arms would have 12 studios, 63 1-bedroom units, 12 2-bedroom units, and one three-bedroom unit for a superintendent. The overlay would apply only to CO (Commercial/Office) zoned land, but would not change the zoning. It would act as an overlay to the existing zoning. Any development would still be subject to review by Orangetown’s land use boards. A proposal to create a zoning overlay in proximity to the Metro North/New Jersey Transit line on Main Street would permit the redevelopment of fallow commercial property in Pearl River. While there are only a few CO parcels large enough (over one acre) to avail itself of the development overlay, the developer’s representative told the board that smaller parcels in the CO zone could be assembled to reach the one-acre threshold. In a presentation to the Town Board last week, the developer, Jefferson Arms LLC, touted the benefits in creating housing opportunities for young professionals, commuters, downsizing seniors, and local workforce residents. Benefits also included additional foot traffic for downtown businesses, as well as enhancing the appearance of the area which is dotted with fallow and underutilized commercial lots. Also discussed was the increase in the taxes the CO lots would pay after conversion to residential use. The owner of the site pays about $69,000 annually in taxes. During the presentation, the owner’s representative alluded to tax revenues from the site many times larger than what is currently levied. The board responded that the 1,000 foot proximity did not make sense, as it could effectively divide individual parcels. A suggestion was made to define the boundaries by streets, not distance from the train station. Changes to the zoning code and the creation of overlays are discretionary with the town board. It has no obligation to act on an application. The Board did not make any decision on the overlay, but referred it to the Town Planner, the Town Planning Board, and the County Planning Department for recommendations and input. BESS Developer Seeks Hardship Exemption From Orangetown Moratorium On Data Centers And Battery Energy Storage Systems A developer of a Batter Energy Storage System (BESS) appeared before the Orangetown Town Board asking for a hardship exemption from the Town’s six-month moratorium on data centers and battery energy storage systems. A BESS is an engineered installation of rechargeable batteries tied to a utility substation that stores electrical energy and releases it on demand. Batteries are charged in the evening when power demand is low and released during the day or when power demand peaks. The Town of Orangetown passed a six-month town-wide moratorium on new data centers and battery energy storage systems in August. The moratorium allowed for discretionary hardship exemptions. The Orangetown Battery Project, hosted behind a warehouse at 524 Route 303 in Orangeburg, would install about fifteen 30-foot containers of rechargeable batteries adjacent to the railroad tracks in Orangetown’s LO district. The applicant negotiated a contract with the owner of the property in May 2025 and was approved for interconnection with Orange & Rockland in December. It has met with the Orangetown Planning Board several times prior to the imposition of the moratorium. The project does not require any variances, waivers, or zone changes. The batteries would connect to the O&R substation on Mountainview Road. According to NYSERDA, energy storage strengthens and modernizes the electric grid by making it more flexible, efficient, and resilient—benefiting communities, businesses, and households across New York. Battery storage systems pose a unique fire risk, and advances in containment and suppression help local governments manage the risk. The applicant advised the town board that it intended to create a “host community agreement” that would require the operator to finance any equipment the local fire district needed to address a potential fire risk. The town board was inclined to grant the waiver, but a representative of AKRF, a planning firm retained by the town to evaluate the application sought additional information from the developer. The developer agreed to provide the information and the matter was rolled forward to the next town board meeting on October 20th. There was no public comment either in favor or opposed to the application. artigo.texto: Imagine que você liga para o seu mecânico e fala: “o carro não pegou hoje de manhã, deve ser a bateria”. Em vez de concordar, ele responde com uma pergunta: “como você usa o carro durante a semana?”. Você estranha. Afinal, o que o seu trajeto até o trabalho tem a ver com um carro que não liga? Tem tudo a ver, e é isso que vamos traduzir hoje. Olá, queridos e queridas! Segunda-feira, 7h40, você gira a chave (ou aperta o botão) e o carro faz um “rrr... rrr...” sem vontade, ou nem isso. O painel acende fraco, o rádio reinicia, e vem o veredicto de sempre: “a bateria morreu do nada”. Mas ontem estava tudo certo, não estava? Bateria quase nunca morre do nada. Leia também - Troca de óleo a cada 10 mil km é regra ou é lenda? - Tudo sobre a gasolina E35: separando fato de boato antes que você acredite em qualquer coisa O que costuma acontecer é que ela vinha avisando e ninguém traduziu. E, em muitos casos, ela nem é a culpada: é só a vítima. Para entender isso, é preciso saber o que ela faz. A bateria não guarda eletricidade; ela guarda energia química, uma reação entre os componentes internos que se converte em energia elétrica na hora que o carro pede. Na partida, ela entrega muita corrente em poucos segundos para o motor de arranque. Mas o trabalho não acaba aí: com o motor desligado, é ela que mantém alarme, memórias e módulos vivos, e com o motor ligado ela ajuda a estabilizar a tensão do sistema elétrico. Quem a recarrega é o alternador. Pense na bateria como a caixa d’água da casa e no alternador como a bomba que a enche. Se a caixa estiver furada, você enche e ela esvazia. Se a bomba estiver fraca, a caixa nunca enche direito. Trocar a caixa d’água quando o problema é a bomba só garante uma caixa nova que nunca enche. E quanto tempo dura uma bateria? Não existe prazo universal, e desconfie de quem prometeu um. Trajetos curtos e frequentes não dão tempo de o carro repor a energia gasta na partida, então a conta nunca fecha. Carro parado por semanas vai se descarregando sozinho. O calor castiga a estrutura interna, e o frio exige mais dela na hora da partida. Um carro cheio de demanda elétrica (multimídia, câmeras, acessórios instalados depois) pede mais da bateria do que um carro simples. Dois veículos iguais, com donos e rotinas diferentes, podem ter vidas de bateria bem diferentes. É por isso que o mecânico perguntou do seu trajeto. Os avisos costumam aparecer antes da falha. Partida mais lenta que o normal, principalmente de manhã ou depois de alguns dias parado. Carro que “acorda cansado” depois de um período sem uso. Luzes que enfraquecem na partida, vidros mais lentos, multimídia reiniciando sozinho. Em carros com Start-Stop, o sistema deixar de atuar ou atuar de um jeito estranho também pode ser sinal, já que ele depende de condições da bateria para funcionar. Mas atenção: sintoma não é diagnóstico. Cada um desses sinais pode ter outra origem, e quem fecha a conta é o teste, não o palpite. Aliás, uma frase que ouço muito na oficina é “medi com o multímetro e a tensão está boa”. Medir só a tensão é como medir a temperatura de uma pessoa e concluir que ela está em forma para correr uma maratona. A tensão em repouso mostra quanto de carga a bateria tem naquele momento, mas não mostra se ela aguenta o esforço da partida. Uma bateria desgastada pode marcar uma tensão aceitável parada e não sustentar a corrente quando é exigida. O que revela a condição real é um teste apropriado, com equipamento próprio. E o teste não termina nela: é preciso avaliar o sistema de carga, ou seja, se o alternador está carregando como deveria com o motor funcionando. Outro engano comum é achar que bateria é tudo igual. Não é. A convencional é a mais simples e atende carros sem muita exigência. A EFB é uma evolução desse conceito, pensada para suportar melhor o ciclo de muitas partidas e paradas, comum em carros com Start-Stop mais básico. A AGM tem outra construção interna, é mais robusta em ciclos de carga e descarga e costuma ser exigida em carros com sistemas mais exigentes. Qual delas o seu carro precisa depende do projeto, e o lugar para descobrir é o manual do proprietário e a especificação do fabricante. Trocar por uma tecnologia inferior à exigida, só para economizar, é uma aposta bem ruim. E mesmo dentro da tecnologia certa, duas baterias de 60 Ah não são necessariamente iguais. O Ah indica a capacidade, ou seja, quanta energia ela armazena. Mas existem ainda a corrente de partida a frio (CCA), as dimensões, a posição dos pólos e as exigências do fabricante. É como dois tênis número 40: o número é o mesmo, mas um é de corrida e o outro é de passeio. Há ainda um detalhe que pouca gente conta: em alguns veículos, principalmente os com gerenciamento eletrônico de energia, a troca pode exigir registro da nova bateria ou algum procedimento específico. Isso não vale para todo carro, e é justamente por isso que vale perguntar antes de sair da oficina: “o meu exige algo depois da troca?”. Já a chupeta, quando bate à pressa, parece a solução óbvia. Mas improvisar pode gerar faísca, inversão de polaridade e danos a módulos eletrônicos. Muitos manuais trazem orientações próprias ou até pontos específicos para partida auxiliar. Se for fazer, faça como o fabricante prevê. E se você trocou a bateria e, meses depois, o problema voltou? Antes de culpar a bateria nova, vale investigar o resto. O alternador está carregando bem? Existe alguma fuga de corrente, algo consumindo energia com o carro desligado? E o seu jeito de usar o carro combina com a bateria que foi escolhida? Voltando à ligação para o mecânico: a pergunta dele sobre o seu trajeto não era conversa fiada, era o início do diagnóstico. Ele queria saber se a bateria está ruim, se ela é a certa para o seu carro e se o sistema que a mantém carregada está funcionando. São exatamente as três perguntas que você deve levar para a oficina. E no fim das contas, quem faz essas perguntas deixa de ser refém daquela frase “troca que resolve”. Pergunte antes de pagar.

artigo.texto: EnOcean Pioneer in self-powered wireless standard According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Battery Free Sensors market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The global Battery Free Sensors market is entering a decisive phase of commercial scale-up, moving from niche, cost-insensitive deployments toward core enablement of low-maintenance monitoring across energy storage and renewable integration systems. The central demand driver is predictive maintenance for battery energy storage systems (BESS), where conventional battery-powered sensors impose recurring replacement labor, downtime, and hazardous-waste liabilities over 20-30 year asset lives. Battery-free sensors that harvest ambient RF, thermal, kinetic, or solar energy eliminate those costs and unlock continuous condition monitoring at scale. Demand is bifurcating between high-reliability nodes for mission-critical grid and industrial assets and ultra-low-cost, high-volume nodes for distributed environmental and condition monitoring across vast renewable fleets. Adoption is not a simple sensor swap: it requires re-architecting data acquisition networks, affecting gateway placement, communication protocols, and backend analytics, which locks in system integrators and controls providers as key channel gatekeepers. Supply chain maturity is uneven, with energy harvesting components and ultra-low-power ASICs facing scale and performance constraints, while mechanical vibration harvesters remain application-specific. Project economics are dominated by total cost of ownership, where eliminated battery replacement labor, downtime, and disposal justify a significant upfront premium. Competitive advantage is shifting from component performance to system integration expertise and software analytics, as value migrates from data collection to predictive maintenance and operational optimization. Regulatory and standards bodies are beginning to formalize maintenance-free monitoring requirements in safety-critical applications, creating compliance-driven demand pull in regulated utility and industrial segments. This report provides a structured, commercially grounded analysis of the market through 2035, covering deployment use cases, buyer environments, upstream dependencies, qualification requirements, pricing architecture, and country capability differences. The baseline scenario for the Battery Free Sensors market through 2035 assumes continued acceleration of renewable capacity additions and grid modernization, with BESS deployments growing at a double-digit pace in most regions. Under this scenario, battery-free sensor demand is forecast to expand at a 14.2% CAGR from 2026 to 2035, lifting the market index to 380 by 2035 (2025=100). The strongest demand pull comes from predictive maintenance for BESS, where operators face mounting pressure to reduce OPEX and safety liabilities associated with battery-powered sensor replacement in hard-to-access or hazardous installations. As BESS asset fleets age, the labor and downtime costs of conventional sensor maintenance compound, making the total cost of ownership case for battery-free sensors increasingly compelling. Adoption will be fastest in utility-scale energy storage and commercial and industrial backup power, where asset criticality and maintenance access constraints are most acute. The commercial and industrial segment will also benefit from tightening functional safety standards and insurance requirements that favor maintenance-free monitoring. Supply-side constraints, particularly specialized low-power PMIC design and fabrication capacity, will moderate growth in price-sensitive, high-volume applications, but will not derail the overall trajectory. Regionally, Asia-Pacific will lead in volume terms, supported by China's dominance in BESS manufacturing and deployment, while North America and Europe will drive value growth through higher qualification and safety requirements. Latin America and the Middle East and Africa will remain smaller but fast-growing markets, underpinned by utility-scale solar and storage tenders. Key risks to the baseline include slower-than-expected BESS deployment, delays in standards formalization, and persistent cost premiums that slow adoption in cost-sensitive segments. However, the structural drivers of maintenance-free monitoring, digitalization of asset management, and the imperative to reduce hazardous waste from battery disposal are expected to keep the market on a strong upward path through 2035. Utility-scale energy storage is the largest and fastest-growing end-use sector for battery-free sensors, primarily driven by predictive maintenance for battery energy storage systems (BESS). As grid operators and utilities deploy massive BESS fleets to integrate renewable energy and provide grid services, the challenge of monitoring thousands of battery modules, thermal management systems, and power conversion equipment becomes acute. Conventional battery-powered sensors require periodic replacement, which is costly and disruptive in high-voltage, hard-to-access installations. Battery-free sensors that harvest ambient RF, thermal, or kinetic energy enable continuous monitoring of cell voltage, temperature, vibration, and state of health without maintenance. Through 2035, demand will be propelled by the need to reduce OPEX, enhance safety, and extend asset life. Key demand-side indicators include BESS capacity additions, average asset age, maintenance cost per sensor, and regulatory requirements for safety monitoring. The sector will increasingly favor sensors integrated with analytics platforms that predict failures before they occur, shifting value from hardware to software and services. artigo.texto: Data Centers (KM Stock/Shutterstock) Publicado em 13 de outubro de 2026 às 21h10. A recente sanção da Lei 15.504/2026, que instituiu o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata), colocou a infraestrutura digital brasileira no centro da agenda econômica no país. Mas, para além de criar um regime tributário para um setor específico, o Redata oferece a oportunidade de aproximar duas agendas que ainda são frequentemente tratadas de maneira separada: o aumento da capacidade de processamento de dados em território brasileiro e o fortalecimento de uma cadeia industrial para tornar essa expansão possível. Data centers são infraestruturas de engenharia de alta complexidade, cujos efeitos ultrapassam o setor de tecnologia, mobilizando verticais estratégicas como energia, construção civil, telecomunicações e serviços especializados. Dentro deles existem muito mais do que servidores de processamento: são utilizados sistemas elétricos, transformadores, painéis e equipamentos de distribuição, UPS, barramentos, sistemas de refrigeração de alta eficiência, automação, controle, cabos, estruturas metálicas e uma extensa cadeia de serviços especializados para instalação e manutenção desses equipamentos. Isso significa que cada novo megawatt de capacidade de data center no país representa também uma nova demanda para uma cadeia física e industrial - muito maior do que normalmente aparece quando se discute economia digital. Cada novo projeto impulsiona a procura por equipamentos, sistemas, engenharia e serviços, fomenta a criação de postos de trabalho e acelera a necessidade de habilidades verdes (green skills) e qualificações técnicas em pilares essenciais para sustentar o avanço da inteligência artificial (IA). Um estudo da FGV Projetos, utilizando a Matriz Insumo-Produto do IBGE, ajuda a dimensionar esse potencial. Para cada R$ 1 de demanda final associada ao setor de data centers é gerado R$ 1,45 em valor de produção na economia, considerando desdobramentos diretos e indiretos. Outro dado é ainda mais relevante para a discussão industrial: R$ 1,16 desse resultado ocorre por meio da ativação da cadeia de fornecedores. O mesmo encadeamento aparece na geração de empregos. Para cada R$ 1 milhão investido, a FGV estima cerca de 7,5 empregos diretos e indiretos, incluindo aqueles originados na cadeia de fornecedores. Esses números contribuem para tangibilizar o fato de que parcela expressiva do impacto econômico de um data center acontece do lado de fora e, quanto maior a participação de fornecedores instalados no país, maior tende a ser a parcela do investimento que permanece e se multiplica dentro da economia nacional. Da mesma forma, quanto maior e mais previsível for a demanda doméstica por data centers, maior será a possibilidade de ampliar a escala, a produtividade e a competitividade da nossa indústria, assegurando novas linhas de produção, investimentos em capacidade produtiva, desenvolvimento tecnológico e qualificação de fornecedores. Estamos falando, portanto, de uma relação de interdependência, na qual data centers competitivos necessitam de uma indústria forte e competitiva, e uma indústria apta a competir globalmente precisa de mercados que gerem escala e demanda tecnológica. Por isso, o debate sobre o desenvolvimento dos data centers no Brasil não pode correr o risco de ser limitado a uma escolha entre “incentivo ao investimento estrangeiro” ou “proteção da indústria nacional”. Essa é uma abordagem míope que apequena uma lógica de ecossistema a uma falsa dicotomia. O que a experiência internacional e a dinâmica dos mercados mostram é que é factível atrair capital, tecnologia e capacidade computacional e, ao mesmo tempo, tracionar nossa cadeia de fornecedores, engenharia, inovação e produção nacional. Isso não implica pressupor que todos os componentes necessários à infraestrutura digital devam ser manufaturados no país – aliás, nenhuma grande economia é autossuficiente na cadeia de infraestrutura digital. Com isso, o desafio de uma política industrial moderna é combinar o acesso competitivo às tecnologias que ainda não produzidas localmente com condições para que a indústria brasileira consolide sua participação à medida em que o mercado doméstico ganha escala. A primeira premissa para a concretização desse cenário, porém, é que novos projetos sejam viabilizados. É neste ponto que reside a importância da regulamentação do Redata e da aprovação do convênio nacional, no âmbito do Confaz, para reduzir o ICMS sobre alguns equipamentos específicos. Afinal, se a infraestrutura brasileira continuar mais cara do que a de mercados concorrentes – e atualmente o custo econômico para um data center no Brasil é 26,7% maior do que nos Estados Unidos, por exemplo – o país perde competitividade na disputa global por esses investimentos. Quando um projeto de infraestrutura digital é alocado em outro mercado, ele leva consigo a demanda que poderia alavancar a indústria local - sem mencionar as atividades econômicas habilitadas na cadeia downstream, que dependem de capacidade computacional, nuvem e IA. Por isso, desenvolvedores de data centers e fabricantes nacionais estão olhando para o mesmo horizonte. Ambos dependem de um ecossistema competitivo, capaz de atrair investimentos, estimular demanda, desenvolver tecnologia e incrementar a produção local. É nessa articulação entre políticas públicas, investimentos privados e indústria de alta eficiência que o tamanho da participação brasileira na nova economia global será definido. *Rafael Segrera é presidente da Schneider Electric para a América do Sul e líder do grupo de trabalho "Fostering Human and Social Development", da Sustainable Business COP (SB COP) *Luciano Fialho é vice-presidente Sênior de Desenvolvimento Corporativo, Energia e Imóveis da Scala Data Centers

artigo.texto: Um ataque com drones ucranianos atingiu o centro de dados principal da Yandex em Vladimir, na Rússia, na manhã de 11 de outubro, forçando a suspensão temporária das operações e interrompendo mais de 80 serviços digitais. Segundo os dados avançados pelo Vietnam.vn, a investida afetou desde aplicações de consumo e ferramentas de inteligência artificial até à infraestrutura corporativa em nuvem da empresa. Terceiro ataque à infraestrutura do gigante tecnológico Este incidente representa o terceiro ataque direcionado aos servidores da multinacional russa num intervalo de apenas quatro dias. A vaga de investidas começou a 8 de outubro com uma ação contra um centro de dados em Sasovo, na região de Ryazan, que provocou um incêndio e obrigou ao encerramento total da infraestrutura responsável por suportar serviços da rede ferroviária russa (RZhD), da operadora MegaFon e de vários órgãos de comunicação social. No dia seguinte, a 9 de outubro, outra instalação em Kaluga, a sudoeste de Moscovo, foi visada, tendo a Yandex confirmado a desativação de múltiplos módulos de hardware. O complexo de Vladimir, visado na ação mais recente, foi projetado para albergar até 2.880 racks de servidores, constituindo um dos polos centrais de processamento do grupo. Serviços afetados e impacto na rede elétrica A interrupção no centro de Vladimir provocou falhas imediatas em várias aplicações de consumo, incluindo a assistente de voz Alice, o Yandex Music, a plataforma de videoconferência Telemost e os sistemas de domótica Yandex Smart Home. No setor empresarial, a plataforma Yandex Cloud registou quebras nos serviços de computação, armazenamento e bases de dados, afetando soluções como Compute Cloud, Object Storage, Managed Kubernetes, PostgreSQL e ClickHouse. As ferramentas de IA da empresa, como a API YandexGPT, o SpeechKit e o Vision OCR, também ficaram inoperacionais. O impacto estendeu-se a plataformas de comércio eletrónico, instituições bancárias, serviços de transporte por aplicação e cadeias de retalho na Rússia e em países vizinhos. Em paralelo, a autarquia de Vladimir confirmou que os ataques danificaram subestações locais e provocaram um corte geral de eletricidade, embora cerca de 80% do fornecimento tenha sido restabelecido durante a manhã. O Ministério da Defesa russo declarou ter intercetado 479 drones em 16 regiões, ao passo que analistas militares apontam que a degradação continuada destas infraestruturas visa comprometer a logística, a governação e as capacidades de comando digital do país.

artigo.texto: Yandex Go taxi and delivery services in Kazakhstan have been disrupted for 36 hours following a drone attack on Russian technology giant Yandex’s data center in Vladimir, leaving users, drivers and couriers unable to access the app. "Yandex Go services are currently operating with errors or may be temporarily unavailable," the company’s Kazakhstan press service said. "We cannot yet name exact timelines, but we are doing everything possible to bring them back as soon as possible." The outage shows how Ukraine’s apparent campaign against Yandex data centers in Russia is spilling into neighboring countries that rely on the company’s services, including Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Belarus and Armenia. Yandex Go Kazakhstan said personal data of Kazakh users is stored on servers in Kazakhstan, but that its services rely on distributed infrastructure. "Individual technological components may be located on servers in different countries. Therefore, technical problems in one component can affect service availability in several countries," it said. The company did not directly confirm that the outage was caused by the attack in Russia. Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development announced Sunday that the servers holding users' personal data were in the country and working normally, but some key components for taxi and delivery services are abroad. It said it was working with Yandex and local providers to restore services. In Uzbekistan, Yandex said some Yandex Go services were unavailable or working intermittently, without saying whether the problem was linked to the attack. Services in Kyrgyzstan were working normally, Russian media outlet TASS reported. Yandex said search, its Alisa voice assistant, maps, mail and taxi services were gradually being restored in Russia, though some functions remain unavailable. The company limited some features of its Disk cloud storage. "We deliberately limited some functions of Yandex 360, including Disk, to preserve the main thing, the operability of services," Yandex told RBC. Yandex said it agreed with cloud providers VK Cloud, Selectel and K2Cloud to quickly host clients’ data and services. Its shares fell more than 5% in early trading on the Moscow Exchange on Monday, TASS reported. Replacing damaged equipment could take about six months, market sources told Kommersant. "These were very large data centers, and since their construction, a global shortage and rising prices for computing capacity began, especially for AI accelerators. Equipping them promises to be expensive and long," said Sergey Kudryashov of Strategy Partners. Russia’s Digital Development Minister Maksut Shadaev said his ministry and the Defense Ministry are working on protecting data centers, TASS reported. Drones struck Yandex data centers in Sasovo in the Ryazan region on Oct. 8, Kaluga on Oct. 9 and Vladimir on Oct. 11, shutting the Vladimir facility completely. Yandex has five data centers, four in Russia and one in Finland that was disconnected because of sanctions. "Two can play at this game," Andriy Kovalenko, former head of Ukraine’s Center for Countering Disinformation, wrote after the first strike, as the Yandex outage spreads beyond Russia.

artigo.texto: Amwins Global Risks (AGR), the specialist global risk division of Amwins, has broadened the scope of its Commercial & Industrial (C&I) insurance facility to include battery energy storage systems (BESS) and electric vehicle (EV) charging infrastructure. The expanded facility enables developers, owners and investors to insure multiple distributed energy assets across different locations under one insurance programme. AGR said the updated offering is intended to meet the needs of businesses developing portfolios of smaller energy infrastructure projects, which may be spread across several sites but form part of a larger investment. “The expansion is designed to support the growing deployment of distributed energy infrastructure, where individual assets may be relatively small, and geographically dispersed, but collectively represent increasingly substantial portfolios for developers, owners and investors,” commented Dr Tom Harries, Director at Amwins Global Risks. “By aggregating assets within a portfolio, AGR provides a consistent underwriting approach across multiple locations while assessing and managing accumulated natural catastrophe exposure at portfolio level.” The facility will provide insurance options for the construction of EV charging infrastructure in the United States, as well as cover for assets once they are operational. AGR said protection can include Delay in Start-Up (DSU) and Business Interruption (BI), addressing risks that may affect project completion or interrupt business activities. The structure also allows deductibles to be adjusted to reflect the size and risk profile of individual installations. According to AGR, this offers an alternative to insurance arrangements developed for utility-scale projects, under which deductibles may be less suited to smaller assets. AGR said the growth of distributed energy infrastructure has created insurance requirements that do not always fit established models. While traditional cover has often focused on individual projects or large-scale energy developments, battery storage facilities and EV charging networks can comprise numerous smaller installations operating across a broad geographical area. “Individual sites can be relatively small, but developers are increasingly building portfolios comprising numerous assets across multiple locations,”added Harries. “Bringing those assets together allows us to underwrite them efficiently at portfolio scale, while still recognising the individual risk characteristics of each site.” The expanded facility builds on AGR’s existing Community Solar offering, which provides portfolio-based insurance for commercial and community-scale solar installations. By adding battery storage and EV charging infrastructure, AGR is extending its approach to cover a broader range of distributed energy assets. Harries said the inclusion of these technologies will allow AGR to assess how a portfolio’s exposure to natural catastrophes changes as further projects are incorporated. The programme is intended to accommodate portfolio growth while taking account of the risk characteristics of individual sites. “The addition of BESS and EV charging infrastructure reflects the increasing convergence of distributed energy technologies,” said Harries. “It allows us to focus on monitoring how the portfolio’s natural catastrophe exposure changes as new projects are added and gives developers the freedom to concentrate on building out their portfolios, knowing their insurance programme can adapt and grow alongside them.”

The global market for Solid State Battery Precursor Free Cathodes represents a pivotal enabler for the industrialization of solid-state batteries (SSBs), addressing the critical bottleneck of scalable, cost-effective electrode manufacturing. Unlike conventional cathode materials that rely on liquid or gel precursors, precursor-free cathodes are synthesized without traditional solvent-based routes, simplifying manufacturing and enhancing electrochemical performance. This market is not a materials science niche but a strategic linchpin for next-generation energy storage, fundamentally driven by automotive OEMs seeking step-change improvements in energy density and safety for electric vehicles. The value proposition shifts from chemical formulation alone to the integration of material synthesis with dry-process electrode engineering, creating a convergence point for battery materials specialists and dry-process equipment innovators. Supply chain risk is concentrated upstream in secure sourcing of high-purity metal oxides and phosphates, and downstream in multi-year qualification cycles with cell manufacturers. Pricing power will accrue to players controlling intellectual property on scalable synthesis routes and demonstrating validated performance in partner cell prototypes. The commercial model is bifurcating: a build path selling active material or coated electrodes, and a partner path centered on IP licensing and joint ventures. Geographic strategy is decoupled, with R&D and IP creation in established technology hubs and future high-volume production dictated by proximity to gigafactories and cost-competitive industrial bases. Regulatory tailwinds from enhanced battery safety and recycling directives indirectly favor SSB adoption, though precursor-free cathodes face distinct regulatory burdens in novel material handling and transportation classification. The competitive landscape is forming around distinct archetypes, with success contingent on securing a defensible position in the emerging dry-process value chain, from powder synthesis to calendaring, rather than attempting full vertical integration across the cell stack. artigo.texto: Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners committed more than €270 million to Kilmarnock South, a 350 MW / 1,400 MWh battery energy storage project in southern Scotland. The investment is being made through Copenhagen Infrastructure IV, the firm’s fourth flagship fund. CIP has taken a final investment decision on the project, and construction is underway. Commercial operations are expected to begin in the first quarter of 2028. Kilmarnock South is designed as a four-hour-duration lithium-ion battery energy storage system. Once operational, it is expected to become the longest-duration battery storage asset in CIP’s U.K. portfolio. The project will store excess Scottish wind power that might otherwise be curtailed and return that electricity to the grid when network capacity is available. Kilmarnock South represents CIP’s fourth investment in transmission-connected battery energy storage in Scotland. The project joins Coalburn 1, Coalburn 2, and Devilla. Coalburn 1 reached commercial operations in August 2026. When all four projects are fully commissioned, CIP’s Scottish battery storage portfolio is expected to provide 1.85 GW of power capacity and 4.4 GWh of energy storage. CIP said that level of storage represents nearly one-third of Great Britain’s current operational battery energy storage capacity. The portfolio would have enough energy storage capacity to meet the electricity demand of more than 5.5 million households for two hours. Kilmarnock South was developed by Noriker Power, which will continue managing the project’s construction phase. The project also has an optimization agreement with Shell Energy Europe designed to provide long-term contracted revenue. KEY QUOTES: “CIP is pleased to add Kilmarnock South to our growing portfolio of UK battery projects, which, once commissioned, will be the longest-duration BESS asset in our UK fleet. Well-sited battery energy storage projects provide valuable power system flexibility which enables the full benefits of low-cost renewables to be captured, strengthening security of supply and helping to both cut and stabilise energy bills for consumers.” Nischal Agarwal, Partner at Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners “A former coal mine at Coalburn is now home to one of Europe’s largest batteries storing clean power, while at Kilmarnock South, a new GBP 232 million battery will store even more Scottish wind power for when it’s needed most. Together, these projects mean less homegrown power going to waste, greater energy security, and lower bills over the long term.” Michael Shanks, U.K. Energy Minister

artigo.texto: Home › Policies & Regulations ›Finance Ministry Clarifies 10 Percent Customs Duty on Stationary and Grid-Scale BESS Finance Ministry Clarifies 10 Percent Customs Duty on Stationary and Grid-Scale BESS The Ministry of Finance has clarified that stationary, grid-scale and industrial lithium-ion BESS qualify for a concessional 10 percent Basic Customs Duty (BCD), while consumer power banks remain subject to the applicable 20 percent tariff rate. October 13, 2026. By Mrinmoy Dey The Ministry of Finance has clarified that stationary, grid-scale and industrial lithium-ion Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) are eligible for a concessional Basic Customs Duty (BCD) rate of 10 percent, distinguishing them from consumer power banks, which are excluded from the concession and remain subject to the applicable 20 percent tariff rate. The clarification follows reports of divergent assessment practices among customs field formations for BESS classified under tariff item 8507 60 00. Some formations had been treating stationary, grid-scale and industrial BESS as power banks and denying them the concessional duty rate. The Ministry has clarified that the term ‘Power Bank’ applies only to lithium-ion battery devices equipped with charging and discharging ports and designed to function as external charging devices for cellular mobile phones or portable electronic devices. Consequently, stationary, grid-scale and industrial lithium-ion BESS falling under the specified tariff item are not covered by the power-bank exclusion and should not be denied the 10 percent concessional BCD rate merely on that basis. The clarification aims to address inconsistent customs assessments by establishing a clear distinction between portable consumer charging devices and stationary energy storage systems. The concessional duty provision continues to exclude battery packs used in the manufacture of electrically operated or hybrid vehicles, lithium-ion batteries or battery packs for cellular mobile phones, and power banks. artigo.texto: Os recentes ataques com drones ucranianos contra os data centers da Yandex resultaram numa queda acentuada do tráfego online de bots na Rússia. No entanto, os dados partilhados pela Cloudflare indicam que a diminuição está associada a processos automatizados da empresa e não a redes de desinformação, ao contrário do que sugerem várias publicações virais. Segundo o Tom's Hardware, um gráfico a circular nas redes sociais levou muitos utilizadores a assumirem que as quintas de trolls responsáveis por espalhar teorias da conspiração e spam tinham sido desativadas. Contudo, o investigador conhecido como antibot4navalny esclareceu na rede social X que os dados medem apenas os pedidos dos rastreadores web da Yandex, usados para indexar sites nos motores de pesquisa e fornecer suporte ao cliente. A Cloudflare confirma que a atividade geral de bots proveniente da Rússia permanece praticamente inalterada. Gráficos falsos e impacto nos serviços A confusão aumentou quando o eurodeputado Tomáš Zdechovský partilhou um gráfico sugerindo que a atividade online em torno do partido político alemão de extrema-direita AfD tinha despencado após os ataques. O informático Raphael Wimmer analisou a imagem e suspeita que esta tenha sido gerada por inteligência artificial, apontando inconsistências como a inclusão de dados referentes a uma data no futuro: 15 de outubro. Wimmer apelou ao fim da partilha de imagens não verificadas, depois de o autor original da publicação ter evitado responder a questões sobre a origem do gráfico. Entretanto, o impacto real dos ataques faz-se sentir na infraestrutura da empresa frequentemente apelidada de "Google da Rússia". A maioria dos sistemas operados pela Yandex continua offline, afetando gravemente serviços como o Yandex Pay, o que impede os utilizadores de realizar transferências, verificar saldos ou fazer compras. Dima Pirogov, responsável pela Yandex Fintech, afirmou em comunicado que a empresa ainda não consegue avançar com uma previsão exata para a recuperação, mas garantiu que a equipa não irá parar até o serviço ser restaurado.

artigo.texto: Cass County residents learn more about proposed Harmony Energy Park data center CASS COUNTY, N.D. (Valley News Live) - Cass County residents gathered in Wheatland Tuesday night to learn more about a proposed data center park, with a vote on a building moratorium just over a week away. The conversation on data centers continued as people gathered to learn about what is being called “Harmony Energy Park”. Harmony Energy Park is a proposed powered data park by Geronimo Power in Harmony Township. The property, set to be located off 32nd Street Southeast and 160th Avenue Southeast, would include two main data center buildings. Project details shared with residents Tuesday night, residents had a chance to learn about the 640-acre project, which would keep buildings at least a mile from any home. “We have noticed in our renewable energy business that the data center companies, the large tech companies have been our biggest customers for the past five or six years. When we saw what the power was going for when we were working with these different tech companies, we thought that we saw an opportunity to bring an even more big, and powerful economic opportunity,” said Blake Nixon, CEO and President of Geronimo Power. With Applied Digital building a data center in Harwood, Nixon said there are pros and cons. “When something new comes to town, change is concerning. Everybody wants to know what is this thing? Why? How is it going to impact me and my community? I think being able to see what a data center looks like is actually a really good thing because it’s just 10 miles away. I think it’s a little bit not good in the fact that, that’s a part of an industrial park and it looks like an industrial park. Which of course where we’re developing, is beautiful rural farmland,” Nixon said. Green space and community input About 80% of the space is expected to remain green space. “We’re asking the community to engage with us and tell us, ‘What do you want us to do with the other 80%? Do you want it to be trees? Grass?’ We can make it so you don’t see the data center if you don’t want to see the data center,” Nixon said. Some residents say data centers can have advantages and disadvantages. “I’m not against it coming in, it just needs to come in properly. Just like any other business, manufacturing elevator, you name it. Even farmers themselves on what they do on the land like I do. I should be cognizant of how I affect the community, too,” said Nathan Faleide, a Wheatland resident. For those who may be leaning toward not wanting a data center in the area, Nixon said: “We want to be a valued, added part of this community like we have been in the other places where we do business. We think the data center can be a big part of that story.” Moratorium vote and public forum Harmony Township has proposed a 24-month zoning moratorium on building solar and wind energy facilities as well as data centers. There is set to be a public hearing and proposed vote on October 22nd at 7 p.m. Residents will have another chance to weigh in on AI and data centers Wednesday. The Challey Institute is hosting a public forum from 5:30 to 7 p.m. in the Oceti Sakowin Ballroom at NDSU’s Memorial Union, looking at what data center growth could mean for North Dakota’s power grid, rates and local communities. The forum is free and open to anyone who wants to attend. More information can be found, here. Copyright 2026 KVLY. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: ‘Yandex Pay’ partially resumes operations after Ukrainian drone strikes on data centers Dmitry Pirogov, the head of Yandex Pay’s fintech division, announced that the company has restored access to transfers and payments for some users. “Many of you can already see your money and manage it. We’re restoring access gradually so the service can handle the load. If some functionality isn’t available to you yet, please wait a little longer,” he wrote in the payment service’s Telegram channel. Pirogov stressed that the service “is still operating unstably”: some functions remain unavailable, and errors are possible during certain operations. Yandex Pay also announced special terms for users from October 11–17, covering savings accounts as well as loan payments. From the start, we built our infrastructure so that data on transactions would be replicated simultaneously across multiple data centers, because we work with literally the most valuable data our users have: data about their money. After the recent drone attacks on our data centers, our engineers had to completely rebuild the infrastructure in order to preserve this key principle and restore access to familiar functions. That’s why our service was hit especially hard, and recovery is taking longer. In recent days, Ukraine has struck three of the six data centers belonging to Yandex: facilities in the Ryazan region, Kaluga, and Vladimir. Many services run by Yandex itself, as well as by its clients, went down. At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. artigo.texto: This year, voters will elect the first new District 72 state representative for the first time in nearly two decades. Longtime Republican state Rep. Ed Clere, who has held the seat since 2008, is not seeking reelection. He’s focusing instead on a 2027 bid for mayor of New Albany, as an independent. Democrat Michele Henry and Republican Darrell Neeley are hoping to fill the role. Both recognize Hoosiers’ financial challenges, and they agree the state has a role in regulating data centers. Neither has held public office, though Neeley ran unsuccessfully for New Albany City Council in 2023. Meet the candidates Henry is a civil rights and worker’s rights attorney. She said she didn’t plan to run, and hadn’t previously considered running for office. But she wants to see changes. “I think that our legislature truly has just forgotten why it exists, and that is to improve the quality of life in our state,” Henry said. “And we haven't been doing that for 20 years now, and it is time to elect people who want to do that.” She said Indiana ranks poorly in some areas, such as public education. “We should be at the top of those lists,” she said. “This is a great state, and District 72 is a fantastic community.” Neeley is an associate pastor in New Albany and served more than three decades in the U.S. Navy. He said he wasn’t seeking the spot but that a lot of people reached out to him when it opened up. He said he sees it as a way to continue his track record of serving people. “This was another aspect in helping people, and being there to support those that think they don't have a voice,” Neeley said. When people asked him about running, “I finally sat down, prayed about it, thought about it, and so here we are.” Big goals Both candidates say they’ve heard from residents about how much they’re struggling to make ends meet, and Henry said focusing on affordability would be a priority. “We know that the rate of foreclosure is at…the highest in Indiana of all the 50 states, and that is largely because people are struggling to afford housing,” she said, adding that the prices of gas, groceries and utilities are also up. One way to help alleviate this, she said, is by eliminating sales tax on utilities and necessary household items, including hygiene products. She also wants to see the state minimum wage raised from its current $7.25 to at least $15. “There's nobody in the United States who could live on $7.25 an hour in any community, and certainly not in Indiana and not in District 72,” she said. She also said leaders should be responsible when bringing in new companies. “If we are going to provide incentives for companies to come to Indiana and bring jobs, we need to make sure that those jobs are quality jobs: that they offer a a salary, an hourly rate, and benefits that allow people to buy a home, to raise a family if that's what they choose to do, to not have to have a second job,” Henry said. Neeley said he wants to continue the state’s economic growth through fiscal responsibility. During his Navy career, he managed $300 million budgets, he said. “I knew how to budget, knew how to use taxpayers' money,” Neeley said. “Because it's not the government's, it wasn't the Navy's. It's the people's money.” He said he also thinks most people just want to make sure their tax money is spent wisely. He noted that 2027 is a biannual budget year for Indiana, which is a “prime opportunity to address the cost of living.” He said legislators need to increase grants and remove barriers for child care, so working families can continue to work. He wants state and local leaders to address what he calls burdensome restrictions on housing, and to see the state’s Residential Housing Infrastructure Assistance Program continue. He said he supports property tax reform, especially when it “addresses our problematic assessment system” and targets relief for seniors and people with disabilities. Getting things done Henry said she hopes Republicans won’t be in the supermajority at the statehouse after the election, which she thinks could make it easier for Democrats to be more effective, rather than continuing what she calls Republicans’ “pro-corporation legislative activity.” “I think there is a very real chance that the Democrats do get out of the superminority this year,” she said. “And once that happens, we will obviously have a lot more play at the table. We'll be able to implement proposals… We'll be able to take action that actually helps people in our communities.” She said even if the partisan gap doesn’t change, she hopes the parties can work together “to actually implement real relief and pro-Hoosier legislation.” Neeley said it’s crucial to work together, and that it’s not beneficial to reject good ideas based on party labels. “These games have to stop,” he said, adding that whether constituents support him or not, “you still have a voice in this district and at the statehouse too. We have to work together, or we're not going to get anywhere.” Both candidates said they would like to continue in the spirit Clere served with for so long. “I have a tremendous amount of respect for Ed,” Henry said. “He’s a moderate person who actually does listen to his constituents.” That’s something she’d like to continue. She also wants to make sure people in the district are represented at the state level. “Southern Indiana folks feel a lot of the time like they aren't heard, that Indianapolis doesn't remember that we are part of the state and not part of, you know, Louisville,” she said. “And so I think it's important that we listen to what the needs are in our community and bring those to the statehouse and then work on solutions that work for our community.” Neeley noted Clere’s focus on health care and legislation for people with disabilities, which he’d like to carry on. “I plan on picking his brain,” Neeley said. artigo.texto: Four-hour battery energy storage systems are now less expensive than open-cycle gas turbines in all 43 markets assessed by Wood Mackenzie, highlighting a major shift in the economics of electricity generation and grid flexibility. The consultancy’s latest global levelized cost of electricity (LCOE) report attributes the trend to expanding battery manufacturing capacity, rising gas turbine costs and fuel price volatility. In the Middle East and Africa, utility-scale solar photovoltaic (PV) remains the lowest-cost power generation technology, with single-axis tracker solar recording an average LCOE of US$37/MWh in 2026. The cost is forecast to decline to US$24/MWh by 2035, while four-hour battery storage costs are projected to fall 33% from US$120/MWh to US$80/MWh over the same period. According to Wood Mackenzie, this decline will make battery storage more cost-competitive than gas-fired peaking generation across every gas market in the region. “This economic shift is decisive and widening,” said Ahmed Jameel Abdullah, Principal Analyst at Wood Mackenzie. He attributed the trend to gas turbine shortages and fuel price volatility, alongside falling storage costs driven by expanding battery manufacturing. The report also highlights the growing cost advantage of renewable energy for baseload generation. Single-axis tracker solar is now the lowest-cost new-build power generation technology in 43 of the 48 markets analysed, while onshore wind leads in the remaining five. In Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE), solar LCOE is projected to fall below US$20/MWh by 2033. Middle East and Africa: Solar and Storage Strengthen Cost Advantage Renewable energy generation costs across the Middle East and Africa remain among the lowest globally. Utility-scale solar continues to set the regional cost benchmark, supported by favourable solar resources and declining technology costs. Onshore wind is also becoming increasingly competitive as Chinese turbine manufacturers expand their presence in the region. Egypt and Morocco are recording particularly low wind generation costs, supported by capacity factors ranging from 40% to 45%. Battery storage is emerging as a key technology for integrating renewable energy into electricity systems. Wood Mackenzie expects four-hour storage costs to decline to US$80/MWh by 2035, strengthening its competitiveness against gas peaking plants and supporting greater deployment of solar and wind power. The consultancy said the combination of low-cost renewable generation and increasingly affordable storage is changing power system planning across the Gulf and Africa. Asia Pacific: China Maintains Global Battery Storage Cost Leadership Utility-scale solar PV remains the most cost-competitive electricity generation source across Asia Pacific, although substantial differences persist between markets. In 2026, solar generation costs in the region’s highest-cost market are more than three times those in the lowest-cost market. The gap is expected to widen to 250% by 2030, despite cost improvements across all markets. Onshore wind is also becoming more competitive, supported by the growing presence of Chinese original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) and the deployment of larger-capacity turbines. These developments are expected to narrow the cost gap between wind and coal-fired generation across South and Southeast Asia. China continues to lead the global grid-scale battery storage market, with benchmark LCOE more than 55% below the Asia Pacific average of US$134/MWh outside China, according to the report. Integrated domestic supply chains and large-scale manufacturing underpin this advantage. Wood Mackenzie expects competitive Chinese battery supplies to reduce the wider Asia Pacific storage LCOE to US$92/MWh by 2036. However, Japan, Australia and the Philippines are likely to retain higher costs because of import duties, elevated installation expenses and domestic manufacturing policies. Offshore wind projects outside China continue to face near-term cost pressures, with more substantial reductions expected from the early 2030s as supply chains mature and turbine sizes increase. Latin America: Solar and Wind Costs Continue to Decline Solar PV with single-axis tracking remains the lowest-cost electricity generation technology in Latin America in 2026. Regional average solar generation costs are projected to decline 38% by 2060, supported by favourable solar resources and high capacity factors in Brazil, Chile and Mexico. Onshore wind costs are also expected to fall significantly. Wood Mackenzie forecasts the regional average wind LCOE will decline from US$73/MWh in 2026 to US$58/MWh by 2030, a reduction of nearly 21%. Increased competition from Chinese turbine manufacturers and the deployment of larger turbines are expected to drive these savings. Grid-scale battery storage is expanding across the region, supported by storage requirements linked to renewable energy projects and standalone procurement to improve grid stability. Storage LCOE is forecast to decline 42% by 2060 as deployment increases and regulatory frameworks mature. Offshore wind remains a longer-term opportunity. Regional average costs are expected to approach combined-cycle gas turbine cost parity in the early 2040s, although development activity in Brazil and Colombia is beginning to support the emergence of local supply chains. Europe: Battery Costs Face Short-Term Pressure Solar PV remains Europe’s cheapest electricity generation technology, with fixed-tilt solar LCOE forecast to decline 22% by 2060 as capital costs fall and technology improves. However, solar capital expenditure is expected to increase 14% in 2026, driven by higher PV module prices. artigo.texto: Trending Failing to regulate data centers could cost Ohioans billions of dollars in higher electricity cost and air pollution, according to a new analysis. The study by Columbus-based analytic firm Scioto Analysis estimates Ohioans would end up spending $16 billion more in electric bills and would suffer $41 billion in air pollution damage without regulations. The analysis estimates under current policies, data center growth could cost Ohio electricity customers $16 billion in higher utility costs between 2027 and 2034. Meanwhile, Ohio’s data center sales and use tax exemption cost the state an estimated $1.6 billion in revenue in 2025. "We are watching a financial crisis develop in real time, and the Ohio Statehouse is failing to respond,” said State Rep. Tristan Rader, D-Lakewood. “We have allowed some of the wealthiest corporations on Earth to receive billions in tax breaks while Ohio families face the prospect of billions more in electricity costs. At this point, our continued inaction isn’t just disappointing - it’s irresponsible.” Rader is working on legislation that he says would reconsider Ohio's "generous" tax exemptions for data centers and establish long-term financial commitments and safeguards protecting existing customers. "Ohio families should not be the venture capitalists for Silicon Valley’s expansion," the legislator said. "We don’t get a share of their profits, and we shouldn’t be handed their bills. The Statehouse needs to act before those bills come due.” According to the tracking group Data Center Map, Ohio has 240 data centers. Another study, by the Goldwater Institute, downplays the threat from data centers, "The bigger problem is an electricity system that hides scarcity from consumers until strain appears as congestion, reliability risks, or higher costs," the institute said. Higher prices would lead to higher efficiency, according to the Institute. "When millions of consumers face fixed prices, demand remains high precisely when the system is under the most pressure, the institute concluded.

artigo.texto: Muita segurança, um edifício (quase) sem pessoas e que parece um organismo vivo, um apetite insaciável por energia elétrica, grandes clientes internacionais de tecnologia em fila de espera: fomos à Start Campus, em Sines, a linha da frente da nova economia da inteligência artificial. "Nunca tinha estado num data center?”, pergunta Luís Rodrigues, enquanto se ouve o som de uma porta de segurança a abrir e entramos num corredor longo sem janelas e com luz branca. Seguimos atrás do segurança que vai abrindo e fechando portas, parte do protocolo apertado. Para chegar ali passámos pelo controlo à entrada - com um grande portão automático de metal e uma cerca de arame farpado -, assinámos um acordo para não fazer imagens dos equipamentos no interior, vimos um vídeo de 10 minutos com as regras do centro e pusemos o telemóvel num saquinho de plástico para bloquear a câmara. “As pessoas que vêm pela primeira vez acham estranho, mas os clientes adoram ver tanta segurança”, diz o diretor operacional da Start Campus, que fica em Sines e é o maior centro de dados em construção na Europa. artigo.texto: OCP 2026: Agentic AI Drives the Data Center's Chip-to-Grid Transformation Key Highlights - OCP is extending its standards mission from servers and racks to the full AI infrastructure stack, encompassing silicon, cooling, power distribution, facilities and utility-grid integration. - AMD introduced its Helion agentic AI rack, while Arm and NVIDIA outlined new CPU architectures and infrastructure requirements for rapidly expanding autonomous workloads. - Meta detailed the engineering behind its Prometheus AI cluster in Ohio, including fabric structures, new optical networking, open-source transport software and AI-optimized concrete. - Broadcom and NVIDIA presented advances in Ethernet networking and optical interconnects designed to overcome the growing physical constraints of accelerator clusters. - New OCP data center and grid-resilience specifications, along with NVIDIA's advances in dynamic power management, signal a shift toward treating the AI factory as a coordinated, grid-aware infrastructure system. Standing before thousands of engineers and technology executives at the opening of the 2026 Open Compute Project (OCP) Global Summit in San Jose, Meta's Santosh Janardhan pointed to the enormous fabric structure surrounding the audience. It was, he explained, an example of the same construction technology Meta had begun deploying to accelerate its massive AI infrastructure buildout. At the company's Prometheus AI cluster in New Albany, Ohio, traditional assumptions about data center construction had given way to an urgent question: What if the next generation of AI infrastructure could be built in months rather than years, using engineered fabric structures instead of conventional concrete-and-steel buildings? "We are actually also training a model while we were building it," said Janardhan, Meta's head of infrastructure. The presentation offered a striking illustration of the larger message emerging from Monday's opening keynotes: The AI factory is becoming a fundamentally different kind of data center. Across presentations by AMD, Meta, Arm, Broadcom and NVIDIA, a common theme emerged. The rapid expansion of AI inference and autonomous agents is forcing new approaches to computing, networking, construction, power distribution and operations. At the same time, the diversity of silicon architectures and the enormous physical scale of deployments are making common infrastructure specifications increasingly important. The result is a significant expansion of OCP's original mission. Fifteen years after the organization began applying open-source principles to hardware design, the industry's next challenge is developing interoperable infrastructure across the entire data center, from processor architecture to the utility connection. OCP's New Mandate: From Chip to Grid OCP CEO George Tchaparian opened the summit by describing an organization whose scale increasingly reflects the industry's transformation. This year's event attracted approximately 15,000 attendees, with another 3,000 on a waitlist. Tchaparian said OCP expects membership to exceed 700 organizations by year-end, while technical contributions are growing approximately 30% annually. The organization has already announced that its 2027 Global Summit will move to San Francisco's Moscone Center to accommodate further growth. More consequential than the attendance figures, however, is the widening scope of OCP's work. Originally centered on open server designs, racks and supporting hardware, the organization's roadmap now encompasses facilities infrastructure, liquid cooling, power distribution, firmware, security, networking and the increasingly complex connections between data centers and utilities. Tchaparian characterized the emerging approach as "chip-to-grid" infrastructure. This reflects a fundamental engineering problem. As hyperscalers and AI infrastructure providers deploy increasingly specialized processors, the electrical, thermal and mechanical consequences of those design decisions extend well beyond individual servers. Higher accelerator densities require new cooling strategies. New power architectures affect rack configurations and electrical distribution. Faster networks alter equipment layouts and cable requirements. Different silicon designs can introduce entirely new facility-level constraints. The traditional process of designing computing equipment and adapting data centers to accommodate it is increasingly difficult to sustain at AI scale. OCP is therefore emphasizing what Tchaparian called co-optimized data centers: infrastructure in which silicon, racks, networking, cooling and power systems are developed with common interfaces and shared design objectives. The challenge is compounded by growing silicon diversity. Hyperscalers are developing custom accelerators alongside commercial GPUs and CPUs, increasing the risk of fragmented hardware ecosystems that require repeated engineering across otherwise similar facilities. OCP also intends to extend hyperscale-derived standards into what it calls the AI computing continuum, encompassing neocloud providers, colocation operators, enterprises and geographically distributed inference infrastructure. The objective is not to eliminate architectural differentiation. It is to reduce the amount of infrastructure that must be redesigned every time the underlying computing technology changes. Agentic AI Gives the CPU a New Mission One of the most consequential themes of the opening keynotes was the renewed importance of general-purpose computing. AMD Chair and CEO Lisa Su described 2026 as the year of inference, estimating that inference now represents approximately 60% of the AI computing market. She pointed to an approximately 14-fold increase in agentic AI traffic during the year, reflecting the accelerating adoption of systems that do more than respond to individual prompts. Instead, autonomous agents can plan tasks, invoke software tools, execute code, retrieve info

artigo.texto: Notebooks com RTX Spark terão centenas de jogos no lançamento Call of Duty em 2027! Veja teste A Nvidia e a Microsoft apresentaram o Surface Ultra, novo notebook ultrafino baseado na tecnologia RTX Spark. O modelo é um dos primeiros adotar a tecnologia, q. A Razer anunciou a chegada da nova linha de mouses topo de linha com foco gamer e ergonômico: o Basilisk V4 Pro é o destaque. O novo aparelho da geração traz melhorias no hardware, como um sensor óptico de 50 mil DPI, além de algumas revisões e adições importantes, principalmente no conjunto de botões. Em termos de design, os novos Basilisk mantêm basicamente o mesmo estilo dos seus antecessores, com aquela saliência lateral que funciona como um descanso. A parte interessante é que as opções de controle foram expandidas para 14 botões personalizáveis, ou seja, bem mais que a geração do V3. Somente na parte lateral, o novo mouse conta com quatro botões, no que a companhia diz servirem a tecnologia Hypershift, controle de IA, e dois botões livres. Como se não fosse o suficiente, a companhia também inseriu um pequeno botãozinho na borda de um dos switches para alternar perfis de configuração. Um dos pontos que a Razer retrabalhou para a linha Basilisk V4, em especial o modelo Pro, foi o anel de rolagem. O Hyperscroll de 2ª geração foi adaptado para entregar quatro modos ao usuário: modo tátil de precisão e padrão, modo de rolagem livre e um modo de rolagem inteligente. Novo sensor e 275 horas de bateria Na parte de dentro, a companhia estadunidense também trocou algumas peças do periférico, como o sensor. Agora, o Basilisk V4 Pro é equipado com o sensor óptico Razer Focus Pro de 3ª geração com sensibilidade de 50 mil DPI, velocidade de rastreamento de 930 IPS e aceleração de 90g. Junto a isso, a fabricante colocou switches ópticos de 4ª geração nos dois botões principais do periférico, projetados para suportar 100 milhões de cliques. A comunicação ocorre através do HyperSpeed Wireless, que promete uma taxa de atualização de 8.000 Hz via dongle. Por falar em conectividade, ele também funciona via Bluetooth e pode ser conectado a até cinco dispositivos. Já sobre a bateria, a Razer promete que o novo Basilisk consegue entregar uma autonomia de até 200 horas ao utilizá-lo no modo de 1.000 Hz (dongle) e 275 horas com Bluetooth. Para a recarga, ele também aceita carregadores sem fio. - Para acompanhar o mouse, a Razer também revelou a nova Mouse Dock V2 Pro para carregamento magnético sem fio; - Essa dock tem um receptor de 8.000 Hz integrado, possibilitando parear mouse e teclado compatíveis; - A companhia também anunciou o Razer HyperFlux V2, uma base de carregamento que também funciona como mousepad; - O Basilisk V4 padrão pesa somente 94g, trabalha com sensor óptico Focus X 33K, 12 botões programáveis e entrega até 140 horas de bateria. A nova geração de mouses Razer Basilisk ainda não tem data para chegar ao mercado brasileiro. No exterior, os dispositivos já estão disponíveis. Confira os preços abaixo: - Razer Basilisk V4 Pro: US$ 170 (cerca de R$ 800 em conversão direta); - Razer Basilisk V4 HyperSpeed: US$ 110 (R$ 550); - Razer Mouse Dock V2 Pro: US$ 70 (R$ 300); - Razer HyperFlux V2: US$ 119 (R$ 600). Por falar na Razer, nós já analisamos o Razer Basilisk V3 Pro e esse é um dos melhores mouses gamer disponíveis no Brasil, mas é caríssimo.
